"Rest is for people who don't want it enough."

Priya looked at her for a long second. "You sound like an autocrat," she said, and handed the clipboard back. "Like a small one. A gym autocrat."

Laurence laughed before she could stop herself, and then didn't apologize for it, and then didn't take the line out of the plan either.

After practice she stayed behind, ostensibly to collect cones. Actually she went to the office alcove where the coach kept her binders, shelves of them, spines labeled by season. She wasn't sneaking, she told herself; she was doing research. In the binder marked with last year's dates she found week-by-week sheets, and each sheet had a word typed at the top that she'd never seen before: microcycle.

"You're in my binders," Ferreira said from the doorway. She didn't sound angry.

"What's a microcycle?"

"Come here." Ferreira pulled a sheet out, one week on a single page, hard days and easy days laid out like weather. "In periodized training, a season gets divided into cycles. The microcycle is the smallest one. It usually lasts about one week." She tapped the page. "That's what you're writing. You're not writing seven days. You're writing one unit."

Laurence looked at the sheet. There was a rest day in it, an actual blank day, and two of the days were marked "activation," which when she flipped back she found meant warm-ups counted as content, not as an apology before the real work. The week was shaped. It had a top and a slope down.

She rewrote the plan that night at the kitchen table, the same table, the same pen. Monday hard, Tuesday easy, Wednesday hardest, Thursday technical with long warm-ups, Friday moderate, Saturday scrimmage, Sunday nothing. Sunday nothing. It looked lazy. It looked like a document written by someone altruistic, someone concerned with other people's hamstrings, and she sat with her discomfort about that until she understood it wasn't discomfort about them. It was discomfort about letting go of the version of herself that believed effort meant stacking.

She also kept one thing. Monday sprints stayed, first thing, no negotiation, because she had decided she was allowed to be a little bit of a tyrant about Mondays specifically.

Friday she handed the clipboard to Ferreira in the gym, under the far basket while the juniors ran their warm-up laps. The coach read it slowly, the way she read everything, and Laurence stood with her hands behind her back and admitted to herself she could not tell from the woman's face whether this was passing or failing.

"Microcycle," Ferreira said finally.

"I found it in your binder. I hope that's okay."

"That's what binders are for." Ferreira closed the clipboard. "Captain's announced Monday."

Laurence nodded and went to set up the cones, arranging them in the pattern for the warm-up drill, and it was only halfway through the second line of cones that she registered what the coach had said. She turned around. Ferreira was already walking toward the juniors, and Priya was jogging over from the storage room with the ball bag, calling out, "Coach, who's the new captain, then?" And Ferreira pointed at Priya, without breaking stride, and said, "Her hamstring approved the week, so she's got my vote, but the team votes Monday."

Laurence stood between the cones with her hand still raised from placing one, and started laughing, and put the cone down.

Maria sat in the corner booth of the Cedar Fork with her hands folded on the table, waiting for the manager. The restaurant smelled like onions and floor cleaner. She had a folder on her lap with one page in it, a page she had rewritten three times since Tuesday. On the page was a single sentence: "Tell me about a time you handled conflict in a group."

Her brother Dev had told her interviews were rigged toward people who could talk about themselves, and that the only fair way to fight that was preparation. He'd printed something off the internet and slid it across the kitchen table. "It's called STAR," he said, chewing a piece of toast. "Situation, Task, Action, Result." He hadn't explained further; he was seventeen and believed explanations were a form of condescension. She'd read the printout herself, twice, then folded it into the folder.

The story she had chosen was the chemistry project from last spring. Priya, Marco, and a fourth kid named Elliot whom nobody had wanted, had been assigned a presentation on water treatment. Elliot had turned out to be bellicose about nearly everything: fonts, slide order, whether the word "flocculation" was too hard for the class. He'd shouted at Priya in the library until a librarian came over, and after that the group had stopped meeting together, meeting instead in pairs, in fragments, in the hallway before class.

The manager came out at four minutes past two, carrying a paper cup. She was shorter than Maria expected, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair. "Maria? I'm Ruth. You applied for the Saturday host position." She sat down across from her, set the cup aside, and opened a small notebook. "First job?" "Yes." "That's fine. Everyone here had one." She clicked a pen. "Tell me about a time you worked with a group and something went wrong."

Maria's rehearsed sentence dissolved. What came out instead was the truth: that the project had gone wrong slowly, in the way things do, that nobody could name the day it failed. She heard herself talking about the library, about Elliot's voice, about Priya leaving the table. Ruth kept writing. Maria thought, with the clarity of panic, that she was telling this badly, in the wrong order, and then she thought about the folded page.

She put her hand flat on the folder but didn't open it. "Let me start over. There's a way to tell these, I practiced it. Situation, task, action, result." She laid it out. The situation: four students, one grade, three weeks. The task: her piece was the research, but she'd also taken on getting the group to function at all, because someone had to. The action: instead of holding a group meeting, which had already exploded once, she went to each person separately, one lunch period at a time, and asked what they needed from the others. Marco wanted Elliot to stop rewriting his slides. Priya wanted an apology, or at least an acknowledgment. Elliot, it turned out, had been sure from the start that the others were going to cut him out, and had decided to be loud before he could be quiet.

Ruth looked up. "And the result?" "We split the presentation into four solo sections so nobody touched anybody else's work. We got an A minus." Maria paused. "It wasn't really solved. It was more like an arbitration nobody agreed to. I made a ruling and they accepted it because nobody wanted another library scene. I still don't know if that was the right thing or just the thing that worked." Ruth stopped writing. She took a slow drink from the cup and studied Maria over the rim.

"You didn't put that on your application," she said. "The part about not knowing." "I didn't think it helped." "Here's what I know after eleven years of this. On Saturdays I have two servers who've filed complaints against each other twice. I've settled it twice. My way of settling it is I underwrite whatever truce they make, meaning if it falls apart on a Saturday night, it falls apart on me. I need someone at the door who can read a room before it goes loud." She closed the notebook. "Can you start this Saturday at ten?"

Maria said yes before she had finished deciding whether she meant it. Ruth stood, then stopped, hand on the back of the booth. "One thing. When you split the presentation into four parts, did the class notice it was four separate projects wearing one title?" "The teacher did," Maria said. "She wrote on the rubric, 'Functioning apart is not the same as functioning together.'" Ruth laughed once, a short sound, and pushed her glasses down onto her nose.

On her way out, Maria passed the two servers, a tall woman and a younger man, setting tables on opposite sides of the room without looking at each other. She recognized the geometry of it, the careful distances, the pairs meeting in fragments. She stopped at the door, then turned back toward the host stand, where the Saturday chart was taped with names in two different inks, and began reading it.

Brooklyn signed her name on the volunteer sheet at the St. Vincent food bank and noticed, beneath it, a column headed "Hours." Behind her, a boy from her school, Dev, was already filling his in.

"You've got thirty-eight written down," she said, looking over his shoulder. "I have zero."

"Deadline's Friday," Dev said. "Graduation's in June, but the school wants the paperwork in before the diploma meeting." He capped his pen. "Forty hours of community involvement, or you don't get the Ontario Secondary School Diploma. I've been putting it off since grade nine."

Brooklyn had known about the requirement for years the way she knew about the periodic table, as a fact that lived in school and never followed her home. Now it had followed her to a church basement that smelled of cardboard and dish soap, where pallets of canned corn stood against one wall and a woman named Ruth was sorting bread with quick, practiced hands.

"Brooklyn, was it?" Ruth said. "You're on the bread table. Check dates, pull anything green or furry, and don't agonize over it. The compost doesn't judge."

She worked through the morning. A man came in with his daughter, maybe four years old, and took a box of rice, two cartons of eggs, a bag of apples that had gone soft on one side. Brooklyn watched him thank Ruth twice, once at the counter and once at the door, as if the first time hadn't been enough. The girl waved at nobody in particular.

In grade ten, Brooklyn remembered, her civics teacher had asked who was volunteering and why, and a girl named Priya had said she tutored immigrant kids in math because her grandmother had been helped that way forty years ago. Another girl had said she did shoreline cleanup because it looked good on applications. The teacher had written both reasons on the board and asked the class which was better, and the class had argued until the bell, and nothing was decided. Brooklyn had said nothing. She had wanted a reason that fit entirely on one line, and she had never found one.

Today she had come, honestly, because of the deadline. Her guidance counselor had flagged her file in April: forty hours still outstanding, and Ontario high school students could not earn the diploma without them. Brooklyn had resented the errand all the way here, resenting most the possibility that she was the kind of person who only showed up when a certificate was held hostage. But by noon she had learned the bread table, and where the dated milk went, and that Ruth had volunteered here eleven years and still got the sorting bins confused on Mondays.

Dev, meanwhile, was intransigent about the scanner. A new inventory app had been installed on the food bank's single tablet, and Ruth wanted the cans logged digitally. Dev insisted the paper list was faster and refused, politely but completely, to switch over. "Two hours I have left to log," he said. "I'm not spending them learning software."

Brooklyn took the tablet herself. The app turned out to be simple, three taps per item, and within twenty minutes she had catalogued a shelf that would have taken Dev an hour by hand. Her arriving late and under compulsion had, in a small way, catalyzed the change; she had no loyalty to the old system, no stake in being right.

"You didn't have to do that," Dev said, watching her.

"I know. It was faster, that's all."

But driving the whole thing home, later, was a confusion she couldn't sort: whether the mandatory hours corrupted the giving or simply got people through the door who would never otherwise have come. The boy at the counter with his daughter didn't know or care why she'd sorted his apples. The soft spot was cut away either way.

Ruth called a lunch break at twelve thirty and put out sandwiches for the volunteers. She sat down across from Brooklyn and peeled an orange in one long spiral, the kind of thing a person learns from doing it ten thousand times.

"Why'd you start so late?" Ruth asked. "Most kids your age bank their hours in grade nine."

"Honestly? It was something I had to do for the diploma. Forty hours, or no graduation." Brooklyn pulled the crust off her sandwich. "That's the whole reason I'm here. I keep thinking that makes it not count."

Ruth considered this while she chewed. "Some people who start for the paper stay for the work. Some who start noble quit in a month. The reason you walked in is the least interesting thing about you by the time you walk out." She pushed half the orange across the table.

Brooklyn took it. She didn't know yet, she admitted to herself, which kind she would turn out to be, and there was no way to find out except to keep coming back after the form was signed. Two hours remained on her sheet. After that, the counting stopped and she would learn what she did when nothing was being measured.

At the end of the shift she wrote "2" in the hours column, capped Dev's pen, and looked up at Ruth sorting bread for the afternoon crowd.

"Same time next Saturday?" she said.

The Herreraons' basement smelled like salsa and radiator dust, and by halftime Payton had claimed the corner of the couch closest to the mini-fridge, because that was where the good seat was and because Mrs. Herreron kept drifting past it, and Payton had noticed she was looking for a place to sit down.

"Jax is on fire," Derek said from the floor, pointing his pizza crust at the screen. "Eight straight points. You don't guard a man like that. You pray."

"He's not on fire," said Marcus, Derek's older brother, home from his first semester of college and apparently determined to prove it. "The hot hand is an illusion. There's a famous study. Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky. They looked at the streaks and found nothing."

"They found the Sixers," Derek said.

"They found that a made shot doesn't make the next one more likely. It's coin flips. People see patterns that aren't there."

Payton had been quiet through most of this, half watching the game and half watching Mrs. Herreron finally settle into the folding chair Derek had dragged over for her without saying anything about it. But the argument snagged on something. Her statistics teacher had made them read a paper in October, one of those things she'd assumed she'd forget, except that she hadn't, and now it was surfacing the way a name surfaces at the second introduction.

"That study's been challenged," she said.

Both brothers turned. On the screen, Jax rose for a three and missed, and Derek groaned as though she'd personally knocked the ball away.

"Challenged how?" Marcus said.

"Two thousand eighteen. Miller and Sanjurjo. They reanalyzed it." She was reaching now, pulling it up out of memory, and she was aware of the risk of reaching wrong in front of a room. "They found a flaw in the statistics. A statistical flaw. And they found evidence of streak shooting. Actual streaks."

"So which is it?" Derek demanded. "Fire or no fire?"

"I didn't say it was one or the other."

"You said the hot hand was real."

"I said the study was flawed." Payton felt her face warm, and she also noticed that Mrs. Herreron had leaned forward, interested, her paper cup of cider held in both hands. That was worth more than winning. Still, she didn't back off. "Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky called the hot hand an illusion, and for thirty years everybody believed them. Then somebody checked the math again."

Marcus had his phone out. "Miller and Sanjurjo," he read, half to himself. Payton watched his expression move from dismissal to something more careful, the way a person checks a price and finds it lower than expected. "Huh."

"Huh what?" Derek said.

"Huh, she's right."

"You're just saying that because she's the only one here who can do your homework."

"I'm saying it because I'm reading it." Marcus turned the screen toward Derek, and Derek squinted at it with the concentration of a man being asked to translate a language he'd only ever spoken.

The game came back from a timeout. Mr. Herreron appeared at the top of the stairs with a second tray of wings, having clearly decided the first tray had been expropriated by the teenagers before it ever reached the table, and Derek intercepted it at the bottom step with an apology that was mostly chewing.

"Bring those here," Mrs. Herreron said, patting the arm of her chair, and Derek brought them, and Payton moved her feet so the tray could rest between them.

"This is a hedonistic spread," Marcus announced, surveying the wings, the queso, the seven-layer dip going cold at the edges.

"It's the playoffs," his father said, as if that explained a philosophy of life, which in this house it did.

In the third quarter Jax scored six straight again, and the basement erupted, and Derek pointed at Payton across the chaos of standing bodies. "Hot hand. Say it. Say I'm right."

"I can't say that," she called back over the noise. But she was grinning, and she stood up too, because Jax was pulling up from the corner and there was no sitting through this. "The 2018 paper found evidence of streak shooting. That's all I can give you."

"That's everything!"

"It's not everything. The first study still exists. They're both sitting there. I don't get to pick one just because it's loud in here."

Derek laughed at that, a real laugh, and even Marcus cracked, and Mrs. Herreron reached up and tugged the hem of Payton's sleeve without saying anything, just once, the way you'd touch a sleeve to say stay.

Jax missed the next two shots and hit the one after. Derek threw his hands up as though the universe were mocking him personally. Marcus held up his phone again, as if it were a ruling. Payton sat back down between the wings and the woman who wanted them, and watched the fourth quarter decide nothing yet, all of it still possible, the scoreboard holding both arguments open at once.

"Next commercial," she said, "somebody's getting my numbers."

The flyer had been taped to the gym door since September, curling at one corner: Build a School, Summer in Kestari, two weeks, applications due Friday. Chase stood in front of it with his phone out, taking a picture, when Priya came up behind him with her own reasons for being there.

"You're applying," she said. It wasn't a question. Priya had been saving for the trip since sophomore year, working Saturdays at her uncle's pharmacy, and she'd told anyone who'd listen that her application essay would be about global citizenship. What she hadn't counted on was the new requirement, printed in small type at the bottom of the flyer: applicants had to submit a one-page analysis of why the destination country needed classrooms. No analysis, no interview.

They ended up in the library during lunch, laptops open. The program's information packet linked to two countries, Kestari and a place called Valden, each with a chart labeled population pyramid. Chase had expected something Egyptian, all triangles and mystery. What he got were two bar graphs turned on their sides, age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top, males on the left, females on the right.

"Which one are we supposed to pick?" Priya asked, tapping the screen. Kestari's chart flared outward at the bottom, wide as a church bell, then tapered to almost nothing at the top. Valden's was the opposite, a narrow base widening into a heavy, blocky crown. Chase turned his notebook sideways and sketched both shapes. "Okay," he said slowly, "so Kestari has a ton of people at the bottom. Young people. The bars are widest for the little kids." He counted the age brackets with his pen. "A pyramid with a wide base and a narrow top means a high birth rate and a young population."

"So?"

"So they're going to need schools. Teachers, classrooms, the whole thing. Look at Valden, it's practically upside down. Nobody's having kids, everybody's old." Priya pulled up Valden's government page and found an article about converting a primary school into a residential care facility, and they sat there for a second without saying anything, the implication settling between them: the same shape that made a country build schools could make another country close them.

Chase started drafting his analysis that night, but the drafting went badly. He kept thinking about his grandmother, who had spent last spring convalescing at Riverside after her hip surgery, and how the ward had been full, the hallway lined with wheelchairs, a nurse telling his mother they were short-staffed again. He'd thought of it as bad luck at the time. Now it looked like a pattern you could read off a graph, the way Valden's shape predicted it, and the thought made him uneasy in a way he couldn't quite name, a low-grade malaise that had nothing to do with the essay and everything to do with what his own country's pyramid must look like underneath the numbers.

The next day he found Priya in the chemistry lab before class. "I wrote it," he said, "but I cut the last paragraph." He'd drafted a conclusion arguing that building schools in Kestari was obviously the right priority, more futures, more potential. Reading it back, it sounded like a person who had never met anyone over seventy. His grandmother had spent her convalescence teaching him gin rummy and telling him about the flood of '87; her value wasn't in her future productivity. He had tried to hold both ideas, the graph's arithmetic and that memory, in the same paragraph, and the paragraph had refused.

"So what's your position?" Priya asked, not looking up from her titration. She had her own problem: her essay draft was all feeling and no evidence, and she knew it, and she needed what Chase had figured out about the shapes. He slid his notebook across the bench, the two sketches side by side, Kestari wide at the base and Valden narrow. "Kestari needs the classrooms. That part's clear, the data says so, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't." He paused, watching the burette drip pink into her flask. "But which country needs more, schools or nursing homes, that's a different question than which matters more, and I don't think the graph can answer the second one. I'm going to write that I'm sure about the first part and not sure about the rest."

Priya copied the sketches without asking, which was fair, since he'd shown them to her. "They might not like uncertainty in an application," she said. "They want conviction. Nascent philanthropists, all of them." Chase laughed, and the bell rang, and he gathered his notebook, the drawings still wet where Priya's sleeve had smudged them, Kestari's wide base blurred into Valden's narrow one at the spine of the page.

The bell over the door of Kessler's Corner Store had a crack in it, so it rang flat, and Nicholas had come to know that sound as the start of his shift. He stacked the chip bags along the top rack while Mr. Kessler counted the till, and between customers he slid his calculus notebook onto the counter beside the register. He had a test on integration in two days, and the shop's dead hours, three to five, were the only quiet ones he got.

His uncle thought he was wasting the summer. "A boy your age should be outside," his uncle had said at dinner, describing the riparian trail along the creek where he fished, the shade, the water smell. Nicholas had said nothing, because the truth was awkward: the area under a curve felt more like a real place to him than the creek did. You could walk into it, in a way. You could measure it.

The problem on his page was from Tuesday's math club, and it had gone wrong in a way nobody had caught at the time. Priya had gotten one answer and Danny had gotten another, both working the same region between a line and a parabola, both showing complete work. Mrs. Okafor had been out of the room, and by the time she came back the club had moved on to voting on T-shirt designs, and the two answers had sat in Nicholas's bag all week like a splinter.

He remembered Danny at the whiteboard, marker squeaking, drawing the line above the parabola on the interval and then writing the parabola minus the line anyway, because the parabola's equation came first on the handout and he had subtracted in the order he'd copied them. Priya had subtracted the other way and gotten a negative number, then flipped its sign at the end without saying why. Both of them had laughed it off. Danny, who everyone would lionize the moment he got into his engineering program, had shrugged and said, "Sign's just a detail." Nicholas hadn't been sure it was.

A customer came in for milk and a lottery ticket, and Nicholas rang her up, made change, watched the door swing shut behind her. Then he drew the two curves again in his notebook, roughly to scale, and looked at them instead of at the algebra. The line sat above the parabola across the whole stretch between the crossing points. That was just a fact of the picture. He shaded the sliver of region between them with the side of his pencil, light, so he could erase it if he was wrong.

And then he saw it, or thought he did. The region had a size, one size, whichever equation you liked better. If the line was on top, then the way to get that size was to integrate the line minus the parabola over the interval where they stayed in that order. Danny had reversed it and had gotten the negative of the true area. Priya had gotten the negative too, but then she'd silently turned it positive, which was like guessing the right answer for the wrong reason. Nicholas wrote both procedures out side by side and found where they diverged, and his pulse did something small and embarrassing.

Mr. Kessler came over to refill the coffee station and glanced at the notebook. "That look like good news or bad news?"

"Good," Nicholas said. "I think." He turned the notebook so the shaded sliver faced his boss. "The area between two curves. You take the upper one minus the lower one, over the part where they're stacked that way." He tapped the line, then the parabola beneath it. "Danny had it backwards, so everything came out negative. Priya just flipped hers without knowing why, which happens to work here, but I don't know if it always works." He stopped, hearing himself pile uncertainty on a man who sold lottery tickets. "Sorry. That's probably not interesting."

Mr. Kessler studied the page longer than Nicholas expected. "My brother surveyed wetlands," he said. "Forest biome, swamp, whatever. He had a whole thing about boundaries. Said the argument was always about where you drew the line, not what was inside it." He went back to the coffee, and Nicholas sat with that, deciding whether it meant anything or whether it was just something an old man says near a notebook.

At five, Priya came in for a soda before her shift at the pharmacy next door. Nicholas slid the notebook across the counter, open to the two columns, before he could talk himself out of it. "From Tuesday. You were negative because of the order, not because of a mistake. Danny's the one who reversed it." She set the soda down and read, and her face did the thing faces do when someone is checking your work and finding you less wrong than they'd assumed.

"So why did flipping it work for me?" she said.

"That's what I can't promise," Nicholas said. "It worked here because the sign was the only thing off. If the curves crossed inside the interval, I don't think you could fix it with one flip. You'd have to split it up. But I haven't done that part yet." He pulled the notebook back and wrote her number at the bottom of the page, then Danny's, and drew a box around the difference so he'd look at it again on the bus.

Priya took her soda and pushed two quarters across the counter. "Text me if the crossing thing breaks," she said. "I want to be there when it does."

The bell rang flat behind her, and Nicholas turned the page and drew a parabola slicing through a line, twice.

Tristan had been sitting at the corner table of the coffee shop for two hours with one cold flat white and a laptop open to the UCAS application. Six courses sat in his list. The system allowed only five. He had read the page four times, hoping the number would change, and it had not.

Nadia slid into the seat across from him, uninvited, carrying a green tea she barely touched. She had her own list folded into the pocket of her denim jacket, and she pulled it out and flattened it against the table so he could see that hers had five lines, five course codes, no hesitation.

"How did you cut yours?" he asked.

"I didn't cut anything. I never had a sixth." She tapped his screen. "Five courses maximum. That's the whole allowance. And it doesn't rank them, you know. The list is unordered. No order of preference. They just sit there, all equal."

"So the sixth one is just gone?"

"The sixth one never existed, officially." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it.

The sixth course was mathematics at a university three hundred miles north. The other five were all within an hour of his mother's flat: two economics, one statistics, one joint honours, one engineering with a foundation year. He had built the list the way you build a wall, each choice braced against the others so nothing could fall. He wanted to subsume the whole decision under a single principle, and the principle he had chosen was proximity. His mother's shifts had been cut in October. Nobody had said out loud what that meant for the spring, and nobody needed to.

"I could drop the foundation year one," he said. "The engineering. That's the weakest."

"You said it was the safety."

"Safe and weak aren't opposites."

"Fine. Drop the one far away, then." Nadia said it while looking at the window, at a man struggling with an umbrella that had turned inside out. She had wanted him to apply north since September, and she had never once said so directly, which was its own kind of statement. Anxiety about choices was endemic this term; half their year had it, teachers kept saying so in assemblies. But hers ran quieter than most, and it surfaced mainly as opinions about other people's decisions.

"It's not that far," Tristan said. "Four hours by train."

"Then keep it."

He looked at the screen for a while. The five-course limit was not a moral test, he told himself, and yet it behaved like one, forcing a ranking onto a system that officially refused ranking. He could keep the wall of five nearby courses, or he could trade one brick for something he actually wanted and let the structure carry a gap. Both were defensible. He could not make both true at once, and no amount of reasoning would make the sixth slot appear.

He deleted the foundation year course. The list rebalanced itself, five items, four of them close and one far, all listed flat and equal, no preference shown anywhere on the page, which was either a mercy or an erasure. He pressed submit before he could reconsider, and the confirmation banner came up green.

"There," Nadia said. "Done."

"Not done. Now we wait."

"Then you can start drinking your coffee like a person." She pushed it toward him. He lifted the cup. It was cold, and he drank it anyway.

Luca turned eighteen on the fourth of October, eleven days before the registration deadline, and the envelope from the county arrived on the ninth: a mail ballot, two thick card pages, a privacy sleeve, and a return envelope with his name already printed in the window. He carried it to the desk in his room and set it beside the keyboard without opening it.

Downstairs, his mother was on the phone with her sister, her voice climbing into the register she used for politics. She had spent the autumn calling the challenger a crook, taping his face to the refrigerator with a magnet, sending Luca links at midnight with subject lines like READ THIS and SHARE. The morning the ballots came, she had said, "I hope you know what's at stake," and left the room before he could answer, which was how most of their conversations about the election ended.

He opened the envelope and read the instructions. You may not show your marked ballot to anyone. Your vote will be kept secret. He read the sentence twice, then typed into the search bar: why is the ballot secret. His fingers paused over the keys. It had not occurred to him that secrecy was a thing someone had to invent.

The results loaded. He skimmed past a page about election laws and found a history site with a picture of a wooden voting booth, and he read part of it out loud, quietly, because reading aloud helped him hold on to things. "The secret printed ballot," he read. "It's called the Australian ballot, because the Australian colonies of Tasmania and Victoria introduced it in 1856." He sat back. So there was a time before this, a time when everyone could watch you vote, when your landlord and your boss and your father could stand behind you and read your choices off a colored card. He tried to imagine his mother standing behind him right now, and did not have to try very hard.

His older sister, Nadia, knocked twice and came in without waiting, the way she always did. She was home from her first semester for the weekend, and she wanted something; he could tell from the way she leaned against the doorframe instead of sitting. "You doing it?" she asked. He said he was reading first. She picked up the privacy sleeve and turned it over in her hands. "Good. You're actually reading it. Dad voted for a school board guy once because the name sounded familiar."

"Did you know the ballot has a name?" Luca said. "It's called the Australian ballot. Tasmania and Victoria, 1856." Nadia raised her eyebrows. "You're going to be insufferable in college," she said, but she smiled when she said it, and then her face went serious again, which was the real reason she had come in. "Mom's downstairs telling Aunt Reza you're voting the right way. Like it's settled." She put the sleeve down. "I just thought you should know she's saying that."

Luca looked at the screen, at the wooden booth, at the date. He thought about the secrecy he had been reading about, the long argument it must have taken to make it law, the whole apparatus of sleeves and envelopes and unmarked folds, all of it built so that no one could ever do what his mother was doing downstairs: assuming his vote, spending it in advance on a phone call. At the same time he thought about her taped-up articles, some of which he had actually read, some of which had been fair. The challenger had taken money from a developer whose project the town had voted down; that part was true even if her acerbic posts about him made everything sound worse than the records showed. Both things were true at once. He did not have a word for that, and he did not need one.

His mother came up while Nadia was still there. She stood in the doorway with her tea and looked at the ballot pages lying flat on the desk. "You want help with the judges?" she asked. "Those races are impossible." He said he had the sample ballot open in another tab. She came closer, close enough to see the screen, and he watched her eyes move from the history site to the blank card pages to his hands. "You know," she said, "I'd feel better if I knew you weren't wasting this. People fought for this."

"People fought for the part where you don't get to know," Luca said.

She stared at him. "I'm not the enemy, Luca. Don't act like I'm the enemy just because that candidate has spent a year trying to vilify everyone who questions him." Her voice had gone quiet, which was worse than loud. Nadia slipped past her into the hall. His mother stayed a moment longer, and then she said something he had not expected, so quietly he almost missed it: "You know I've never actually missed one. Since I was twenty. My mother couldn't. It wasn't that kind of country." She picked a thread off her sleeve, an encumbrance she'd worn all day and only now noticed. "I just want to see it filled in. Not how. Just filled in."

After she went down, Luca sat for a while with his hand flat over the ballot pages. Then he picked up the pen, marked the races one by one, some the way his mother would have, some not, and slid the card into the sleeve. He carried it to the top of the stairs and held it up so it caught the light from the kitchen, and called, "It's filled in."

The two articles had been open on Vanessa's laptop since Tuesday, and by Thursday night they had stopped being articles and started being two people arguing across her kitchen table while she sat between them, unable to side with either. The first, from a ecology journal with a matte cover she'd found through the school database, claimed that montane bird species were shifting their ranges uphill as temperatures warmed, following the cool air they'd evolved to need. The second, published three years later by a team that had visited fewer sites but over more years, found no consistent shift at all, and suggested the first paper's pattern was an artifact of where its researchers had happened to place their survey points.

Her mother set a mug of tea down beside the keyboard, not asking, just setting it down, the way she did when she could tell a night was going long. The kitchen clock said nine-forty. Vanessa's draft, due Monday, was supposed to be a critical review, which her assignment sheet described as "a considered position on a scholarly debate," and so far her considered position was that she had typed the word "however" eleven times and deleted it eleven times.

"Still the birds?" her mother said, sitting across from her with her own mug.

"Still the birds."

She read the methods section of the first paper again, slowly, the way her junior-year English teacher had cajoled the class into reading poetry, one line at a time, resisting the urge to skim toward the conclusion. The first team had sampled forty-two ridgelines across two summers. The second team, eleven watersheds across nine years. Forty-two sites, two years. Eleven sites, nine years. She wrote both on a napkin and stared at them like they were scores from two different sports.

The problem, she realized, was that both papers could be describing the same mountains. A bird population could drift uphill in a hot year and drift back down in a wet one, and two studies watching different slices of time would each see only their own slice and swear it was the whole weather. She pushed the napkin away, then pulled it back. Somewhere, she thought, someone must have noticed this problem before her, someone with more than a napkin.

She searched the second paper's reference list for anything with the word "review" in the title, then tried "synthesis," then, on a guess, typed both authors' names together. The database returned a third paper, one neither article had cited much, published just last year. Its abstract began with a sentence she read three times: the authors had combined the results of dozens of studies on exactly this question, the upslope shift of montane species, in order to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could.

"Wait," she said out loud.

"What?"

"Hang on." She was already skimming the methods, where the phrase appeared again in bold-faced certainty: a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question. It pooled the forty-two ridgelines and the eleven watersheds and forty other datasets besides, and what it found sat between the two papers like a referee: a small uphill shift overall, real but modest, smaller than the first paper claimed and larger than the second allowed.

She called her friend Priya, who was also writing a review, on hormones and adolescent sleep, and who answered on the second ring with her mouth clearly full of something.

"Did you find the thing where they pool all the studies?" Vanessa said.

"The what?"

"A meta-analysis. It combines the results of a bunch of studies on the same question, so it can estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can. Both of my articles are inside it. Like, statistically inside it."

Priya stopped chewing. "That exists?"

"Both of my authors are in the author list of the thing that proves them both partly wrong. It's brutal. It's beautiful."

After she hung up, she sat for a while with her hands flat on the table, the way her grandmother used to do before deciding whether bread dough had risen enough, a patience Vanessa had always read as discernment rather than delay, though she couldn't have said how she knew the difference. Her grandmother had been dead two years, and Vanessa thought, not for the first time, that the woman would have understood the napkin with the two numbers on it, the weighing of small evidence.

Because here was what the night had actually taught her, and it wasn't the answer. The meta-analysis gave an answer, a pooled slope, a confidence interval, but its own final paragraph flagged exactly the thing she'd guessed at on the napkin: study design varied, some datasets were short, some surveys were placed in ways that might bias the result. The referee was better informed than either fighter and still not omniscient. Her review, she saw now, would not be a verdict. It would be a description of how the two papers disagreed, why, and what a pooling of all the evidence so far suggested, with its edges left visible.

She opened a new document and typed the first real sentence she'd written all week: "These two studies reach opposite conclusions not because one is wrong, but because each saw part of a pattern." Then she deleted "not because one is wrong," because she wasn't sure that was true, and because she was starting to distrust sentences that settled things. She retyped it: "Each study saw part of a pattern, and only part."

Her mother came back for the empty mugs. Vanessa turned the laptop so she could see the forest of little squares on the meta-analysis's summary figure, each square a study, each horizontal line the uncertainty around it, the diamond at the bottom the pooled estimate that no single square could have drawn alone.

"That's tomorrow's you talking," her mother said, tapping the diamond.

"That's Monday's me, actually," Vanessa said, and saved the file.

The party had spilled from the Kowalskis' kitchen onto the lawn, and Isabella stood near the fence holding a cup of punch she hadn't touched, watching her classmates invent dances that would embarrass them by August. Someone had strung lights between the porch and the maple. Everyone she could see was going somewhere in the fall: state schools, a conservatory in Boston, one gap year that nobody believed would last only a year.

She found Devon by the cooler, turning a can of soda in his hands without opening it. "You counted the yard yet?" he asked. "Like a census. I keep doing it without meaning to."

"Counted what?"

"Who's here." He nodded toward the lawn. "Four hundred and six of us started ninth grade together. Or close to that. There are maybe three hundred backdrops back there."

Isabella did the subtraction in her head and didn't like the remainder. "Some moved. Some went private. Marcus went to that academy in his dad's city."

"Sure," Devon said. "But not all of them." He popped the can, took one sip, and set it on the fence post like evidence he intended to return to. "I looked it up last night, because I couldn't sleep. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in 2021-22. Eighty-seven. I kept saying it to my ceiling."

"That's the whole country, though. Not us."

"We're not special," Devon said, and wandered off toward the music, leaving her with the number.

She followed the fence line, and the arithmetic walked with her. Thirteen percent somewhere, distributed across four years, invisible until you stood in a backyard and noticed the absences the way you notice a missing tooth. Her younger self had assumed that everyone who started simply kept going, the way a river does, and the correction felt less like information than like a debt she hadn't known she owed.

In her back pocket, her phone held a message she'd received in March and never answered. She stepped behind the garage where the music thinned and read it again, the way she'd read it a dozen times. It was from Renata, who had sat beside her in biology sophomore year and then, by junior year, sat nowhere. "i know this is weird. i'm getting my GED in june instead of walking. i didn't drop out, i want you to know that, it just looked exactly like dropping out from the outside. my mom got sick and somebody had to be home. anyway. you were the only person who noticed i stopped coming. you don't have to reply. it just felt wrong to graduate without telling anyone why i wasn't there." Isabella had drafted four replies and deleted each one, afraid that sympathy would sound like pity, afraid that silence was its own verdict. Now she typed the simplest true thing: "i noticed. i'm at a party and it's strange and you should know you're the reason it's strange. GED in june is graduating. come find me after." She pressed send before she could litigate the sentence further, and watched the word delivered appear beneath it.

The Kowalskis' dog, a belligerent little terrier who had spent the evening defending the sandbox from toddlers, streaked past her and hurled himself at the fence, barking at nothing on the other side. She watched him and thought that everyone at this party was standing on some substrate they never examined, the four quiet years of attendance and passing grades, and that Renata had been standing on something too, just a different and harder material, one that didn't come with a ceremony.

Devon reappeared at her elbow with two cups of punch and handed her one. "You look like you found a name in the missing column."

"Renata Alvarez. Junior year. Her mom got sick." Isabella took a drink, and the sweetness surprised her. "I'm not sure that's all of it either. But it's part of it."

"You going to track the rest down?" He said it lightly, but she understood he was asking whether she intended to turn the evening into an accounting, a ledger of everyone the cohort had quietly set down along the way, or whether she could hold both things at once: the joy of the lit yard and the fence-line of people who should have been in it.

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe some. Probably not all." The lights hummed above them; someone had put on a song from freshman year, and the whole lawn shouted the chorus like a promise made in the dark. Her phone buzzed once against her hip, and she reached for it.

Elijah arrived at the community center gym twenty minutes early, the way he had every Tuesday since October, and found Marcus already there, shooting free throws with his back to the door. The league was a patchwork thing, six teams of boys who mostly did not go to school together, and their team, the one sponsored by Delgado's Hardware, had started the season 4 and 1. Then they lost three in a row, and the losses had a sound to them: Marcus yelling at Dev for not passing, Dev calling Marcus a ball hog, the younger kids going quiet on the bench. Elijah wanted one thing, which was to finish the season with a team that still liked each other. He was not sure this was the same thing as winning, and he kept trying to decide whether it was.

The fight that night started over a screen. Marcus set it late, Dev's defender slipped under it, Dev turned the ball over, and on the walk back up the court Dev said, "You want forty shots a game, just say it." Marcus said, "I want to win, which is different from what you want." By the time they got to the locker room, Coach Reyes had stopped trying to forestall it. He stood in the doorway with a folded piece of paper and put it on the bench where Marcus could not miss it.

The note was short. Elijah read it over Marcus's shoulder: "Storming. Look it up. Practice Thursday." Marcus crumpled it and threw it into the corner, which was its own kind of answer, and left. Elijah picked the paper back up, smoothed it against his thigh, and took it home.

At his kitchen table he typed the word into his phone. What came up was a psychologist named Bruce Tuckman, who proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. He read it twice. The names sounded like something from a worksheet, but he recognized the shape of it immediately, the polite first weeks, then the arguments, and something after that he could not picture yet. He texted his older sister at college, because she was studying psychology and he wanted to check that the internet had not invented it.

"Real thing," she wrote back. "They made us memorize it. Forming, storming, norming, performing. Tuckman, 1965. Why, did your team finally start fighting?"

"Coach left it on a note," Elijah typed. "Marcus threw it out."

"Of course he did," she wrote. "Wanting to be the guy who scores is its own philosophy. Everything Marcus does has a logos. The question is whether the team's is the same one."

Elijah set the phone down and thought about Marcus's want, which was not a mystery: Marcus believed he was the best player on the floor, which was true, and believed that this meant the offense should run through him, which had stopped being true the moment teams started doubling him. Dev wanted touches, the younger kids wanted minutes, and Elijah wanted whatever held all of it together, though he could not have said in one sentence what that was. On Thursday he brought the note to practice and left it on the bench again, unfolded this time.

Dev found it first. "What's forming, storming, norming, performing?" he said, reading it aloud, pronouncing the words carefully like a list he was being tested on. Marcus came over and looked at the paper, and Elijah said, "Some psychologist, Tuckman. He says groups go through it. We're supposed to be in the storming part." Marcus read the screen of Elijah's propped-up phone for a long moment, then said, "So we're normal," and walked back out to the court. It was the closest thing to an apology anyone had offered all season.

The norming happened without ceremony. Dev started calling screens early so Marcus could hear them, and Marcus started throwing the skip pass he had hoarded all year, and the younger kids got their minutes in a blowout against the church team that they won by nineteen. The performing, if that was the word, arrived on a Sunday in December, the last scheduled game, against the league's best team: they ran a set play with four passes and no words, and Elijah, who had not scored all afternoon, cut to the basket and laid it in at the buzzer. In the locker room afterward the noise was all of them at once, and Reyes stood in the corner with the box scores and a new piece of paper.

"League's folding," he said. "Center lost the gym rental budget in the county vote Tuesday. We already played the last game." He held up the paper, which was a flyer for a winter clinic at a gym across town, and Marcus took it from his hand and folded it into his pocket before anyone else could move.

The enrollment form came in a plastic sleeve with a pen chained to the clipboard, which Stella thought was an odd way to begin a lesson in trust. She was sixteen, third in line at the counter of Ridgeline Driving Academy, and behind her the Tuesday class was already filling plastic chairs. The man at the counter, Mr. Okafor, slid the sleeve toward each student like a dealer. "Read it, sign it, initial page four," he said, and the girl ahead of Stella signed without sitting down.

Stella sat down. The form was dense, and the language had a way of moving just as she reached for it: release, indemnify, assumption of risk. On page four, a paragraph in slightly larger print said that any dispute would be settled through binding arbitration rather than in court, and that by signing she waived participation in any class-action lawsuit. She read it twice. She had seen the word arbitration before, last month, in her father's kitchen, hunched over his laptop scrolling through the endless terms of his new phone app.

That night came back to her clearly. Her father had beckoned her over with two fingers, the screen's glow on his glasses. "Look at this," he had said. "I clicked agree on this app months ago. Apparently I agreed not to sue them in court. If something goes wrong, we go to some private thing instead. And we can't join together with other people who got the same raw deal." He had laughed, a small dry laugh, and said, "They buried it in the conditions where nobody reads." Stella had ascribed her father's amusement to his usual habit of finding catastrophe funny, but she had gone to bed uneasy, the way you do when you learn the floor of a familiar room has a trapdoor somewhere.

Now she looked up at Mr. Okafor. "What does this paragraph mean, exactly?"

"Arbitration clause," he said pleasantly. "Standard."

"I mean, what happens if something goes wrong."

"Then we settle it privately, not in a courtroom." He was already reaching for the next clipboard.

The girl behind her, a compact person in a wrestling hoodie, leaned over Stella's shoulder. "You're actually reading it?"

"Somebody has to."

"It's driving school, not a kidney transplant."

"Same principle," Stella said, and meant it, though she could not have said exactly what the principle was, only that it involved the difference between agreeing and consenting, which her mother insisted was not the same thing at all. Consent, her mother said, required knowing what you were saying yes to. Her mother had said this about doctors, about boyfriends, about a landlord once, standing in the doorway of their old apartment with her arms folded.

The trouble was concrete: Stella wanted the class. Her mother worked the early shift and her father's car sat in the lot all day, and without a license Stella was asking favors every week, small favors that accumulated like interest. And the class was cheap, cheaper than the other school across town, which now seemed less like luck and more like a clue. She thought of her father's screen. She thought of the girl ahead of her who had signed standing up.

She raised her hand again. "If I cross this out and initial it, can I still take the class?"

Mr. Okafor blinked. "Nobody's ever asked."

"But can I?"

He looked at the paragraph, then at her, and something in his face shifted, less irritation than recalibration. "Let me call the owner." He picked up the phone, and while he dialed, the wrestling girl slid into the chair beside Stella and started reading page two aloud in a courtroom voice, "'The student ascribes all risk of somatic injury to their own person,' which I believe is Latin for 'ouch is your problem,'" and Stella laughed despite herself, a bright involuntary sound that felt like the first crack in a frozen lake.

The owner said no to the cross-out, but offered a verbal assurance, which everyone in the room understood was worth the paper it was printed on, which was nothing. Stella sat with the pen hovering. She thought of her mother in the doorway, arms folded. She thought of the car in the lot, keys eventually in her own hand, the specific exhilaration of a first highway on-ramp, the pedal under her foot. She thought: I can sign this and know what I signed, or refuse it and stay home, and neither choice is clean.

She wrote her name, then, underneath, in small careful letters, "signed under protest," and handed the clipboard back. Mr. Okafor looked at the addition, opened his mouth, closed it, and stamped the form.

"First lesson is Saturday," he said. "Eight a.m."

Behind her, the wrestling girl was still on page six, reading slower now.

The office smelled of toner and the lemon polish Mr. Aduba used on the counters every morning, and by the second week of her summer job Laura had learned to tell the time by the door. Ten o'clock brought the renters, clutching printouts, asking whether the deposit on a two-bedroom was really one month's rent plus a fee, and whether they would get any of it back if the blinds were already bent when they moved in. Two o'clock brought the buyers, quieter people who sat across from Mr. Aduba's desk with bank statements folded into squares, talking about down payments as if the words were fragile. Laura filed their paperwork, marked the keys in, made coffee, and listened.

Her own problem sat in her bag all afternoon: a letter from the housing office at the college she'd start in September, listing the dorm fee next to a smaller figure for sharing an off-campus apartment with three strangers. Her mother had said, over dinner, that they'd work it out, and then changed the subject to her aunt's knees, and Laura had understood that "work it out" meant she was supposed to work it out.

On Thursday her cousin Denise came in at four, still in her hospital scrubs, carrying a folder she dropped on the counter like something hot. "Five years," she said. "Five years of paying every single month, and I looked it up today and I still owe almost exactly what I borrowed. Where did the money go, Laura? Tell me where it went."

Mr. Aduba, who was phlegmatic about nearly everything, including burst pipes and a tenant who once kept goats, looked up from his screen. "Standard repayment loan," he said. "The early payments go mostly to interest." He turned back to his screen, as if that settled it, and for him it had.

Denise hadn't heard it that way before either. "So the bank takes its share first," she said slowly, "and only later does the money actually start bringing down what I owe."

Laura pulled the amortization sheet out of Denise's folder and ran her finger down the columns, curious now in spite of herself. The monthly number never changed, but its two halves shifted as the years went by, the interest slice shrinking and the other slice growing, until near the end nearly everything went to the borrowed amount itself. It was like watching a tide change direction so slowly you had to mark the waterline to prove it. She thought of her mother's old joke that the universe was patient because it could afford to be.

"Meanwhile I've been renting," Laura said, mostly to herself, "and I understood that part. You pay, you live there, the money's gone, and the deposit is the only piece that might circle back to you if you leave the place clean." She looked up. "I thought buying was the opposite. Money in, house yours. Nobody told me it's a long argument with the bank first, and for the first stretch the bank wins every month."

Denise laughed, a short, tired sound. "You'll be a freshman and you already prognosticate better than my loan officer." She squared the folder against the counter. "At least now I know the payments weren't wasted. They were just, what's the word, front-loaded."

Mr. Aduba slid a listing across the desk to a couple by the window, and the office hummed with its usual throughput of phone calls, key tags, and people carrying their futures around in envelopes. Laura photocopied the amortization sheet and folded it next to the housing letter in her bag, then sat at the front desk and did the arithmetic she'd been avoiding. Dorm fee times eight semesters. Off-campus rent times the same months, minus her share of a deposit she might never see again, plus a bus pass. The two totals sat near each other, close enough that the difference wouldn't decide anything by itself. What she couldn't price was quieter: whether she wanted to learn a city through a landlord's rules or through a roommate's dishes in the sink.

She understood something else, too, though it was less comfortable. Denise's payments hadn't vanished; they had gone somewhere, just not where Denise had pictured, and Laura liked knowing that the system had a logic even when it wasn't her logic. What she couldn't yet say was whether the logic was fair. Maybe the bank deserved its interest for lending the money at all, and maybe that was exactly the kind of sentence people said when the money wasn't theirs. She held both possibilities open the way you hold two keys, trying each in the same lock.

At closing time she wiped the counter, switched off the printer, and pulled the folded paper out again. On the back of the amortization sheet, in the margin, she wrote the dorm number, the rent number, and then, underneath, a small question mark that she didn't try to answer. Denise knocked on the glass from the parking lot, holding up her car keys through the window, and Laura clipped the page into her notebook, waved back, and went to lock the front door.

The video arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, forwarded from Dex with three fire emojis and the caption "bro look at this NOW." It showed a shopping mall in flames, smoke rolling against a sky the color of dishwater, people running with their jackets over their mouths. A caption in the corner gave a city and yesterday's date. Loic was alone in the living room, his mother asleep down the hall, and his thumb hovered over the forward arrow for the group chat before he noticed that his own heartbeat had picked up, as though the fire were something happening to him.

He sent it. Fourteen people received it in the next ninety seconds, and the replies stacked up fast, the little word bubbles portending a night of outrage. Dajah wrote "this is terrifying." Someone Loic barely knew from his sister's graduation wrote "what is WRONG with people." Loic typed "exactly" and felt the warm certainty of agreeing with everyone at once, the feeling he would later recognize as the cheapest thing he owned.

Then Nadia replied, three minutes later, with a screenshot. "This photo is old," she wrote. "It's been online since like 2017." She had run the still frame through something called TinEye, a reverse image search engine, and she'd sorted the results with the oldest first, which showed her when the image first appeared online, years before yesterday. Loic read the message twice. The fire emojis in his own forward suddenly looked insouciant, the seal of someone who had cared only about being first.

He didn't apologize right away. First he argued, because the first feeling is always that the correction is an attack. "The video format is different," he typed. "Someone re-uploaded it, so maybe it's new footage of the same thing." Nadia sent a link. He sat in the lamplight of the living room, the TV off, his mother's magazines fanned on the coffee table, and opened his laptop on the arm of the couch.

He dragged the frame into the search bar himself. He didn't want to take her word for it; he had decided at some point that year, without announcing it, that he was going to be a person who checked things, a small-time autodidact with a laptop and a grudge against being fooled. The results loaded, and he found the oldest-first option and clicked it, and there was the same smoke, the same dishwater sky, dated years back, on sites he'd never heard of, some of them dead now, the page still standing like a burned building left standing.

He typed an apology into the group chat. It felt insufficient and he sent it anyway. "I shared something fake," he wrote. "The photo's from years ago. Sorry, everyone, check before you forward." A couple of people replied with thumbs. Dajah wrote "good looking out." Someone else wrote "lol it's not that deep," and Loic sat with that for a while, the possibility that it wasn't, that he had turned a Tuesday night into a seminar nobody had enrolled in.

He called Nadia instead of texting, because some things you want to hear in a voice. "How'd you even know to do that," he asked. She was folding laundry, he could hear the fabric. "My cousin got burned during the election," she said. "Shared a thing, got quoted at a family dinner, spent a year being the cautionary tale." She laughed a little. "TinEye's been around since 2008, so it's not like it's a secret. People just don't use it."

He told her he'd run the oldest-first sort himself, that he'd seen the earliest result with his own eyes, and she said "then you did it right." It was a small compliment and he held on to it harder than he meant to. After they hung up he scrolled back through the group chat, past his fire emojis, past the fourteen forwards, and found that two people had sent the video on after his correction, probably without reading up that far. He couldn't reach those threads. He knew that now, and it didn't portend anything good, it was just true. He closed the laptop and sat in the quiet living room, then picked up his phone and opened his sister's chat, where the video sat unsent, and typed: "Before you share anything, there's a thing you should see."

The lab smelled like wet dirt and coffee, which Kyle decided was what a real science lab should smell like, even if the posters on the wall were about something he'd never heard of before this spring: the soil microbiome, all the fungi and bacteria living in a handful of forest floor. Dr. Okafor had taken him on as a summer mentee after his chemistry teacher sent an email Kyle hadn't even known was being written. Now he sat at a stool beside the fume hood, pipetting liquid into little tubes with hands that were steadier than he expected, while his phone sat face-down in his backpack and vibrated against a spiral notebook.

He didn't check it. He had a rule about that, invented twenty minutes ago.

The vibration was almost certainly Mr. Duvall from the landscaping company, calling to confirm whether Kyle could start Monday. Fourteen dollars an hour, forty hours a week, all summer, real money by August. The research position here, by contrast, was unpaid, and its rewards were the kind adults praised in a language Kyle privately thought of as rain-word, vague and falling everywhere at once. Experience. Connections. A line on an application.

"So you're the new one," said Priya, a lanky girl in a college hoodie who had wandered over from the greenhouse bay. She watched him pipette with an expression of polite horror. "You're pushing too hard. Let the drop fall on its own."

Kyle eased his thumb. A drop detached, tidy as a bead.

"What are you doing this summer?" she asked. "Here, or the thing?"

"The thing?"

"Some people do the summer program and then leave in July for jobs." She shrugged. "Dr. Okafor pretends not to mind. My mom thinks I'm insane for staying. She keeps bringing up this study. The marshmallow one. Little kids, one treat now or two if they wait." Priya rolled her eyes toward the ceiling. "She read that a 1990 follow-up of those preschoolers found the kids who'd waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers. So now every time I choose homework over a shift at the pool, she's smug about it for a week."

"Wait, they followed them for years? Actual years?"

"Twelve or something. I don't know. My mom tells it like a fable." Priya drifted back toward the greenhouse, and Kyle stood there with his pipette suspended, a drop trembling at its tip.

He wanted to dismiss it. It was a fable, obviously, the kind of thing adults used to make patience sound like virtue instead of what it usually was, standing around while other people got the good seats. One afternoon with a marshmallow couldn't reach across a decade and grab a number out of some kid's future. But then, the landscaping job was also a single afternoon's decision, and everyone acted as if it would reach forward and grab his. Mr. Duvall had said the crew he joined this summer often came back every year through college, which sounded either like loyalty or like a trap, depending on the hour at which Kyle thought about it.

At the break, he used the old desktop in the lab's corner, the one with the screen the color of weak tea. The library database gave him the study without much digging: preschoolers, treats, the waiting, and then, in a 1990 follow-up, the longer waiters tending toward higher SAT scores as teenagers. He read it twice. The word that snagged him was "tended." Not guaranteed, not always, just leaned, the way a slope leans. He tried to recalibrate around it, to hold both things at once: that a choice made in one afternoon seemed to lean on a person for years, and that leaning wasn't deciding. Somewhere under all that was the fact that no one had ever offered him a second marshmallow for waiting. Waiting, in his house, had just been waiting.

Because that was the part he hadn't told Dr. Okafor, or Priya, or anyone. The word he kept behind his teeth. His mother had started picking up extra shifts in March, and the second-shift differential didn't cover what the hospital had started sending in envelopes she left on the microwave, turned address-side down. Kyle had done the arithmetic on the bus. Fourteen dollars an hour, forty hours, eleven weeks. He could carry the fall by himself, the way she'd carried everything since June of last year. That was the calculation sitting in his backpack, buzzing.

Dr. Okafor came back from the staff room with two cups of tea and offered him one, and when Kyle took it she became unexpectedly effusive about his pipetting, saying he had good hands, that good hands were rarer than good grades, that the bacteria in sample seven had done something under the microscope this morning that she wanted to show him. She leaned over the scope and adjusted the fine focus, and the screen filled with a smear of life, threads and dots moving through soil water like a slow city. "This biome," she said, tapping the screen with one finger, "has been developing in that jar since February. Every day it becomes more itself. You cannot rush it and you cannot skip ahead and see what it will be in August."

Kyle looked at the jar. Then, in a way that felt like stepping off a curb he'd been standing on all day, he took his phone out of the backpack. The screen said one missed call, one voicemail. He stood in the doorway of the lab where the dirt smell was strongest and pressed the phone to his ear, and Mr. Duvall's voice came through flat and cheerful, saying the crew slot was his if he wanted it, saying to call back by five, saying no rush, kid, it's your summer.

Behind him Dr. Okafor was still bent over the microscope, patient as soil. He looked at the clock above the sink, then at the screen, where the threads kept moving through their dark, unfinished city. He dialed.

"Mr. Duvall? It's Kyle." He watched a single bead form at the tip of his abandoned pipette, hanging there, holding on. "I need to ask you something before I answer."

The kitchen smelled of Grandpa Walt's coffee, bitter and old, and Jordan set his shoebox of alum crystals on the table between the sugar bowl and the window geranium. The largest crystal sat on a folded paper towel, blue-white and faceted, and beside it his lab notebook lay open to the page where he'd weighed everything twice.

"They're smaller than the ones in your photograph," Grandpa said, turning the box with one finger. He had the saturnine face of a man who had spent forty years underground in the gypsum mine, and he looked at the crystal the way he looked at most things, as if it had already disappointed him somewhere.

"That's the problem," Jordan said. "I started with twenty-five grams of alum. That's potassium aluminum sulfate dodecahydrate, molar mass four hundred seventy-four grams per mole. So I divide, and I get about zero point zero five three moles of the stuff, and since it comes back out of solution as the same compound, the theoretical yield is twenty-five grams. But the crystals only weigh twenty-one point four grams." He slid the notebook across. "I lost almost four grams somewhere."

Grandpa studied the figures without touching them. "And what do you call that. The number you're after."

Jordan had written the division on the back of an envelope that morning, on the bus, and he'd been carrying the answer around all day like a stone in his pocket. "Percent yield. You take the actual mass you got, divide by the theoretical yield, multiply by a hundred. Mine's eighty-five point six percent." He said it flat, because the number still embarrassed him. At the regional fair in March, a judge had asked him for it, and he'd stood there with his mouth open, having never computed it at all.

"You were supposed to win that thing," Grandpa said. It wasn't a question. Two springs ago they had driven down to the fair together in the truck with the rusted wheel well, and Jordan had taken second, and on the drive home Grandpa had said the judges wouldn't know a decent crystal if it fell on them. That was the last good stretch between them. Afterward came the silent autumn, when Jordan stopped visiting because Grandpa had told his father, at Thanksgiving, that a boy who spent his weekends washing glassware was wasting the only youth he'd get. His father, who could pontificate for a full hour on the dignity of manual labor without ever having held a shovel he wasn't photographing, had returned fire, and Jordan had spent the holiday in the car with the radio on.

"Some of it's still in solution," Jordan said. "The water holds a little alum even when it's cold. Some stuck to the filter paper. Some probably splashed when I poured." He tapped the envelope. "But I can't prove which. That's the part that got me. I know how much I lost, not where."

Grandpa got up and refilled his cup, and the chair scraped the linoleum in the way Jordan had memorized without meaning to. In the mine, Grandpa had said once, you measured what came up the shaft, and what didn't come up, you didn't guess at. You just dug differently next week. Jordan had thought that was a hard way to live. He wasn't sure now. His own method had been to calculate until the numbers matched, and when they didn't match, to decide the scale was wrong.

"Eighty-five and a half," Grandpa said, sitting back down. "In the mill that would've been a good week."

"Dr. Okafor says above ninety is excellent for a first recrystallization." Jordan heard himself and laughed a little. "But she's not the one who has to write it on the poster."

"So write it." Grandpa pushed the envelope back toward him. "Write that you know what you got and you know what it should've been. A man who hides the shortfall hides it the second time too."

Jordan looked at the crystal, at the small perfect faces of it, grown atom by atom from the water in a mason jar on his desk while he slept. He had wanted, all spring, to be the boy whose numbers came out clean. What he had instead was a number with a gap in it, and the honest sentence that the gap was real and its cause was not. He picked up the pen and began printing neatly beneath the division: actual mass divided by theoretical yield, times one hundred, equals 85.6 percent.

"Next year," he said, "I'll cool it slower. Filter it twice." He glanced up. "If I'm still welcome to use the garage for the evaporation dishes."

Grandpa turned the crystal once more in the light from the window, and the facets threw small bright coins across the tablecloth.

"Wash them when you're done," he said. "Both of you. You can tell your father that."

Jordan had until five o'clock tomorrow to submit a written critique of a Frida Kahlo painting for the community studio's youth show, and the studio had decided, in its mysterious apportionment of good and bad luck, that his assigned painting was the one with the wounded deer.

He'd spent the evening sprawled on the paint-spattered couch with a print of it, feeling torpid, while Priya across the room worked on her own critique with the smug efficiency of someone who had already finished a draft. "You could just describe it," she said. "Deer, arrows, ocean, done."

"That's a list, not a critique." He held the print at arm's length, then closer, then tipped his head sideways until Priya laughed at him. "Ms. Okafor wants formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Three paragraphs, apparently, or the universe collapses."

"So write the paragraphs."

The problem, which he could not explain without sounding like an idiot, was that he had two ideas about the painting and they refused to sit in the same paragraph. One idea was technical: something about how the greens of the forest and the red of the deer's wound and the sky's streaks pushed against each other, so the whole surface seemed to hum. The other idea was about Kahlo putting her own face on a pierced animal, which was either the saddest self-portrait ever made or a joke at the expense of everyone who expected women to paint flowers. He couldn't tell which idea was the real one, and every draft he started collapsed into either art-vocabulary soup or feelings with no evidence.

The deadline was real because the youth show opened Saturday and the critiques would hang beside the paintings. Priya had already read hers aloud twice, partly to help him and mostly, he suspected, to aggrandize herself, since her critique of the Diego Rivera print contained the phrase "monumental dignity of labor" four times.

"You're overcomplicating," she said. "Pick the hummingbird. Write about the hummingbird."

"I can't just pick symbolism. It has to connect to how the painting is built." He flattened the print on the table and squinted at the deer's neck, where the wound ran red against leaves so green they looked lit from inside. Something about that pairing kept snagging him. He dragged out the studio's big wooden colour wheel, a wheel Priya called the pizza of knowledge, and spun it until he found what he was looking for. Red sat directly across from green, opposite each other on the wheel.

"Complementary colours," he said. "They sit opposite each other on the wheel, like red and green."

"So?"

"So look." He held the wheel beside the print. "She puts them side by side everywhere. The wound against the leaves, the ribbon against the branches. And when they're side by side they make each other look brighter. That's why the painting vibrates. It's not just blood, it's blood made louder by green."

Priya came over, which he counted as a victory. She looked, really looked, tilting her head the way he had, and said, "Huh," in the tone of someone annoyed to be interested. "So the hummingbird's not just a symbol, it's also red hanging in green."

"Right. Or, wait." He turned the print over and back, as if the back might hold the answer. "It's both. The colour makes you look, and then what you're looking at is the wound. The brightness is the argument. Kahlo builds a glowing painting so you can't look away from the thing that hurts." He said it out loud and heard, for the first time, his two ideas snapping together like magnets.

He wrote fast, filling the margin with crossed-out words, while Priya read over his shoulder and periodically said "monumental dignity" to annoy him. At one point she leaned on his arm mid-sentence and he wrote "grn" by accident and had to fix it.

By eight, he had a draft with a real thesis: that the composition led your eye in a circle, down the neck, through the ocean, back up the antlers, so the deer never got to rest, and the complementary reds and greens kept the whole loop humming. In his last paragraph he admitted the thing he still couldn't settle, which was whether the deer was despair or defiance, and argued that the painting refused to choose, and that maybe refusing to choose was the point. Priya read that part twice.

"It's better than mine," she said. "Don't tell anyone I said that."
