Rose found the violin in her grandmother's hallway closet, behind a box of winter coats, and carried it to the kitchen table the way you carry something that might still be alive. Her grandmother looked up from the sink, dried her hands, and said only, "The E string is flat. It's been flat since 1987."

She had played clarinet for six years, sight-read anything put in front of her, and had assumed that reading notes was what playing an instrument meant. But the violin had no holes for her fingers, no keys, no map. Her grandmother tuned it for her, placed her fingers on the strings one afternoon, and then did something Rose didn't expect: she hummed a phrase from an old folk song and said, "Now play that back." When Rose asked for the sheet music, her grandmother laughed. "I never had any. There wasn't any in the house."

The problem arrived on Saturday in the form of Birdie, nine years old, who lived two farms over and took the bus to the house every week for a lesson her grandmother gave for nothing. Rose thought that was altruistic of her, though she also suspected her grandmother simply liked the company. Birdie could play. That was the humiliating part. She set her small violin under her chin and produced a clean, singing "Go Tell Aunt Rhody" while Rose stood in the doorway holding the sheet music she had transcribed the night before, her version of being prepared.

"You read it off the paper," Birdie said afterward, squinting at Rose's pages. "What are all those flags for?" She genuinely didn't know. She could play a dozen songs and could not name a single note on the staff. Rose felt something twist that wasn't quite contempt and wasn't quite envy, some hybrid she couldn't file. She had spent years building a system of reading, and here was a child who bypassed it entirely, the way, Rose thought and then stopped thinking, a toddler talks long before anyone hands it an alphabet.

She cornered her grandmother at the kitchen table that evening, the fact sheets spread out. "How does she do that without reading?"

"It's how she was taught. The Suzuki method. Shinichi Suzuki, the Japanese violinist. He started children playing by ear before they ever read music, the way they learn to speak before they learn to read."

"Then she's missing half of it," Rose said.

"Or you are."

They did not settle it. Rose went to bed angry in the clean, useless way that keeps you awake counting ceiling cracks. In the morning she found Birdie on the porch steps sawing through "Twinkle, Twinkle" and sat down beside her with the transcript. "Trade," Rose said. "You teach me the song by ear. I teach you the notes." Birdie considered this with the gravity of a customs officer. "You have to promise not to abrogate," she said, and Rose, who had taught her that word two days earlier from a crossword, promised not to abrogate.

The lesson was harder than either expected. Birdie could not understand why Rose kept stopping to look down at fingers that wouldn't obey, and Rose could not understand how Birdie's hands knew where to go without ever asking permission. "You just hear where it goes," Birdie said, and when Rose snapped that that wasn't an answer, Birdie played the next phrase wrong on purpose, so slowly that Rose could hear the right note arriving before Birdie's finger landed on it. Rose copied the correction. Then copied it again. On the fourth try the phrase came out whole, and she had not looked at the paper once.

Her grandmother came out with lemonade and the mail, and set down a postcard from the clinic reminding her that her allergy shots were due. "Antigens," she said vaguely, reading it, "little troublemakers they inject so your body learns the tune." Rose thought about that longer than the postcard deserved. A small dose of the thing that hurts, given on purpose, so the system learns to answer it.

She didn't conclude anything tidy. Some days she still believed reading was the spine of music and Birdie was a trick pony; other days, playing "Aunt Rhody" in the dark barn with her eyes shut, she believed the opposite. She decided she was allowed to hold both. On the last night of the visit she played the folk song through, twice, no music stand, and her grandmother called from the kitchen, "The E string's still flat."

"I know," Rose called back. "I like it now."

The line outside the food bank reached the corner of the parking lot before the doors opened at ten. Eva stood behind a folding table stacked with canned tomatoes and wondered whether she should have chosen a Saturday, when she imagined the volunteers would outnumber the visitors. A woman in a lanyard named Priya handed her a clipboard and said, "You take names and household sizes, I bag." The first man through the door gave his name in a voice so quiet Eva had to lean over the table.

By eleven her handwriting had gone small and cramped. A boy from her school, Daniel, came through with his younger sister, and they both pretended not to recognize each other, which was a courtesy she understood and accepted. He counted for a household of four. After he left, Priya glanced at the line still folded along the wall and said, "It's a Tuesday. You'd think a Tuesday would be slower."

Eva looked it up on her phone during her break, crouched beside the milk cooler. Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 had recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. She read the sentence twice. A record for a single month. She had expected the number to be large, but not a record, and she had not expected the record to be now, in an ordinary month with no holiday and no crisis she could name. She sat with the milk sweating against her knee and felt the fact ferment in her, slow and sour, changing shape the longer she held it.

Her mother had sent her here with an injunction she had repeated at the door: be useful, stay quiet, don't stare. Her civics teacher, on the other hand, had spent a unit on structural causes, poverty as a design flaw rather than a personal one, and had told them that charity could soothe the conscience without fixing anything. Eva had written that in an essay and gotten an A. Standing at the table, she found the two positions did not fit together the way they had on paper. Handing a man a bag of rice was not nothing. It was also not enough, and both of those things were true at once, and she could not make them into one sentence.

At noon a volunteer named Gerald, older and obdurate about procedure, refused a woman a second bag of formula because the sheet said one per household per visit. The woman said her sister and the baby were waiting in the car and were a separate household. Gerald said the sheet didn't say that. Priya came over and put her hand flat on the clipboard and said, "Write it as two households. I'll initial it." Gerald's jaw worked, but he stepped back, and Eva wrote the second entry while the woman held her sister's ID against the table edge to keep it steady.

Eva discovered that she had opinions about the clipboard. Rules existed so the supply lasted, and the supply had to last, because there were 2.2 million visits in a single month and this was only one food bank on one Tuesday. But the rules were written somewhere else, by people who had not seen the sister waiting in the car. Priya's initials were a small, local correction, the kind Eva's teacher would probably call a bandage. Eva was not sure the teacher was wrong. She was also not sure that mattered to the woman walking out with the formula, whose problem today was not structural.

Daniel came back near closing because his sister had left her scarf on a chair. He stood at the table while Eva looked for it under the coat rack, and he said, "You can't tell anyone, right." It was not really a question. She found the scarf, gray with a hole at one end, and held it out.

"I won't," she said. She signed out on the volunteer sheet, wrote her hours, and noticed her hand was still cramped from the morning's names. Priya called from the doorway that Tuesday next week she should come early, before the line reaches the corner. Eva zipped her jacket and said, "I'll be here at nine thirty."

Laurence found him at the third row of the bleachers, holding two cups of hot chocolate even though the game wouldn't start for twenty minutes, and she understood immediately that he had been worried about the same thing she had been worried about, which was having nothing to do with his hands. "I didn't know if you liked it," Dev said, offering one cup. "I guessed. Sugar's in the packet, not the cup, because I read once that people are particular." She took it. The night had that September smell of cut grass and cigarette smoke drifting from the parking lot, and the floodlights turned everyone's faces the same flat orange, which felt merciful, since it hid whatever her face was doing.

She had spent the drive here composing herself into someone blasé, a girl who watched football with mild amusement, who laughed at the right moments without investing anything, and the plan had already failed in the parking lot when she'd tripped on a chain and he'd caught her elbow and she'd said thank you twice, the second thank you quieter, as though the first had been a mistake. Now she sipped the hot chocolate and it was good, actually good, and she resented that, because it was harder to be cool about something good.

The marching band came out and scattered across the field like an archipelago, each cluster of brass and drums its own small island of noise. Dev leaned toward her to be heard over the drums. "You know my sister's in the clarinet section? Third row. She's been talking about this game for two weeks." He pointed, and there was a small wave from a girl in a green uniform, and Laurence waved back, and something about the wave, its unembarrassed eagerness, made her like him more, which she filed away as information she would examine later, alone.

By halftime she had accumulated a list of failures she kept without wanting to. She had misheard his joke about the referee and laughed two beats late. She had talked for what felt like four straight minutes about her intended major, urban studies, and had used the word "problematize" out loud, in a sentence, at a football game, and watched his expression go politely blank. When he'd asked whether she wanted a soft pretzel, she'd said "I'm good" in a tone that must have sounded like rejection of the entire category of pretzels, of shared food, possibly of him. The score was 21 to 14 and she could not have told you who was winning.

When the third quarter ended, Dev's phone buzzed and he looked at it too long. "My mom," he said. "She wants me home by eleven, she's, my grandpa's visiting and she wants the car in the driveway before he wakes up, he sleeps weird hours." He stood there holding the phone, not moving, and then he said, "I'm sorry. I know this is the worst possible timing. This was really..." He stopped, restarted. "I don't want to go."

Laurence walked him to the gate because it seemed like the thing a person would do, and the whole way she was composing the post-mortem: he couldn't even wait through the fourth quarter, he stood there struggling to say the date was anything at all. At the gate he turned around. "Can I be honest about something?" he said. "I've spent the entire game thinking you were bored. Like you came because your friend Priya said I was nice and now you're stuck here until the clock runs out. You kept looking at the field instead of at me, so I figured the field was more interesting, which, fair, but." He pushed his hands into his jacket pockets. "I kept trying to think of a way to ask if you were hating it without asking if you were hating it."

She stood there with her cup going cold in her hands. The field, the band, the whole roaring stadium was behind her, and she had been looking at it because looking at him was too much, and it had never once occurred to her that the direction of her eyes might have been read as a verdict on him. "I looked something up before tonight," she said. "Because I do that, I look things up, I looked up what to expect on first dates. There's this thing where after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them. And how much they enjoyed their company. Both of those, it's the whole finding." She heard herself speeding up and made herself slow down. "It's called the liking gap. People walk away from first conversations and the other person liked them more than they think. That's what the study said."

"So you're saying," Dev said, "that I've been sitting there thinking you hated me, and you've been sitting there thinking I hated you, and we were both, statistically." He laughed, and she laughed, and then he wasn't laughing anymore, he was saying, "Text me when you get home, okay, not because I'm worried, just because I want to know," and then he jogged toward the parking lot, one hand raised, and she stood at the gate in the floodlight noise and took out her phone and typed, before she could curate it, "I did not hate a single minute."

The used car lot sat behind the school like an archipelago of metal islands, and every afternoon David cut through it on his way home, slowing past the blue sedan with the faded FOR SALE sign in the window. He had two thousand dollars saved from three summers of mowing lawns, and his mother had promised, quietly, in the kitchen, that if he could cover half, she would help with the rest. The sedan was six thousand. The math felt possible in a way that made his chest tighten.

In geology that spring they had been forced to memorize rock types, and Mr. Okafor had passed around a chunk of obsidian, black and glassy, an igneous stone born from cooling lava. David had held it longer than he needed to. His grandfather had kept a chunk like it on his dresser, next to a savings passbook, and David remembered being nine, sitting on the bed's edge while the old man showed him the small deposits and the tiny sums the bank added each year, unearned, arriving like weather. "Money that sits still can grow," his grandfather had said, tapping the booklet, and David had believed it the way children believe things, without mechanism, without question.

Then the letter came. It was addressed to his mother, from the credit union, and she left it open on the counter while she made dinner, so David read it standing up, a spoon in his hand. The savings account had earned four percent last year; the balance, which had dipped after his father left, was climbing again, dollar by patient dollar. His mother watched him read it over his shoulder. "Grandpa would like that," she said, and handed him the carrots to peel.

At the dealership on Saturday, the salesman was a big, warm man named Ruiz who called David "young man" and his mother "ma'am" and brought them bottled water without being asked. The blue sedan was there, freshly washed. Six thousand dollars, Ruiz said, or they could finance it. He slid a paper across the desk: seventy-two months, one hundred and five a month. His mother's shoulders dropped a little with relief. David knew what her paycheck looked like; he knew one hundred and five was almost possible and one hundred and sixty was not.

"Or forty-eight months," Ruiz said, tapping another column, "but that's one thirty-five." David took the pen and added down both columns, twice, because the first answer seemed wrong. Forty-eight months at one thirty-five came to six thousand four hundred eighty. Seventy-two months at one hundred and five came to seven thousand five hundred sixty. He showed his mother the two totals. "The longer one has the smaller payment," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke, "but it costs more in the end. Like more than a thousand dollars more." Ruiz didn't argue. He looked at the paper, then at David, and something in his face shifted, less salesman, more uncle. "That's true," he said. "That's just how it works. At the same rate, more months means more interest over the life of the loan."

His mother was quiet in the car afterward. "We could do the four years," she said. "Tight, but maybe." Then, half a block on, the twist of the afternoon: Ruiz came jogging out of the lot with his jacket unbuttoned and caught them at the light. He handed David a card. "The sedan's owner trades with us," he said. "He'd probably take fifty-two hundred cash. No loan at all. I just thought somebody should mention it." He shrugged, embarrassed, and walked back before either of them could fully thank him.

David thought about it that night instead of homework. The cash offer would expropriate most of his savings in one gesture, the whole two thousand plus his mother's share, and the letter's patient four percent would have nothing left to work on. But no payment would arrive every month either, no stream of small subtractions, and his mother would keep her margins. He tried to hold both pictures at once: money growing because it sat still, and money spent because it moved something real into their driveway. He could not make the two pictures agree.

He texted his mother from bed: "We could pay cash and start saving again. Slower but no loan." She replied a minute later with a single thumbs up, then, after a longer pause: "Monday we offer 4900. If he says no, we do the 4 year loan. Deal?" David typed "deal," put the phone face down, and lay listening to the furnace tick. On Monday he would walk through the archipelago of cars one more time, and maybe drive one of them home.

Sophie knelt in the frozen grass between her mother's shoes and the headstone with the name HAMIDI chiseled deep enough to catch shadow, and she said, "Tell me again how she did it." Her mother's breath came out in slow white clouds. "She didn't do anything, that was the thing. She just sat there and everyone knew where to stand." Above them the January sky was the flat gray of an unwashed window, and the cemetery held only the two of them and a crow that kept landing on the fence and leaving, as if it couldn't decide.

The plan had come out of the November kitchen, out of the last iftar before her grandmother died. Sophie had been seventeen for a month and a half, and her aunts had been passing the dates over her head all her life. During Ramadan the whole family broke each day's fast at sunset with the meal they called iftar, and it always began the same way, with one date, the way the Prophet Muhammad had done it. Her grandmother had kept the dates ready for the moment the sun went down, every single evening of every Ramadan for fifty years, and when she died in December, nobody had said out loud who would take it over. Sophie had asked for it the way you ask for something you're afraid will be refused: quickly, at the sink, with her back turned. Her mother had said, "You know it's not just food. It's the timing." Sophie had said she knew.

Now it was her problem, and the problem had a shape she hadn't expected. Half the family wanted the iftar held the old way, at the house on Delancey Street, with the prayer before the dates and her uncle calling the adhan from the hallway because the speaker had broken years ago and nobody had fixed it, which had somehow become tradition itself. The other half, the younger half, had proposed something at the community center, catered, efficient, with a printed schedule so the fast could be broken on time without anyone standing in a kitchen all afternoon. Sophie had listened to both sides over a holiday dinner that was not the holiday dinner, and had understood that the argument wasn't really about venue. It was about whether a thing survived by staying exactly where it was or by being allowed to move.

She had come to the cemetery because the argument needed a third opinion and the third opinion was under the grass. "You'd tell me to stop being dramatic," she said to the headstone. Her mother laughed, a short sound, startled out of her. "She would. She'd say, feed them, the rest follows." Sophie looked up at her. "But that's the part I don't know. Does it?" Her mother pulled her scarf tighter and didn't answer, which Sophie had learned, recently, was its own kind of answer, the recalcitrant silence her grandmother had also used when a question was better left to ferment in the person asking it.

The concrete task was this: Sophie had to have the dates ready at the second of sunset, not ten minutes after, and she had learned, testing herself, that she could not trust her own eyes to know when the sun had gone. She'd looked up the calculation instead, and had spent a full afternoon in her room with the prayer times and the compass on her phone, until her aunt caught her at it and said, "You're doing what your grandmother did, the week before Ramadan, every year." That had been a strange comfort, that the worry was inherited, that her grandmother had also once sat somewhere with a piece of paper and no idea what she was doing. It might have been happenstance that the woman who became the family's keeper of iftar was the one who worried hardest, but Sophie didn't think so.

She had also gotten something wrong, and found out at the worst time. Last week, at the trial run she'd organized for the cousins, she had put out dates and water, and she'd watched the second hand of the kitchen clock tick past the calculated minute, and she had let everyone eat, and then her cousin Yusuf had looked at his own phone and said, "It was two minutes ago. The sun's been down." Two minutes. Nobody had made it a crime, but Sophie had felt it like one, because the whole point of the date was the moment, the first thing to touch a fast that had lasted since dawn. She had redone the calculation that night and found her mistake, a daylight savings setting she'd overlooked, and had sworn at her phone in a whisper in the dark.

The two sides of the family argument came together in her head on the walk back down the cemetery path, not because she forced them but because the frozen ground made her walk slowly and the walking did it. The community center people were right that a thing can be carried. The Delancey Street people were right that some things soak into walls. What she settled on, and she knew settled was too strong a word, was the house, the old way, but with the schedule printed anyway, taped to the refrigerator where the adhan speaker used to be, because the adhan could come from a phone now and a wrong clock could not be allowed to happen twice. Her mother walked beside her with her hands in her pockets and offered nothing, which Sophie understood as permission of a kind, though she could not have said of what.

The evening before the first fast, Sophie stood in the Delancey Street kitchen alone, the way she imagined her grandmother had stood, with the box of dates open on the counter and the small glass plates laid out, one for each person, eleven in total. She picked up a date and turned it in her fingers, this unremarkable brown thing that had to be in a hand at the second the light left. From the hallway her mother called, "Are you ready for tomorrow?" Sophie set the date back in the box, on top, where she would see it first. "The sun sets at 5:47," she said. "I'll be standing right here at 5:46."

The guidance counsellor's office smelled like instant coffee and the lemon disinfectant they used on the desks between periods, and Hannah had been sitting in the orange chair for eleven minutes because Mrs. Okafor's door was shut and someone was crying in there, audibly, in the way of a person who wanted to be heard through the door.

She had come to drop Calculus. The form was already filled out, folded twice, warm from her pocket. The deadline was four o'clock today; after that she was locked in for the semester, and the semester average she needed for the scholarship was not something she intended to titrate against a unit on integrals. She had done the math. She was good at math, which was the annoying part.

Her phone buzzed. Dev again. can u cover sat? my shift. third time this month. Dev worked the front desk at the rec center with her, had worked it since September, and had developed a talent for discovering, always on a Saturday morning, some obligation that outranked the schedule. He was charming about it, effusive in his apologies, and Hannah had covered twice because the alternative was explaining to their supervisor, whose management style could generously be called autocratic, that Hannah's coworker was a mirage.

The crying in Mrs. Okafor's office stopped. The door opened and a junior Hannah vaguely knew came out with red eyes and a parking pass application, and Mrs. Okafor beckoned her in.

"So," said Mrs. Okafor, reaching for the drop slip before Hannah had fully unfolded it. "Tell me why."

"Calculus is going to wreck my average," Hannah said. "I can take it in college. It's one course. It doesn't matter that much."

Mrs. Okafor didn't answer right away. She was looking something up on her laptop, turning the screen slightly, the way she did when a student's file said something different from the student's mouth. "Your grade is an eighty-one," she said. "That's not wreckage."

"It's going to be a sixty by finals." Hannah sat back. "It's one decision. One semester."

While Mrs. Okafor typed, Hannah's eye drifted to the bulletin board, to a photocopied page pinned between a poster about sleep and a flyer for votech programs. It was a summary of some study, Dunedin, a place in New Zealand, it said, following a thousand people born in one year across their whole lives. An analysis from 2011 had found that children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poorer health, less wealth, and criminal convictions. Hannah read it twice. It did not say how. It didn't say what happened in between the children and the adults, whether anyone had intervened, whether a single dropped calculus course was the same species of thing at all.

Her phone buzzed against her thigh. Dev. please please

"I know what you're thinking," Hannah said to Mrs. Okafor, before the counsellor could say it. "That the small stuff adds up. There's a whole page about it on your board."

"I was thinking about parking," said Mrs. Okafor. "But go on."

"There was this analysis, 2011, of the Dunedin Study. Kids with lower self-control ended up worse off. Health, money, criminal record." She heard herself say it and felt the argument land on her own head like a dropped textbook. "But that's children. Over decades. I'm deciding about one class in one semester. That's different. That's a single, rational, contained decision."

"Is it," said Mrs. Okafor, in the tone of a woman who had filed this exact form four hundred times and could probably predict the date of the final in question.

Here was the thing Hannah could not get around: she liked hard things when she chose them, and she avoided things she hadn't chosen, and Calculus had been her idea until it stopped being fun. Dev, she suspected, was the same. Dev did not think of himself as a person who abandoned his shifts; he thought of himself as a person with extenuating circumstances, each one reasonable, each one single and contained. Whereas the study on the bulletin board said the single and contained decisions were possibly the whole mechanism, or possibly not, since it didn't say, and neither did Hannah.

She picked up her phone. no, she typed to Dev. your shift is your shift. Then she deleted it for something kinder: can't. also you should know the swap list is three people deep and Bev is counting.

"The slip," said Mrs. Okafor, holding out her hand.

Hannah looked at the form, still folded, still warm. Outside, someone's class change rang through the hallway speakers, and she calculated, in the way she calculated, that she had until three fifty.

She tore it in half, once, neatly, and put the pieces in her pocket.

"Wise," said Mrs. Okafor, reaching for her stamp.

"It's one semester," Hannah said. "Ask me in December."

"Ask yourself in thirty years," said Mrs. Okafor, stamping something that was not, after all, her drop slip, and handing her a pass back to class.

Megan had chosen the bowling alley herself, mostly because it was impossible to be awkward somewhere that smelled like rented shoes. Her date, Daniel, had suggested a coffee shop, and she had countered with Tuesday night league lulls and half price games, and now here they were under the black lights, holding shoes in two plastic bags like trophies from a very small war.

The first game went well. Daniel bowled a respectable gutter ball and laughed at himself without performing the laughter, which Megan logged as promising. They talked about orientation schedules and roommates and the cafeteria's alleged burrito bar, and the conversation moved at the pace of two people testing a bridge with one foot on each plank.

By the second game, the planks ran out. Daniel asked what her major was, and she had already told him. She asked if he had siblings, and he had already said two, a younger sister, and a brother in Denver whose whole personality was apparently the Broncos. Megan watched the pins reset themselves with a mechanical clatter and tried to resuscitate the small talk, which lay between them on the lane like something that had been left out too long.

Then Daniel said, "Okay, I have an idea, but it might be weird." He wiped his palms on his jeans. "My psych teacher told us about this study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal, and afterward the pairs felt closer than pairs who just made small talk." He let that sit for a second. "We're out of small talk. I'm just saying."

"You want to run a psychology experiment on our first date."

"I want to cheat, technically. Same thing."

Megan pretended to consider it, though she had already decided, the way she decided most things, quickly and then slowly after. Her mother would say it was rushing intimacy, that closeness you built out of a questionnaire was a house with no foundation. Her brother would say the foundation was the questionnaire, that anything that worked was real the moment it worked. Both of them were probably a little right, which was the most annoying possible arrangement.

"Fine," she said, picking up her ball. "But we bowl between questions. And I go first. Question one, and I'm starting easy. What's your actual worst fear, spiders excepted?"

"You said starting easy."

"Spiders are the universal exception."

He answered while she rolled a seven, something about being forgettable, which was a better answer than the question deserved. Then his turn, and his question came while the ball was still traveling: what she would save from her childhood bedroom if it burned. She said her grandmother's recipe box, then admitted she had never cooked anything from it, and Daniel said that somehow made it mean more, not less, and she felt the consonance of that, two notes she hadn't expected to line up.

The questions climbed the way the study apparently promised, one rung at a time. Somewhere around question eleven, which Daniel delivered in the tone of a person defusing something, Megan realized she had told him about her parents' divorce, a subject she usually rationed out over three months of friendship, and that he had told her about his brother in Denver being sick last year, the real story, not the Broncos story. She also noticed she had stopped keeping score. The screen was keeping score anyway, indifferent and accurate, flashing her losses in orange while she failed entirely to mind.

By the last frame, the questions had reached a place where the answers had weight to them, and Megan found herself thinking that her mother and her brother were describing the same bridge from opposite banks. The closeness wasn't fake just because the questions came from a study, and it wasn't guaranteed just because a study said strangers had felt it before them. What stayed uncertain was the part no experiment covered, which was what happened after the thirty six ran out and you were left with only whatever you'd built. She didn't say any of this. She was eighteen, not a fortune cookie.

"Question thirty six," Daniel said. "Last one. The study doesn't say what it is, so I'm making it up, which I feel is within the spirit of the thing." He stood at the line with his ball, not bowling, waiting. "If this goes horribly, statistically we still had a better night than the small talk couples. And if it doesn't go horribly, what do you want to do next Saturday?"

Megan looked at the pins, ten of them, white and patient under the black light.

"Gutter ball decides nothing," she said, and rolled.

Mr. Okonkwo had divided the class into two benches, and Aidan had drawn the side defending algorithmic bail decisions, which was a problem because he had spent the whole weekend failing to write his opening argument.

"You're overthinking it," Marcus said, sliding into the seat beside him. "It's a debate. You argue whatever side you get."

"I know how debates work." Aidan pulled up his laptop. The classroom's old projector hummed above them, casting a torpid blue wash over the whiteboard, where Okonkwo had written only one word: NEUTRAL. "I just don't believe my side."

"So fake it."

The door opened and Priya came in early, the way she always did, carrying a folder of printed articles because she distrusted screens in arguments. She sat across the aisle and began arranging her pages. Aidan could see headlines upside down, and one of them had a word he recognized from somewhere, COMPAS, though he couldn't place it.

When the bell ended, Okonkwo clapped his hands once. "Computers should decide bail because they are neutral," he read from the board. "Bench one, you defend. Bench two, you dismantle. Five minutes to prepare."

Marcus leaned forward immediately. "Look, a judge has a bad morning, a fight with his wife, he's biased and doesn't even know it. An algorithm never had a bad morning. Same inputs, same outputs. That's your opener."

"That's fine," Aidan said, but he was watching Priya. She had flipped to a specific page and marked it with a yellow tab. He typed into his own laptop, not the debate prep document, just the search bar: COMPAS.

The results loaded and he read the first one twice. He looked up at the clock, which gave him three minutes.

"Bench one," Okonkwo called. "Your case."

Marcus stood. He gave the bad-morning-judge speech, then the part about consistency, then a line about how a tool that treats everyone the same is the definition of fairness. He sat down and nudged Aidan's elbow. "Your turn. Finish strong."

Aidan stood. "I had a second argument," he said. "I don't have it anymore."

"Take your time," Okonkwo said.

"In 2016, ProPublica investigated a risk tool called COMPAS, the kind used in bail decisions." He kept his eyes on Priya, who had stopped arranging her pages. "They found it misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants."

Nobody in the room moved. Someone at the back said, "Twice?"

"About twice the rate," Aidan said. "Same tool, same claim of neutrality." He turned toward his own bench. "I was going to argue that a computer has no volition, so it can't discriminate. But somebody chose the data. Somebody chose what to measure. The neutrality isn't in the machine. It's a claim people make about the machine." He sat down before he could soften any of it.

Marcus stared at him. "You just torched your own side."

"Yeah."

Priya stood slowly. She didn't gloat, which somehow made it worse. "I was going to use the same study," she said. "I spent Sunday deciding whether to say the word COMPAS out loud in this room." She didn't explain why that had been hard, and Aidan didn't ask, though he understood it had something to do with being the only student in the class who would ever have that hesitation.

"Then you agree with me," Marcus said to Aidan, "that the technology is fine and the data is bad? Fix the data, ship the tool."

"I don't know." Aidan heard how weak it sounded and kept going anyway. "Maybe. But we keep hearing that automation removes human judgment, and every example we've studied, the bail tool, the hiring filters, the school surveillance cameras Principal Reyes wants, replaces human judgment with somebody else's judgment, baked in and hidden. At least a judge can be questioned. A score just gets printed."

Okonkwo had been writing on the board through all of this. He underlined NEUTRAL, then crossed the word out, and the dry marker squeaked against the silence. "For Thursday," he said, "you'll each write a position statement. It must contain at least one thing you are still unsure about. I'll fail anything completely certain."

The room emptied in its usual noisy rush, but Priya waited by the door. She held out the yellow-tabbed article. "You should read the whole thing. My printer's dying anyway, so consider it a donation."

Aidan took the folder and slid it into his backpack without breaking it down, the paper stiff against his textbooks. Marcus was already in the hallway calling that he wasn't mad, exactly, but Aidan walked the other way, out toward the parking lot, where the district's new security cameras turned slowly on their mounts above the bike racks, tracking nothing in particular, recording it anyway.

Luca had until Friday to finish the drawing for his application portfolio, and the chair he'd chosen as his subject sat in the reading room of the public library like an accusation. He had picked it because it looked simple: wooden, straight-backed, older than anyone in the building. Three afternoons in a row he had sat cross-legged on the carpet with his sketchbook, and three afternoons the legs had come out wrong, the back slats leaning where they should have stood straight, the whole thing warping on the page like something seen through water. He pressed his pencil down until the lead snapped, then sat very still while the shard rolled off the page onto the carpet.

He had told his mother the portfolio was nearly done. That was the part that sat worst with him, worse even than the drawing. She'd cleared the kitchen table for him and kept his little sister away from his pencils, and every night she asked how it was going, and every night he said good, good, almost there. He knew a word for what he was doing, from a novel he'd read in the fall: mendacity. It had sounded lofty in the novel, almost elegant. In his mouth it just tasted like lying to someone who trusted him.

A girl from his art class, Deja, came through the reading room on Wednesday carrying a stack of returned atlases. She stopped behind him, looked over his shoulder, and said, "That chair looks like it's melting."

"I know." He turned the page sideways, as though the problem might be orientation. It was not orientation.

Deja set the atlases down on the shelf cart and folded herself into the seat across from him. "My grandmother taught me a trick," she said. "You don't draw the chair. You draw what's around the chair. The empty parts. Between the legs, around the back." She tapped the air between two of the chair's legs with one finger, not touching it, like a priest blessing a very small font.

"That makes no sense."

"It's called negative space," she said. "The empty area around and between things. Artists draw that to get the outline right." She picked up his spare pencil, the one he kept behind his ear, and on the corner of his page drew the shapes between the legs: tall thin polygons, a triangle of window light, the wedge of floor shadow. Then she handed the pencil back and went to shelve the atlases, because she was, as she'd told him once, the only sophomore the library would actually pay.

Luca sat for a long moment feeling truculent about it, wanting to tell her that a chair was a chair and you drew a chair by drawing a chair. But the corner of his page sat there with its odd geometry, and the shapes were right. He could see that they were right in a way his chair had never been. The empty parts didn't wobble. They didn't lie.

He started a new page and drew nothing. That was how he thought of it, at first, and it made him laugh under his breath, quietly enough that the man at the microfilm machine didn't glare. He drew the gap between the second and third slat, then the gap between the third and fourth, then the rectangles of window framed by the space around the back, then the air beneath the seat. When he stepped back to the table to look, the chair was there. It had arrived on the page without him drawing it, outlined by its own absence, straight and solid and old. His heart palpitated once, hard, the way it did when a jazz track changed key or when Deja had sat down next to him in September. He looked at the drawing for a full minute before he let himself shade a single plank of the seat.

He was signing his name in the corner, small, when the librarian on desk duty walked over. Mrs. Okafor was heavyset and unhurried and had never once spoken to him except to point at the quiet sign. She looked at the drawing, then at the chair, then back. "You drew the light," she said.

"I drew the gaps," Luca said, which he understood, even as he said it, was the same thing, or near enough, or possibly not the same thing at all, and he decided he could live without deciding.

"Can I put it on the wall by the front?" she asked. "We rotate local student work. It stays yours, you get it back whenever."

He thought of his mother, of telling her tonight that it was done, actually done, done and hanging in a public building. He thought of the strange honesty of the method itself, that you could get at something true by drawing around it rather than at it, and he thought that his whole application essay, maybe his whole next year, might work like that, and then he thought that he might be wrong about all of it, that Friday might come and the portfolio reviewer might want chairs drawn the ordinary way.

"Okay," he said. "Yes."

Mrs. Okafor lifted the sketchbook page with both hands, careful of the corners, and carried it toward the front desk, where the afternoon light came through the tall windows and lay down across the carpet in long, exact shapes.

Justine had written her grandfather's name on the first cup of juice and her own on the second, and now she stood in Aunt Carol's kitchen holding the two cups like evidence in a case she hadn't meant to open. For eleven years Grandpa had led the Seder from the head of the table, and nobody had said out loud that this year would be different, but this year would be different, because he was in the sunroom with a blanket over his legs, dozing before the soup even came out, and her mother had said, quietly, last Tuesday, "You know it. You've watched him your whole life. Just do what he does."

The Haggadahs were stacked by the door, the same battered stack as always, and Justine counted them twice because counting things was what she did when she was about to be responsible for things. At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Her brother Theo was seven now and had been practicing for three weeks, whispering the first question to himself in the bathtub, in the car, once to a cashier at the grocery store who had given him a sticker for it. But Theo got nervous. Theo froze. And when Theo froze, he cried, and when Theo cried, the whole table tilted toward him, and Justine knew, with the certainty of someone who had been an older sibling for seven years, that her first Seder as leader could collapse in the first ten minutes if she didn't plan for it.

"You could just ask them yourself," said her cousin Maya, leaning against the counter, stealing an olive. "You're leading. Nobody would stop you."

"That's not how it works," Justine said. "It's his job. He's the youngest who can."

"So coach him. You're the coach now, apparently. Coach." Maya said the word like it was slightly ridiculous, and it was, and Justine took the olive jar away from her anyway.

The problem was that coaching and leading were two different shapes of attention, and she couldn't be in both at once. If she sat next to Theo and prompted him through the questions, she wasn't at the head of the table holding the order of things together. If she sat at the head, she could see Theo's face going pale from across the room and could do nothing about it. She thought about it while setting the table, while hiding the afikoman under the good napkins, while her mother said, "You're being very quiet," in a tone Justine declined to answer. She was not going to solve it by agonizing. Her grandfather had never agonized; he had improvised. Once, when the candles wouldn't light, he'd declared, "We remember them lit," and everyone had laughed and moved on. Arbitration, that was what he did all night, small rulings on who poured and who read and when the food came, and nobody had ever called it that, but Justine understood suddenly that leadership at this table was mostly just deciding things before anyone had to argue.

So she made a ruling of her own. She put Theo's chair not beside hers but at an angle, close to the head, close enough that she could reach his shoulder without standing up. Then she found him in the hallway, hiding in his dress shirt.

"Here's the plan," she said. "You ask. If you get stuck, I ask the first word of the next line, and you take it from there. Nobody will even notice."

"What if I cry?"

"Then you cry and keep asking. Grandpa mixed up the plagues two years running and nobody fired him."

Theo considered this. "Nobody can fire you if you're grandpa."

"Exactly," Justine said, though this was not exactly what she meant.

Dinner began badly, which is to say it began the way family dinners begin, with her uncle declaring the gefilte fish an abomination and Aunt Carol calling him a philistine and both of them enjoying it thoroughly. When Justine raised her cup for kiddush her voice came out smaller than she'd rehearsed, and she had to start the blessing again, and her ears burned, but the second time was steady, and her grandfather opened one eye from the sunroom doorway and said, "Louder, they're all deaf," which was untrue and helpful.

Then it was time. Theo stood up. His hands found the hem of his shirt. "Why is this night," he said, and stopped, and the table went still in the way tables do when everyone is pretending not to watch. Justine leaned toward him and said only, "different." "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Theo finished, and then the rest came out of him in a rush, all four questions, dipping and reclining and bitter herbs, barely stopping to breathe, and when he sat down he was grinning so hard he looked like he might tip over sideways. Maya raised her glass to Justine from across the table. Justine noticed, at that exact moment, that she had skipped a paragraph in the order of the service, and decided, in the spirit of her grandfather, to fold it in later without announcing the error. She had gained the table and lost the certainty of doing it right, and both of those things were true at once.

Later, after the meal, after her uncle's third monologue about a neighbor whose spending habits he described as profligate, after Theo found the afikoman and held it for ransom with terrifying confidence, Justine went out to the sunroom with a plate of macaroons. Her grandfather was awake, watching through the doorway as she broke the matzah and distributed it.

"You missed the part with the rabbis in Bnei Brak," he said.

"I put it after the meal. Nobody noticed."

"Everybody noticed," he said. "Nobody minded." He took a macaroon and ate it slowly. "Next year, do the rabbis earlier."

"Next year?"

"Next year," he said, and closed his eyes again, and Justine sat beside him and let the evening go on without her for a while.

Kyle had told himself, more than once on the walk from the hardware store, that the chair was entirely for his own satisfaction, and by the third telling it had become almost true. It was a folding lawn chair salvaged from behind the garage, its frame sound but its canvas gone to mold, and he intended to replace the canvas himself and paint it before his sister left for the airport on Sunday. He had four days. He had never painted anything that mattered.

He set up in the backyard because his mother's kitchen was still being repainted by professionals, a fact his father had lambasted at dinner for two nights running, calling it money spent on walls that nobody looked at. Kyle had agreed out loud and disagreed quietly, which had lately become his standard arrangement with his father, and which he did not intend to examine too closely.

The new canvas stretched and laced onto the frame well enough, but the painting went wrong almost immediately. He had bought five tubes of paint on impulse at the store, reasoning that more colors meant more choices, and now he sat cross-legged in the grass with them lined up like evidence against him. The blue and the red he had laid down in wide bands curdled against each other, vibrating in a way that made his jaw tighten. It looked petulant, the whole thing, like a tantrum in pigment. He had wanted something steadier for Nadia, something that said he had thought of her, and instead he had produced stripes that fought.

He scraped the worst of it off with a palette knife and went inside to his phone, telling himself he would look for ten minutes. His search for why red and blue hurt each other led him somewhere he did not expect. A physics man, of all people, had something to do with it. Kyle read the page twice, then a third time, because the date seemed too precise to be real.

"Newton," he said aloud to the empty kitchen. "In 1704. In a book called Opticks." He carried the phone back out to the grass and set it face up on the patio stone beside his brushes. Isaac Newton, who had thought about gravity and light, had arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle, and that circle was an early version of the color wheel artists used today. Kyle sat with that for a while, turning his brushes over. He had assumed the wheel belonged to painters, that some seventeenth-century craftsman had mixed his way to it by feel. Instead a physicist had bent the rainbow into a ring, and painters had inherited the geometry of it.

The wheel told him about opposites. He found a version online, turned it until the red he had used faced its opposite across the circle, and understood that the pair was useful to him for exactly the reason it had wrecked him: the two pushed against each other. So he stopped trying to make the red and blue sit side by side and gave each of them a thin border of the other's opposite, a margin of green around the red, a whisper of orange under the blue, and the bands stopped fighting. They held their ground like neighbors who had finally agreed on a fence.

He worked until the light went long and the sprinklers two yards over came on with their tin hiss. His father came out with a beer and stood at the edge of the patio, saying nothing for the length of a full minute, which Kyle had learned was how the man approached anything handmade.

"Your mother says you learned that circle thing from a scientist," his father said.

"From Newton," Kyle said. "1704. It's in Opticks." He did not add that he had chosen the whole scheme to be calm, or that the calm was for Nadia, or that some part of him had angled the chair on the lawn so it would be visible from the patio. His father drained a third of the beer and looked at the canvas, and the silence stretched, and Kyle noticed that he was holding his breath in a way that had nothing to do with paint.

It was not, he had to admit, a matter of doing it only for himself. He wanted it liked, and he wanted to seem indifferent to whether it was liked, and he could not fully have both. What he could have was the chair, which by dusk was dry enough to touch, its bands lying flat and settled against each other, a consonance he could not have named before this week and which he now saw everywhere he looked: in the fence slats against the grass, in the orange porch light against the coming dark. He folded the chair and carried it toward the garage, and behind him his father said, "Huh," which was not praise and was not nothing, and Kyle kept walking and let it be whichever it was.

Laurence had the ballot spread on the desk beside the keyboard, the paper as long as her forearm, and she was going down the list of judges with three tabs open, because she refused to vote for someone just because their name sounded competent. She was eighteen as of the ninth of this month, which still startled her when she wrote it on forms. Her mother kept passing the doorway with laundry, slowing down each time as if Laurence were performing surgery.

"Grandpa's coming by at four," her mother said on the fourth pass. "He'll want to see that you voted. Try to look excited, or at least awake."

"I'm not excited. I'm reading about a drainage district commissioner." Laurence turned the laptop so her mother could see the candidate's page, a wall of text in a font from another decade. "This guy has been in office since before I was born and his whole statement is two sentences about fiscal responsibility. That's it. That's all he's telling the voters."

Her mother set down the towel she'd been folding. "Then vote for the other one, or don't vote for that one at all. Nobody will arrest you."

"That's not the point." Laurence pulled the laptop back. "If I skip it, I'm letting everyone else decide, and if I vote on nothing, I'm just making noise. I want it to mean something, and I can't tell if it does." She said the last part more quietly than she meant to.

When her grandfather arrived he came in carrying a paper bag of oranges from the tree he babied through every frost, and he put two of them on the desk next to the ballot without comment, which was his way of noticing that she hadn't eaten lunch. He read over her shoulder for a while, hands behind his back, while she clicked between a county measure and an editorial about it.

"Does it matter?" she asked him finally, spinning her chair. "One vote. Everyone says it doesn't."

He picked up an orange and started peeling it in one long spiral, the way he did everything, slowly and without waste. "You know why you get to do this at eighteen?"

"Because of the Constitution. Amendment something."

"Twenty-sixth," he said. "But the push for it had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Eighteen-year-olds could be drafted for Vietnam, and people said that if you can be drafted, you should get the ballot." He handed her half the orange and sat on the edge of the bed, leaving the rest of it there, not elaborating, which for him was a kind of discipline.

Laurence ate the orange and thought about her grandfather at eighteen, about which of those two things he would rather have been given. She opened a new tab and typed the slogan in, and the results were all there, the marches, the buttons with the words printed in a circle, senators quoted saying exactly that. She read for ten minutes with the peel smell still on her fingers. "So people my age were handed a rifle first," she said, "and the vote was the consolation prize. Or the apology."

"Something like that," her grandfather said. "Depends who you ask."

She looked at the ballot again. The framing helped and it also didn't; the vote wasn't a promise that anything would go her way, and she understood that the slogan was a kind of synecdoche, the draft standing in for every way the country could use you before it let you speak. That didn't make her one ballot weigh more. If anything it made the whole thing feel smaller, a modest, parsimonious little power doled out exactly as far as it had to go and no further, circumscribed on every side by districts and electoral math and commissioners running unopposed since the nineties. And still people had marched for exactly this, this thin slice, because it was what was on offer.

"Okay," she said. She pulled the ballot closer and filled in the drainage race for the challenger, who had at least written a paragraph, and left one judicial race blank where both candidates had given her nothing at all. "I'm not voting in that one. I couldn't tell you why either of them wants the job."

"That's allowed," her grandfather said. "Blank is a answer too."

Her mother appeared in the doorway again, empty-handed this time, and Laurence signed the envelope, licked it, and held the sealed ballot up between two fingers like evidence.

"One vote," she said. "Old enough to fight."

The municipal pool had the smell of every pool Savannah had ever swum in, chlorine and hot rubber, and a record board so old its letters had the authority of antiquity, times posted by girls who now had children of their own. She read it while waiting for dryland to start, because reading it was easier than looking at Rosa, who had been named putative captain by a vote so close the coach refused to announce the number.

Dryland that Thursday was not dry. Coach Okafor had dragged a battle rope and a thick tow line onto the deck, and after the usual squats he split the team in two and pointed at the deep end gutter, where he had looped the rope through a stainless rail. "Tug of war," he said. "Winners choose the lane order for the relay on Saturday." A cheer went up, thin, because everyone was sore from Tuesday, and Marisol asked whether falling in counted as a forfeit, and he said only for her, which made even Rosa laugh.

Savannah's team lost the first pull in about eleven seconds. She had braced her heels, gripped until her palms burned, and felt, through the rope, a strange softness, as though the other four were holding back a little, saving something, or simply trusting that someone else would take the load. When they regrouped, dripping, Coach Okafor was squinting at them all with the expression of a man doing arithmetic in his head.

"Okay," he said. "New experiment. One at a time. Grip here, pull as hard as you can against the spring scale I clipped to the rail." He held up a rusted spring scale, the kind from a physics classroom, and it turned out the high school would lend anything to anyone who signed a form. Savannah went last. Alone, straining backward against the dial, she watched the needle swing further than it had for anyone else, and she heard Rosa, behind her, say "huh" in a small voice.

The numbers went up on the whiteboard in dripping marker, and then Coach Okafor added a second column, the totals from the group pull divided by five, and the whole deck went quiet in the way a classroom does when something embarrassing becomes visible. Every girl's group number was smaller than her solo number. Every one. "Look at that," Marisol said. "We're a scam." And Savannah, thinking of her psychology textbook, which she read at night the way other people read mysteries, remembered a page she had almost skimmed: a French engineer, Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had people pull a rope and found that each person in a group pulled less hard than the same person pulled alone. She had assumed it was about lazy factory workers in mustaches. It was about her. She said it out loud, carefully, giving the engineer his due.

From where Rosa stood, toweling her hair, the interesting thing was not the scale. It was Savannah's face while she recited the fact, the way she recited everything, like handing over evidence at a trial. Rosa had voted for herself for captain, obviously, and had won or lost by some number nobody would say, and for two weeks she had been waiting to find out what kind of person Savannah actually was. A person who pulled hardest alone, that much was certain now. What Rosa wanted to know was whether such a person could want anything that required other people.

"Okay," Coach Okafor said, "so science says you're all slightly useless together. Excellent. Same teams, pull again, and this time I want you calling your own name when you feel yourself easing off." This was the part he could not abrogate, the ancient rule of Thursday dryland that any drill ending in failure must be repeated until it ended in laughter, and he enforced it with the patience of a man who had run this team for nineteen years.

The second pull lasted a full minute. Savannah called her own name twice, hoarse and ridiculous, and heard Rosa call hers three times, and Marisol once, followed immediately by the slap of Marisol's feet skidding out from under her and the enormous ceremonial splash of a ninety-pound girl entering the deep end fully clothed in a team shirt. Everyone laughed, including Coach, including Marisol from the water, arms spread on the gutter like a woman reclining in a very cold bath. The rope went slack on both sides. Nobody had won. On the whiteboard, in the space for the second pull's totals, someone had drawn a wave.

Saturday, the relay went third. Savannah swam anchor, and when she dove in, trailing by half a body, she thought about the whiteboard and the number that had been smaller than her number, and about Rosa on the second leg lifting her head to call her own name into a silent natatorium, and she could not decide, even mid-stroke, whether the team had taught her to pull harder alone or whether pulling alone had taught her nothing the relay could use. She touched the wall. Somebody's hand was already there. When she pulled off her goggles, Rosa was hanging on the lane line beside her, breathing hard, saying, "Tell me the scale again. I want to write it on my mirror."

The march came through the floorboards before Peyton was fully awake, which meant her brother had gotten to the stereo first, which meant today was the day her mother had decided to make ceremonial. She lay in bed and listened to the trumpets loop around the same eight bars, the way they had looped every June of her life, and thought about how strange it was that a person could know a piece of music this well without knowing the first thing about it.

"Band practice at ten," her mother called up the stairs. "And your grandmother's coming to the ceremony, so wear the dress with the buttons."

Peyton had been avoiding the ceremony for weeks, quietly, the way you avoid a thing you can't actually escape. She had tried subterfuge. She had mentioned, at dinner, that plenty of people skipped graduation, that it was long and hot and the speeches were written for parents. She had left a college orientation brochure on the counter with the dates circled, though the orientation wasn't until August. Her mother had absorbed all of it without comment, the way a sea wall absorbs weather, and had gone on ironing.

At ten she was in the band room with her clarinet, running the march for the twelfth time that week, and it was there, counting rests, that the question finally calcified into something she couldn't ignore. "Why this song?" she said, during a water break. "Every school in the country. Every movie. Why do we all play this one?"

"Because it's tradition," said Marcus, who played baritone and considered tradition a sufficient answer to most questions.

"Traditions start somewhere." She was already typing with her thumb, one-handed, the way people did when a question had been sitting in them too long.

What she found was this: the march had become graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music. She read it twice, then held the phone out so Marcus could see. "Yale. 1905. They gave the composer a doctorate and played his march, and somehow that turned into every cap and gown on earth."

"Creepy," Marcus said, meaning interesting.

"It's not creepy, it's..." She looked for the word and didn't find it. "One school did it once, and now my grandmother is wearing a corsage because of it."

Her grandmother arrived that afternoon, early, while Peyton was still in her robe, and installed herself at the kitchen table with the tea her mother made without being asked. Peyton sat down across from her, mostly because leaving would have required an excuse she didn't have. Her grandmother had grown more ascetic over the years, having given up television, then sugar, then most of her opinions, or at least the sharing of them, so that a visit now felt like sitting with a very calm question.

"I hear you'd rather not walk," her grandmother said.

Peyton examined her tea. "It's a show we put on for other people. I don't need two hours of my name not being called to know I finished."

"You don't," her grandmother agreed, which disarmed her completely. "I skipped mine. 1968. I stood outside in the parking lot in my gown because it was June in Ohio and the gym had no air, and I listened to that same march through the doors." She turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "I remember the music more than I remember deciding anything about it."

Peyton had assumed the argument would be about pride, or photographs, or things her mother could frame. This was something else, and she sat with it while her grandmother drank her tea. There was a version of herself, the one who had tried the brochures and the dinner remarks, that wanted to treat the whole ceremony as an inherited reflex, a thing people did because Yale had done it in 1905 and nobody had thought to stop. But her grandmother standing in an Ohio parking lot in a rented gown, listening through gym doors, was not a reflex. That was a person choosing to be near a thing, even at the edge of it, and Peyton could not make the two ideas sit still together. Maybe the ritual was arbitrary and it meant something anyway. Maybe it meant something because it was arbitrary, because everyone had agreed to it, the way people agreed to a language.

"I'll walk," she said. Her grandmother nodded once, as though Peyton had reported the weather, and asked for more hot water.

At the ceremony the next evening, the band filed in first, and Peyton took her seat in the clarinet section with a good view of the whole procession. When the trumpets came in, she watched her grandmother in the fourth row, leaning slightly forward, doing the same thing she had done in a parking lot in 1968, and Peyton understood that she herself was now part of the reason, the small link that kept the thing running from 1905 to a folding chair in a gym in June. She would not have said that out loud. She wasn't even sure it was true, exactly, and she held onto the uncertainty on purpose, the way she held the clarinet, lightly, at the ready.

She lifted the reed to her lips and came in on the downbeat, half a beat late, and played.

The letter from the tenant arrived on a Tuesday, and Sebastian's grandfather read it twice at the kitchen table before setting it under the sugar bowl as though to weigh it down. "Mr. Okafor wants his deposit back," he said. "All six hundred of it."

Sebastian had come to the house for the last week of summer, planning mostly to eat his grandmother's cooking and avoid thinking about the fall. Instead he found himself in the passenger seat of the Buick the next morning, riding across town to the little yellow duplex his grandparents had bought decades ago, back when the mortgage on it had seemed to his grandfather like a rope around the neck. "Thirty years we paid," he said at a red light. "Every month. And the bank held the deed until the end, like a hostage." Sebastian had known, in a vague way, that houses were paid for over time, but he had never pictured his grandfather at twenty-five, signing papers at a bank, putting down what he called "the down payment, the part you have to have up front or they won't talk to you at all."

The tenant, Mr. Okafor, met them on the porch. He was maybe thirty, with a moving truck half loaded behind him in the drive, and he wanted, plainly, his money. "I left that place better than I found it," he said. "I painted the kitchen myself. Paid for the paint out of my own pocket."

Inside, the apartment smelled of cardboard and lemon cleaner. Sebastian's grandfather walked the hallway with his hands behind his back, the way he walked his own garden, and stopped at the living room wall where a row of small nail holes marched along the picture rail like a constellation. "There," he said. "Holes in the wall. That's damage. That comes out of the deposit, that's what a deposit is for."

"No," Sebastian said, and both men turned to look at him, and he felt his face go hot, because he had not planned to say anything. But he had spent the previous night at the kitchen table with his grandmother's ancient laptop, wading through an interminable stretch of tenant-rights pages, some written in a lawyerly dialect that assumed an erudition he did not have, until he found one written in plain sentences and read it three times. "The deposit covers unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear," he said. "Small nail holes are ordinary aging. Where we live, a landlord can't deduct for that."

His grandfather's mouth worked for a moment without sound. "It's my wall," he said finally.

"It's ordinary aging," Sebastian said. "It's on the state website. I took screenshots." He had also done something else, and this was harder to bring up. "Grandpa, I photographed every wall yesterday when we came to measure for the new blinds. Every room, every ceiling corner. Because if Mr. Okafor wants to argue later, you'll want proof of the condition, and so will he."

Mr. Okafor had gone quiet at the mention of the website, and now he cleared his throat. "There's something else," he said. "The back bedroom. There was a leak from the bathroom above it, back in March. I told you about it on the phone." Sebastian's grandfather said that he remembered, and that he had called a plumber. "The plumber patched the pipe," Mr. Okafor said. "The ceiling stain stayed. I didn't cause it, but I didn't fix it either, because it's your building. I figured it would come out of the deposit fight, so I want to say now, before you decide: that stain is mine to live with and yours to fix, and neither of us should pay the other for it."

Here was the twist, and Sebastian watched it happen slowly, like weather changing. His grandfather walked to the back bedroom and stood under the brownish ring on the ceiling for a long time. "That's water damage," he said. "Not from you." He turned around. "I was going to take the six hundred dollars and repaint the whole unit. I had it figured that way. New tenant in September, new paint, and the deposit pays for it."

"Paint wears out," Sebastian said quietly. "Like nail holes."

His grandfather looked at the ceiling, then at the boy, then at the man who had rented his rooms for four years and had never once been late with the rent, and something in his shoulders came down an inch. "The kitchen paint you bought yourself," he said. "What did that cost you?" Mr. Okafor said about eighty dollars. His grandfather took out his checkbook, the old leather kind with a pen loop, and leaned on the windowsill to write. "Six hundred for the deposit," he said, "and eighty for the paint. And you'll indemnify me for nothing, because there's nothing to indemnify. It's just a wall."

Driving home, the windows down, his grandfather was silent for most of the highway. Near the exit he said, "Your grandmother told me you stayed up past one reading that website." Sebastian said that he had. "Good," his grandfather said. "When you get your own place someday, save for the down payment first, then the deposit, and photograph everything, both times, moving in and moving out." He pulled into the driveway and shut off the engine. "Now come inside. She made the plum cake, and she will not cut it without us."

Michael had chosen the cello at the start of term because it looked dignified, but the only instrument left in the storeroom that Friday was a violin with a fine layer of chalk dust along its ribs, so he took it. The music room smelled of rosin and the custodian's lemon floor polish, and the radiators clanked like a stubborn percussion section. Ms. Oyelaran, who ran the after-school ensemble and never wasted words, handed him the bow and said, "Four strings. Everything starts there."

He plucked them that first afternoon, one after another, and they gave back G, D, A, E, lowest to highest, though at the time he only heard four different voices arguing. In the practice rooms along the corridor, other people's scales leaked through the walls, and he wondered whether the intervals between those strings were chosen for a reason, or whether somebody, centuries ago, had simply liked the way they climbed. He had a habit of asking questions like that, and his older sister had once told him he could pontificate about a doorknob. He had looked up the word afterwards, then used it back at her, which she found less amusing than he had hoped.

The ensemble met Tuesdays after last bell, and beside him sat Priya Raman, a tiny pugnacious first-year who had been playing violin since she was six and had opinions about everyone else's posture. Across the stands was Colm, who read music the way other people read street signs, without apparent effort, and who had cornered Michael once at the water fountain to declare that a pianist named Ólafur something-or-other was "the whole zeitgeist now, honestly, the spirit of the age, if you even know what that means." Michael had said he didn't, and Colm had nodded, satisfied, as though this proved something.

The concrete problem arrived in November, three days before the winter showcase, when the second violinist in their quartet broke her wrist on the ice behind the gym. Ms. Oyelaran put a photocopy of the second violin part on Michael's stand and said only, "You know the fingerings. Learn the thinking." Priya leaned over during the break, tapping the four strings with her pencil, one, two, three, four, and recited, like a spell she'd been given long ago by her first teacher: "Good Dogs Always Eat." She pointed from the thickest string upward as she said it. Then she went back to arguing with Colm about tempo, leaving Michael to work out for himself that the letters in her sentence were the names of the strings, that G sat lowest, that E sang highest, and that they were spaced, she mentioned later while packing her case, in perfect fifths, each string to the next.

That night he wrote to his sister at college, because she was the only person he could admit things to. "I got promoted out of desperation, not talent," the letter said. "The second violin part is all inner voices, the plumbing of the piece. Nobody hears you unless you vanish, and then they notice the silence. Also I learned the strings are G, D, A and E, lowest to highest, each a fifth apart, and there's a sentence for it, Good Dogs Always Eat, and I keep saying it in my head like a prayer before every entrance. Is it cheating to use a sentence instead of just knowing? Is that how knowing starts?" He sealed it before he could edit himself into sounding less lost.

The showcase was in the gym, under banners from a fundraiser nobody remembered, and the folding chairs filled with parents holding phones like candles. Colm's opening phrase was clean and a little cold. Priya played with her chin up, daring the audience. Michael came in late on his first entrance, half a beat, and nobody died. On his second entrance he was early, and the chord that resulted was sweeter than the one written, which confused him so much he lost his place for two bars and found it again by feel, by the hum of the G string under his knuckle.

Afterwards, Priya's father took a photograph of the quartet, and Ms. Oyelaran shook each of their hands as though conferring knighthoods. In the coat queue, Priya said, "You dragged on that third phrase. Deliberately?" Michael said maybe, that it had sounded like it wanted to linger, though he couldn't say whether the wanting was his or the music's. Priya considered this the way she considered Colm's tempo arguments, then shrugged and said it had worked. He watched Colm's mother mouth something at Colm across the hall, and Colm, grinning, raised his violin case in answer.

He walked home with the case knocking his hip, saying Good Dogs Always Eat to the frosty street, wondering whether every hard thing began as somebody else's sentence that you slowly earned the right to mean. At his corner he stopped, lifted the case, and unlatched it under the streetlight, just to look at the four strings lying in their perfect ladder. He plucked the E, thin and bright against the cold.

Kayla arrived early to philosophy on Tuesday because she wanted the desk by the window, the one where you could hear the radiator ticking and feel slightly outside the room. Mr. Osei had written two words on the board before anyone else came in: unintended consequences. She copied them into her notebook and then, feeling dishonest, underlined them twice.

The problem she carried in with her was a family one, small and specific. Her mother had agreed, over lasagna on Sunday, to pay Kayla's younger brother Devon five dollars per chore, and Devon had gone radiant and cooperative for exactly two days. Kayla had proposed the scheme herself, at the dinner table, as a fair system, fairness being a thing she could defend with arguments. Her mother had set down her fork and said, "In 1902, the French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew." Then she had gone back to her lasagna as though she had said nothing at all. Kayla had spent the night since then being quietly furious, because the story implied she was the kind of person who creates more rats, and because she suspected it might be true.

"Incentives," Mr. Osei said now, walking between the desks. "We reward a behavior and we expect more of it. But what we reward and what we want are not always the same thing. So today, a proposal." He handed a sheet to each row. "The school is considering a new attendance policy. Any student with perfect attendance this term receives a fifty-dollar credit at the campus store. You will argue it in teams, then we will vote."

Kayla's team drew Marcus, who talked like he was being timed, and Priya, who said almost nothing until she had decided something was wrong. They were assigned to defend the policy, which Kayla found convenient and then, on reflection, uncomfortable, because she did believe kids should come to school, and being paid to believe it felt like a corruption she couldn't locate precisely.

"Kids skip because home is bad or school is bad," Priya said, when Marcus had finished a paragraph about responsibility and personal accountability. "Fifty dollars doesn't fix either."

"Nobody's saying it fixes it," Marcus said. "It's a trade-off. We accept imperfect outcomes all the time. Every policy trades something away."

Kayla wrote trade-off in her notebook, next to unintended consequences, and disliked how tidy they looked side by side. She remembered Devon that morning, sweeping the kitchen in a way that moved crumbs from one zone to another so that the counter, his counter, gleamed and the floor got worse. Four days into the system, the chore chart showed a boy in strict compliance with a house that was dirtier than when they started.
