She had not told her mother, partly because tattling was beneath her and partly because she was still working out whether the dirtier house was Kayla's fault or the system's, and whether that distinction even held.

The debate itself was brief and lopsided. Marcus was fluent and even the opposing team conceded that attendance would probably rise. Mr. Osei called the vote, and it passed easily, and then he said, "One more thing. Beginning Monday, any student who misses a class, excused or unexcused, forfeits the credit." He collected the sheets. "Same policy. One sentence added. Argue with me about it tomorrow."

Walking out, Priya caught Kayla's sleeve at the door. "The sick kids," she said. "The ones who stay home with a fever so they don't infect everyone. The policy maligns them for doing the right thing." Kayla heard her own voice say "exactly" before she had finished thinking it. She pictured the flu moving through the junior class in November, each infected student a small monument to perfect attendance, the credit converting a virtue into an incentive and the incentive back into a harm nobody had voted for.

That night she found Devon on the living room floor, cutting a chore chart out of construction paper, a second chart, subdividing each chore into parts. Dishes would now count as dishes-wash, dishes-dry, and dishes-put-away. He looked up at her with the serene rectitude of a boy who had found the letter of the law and intended to live inside it. "Three chores a night," he said. "Fifteen dollars."

She sat down across from him on the carpet. She had planned to explain the rats again, the way her mother hadn't, and she had a speech half-built about consequences that spread past the moment you stop watching. Instead she said, "What if Mom pays for the week being done, not for each chore? One price. The whole kitchen."

Devon considered it with the gravity of a person renegotiating a treaty. "Then I'd have to do the floor too," he said slowly.

"Right. The floor too." She didn't say that her new system would have its own tail-clipping, some corner she couldn't see yet, some kid at school dragging herself in contagious because fifty dollars mattered more than a fever, and no board, no mother, no sister designing the rules from inside them. She only knew the difference between trying to control an outcome and pretending she could see all of them.

"Fine," Devon said. "But I want it in writing." He slid the construction paper across the carpet toward her, scissors still in his hand.

The printer at the back of the Fairview Public Library took quarters, which Ryan had, and gave instructions, which he ignored. He had twenty minutes before the climate club meeting and one design, a drawing of a drowned street sign he had inked at two in the morning, and a plan he described to himself as "figure it out at the machine." The library enfranchised anybody with sixty cents into the whole world of publishing; that was how he thought of it, anyway, since the art room at school now required a permission slip for the paper cutter.

He had quit art class in March. Not dramatically, in the way he sometimes rehearsed quitting things, but by simply not turning in the self-portrait, and then not turning in the apology for the self-portrait, and then letting the weeks accumulate like silt until Ms. Okafor stopped asking. The portrait had been honest, which was the problem. It showed his face the way he actually suspected it looked to other people, and the class had gone quiet in the wrong way. His mother said he'd traded one kind of honesty for a cheaper one. He was still deciding whether that was fair.

The poster was, in his private taxonomy, the first thing he'd drawn since. Flyers were their own phylum of object, halfway between litter and art, and he wanted this one to be art that was not afraid to become litter. He fed a sheet of A3 into the tray and pressed the button for 100 percent, because scaling felt like a negotiation he wasn't qualified for.

The sheet came out with the drowned street sign floating in too much white. Behind him, a kid of about eleven watched over his shoulder with the frank entitlement of someone who intended to comment.

"It's too small," the kid said.

"It's A3."

"What's A3?"

"Big paper," Ryan said, and immediately felt the answer was beneath both of them.

He tried again at a larger percentage, but when he asked the machine for A4, something happened that he stood looking at for longer than he would admit. The shrunken printout was the same drawing, and the shape of the page was the same shape. He held the A4 up against the A3 against the window, where the late light lay alluvial across the tables, and the edges lined up corner to corner, the big page exactly a doubled version of the small one. He cut the A3 in half with the blunt library scissors, and the two halves were A4, and each half matched the printout's proportions exactly.

"Those are ISO 216 sizes," the kid said, with the air of someone reciting something off a cereal box. "The sides are one to the square root of two. Cut it in half, you get the same shape again."

Ryan looked at him. "How do you know that?"

"My dad's an engineer. He cries at paper."

What the kid's father apparently wept over, Ryan now tested: he printed the poster at A4, and it matched the half of the A3 perfectly, and the half of the half, an A5 he cut with growing confidence, matched again. One drawing, descending through sizes like a set of nested spoons. The small versions were not degraded copies. They were the poster, fully themselves, asking nothing of the big one. He thought, without wanting to, of the self-portrait, which had existed at exactly one size, in exactly one room, in front of exactly one audience, and had died there.

The club's co-president, Dara, arrived with a USB drive and an agenda. She wanted forty flyers by Saturday and had assumed they'd photocopy his design "whatever size, whatever, people will get it." Ryan laid his cut sheets in a row on the table, A3 to A5, and said the design would hold at any size, that a flyer could be folded into a smaller flyer and still be true, and Dara said, "Ryan, it's a street sign, not a manifesto," which was fair.

Then came the part he hadn't planned. Ms. Okafor was at the next table, returned books stacked beside her, and she had been watching the row of diminishing pages for some time. She didn't say anything about March or the portrait. She picked up the A5, held it at arm's length, and said, "This one. Print this one forty times."

"The small one?"

"The small one," she said, and put on her reading glasses. "It looks like you finally stopped apologizing for the size of things."

He didn't know if that was true, or if a drawing could apologize, or whether quitting in March had been cowardice or just a kind of waiting. What he knew was that the machine took quarters and he had four, and that the kid was still there, and that some truths could be cut in half forever without changing shape.

He fed the tray and pressed the button.

The departures board flickered above Gate 14, and Lucas opened his laptop on the seat beside him because the middle seat was empty and might stay that way. His flight to his grandmother's was delayed two hours, which his mother had predicted, and which he had refused to believe until the word DELAYED appeared in amber letters where his departure time used to be. He had a chemistry test to study for and a presentation to finish, and only one of them was due tomorrow, by video, from wherever he happened to be.

The presentation was for his civics class. They were role-playing a town meeting about a proposal to build new housing on a piece of land near the river, and Lucas had been assigned the role of the county's floodplain analyst, which meant he had to sound like somebody who knew things. He did not entirely know things. He had spent three evenings in a geographic information system his teacher had set up, dragging a flood risk layer over a housing layer until the neighborhood he'd grown up in turned blue in some blocks and stayed ordinary gray in others. The overlay was beautiful in a way that unsettled him. His aunt's street was blue.

He had written a draft with the number of houses in the flood zone, forty-one, and he had been almost satisfied with it until he read the assignment sheet again in the airport's harsh light. The mock town council, it said, would ask about residents, not just structures. He stared at the sentence. A council member, playing an obstreperous retired engineer named Mr. Vasquez, was instructed to ask how many people lived in the flood zone, and Lucas's draft answered with houses, which was not the same question and might even be a way of dodging it.

He opened the map and clicked on one blue polygon, a building near the water. A table appeared at the bottom of the screen, and the row that came up had columns: an ID number, a flood classification, a count of residents. He clicked another building and another row rose into the table. So that was how it worked. Each feature in the layer linked to a row in an attribute table, which meant the data attached to buildings, things like the number of residents in each one, could be totaled if he selected an area. He highlighted the whole flood zone, all forty-one polygons, and the table showed him the sum.

Six hundred and twelve people.

He sat with that. Forty-one had felt like a statistic. Six hundred and twelve felt like the gym at his old middle school, which held about that many and looked enormous when it emptied out at the end of an assembly. He texted his aunt, because she actually lived on one of the blue blocks and because she answered faster than anyone he knew.

"Doing my town meeting thing. Did you know there are 612 people in the flood zone by the river?"

Her reply came while the gate agent was announcing something about rebooking. "Who counted us?" she wrote. "Tell whoever it is that the number doesn't include my neighbor's mother, who is in the basement apartment and half the time doesn't answer the door. Also it doesn't include the people who will live in whatever they build. Bring me a coffee when you land."

Lucas read the message twice. She was doing what she always did, taking his clean number and putting a crack in it. The map said six hundred and twelve, and the map was built from data somebody had collected, and data had edges. His aunt's neighbor's mother might be counted or might not. The new residents, if the housing was built, would not be in the table at all yet. He revised his script: he would give the total, and then he would say what the total could not tell them.

He worked until his eyes burned, then bought a sandwich he couldn't really metabolize quickly enough to feel less hungry, and read half a page of enthalpy diagrams for the chemistry test without retaining anything except the shape of the curves. When he boarded at last, the middle seat had been taken by a man who fell asleep before the safety demonstration, and Lucas typed the final lines of his script into his phone with his thumbs.

At the virtual meeting the next afternoon, from his grandmother's kitchen table, Mr. Vasquez performed his role perfectly, arms crossed over a blazer. "Houses, shouses," the boy playing him said. "How many people live in that flood zone, analyst?" Lucas let the pause last one breath, the way he'd practiced.

"Six hundred and twelve," he said. "Each building in the layer links to a row in an attribute table, so I could total the resident counts for the whole selected area. That's six hundred and twelve people today. What I can't tell you is who's missing from that count, or who'd be added if we build." Mr. Vasquez uncrossed his arms. Somewhere behind him, his grandmother's screen door banged, and she called from the porch, "Lucas, honey, come look at this rain."

Dominic stood at the counter with his grandfather's Bible open beside a cutting board, the way other people might set a phone next to their dinner. His mother had told him that if he was going to argue with Grandpa Joe about Friday meat, he should at least know what he was arguing from. The lasagna in the oven was the meatless kind, spinach and ricotta, and the smell of it filled the kitchen like an argument already conceded.

"You're doing homework on us now," Grandpa Joe said from the doorway. He set a paper bag on the table. Inside it, Dominic knew, was a pound of ground beef, bought on purpose, a test.

"It's for Mr. Ruiz's class," Dominic said. "We have to debate whether an old religious rule still applies. Using the text itself. Not just feelings about it." He watched his grandfather take down the good knife. "I picked Friday abstinence."

Grandpa Joe began slicing an onion with the patience of a man who had done it fifty years. "You picked a fight, you mean. The McAfees eat burgers on Fridays and sit three pews ahead of us. You want to know if I think they're wrong."

"I want to know why we don't. That's different." Dominic turned the Bible toward him. "The text isn't the problem, Grandpa. It says nothing about beef. It says fasting and abstinence, and it says obey the Church. That's the whole thing."

His grandfather put the knife down. "You finished already? At eighteen?"

Dominic had done research that afternoon, and he was almost afraid to use it. "I found something. Nineteen sixty-six. Pope Paul the Sixth. Paenitemini." He said the word carefully, the way Mr. Ruiz had taught them to say anything in Latin they weren't sure of. "It let the bishops' conferences, the national ones, replace the traditional fast and abstinence with other penance. Prayer. Works of charity. Stuff like that. So it's not that the McAfeys are cheating. It's that somebody changed the rule, and we kept it anyway."

The onion lay in pale rings on the board. Grandpa Joe wiped his hands on the dish towel and did not pick the knife back up. "Who told you that?"

"The Vatican website. Sort of. I had to piece it together." Dominic closed the Bible, then opened it again, because closing it felt like giving up an advantage. "So here's my problem. If the rule can be changed by the same authority that made it, then what makes our way better than theirs? We skip meat. They visit the hospital or whatever. The Church says both count."

"Both count," his grandfather agreed. He sat down at the table across from the beef, which sat there in its wax paper like a third participant. "So go be a McAfee."

The oven timer clicked. Dominic ignored it. "That's not an answer, that's a dare."

"It's an answer. You asked whether the rule still applies. The Church said pray instead, give instead. Fine. So the rule applies, and the shape of it changed." Grandpa Joe folded his arms. "But you want me to say the old shape was nothing. I won't."

Dominic took the lasagna out barehanded, then set it down too fast and sucked his thumb. While he ran it under the cold tap, he thought about Mr. Ruiz's warning that a debater who loved both sides would lose to a debater who loved one. "Here's what I think," he said finally. "The text itself lets the practice change. That's tenable, I can defend it from the documents. But it doesn't say the old practice was wrong, and it doesn't say the new one is equal for every person. Maybe the bishops gave us options because people are different, not because meat was never the point."

"Look at you," his grandfather said, but not unkindly. He stood and got two plates. "Your grandmother used to expatiate on this at dinner. Twenty minutes on sacrifice and hunger, and I'd fall asleep in my chair. You gave me the short version."

"There's a part I can't fix," Dominic said. "For the debate. The other side will ask why we keep the old way when we don't have to. I can say tradition has value. I can say the Friday hunger is a kind of recompense for a week of taking whatever we want. But I can't prove those from the text. They're ours, not its." He served his grandfather the first piece of lasagna. "So I'm going to stand up there and argue the rule still applies, and then admit the part I can't settle. Mr. Ruiz says that costs points."

Grandpa Joe ate one bite, then pushed the plate a few inches away, which for him was an eloquence. He took the pound of beef and put it in the refrigerator, on the bottom shelf, behind the milk where things went to wait for Saturday.

"Put the onion in the fridge," he said. "Half of it's still good."

"You didn't answer about the points."

"Tell your Mr. Ruiz," his grandfather said, "that some questions you lose on purpose."

The licensing office smelled of floor wax and paper, and the number ticket in Anais's hand read 47, which felt like a prophecy of waiting. She had turned eighteen three weeks ago, the last of her friends to do so, and the last to get a learner's permit by an even wider margin. Behind her in line, a boy with a lanyard flapping against his chest kept checking his phone, then checking it again, as though the screen might have changed the posted wait time out of pity.

"Forty-one," the clerk called, and a woman with a toddler on her hip shuffled forward. Anais settled into a plastic chair and read the laminated sign on the wall for the fourth time, mostly because there was nothing else to read. The sign laid out the steps: a learner's permit first, then, after holding it and passing a road test, a provisional license with restrictions, and only then, later, a full license. She had assumed, when she'd imagined this day, that there would be one permit and one test and then freedom. The sign was suggesting something more gradual, an idea she turned over the way she turned over most things her father said too quickly to be examined.

The boy sat down two chairs away. "You here for the road test?" he asked, hopeful, the way people ask in order to be asked back.

"Permit. I'm just starting." She said it plainly, without apology, which surprised her a little.

"Same," he said. "I got mine last month in the next county over. I'm here because we moved." He leaned closer, lowering his voice as if sharing stock tips. "Once I pass the road test next week, my friends and I are driving to the lake. All of us. Someone's got a truck."

Anais glanced back at the sign. "Does the permit thing end when you pass the test?" she asked. "It says here there's a middle step. A provisional license. It has restrictions on it before you get the full one."

He stood up to look, dragging his lanyard along her shoulder in a way that felt accidentally munificent, like being knighted by someone's keys. His face changed while he read. "Restrictions," he said, flatly. He read the line again, mouthing it, as if a second pass might make it say something friendlier. "So I can't just drive my friends around right away."

"Doesn't look like it." She felt the small, mean comfort of knowing something before someone else did, and then felt embarrassed for feeling it, because she had learned it from a sign four minutes ago. She was a neophyte in the exact sense of the word, and the word did not discriminate about how recently the ignorance had been cured.

"That's," he said, and stopped, gesturing at the sign as though it owed him a better verb.

"Forty-seven," the clerk called, and Anais went up to the counter, where a woman with reading glasses on a chain took her paperwork, had her sign a line, and told her to look at a small red dot for the vision check. "Passed," the woman said, with the enthusiasm of a person who said it two hundred times a day, and then: "Instructor's out front, white car. You're her three o'clock."

The white car was parked at the curb with STUDENT DRIVER signs suctioned to both doors, which Anais found both mortifying and weirdly protective, like a sign preempting every possible opinion the surrounding traffic might form about her. The instructor, a small woman named Dot with a clipboard and a thermos, had her adjust the mirror, then the seat, then the mirror again. "Tell me what you see," Dot said, and Anais told her: the curb, a mailbox, a man carrying a birthday cake flat across a parking lot like a pizza.

She pulled out of the space on her second attempt, and the car moved, and it was hers in the way borrowed things can be yours for an hour. At the first stop sign she braked too hard and both of them rocked forward. "Gentle," Dot said, sipping from the thermos without apparent concern for her own life. "You have time. Everything today is gradual." Anais laughed, surprising herself, because that was the second time today someone had told her that, and she was beginning to think the licensing office knew something the rest of the world was too polite to say. When they turned back toward the lot, the boy with the lanyard was standing at the curb, phone at his ear, holding up a hand as if to wave or to ask a question.

Anais rolled down the window, and he leaned in and said, "So how bad is it, out there?"

The clock above the whiteboard read 10:47, and Ava had promised herself she would not look at her phone until lunch. Mr. Ferris had left the classroom for the copy room, which meant thirty-two minutes of unsupervised study hall, which meant her application status sat one login away in her pocket like a stone. Around her, the AP Gov class she was technically auditing argued about a populist senator from Ohio, someone who had apparently promised to defund the very agency he'd once run. Her friend Deshawn kept calling him a genius of resentment. Her notebook was open to a page that said, in her own handwriting, nothing about any of it.

What it said instead was a list she'd made at two in the morning: reasons Wellesley, reasons State. Under reasons Wellesley she'd written small classes, the lake, the tour guide with the clogs. Under reasons State she'd written money, and then, because she was honest even at two in the morning, near Mom.

The tour had been in October. She and her mother had flown east on miles her mother had saved from work trips, and on the second morning a senior in clogs had walked them backward along a brick path, narrating the buildings like a person who had memorized a poem. At the admissions office she stopped and gestured at the glass doors as if presenting a cathedral. "Our yield this year was the highest in a decade," she said, and half the parents nodded as though they knew what that meant.

Ava hadn't known. She'd raised her hand, feeling like the only person in the group willing to be the ignorant one. "What's yield?"

The guide had smiled, the practiced smile of someone who got this question twice a day. "Yield is the percentage of students a college admits who actually accept the offer and enroll."

That was all she'd said, but Ava had turned it over the whole flight home. A college admitted a hundred people and only some came. The college was guessing, the same way she was guessing, and its prestige depended on being guessed right. Her mother, watching the clouds, had offered something jaundiced about how the whole thing was a beauty contest where everyone pretended not to care who won. Ava had argued with her then. She was less sure now, three days after the email that said her file had been deferred to regular decision, which was the admissions office's way of saying maybe without saying it.

Now the clock said 10:52. Deshawn leaned across the aisle. "You're going to wear a hole in that page. Just check it."

"My brother absconded with my charger, my phone's at nine percent, and if it dies mid-decision I'll lose my mind."

"Then wait for a plug."

"Then wait forever." She said it lightly, but the truth underneath it was heavier: part of her preferred the waiting, because the waiting had two doors in it. In April, or whenever the letter came, there would be only one. She had been turning that over too, the strange double vision of it. From the outside she was a supplicant, a percentage point the college would either claim or not. From the inside she was the one choosing, with a list on one page and a mother on the other, and the college's yield was made of nothing except thousands of girls exactly like her deciding. Both things were true at once, and she couldn't make them into one thing, and she was starting to think she wasn't supposed to.

Mr. Ferris came back with his copies, and the argument about Ohio resumed, and at 10:58 Ava gave up and slid the phone out under the desk. The login screen loaded slowly, the way screens do when they know. She typed her password wrong once, then right. The wheel spun. Deshawn had stopped pretending to read.

The page resolved. There was a block of text, and at the top of it, before she could read a single word, one line stood out in bold: Congratulations on your admission.

Her thumb hovered over the screen. Somewhere in Ohio a senator was promising things, and somewhere on a brick path a girl in clogs was still walking backward, and Ava had until May 1 to decide. She looked up at Deshawn.

"Get me a charger," she said. "I have to call my mom."

Angelina arrived eleven minutes early, which she decided was the correct amount of early: enough to claim the good table by the window, not so much that she looked desperate. She ordered a cappuccino she didn't especially want, because holding a warm cup gave her hands something official to do, and spread a paperback across the table's second chair so no one else would take it. The book was her roommate's, a fat psych text she'd grabbed on the way out the door for exactly this purpose, a prop, a shield.

The date was with Theo, whom she'd met at orientation where he'd spent forty minutes defending the campus poetry slam to a table of skeptics, not preaching so much as proselytizing, though he did it with such goofy charm that even the skeptics had softened. When he walked into the coffee shop he was carrying a paper bag that leaked the smell of cinnamon, and he held it up like evidence. "I didn't know what you'd want," he said, "so I got three kinds of pastry. This is either thoughtful or alarming."

"It's both," Angelina said, and moved the book so he could sit.

They talked the way people talk when everything about a person is still unverified. He told her about his brother, who worked at a shelter downtown and came home every night furious and energized, impossible to talk to about anything except the residents, the indigent men who'd become, in his brother's telling, more real to him than his own family. She told him about her mother's restaurant, the year it nearly closed, the regulars who'd quietly paid for other people's meals. He listened with his whole face. She kept noticing that she was noticing it.

Then, because the universe apparently had a sense of humor about first dates, the espresso machine behind the counter died with a sound like a car backfiring, loudly, inches from Angelina's shoulder. She startled so hard she knocked the cappuccino into her lap. The barista, a broad-shouldered woman named Kim according to her nametag, vaulted the counter with a towel before Angelina had finished gasping, pressing it against the spill on the table and then, more gently, offering a second one for Angelina's jeans. "You okay? That thing's been threatening to blow for a week." Theo had jumped too, his chair legs shrieking against the floor, and now they were both standing, both shaky, both laughing at nothing in particular.

They sat back down, and Angelina found that her heart was pounding, hard, and that she felt strangely, vividly alive, the way the room looked after lightning: every edge sharper. She looked at Theo, at the concern still crinkled around his eyes, at the pastry bag he'd half-risen to protect, and something in her chest performed a small, definite flip, and she thought, with the certainty of a person who has just been frightened within an inch of her life: I really like him.

For a while she rode that feeling. He refilled her water without being asked; she caught herself smiling at the ice in the glass. But a doubt began to gnaw at her, because she'd been ambivalent about this date all week, and ambivalence doesn't usually dissolve in one loud noise. She turned her phone over and over on the table. Finally, feeling like a fraud, she opened a text to her roommate and typed: how do you know if you like someone or if you're just scared of espresso machines.

The reply took a minute. Then: omg open the book. Ch 11. She was still under the table fishing for the textbook when Theo asked what she was doing, and she decided, on impulse, to be honest, or at least honest-adjacent. "My roommate told me something's in here that I need to read. It's about tonight, possibly. It's very embarrassing." She found the chapter, thumbed through it, and read faster than she'd ever read anything, her cheeks heating while Theo watched with open fascination.

"Okay," she said, setting the book down flat between their cups. "So there's this thing. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal. A racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby."

Theo blinked. "So the espresso machine."

"So the espresso machine." She pulled the book back before he could read over her shoulder, because the margins were now mortifyingly relevant. "The problem is that knowing about it doesn't turn it off. My heart doesn't know it's been caught. So I can't tell which part of what I'm feeling is you and which part is a broken machine, and I might not be able to tell for a while. Possibly ever. I just didn't want to sit here pretending I was sure when I wasn't."

He tore the bag open between them, releasing cinnamon into the air, and set the largest pastry on her napkin. "Then we'll have to do it again," he said. "Somewhere with no machinery. A field, maybe." Angelina laughed, and noticed, carefully, the way her heartbeat answered, and left it there, unresolved, still pounding, while she reached for the pastry and broke it in half.

The last box in Victor's room was labeled MISC, which was a lie, because he knew exactly what was in it: the folded map of Cedar Run with everyone's houses marked in pen, a stripped bike chain, half a deck of cards, and a photo from junior year that he kept face down at the bottom so his mother wouldn't ask about it. The truck came at seven in the morning. That gave him one evening, and Marcus had already texted three times asking whether he was coming to the quarry or whether he was going to be a ghost about it.

He went. The water was still cold for May, and they jumped off the low ledge because the high one belonged to a summer they weren't going to share. Marcus tried to excoriate him on the walk back, saying Victor had gotten quiet weeks ago, that he'd started leaving early, that a person could at least pretend he was being torn apart. Victor let him run out of words, because most of it was true, and because the alternative was saying what he actually suspected: that leaving might not tear him apart, and that felt worse.

At dinner his sister Priya, home from her first year of college, was scrolling through her psych notes with her laptop propped against the ketchup. "Help me study," she said, shoving it across. "Flashcards. I'll test you." He was in no mood, but the alternative was taping boxes, so he read while she ate.

One card stopped him. Robert Zajonc, 1968, experiments on what the card called the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often. He read it twice. Priya, chewing, said, "Mere-exposure effect. It's on the exam." He set the card down like it was warm.

"Say the answer anyway," she said.

"People tend to like things more simply because they've seen them more often. Zajonc, 1968."

"Good. Next."

But he wasn't hungry anymore, and he wasn't exactly upset. He was working something out, sitting there with his fork down. He thought about how, in fourth grade, he'd hated the smell of the cafeteria until he didn't. He thought about Marcus himself, whom he'd disliked for the first month of seventh grade, before their lockers happened to be adjacent and the dislike quietly expired. He thought about Priya's roommate, who had hated her bus route in a new town and found it almost comforting a month later, a story Priya told every Thanksgiving that he had never once believed until now.

"What if that's the whole thing," he said. "Not just bus routes. What if I'm not even going to miss this place the way I think I will. What if it's just exposure, and the new town becomes the familiar thing, and Cedar Run becomes the strange one, and I don't get a say in any of it."

Priya closed the laptop halfway. "That's not what the card says. The card says you'll like the new stuff more than you expect. It doesn't say you'll like the old stuff less." She looked at him the way she did when she was deciding whether he could take the truth. "You could take the card as mercy. Or you could take it as an insult to everyone you love. It's not deciding for you."

He didn't answer, because he had asked himself the same question in the shower for two weeks and never gotten further than the question. Whether Marcus was a person or a habit. Whether either of them would still recognize the difference by Christmas.

At ten he drove to Marcus's house, which was against the plan, because the plan had been the quarry and then goodbye, and plans had a way of becoming the shape of a thing if you let them. Marcus was on the porch. The porch light was on and moths worked at it, and the map was folded in Victor's back pocket.

"Come see something," Victor said, and spread the map on the porch boards and took out the pen. He drew the route to the new town, the highway, the exit his father had already driven twice. Then he marked the new house with a small square, the way their own houses were marked. "This is going to be a real place," he said. "I'm going to see it every day. And apparently that's how liking starts, whether or not I want it to." Marcus looked at the map, then at him, and Victor said, "It might happen to you too. This place without me in it. It's not a decision anyone makes."

Marcus picked up the pen, turned it once in his fingers, and drew a line from his own marked house straight to the new square, longer than any line on the map, crossing three towns and a river that the highway didn't even cross. Then he wrote along it, in small letters, exposure.

They sat with the porch light on until Victor's phone buzzed with his mother's curfew, and the moths kept circling, faithful to the one bright thing they knew.

Maika sat cross-legged on her bed with the schedule from the ice rink spread in front of her and her phone propped against the pillow. Three shifts were open on Saturday: morning skate guard, afternoon birthday parties, and the evening public session. She could take only one, because her mother had already claimed the other hours for her uncle's moving day. She wrote all three at the top of a page, then began adding them up: morning, forty-two dollars; afternoon, fifty; evening, sixty plus a share of tips. One hundred fifty-two dollars, then, that Saturday was worth, and she was losing all of it to a truck full of her uncle's furniture.

The math bothered her in a way she couldn't place at first. She texted Jolie, who worked the concession stand and was doing the same accounting for her own weekend. Jolie replied with a photo of her own list, three columns, a total circled at the bottom. "i'm missing like 160" the message said. Maika stared at the number and felt the wrongness sharpen. They weren't both missing everything on their lists. If Jolie took the evening shift, she wasn't missing the morning, because she'd never been able to take the morning anyway. Something was being counted twice, or counted that had never existed to be lost.

She called her. Jolie answered on the second ring, chewing something. "You're adding all three," Maika said. "But you can only work one. You're not giving up three shifts. You're giving up the best one you didn't take." There was a pause, then the sound of a chip being finished. "My brother kept saying that word," Jolie said. "Opportunity cost. He says it's only the next-best one." Maika wrote the phrase on the page and underlined it, then crossed out two of her three numbers and circled the evening shift at sixty plus tips. If she took the morning instead, what she gave up was the evening, not the evening plus the afternoon plus the morning stacked into a turgid total that looked like a real loss and wasn't.

The choice itself didn't get easier. The evening shift ended at ten, which meant she'd miss Devi's going-away dinner, the one where everyone was bringing a dish and Devi's mother had asked specifically whether Maika would come. Maika had said probably, which both of them understood to mean no. The morning shift ended at noon. She could guard the ice from eight to noon, earn forty-two dollars, and be at Devi's table by six with a bowl of something. The evening was worth twenty more dollars and the tips. She sat with her back against the headboard and tried to make the two things comparable, which was like weighing water against an hour.

She tried to circumscribe the problem, to draw a line around what actually counted. The dinner wasn't the money she'd spend on it, and it wasn't even Devi exactly, since Devi would be at college in the fall either way and they'd already agreed to write. It was the table, she decided. The specific table with the specific people, on the last night those people would be in one room for at least a year. That was the next-best alternative to the evening shift, the single thing standing behind the door she didn't open. The afternoon birthday parties were nothing. They were a door she'd already walked past.

There was a small bathos in realizing this, like climbing a staircase that turns out to have one fewer step than expected. She had wanted the decision to feel large, and instead it had a flat, ordinary bottom: twenty dollars and tips against a dinner. She picked up her phone and typed the text to her supervisor, then set the phone face down on the quilt without sending it, and got up to look out the window at the parking lot, where her uncle's truck was already half loaded with boxes although it was only Thursday.

From the window she could see her mother carrying a lamp to the truck, setting it down on the asphalt, going back for another. Her mother moved in short decisive trips. On Saturday, Maika would be at the rink for one of the three shifts or at the dinner, and the other possibilities would not pile up anywhere, would not sit in a ledger waiting to be mourned. They would simply be the one next-best thing, and then gone.

She went back to the bed, picked up the phone, and sent the message. "Can I take Saturday morning?" She put the schedule in her desk drawer, then took it out again and folded it into her back pocket, and went downstairs to ask her mother what she should cook for Friday, since there wouldn't be time to make anything on Saturday.

The week before Noah left for college, his father handed him a shovel and pointed at the fence line where the last strip of switchgrass separated their bean field from the Halversons' plowed ground. "Pull it out if you want," his father said, "or leave it. It's yours next summer either way." Four acres of grass, four acres that could have been beans at fourteen dollars a bushel, standing there like a spare tire nobody needed. Noah had spent all of July building the case against it, rehearsing numbers in his head the way his debate coach had taught him, but he hadn't said any of it aloud yet.

Then the orientation schedule arrived, and his first Friday of classes included a field trip to the Okafor farm, forty minutes south of campus, for everyone in the agricultural systems survey course. Noah almost skipped it. He had grown up on a farm; he knew more about dirt than the professor did, probably. But attendance was ten percent of the grade, so he boarded the bus with his earbuds in and his arms crossed, watching the tile lines scroll past the windows.

Mrs. Okafor met them at the gate in a canvas jacket, the wind pulling at her collar. She was younger than Noah expected, and she didn't lecture. She just started walking the boundary of her west field, and the class trailed after her through stubble and loose chaff, and when the wind gusted she stopped and let them all feel it, grit ticking against their jacket zippers like sleet. "Notice where it stings and where it doesn't," she said, and kept walking.

The field was striped. Bands of corn ran between bands of tall grass, maybe twenty rows of each, all the way to the creek. A girl from Chicago asked why the farm looked like that, like a barber pole, and Mrs. Okafor squatted down and pulled up a fistful of grass, roots dangling a foot and more below it, pale and matted and heavy with soil. "In the Dust Bowl, the Plains' native grasses got plowed up, and with them the deep roots that held the soil. Then the drought came and the wind carried the topsoil away." She let the root mass dangle a moment longer, then set it back in the ground and tamped it with her boot, as if returning a borrowed thing.

Noah stood at the back of the group and felt his argument rearranging itself under him. He had been thinking about the grass strips as sentiment, his grandfather's habit dressed up as virtue, something you paid for out of nostalgia. He hadn't thought of them as machinery. The wind was still coming off the Halversons' side of the fence line even here, forty minutes from home, and it stung on the bare patches and went quiet in the grass, exactly as she'd said it would.

On the bus back he called his father. "I'm not pulling the switchgrass out," he said. His father said nothing for a while, long enough that Noah could hear the radio in the kitchen, the grain report, noxious weed notices for two counties over. "You had that whole speech ready," his father said finally. "I could hear you practicing it through the screen door. Fourteen dollars a bushel. I know the number." Noah looked out the window at a tractor turning on a far field, its dust plume rising and leaning east. "The grass is holding the field down," Noah said. "That's income too. It's just income you can't see until the year you'd lose everything else."

There was a silence on the line that Noah couldn't read, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it. Maybe his father was proud. Maybe he was recalculating the farm's whole ledger. Maybe he was just tired and had stopped listening. Noah's roommate, a business major who heard only the word income, leaned over from the next seat and said, "So did you convince him, or did he convince you?" and Noah said, "Neither, I think. I changed my own mind with somebody else's information," which sounded clumsy out loud, and which his roommate repeated in a mock-elocution voice, hand to his chest, until the girl from Chicago told them both to shut up.

That Sunday, the wind came up hard out of the northwest, thirty miles an hour and rising, and Noah drove home to walk the fence line before he left for good. The Halversons' field, disked bare for winter wheat, had already begun to travel; a brown haze hung over the low ground, and the ditch on their side of the fence had a new shoulder of fine soil drifted against the wire, soft as ash. On his family's side, the bean stubble was brown and ugly but fixed, and the switchgrass ran down the slope in a gold line, hissing, its seed heads bent all one direction, and along its upper edge the drifted soil had piled six inches deep, held there, bought and paid for in a currency no market quoted.

His father came down the fence line to meet him, hands in his pockets, and stood looking at the drift. "Halverson called this morning," he said. "He wants to know if we've still got seed for that grass." Then he laughed once, short, almost regretful. "Forty years I've been telling your grandfather those strips were wasted ground. Now the man who out-yielded me every season of my life wants my weeds." He bent and picked up a handful of the drifted topsoil, let the wind burnish it off his palm grain by grain, and said, "Go get the seed catalog out of the truck."

Edouard set the lasagna down between his mother's geraniums and his brother's phone, and immediately his father began. "So the hero of the hardware store returns. Tell them what you did."

The facts were simple enough to say out loud, though they had been undulating in Edouard's head all afternoon like something alive in a jar. On Tuesday he had suggested to Mr. Kastner, the owner, that the store stay open an hour later on weekdays. More contractors would come after their jobs ended; the numbers Edouard had pulled from the register tapes supported it. Mr. Kastner had clapped him on the shoulder and said he'd think like an owner someday. Then, on Thursday, the new schedule went up, and the closing shift started at six, which was exactly when the last bus to Cedar Heights left the depot. Rosa, who had worked closings for nine years, lived in Cedar Heights. So did Marcus and the two college kids hired in May.

"Edouard," his mother said. "Your father is being facetious. Eat."

"I'm being serious. This is a serious dinner." His father forked a piece of garlic bread and pointed it like a citation. "My son improves the store's revenue and strands three employees at the curb. That's a trade-off, that's what that is. You learn about those in your ethics class? They have a name for everything now."

"They have a name for this one, actually." Edouard had spent his lunch period in the library with his phone face down on the table, searching until he found it. "There's a professor, Freeman, wrote a book in 1984, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. He argued that a business should consider everyone affected by its decisions, not only the owners. Anyone affected counts as a stakeholder. Customers, workers, the neighborhood." Saying it aloud at the table felt strange, like reciting something in a language he was not yet fluent in.

His brother, Timmy, looked up from his phone long enough to say, "So the bus people are stakeholders and Dad's a stakeholder and the store's a stakeholder. Everybody's a stakeholder. Great system, very rigorous."

"Everyone affected," Edouard said. "That's the point. That's the whole point, actually." He was surprised by how steady his voice came out, because inside he was not steady at all. He had made a recommendation with a spreadsheet and a guess about traffic, and the spreadsheet had been right, and the guess had been right, and Rosa had still ended up standing on Delaware Avenue at six-fifteen yesterday, waiting for a ride that came forty minutes late. He'd seen her from the bus window on his way home. He had almost gotten off. He had stayed in his seat, which was its own decision, and he could not stop weighing it.

"Did you say anything to Kastner?" his mother asked. She had stopped eating, which in her case was the equivalent of standing up and shouting.

"I went back this morning before school. I told him about the bus." Edouard pushed the lasagna around his plate, red sauce pooling in the trench his fork made. "He said he'd look at carpooling options. He said, and this is a quote, 'Good catch, that's why I pay you to think.' Except he doesn't pay me to think about that part. He pays me to think about the register. I thought about the register and something else happened, something I wasn't looking at."

"Unintended consequences," his father said, with the grim satisfaction of a man who had predicted rain all day and was now watching it pour. "You didn't intend to strand Rosa. Intentions don't carry people home, though."

"Right, but here's what I keep going back and forth on." Edouard put his fork down, which his family all noticed, because he never put his fork down. "If I'd thought about everyone affected, if I'd actually applied the thing instead of just finding it Thursday night like a lawyer hunting for a precedent to excuse himself with, would I have made a different recommendation? Maybe. Maybe I'd have said close at five-thirty and open earlier. Or maybe I'd have said the same thing, because the store is struggling, because Mr. Kastner has three kids in college, because he's a stakeholder too, and the whole thing is a trade-off between people who all have real claims. The book gives you the question. It doesn't do the arithmetic for you."

Timmy lowered the phone entirely, which had not happened at a dinner table since March. "So what are you going to do?"

"Monday I'm going to ask Mr. Kastner for the schedule through August, before it's posted, not after. Not to reverse anything. Just to look at all of it at once, bus times and register tapes together, and see what's actually possible." He picked the fork back up. "Maybe nothing changes. Maybe the honest answer is that the extra hour pays for a shuttle van. I don't know yet. I'm telling you I don't know yet, and I'd rather say that than pretend I solved it in the library at lunch."

His mother spooned more lasagna onto his plate without asking, which was how she said she was listening. His father opened his mouth, closed it, and ate the garlic bread instead. Through the window the geraniums moved in the evening wind, and Timmy said, "Stakeholder theory at the dinner table. Verisimilitude achieved. This family finally resembles an actual household."

"Shut up and pass the bread," Edouard said, and passed it to Rosa in his head, forty minutes late, still waiting under the streetlight.

I didn't care that Deacon had a new helmet. That's what I told Priya at lunch, twice, which should have been my first clue that I cared. What I actually wanted was to win the ethics unit, because Mr. Okafor had promised the best essay would be read at assembly, and my mother had already missed two of my assemblies this year. A win felt like a way to suture the gap without ever having to say anything out loud.

The helmet was white with a black stripe, and Deacon wore it to fourth period like a crown. "Full face, MIPS, the works," he said, tipping it back on his head. "I can bomb the Lark Street hill now and nothing happens."

"Nothing happens anyway," Priya said. "You crawl down it."

"Not anymore."

That afternoon I watched from the chain-link fence as he took the hill standing on the pedals, faster than I'd ever seen him go, the helmet bright against the asphalt. He made it, obviously. He waved both hands, which was its own kind of argument. In fifth grade, before any of us wore helmets, he used to ride down that same hill with his arms crossed like a magician, and once he skidded into the hedge and came up laughing with a leaf in his teeth. I remembered that while I stood at the fence, and I remembered, too, that he'd gone slower back then.

I was in the school library that night because of the essay, not because of him. Mr. Okafor had listed concepts on the board: responsibility, trade-offs, unintended consequences, and told us to find one real example and argue it honestly. I'd been planning to write about my mother, some specious thing about sacrifice, and I'd been planning to make it neater than it was. But I opened a behavioral economics book at the next table and found a chapter on safety measures that didn't deliver what engineers predicted. There was a term for it. Risk compensation, the book said: people behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure delivers less benefit than predicted. I copied it into my notebook and then sat without writing anything else for a while.

"Risk compensation," I said to Priya the next morning, showing her the page. "That's Deacon. The helmet didn't make the hill safer. It made him faster."

"So tell him to slow down."

"It's not that simple. He's not wrong to wear it. If he falls, it still helps. It's just that the benefit is smaller than the box promised, because he changed his behavior." I heard myself lecturing and stopped. This was the problem with the concept: it cut both ways, and I hated things that cut both ways. My mother took the night shift for the money that let us stay in this school district, and the money came with her absence, and whenever I called that a trade-off she said I was too young to use that word about her choices, and whenever I said her choice had an unintended consequence, which was me eating dinner alone, she stopped answering texts for a day. Responsibility, I had started to think, was mostly a word adults used to close conversations.

I caught Deacon at his locker. "You went twice as fast down the hill yesterday."

"Yeah. It's safe now. That's the point of a helmet."

"The point of a helmet is if you crash. It doesn't cancel the crash." I turned my notebook around so he could see the photocopied page. "Risk compensation. It's a real thing. People act less carefully when they feel protected, so the safety thing doesn't help as much as it's supposed to."

He read it, jaw working. "So what am I supposed to do, wear the helmet and ride like I don't have it?"

"Basically, yeah."

"That's the most boring advice anyone's ever given me." But he said it looking at the page, not at me, and on Friday I saw him take the hill seated, braking in pulses, the white helmet moving at a speed I almost didn't recognize. He waved at the fence with one hand only.

I wrote the essay that weekend. I wrote about Deacon and the hill and the term from the library, and then, near the end, without planning to, about the night shift, though I kept my mother's name out of it. I didn't resolve it. I wrote that some protections are still worth taking even when they change us, and that you can't always tell which part of a person is the trade-off and which is just who they became, and Mr. Okafor wrote "honest" in the margin in green ink. The assembly was Thursday. My mother texted that she'd try to make it, and then, an hour later, that the shift swap hadn't gone through.

I sat in the third row next to Priya. On stage, Mr. Okafor adjusted the microphone, unfolded a paper, and said my name.

The cake had his name on it in blue icing, which Brayden took as a small omen, since blue was the color of the college logo on the banner his mother had taped above the buffet. He had not yet told anyone that he was thinking of deferring a year, and the banner seemed to presage the conversation he would have to have before the ice cream melted. He stood near the deviled eggs and practiced openings in his head.

His grandfather arrived late, as always, holding a folded newspaper under one arm like a man reporting for duty. He shook Brayden's hand formally, then ruined it by pulling him into a hug that smelled like spearmint and engine grease. "Eighteen," he said. "Legal adult. You can now be sued."

"I'll try to avoid insolvency," Brayden said, mostly to make his cousins laugh, and they did, except for the youngest, who asked what insolvency meant and was told to eat his potato salad.

Dinner was long and loud. An uncle who had once declared bankruptcy, a fact the family handled the way it handled weather, held forth on the stock market with a jaundiced eye, and Brayden's mother kept refilling glasses as though hydration were the family's only remaining defense. When the toasts began, his grandfather stood, tapped his glass, and did not say what everyone expected.

"I never graduated," he said. "High school, I mean. I left in eleventh grade."

The room recalibrated. His mother set down a pitcher. Someone's fork stopped halfway.

"I went in the Army instead," his grandfather continued, apparently addressing the potato salad. "And afterward, I got the GED. That test they made in 1942, so service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school could show they had the skills anyway. That was me. I took it after I got out."

"The same year," Brayden's aunt said, "as the Chopin concert?"

"The same lifetime," his grandfather said, and sat down, having concluded his remarks.

Later, Brayden found him on the porch with a slice of cake he wasn't eating, the fork laid across the plate at a precise angle. The yard was turning the color of late evening, and somewhere a sprinkler ticked against a fence.

"You never told me that," Brayden said.

"Never came up."

"I've known you eighteen years."

"Seventeen and some months. You weren't conversational at first."

Brayden sat on the step below him. In the window behind them, his mother was cutting more cake for cousins who hadn't finished their first pieces, an act of optimism the family had long since learned not to question. He had been rehearsing a speech all week about the gap year, the job at the machine shop, the idea that a diploma was a door and not a floor, and now every version of it sounded different in his head.

"I've been thinking about not going," he said. "In the fall. Right away, I mean. Working first."

His grandfather didn't answer right away. He picked up the fork, then set it down again, and Brayden understood that this was the older man thinking, not dismissing.

"You know what I used to think the GED was?" his grandfather said. "Secondhand. A substitute thing. Took me years to notice nobody who mattered ever asked which one I had. Then I trained fellows who had the regular diploma and couldn't read a schematic, and I stopped sorting people that way, including myself." He looked at the yard. "On the other hand, the Army didn't give me a choice about waiting. You have one. That's not nothing either."

"So which is it?"

"If I knew that, I'd have written a book instead of engines." He handed the plate down. "Take this in, would you. Your mother's giving me the look."

Brayden carried the cake through the sliding door, past the banner, past the uncle now explaining interest rates to a teenager who was texting under the table. His mother met his eyes across the room with a question in them, and he realized he still didn't have the answer, only something closer to it, and that his grandfather had left both pieces of it on the porch, next to a fork nobody had used.

He set the plate on the buffet, and before he could turn around, his mother said, "Brayden. Come here a second."

Anthony got to statistics early because the only seat near the window was in the back, and he liked watching the parking lot fill. Mr. Ruiz had written a number on the board before anyone arrived, 48 to 46, and beneath it the words "City Council Poll, Channel 5." When the bell finished, Dana Vasquez stood up before Mr. Ruiz could say anything.

"Can I present?" she asked. She had been trying for two weeks to get the school to fund a student survey project, and Mr. Ruiz had told her she could have five minutes of class if she brought data. She walked to the board with her laptop and clicked to a slide with a bar chart. "I put a poll on the school's app asking whether we should keep open lunch or go to closed blocks. I got 1,400 responses. Nine percent more said open. So the student body wants open lunch, and I want the administration to actually look at it at the next board meeting." Her voice was steady, but her thumbnail was pressed white against the clicker.

Anthony liked Dana, and he wanted open lunch too, but something about the slide bothered him, the way the bars were drawn tall and certain. He raised his hand. "Who answered?"

"People who use the app."

"Who uses the app?"

"Mostly freshmen," she admitted. "Because the freshmen got the orientation push."

Marcus, two rows over, leaned back in his chair. "It's 1,400 people, man. Out of like 2,000 in the school. That's basically everybody. If that many people say it, it's right." A few people nodded. Marcus wanted the argument settled quickly; he had a calculus test next period and no patience for a debate that would eat the review time.

Anthony didn't have an answer ready, so he said the only true thing he had. "Big doesn't automatically mean right." It sounded weak even to him, a slogan without a body. Mr. Ruiz, who was leaning against the radiator with his arms folded, said nothing, which Anthony had learned meant the teacher thought the question was live.

At lunch Anthony went to the library and typed "famous wrong polls" into a search, half expecting nothing, and the screen filled with the same story three times. In 1936 a magazine called the Literary Digest mailed out a survey about the presidential election and collected about 2.4 million responses, and on the strength of those numbers predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt then won in a landslide. Anthony read it twice. He wrote nothing down and then wrote it down anyway, the number and both names, because 2.4 million felt impossible to hold in his head. Whatever it was that made a poll wrong, it wasn't a shortage of people. Something else decided.

He found Dana in the hallway before seventh period, by the water fountain where the noise covered conversation. "That thing you said about 1,400 being basically everybody. There was this poll in 1936, the Literary Digest. They got 2.4 million responses and said Landon would beat Roosevelt, and Roosevelt won in a landslide."

Dana looked at the number on his notebook. "2.4 million."

"Yeah."

"So what was wrong with it?"

"I don't know yet. I'm working on that part." He could have guessed, something about who ended up in the sample and who didn't, freshmen and app users and magazine readers in 1936, but he didn't want to dress a guess up as knowledge. What he did know was the shape of it: the size of a sample and the truth of a claim were different axes, and the first did not guarantee the second. He told her that much, and she chewed her lip, and he could see her weighing her board meeting against it.

That night they sat in his kitchen with the textbook open to the chapter they hadn't reached yet, the one on sampling distributions. There was a formula for how far off a percentage could plausibly be, called the margin of error, and it shrank as the sample grew, but slowly, like a door closing by degrees. They ran Dana's numbers. With 1,400 responses her 9 percent lead survived, comfortable even. Then she pulled up the breakdown by grade and the floor dropped out of the argument: seniors were nearly absent from her data, and seniors were the ones who remembered the closed-block year. Whether the whole school preferred open lunch depended on people who hadn't answered, and no amount of arithmetic could allay that doubt. It wasn't happenstance that her sample skewed young, either; the orientation push had built the skew in, quietly, a subterranean bias under an impressive-looking total.

"So I can't take it to the board like this," Dana said. She said it flatly, and then, after a minute, "Unless I take it like this. Nine percent overall, but the sample is mostly underclassmen, and I need two hundred more seniors before the number means anything."

"That's more honest than the slide was."

"It's less persuasive."

"It might be more," Anthony said. "They're the ones who always say student government fakes its data."

They stayed at the table past ten, drafting the email she would send out, deciding to go classroom to classroom in the senior wing on Thursday instead of relying on the app. Dana typed the subject line, erased it, and typed it again. "Seniors," she read aloud, "we want your answer, even the ones of you who never check anything."

"Especially those," Anthony said, and reached over her shoulder to hit send.

Henry arrived at the Beanery eleven minutes early, which he told himself was a matter of the bus schedule and nothing else, and which was, in fact, a matter of wanting to choose the table near the window before Marisol got there so that he would appear to have been there for ages, casual, at home. He set down his backpack, took out his history notes on the Mongol expansion across the steppe for Tuesday's quiz, and then put them away again because studying on a date, even before the date technically began, seemed like something a person would do to seem interesting rather than something an interesting person would do.

Marisol came in at 4:02, shaking rain off her jacket, and Henry stood up so fast he knocked his spoon to the floor. He had liked her since the group project in October, when she had eviscerated his draft thesis in one sentence and then spent forty minutes helping him rebuild it, and he had decided, over three months of deliberation, that this was a good sign and not a warning. He got in line with her, bought her drink even though she protested, and carried both cups back to the window table with the concentration of a bomb technician.

They were eight minutes into a genuinely decent conversation about whether the school's new bell schedule was gratuitous cruelty or merely incompetence when Priya walked in with Dylan. Priya was Henry's best friend since sixth grade; Dylan was two years older, had a car, and had been dating her for five weeks. Henry watched them order, and he watched Dylan take Priya's wrist to steer her toward a table, and he watched Priya's face do something brief and small that she smoothed over immediately. Henry noticed all of this and told himself he noticed it because Dylan was, objectively, a jerk, and not for any other reason, and certainly not because Priya had once, in eighth grade, held his hand during the whole of a thunderstorm and neither of them had ever mentioned it since.

He kept half his attention on their table while Marisol described her brother's wedding disaster. Dylan reached across and gripped Priya's forearm when she reached for her phone, hard enough that she set the phone down and laughed, a laugh with no floor under it. Twice. Three times, over twenty minutes. Henry was not counting, except that he was.

"Sorry," he said to Marisol. "My friend's over there. Her boyfriend keeps grabbing her arm and it doesn't look like a joke kind of grabbing."

Marisol glanced over, unhurried. "That's the third time."

"You were counting too?"

"Hard not to." She wrapped both hands around her cup. "Is she the type to say something if you ask?"

Priya was the type to eviscerate anyone who suggested she couldn't handle her own life. That was the problem. Henry had a page torn from a health class handout folded in the front pocket of his backpack, something he'd shoved there in September and rediscovered last week while looking for a pencil: the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which had found that about one in twelve US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. One in twelve. He had read it twice on the bus, wondering which twelve-person rows of his classes it applied to, and whether the numbers counted only the people who reported it, and what the unreported rows would look like. He had not thought, at the time, that he might someday watch it happen from four tables away.

"I read this thing," he said now, quietly, because Marisol was watching him and he did not want Priya to hear. "A CDC survey, 2021, the Youth Risk Behavior Survey. About one in twelve high school students who'd dated reported physical dating violence." He heard how it sounded, like a lecture, like a trivia card. "I'm not saying that's her. I'm saying it's common enough that it's not crazy to say something."

"It's not crazy," Marisol said.

"It might be me being a bad friend instead. Or a jealous one." He said it before he could stop himself, and it sat on the table between them alongside the two cups. Marisol didn't reach for it or brush it away, which he appreciated more than he could have said.

He got up, crossed the four tables, and stood beside Priya's chair with his hands in his pockets. "Hey. Can I borrow you for a sec? Help me pick a drink for Marisol."

Priya followed him to the counter, and Dylan watched them go with an expression Henry decided not to interpret. At the counter Henry looked at the menu board as though it required study, and then at her forearm, where the marks were already fading.

"Dylan grabs you," he said. "Your arm. I've seen it three times tonight and you don't look like you like it."

Priya stared at the pastries case. "It's not a thing."

"If it's not a thing, then it's not a thing to talk about either. So talk about it."

"It's a thing," she said finally, very quietly, to the glass.

"Okay," Henry said. "Then you don't have to figure it out standing at this counter tonight." He nodded toward the window table, where Marisol had turned her chair to give them privacy, or the appearance of it. "Come sit with us. Bring your coffee."

Priya glanced back at Dylan, then at the door, then at the window.

"Okay," she said.

Olivier had folded the population pyramid of Japan into his jacket pocket before leaving the house, and by the second switchback of the trail it had gone soft with sweat, so that when he pulled it out at the overlook it opened like something alive. His uncle's dog, a gray-muzzled thing called Pim, sat down beside him and watched the paper as though it might bolt. The graph was for his first college assignment, due in nine days, though the professor had said the deadline was the least interesting part of it. On the left of the pyramid the bars ran long and fat near the middle, like a barrel cinched at both ends. On the right, near the top, the bars flared out wider than their neighbors on the left, and Olivier had been staring at that asymmetry for two days without making sense of it.

He had tried asking his younger sister, Marta, who was good at guessing. "Maybe they counted wrong," she'd said at breakfast, chin in her hand. "Or maybe more men leave the country." Then she had leaned closer, tapped the widest bar at the very top of the right side, and said, "Or maybe women just live longer than men, and that's all it is." She'd shrugged and gone back to her toast, leaving Olivier with the strange feeling of having been handed an answer that was either obvious or wrong, with no way to tell which.

The trail continued up through pines, and he kept walking with the paper refolded, Pim trotting ahead. The assignment wanted a prediction: from the pyramid alone, would the country need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years. The professor had warned them against what she called charlatan confidence, people who read one demographic shape and pronounced the future like oracles. Olivier liked that warning. It made the work feel less like arithmetic and more like judgment, though he wasn't yet sure what judgment consisted of besides noticing things slowly.

He noticed, first, the base of the pyramid: narrow. Fewer children being born than there were people in the middle ages, which meant the middle would thin over time, and the whole shape would drift upward like oil in water. More schools or more nursing homes. The question had seemed almost insulting in its simplicity until he understood that the answer was both, in different decades, and that the pyramid could tell you the order. A country could need classrooms now and wards later, and the graph held that sequence in its silhouette the way a tree ring held a drought.

What he couldn't reconcile was the tilted top. If Marta was right, if women lived longer than men on average, then the right side of the pyramid, which was the female side, would naturally widen at the top, and the widening told you nothing about births or policy; it was, he thought, extrinsic to the question, a feature of the shape that came from longevity rather than from any decision the country had made. But then he stopped himself on the trail, because was that true? A nursing home population was mostly women if women mostly lived to fill it. The asymmetry wasn't beside the point. It changed who the nursing homes were for.

He sat on a granite slab near the third overlook and ate half a sandwich while Pim investigated a chipmunk hole with professional seriousness. His professor had said something in the first lecture about learning to historicize a statistic, to ask when and where it was true before trusting it, and Olivier had written the word down without feeling it. Now he felt it. The pyramid was a photograph of one country in one year, and every bar was a generation carrying its own history upward. The wide middle bars were his own grandparents. The narrow base was, roughly, him.

He texted Marta a photo of the pyramid with the top circled. Can I use your guess, he typed, or does that make me a plagiarist. She wrote back within a minute: you can use it if you admit you didn't see it yourself. He laughed out loud, which made Pim look up from the chipmunk hole. That seemed fair, and also more than fair, because the honest version was better: a friend had looked at the shape and seen the reason before he had, and he could build on it without pretending otherwise. He would write that the top of the pyramid held more women than men because women lived longer than men on average, and that this shaped the demand for care as surely as the narrow base shaped the demand for schools.

What stayed uncertain, he decided, walking the last mile down with the light going amber through the pines, was everything the pyramid couldn't say: whether families would change, whether migration would widen the base, whether thirty years from now anyone would look at his prediction and call it obvious or call it naive. He would have to write that part too, the not knowing, and let it stand next to the parts he was sure of. At the trailhead he refolded the pyramid along its worn creases and held it out to Pim, who sniffed it once, thoroughly, and sneezed.

"All right," Olivier said, pocketing it again. "Home, then. We've got a future to get wrong."

The hardware store sat at the end of the plaza, sharing a back hallway with the grocery next door, and Sofia learned this in her first ten minutes of work because Mr. Aldrich, who owned both, walked her through the doorway with a key on a stretchy coil around his wrist. He had hired her on the strength of one interview and a note from her neighbor, who bought birdseed here every Saturday. Her job, he said, was the register, the seed rack, and restocking shelf paper for the paint department. She had spent the night before the interview reading the federal child labor rules on her phone, not because anyone told her to, but because she could not sleep and reading regulations felt like a way of holding still.

Her foreboding about the job had been vague until then, something about register codes and being trusted with money, and by noon it had faded into ordinary nervousness. She sold a woman three packets of beefsteak tomato seeds and a trowel. Behind her, Denzell, the other part-time hire, a seventeen-year-old who had been working here since June, was organizing the seed display by packet color. He held up two packets of the same variety and said the plants would still come out different, all that phenotypic variation, genes plus weather plus whatever the soil was doing. Sofia said she had not thought about tomatoes that way. He said nobody did, that was the problem.

At two o'clock Mr. Aldrich came through the back hallway fast. Rosa, the deli woman at the grocery, had called in with a flooded basement, and he had a line of lunch customers. He looked at Denzell first, because Denzell was older, and asked him to run next door and cover the slicer until Rosa showed up. Denzell did not move. He said he could work the register, the produce scale, the coffee machine, but not the slicer. Mr. Aldrich said it was a deli, not a chemistry lab, and that a slicer was a slicer.

"Under federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen can't operate power-driven meat slicers," Denzell said. "Even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant."

Mr. Aldrich stood there with his hand still raised, halfway through pointing at the hallway. Then he turned and looked at Sofia, and Sofia felt the question arrive before he said it, and she heard herself say the same thing Denzell had said, that under eighteen meant under eighteen, that she had read it the night before and it had not seemed like information she would ever need. She was surprised by how steady her voice came out.

Mr. Aldrich did not argue. He went to the office and came back with a laminated federal poster, the same one Sofia realized she had passed in the hallway without reading, and stood under the light with it, moving his finger down the lines. A man came in for pipe tape and Sofia sold it to him while Mr. Aldrich read. When the man left, Mr. Aldrich said, to nobody in particular, that he had been nineteen when he started and had run slicers since, and that he had not known a rule could reach all the way into a small store like his. He said he supposed that was the point of rules. He put the poster back.

Then he called his sister-in-law, who was forty-one, and while the phone rang he stood in the doorway between the two stores with his shoulders lower than they had been all day. Sofia could not tell whether he was angry. He had every reason to be annoyed at losing an hour of coverage, and instead he had lost it twice, once from Denzell and once from her, and she had volunteered her refusal without being asked, which was either loyalty or something worse. She thought of the way Denzell had said no, flat and fast, like a coin dropped on a counter, and the way she had said it, testing each word as it left. One of them had been sure. She was not sure she was the one.

Denzell went back to the seed rack. He lined up the tomato packets in pairs, two beefsteaks side by side, and said the plants would come out different anyway, even from the same packet, even in the same yard. He said his bio teacher would be proud of him for using the word twice in one day. He said the slicer thing had come up in June, his first week, when Rosa had asked him to cut a pound of turkey and he had stood there until she laughed and did it herself, and after that he had looked the rule up on his phone in the break room so he would have it ready.

Through the open hallway door Sofia could hear the sister-in-law arriving at the deli, her keys, her voice asking what was still needed. Mr. Aldrich came back through and stopped at Sofia's register. He put a roll of quarters on the counter, the float for tomorrow, and slid it toward her. "Same time Saturday," he said. "You'll take the early shift, and if Rosa's out again, I'll be the one cutting the turkey."

Dylan counted the numbers on the napkin three times before he was willing to believe them, and even then he believed them the way you believe weather forecasts, provisionally, with a coat. He had worked nineteen hours at Marzano's at nine dollars an hour, which should have been a hundred and seventy-one dollars, and the check in his hand said one hundred fifty-two. He turned it over as though the missing nineteen dollars might be hiding on the back, perhaps with an apology.

"Take it up with Rosa," said Marcus, the shift lead, who was extruding dough through the pasta machine with the calm of a man who had done it ten thousand times and intended to do it ten thousand more. "She does the payroll. But fair warning, she'll make you do the math yourself. She thinks suffering teaches."

Rosa was in the back office, which was really a closet with ambitions, filing receipts into a binder that looked older than the restaurant. When Dylan asked about his check she didn't look up. "How much did you expect?"

"A hundred seventy-one."

"How much is on it?"

"A hundred fifty-two point oh six."

"Then the difference is?" She still hadn't looked up. Dylan did the subtraction on the receipt paper. Nineteen dollars, give or take.
