She stood in the doorway holding her cap, still flat in its packaging, and watched him loosen a bolt that did not need loosening.

"You're hiding," she said.

"I'm maintaining equipment." He set the wrench down and looked at her gown, which she had put on early because her mother wanted pictures before the heat arrived. "You could help me with this bolt."

She crouched beside him and held the nut steady while he turned. This was how they had always talked, side by side, hands busy, neither of them required to look at the other. He asked whether she had decided about the deferral yet, and she said no, and he said nothing, and she was grateful for the nothing.

The trouble was this: the university had offered her a place in the fall, and the wildlife center two towns over had offered her a paid internship for the same months, with housing above the raptor barn and a supervisor who had once let her transcribe a whole season of migration logs just because she asked. Her mother thought the internship was a detour dressed up as a calling. Her father thought whatever she thought, mostly, which was its own kind of pressure. Charlotte had spent two weeks making lists, and the lists had become two small saturnine piles on her desk, each one refusing to collapse into the other.

Her friend Priya arrived at noon with a garment steamer and a bag of bobby pins, having declared over text that Charlotte's household clearly could not be trusted with wrinkles. In the kitchen Priya steamed the gown while Charlotte's mother fanned the fabric with a cutting board, and for a while the room was just steam and laughter and the smell of the lemon cake cooling on the sill.

Charlotte said, mostly to the steam, "I keep feeling like it's a funeral for something."

"For what?"

"For being this. For this house, this kitchen. Everything I know how to be." She heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "Four years and then it's over, and they hand you a hat."

Priya lifted the gown off the hanger and held it up to the window light, checking her work. "You know what the ceremony's actually called," she said. "Commencement. It means beginning. That's why they used the word, because you begin a new status. Like being a bachelor or a master." She shook out a crease at the hem. "So it's not a funeral. It's a launch, technically."

"Technically," Charlotte said, but something in her chest rearranged itself slightly, the way furniture moves when you finally stop dragging it sideways.

At the school, under a sun that made the bleachers shimmer, Charlotte sat between Priya and a boy named Marcus who had cried at the winter concert and was now crying again, discreetly, into his sleeve. She passed him a tissue from the sleeve of her gown without looking, and he took it without looking, and that small machination of kindness passed between them the way such things do, unannounced. When the principal read her name, her mother's camera flash went off three times, too early, and her father stood up in the fifth row before anyone else in the row did, hands in his pockets, then out of them, then in again.

Afterward, in the parking lot, the deferral still undecided in her pocket like a stone, Charlotte found Priya by the chain-link fence. "Beginning a new status," Charlotte said. "Bachelor or master."

"Or intern," Priya said.

"Or intern." Charlotte turned her cap over in her hands, the tangle of the tassel catching the light. "I still don't know which one, though. That part they don't put in the word."

"They don't," Priya agreed. She took the bobby pins out of Charlotte's hair, one at a time, and dropped them into the cup of her palm. "You've got until Monday to call them. Come on, your mom's holding cake hostage until you get in the picture."

Charlotte followed her across the hot asphalt, cap in hand, and behind them the empty stadium doors swung slowly shut on their own.

The moving truck had left, and Noemie stood in the empty living room where the rectangles of unpainted wall marked where her mother's paintings had hung for eleven years. In four days she would start at Kingsbridge High, junior year, in a town whose name she had not known how to pronounce until the realtor corrected her twice. Her boxes were stacked in the new house already, but she had insisted on coming back once more, alone, on the bus, to walk the old rooms. What she wanted was simple and impossible: to be in two places at once, the way she had been all summer, half here and half already gone.

On Monday the school was louder than her old one, or maybe the same volume arranged differently, so that everything sounded like a language she could almost speak. In third period the teacher gave them a warm-up question, something about where they were from, and Noemie watched a boy named Deshawn answer for the whole class as if it were a game he had won before. When her turn came she said the name of her old town and felt it land in the room like a coin dropped on carpet, noticed by no one. She wrote it in her notebook instead, and under it she wrote the names of Priya and Kas, her two best friends, who had promised to call every Sunday and who had called twice.

Wednesday she ate lunch in the library because the cafeteria had a geography she could not read yet, every table a country with closed borders. The librarian, Ms. Okafor, did not try to talk to her, which Noemie appreciated, and instead slid the day's newspapers across the counter for anyone who wanted them. Noemie read them the way she read everything lately, hungrily and without direction, looking for a reason to feel the way she felt. On the second page she found it, not a reason exactly but a word.

The article said that in May 2023 the US Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, had issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States. She read the sentence three times. An advisory, she gathered, was not a law or a warning exactly, more like a formal way of saying pay attention. She had thought of epidemics as things that happened to bodies, fevers and coughs, and here was one that happened in the spaces between people. It destabilized something she had been telling herself, that what she was going through was private and therefore hers alone to endure. If it was an epidemic, then it was common, which should have been depressing and was, oddly, the opposite.

She copied the sentence into her notebook, and a boy at the next table leaned over. "Homework?" he asked. He had a laminated schedule sticking out of his back pocket and a way of sitting that suggested he had decided she was interesting before she had decided anything about him. His name, when he offered it, was Theo.

"No," she said. "It's real. The Surgeon General called it an epidemic. Loneliness. This May."

"Huh," Theo said. "So it's, like, official." He looked at the paper, then at her, and she could see him doing the same math she had done. "That's kind of terrible and kind of nice at the same time."

It was a better sentence than she could have made, and she wrote that down too, which made him laugh. They talked through the rest of lunch, not about loneliness but about the library's broken printer and the fact that the school's one good window faced the parking lot. Still, the fact sat under the conversation the way a table sits under a meal. She found she was doing something she recognized from her old friendships, testing him with small true statements to see which ones he would catch.

That night she lay on her mattress on the floor of the new room and thought about calling Priya. The problem was not the call itself but what it would mean, because Priya communicated in two registers, the affective one, all hearts and voice memos, and the analytical one, which Noemie's mother called arguing for sport and Priya called rigor. Noemie's own position had always floated between them, and lately she had been trying to pin it down. Was she lonely in the way the article meant, or was she just new, and were those different things? She honestly did not know, and she was tired of pretending the not-knowing was a failure.

She called Priya on Sunday, not the scheduled hour but eleven at night, when the wanting outweighed the pride. Priya answered on the second ring, voice thick with sleep, and did not say where have you been. "I read something," Noemie said. "The Surgeon General, in May, he put out an advisory saying loneliness and isolation are an epidemic in the US." There was a silence long enough that she checked the screen to see if the call had dropped.

"That's either devastating or the best news I've ever heard," Priya said, and laughed, and Noemie laughed, and then neither of them said anything for a while, but it was the good kind of nothing, the kind that used to fill the back of Priya's car on long drives. Eventually Priya said, "Kas says hi, by the way, she's asleep on my floor, she'll be furious she missed this." Noemie asked how furious, on a scale, and Priya said a nine, and Noemie said only a nine, and Priya said fine, a nine point five.

They talked until Noemie's phone was hot against her ear, about nothing that mattered and everything that did, and when Priya finally yawned herself off the line, Noemie did not hang up right away. She sat on the floor with the dead phone in her lap, looking at the window, where the streetlight made a small bright country of the sidewalk. Tomorrow she would find Theo at lunch, she thought, and sit where he could see her. She picked up her notebook and, under the sentence she had copied, drew a second rectangle beside the first, the way the unpainted walls had looked, and wrote in it: Day one was May something, or maybe it was today. Then she turned off the light and lay listening to the unfamiliar house settle, tick by tick, into its own slow rhythm, and somewhere down the hall, faint through the wall, she heard her mother turn over in her sleep.

The band room smelled like cork grease and old carpet, and Nevaeh had been alone in it for forty minutes, failing at the same sixteen bars. The solo in the Holst suite was supposed to flutter, all sixteenth notes in the upper register of her oboe, and every time she pushed the tempo her tongue tangled and her fingers arrived late, as if they were getting their instructions from somewhere far away.

Marcus came in for his trumpet, saw her red-faced over the reed, and dropped into the chair beside her. "You're rushing the hard part," he said. "Everybody does. My teacher says don't pathologize it, it's just hands being slower than ambition." He pulled her metronome across the stand and dialed it down until the numbers stopped somewhere near the bottom.

"Sixty," he said, tapping the casing. "That means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second."

She had assumed practice meant playing it correctly at performance speed, over and over, until correctness took. That was her mother's philosophy, applied to piano at age eight and chemistry now: repetition at full difficulty builds character. Marcus believed the opposite, that you earned speed the way you earned trust, in small, boring increments, starting from wherever you actually were. She had always thought his way sounded like an excuse for going slow. Now she set her lips to the reed and played the passage with one note per tick, and it was so slow it embarrassed her, every sixteenth note landing on a second like a dropped coin.

But nothing tangled. The fingering that had been impossible was merely easy, and that difference felt like a trick being played on her. She raised the tempo by eights, and at seventy-two her tongue slipped on the turn, so she went back down, and the little weight on top of the metronome swung left and right through the silence like a tiny metronome of its own. Through the high windows the late light came down in a diaphanous column, catching the dust the percussive chaos of fourth period had left in the air.

"You know what my grandma says," Marcus said, feet up on a chair. "Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. Her whole generation is built on some aphorism like that." Nevaeh rolled her eyes at him, but quietly, because the saying had just proved itself on her own reed, and it was annoying when wisdom arrived in a form you could get embroidered on a pillow.

By the time the custodian's cart squeaked past in the hallway, she could play the passage cleanly at ninety-two, still short of the printed one hundred twelve, and she understood something she could not yet say in a sentence. Her mother's way was not wrong; the piece did demand eventual speed, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of cowardice. But speed was a result, not a method, and treating a method like a result was why she had spent three nights in a row quitting early and calling herself talentless. She could hold both ideas now without either one cancelling the other, though she still wasn't sure what to do on the days when slow practice stopped feeling like patience and started feeling like defeat. That part she would have to find out the same way she had found this out, one second at a time.

She packed the oboe, swabbing the bore, easing the reed into its little plastic coffin. At the door she paused, then went back, set the metronome to sixty, and played the sixteen bars once more, slow and perfect, the tick and the notes locking together like a latch.

"One beat per second," she said to Marcus, and turned out the lights.

The ice cream shop had a hand-lettered sign that said two scoops for the price of one on Thursdays, which was how Alyssa ended up on a first date that doubled, technically, as a discount. She had suggested Thursday herself, in a text she rewrote three times before sending, and now she sat at a wobbly table by the window watching the door and pretending to study the flavor board as though she might still change her order.

Marcus arrived four minutes late, holding the door for a stroller and then for a woman who wasn't going anywhere near the door, which made her like him and also made her nervous, because a person that courteous could not possibly be comfortable with the silence she was already planning to fill badly. He ordered cardamom pistachio. She ordered vanilla, then worried that vanilla made her sound like an ascetic, a person who had renounced pleasure entirely, and added rainbow sprinkles with the defiant air of someone making a point.

"You went simple," he said, sliding into the chair across from her. "Respect."

"I contain multitudes," she said, and he laughed, an actual laugh, not the polite exhale she'd been braced for.

The trouble was that she had prepared for this date the way she prepared for exams, which was to say she had researched it. Her sister had left a psychology textbook behind when she moved out, and Alyssa, unable to sleep the night before, had read a chapter on conversation while eating toast at one in the morning. One study had snagged in her mind. It was from 2018, by Erica Boothby and colleagues, and it had found something the researchers called a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. She'd read the sentence twice and felt briefly, unreasonably consoled, as if a fact could be carried into battle.

It could not, it turned out, be carried into battle, because halfway through her second scoop she knocked over the napkin dispenser, and while gathering napkins off the floor she said "flaccid" when she meant "flat," describing a book she'd read, and Marcus said "flaccid?" in a tone she spent the next several minutes trying to decode. He was cerebral, that much was clear; he'd brought up a documentary about Antarctic drilling and used the word "solvent" correctly. She kept up. She thought she kept up. She had no evidence either way, which was the entire problem.

"So this was fun," Marcus said when they were scraping the bottoms of their cups, and she heard the word "fun" as a formality, the verbal equivalent of a handshake. He paid for both of them despite her reaching for her wallet, and then he stood there outside the shop with his hands in his pockets, rocking slightly on his heels, and said, "Okay. Well. See you, maybe?"

"Maybe," she said, and watched him walk toward the bus stop without looking back, which she took as a verdict.

Walking home, she began the autopsy. There was the napkin disaster. There was the moment he'd mentioned a band and she'd said she'd "heard of them" in a voice that implied she had heard of them the way one hears of Luxembourg. There was the long pause after she'd asked about his brothers and he'd said it was complicated. She replayed each one, trying to suture the evening back together into something she could evaluate, and every seam she closed made the whole thing look worse. He hated it. Obviously. He said "maybe." People who liked things said things more definite than "maybe."

Then the fact from the textbook surfaced again, unhelpfully, like a lifeguard arriving after the drowning. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them. Usually. She stood on the curb outside the dollar store and had it out with herself. One voice said: you have direct evidence, Alyssa, you were there, you experienced every limp laugh in real time. The other voice said: you experienced yourself, not him. His experience happened inside his head, where you have never once been, and a study that went and looked inside people's heads found that the person doing the judging tends to guess low.

Both voices were hers, which was the annoying part. She could not dismiss either one. The evidence of her own memory said the date went badly; the evidence of the research said her memory was probably a biased witness. Somewhere between the two, a position assembled itself: she did not know how it went. She could not know, tonight, from here. What she could do was act as if the gap were real and see what happened, which felt less like confidence than like running an experiment on herself.

She took out her phone and typed, deleted, and typed again. "I had a good time. The flaccid thing will haunt me forever but the ice cream was solid." She sent it before the first voice could file an objection, then put the phone face-down in her jacket pocket and walked the last three blocks at a pace that pretended not to care.

On her street, half a block from home, the phone buzzed. She stood under the streetlight to read it. "I actually laughed so hard at flaccid that I almost dropped my cup. Also I got the wrong bus because I wasn't paying attention. Do you want to get ice cream again, or like, actual food?"

Alyssa read it twice. She looked up the dark street, then back down at the screen, and started typing, "actual food," with one thumb, while a moth circled the light above her head in patient, idiotic loops.

The debate about the third period had started, as most things in Mr. Okafor's classroom started, with Marcus leaning back in his chair and saying something he had not fully thought through. "If a president is doing a good job, why can't he just keep running? Wouldn't the people decide?" Mr. Okafor, who disliked answering questions he thought students could dismantle on their own, wrote parliamentary on one side of the board and presidential on the other, and said nothing. Jordan, three rows back, recognized the silence as an assignment.

Jordan wanted the scholarship to the summer program in political science, and the application asked for an essay comparing how a parliamentary system and a presidential system each choose and remove a head of government. He had written two pages already, both of them, he suspected, wrong in ways he could not yet name. Now Marcus had handed him the exact question his essay kept circling. He pulled his legal pad out from under his chemistry folder and began a list: PM chosen by the party, president chosen by the voters. PM removed by a vote of no confidence, president removed by impeachment. He stared at the list, waiting for it to become an argument, and it refused.

"Jordan," Mr. Okafor said, without turning from the board. "You've been writing for four minutes. Say something."

He had not expected to be called on, and the page in front of him was still just two columns. "In a parliamentary system," he said slowly, "the head of government isn't elected by the whole country. The party picks the prime minister, and the parliament can remove him whenever he loses their support. A vote of no confidence. So it's faster. But it means the voters never chose him directly."

"And presidents?" Marcus asked, still tipped back in his chair.

"Directly elected. Fixed terms. But here's what I keep getting stuck on." Jordan tapped his pen against the pad. "Removal is supposed to be hard. Impeachment takes a whole machinery, a whole process. It's not designed to be quick."

"Which is better?" Priya asked from the window row, and Jordan said, honestly, "I don't know yet," and a few people laughed, but Mr. Okafor didn't.

At lunch, Jordan found Marcus by the vending machines, holding a bag of chips he wasn't eating. "Your question this morning," Jordan said. "The popular president running forever. I looked it up during study hall. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice."

Marcus frowned at his chips. "So even if everybody wanted him?"

"Even then. Twice, and that's it." Jordan watched Marcus turn this over, watched him arrive somewhere. "So it's a third thing," Marcus said. "Not choosing, not removing. A limit that happens before either one. Like the system doesn't totally trust popularity."

Jordan wrote that down on his hand because his legal pad was in his locker. That afternoon, sitting on the bleachers behind the gym with the essay open on his laptop, he remembered his grandfather, who had told a story every Thanksgiving about a council in the village where he grew up, how the elders could stand up at any meeting and withdraw their confidence in the man who spoke for them, and how the speaker would simply walk home before dinner. Jordan had been eleven and had thought it sounded brutal. His grandfather had said, "It wasn't brutal. It was ordinary. He'd be back the next week, arguing again, just not standing in front." He had liked watching his grandfather introspect in that slow way of his, turning a memory over before releasing it. It occurred to Jordan now, with the laptop warm on his knees, that he had been raised on two vocabularies without noticing: the fixed and the flexible, the term and the confidence.

He tried to put both on the page. The presidential system, he wrote, makes the head of government rigid in office, protected by fixed terms and a difficult removal, and the parliamentary system leaves the same figure ductile, shaped continuously by the parliament that made him. Then he deleted "shaped continuously" because it sounded like a thesaurus. He kept "ductile" because it was the true word, and because the essay was supposed to sound like him.

His younger sister, Devi, found him there after her soccer practice, backpack still on, and read over his shoulder with the shamelessness of a ninth grader. "So the prime minister can just be fired? By his own people?"

"Not fired exactly. Removed. If parliament votes no confidence, he has to go."

"That seems worse for him."

"It might be better for everyone else," Jordan said. "That's the part I haven't figured out. Whether stability is the same thing as safety." He looked at the screen, at the sentence he had just typed, and left it there, unresolved, with a colon after it and nothing following, a small hole he had decided not to fill with something easy.

Mr. Okafor, passing the bleachers on his way to the parking lot, paused with his keys in his hand. "The essay for the scholarship?" he asked, and Jordan nodded. "If a pedagogue tells you the answer, it isn't yours," Okafor said. "I'm told I have a reputation. Try to keep my fingerprints off it." He walked on toward his gray sedan.

Devi sat down beside him, unzipping the backpack, producing two granola bars and handing him one. Jordan took it, typed a question mark into the hole in his paragraph, and then deleted the question mark too, leaving the sentence bare. Somewhere across the field the sprinklers came on, ticking across the grass in slow arcs, and he hit save.

The mock election was Mr. Okafor's idea, a dress rehearsal two days before the real one, and the classroom had been arranged into rows of folding tables with cardboard voting booths at the front, the kind borrowed from the county whenever the school ran out of ways to make civics feel urgent. Morgan had turned eighteen on the fourth of October, which meant that Tuesday would be her first actual vote, and she kept thinking about that with an odd, hollow excitement, like holding a ticket to somewhere she had never been.

The trouble began when Deshawn leaned across the aisle before the bell. "Half of us don't even show up," he said. "You know that, right? Young people. Everybody talks like our generation decides elections, and then half of us stay home."

"That's not true," Priya said, spinning in her chair. "It was way higher last time. Everyone voted."

"It was fifty percent," Deshawn said. "I read it somewhere. Half. Exactly half."

"You're making that up."

They looked at each other, and then, because there was no one else to ask, they looked at Morgan, who was known for checking things. She didn't know. She had a phone in her pocket and a number in her head that she couldn't verify, and the bell was ringing, and Mr. Okafor was already saying that the booths would close at the end of the period, forty-two minutes, and that every student who intended to vote in the mock election had to decide before then.

The debate section came first. Priya argued that low turnout among young voters was a myth spread by people who wanted youth to feel powerless, a way of keeping them quiet; Deshawn argued that if you couldn't be bothered to show up, your complaints were theater. Mr. Okafor moved between them like a referee, offering nothing. "Morgan," he said once, "you've been quiet." She said she was thinking, which was true but also a way of not saying she was calculating, because there was a second problem she hadn't told anyone about: her registration had been returned for a wrong apartment number, and the corrected form had to be postmarked by Saturday, and her father, whose car she needed, worked until six.

She asked to use the classroom computer for five minutes. What she found was a research center at Tufts University called CIRCLE, which had estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election. She read it twice. Half had come out, half had not, and the number sat strangely between Deshawn's cynicism and Priya's faith, refusing to belong to either. She wrote the figure on the whiteboard in dry-erase marker and stood back.

"Fifty percent," she said. "CIRCLE, at Tufts, for 2020. So you're both a little right, and you're both using it wrong." Priya protested that fifty percent was nothing to celebrate; Deshawn said it proved his point about apathy; and Morgan, feeling something assemble itself inside her, said no, it proved neither, because a number like that wasn't a verdict, it was an opening. If half showed up, the other half was not a fixed quantity. It was a margin. And margins could move.

"But which argument does the number support?" Priya demanded. The booths were open now. Students were filing forward, marking pretend ballots, and the countdown on the board said eleven minutes, and beyond the classroom window the October light was already going amber, and somewhere across town a post office would close at five tomorrow.

"Neither," Morgan said. "That's what I keep trying to say. You want the number to be a weapon, and it's not, it's a description. It tells you where we are. It doesn't tell you where we have to stay." She heard her own voice waver and pushed through it. "Deshawn, if turnout is only half, then the ones who do come are worth more, not less. Priya, if it's only half, then we can't pretend the work is finished. The same fact. Two directions. I think you hold both at once, and I think that's the honest position, and I'll admit I don't know how to make the other half move. I don't. But I know which half I'm going to be in."

She walked to the booth, pulled the cardboard flap shut, and marked the ballot in the blue pen that hung from a string. Then she came out, folded her paper into the collection box, and took out her phone. Three texts sat unsent to her father, drafted and deleted. She typed a fourth, asking him to leave work early, and added the address of the post office on Fenwick, and pressed send.

Deshawn was watching her from the doorway. "You actually registered," he said. It wasn't a question.

"Ballot's in the mail by five tomorrow," she said, "or it isn't." She shouldered her bag and walked past him into the hall, phone flat against her palm, waiting for the screen to light up.

The paycheque lay flat on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a bowl of unfinished cereal, and Ashton read it the way other people read the fine print on lottery tickets, which was to say suspiciously and from top to bottom. He had worked sixty-two hours over three weeks at Marconi's, the Italian place on Dundas where he bussed tables and refilled water glasses until his wrist ached, and the number at the top of the stub said $744. The number at the bottom said $623.51. He set the paper down, picked it up, and read it again.

"Mom," he said. "They took over a hundred dollars."

His mother was at the other end of the table with her own paperwork, a shoebox of receipts and a laptop she treated like a hostage negotiation, opening one tab at a time. "That's income tax," she said without looking up. "Federal and provincial. And there's CPP and EI on there too, probably." She had her own want this evening, which was to finish her tax return before midnight, because last year she'd filed late and the delay had eaten a month of her refund, and the refund was going to fix the dryer that had started making a sound like a dying accordion.

Ashton pulled the stub closer. The deductions were itemized in a font so small it seemed designed to discourage exactly the scrutiny he was giving it. Federal tax, provincial tax, Canada Pension Plan, Employment Insurance. Each line was only a few dollars or a few dozen, but together they had quietly subtracted $120.49 from what he'd understood to be his. He was saving for a used keyboard, a Yamaha someone in his building was selling for $600, and he had been counting his hours times his wage in his head all month, which now struck him as a kind of pleasant fiction.

"There's more of it everywhere," his mother said, almost cheerful about it, and slid a restaurant receipt across the table. It was from the dinner she and Ashton had grabbed after his shift on Friday, pasta for her, pizza for him. "Look at the bottom."

He looked. Total before tax, $34.50. Then a single line, HST, $4.49. Then total, $38.99. He frowned at it, because he'd expected two lines. He'd seen American receipts online, in the group chats where people argued about prices, and those had separate lines for state tax and whatever else. This one had only one.

"It's the Harmonized Sales Tax," his mother said, peering at it briefly. "Ontario combines the federal GST with the provincial sales tax into one thirteen percent line." She tapped the receipt with one finger, a gesture that closed the subject as far as she was concerned, and returned to her shoebox.

Ashton did the arithmetic on the back of an envelope, because there was a satisfaction in doing it by hand that he couldn't have explained and didn't try to. Thirteen percent of $34.50 was $4.485, which rounded to $4.49. One line, one rate, no split. So when he'd been telling his friend Deshawn that everything in this city cost some secret extra amount on top of the sticker price, he'd been right in a way, but wrong in the shape of it. It wasn't hidden and it wasn't layered. It was sitting there in the open, one line, thirteen percent, added to nearly everything he bought, which meant it was added to the keyboard too. Six hundred dollars was actually six hundred and seventy-eight. He sat back in the chair and stared at the ceiling, mesmerized less by the number than by the realization that the whole economy was speaking a language he had been hearing his entire life without translating.

"The return's asking if I want to answer all these questions about climate incentives," his mother muttered. "It's so prolix. Paragraph after paragraph for a checkbox."

"Then don't read it," Ashton said.

"I have to read it. If I check the wrong box I get a letter in April and then I panic until June." She rubbed her eyes. "Do yours."

"Mine?"

"You worked. You paid tax on income. You file a return." She turned the laptop toward him. "You probably get most of it back, you made almost nothing."

He had planned to watch videos and go to bed. Instead he pulled the laptop across the table, and for the next forty minutes the two of them worked in parallel, the shoebox slowly emptying on her side, his T4 slip, which he'd folded into his back pocket and sat on for a week, smoothed flat on his. The form asked him things he didn't know the answers to at first, and then, line by line, he found he did know them, because the answers were on the paycheque stub he had already interrogated. Income here, tax already paid there. The form subtracted one from the other in front of him.

He was halfway through when he stopped and reread the line about tuition credits and then a line about the disability amount for his mother, which he'd never considered, and a thought surfaced slowly, the way water moves through an aquifer, unseen and under pressure, arriving at a well nobody drilled on purpose. All month he'd been thinking of tax as a thing that was done to him, a subtraction, a hand in his pocket. But the return was running the arithmetic backwards, and the backwards arithmetic ended in his favour. He'd been counting his wages wrong the whole time, in both directions. The sticker price of the keyboard was bigger than the sticker. His paycheque was smaller than his pay. And the system that took from him in April gave some of it back in spring, or was supposed to, if you filled in the boxes and didn't panic until June.

"Eighty-one dollars," he said finally, leaning back.

"Refund?"

"Refund." He looked at the number on the screen, then at the paycheque stub, then out the dark window toward the building across the lot where the Yamaha waited in somebody's basement. Six hundred and seventy-eight with the tax. He had $520 saved, plus the eighty-one coming, plus two more shifts this week. His mother submitted her own return a few minutes later, closed the laptop with ceremony, and announced that the dryer was going to live.

"I thought this stuff was going to be boring," Ashton said, stacking his envelope, his stub and the receipt into a pile and squaring the edges against the table.

"It is boring," his mother said. "That's not the same as useless." She stood, then paused with her hand on the back of her chair. "What's the keyboard cost again?"

"Six seventy-eight," he said. "One tax line. I checked."

The news broadcast came from a laptop balanced on Grandad's kitchen table, where the smell of burnt toast still hung in the air. Felix had come to the house for two quiet days of revision before his politics entrance interview, and instead the lower house of some parliament he couldn't yet locate on a map was voting, live, on whether its government still had its confidence. He watched the division numbers crawl up the screen. The government lost.

"So what happens now?" he asked, because Grandad was the only other person in the house and the question had to go somewhere.

"Dunno. New prime minister by Friday, I'd have said." Grandad buttered a second slice of toast without looking at the screen.

"That's the thing," Felix said. "I don't think that's right." He pulled his notebook toward him, the one with the comparison charts he'd been building for three days, and felt the floor of his preparation tilt. His interview was in forty hours. He was supposed to argue which system was better at choosing and removing a head of government, presidential or parliamentary, and he had written two pages on the presidential side because it was the side he actually knew. He had watched that side his whole life. Fixed terms, a single name on a ballot, a removal process so long and so rare it had only ever been a paragraph in his textbook. He had written almost nothing about parliaments because they confused him, and now one was falling apart on the table in front of him.

He called his mother first, but she was in a meeting. Then he sat on the back step with the laptop and read, properly read, the coverage. The losing prime minister would not simply be replaced by Friday. A government that lost this kind of vote in the lower house, the reporters kept repeating, had to resign or call a general election. He said it aloud once, to the wet garden and the pigeon on the fence. "Has to resign, or call a general election." Not maybe. Not usually. Has to. The whole cabinet, the entire government, because one chamber had stopped believing in it, on an ordinary Tuesday.

He took it back inside to test it against Grandad, who was filling in a crossword in biro. "Say the president we've got," Felix said. "Say congress just decided, tomorrow, that they'd stopped trusting him. Nothing happens, right? He serves out the term."

"Good," said Grandad. "I voted for the man, not for four hundred other men. Your lot over there, they can chuck a government out on a whim."

"Except it's not a whim, it's a vote, and the government's gone the same day." Felix heard the argument assembling itself, faster than he could write. "And it works the other way too. They chose that prime minister through parliament, not through us. You get the head of government the legislature will tolerate, and you lose them the moment it won't."

Grandad tapped his biro twice. "And I'd rather have a lemon for four years than a revolving door."

"That's actually the trade," Felix said, and it came out before he'd checked it, and then he sat with it. He'd spent three days trying to pick a winner and here, between the toast crumbs and the crossword, was the actual shape of the thing: one system underwrites stability with a fixed term you can't shorten, the other underwrites accountability with a removal you can't refuse. He couldn't have both. Nobody could. He wrote that in the notebook, then crossed out "nobody could" because it sounded too much like wisdom and he hadn't earned it yet.

Later they watched the evening bulletin together, the follow-up, the same chamber half empty now. Grandad was quiet through it, which Felix had learned meant thinking rather than agreement. On the screen a junior minister was being interviewed on a street corner, saying the words "no confidence" as if everyone watching had been born knowing them, and Felix realized his nascent command of all this, forty hours old and borrowed from a Tuesday broadcast, would have to be enough.

"They'll call the election," Grandad said at last, not asking. "They always do, eventually."

"Or resign," Felix said. "It's one or the other. That's the rule." He closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again, because he wanted to keep the picture of that chamber in his head: the doors, the counting, a government ending on a voice vote. His interview would ask him to defend a side. He still didn't know which side he'd defend, only that he finally understood both, and that somewhere between the fixed term and the fallen government there was a position he could hold honestly, even if he couldn't yet say it out loud.

He went back to the notebook and wrote, at the top of a clean page, "Which do I actually believe?" Grandad put the kettle on and said, from the kitchen, "You'll want tea for this part."

The volunteer office at the community center smelled of burnt coffee and old construction paper, and by August Justine had habituated to both so completely that she only noticed them on Mondays, after the weekend scrubbed her senses clean. She had taken the summer job because the application for the state scholarship wanted three hundred hours of service, and because her mother had said, gently, that sitting at home revising her personal essay for the fourth time was not the same as living. She filed forms, restocked the snack table for the after-school program, and answered the phone when Mrs. Alvarez, the coordinator, was mid-crisis with a printer.

The crisis that Wednesday was bigger than a printer. Mrs. Alvarez stood at her desk with a legal pad covered in crossed-out lines, pressing the phone between her ear and shoulder while she typed. "No, the picnic is still on," she said. "Yes, we moved it to the twentieth. I'm emailing all the families right now, this afternoon, before anyone else calls." She hung up, rubbed her eyes, and pulled a spreadsheet toward her. Fifty names. Justine knew the number because she had alphabetized that spreadsheet herself two weeks earlier, sorting the parents of every child in the summer program by last name while Mrs. Alvarez taught a CPR refresher in the gym.

Justine carried a stack of permission slips across the room, and as she set them down she saw the email taking shape on the screen. The cursor blinked in the To field, and Mrs. Alvarez was pasting the whole column of addresses in a single block, one name after another, fifty addresses marching across the line like a train with no end. Something in Justine's chest tightened, though she could not immediately have said why. She thought of her own mother, who guarded her email address the way some people guarded their house keys, and who had once spent an afternoon unsubscribing from everything after a school newsletter went out with every parent listed in plain view.

"Mrs. Alvarez," she said. Then, when the coordinator looked up, "Sorry. Quick question about that email."

"It has to go out in ten minutes, Justine."

"I know. It's fast, I promise." Justine leaned toward the screen, careful not to touch anything. "If you put all fifty addresses in the To field, every parent who gets it can see every other parent's address. People who don't know each other." She had learned this the hard way in the spring, when a group organizing her college visit weekend had sent a message with forty addresses exposed, and a man named Gerald had replied to all, twice, about parking. "If you use Bcc instead, the recipients are hidden from everyone else. Nobody sees anybody's address but their own."

Mrs. Alvarez's hand stopped on the mouse. "Blind copy," she said slowly, reading the field label as if seeing it for the first time in twenty years of emails.

"That's the one. You put one address, yours or the office's, up in To, and everyone else down there." Justine pointed at the row of small letters stacked along the edge of the compose window. "Fifty parents who've never met can't end up with each other's information."

For a moment Mrs. Alvarez did not move, and Justine braced herself. She had heard the coordinator argue with the fire marshal about occupancy limits; she had watched her go belligerent with a vendor over spoiled fruit, chin out, refusing to yield an inch. But now the woman only exhaled, long and tired, and said, "I've been sending these lists for three summers." She said it without defensiveness, more to herself than to Justine, the way a connoisseur of her own mistakes might catalogue a flaw in a favorite painting. "Three summers, and nobody ever said anything."

"Maybe nobody wanted to correct you," Justine said. "You're kind of the boss of the building."

Mrs. Alvarez laughed, a short sound that cracked into something warmer. She highlighted the long chain of addresses in the To field, cut it, and pasted it into the Bcc row instead. Then she typed her own address at the top, checked the subject line, and paused. "The picnic's still the twentieth. You think I should say that first, before anything else, so nobody skims past it?"

"Yes. Short paragraphs. And maybe put the rain plan in its own line so people can find it without reading everything." Justine pulled a chair around beside the desk, not waiting to be invited, and read over the draft as Mrs. Alvarez reshaped it: the date up front, the potluck request on its own line, a courteous closing that thanked parents for their patience with the scheduling change. Where the draft had said "as previously indicated," Justine suggested "as we mentioned last week," and Mrs. Alvarez nodded and made the change without fuss.

The send button sat there, gray and patient. Mrs. Alvarez rested her fingers above the keyboard and glanced at Justine. "Anything else I'm about to get wrong?"

Justine smiled and shook her head, though privately she held a small uncertainty in reserve, a wondering about whether some parents might have wanted to see each other's names, might have wanted the picnic to be a place where lists of strangers became a community. She did not say it. Some things could stay unresolved until the replies came in.

Mrs. Alvarez clicked send, and the fifty addresses folded themselves invisibly into the dark.

The festival smelled of fried dough and cardamom, and Arianna kept one hand on her phone in her pocket like something she was guarding from her mother. She had told her, twice on the drive over, that she had already checked the academic calendar, that Eid would fall safely after finals, that there was no conflict at all. This was true in the sense that she had thought about checking it very hard while lying on her bed the night before.

"Smile at least," her mother said, handing her a paper plate of kebab. "People will think you're here under arrest."

"I'm smiling."

"You're displaying the general arrangement of a smile."

Her little brother Sami had already disappeared toward the henna tables, and her father stood near the stage with the other uncles, arguing happily about something that would end in someone buying everyone tea. Arianna took a bite and felt the torpid weight of the whole school year settling over her, the exams that began Monday, the history outline she had not written. She had counted on June. Eid had been in June last year, blazing and easy, the whole block closed off for the parade, and she had assumed, the way you assume the tide stays where you left it, that it would stay.

Her phone buzzed. She turned her shoulder away from her mother.

From Nadia: ok don't panic but the exam schedule came out. Your history final is Tuesday morning. From Nadia: which is Eid. From Nadia: I'm sorry. I know you said it moved after exams.

She read it three times. Around her, children were chasing each other between the folding tables, and a man at the sound system was testing the microphone, and nothing about the festival had changed at all except that it had happened in the wrong season, arriving like a guest who keeps earlier appointments every year.

Her mother was watching her, though, so Arianna typed back: I'll email the teacher tonight. There's a policy for religious observance. It'll be fine. She put the phone away. She was not going to ruin her mother's one good day this month over a scheduling problem she had created herself, because that was the part she was beginning to admit: nobody had moved Eid. Eid moved. Someone at the volunteer booth, an older girl she half knew from the mosque, had said it casually last summer, that the calendar ran on the moon and came ten or eleven days earlier every year, so Ramadan would slide backward through spring and then winter before anyone noticed. Arianna had nodded and filed it nowhere. If she had filed it, she would have known June was never coming back.

Her mother took the empty plate from her. "You have that face."

"What face."

"The one you had at nine years old when you broke the vase and rearranged the shelf to hide it."

"I don't have a face," Arianna said. "I have a situation."

Her mother walked with her to the edge of the festival, past the banner strung between two lampposts, past the aesthete uncle who was photographing the lanterns from six angles and complaining that the string lights had been hung without any sense of rhythm. At the curb, the noise dropped away and they could hear traffic again, the ordinary city going about its Saturday.

"Tell me," her mother said.

"History final is Tuesday morning. It's Eid. There's a form I can file for religious accommodation, but I have to do it Monday, and I have to actually study this weekend, which is this weekend, meaning now." She heard her own voice compress everything into logistics, delimiting the problem neatly so it wouldn't spill into anything larger. "And I told you it wasn't a conflict. I told you I'd checked. I didn't check. I decided it."

Her mother was quiet for a moment. Down the block, Sami came running with a smeared henna design on his palm, shouting that he'd gotten a lion, and it looked more like a duck, and their father was laughing somewhere behind him.

"So file the form," her mother said. "And study tomorrow, and study Sunday, and Tuesday morning you take the exam and Tuesday afternoon you eat like a horse. You think this is the first time Eid landed somewhere inconvenient? Ask your grandmother about fasting through final exams in Karachi. Ask her about fasting in July." She straightened Arianna's collar, a small unnecessary adjustment. "You're not in trouble with me. You might be in trouble with the registrar, but the registrar doesn't make kheer."

"I'm sorry I lied," Arianna said. "Sort of lied."

"Sort of is the only way anyone lies," her mother said, and started walking back toward the music.

Arianna stayed on the curb a moment longer and opened her email, thumbing out a draft to the history teacher, requesting the accommodation form, deleting the apology, putting it back in. Behind her the microphone crackled to life and someone began the call to gather everyone for the afternoon prayer, the old words rising over the bunting and the paper lanterns, and she pressed send.

The flyer had been taped to the gym door since September, curling at one corner like a leaf that refused to fall: Spring Trip, Washington D.C., $640, deposits due by February. Ava stopped in front of it every day on her way to fifth period, and every day the number sat there, patient and indifferent, the way numbers are. She had $212 in a savings account her grandmother had opened when she was nine, and four months.

At lunch she spread the problem in front of her friend Denise like a hand of cards. "If I put in eighty a month from my paycheck, that's what, three-twenty plus the two-twelve. I'm still short." She tore the crust off her sandwich and lined the pieces along the table's edge, sedimentary layers of bread, each one settling on the last. "Unless it grows somehow. Does money in savings grow?"

"Mine has interest," Denise said, thumbing through her phone. "Like point-something percent. My mom calls it sad money. It grows, but slowly."

"Slowly how?" Ava leaned over. On the screen, a calculator app, and Denise typed in numbers with the flat authority of someone who had done this before, which she had, because Denise's mother made her balance the family checkbook as punishment for various crimes. "Two hundred at two percent," Denise said. "Four dollars a year. It doesn't just add four forever, though. After the first year it's two-oh-four, and the two percent works on that. So the next year it's a little more than four."

Ava sat back. The interest fed on whatever was there, and what was there kept getting bigger, so the interest kept getting bigger too. "So waiting is worth something," she said slowly. "Even boring waiting."

That afternoon her brother Marcus picked her up in the Camry he'd bought in August, used, from a lot off Route 9 with flags snapping in the wind. He was twenty-one and treated the car like a wound he was proud of. At a red light he pulled his phone from the cup holder and frowned at it, and Ava, who noticed everything when she was curious and nothing when she wasn't, noticed the frown.

"What."

"They sent the loan statement." He held it out. Four payments made, it said, and beside it the remaining balance, and Ava did the subtraction in her head and then did it again because the answer didn't move. He'd paid almost seven hundred dollars and the balance had dropped by barely more than three.

"That can't be right." She took the phone and scrolled, as if the missing money might be hiding further down. "You paid seven hundred and it only went down three-something?"

"That's what the guy said it would do," Marcus said, gripping the wheel as the light turned. "Each payment's interest gets charged on what's left, so the early payments mostly go to interest. Later they go more toward the actual loan." He said it flat, like reciting a scar. "Front-loaded. I didn't really get it until I saw it."

Ava looked at the statement, then out the window at the strip mall sliding past, the nail salon, the payday loan place with its neon OPEN sign, the bank with its quiet stone front. Two directions, and money traveling both. In the savings account, interest landed on a balance that grew, so the growth fed itself. In the loan, interest was taken first, off the remaining balance, so the balance she and Marcus actually wanted to shrink shrank slowly at the start, faster later, like something paying its dues before it was allowed to leave. She didn't know yet whether the two were opposites exactly, or only mirror-ish, and she held the question the way you hold a stone you intend to look at again later.

"Could you pay extra?" she asked. "Toward the balance part?"

"The principal. Maybe. I'd have to ask."

"Ask." She handed the phone back. "Because if extra knocks the balance down early, then there's less for the interest to feed on the whole way. That's how it works, right? Less there, less charged."

Marcus glanced at her. "When did you become a bank."

"I need six hundred forty dollars by February and I'm trying to think like money does."

He laughed, short and surprised. In the driveway she sat in the car a minute longer after he took the phone inside, doing arithmetic on the fog of the window with her fingertip. Eighty a month, plus what she had, plus whatever the interest added, and it wouldn't be enough, probably, unless she picked up Shira's Saturday shifts at the bakery, and she was still deciding whether she wanted the trip more than she wanted the Saturdays. Inside, Marcus called out, "Hey, I'm calling the loan place," and she wiped the numbers away with her sleeve and went to hear what they said.

The parking lot behind the shuttered Kmart still had its lines, faded to the color of old milk, and Justine's father had chosen it for exactly that emptiness, arriving at seven on a Saturday so no one would see her stall the car. His own want was barely concealed: he had waited sixteen years for a child old enough to want the keys, and he had spent the drive over narrating his father's driving habits as though handing down scripture. Justine knew he wanted this hour to be a thing they shared, an inheritance, and she half wanted that too, which made it harder when she didn't.

Her friend Priya had ridden with her to the lot, sprawled in the back seat with a slushie, and had already issued her doctrine. "Two seconds," Priya said, leaning between the front seats. "You count one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, and if you pass the same spot before two, you back off. Two is plenty. My brother taught me and he's never had a ticket."

"Three," her father said, not turning around. "At least three seconds."

"That's what old people do," Priya said, and sucked loudly at the straw.

He eased the car to the far end of the lot and they swapped seats, and Justine put her hands where the instructor poster said ten and two, though her father immediately said nine and three was better now, and she changed, feeling the day begin to accumulate small corrections. She let off the brake too fast and the car lurched, and she laughed the way you laugh to keep something else from happening in your face. Her father only said, "Again," in the voice he used when he was trying very hard not to be the kind of man who yelled.

For a while it was only starts and stops, the wheel surprisingly light in her palms, the lot a slow geometry of turns. Then her father pointed at the service road beyond the lot's broken gate, two lanes of Saturday traffic, and said, "You're ready for that." Priya said, "She's not," and he said, "The lot doesn't teach you anything but the lot." Justine pulled out anyway, because she wanted the road more than she wanted to be careful, and it was on the road, behind a hatchback with a mattress strapped to its roof, that the two doctrines collided.

"Count it," her father said. "Pick a line on the pavement, a sign, anything fixed. When the mattress car passes it, start counting. See how long until you reach it."

"One-one-thousand, two-one-thousand," Justine said under her breath, and reached the painted arrow before she finished the second. She eased off the gas until the count ran to three and felt the road widen around her, the hatchback shrinking into something she could think about instead of react to. Priya made a scornful noise from the back, and Justine said nothing, but she noticed that when a drizzle started, beading on the windshield faster than the wipers could sweep it, three seconds felt suddenly small.

"It's raining," she said. "Does that change it?"

Her father was quiet a moment, in the way of a man checking whether he actually knew. "You add a second for each difficulty," he said. "Bad weather, heavy traffic. So rain makes it four."

"Who decided that?" Priya demanded.

"The National Safety Council recommends it," he said, which was the most authoritative thing he'd said all morning, and also the least like him, a borrowed certainty. Justine counted to four behind the mattress car and watched the gap open, and thought that Priya's two seconds were not exactly wrong so much as made for a world with no rain in it, and her father's three were not exactly right so much as made for a world where everything might go wrong at once. The truth she could hold was somewhere between: the count wasn't a number you learned once, it was a number you earned again with every new thing the road did.

She would have liked to say this out loud, some announcement of her own perspicacity, but the moment for announcements passed; the light ahead turned yellow and she braked harder than she meant to, and the car behind them honked, and Priya said, "See, that guy was at two," and her father laughed before he could stop himself. Justine realized he was not laughing at her. It was the honk, the rain, the mattress, the whole rattling pageant of the road, and he looked younger than he had at breakfast.

Later, back in the Kmart lot, the rain stopped and they sat with the engine ticking. "Again next Saturday?" he said, and she heard how carefully casual it was, how much it mattered to him that she say yes, as if the lessons were a way of inculcating something larger than driving, some habit of counting and looking ahead that he wanted planted in her before September took her three hundred miles away. She said yes. But when she dropped Priya at home that afternoon, Priya leaned in the window and said, "Two seconds, Juste. Don't let him turn you into a paranoid." Justine put the car in drive, found a seam in the pavement, and counted, under her breath, all the way to three.

The gown was too hot before the ceremony even started. Jason stood in the staging area behind the football field bleachers, among two hundred classmates arranged in alphabetical order, waiting for the band to begin. The person beside him, a girl named Priya whom he knew only as the one who beat him in eleventh grade calculus by half a point, was humming under her breath, and it took him a moment to recognize the tune.

"That song," he said. "Do you know where it actually comes from? I've heard it at every graduation since kindergarten and I never once asked."

"Pomp and Circumstance, March Number One," she said. "Edward Elgar. It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool."

He looked at her. "How do you know that?"

"My grandfather played trumpet. He told me the first time I hummed it, which was apparently the same age you were when you started wondering." She said it without smugness, the way his calculus teacher used to say a lemma, a small stepping stone you proved on the way to something larger, and you either knew it or you didn't. Jason had spent four years trying to know things like that. Priya had spent four years knowing them without visible effort.

His phone buzzed in the pocket under his gown. His father: On my way. Traffic on Route 9. He read it twice, then put the phone away. His father had said he was on his way to the regional science fair in tenth grade too, and to the playoff game last spring, and neither time had the arrival actually occurred. There had been a period, after the divorce, when his father claimed to be nearly destitute, and Jason had believed it, and then had seen a photograph of a new truck on his uncle's phone. He didn't know what to do with the contradiction then and he didn't now. He wanted his father in the bleachers. He also wanted to not care whether his father was in the bleachers, and those two wants had been living in him all morning like tenants who refused to speak to each other.

The band started. The sound came across the field thin and slightly late, the way sound did outdoors, and the line began to move. Priya walked ahead of him, alphabet working itself out with perfect indifference to anything either of them had ever done. Jason followed. He thought about the march itself, how something written in 1901 in Liverpool had crossed an ocean and installed itself in every gymnasium and football field in North America, how nobody in the ceremony had chosen it and yet everyone was walking to it. It seemed to him that most of his life so far had that quality. The colleges, the applications, the courses he'd taken because they stacked correctly on a transcript. He had chosen his path the way the school chose its processional music, by inheritance.

He found his chair. The speeches began. The principal enunciated every word carefully, as though the microphone were a stranger she was being formally introduced to, and Jason sat with his hands folded and watched the gate at the far end of the field. A man in a green shirt arrived at the gate and was stopped by an usher, and Jason's whole chest tightened, and then the man turned and it was nobody, some uncle of somebody, and the tightening loosened into something he didn't have a name for.

They called names. Rios. Roberts. When it was his turn he crossed the stage, shook the hand offered to him, took the leather folder, and looked out once at the bleachers, at a blur of hats and sunglasses and small waving hands, and could not tell anything from it. He descended the stairs on the other side and sat down again in the section of chairs reserved for the already-graduated.

Afterward, in the parking lot, gown unzipped, his father was leaning against a car that was not a new truck but not a destitute man's car either. He was holding a grocery-store bouquet, carnations, the kind of thing bought at the last possible minute, and Jason understood that the man had missed the walk itself, the whole processional, Elgar and all, and had arrived in time only for the part where his son already had the folder under his arm. His father raised the flowers slightly, an offering, an apology, an admission, impossible to tell which. Jason stood there holding everything he had decided in the bleachers, that it didn't matter, and everything he had decided on the stage, that it did, and found that he could hold both and still walk.

"You missed the music," Jason said. "It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool."

"Then I'll hum it," his father said, "if you tell me how it goes."

The parking lot behind the middle school still had the faded cones from summer, and Grayson's grandfather sat in the passenger seat adjusting the mirror as though the mirror were the thing that had to be taught first. "Both hands at nine and three," he said. "And if you ever have to stop fast, pump the brakes. Pump them till you stop. That's how I taught your mother, and she never put a dent in anything I paid for." Grayson nodded, put the car in drive, and let it roll forward over the painted lines while his grandfather hummed something without a melody.

That had been two weeks ago, in the same family sedan his mother was now sliding into the driver's seat of, a driving instructor named Mr. Okafor already waiting by the lot entrance with a clipboard. He was quiet in the way of a man who had spent thirty years watching teenagers discover the width of their own bodies, and he didn't stigmatize the nervous ones, which Grayson appreciated, because his cousin had failed twice and everyone at the dinner table had treated it like a character flaw rather than a bad Tuesday. "You've had some practice," Mr. Okafor said, reading the form. "Ten hours." He handed Grayson the keys. "Show me a left turn out of the lot, then we'll take the road by the canal."

The road by the canal was narrow and tree-dark, and Grayson drove it at the speed of a person carrying something breakable. He thought of his uncle Danny, who called himself a car guy but had never changed his own oil, a dilettante in coveralls, and who had once told Grayson that modern cars did everything for you anyway. His grandfather, on the other hand, was genuinely sagacious about most things, taxes, tomatoes, the temperament of dogs, and yet on this one subject he had been firm. Pump the brakes. Grayson had said nothing at the time, because at sixteen he had said nothing at the time about a lot of things.

They had done lane changes and a three-point turn when Mr. Okafor asked him to pull over and swap seats, and it was while Grayson was checking the mirror for the hundredth unnecessary time that the dog came. It came out of the reeds at the canal edge, low and fast, a brown shape with no collar and total commitment, and it crossed the road maybe four car lengths ahead. Grayson's foot went to the brake the way his grandfather's voice had trained it, and it started to come off, to pump, and then it didn't. He pressed down hard and held it there, and the pedal made a sound like grinding gravel and shuddered against his foot, and while the car was still slowing he turned the wheel, gently, the way you'd turn a doorknob, and the sedan came around the dog with a lane's width to spare and stopped on the shoulder, ticking.

The dog stood in the road, looked at them, and trotted back into the reeds as though it had an appointment. Mr. Okafor's hand, which Grayson now noticed had been hovering near the wheel the whole time, returned to his knee. "You okay?" Grayson said, "yes" before his voice caught, then, "yes," for real. The shuddering in the pedal had frightened him more than the dog had. He sat with his hands at nine and three and asked, because he wanted the man's answer rather than the internet's, "That noise, that's the anti-lock brakes?"

"That's them working," Mr. Okafor said. He looked at Grayson a moment longer. "Where did you learn to do that? Most students pump."

Grayson told him about the parking lot, the cones, the humming. He told him that afterward he had gone home and read the owner's manual cover to cover, which was the kind of thing he did and had decided at some point to stop apologizing for, and that the manual had said to press firmly and hold it, not pump, that these cars had anti-lock brakes and you could keep steering even while braking hard. His grandfather's advice was from a different car, a different decade, given with total confidence. "He wasn't wrong for his car," Grayson said. "He's just still driving it." He heard how that sounded, like a judgment about more than brakes, and let it stand there without deciding whether he meant it.

"He taught you everything else, though," Mr. Okafor said. "Nine and three. Checking the mirror. You did all of that before you touched the brake." He made a note on his clipboard. "Ready to drive back?"

Grayson pulled onto the road. He was thinking that his grandfather would want the whole story tonight, would want to know what the pedal had felt like, and that somewhere in the telling Grayson would have to say that the advice had been out of date, and he did not yet know whether to say it like a correction or like a discovery he happened to have gotten to first. Both might be true. The canal slid past on his side, bright where the sun got through the trees.

At the lot, his mother was leaning against her end of the sedan, phone down, watching them come in. Mr. Okafor got out and said something to her that Grayson couldn't hear, and she laughed, then pressed her hand flat over her mouth the way she did when she was about to cry instead. When Grayson parked and cut the engine, she opened his door before he'd fully stopped moving. "Ten hours," she said. "Your grandfather says four was plenty in his day."

Amy had claimed the good corner of the couch an hour before kickoff, which her brother Danny considered an act of war and which she considered strategy, and now the room was filling up anyway: Danny, their dad, the Nguyens from next door, and Amy's nine-year-old cousin Theo, who arrived carrying a pillow like a shield.

"Giants," Theo announced, "are going to win by a thousand."

"That's not a score anyone can achieve," Danny said, taking the last pretzel.

"It's a vibe," Theo said, and Amy laughed so hard she almost spilled her drink on the remote, which would have ended the game for everyone and made her, briefly, the most hated person in the living room.

The trouble started on a third down in the second quarter. The Giants, down by four, needed six yards, and the yellow line glowed across the field like a strip of raked sunlight. Theo leaned forward, squinting at the screen.

"Why is it yellow?" he asked. "Is it slippery?"

"It's paint," Danny said. "They paint it on the grass."

"They repaint it every first down?" Amy said. "With what, a very fast man and a very long brush?"

Danny shrugged. "Groundskeepers. Professionals."

Amy looked at the line. The camera cut to a sideline shot, then back, and the yellow appeared again, perfectly straight, perfectly placed, following the field like it knew where the sticks were. She thought of her physics teacher, who liked to say that the most rationalism ever achieved by humankind was probably hiding inside a television broadcast, unthanked. If the line were paint, it would smudge when a player slid across it. She had watched receivers slide across it all season. It never smudged.

"Theo," she said, "when the camera zooms in on a player standing on the line, what happens?"

Theo watched. A receiver caught a pass exactly at the yellow stripe, and the camera pushed in tight, and Theo's mouth opened. The yellow wasn't on his shoes. It wasn't on the grass, not really; it was just there, under him and over him and somehow not anywhere at all.

"Whoa," Theo said.

"Whoa what?" their dad said, looking up from his nachos.

"The line's not paint," Theo said. "It's a ghost."

Amy already had her phone out, thumbs moving, because she was the kind of person who could not leave a ghost uninterrogated. She read, and read again, and then held the phone up like a trophy.

"The yellow line is computer-drawn," she said. "It's not on the field at all. It only looks like it is."

"Then where does it come from?" Theo demanded, as if she had personally installed it.

"A company called Sportvision," Amy said, reading. "And get this. The first broadcast with it was ESPN, September 27, 1998."

"That's before I was born," Theo said, in the tone of a man discovering the earth was older than his house.

"That's before Danny was born," Amy said.

"Barely," said Danny, who was twenty and sensitive about it, and the Nguyens' dad said, "Barely is doing a lot of work in that sentence," and the room broke up laughing, even Danny, eventually.

Here was the thing Amy kept turning over while the fourth quarter tightened and everyone shouted at a holding call: she had been wrong about being wrong. She had assumed Danny's explanation was lazy but harmless, the kind of small untruth that underwrites family peace, and instead it had sent Theo believing in magic paint, and it had sent her, for years, never once asking. The lie wasn't deleterious because it hurt anyone; it was deleterious because it was comfortable. She liked knowing things. She liked it less, she was discovering, to notice how many things she'd absorbed without checking, and she could not decide whether that made curiosity a virtue or just a habit with better marketing.

"Ames," Theo whispered, during the two-minute warning, "if the line's not real, is the game real?"

"The game's real," she said. "The line's real too. It's just real somewhere else."

"In the computer?"

"In the computer."

Theo considered this with the seriousness of a philosopher nine years into a hard problem. "So the players can't see it."

"Nope."

"That's so sad. They're just guessing."

"They're not guessing," Danny said. "They have the actual chains on the actual field. The yellow line is for us. We're the ones who needed help."

"A ghost to help us," Theo said, satisfied, and settled back into his pillow.

The Giants drove to the twelve and stalled, and kicked a field goal to tie it, and Theo declared this unacceptable, and Amy found she was smiling at the screen where the yellow stripe lay across the grass like something the world had agreed to pretend. On fourth and one, with eleven seconds left, her dad stood up, blocking the television entirely.

"Dad," everyone said at once.

"Who's thirsty?" he asked, not moving.

Jasmine had never once been wrong about money, which is why she kept the receipts. She kept them folded in the front pocket of her binder, every Tim Hortons cup and drugstore lip balm, because Ms. Ferreira had said in September that sales tax showed up on receipts whether you looked at it or not. 13 percent in Ontario, blended into the total or listed beneath it, and Jasmine had started seeing it everywhere, a quiet subtraction attached to nearly everything she bought. She was the kind of person who noticed. She told herself she was the kind of person everyone else wished they had around.

The business classroom smelled like dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust. Third period, Grade 12 accounting, and Ms. Ferreira was walking them through a sample paycheque projected on the whiteboard: gross pay, then the deductions carved out of it, income tax withheld, employment insurance, Canada Pension Plan. Net pay sat at the bottom in a smaller, sadder number. "This is not the money you earned," Ferreira said, tapping the gross. "This is the money you get to keep." Danny Kowalski muttered something about robbery, and half the class laughed, and Jasmine didn't, because she was copying the paycheque into her notes with the concentration of someone transcribing scripture.

The unit ended with a field trip to the bank on Ridgeline Avenue, which was really just a walk with permission slips. It was March, refund season, and the branch had put up a curling banner about fast refund deposits. While they waited for the tour to start, Danny stood at the counter beside his older sister, who was cashing her return. When she came back to the cluster of students she was grinning, holding up her phone with the deposit confirmation. "Eighteen hundred bucks," she said. "Free money, baby. Like winning the lottery."

Jasmine felt the correction rise in her before she'd finished deciding whether to say it. "It's not free money, though," she said. "Not extra income either. It's your own money coming back. If you get a refund, it means more was withheld from your pay during the year than you actually owed. It's an overpayment being returned." Danny's sister looked at her the way people look at a red light they didn't want. "Whatever," she said. "It showed up in my account. Felt free to me." Danny excoriated Jasmine all the way back to the school, not cruelly but at volume, calling her the tax police, the receipt girl, asking whether she itemized her birthday cards. She let him. She was right, and being right, she had learned, cost a certain amount of being liked at any given moment.

The part she didn't say out loud, walking back with her hands in her pockets, was the part she wasn't sure about. Her father had been explaining his own return at the kitchen table the night before, forms spread across the counter like a dissection, and he had seemed pleased about his refund too, in a way that suggested she might be missing something. If the money was only ever hers, why did getting it back feel like a windfall to everyone she'd ever met? Maybe there was a whole phylogeny of how people related to their own money, some evolutionary tree of feelings about it, and she occupied a lonely branch. She'd read that word in biology that morning, phylogeny, and liked it, and liked even less admitting that Danny's sister's happiness might be as legitimate as her accuracy.

The following Monday, Ferreira handed back their unit projects. Jasmine's was the paycheque analysis, hers marked ninety-four, with a note in green pen: "Careful with tone when you correct people. Accuracy is not the same as persuasion." She read it four times. She had assumed the note would say something else, something admiring, and for a second she genuinely could not tell whether Ferreira was wrong or whether she was.

At lunch she found Danny's sister outside the bank, back for something, standing near the creek that ran behind the plaza, the riparian strip of dead grass and crushed reeds marking where the water rose in spring. Jasmine had her binder with her, receipts still in the pocket, though she wasn't sure anymore what she planned to do with them. "Hey," she said. "I wasn't trying to ruin it. The eighteen hundred." Danny's sister shrugged, scrolling her phone. "You didn't ruin it. I already spent it." Then, pocketing the phone, she said, "You know what I mean, though. All year it's gone, gone, gone, and then one day it comes back."

Jasmine looked at the creek, at the grey water moving under the last of the ice, and didn't answer, because both things were true and she couldn't yet say how. Danny's sister started walking toward the bus stop, and Jasmine stood a moment longer, then opened the binder and smoothed one receipt flat against her knee, the sales tax printed small at the bottom, and put it back.

Vincent had forty-one tabs open, but only one mattered. It was the dashboard his school had rolled out that September: every student's name in a column, and beside each name a number that shifted, sometimes hourly, according to how the district's new system scored their behavior on school accounts. The system watched logins, typing cadence, flagged words in email drafts, even how long a cursor idled over a page before scrolling.
