The vote was called, and Victor watched the clerk tally the standing bodies in the aisles. Twenty-two for, seven against. A majority, an ordinary miracle, accomplished without anyone changing their mind about anything except him. Priya declared the bill passed, and the house moved on to the next order of business before his pulse had slowed.

The closing ceremony simulated royal assent. The Speaker, an actual retired MLA who had agreed to attend, sat beneath the carved provincial crest and read the titles of the bills that had survived the weekend, Victor's among them, in a flat ceremonial voice. "The bill receives assent and is now law," she said, and there was a small smattering of applause, mostly from parents who had drifted in for the last hour. Victor stood with the others while the Sergeant-at-Arms carried the mace out of the chamber, the old brass catching the light, the whole thing over.

Outside, in the parking lot, the evening had gone cold and the real buses were already idling. Ellis was loading a duffel bag into a minivan. "Your law's got a hole in it," he called across the asphalt. Victor shrugged into his jacket. "So does every law," he said. "I read the rest of the order paper." Ellis grinned and shut the van door, and Victor stood a moment longer listening to the engines.

The summer research slot came down to one afternoon in the optics lab, and Makayla had planned for it the way she planned for exams, which was to say too much and then sleep badly. Forty seniors from her school were rotating through the university's physics building in groups of six. Her group had drawn the spectroscopy bench on the third floor, where a graduate student named Corinne handed each of them a printed card and told them to record what they saw through the eyepiece.

Priya went first. She looked for a long time and wrote "faint dark lines, maybe three, hard to say." Then Corinne tapped the card and said, "For this demo, you're looking for bright emission lines in the green region. Four of them." Priya leaned back in, and within thirty seconds her pencil was moving. "Oh, yeah," she said. "Four. They're right there. I don't know how I missed it."

Makayla kept her eyes on the bench while the other four took their turns. Every one of them saw four lines after being told to expect four. When her turn came, she looked before Corinne said anything to her, and she saw what Priya had seen at first: dark lines, indistinct, count uncertain. She wrote that down. Corinne read it, then read it again.

"Interesting," Corinne said. "You're the only one who recorded dark lines."

"I wrote it before you told me what to look for," Makayla said. "Does that matter?"

Corinne didn't answer directly. She pulled a stool over and sat, which the other grad students in the room did not do. "Have you heard of René Blondlot?" she asked the group. Nobody had. "A French physicist, claimed to discover a new kind of radiation. He called them N-rays."

"Like X-rays," said Dario, the boy next to Makayla.

"Right. In 1904 another physicist, Robert W. Wood, went to Blondlot's lab and secretly removed a key prism from the apparatus. The observers still reported seeing the N-rays." Corinne stood up and straightened the eyepiece. "Wood didn't announce what he'd done until after. That's the part people remember."

Makayla turned her card over. On the back, in the margin, she had written her prep notes that morning, half of them definitions she'd exhumed from an old textbook in the school library, because the research program's application asked for a short essay on "how we know what we know." One of the notes said logos, from her English class, argument that persuades by reason. She had underlined it twice. Now the word looked thin to her, like it assumed reason was a thing one person could hold whole in one hand.

"Is this demo rigged, then?" Priya asked. There was an edge in her voice, and Makayla understood it. Priya had already emailed the program coordinator saying the lab visit confirmed her interest in optics.

"It's not rigged," Corinne said. "The lamp is exactly what I said it is. The question is what a single observer is worth."

Makayla thought about that on the walk to the next station, and she thought about it through the boring part of the tour, the clean room with its yellow light, and the part where Dario asked whether the university had ever retracted a paper. One result wasn't anything, she'd known that in an abstract way, but she hadn't felt it until Priya's pencil started moving. Still, she wasn't sure the feeling was fair. Priya wasn't lying. Corinne's tip about the green lines was presumably true, and Priya's second look was presumably better than her first. Expectation could point you at something real. The problem was that the pointing and the seeing felt identical from the inside, and only one of them counted as evidence.

At the bus turnaround she caught up with Corinne, who was carrying a crate of extension cords to a van. Makayla said she wanted to apply for the slot and asked, since it would come up in the essay, whether Corinne thought a study should be thrown out when the observers knew what they expected.

"One observer, one afternoon? That was never a study," Corinne said. She shifted the crate to her hip. "You'd repeat it, other people would repeat it with different instruments, people who wanted you to be wrong would repeat it. Then you'd know something."

"Unless they were all expecting the same thing," Makayla said.

"Then it takes longer," Corinne said. She loaded the crate and shut the van door.

On the bus Makayla wrote two sentences in her notebook and crossed out the second one, which had claimed too much. The first said that she had seen dark lines and had no way, from inside her own head, to certify them, and that the certification would have to come from outside her, repeatedly, from people with no stake in what she'd written. She looked at Priya two rows up, headphones in, filling out the program's online form on her phone. Priya typed fast, and stopped once, and looked out the window at the loading dock, and then typed again.

The pay stub was thin paper, the kind that turned soft with sweat in a back pocket, and Lea read it twice under the fluorescent glare of the warehouse break room. Wages, overtime, and then a line she had never noticed before her eighteenth week of summer work: union dues, eleven dollars and change, taken off like tax. She had never joined anything. She had signed one form, the day she was hired, and a woman named Carol had checked her forklift certification and pointed her at aisle nine.

"You look like someone stole your lunch," said Marcus, dropping onto the bench across from her with his own stub held up to the light. He was twenty, quiet most of the time, with a scar on his forearm he never explained.

"Someone's taking money off my pay and I didn't sign up for it."

"It's called the Rand formula." He said it the way he said aisle numbers, flat, obvious. "Justice Ivan Rand, 1946. Came out of the Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario. Everyone covered by a union contract pays dues, whether they joined or not."

Lea turned the stub over as if the back might hold more. Outside the loading bay doors, trucks reversed in long beeps, and the dock plates clanged down one after another. "That doesn't seem fair," she said, and meant it, and also heard how young it came out.

Marcus shrugged. "Wage scale's fair. Overtime after forty-four hours is fair. You think this place gives that out of the goodness of its heart?" He tore the perforated edge off his stub and rolled it between his fingers. "My first year, before I understood anything, I resented it too. Then I watched the committee argue down the speed-up on the sort line, and it cost them three weeks of meetings after shifts, and they still showed up. I decided to internalize it differently. Dues are the price of the door staying open. Most of the time you don't see what the door is for."

The subtext sat between them, heavier than the words. Lea knew her mother had worked non-union at a laundry through her whole childhood, no pension, no wage scale, let go in a slow November with two weeks' pay and an apology that meant nothing. Her mother had put whatever she could into an annuity in those years, small deposits, disciplined ones, and she still called it the thing she was proudest of, because it was hers alone, because no committee had voted on it, because nobody could take it back. Two houses, two ways of thinking about what safety looked like. Lea had grown up inside the second one and was standing in the first.

She spent her lunch walking the long corridor to the union board, a corkboard thick with paper: minutes of meetings, a grievance about heat in the summer, the wage grid with its neat ascending rows, the shift premium, the safety clause about ventilation that someone had highlighted in yellow years ago. Carol was there tacking up a notice, and Lea asked her, half a question, whether the eleven dollars bought anything for someone who was leaving for university in September anyway.

"Your contract covers you while you're covered," Carol said. "That's all it promises. The rest is longer than you." She tapped the wage grid. "Kid before you, kid after you, same rows. You pay into the rows, you get the rows. You go, and it keeps going."

That night Lea sat on her bed with the stub flattened on her knee and thought about her mother's annuity statement, the tidy column of deposits, hers alone. The dues were the opposite kind of thing: money that went out into a common account she would never see itemized, spent partly on her, partly on strangers, partly on people not yet hired. Her mother would call that a bad bargain. Marcus would call it the only reason the bargain existed at all. Lea could not decide which was truer, and suspected the honest answer was equivocal, that the same deduction could be theft or inheritance depending on which month you looked at it.

In the morning she pinned the stub above her desk, next to the acceptance letter. At the end of her last shift, Marcus met her at the time clock with two coffees, and they drank them standing in the bay while the first truck of the night backed in, its beacon sweeping the concrete. "You never came to a meeting," he said. "I know," Lea said, and watched the dock plate fall.

The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and warm paper, and the air conditioning reached only the first three feet of the room, so Carter's collar was damp by the time he reached the teller line. He had forty dollars folded into his pocket, two twenties that had been one twenty until this morning, and a question he had been rehearsing since he left the house. Ahead of him a woman argued softly about a hold on a check, and the word liability drifted back over the velvet rope as though the bank itself were made of such words.

The teller who waved him forward was young, maybe twenty, with a name tag that said Priya and a lanyard heavy with pins. "Opening an account?" she asked. "Student checking takes ten minutes. You'll need to read the terms and conditions, and there's a signature card at the end. That's the consent part, basically. Your signature is you agreeing."

"I sold something," Carter said. "For twenty dollars. And I want to know if I can undo it."

Priya glanced at the queue behind him, three deep now, and lowered her voice. "Sold what?"

He told her about the bike, though telling it meant going back to yesterday evening, to the gravel drive beside Mr. Aldous's garage where the light had gone long and orange and the tire of the racing bike had spun slowly in his hand. Mr. Aldous had come out with his watering can, looked at the bike leaning against the fence, and said, "I'd give you twenty for that." Carter had needed twenty dollars. Not wanted, needed, by Friday, for the deposit on the cabin trip everyone had already paid, and the offer had seemed like a small synchronicity, the universe sliding the solution across the counter at the exact hour of his desperation. He had shaken on it right there, gravel gritting under his sneakers, the watering can dripping a dark coin of water onto the concrete.

"It's worth three hundred," Carter said now. "Maybe more. I checked online last night."

Priya pulled a blank deposit slip toward her and turned it over, as if the answer might be printed on the back. "Was it a fair price?" she asked, and when he shook his head she said, almost to herself, "Under common law, consideration just has to have some value. It doesn't have to be a fair price." She slid the slip back. "Courts don't sit around judging whether you made a good bargain. I'm doing law at night school, that's the only reason I know. Was it cash? Did you sign anything?"

"He wrote it on a napkin. From his porch. Both our names."

"Then it's signed."

The room seemed to tilt a little, the way it had in fourth grade when he learned that the sun would eventually swallow the earth, a fact too large to feel anything about in a carpeted building at eleven in the morning. Behind him a man cleared his throat. Priya's eyes went to a screen only she could see, some counter of accounts opened today, and Carter understood suddenly that she had a number to hit too, that everyone in the building was standing inside some bargain whose terms they had agreed to without reading, himself included. The whole morning had a turbid, stirred-up feeling, like the creek after rain, everything he thought was settled now moving in the water.

"Ten minutes for the account," Priya said. "It's a good one, no monthly fee if you keep a balance. And you should still go talk to him. He can undo a deal if he wants to, that's different from having to."

He opened the account because the twenty, folded and warm from his pocket, had nowhere else to live, and because the signature card waited with its empty line like a small door. He read the terms and conditions while Priya typed, the clauses rising off the page in a gray procession, liability limited, conditions subject to change, and he signed at the bottom and felt the pen drag slightly, leaving his name in blue ink, and thought of the napkin with both names on it in Mr. Aldous's careful draftsman's hand.

He walked home the long way, past the creek, and cut up Mr. Aldous's street without quite deciding to. The bike was there, leaning against the porch railing, polished, the chain oiled, the seat adjusted higher, which meant someone had ridden it already or meant to. Mr. Aldos came out with his watering can and saw him standing at the edge of the drive.

"I've been thinking about that price," Mr. Aldous said, and set the can down on the step.

"So have I," said Carter.

The essay question sat at the top of Addison's laptop screen like an accusation: Is it possible to describe the past without taking a side? She had come to her grandfather's house for the weekend because the internet at home was down, and because her mother had said, gently, that Grandpa could use the company.

The house was spartan since Grandma died, the spare furniture arranged as if for inspection, the study still crowded with boxes nobody had opened. Addison set up at the kitchen table while her grandfather washed the same pan he had washed before lunch. She had found the quote in her notes from class. In 1824, the German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past "as it actually was", rather than to judge it or instruct the present. Her job was to decide whether that was even possible.

"How's the paper?" her grandfather asked, drying his hands.

"Fine." She closed the laptop halfway. "Do you have any old letters? Like, from when you were young. Primary sources. My teacher wants primary sources."

He was quiet long enough that she thought he hadn't heard. "There's a box in the study. Your grandmother's side of the closet."

The study smelled of cedar and dust. Addison found the box under a stack of tax returns: bundled letters, a photograph album, a newspaper clipping from 1968 with a crease down the middle. She carried it to the kitchen table and began sorting, and her grandfather stood at the counter with his coffee, not quite watching, not quite not watching.

The clipping was about a student protest at his university. The article called the organizers "disruptive elements" and quoted the dean at length. There was no quote from any student. Addison turned the clipping over. On the back, in her grandmother's handwriting, was a single line: He was there. Ask him what he saw.

"Grandpa. This protest. Were you there?"

The coffee cup stopped halfway to his mouth. "That was a long time ago."

"That's not an answer."

He set the cup down. "I was there. It wasn't what the paper said."

She thought of a night three years ago, before Grandma got sick, when the two of them sat on the porch and Grandma told stories about her brother, the one nobody else mentioned, who had written pamphlets and lost his job for it and moved away. The family, Grandma said, had spent thirty years trying to exculpate themselves, as if his opinions were a crime they could prove they hadn't committed. Addison had looked up from the porch steps to see her grandfather standing inside the screen door, listening, saying nothing, going back to the dishes.

"The paper says the protest turned violent," she said now, tapping the clipping.

"The police turned it violent. Some kid threw a bottle, maybe. Then they waded in. I got pushed against a fence. A girl next to me got hit with a baton." He said it flatly, the way he said things that cost him. "The paper printed the dean's version. Nobody asked us."

Addison opened her laptop again. "So the newspaper is a primary source and you're a primary source, and they don't match."

"That happens."

"So which one do I believe? You're my grandfather. I want to believe you. Doesn't that mean I've already taken a side?"

He almost smiled. "Sounds like your paper's writing itself."

"It isn't." She pulled one of the letter bundles toward her. They were Grandma's letters to her sister, dated that same spring. Addison skimmed, stopped, read one twice. In it, Grandma described the protest, the fence, the baton, the girl, and one more thing: a list of names being circulated, students identified as organizers, and one of the names was her brother's, though the article had said nothing about any list. Addison looked up.

"There's a list in here that the newspaper never mentioned."

"Your grandmother kept everything." His voice had gone careful. "Even things that were dangerous to keep."

"That's why she wrote it down. Because the paper wasn't going to."

He sat down across from her, slowly, and for a while neither of them spoke. Outside, a mower started two houses away.

"So Ranke," Addison said, mostly to herself, and her grandfather raised an eyebrow. "This historian. He wanted to show the past as it actually was. No judging, no lessons for the present. Just what happened."

"The fence was real," her grandfather said. "The baton was real."

"But which things got written down, and which didn't, that's a choice somebody made. Even Grandma chose. She saved the clipping and the letter together, like she knew one wasn't enough."

She typed for a while, then stopped. "Here's my problem. If I only use the newspaper, I've taken the dean's side without meaning to. If I only use you and Grandma, I've taken yours. And if I use everything, somebody still decided what everything was."

"Then say that."

"Say what?"

"That you don't know for sure. That's what your grandmother would have said." He stood, took his cup to the sink, ran water over it. "She'd have made you put the clipping in the paper, though. Face up."

Addison flattened the crease with her thumb, then let it fold back along its old line. She set the clipping beside the letter, side by side on the table, and opened a fresh page.

"Can I copy the letter?" she asked. "The whole thing?"

"Take the box," he said, and turned off the tap.

Nicholas had never been inside a courthouse before the morning he was assigned to argue both sides. The marble corridor smelled like floor wax and old paper, and his shoes made a sound on the stairs that seemed too loud for the building's hush. In his messenger bag he carried two sets of notes, one for the school district and one for the student, because Coach Reyes had drawn his name for the hardest format: each speaker at the regional mock Supreme Court tournament would have to argue the case twice, once as petitioner, once as respondent, and be credible both times. The case was a real one. A high school student had posted something angry on Snapchat over the weekend, off campus, and the school had punished her for it, and the Supreme Court had taken up whether that punishment was allowed.

He found his team's bench near the windows, where the crepuscular light of the late afternoon would eventually arrive, though right now it was only ten in the morning and everything was flat and bright. Priya was already there, highlighting a printed opinion with a green marker as if green could make the law grow clearer. "You got Mahanoy?" she asked. "Lucky. It's only the most important student speech case in decades."

"That's what I keep reading," Nicholas said, though luck was not how it felt. He had spent the whole week trying to hold two contradictions in his head at once, and instead of clarifying, they had coagulated into something thick that he could not pour into an argument. The school side said adults had to supervise teenagers who were cruel to each other. The student side said a snap sent from a bedroom on a Saturday was nobody's business but the sender's. He believed both, depending on the hour.

Their first round was called at eleven, in a courtroom with a real judge's bench and a retired judge sitting behind it, smiling at them the way people smile at pigeons. Nicholas stood, squared his notes, and argued for the school district. He talked about teams and morale and the way a cheerleading squad was a small biome, its own fragile ecosystem of trust that a toxic post could collapse. The judge nodded once. Priya passed him a note that said "good," which was the highest compliment available.

Between rounds, in the hallway, a girl from another school sat alone on the wide stone steps, scrolling her phone with her thumb moving fast, the way you scroll when you are looking for something and afraid of it. Nicholas recognized her from the pairings sheet. "You okay?" he asked, because it seemed like the thing to ask, and she looked up with the guarded face of someone much younger than sixteen.

"I made a post last weekend," she said. "About my coach. It was stupid, but I didn't think it was illegal stupid. My school suspended me Tuesday." She turned the phone toward him and then pulled it back before he could read anything. "So I looked up whether the Court ever said anything. Mahanoy. Mahanoy Area School District versus B.L., 2021. The Supreme Court ruled eight to one that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Eight to one. That's basically everybody." She said the case name carefully, like a spell she had memorized in case she needed to say it out loud to an assistant principal.

Nicholas sat down on the step beside her, not too close. He had been carrying the case around all week as an exercise, a tournament problem, a thing to be sliced into arguments, and here it was sitting on a stone stair in the body of a girl with bitten nails. "I have to argue against you in about twenty minutes," he said. "The school's side. It's a mock thing, but I still have to say the words." She laughed, one syllable, surprised out of her. "Then say them," she said. "I want to hear if they're any good."

At one o'clock he stood at the podium again, this time for the student, and the words came differently, or the same words came with different weight, and he could not decide afterward whether the difference was in the argument or in himself. The judge asked him whether schools should have no authority at all over weekend posts, and Nicholas said no, that was not his position, that he did not know exactly where the line was, and that the Court itself had left the boundary unsettled. It was, he understood as he said it, a strange way to win, by admitting the map had blank spaces. When the round ended, Priya squeezed his shoulder, and the girl from the steps was standing at the back of the courtroom, arms folded, waiting for him at the doors with her phone in her hand.

The marble steps of the courthouse were slick from rain, and Sophia climbed them with her binder pressed against her chest, the one holding two sets of notes she had not yet managed to reconcile. Inside, the mock court would convene in forty minutes. She was arguing Tinker v. Des Moines reimagined for the digital age, a fictional case in which a student, suspended for an online post, claimed her First Amendment rights were violated, and Sophia had drawn the unlucky position of preparing both sides.

Her partner for the respondent, Marcus, was already in the lobby, leaning against a radiator that looked like something salvaged from an antiquated ship, all valves and dull brass. "You look like you didn't sleep," he said.

"I didn't. I keep finding holes in my own case." She opened the binder to show him: her petitioner pages argued that the school had punished speech, which the government could not do; her respondent pages argued that the platform hosting the post had removed it first, before the school acted. She had underlined a sentence three times and then crossed it out three times.

"Which side do you actually believe?" Marcus asked, and she hated the question, because last spring she had organized a walkout and then told a younger student, briskly and with total confidence, that the website deleting their event page was a First Amendment violation. She had said it into a microphone. She had been wrong in front of two hundred people, and no one had corrected her, because no one knew.

"Neither," she said. "Both. That's the problem."

They went up to the courtroom, where rows of folding chairs faced a bench borrowed from a real judge's chambers, dark wood, scarred. Other students milled around in blazers that did not quite fit. Sophia found her seat and read her opening lines again, mouthing them.

When her turn came, she stood and argued for the student: schools are arms of the government, the First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech, and punishment for a lawful post was state action, pure and simple. The student judges leaned forward. One of them, a girl with a pen behind her ear, scribbled something. Sophia felt the argument hold, solid and warm, like a wall she could put her back against.

Then the presiding judge said, "Ms. Okafor, the post was also removed by the platform itself. Does your client have a claim against them?"

Sophia opened her mouth to say yes, and the words from last spring rose up, the microphone, her own certainty, and she stopped. Across the room Marcus gave her a look that was almost kind. "No," she said slowly. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It does not by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. The platform is private. My claim is against the school alone." The judge with the pen nodded and wrote for a long moment, and Sophia sat down with her heart knocking, because she had just handed the other side a gift.

When they switched, she stood to litigate the respondent's position herself, and it was stranger than she expected, dismantling the wall she had built an hour before. She offered the counterpoint gently: schools may regulate speech that substantially disrupts learning, and the post had caused a hallway confrontation the day after it appeared. She believed it, in this room, under these lights. She had also believed the opposite. Both could not be true, and yet each had felt true while she argued it, and that frightened her a little, the way a smooth floor frightens you when you first feel it give under your shoe.

Afterward, in the corridor, the younger student from the walkout, Priya, was waiting by the water fountain. "I saw the case summary," Priya said. "The part about the private website. Is that why our event page came down last year? Nobody did anything illegal?"

Sophia looked at her, at the binder under her own arm, at the rain streaking the tall windows. "That's not what I said," she answered. "I said nobody could sue over it as a First Amendment claim. There's a difference." Priya's face did something complicated, and Sophia did not know yet whether she had made it better or worse, so she held out the binder, opened to the crossed-out sentence, and let Priya read it for herself.

Eric had promised himself he would finish the hallway drawing before fifth period ended, and he had forty minutes left, a pencil sharpened to a needle, and a hallway that refused to be a hallway. It lay on the paper like something flattened by a steamroller, a row of lockers marching across the page with the depth of a filing cabinet. He had drawn the drinking fountain three times. Each time it sat on top of the lockers instead of beside them, like a very clean frog.

"You've redrawn that fountain so many times it's going to ask for a contract," said Priya from the next stool, not looking up from her print of crows. She and Eric had a running arrangement: she critiqued his drawing, he critiqued her titles, and both of them ignored the teacher's suggestion that they critique their own work for once.

"The hallway's broken," Eric said. "It's a hallway for people with no depth perception. Flatland High School."

Priya leaned over, held her pencil at arm's length against his paper, and squinted like a pirate. "Everything's parallel. Your lockers are all the same size, and the door at the end is the same size too. That's why it looks like a poster for a very boring school."

He knew she was right, and he hated how right she was, because he had spent two nights on the tile pattern alone. The tiles. He had drawn a hundred tiles, each one exactly, obediently square, and somewhere in the back of his mind a suspicion had been forming that the tiles were the traitors. When he stood in the actual hallway, the far tiles looked smaller. He had never once drawn them smaller. He had, apparently, been running a hallway according to his own private laws of geometry, laws the hallway had never agreed to follow.

He flipped to a clean page and started over, this time being sneaky about it. He drew one point in the middle of the paper and then, feeling like a con artist, made the locker edges run toward that point like they were late for a bus. The tiles shrank as they went. The door at the end came out small, and strange, and then, all at once, deep. The hallway opened like a drawer sliding out of the page. He sat back so fast his stool squeaked.

"Whoa," Priya said. "What did you just do?"

"I don't know. I made the lines go toward one spot." He tapped the point with his eraser. "It's like everything's running away from the viewer to hide back there."

"That's a thing," Priya said, already pulling out her phone with the guilty speed of someone who knew the teacher would confiscate it in a heartbeat. "My brother did a report on it. Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. Drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point, to show depth on a flat surface."

"So I accidentally invented it in an art room in Ohio."

"You're about six hundred years late and an ocean short, but sure, Columbus it however you like." She grinned. "Brunelleschi would be furious that you tried to expropriate his idea with a number two pencil."

"It's not expropriation if I didn't know it existed. It's independent rediscovery. It's very dignified."

The teacher drifted past, looked at the new drawing for a long moment, and said only, "Better," which from her was a standing ovation, and moved on. Eric looked at the vanishing point and felt both pleased and slightly cheated. He had wanted to invent something, and instead he had reinvented something, which meant either that he was six centuries late or that the idea was so true that a seventeen-year-old with a mechanical pencil could stumble into it on a Tuesday. He could not decide which of those he preferred, and the point itself, that small dot where the whole hallway went to disappear, gave him no help at all.

"Draw the drinking fountain now," Priya said. "It can finally live beside the lockers instead of on them, like a civilized amphibian."

Eric positioned his pencil, then paused. "One problem. If everything runs to the point, the fountain's edges have to aim there too, and it's off to the side. Do I give it its own point?"

"That's not a problem, that's Thursday."

He laughed, sharpened the pencil again, and began the fountain for the fourth time, angling its lines carefully toward that one small dot at the end of the hall.

Rose found the notice taped to the circulation desk of the public library, between a flyer for toddler story hour and a laminated map of the county bus routes. First-time volunteers welcome, it said, Saturday, seven a.m., dress for mud. She had been meaning to do something that wasn't school, something that would look less like a line on an application and more like a fact about her, and she had been circumspect about which something, because she distrusted her own motives and didn't want to be the girl who photographed her own kindness. She copied the address onto the back of a receipt and checked out a novel she would not read.

Saturday came cold and clear. The food bank's van waited in the library parking lot, which served as the meeting point, and beside it stood a man in a canvas jacket counting heads on a clipboard. Eleven volunteers, most of them older than Rose, all of them strangers. The man, whose name was Teodoro, drove them out past the edge of town to a farm where the squash field had already been picked over once by the crew that mattered, the paid crew, the main harvest.

"You'll see squash out there still," Teodoro said as they stepped down into the rows. "Anything you gather goes to the food bank. It's called gleaning." He said it the way he might have said the word for a bird or a tool, and then he handed out crates and gloves and walked off toward the far end of the field.

The rows were messy in a way Rose hadn't expected. The plants lay half flattened, and under them the squash had gone pale where the ground had touched them, scarred where a machine had brushed past. She picked one up, turned it over, and hesitated over a soft brown patch the size of her thumb. Whole or not whole. She looked up to ask someone and saw that the other volunteers had already scattered, bent and working, their crates filling without ceremony. Nobody was going to tell her. She set the blemished one aside and kept the rest.

Dana, the volunteer nearest her, was maybe sixty and moved with the ease of a person who had done this many seasons. "Soft spots mean it won't store," Dana said, not looking up. "Hard ones are just ugly. People think food bank means perfect produce, and then it rots in the field because nobody paid for it." Rose asked whether the farmer couldn't sell it, and Dana shrugged one shoulder. "After the main harvest, what's left isn't worth the labor to him. But it's still food. So we come." Rose worked that around while she worked the row. It seemed to her a strange economy, that a thing could be worthless and good at the same time, and she tested the idea against each squash she lifted.

By mid-morning the problem found them. The crates were full, more than half the field still unpicked, and the van had room for only what was crated. The second shift, Teodoro announced from the end of the row, had fallen through, so whatever they didn't get today would be disked into the soil on Monday. Rose watched the volunteers glance at each other, at the sun, at their phones. One by one they began to say they had things, errands, a granddaughter's recital. Teodoro didn't argue. He began stacking crates with the flat efficiency of a man preparing to lose.

Rose had been quiet all morning, and quiet people can sometimes say a thing plainly. "We don't all have to stay," she said. "Some of us could keep picking while the van runs the first load over. Then it comes back for the rest." Dana looked at her, then at the field, then at Teodoro. Teodoro turned his clipboard over as if the answer might be written on the back.

From where Dana stood, it looked like this: a girl of eighteen, mud to the knees of a jacket too thin for the weather, holding a scarred squash in both hands like evidence in a case she was still arguing with herself. Dana had spent enough years in this work to know that schemes hatched at eleven in the morning often died by noon, and she was not going to flatter the girl by pretending otherwise. But she had also spent enough years to know that a full crate driven to the pantry at noon fed someone at six. "I'll stay for the second round," Dana said. "I've got nothing until four." Two of the recital people, cajoled less by Teodoro than by their own shame, muttered that they could stay an hour, and the numbers on the clipboard stopped being a countdown.

The van went loaded and came back empty in time for lunch. Rose's arms ached in a way that felt specific, one muscle for lifting and another for bending, and she had learned that a soft spot was a judgment and an ugly skin was nothing at all. She still wasn't sure, when she thought about the morning, whether she had done a good thing or a merely sensible one, or whether there was a difference, and she decided she would have to come back another Saturday to find out. She stood at the tailgate stacking the last crates, and Dana handed her a squash with a long green scar down its side. "Perfect," Dana said.

Jacob checked the mailbox at 4:15, the way he had every afternoon for nine days, though the mail never came before five. The box was empty except for a coupon circular and a water bill, and he stood there holding the little door open as if another letter might materialize behind the first one. His father had installed the mailbox at the edge of the gravel drive fifteen years ago, sinking the post in concrete, and over time the ground around it had turned friable, so that the whole thing listed toward the road like a man listening for something. Jacob straightened it every so often without thinking. Today he held it upright while he counted the days left before the state university's reply deadline, which was not really a deadline at all, just the last day he could say yes.

The letter, when it came, would be the fourth. Two colleges had already said no, and one had said yes but wanted thirty-eight thousand dollars a year, a figure he had read aloud to his mother and then never mentioned again. The state university was the one he could actually pay for, more or less, which was why his older sister, Dani, had taken over the kitchen table for the past three nights.

He could see her through the window when he came back up the drive, hunched at the laptop with their mother beside her, both of them lit by the screen in the dark kitchen. They were filling out the FAFSA, the form for federal financial aid, and Dani kept explaining it to him in fragments whenever he passed through. "It's how you get the Pell Grant," she said once, not looking up. "Federal money you don't pay back. And federal loans, the ones with the better rates." Another night she added, quieter, "It's not just the federal government. The state uses it too, and the colleges themselves. Almost everybody bases their aid on this one form." Their mother typed the tax numbers with one finger, then two, then asked Dani to read the line back. The state's aid deadline was tomorrow at midnight, and Dani wanted her own answer, a transfer out of the community college and into the nursing program, and that want was tangled up in the same form, the same numbers, the same parents' income.

Jacob had spent the whole application season telling anyone who asked that it was simple math. You ranked the schools, you weighed the costs, you picked the highest expected value. He called it rationalism, half as a joke, when his uncle asked at Christmas how he was choosing. But the math kept refusing to stay simple. The yes for thirty-eight thousand sat in his desk drawer, and every time he opened the drawer for a pencil he felt the weight of it, and he could not make it into a number that behaved. He wanted the big school the way you want a person, which was to say irrationally, and he wanted to be the kind of person who didn't want things that way.

On the ninth night, near eleven, Dani called him into the kitchen. "Read this," she said, and turned the laptop toward him. The form wanted to know whether their parents had filed a joint return, and then it wanted a figure from line something of that return, and their mother had gone to bed with a headache, leaving the question half answered and the deadline two hours off. Jacob found the return in the filing cabinet himself, his hands steady in a way his stomach was not, and read the number while Dani typed it. "So the aid just follows from this?" he asked. "One form, all of it?" "Federal, state, the schools' own money," Dani said. "It all starts here." She hit submit at 11:41 and then sat back and put her hands over her face, and Jacob stood there awkwardly until she said, through her fingers, "Go check the mail. Just in case."

There was nothing, of course. But he stood at the box in the cold anyway, and it was there, with the post leaning against his palm, that he understood something he could not have put in an essay. The form Dani had just filed was a machine for turning one family's circumstances into money, and the machine did not care what he deserved or what he dreamed. That should have made him feel reduced. Instead it felt almost like being absolved. The choice had never been only his; it had been made partly by tax returns and deadlines and whatever Pell Grants added up to, and he could stop treating the wanting as a personal failing.

He came back in and found Dani at the sink, drinking water, the kitchen dark again except the light over the stove. "I decided something," he said. "If the state school takes me, I'm going. The thirty-eight thousand one, I'm letting it go." Dani set down the glass. "Last week you said it was worth the debt if you got in." "Last week I was doing math with feelings and pretending they were numbers," he said. She laughed, a short surprised sound, and then grew serious. "Then maybe I can stop feeling guilty about wanting the nursing program," she said. "Mom keeps saying we can't both." Jacob shrugged. "The form says what it says. We'll see what it says."

The next afternoon he walked down the drive at 4:15 again, knowing better, and stopped anyway when he saw the white edge wedged among the coupons. The envelope was thin, which the internet said could mean anything. He carried it back to the porch steps and sat down with it unopened on his knee, and from inside the house he could hear Dani at the kitchen table, already back on the laptop, looking up the nursing program's aid page. He slid his thumb under the flap and lifted the edge, and the porch boards creaked under him as he leaned forward to read the first line.

Jessica's father tossed her the keys the way he might have tossed her a softball, underhand and unremarkable, and she caught them against her chest in the driveway while the June heat pressed down on the both of them. She had turned seventeen two weeks earlier, which meant she could finally predicate her independence on a piece of plastic from the DMV, but first she had to survive her father's teaching, and she knew from her cousin that this was no small thing. He had already reorganized the passenger seat three times, moving a water bottle, then a phone charger, then the water bottle back, as though the car's interior were a paragraph whose syntax had to be exactly right before anything could proceed.

"Seat, mirror, seatbelt," he said. "In that order, every time."

She adjusted the rearview mirror until the whole rear window sat inside its frame, then leaned sideways to fix the left mirror, and he watched without correcting her, which felt like a kind of applause. The engine started louder than she expected. She eased the car down the driveway with her foot hovering over the brake the way a pianist hovers over a wrong note, and they rolled out onto Farrow Street, where the speed limit was twenty-five and the maple branches made a shifting ceiling of light.

"The steering wheel isn't a suggestion," her father said after a hundred yards of small, anxious corrections. "You can commit."

So she committed, and the car straightened, and for three blocks she understood what everyone had been talking about. The whole street opened up in front of her. She could see the crosswalk ahead, the stop sign, the woman walking a dog, and she signaled for a right turn and took it wide, then tighter, and her father said "better," and she believed him.

They turned onto Miller Road, which had two lanes in each direction, and her father told her to get into the right lane for the turn at the pharmacy. She checked the right mirror. Empty road, silver and still in the afternoon glare. She put on the signal and began to drift over, and her father's hand came off his knee and pressed the wheel back toward its lane, and at the same moment a blue hatchback slid past on her right, close enough that she could see the driver's face, a college-aged guy mouthing something at her through his window.

"Whoa," she said, or something like it, her pulse in her ears. "I looked. I looked in the mirror."

"There's a spot the mirror can't cover," her father said. "Called a blind spot. You have to turn your head."

She pulled over at the pharmacy lot, her hands still shaped around the wheel, and turned her head to look at the space beside the car where the hatchback had been. Nothing there now, just hot asphalt and a shopping cart. "So even with the mirror," she said slowly, "there's an area I can't see at all. From the seat. No matter how I adjust it."

"That's why you turn your head before changing lanes," he said. "Mirror, then shoulder, then move."

She sat with that for a moment. It bothered her in a way she couldn't immediately name, and then she could: she had believed that seeing was mostly a matter of arranging the instruments correctly, the way she arranged her desk before studying, the way she built an essay's structure before writing a word of it. Arrange everything and the whole field would be visible. But the blind spot didn't care about arrangement. It was a permanent gap in the machine's perception, and the only remedy was for her to physically turn and look with her own eyes, to accept that no setup was complete.

"That guy was so close," she said, and heard her own voice come out petulant, which embarrassed her, so she straightened it out. "I'm sorry. I really thought the mirror was enough."

"He'll forget it by dinner," her father said. "You won't. That's the trade."

They did the pharmacy turn, then drove out to the old airport road where the traffic thinned to nothing, and she practiced the sequence until it became something other than thought: signal, mirror, shoulder, wheel. The first few times she overdid it, turning her whole torso and drifting in the lane, and her father laughed and said, "Your head, not your whole biography," and she laughed too, the sound startled out of her. By the fifth attempt she could glance over her shoulder and keep the car straight at the same time, and the glance had stopped feeling like an admission of failure and started feeling like what it actually was, a habit of humility built into the motion of driving.

Driving home, she caught herself wondering whether the mirrors could be positioned to shrink the blind spot, angled further outward, maybe, and whether her father's method was simply the old way of doing things. She asked him, and he shrugged and said some people did angle them differently, and that she could experiment when the car was hers. She liked that answer better than a lecture. She liked that there was a question left over, something she would have to work out with her own shoulders and her own mirrors, on her own roads, after he stopped riding beside her.

Back in the driveway, she parked crooked and had to try twice, and neither of them mentioned it. She cut the engine and sat with her hands on the wheel.

"Same time Thursday?" her father said.

"Same time Thursday," she said, and turned her head, out of pure habit now, to check the empty street behind her before she opened the door.

Ella had been sick for three days with something the campus nurse refused to name, a flu that would have debilitated a less stubborn person, and she had waited until the last hour of voting to drag herself to the fire station on Delancey Street. The line inside was short. Outside, on the curb, two people she knew from the mayoral campaign office were already arguing, and they were arguing loudly enough that a poll worker came to the door and told them to take it to the sidewalk.

"Ella," Marcus said, grabbing her sleeve before she could get in line. "Tell her. The Herald poll has Rivera up two points and the margin of error is four. Two is smaller than four. It's a tie. Dana thinks Rivera's winning."

"I'm not saying he's winning," Dana said. She had a clipboard against her hip and a stack of door-hangers going soft in the drizzle. "I'm saying two points is two points. The number says Rivera."

"The number says nothing. Within the margin of error means tied. That's what it means."

The poll worker leaned out again. "Polls close at eight. It's quarter past seven. If you're voting, get in line. If you're not, move along."

That was the real deadline, and all three of them knew it. The campaign had forty volunteers sitting in cars along Fourth Avenue, waiting for one phone call: either push the last three precincts for Rivera in the final forty-five minutes, or stand down and save the money for the recount fund. Dana had the call sheet in her back pocket. Marcus had the campaign manager's cell number queued on his phone. They had been standing on this curb for twenty minutes going in circles.

Ella pulled her hood up and thought about her statistics elective, which she had taken only because the ceramics studio was full. She thought about the exercise the textbook had made them do twice, and she was careful now, because she did not want to say it wrong in front of both of them.

"Listen," she said. "It's not a tie. I'm pretty sure it's not a tie. When the lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll can't say with confidence who's ahead. That's all it can't say. It doesn't mean the race is exactly tied. Two points is still two points. The poll just can't tell you it's real."

"So we push," Dana said.

"So you don't know," Ella said. "That's the honest answer. The poll can't tell you Rivera's ahead and it can't tell you he isn't. It's not zero."

Marcus stared at the flyer stapled to the telephone pole above them, one of Rivera's bombastic ones, four exclamation points and a promise to "take back the city by storm." He said, "So what do we do with forty minutes and forty volunteers?"

"You do what you'd do if you didn't have the poll at all," Ella said. "You knock on the doors of people who always vote and always vote for you, and you make sure they got out. That doesn't cost you anything if you're behind, and it doesn't waste much if you're ahead."

Dana was already dialing. Marcus stood there a second longer, working it through, and Ella could see him letting go of the word "tied" the way you let go of a rung you thought was solid. "Okay," he said. "Okay, that's actually not the same as a tie."

Dana got through. "Push the three precincts," she said into the phone. "Yes. Ground game only, no literature drops. Yes, I know it's raining." She hung up and looked at both of them. "Done. Now go vote, both of you, before they lock the doors."

Inside, the line had shrunk to six people. A woman ahead of Ella was reading a voter guide about the county question on laboratory animal standards, out loud, half to herself: "Whereas the party of the first part acknowledges the capacity for sentience in..." She trailed off and flipped the page. Ella checked in at the table, signed her name in the box next to a signature card from six weeks ago, when she had registered on her eighteenth birthday with her mother standing behind her holding the umbrella.

The booth gave her a stubby pencil and a ballot with tiny ovals. She filled in the mayor's race first, then the county question, then the judges she had never heard of, and she thought, briefly, that her single oval was one data point in a pile so large it would never be separable again. At seven fifty-five she fed the ballot into the scanner, which chunked it down with a sound like a mail slot, and the machine displayed a number on its counter, one higher than before.

Outside, Marcus and Dana were gone, and the rain had stopped. She could see the headlights of cars turning onto Fourth Avenue, one after another, all going the same direction.

Sarah had been at the community center every Tuesday and Thursday since September, first for open gym and then, when the rec league needed a fifth, for the volleyball team that practiced in the echoing gym with the cracked scoreboard. Her father had wanted her to find something structured before college, some discipline to inculcate a routine into her last summer at home, and she had agreed mostly to stop the conversation. Now it was October, and the season was down to three games, and Priya had a doctor's note folded into her sock.

Priya had taken a ball to the temple two weeks earlier, off Sarah's own serve, a shank that nobody could have called. Since then she had come back in stages, and Sarah had learned the shape of it almost without meaning to. First Priya only watched, sitting on the folded mats with the lights dimmed for her. Then she did light jogging along the sideline. Then, last Thursday, she was cleared for the non-contact drills, and tonight she was supposed to try actual play, scrimmaging, the last step before full games.

"Read my note if you want," Priya said, pulling it out of her sock in the hallway by the water fountain. "It says every step, rest to full play, and I only move up if I stay free of symptoms the whole way. One headache and I drop back down." Sarah read it twice. The paper was soft from being carried.

They were eleven minutes into the scrimmage when Sarah noticed Priya standing still at the net, one hand pressed to her eyebrow. Not hurt the way a rolled ankle hurts, but paused, the way you pause in a library. Sarah called the ball early, took the set herself, and put it down flat so the rally ended. Then she walked over.

"Head?"

"Kind of," Priya said. "Started when I tracked Dara's serve. It's not bad."

Coach Reyes blew the whistle and came over, arms crossed, and Sarah watched him weigh it. They needed tonight. Thursday was the semifinal, and Priya was their only real blocker, and everyone on the court knew it. "If it's not bad," he said slowly, "you could sit five and see."

Sarah heard the offer for what it was, and it wasn't dishonest, exactly, but it was specious, a reasonable-sounding cover for wanting her on the floor. She thought of her father, who had argued last week that a promise to yourself was the only contract nobody else could break, and of Priya's note, which said the opposite in a way: that you advanced only when nothing in you objected. For a second the two ideas sat side by side in her head, neither one winning.

"It says while," Sarah said. "You move up only while you're symptom free. Not five minutes of being symptom free." She hadn't planned to say it out loud, and she felt Reyes's eyes on her, but Priya was already nodding, already reaching for her knee pads' strap.

"I know," Priya said. "I go back a stage. Light drills, no scrimmage." She looked at Reyes, and something in her face made the decision hers, which Sarah understood was the only way it could stand. Reyes exhaled through his nose, then shrugged, and told Dara to switch to the net.

After practice Sarah helped Priya carry the ball cart to the equipment closet, because Priya wasn't supposed to lift much yet and because it was a small thing that cost Sarah nothing. They stood in the hallway under the humming fluorescent panel while Priya re-read her own note.

"I'll be honest," Sarah said. "I don't know if the doctor's way is right about everything. Maybe you'd have been fine. Maybe five minutes' rest fixes it and nobody knows." Priya tilted her head, considering, not arguing. "But you're the one who has to live in your head all year," Sarah went on, "and I only have to live with losing Thursday. That math seems pretty easy."

Priya laughed, folded the note, and slid it back into her sock. In the gym, Reyes was killing the lights one bank at a time, and the last square of brightness shrank toward the door where the two of them stood.

"Walk me out," Priya said.

Gabrielle arrived at the farmers' market with her grandmother's canvas bag, forty dollars of her own babysitting money, and a plan she had defended at the kitchen table the night before. Her father wanted spaghetti and meatballs, the same dinner they had eaten every Sunday since she could remember, a tradition she privately considered parochial, as though the family palate had stopped exploring somewhere around 1998. She wanted to cook the pork loin from the Hsu farm stand, with the plums and the rosemary, the recipe she had torn from a magazine and taped inside her notebook like a confession. In the end she bought both, because in her family refusing anyone anything was a kind of arson.

She moved through the stalls with purpose, joking with Mr. Alvarez about whether his tomatoes were as good as he claimed, and letting him eviscerate a competitor's melons with one raised eyebrow. She counted her change. She argued herself down from the flowers and then, at the last stall, argued herself back up. By eleven she was carrying pork, plums, rosemary, a bag of tomatoes "for the meatballs, in case," and a terrible confidence that dinner would prove something, though she could not have said what.

Her brother Theo had left for college in August, and he texted while she was waiting in line for bread. "Cooking the family meal? Who are you and what have you done with my sister." Then, a second message: "Seriously though. Dad will say it's too fancy. Mom will say it's delicious to spite him. Report back." She read it twice, smiling, and did not answer yet, because answers felt like promises.

She cooked in the late afternoon with the kitchen windows open, the plums collapsing into the pan, the pork seared and then resting under foil. Her mother drifted through and stole a plum. Her father drifted through and said, "Smells like a restaurant," which in his dialect could mean anything. He changed his mind before dinner, though, out loud, at the table, which for him was practically opera. "This," he said, pointing his fork at the plums, "is better than the meatballs. Don't tell the meatballs." Everyone laughed, even Gabrielle, even the dog, who was hoping to be consulted.

Afterward they sat on the back porch in the blue evening, and it was hot, the kind of hot where the porch swing complained and the lemonade went watery. The platters came out with them, because no one wanted to go back inside, and the pork sat in its juices on the table while they argued about whether Aunt Rosa's new boyfriend was truly terrible or just boring, a debate with a long and distinguished history. Gabrielle looked at the meat and felt a small cold thought arrive.

She went inside and found the thermometer magnet on the fridge, the one from a food safety pamphlet her mother had never read. Her phone was faster. She searched, and there it was, plain as arithmetic: perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or for more than one hour when it's above 90. She read it twice. She stepped back onto the porch, where the air itself felt like a held breath, thick and ninety-something, and looked at the clock inside her own head. They had been out here longer than one hour. Longer than two.

"Everything's done," she said, gathering the platters, and her father said, "Done?" and she said, "Done for. The meat. It's been sitting out in this heat, and the rule is two hours in the danger zone, one hour if it's over ninety, and we are way past one." Her mother said, "The danger zone," slowly, as though tasting the phrase. "That sounds like a movie your brother would like." Gabrielle scraped the pork and the plums into the trash while her father mourned quietly and dramatically, one hand on his chest, and the dog watched the garbage can with frank theological despair.

Later, alone in the kitchen, she washed the pan and thought about her grandmother, who had raised five kids on leftovers and prayer and would have laughed at the waste, and about Theo's food science textbooks, which he quoted at dinner like scripture. Two inheritances, and she could hold both, she decided, roughly; she would trust the thermometer and the rule, and she would cook less next time, and she would still not tell her grandmother. The plums had been perfect, though, and the pork was gone, and there was no version of tonight without that.

She texted Theo a photo of the empty trash can and the thermometer magnet. "You were right about the danger zone. Dad loved dinner and then I eviscerated it, per USDA. Consanguinity entitles you to half the blame for my cooking genes." She dried her hands and set the pan back on the stove, and outside, faintly, she could hear her father and the dog, negotiating over the last piece of bread.

Jackson had been volunteering at the Harbor Street Community Office for six weeks, and until Tuesday morning nobody had asked him to write anything.

Mrs. Adeyemi, the coordinator, called him over to the desk by the window. "I need a favor," she said. "Dara's out sick, and this email to the parks department has to go out by noon. The grant meeting is Thursday, and if we don't confirm the picnic shelter by then, we lose it." She slid a printout across the desk. "Read this and tell me what you think."

Jackson read it. Dara, the part-time staffer, had written a page and a half about the history of the summer program, the weather last July, a complaint about a broken water fountain, and then, in the final paragraph, a request to reserve the Riverside shelter on August 12. It meandered like a river deciding where to go. He could tell Dara was trying to sound professional, stacking formal phrases to burnish the message, but the polish hid the point instead of brightening it.

"It's polite," he said carefully. "It's just that the ask is buried."

"Can you fix it by eleven?" Mrs. Adeyemi was already halfway back to the phone, where a parent was asking about bus passes. "Keep it respectful. Mr. Okafor over there can be touchy about tone, so don't be blunt."

Jackson sat down at the volunteer computer. He typed a draft, deleted it, typed another. The question he kept circling was simple and stubborn: what did a professional voice actually sound like? He'd written school essays meant to impress a teacher, but this was different. Somebody on the other end had forty other emails and a shelter calendar, and the kindest thing might be to stop performing and just say the thing.

He was still rearranging paragraphs when Ren, the college intern, leaned over his shoulder with a granola bar. "What's the mess?"

"Trying to figure out where the request goes," Jackson said. "Dara put it last, like a reveal."

Ren chewed for a second. "My cousin's in the Navy. She drills this into everybody. 'Bottom Line Up Front', BLUF. It's a US military writing standard. You put the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details."

"So the ask goes first, and the reasons come after."

"Exactly. She says nobody overseas has time to hunt for the point."

Jackson turned back to the screen. It felt almost rude, like walking into someone's office and talking before saying hello. But maybe, he thought, leading with the request was a form of respect, an admission that the reader's time mattered. He wrote a new draft.

Dear Mr. Okafor,

I'm writing to confirm our reservation of the Riverside picnic shelter for August 12, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., for the Harbor Street summer program's family day, roughly 80 attendees.

If the shelter is available, could you reply by Wednesday so we can finalize the grant paperwork? Below is the background, in case it's useful.

He kept the history Dara had gathered but cut it to four sentences. He left out the water fountain complaint entirely, then second-guessed himself and added one line, since Dara had clearly wanted it mentioned: "Separately, we'd appreciate knowing when the drinking fountain near the east entrance might be repaired." Maybe that was wrong, mixing requests. Maybe it was honest. He couldn't decide, and he let it stand.

Mrs. Adeyemi read it at 11:20, her face dour with deadline worry until the second line, when it eased. "This is good. Short and clear." Then she paused. "The fountain thing. He'll read that as a criticism of his department."

"Is that bad? Dara wanted it on record."

"It's a question of whether we need the shelter more than we need the complaint." She handed it back. "Your call. You're the one writing it."

Jackson sat with it for a moment. Two instincts pulled at him: Dara's instinct to document everything, soften everything, wrap the point in velvet; and the BLUF instinct to state the point and get out of the way. Neither felt complete on its own. The email could be direct and still be generous. He moved the fountain line to the end, after the background, and reworded it: "One small unrelated note, no urgency: the drinking fountain near the east entrance has been out of service, and families would be glad when it's working again."

He hit send at 11:52.

At 2:40 the reply came. Mr. Okafor confirmed the shelter, said he'd have the permit signed by Wednesday morning, and added a single line about the fountain: a work order had been filed in June, and he would check on its status. Then, at the bottom: "Thank you for making your request easy to find."

Mrs. Adeyemi printed it and pinned it to the corkboard above the office printer. "Dara should see this when she's back," she said, and Jackson noticed she'd circled the last sentence in red pen.

He stood there a minute longer than he needed to, reading it again. He still didn't know whether he'd been right to keep the fountain line at all, or whether softening it had been wisdom or cowardice. That part stayed unresolved, the way real things did. But he copied the email into a file he labeled "forms and templates," and saved it under a new folder name: BLUF, and other things I don't know yet.

Ren passed by with the last of the granola bar. "So what's the verdict? Military style?"

"Half," Jackson said. "Blunt up front, polite at the back."

"Sounds like stoicism with manners," Ren said, and laughed.

Jackson didn't answer, but he wrote that down too.

The argument John had prepared was about heredity and choice. He had written it on two sides of an index card the night before: that a person's observable traits, the phenotype, set certain conditions, but that conditions were not commands, and that anyone who claimed genes dictated a life had skipped a step. He wanted to say it well. He had been quiet in this class since September, and Mr. Okafor had asked him twice, gently, whether he had thoughts he was saving for later. Today he had a card with him, and a raised hand, and the small honest want of a boy who wanted to be heard getting it right.

The discussion had already started when the bell stopped ringing. Marcus was talking, leaning back with his chair on two legs, about a magazine article claiming that scientists had proved people were born criminals. "So if your genes say you're going to steal," Marcus said, "punishment is basically pointless. That's the logical conclusion of the whole genetic position." A few people nodded. Someone near the window said, grimly, that he refused to believe humans were just meat programs.

John put his hand up and made his argument, reading partly from the card and partly from somewhere braver. He said the phenotype was a starting condition, like the terrain a road is built on, and that roads went many ways across the same terrain. He said the evidence for influence was not evidence for fate. When he finished, the room was quiet in a way he could not read, and then Marcus dropped his chair forward with a bang.

"So you're saying it doesn't matter how kids are raised," Marcus said. "If it's all in the genes anyway, then bad parents are off the hook, and we can just malign poor families for their DNA and call it science. That's what you're defending." He spread his hands, as though the conclusion were obvious and a little dirty. Around him, people were frowning, but the frowns were aimed at John now, at the ugly thing Marcus had placed in his mouth, something about eugenics and excuses, a position John had never taken and would never take.

"That's not what I said," John managed. His voice came out thinner than he wanted. "I said influence, not control." But Marcus was already talking over him, generously offering to agree to disagree, as if he had done John a favor by dismantling him. John looked down at his index card, at his own tidy handwriting, and felt the strange vertigo of being defeated by an argument that had never touched his own.

Across the room, Dana had stopped doodling. She had written down both claims in her notebook, in her cramped shorthand, one under the other: John's actual words, and Marcus's reply. The two did not match. Marcus had not answered the road built across terrain; he had answered something easier, a flimsier version standing where John had been standing, and he was swinging at it as though it were the same thing. She raised her hand, and when Mr. Okafor nodded to her, she turned toward Marcus rather than the teacher.

"That's a straw man," she said. "You attacked a weaker, distorted version of his argument instead of the argument he actually made, and you're acting like the two are the same." Marcus opened his mouth, and Dana pointed at her notebook, which was not a normal thing to do, and read John's sentence back verbatim, then read Marcus's rebuttal verbatim. "He said influence, not control," she said. "You answered control. If it's a fallacy, the whole reply just falls off the argument, like knocking over a dummy and claiming you beat the man." The class was very still. Marcus said, "Fine, then he should have been clearer," which was not the same as conceding, and everyone seemed to know it.

Mr. Okafor asked whether John wanted to respond, and John found that the moment had changed shape on him. He had planned for opposition, for a real counterargument about twin studies or free will, and what he had gotten instead was a distortion, which required a different move: not to defend his claim harder, but to first restore it, to say, "Before you argue with me, argue with me." He said that, almost exactly, and heard a couple of people laugh quietly, the good kind of laugh. Then he said the part he was less sure of, because it was true. "I don't actually know where influence ends," he said. "I know it's not everything. I can't tell you the percentage, and I don't think anyone in this room can. If you want to beat my real argument, that's the place to hit it, because that's where I'm standing."

Marcus looked at him for a long second, chair flat on the floor now, and then said, "All right. Say more about the percentage thing." John put the index card face down on his desk, because he was about to go off it, and started talking.

Hunter paid for two hot chocolates he didn't want, because Marisol had said yes to a football game and a football game meant cold bleachers, and a spartan concession stand offered nothing else. He was eighteen and this was his first real date, a fact his friend Dex had found hilarious for the entire week leading up to it.

They found seats at the top of the visitor side, away from the marching band. For the first quarter it went well. She laughed at his joke about the opposing team's mascot, a costumed antelope with a broken snout, and she explained which players were her cousins. Then the second quarter began and the conversation thinned out like fog burning off, and by the two-minute warning they were watching the scoreboard more than each other, and Hunter understood that silence between strangers is different from silence between friends, though he couldn't have said how.

"So," Marisol said, and the word hung there like a pass with no receiver.

In his pocket his phone buzzed. A text from his sister, Wren, who was home with a broken wrist and her own agenda: "If the date is bad, tell her about your sabbatical from gaming. Girls like reformed boys. Also bring me a pretzel. THIS IS MY ONLY WANT IN LIFE." He typed back "no such thing as reformed" and put the phone away, which Marisol noticed, and which he had to explain, which made her laugh again, which gave him the nerve to try something.

"Can I propose an experiment?" he said. "I read about this study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and afterward they felt closer than pairs who just made small talk."

"Thirty-six," she said. "At a football game."

"We don't have to do all of them. We could just do some. Trade harder questions."

She pulled her scarf up to her chin, considering. "Fine. But I go first. Question one: why did you actually ask me out? Not the version you told Dex."

He hadn't expected the study to be turned on him so fast. "Because you argued with Mr. Ferreira about the ending of that story and you were wrong, but you were wrong in a way I kept thinking about for a week. Your turn. What do you want that you've never told anyone at this school?"

The game went on below them, small helmets colliding, and neither of them watched it anymore. Her answer involved veterinary school and a mother who thought it was impractical. His next question, borrowed from what he remembered of the study's spirit, was about what she'd want to know about her own future if she could. Hers was about embarrassment, and she answered hers first even though she'd asked it, which he liked. Somewhere in the third quarter the questions stopped being a game and became just talking, though he couldn't locate the exact moment the change happened, the way you can't say when dusk becomes night.

"I have to ask the pretzel question," he said finally. "My sister's want. She's home with a cast on her arm and the emotional leverage of a Victorian orphan."

"Get two," Marisol said. "I'll go with you."

They climbed down through the crowd, and on the walk to the concession stand she asked the last question of the night, the one he turned over all the way home. "Do you think it works," she said, "the study? Do you think we actually feel closer, or we just think we do?"

Below them the band played, and the antelope mascot danced badly near the fence, and Hunter considered the question honestly, because it deserved that. "I don't know if those are different things," he said. "I can't tell yet. Ask me question thirty-seven tomorrow."

She was already writing it down on the back of her ticket stub.

Landon found the cap first, then the gown, then the tassel, in that order, in three different places: the cap under his bed, the gown on the laundry hook where it had been since March, the tassel in a mug on his desk that said WORLD'S OKAYEST FISHERMAN, a gift from an uncle who had never seen him fish. The ceremony was in nine hours. His mother was already in the kitchen making potato salad for the party, halving eggs with a serrated knife, which he had told her a hundred times was wrong and which she did anyway.

The problem was the speech. Two weeks earlier, when Mr. Ruiz had asked him to speak for the class, Landon had said yes because it was easier than saying no, and now he had a legal pad with four false starts on it and a fifth one that ended mid-sentence at the word "meanwhile." He had tried solemn. He had tried funny. Both had desiccated on the page, the jokes curling up like the edges of the eggs his mother was currently butchering. He sat at the kitchen table with the pad while she worked, and she did not ask about the speech, because she knew him well enough not to.

The party started at two, in the backyard, under a canopy his stepfather had borrowed from a man at work. People came in a slow tide: aunts, neighbors, kids Landon had known since trundle beds, kids he had met in eleventh grade and liked fine. Dana Okafor arrived with her grandmother and a casserole and the expression of someone surveying a land she had once ruled. Gus came late, as Gus did, carrying a basketball even though there was no game planned.

It was Gus, actually, standing at the drink table with a red cup, who said it. "Where's Ricky Solano? And those O'Malley twins. I figured they'd be here even if they didn't walk." He counted on his fingers, half joking, and then stopped counting because the list got longer than a joke could carry. "We started with like 340."

"There's, what, 290 walking tomorrow," Dana said. She had a way of saying numbers like she was handing you change. Landon watched her do the arithmetic in her head and then pull out her phone, because even Dana checked. She scrolled, frowned, scrolled again, and turned the screen toward them. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." She said it flat, like reading a train schedule. "That's the whole country, that year."

"So we're average," Gus said.

"We're a data point," said Dana, and put the phone away, and took a cupcake.

Landon had been drifting toward his own speech problem all afternoon, the way a loose tooth finds the tongue, and now he could not stop pressing on it. He walked to the far end of the yard, past the canopy, where the grass turned to dirt near the fence, and stood there doing what he always did with numbers: turning them into faces. Ricky Solano, who had moved junior year and sent one Snap after that. The O'Malley twins. A girl named Priya who had left mid-October of sophomore year without a word, whose locker he had watched get taped over and reassigned. Thirteen percent of somewhere. But that was the country, that year, not his class, and his class was not a fixed thing either, kids arriving and leaving like weather. He understood the statistic and did not understand his class, and he understood his class, in the face-by-face way, and could not fit it to the statistic, and both of those were true, and he stood in the dirt trying to hold them at once.

His mother found him there. "You're hiding," she said.

"I'm drafting."

"In the dirt."

"Where no one can see me delete things."
