Marcus erased his sentence with the dedication of a man removing evidence. "So what do I write?"

"The truth. That one group found this, and other people are checking it, and that's how it works. Ms. Betancourt will like that better anyway. She told me last year she can always tell when somebody copied a claim." Peyton had learned that lesson late, in a recycling bin, but Marcus didn't need the whole autopsy.

He wrote for a while, tongue between his teeth. Peyton went back to her table and her own work, an application essay with the cursor blinking at her like a heartbeat monitor. Across the floor, two women by the microfilm machine were arguing in furious whispers about whether the machine still worked, which it did not; it had not worked since at least the Clinton administration, and every few months someone tried anyway, out of loyalty or spite.

Marcus reappeared at her shoulder twenty minutes later with the poster board under his arm. "I changed it. It says 'One study suggests, and other scientists are testing it.' And I cited it as a preprint." He said the last word carefully, newly owned. "Devin's cousin says that's the honest way."

"It is."

"Is my poster still good?"

"Better," she said. "Judges like a guy who knows what he doesn't know yet."

He considered this, then carried the poster down the stairs, holding it flat and level like something that could still spill. Peyton watched him go, then looked back at her essay, at the cursor, at the sentence she'd written about being certain of nothing except her willingness to find out. She deleted the whole sentence and started typing just as the microfilm machine, against all evidence, hummed to life behind her.

Megan spread the watercolor set across the library table with the care of someone handling evidence, though the evidence was only twelve pans of pigment, half of them dried to chalk. She was making a birthday card for her grandmother, who had come home from the hospital two weeks ago to convalesce on the couch by the window, and who had once told Megan that yellow was a coward's color unless you paired it bravely. Megan had been staring at the yellow pan for twenty minutes.

The problem was the border. She wanted a ring of color around a painted window, the window her grandmother looked through all day, but every arrangement she tried turned muddy or flat. Opposite the table, a boy from her chemistry class, Dev, sat buried in a textbook, mouthing formulas. She watched him write "enthalpy" in the margin of his notes three times, underlining it, and she thought that at least his problem had an equation attached.

"Dev," she said. "How do you arrange colors so they don't fight?"

He looked up, wary, as if she might be quizzing him. "You're asking me? I wear the same hoodie every day."

"You have a system, then. Systems are what I need."

He came over anyway, rubbing his eyes, and stood over her sketch: a window with a garden beyond it, no border yet. He said the obvious thing, that you put opposite colors across from each other, blue against orange, red against green. Megan said she knew that, everyone knew that, but which circle, whose order, starting where. She wanted it to be correct, not just pleasant. She had a suspicion that pleasant was a compromise.

The reference shelf had a book on color theory with a wheel inside the front cover, and next to it, thinner and older in spirit, a history of science. Megan pulled both. In the second book she found a page about Isaac Newton, and stopped with her finger under a line. Newton had arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, and that circle was an early version of the color wheel artists use today.

"Look at this," she said, turning the book so Dev could see. "The color wheel. It started with him. Opticks, 1704."

"A physicist invented the thing painters use?"

"A physicist bent the spectrum into a circle," Megan said, and heard how it sounded, like something her grandmother would call bombastic, and liked it anyway.

She copied the circle into the margin of her sketch, spacing the colors the way the page showed, and here she paused. Part of her had wanted a rule she could follow exactly, a chemistry of paint, and Newton's circle gave her that, an order that had survived three centuries. But her grandmother's window at dusk was not a spectrum. It was violet leaning into gray, gold gone thin, and no circle anywhere could tell her how much water to add. Dev suggested she put the red where Newton would not, just to see. She tried it, and it was wrong, and then it was wrong in a way she almost liked, which was more confusing than before.

A librarian came by with a cart and slowed, noticing the two of them bent over the book. She didn't explain anything or correct anything. She only set down a cup of water for rinsing brushes, because she had seen the paints, and a folded paper towel, and said the good paper was in the drawer if Megan wanted something that wouldn't buckle. Megan thanked her and took two sheets, one for the failure and one for after.

She painted the border twice. The first followed Newton's circle as she had copied it, each color in its inherited place, and it looked orderly and a little dead, like a diagram of a garden rather than a garden. On the second sheet she kept the circle but let it wobble, letting the gold stretch wider where the window's light would fall on her grandmother's face, letting the violet crowd in at the corner where the couch sat. She could not have said which version was more true, and she suspected the honest answer was that the order mattered and the disobedience mattered too, though she could not prove either half. She wrote nothing clever inside the card. She wrote, "The window misses you being at it."

Dev packed up at closing time and paused at her table. "The enthalpy thing," he said, tapping his notes, "turns out it's just where the heat goes. All that worrying for one word."

"Tell me about it," Megan said, and held the wet card flat on both palms, level, all the way to the door.

The phone store smelled of floor cleaner and warm plastic, and Sebastian had been standing at the counter long enough to memorize the ceiling tiles, forty-one of them, four stained. His own phone lay dark on the glass between him and the clerk, drowned in Tuesday's storm when he had run the half mile from the bus stop with it in his jacket pocket. He was leaving for college in the morning, eight a.m., a drive of six hours, and without a phone his mother had said it would be like sending him off with a paper map and a flare gun.

"Insurance claim first," the clerk said, typing. "Then the upgrade. You'll need to sign the terms and conditions before I can process anything, and we close at nine."

Sebastian signed the first screen without reading it, then stopped himself, thumb hovering. He was the kind of person who read the back of cereal boxes. He scrolled back up. The clause at the top ran for two paragraphs about liability, about how the company was not responsible for acts of God, and that phrase stopped him, because he had seen it somewhere else, recently, somewhere that mattered.

"My concert tickets," he said. He pulled the drowned phone toward him uselessly, then remembered and borrowed the clerk's display tablet instead. He logged into his email and found the message from the venue. The show, the one he had bought tickets for in June with money from mowing lawns, the one that was supposed to be tonight, had been canceled. The storm had taken part of the roof off the amphitheater. The email offered his money back as credit toward next season, and beneath that, in gray nine-point type, sat the sentence he had skimmed three days ago and not understood: per the force majeure provision of the ticket terms, no cash refunds would be issued.

"What's force majeure?" he asked the clerk.

The clerk glanced at the tablet and shrugged. "It's in every contract we have too. Force majeure frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, like a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing." He said it flat, the way he probably said it forty times a week, and went back to typing.

Sebastian read the clause again. The storm had prevented the venue from holding the concert; the venue had not chosen to cancel it out of laziness or greed, at least not provably. So the venue was freed from its obligation to put on a show, and, apparently, from its obligation to give him back his sixty dollars. He felt two reactions push against each other. One was simple indignation: he had paid for a concert, and there had been no concert, and money should travel backward along that broken promise. The other was a stranger, more reluctant feeling, an interest in how the machine worked, an almost admiring recognition that somewhere a lawyer had sat down and imagined storms and wars and roof failures in advance and written a door for the company to walk through.

"The thing is," he said slowly, "I get it. If a war started, you couldn't exactly demand the band play. It's not their fault." He turned the tablet toward the clerk. "But it's not my fault either. Why does the clause only open the door for them?"

The clerk looked up for real this time. "What's your major?"

"Undeclared. I leave tomorrow."

"Then take a law class." He slid a second screen across the counter. "Device payment agreement. You're financing three hundred dollars over twenty-four months. Read that one, actually. People always skim that one."

Sebastian read it. He read the part about consent, how signing indicated his agreement to be bound. He read the liability section, which capped the company's responsibility at the phone's purchase price. He read about arbitration, a word he liked the shape of without fully trusting it. Around him the store was emptying; a mother negotiated with a small boy over a case with cartoon dogs on it, and a delivery guy in a rain jacket waited for a screen repair, and the fluorescent lights hummed at a pitch that seemed designed to be ignored.

His mother texted from the demo phone's message relay, a service the clerk had set up out of what Sebastian suspected was pity: Are you getting it or not, we need to pack the car tonight. He noticed he was doing something he recognized from arguing with his father, which was holding two positions at once without collapsing them. The venue had behaved reasonably under a rule that was itself reasonable, and he had still lost sixty dollars, and both of those things were true, and neither one erased the other. He could not find a principle that made the loss fair. He could only find a principle that made the loss legal, and he was surprised, scrolling through the gray text, by how much distance could fit between those two words.

"Okay," he said, and signed. Then, before the clerk could take the tablet back, he opened the venue's website and found the contact form. He did not demand a refund. He wrote instead: I accept the force majeure terms. I'm asking for the refund anyway, as a courtesy, because I'm a student and the show would have been my last one before moving away. He hesitated over the word courtesy, worried it sounded like equivocating, and left it in, because it was honest: he did not know if he deserved the money, and he wanted it, and he was unwilling to pretend one of those feelings didn't exist.

"Smart," the clerk said, reading over his shoulder with the frankness of someone who had stopped caring about boundaries hours ago. "The folks who yell get form letters. The folks who quote the clause back at us get listened to." He boxed up the new phone, white and boxy in its shrink wrap. "You'll have it activated in ten minutes. Sign here, initial there."

Sebastian's pen moved through the boxes, his initials appearing one after another like a small procession, and he thought briefly of the word acolyte, which he had learned for the SAT and never used, and how he was signing his way into a church of terms he had only partially read. The phone came alive in his hand, screen bright, and the first message through was his mother's: I packed your rain jacket. Check the weather before you go. He looked out the store's front window at the drying parking lot, at the sky still bruised in the west, and then he checked.

Julia had the whole Saturday planned down to the quarter hour, and the farmers' market was eating the plan alive. She had promised her mother a real dinner, a soup made from scratch, before her brother Marcus flew back to his second year of college on Sunday, and she had allotted exactly twenty minutes to buy onions, carrots, and a chicken from the Halloway farm stand. But Mrs. Halloway wanted to talk about Julia's upcoming departure too, and about her own daughter who had just started nursing school in Cleveland, and there was no polite way to hurry a woman handing you a free bag of carrot tops for stock.

"Your mother says you're doing the dinner tonight," Mrs. Halloway said, wrapping the chicken in butcher paper. "Marcus texted me about it. That boy valorizes your cooking like it's a religion, you know. Every time he comes home he tells me his sister makes better soup than anybody."

"He exaggerates," Julia said, though privately she held the opinion closer to fact than exaggeration. Tonight was supposed to prove something, though she would not have said what. That the kitchen could still be a place the family gathered, maybe, even after this year of dinners eaten in shifts. That she could leave for her dorm in two weeks having built something that would outlast her.

Marcus appeared at the mouth of the stand with a cup of cider and an expression of pure teenage grievance. "Mom says I have to help," he announced. "I'm being conscripted."

"You're being included," Julia said. She paid Mrs. Halloway, hefted the bag. "There's a difference. You can carry the onions."

At home the kitchen was warm and smelled faintly of the morning's coffee. Julia set out the cutting board and the three yellow onions from the bag, and she was circumspect about the knife, checking its edge against her thumbnail the way her father had taught her before he stopped cooking altogether. Marcus was assigned carrots and immediately began complaining about the peeler. Their mother drifted in and out, pretending to look for a ladle, plainly wanting to be asked to stay.

"You cry every time," Marcus said when the first onion was half chopped and Julia's eyes had begun to sting and stream. "It's an onion. Emotionally unstable behavior, honestly. Should we talk about your feelings?"

"It's not crying," Julia said, blinking hard, wiping her cheek with her wrist. "It's chemistry. Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, and that vapor irritates your eyes and makes them tear. It's a gas. It has nothing to do with my feelings."

"Syn-pro-what?"

"Propanethial-S-oxide. I read it. It's in the food science thing I've been looking at for school." She said it with more certainty than she felt. She had read it twice, actually, because the first time she had been half asleep, and she liked knowing the name of the thing that got her every single time. It was satisfying, in a way, to have an explanation that nobody could tease her about. Though she noticed Marcus chopping his own onion now, at the far end of the board, and his eyes were going red too.

"Okay," he admitted, sniffing. "That's real. Why does it feel like mace?"

"Because your eyes think it is," Julia said, and slid her board to the window ledge, where the breeze off the yard came through. That helped, somewhat. She went back to the pot, softening the onions in butter, and her mother finally sat down at the table with the peeler and a pile of carrots, taking over Marcus's abandoned post without being asked. Marcus leaned against the counter and told a story about his roommate, and the kitchen filled with the low heat of the onions going translucent, and Julia thought about how the cell walls were breaking down in the pan, the substrate of the whole soup turning sweet, everything sharp becoming something else.

"You know what I want," Marcus said suddenly, mid-story, apropos of nothing Julia could track. "When you're at school. Text me what you're making sometimes. Not a big thing. Just, like, Tuesday, you made soup. Because the food here is the only thing I actually miss."

"You miss Mom and Dad."

"I tolerate Mom and Dad. I miss the food." He grinned, but there was something careful underneath it, and Julia understood that he was asking for a thread, a small one, and that he had chosen this ridiculous way to ask because the plain way would have embarrassed them both.

She considered, while stirring, two ideas she had been carrying around all summer like coins in the same pocket. One was from her chemistry teacher, that everything worth knowing had a mechanism, a name, a reason the tears came. The other was older, from her grandmother, that you couldn't explain a good soup, you could only stand over it and pay attention. She had thought for a while that she would have to pick, that college meant choosing the explaining kind of life and letting the other one go. Standing at the stove with the market bag empty on the counter and her brother describing the vapor still stinging his eyes, she suspected they were not actually opposites. The gas had a name and the soup had a name and neither one was the whole of it, and she could not yet say how the two fit together, only that both had felt true in her hands today.

"I'll text you," she said. "Tuesdays and Sundays. Soup report." She dipped the wooden spoon, blew on it, and held it out across the stove for Marcus to taste. "Careful. It's hot."

The county archive occupied the second floor of the old library, above the children's room, and Katherine had chosen it because the high school library had nothing on Marco Polo except a picture book with camels on the cover. Her report was due Thursday. She had two days, a partner named Daniel who had not read anything, and a thesis she had written on the bus that morning: Marco Polo's journey opened China to Europe.

The archivist, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor, set her up at a table near the window and brought a slip case of holdings. "Most of what we have is secondary," she said. "Travel narratives, mostly nineteenth century. There's one odd one in there."

Katherine worked through the stack in order. The first books gave her what she expected: seventeen years at the court of Kublai Khan, the Description of the World, the prisons of Genoa where Polo dictated his story to Rustichello. She copied quotations and kept a running page count. By eleven she had half the report drafted in her notebook, and Daniel had texted twice asking if she'd done his half too.

The odd one was a dark blue hardback with a cracked spine, shelved wrong among the admirers. Did Marco Polo Go to China? by Frances Wood. Katherine read the title twice, then the inside flap, then the first chapter standing up because she didn't trust herself to sit still. Wood had argued that Marco Polo might never have reached China at all. Her evidence was the book itself, what it left out. It never mentioned tea. It never mentioned foot-binding. It never mentioned the Great Wall.

She read for an hour without taking a note. When she finally copied the three omissions down, her handwriting came out cramped, as if her hand had a different opinion than her thesis did.

Daniel arrived at noon with a bag of chips and no sources. "Tell me what to say," he said, dropping into the chair across from her. "I'll do the map part. I found a map online."

"Look at this." She turned the blue book toward him and tapped the title.

He glanced at it and pushed the chips aside. "That's dumb. Everyone knows he went. It's like, the most famous trip ever."

"That's the point. She's not saying he lied. She's saying maybe he never reached China, and the book's full of things a person who'd actually lived there would probably mention. Tea, Daniel. Sixteen years in China and no tea."

"So one person says he didn't go. So what? Our report's due Thursday."

Katherine sat back. She wanted to tell him he was missing it, that the report was better now, not ruined, but she could hear how the sentence would sound, like pedantry, like she was grading him instead of persuading him. Mrs. Okafor passed behind them with a cart of document boxes, paused, and said nothing, which somehow felt like permission.

"It's not one person against everyone," Katherine said instead. "It's a question. Historians disagree about him because the sources are partial. We only have his book, and his book doesn't say what we want it to say. Either direction."

"So which side are we on?"

She looked at her notebook, at the thesis she'd written on the bus. Opened China to Europe. It was pithy, it filled a line, and she had believed it that morning without ever having checked whether the journey itself was even settled. She tried to hold both ideas at once, the famous Polo and the doubted one, and found she could do it if she let go of the need for one of them to be wrong. "We're on the question's side," she said. "We present what the book says, then what Wood says, then what we can't know."

"That's not a thesis."

"It is. It's just not the one I started with."

Daniel ate his chips while she drafted. He would still probably only do the map, and she would still probably let him, because she had learned to compartmentalize, to file Daniel under partner in a drawer separate from friend, and to close that drawer when the work mattered. But she drafted differently than she had on the bus. She wrote the admiration first, the courts and the paper money and the years of travel, and then the doubt, set down plainly, without pretending she could settle it: that a traveler who never mentioned the Great Wall had left a crack in his own story, and that historians had been looking through that crack ever since, each one seeing a slightly different China on the other side.

At four Mrs. Okafor came to collect the books. Katherine slid the blue hardback across the table last. "Can I come back tomorrow? I want to reread the chapter on omissions."

"It'll be here," Mrs. Okafor said, and then, almost smiling, "That's the trouble with archives. The books don't change. Only the readers do."

Katherine zipped her notebook into her bag, where it pressed against the folded map Daniel had printed and left behind, the Great Wall drawn across it in a thin red line.

The suite smelled like buffalo sauce and wet coats, and Carson had exactly twenty-two minutes until the halftime trivia board lit up on the jumbotron, twenty-two minutes to decide whether his grandfather was a liar or just old. The contest had been announced at the end of the first quarter: one question per suite, answers texted in before the second half kicked off, and the prize was a locker room tour, which Carson wanted more than he had admitted to anyone, including himself.

"It was the Packers," Grandpa Ray was saying, wedged into the corner seat with a plate balanced on his knee like a man who had done this a hundred times. "Packers and the Chiefs. I remember it like yesterday." He was a gourmand of halftime spreads even now, working through the chicken wings with a methodical devotion, pausing only to gesture at the field below with a dripping bone.

Carson's mother rolled her eyes from across the room. "Dad, you were four in 1967." She said it lightly, the way she said most things about Grandpa Ray, but Carson had learned that lightness could carry weight, the way a paper airplane carries a stone if you fold it wrong.

"Five," Grandpa Ray said. "And I remember the score. Thirty-five to ten." He pointed the bone at Carson. "You think I make things up."

Carson didn't answer that, because the honest answer was sometimes, and the second honest answer was that he wanted Grandpa Ray not to have made this up. The trivia question had blinked onto the screen at the end of the first quarter: WHEN AND WHERE WAS THE FIRST SUPER BOWL PLAYED, AND WHAT WAS THE FINAL SCORE? His cousin Priya had already started typing "Green Bay" into the family's shared answer, because everyone knew the Packers were a Green Bay team, and something about that had snagged in Carson's mind like a sleeve on a nail. His grandfather had said Los Angeles. On the screen, the Chargers' kicker lined up for a field goal, and the whole suite went quiescent, even the twins, even the dog, waiting while the ball sailed wide left and the room broke into groans.

"Wait," Carson said, and Priya's thumbs stopped. "Grandpa, you said it was in Los Angeles. Not Green Bay."

"Of course it was in Los Angeles." Grandpa Ray looked faintly wounded, the way he did whenever anyone demanded evidence for his memories. "Big stadium out there. January. Cold everywhere else in the country but not there." He licked sauce off his thumb. "Fifteenth, I think. January fifteenth."

Priya was frowning at her phone. "That can't be right. Why would they play a Packers game in LA?" But she said it as a question, not a verdict, and Carson recognized the tone because it was his own, the little hitch before you commit to believing something. Fourteen minutes to kickoff of the second half. He thought about how they had all spent years humming to Grandpa Ray's stories, letting him have them the way you let a kid win at cards, and how it would be a strange kind of cruelty for this to be the one story that was true. It would also, he admitted to himself, be a strange kind of gift.

He got up and found his uncle Devin by the window, the one family member with actual data on his phone, the one who had made a small fortune in fantasy football and treated every dispute like a courtroom. "Uncle D. First Super Bowl. Don't tell me who told you what. Just look it up."

Devin looked at him for a long second, and Carson understood that his uncle had already heard the argument from across the room, and had already, probably, looked it up, because that was who Devin was. "You asking for Ray or for the trivia?"

"Both. Separately."

Devin turned the screen toward him. Carson stood transfixed by it for a moment, not because the information was dramatic but because it was ordinary, plain black text: January 15, 1967, Green Bay Packers 35, Kansas City Chiefs 10, Los Angeles. Every number where his grandfather had said it would be. Down on the field, the halftime crew was hauling the stage pieces into position, and somewhere a clock was running that Carson couldn't see.

He walked back and sat down next to Grandpa Ray without saying anything, then took Priya's phone and typed: January 15, 1967, Los Angeles. Packers 35, Chiefs 10. He hit send with nine minutes still on the clock, before he could think better of it, before he could weigh whether he was doing it for the locker room or for the old man. The answer could only be submitted once. Priya made a small sound of protest that trailed off into nothing.

The jumbotron flickered. Then, in letters ten feet tall: SUITE 114. CORRECT.

Grandpa Ray set down his plate. For a second he didn't say anything at all, just looked at the screen, and Carson watched his throat move.

"Told you," he finally said. "Like yesterday."

The sled drill came at the end of every Tuesday practice, after the passing patterns had been run into the grass and the cones stood crooked where cleats had knocked them. Coach Reyes had three of them load the weighted sled and push it twenty yards as a unit, shoulders against the bar, and he stood at the far sideline with a stopwatch he never seemed to read. Dominic took his spot at the left end and waited for the whistle.

They were slow. Not just Tuesday but every Tuesday that September, slow in a way that didn't match how any of them moved alone. Dominic had watched Femi sprint the length of the field in the last minute of a match and arrive at the far post still furious with energy. He had watched himself, in the mirror of his own body, chase down a breakaway in the season opener and feel his lungs open like a door. Yet when the three of them leaned into the sled together, the thing crawled.

"Again," Coach Reyes said that Tuesday, and then, quieter, almost to himself, "You each push harder when I time you one at a time. I've been watching it for a month."

That night Dominic sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open, collating what he could find: a name, Ringelmann, which he typed into a search bar and then into another. He read slowly, twice. A French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone. Dominic read the sentence out loud to the empty kitchen, then copied it into the notebook he kept for calculus.

He brought it to Femi before Thursday practice, holding the notebook open between them on the bench. Femi read it with his shin guards still in his hands.

"Ringelmann," Femi said. "Never heard of him."

"He measured it. Rope, groups, 1913. Everybody pulls less when they're in the group." Dominic closed the notebook. "It's not just us being lazy. It's what happens."

"So what do we do about it?"

Dominic had thought about this on the walk over, past the tennis courts where the nets sagged and a single player served balls to no one. Part of him wanted to say that knowing was enough, that a named thing was a handled thing. Another part, older and more skeptical, suspected that a fact like this was less an answer than a description of the problem. "I don't know yet," he said. "Maybe we count our own steps. Maybe we agree that each of us is responsible for his own push, and nobody assumes the other guy is carrying it."

"Meaning we all secretly think the other two have it," Femi said. "That's kind of comforting, actually. I thought I was just getting soft."

The infield grass was still wet when Coach called the sled drill on Thursday. Dominic lined up at the left end again, with Femi at center and Elias, a junior who rarely spoke, at the right. Before the whistle, Dominic said, without turning his head, "Your own push. Don't worry about ours." He heard Femi laugh once through his nose.

The sled moved. Not beautifully, not like a machine, but it moved the way it moved when Coach timed them individually, and Dominic felt his own thighs burn in a way he recognized from the opener. Afterward, doubled over with his hands on his knees, he tried to be honest with himself about what had changed. Perhaps the words had. Perhaps only Tuesday's rest had, or the cool in the air. He wanted to credit the sentence in his notebook and could not entirely.

At the water table, Elias drank and then said, "Was that real, or did we just want it to be?"

"That's the problem," Dominic said. "I can't tell the difference yet."

Over the next three weeks, the question stopped being a project and became a small persistent habit of mind, the way a player keeps checking his shoulder. He noticed it in the matches too. When the team defended as a block, each of them seemed to run a half step less than he did when the play broke and only one man was back. It felt endemic to them, not a flaw anyone had chosen but something grown into the structure, the way the goalposts leaned very slightly toward the south end. Whether it could be cured, or only watched, he didn't know. Coach Reyes, who had a reactionary streak about anything that smelled of sports science, dismissed the stretch bands a trainer once suggested and kept his stopwatch in his pocket, so Dominic assumed the sled drill would continue exactly as it was, unmeasured, which in its own way suited him.

On the last Tuesday of the season, the air had the smell of cut grass going cold, and the light failed early enough that the far goal stood half in shadow. Coach called the drill a final time. Femi, Elias, and Dominic took the bar, and before the whistle, Elias said quietly, "Own push," as if reminding himself of a word in a language he was still learning.

They pushed. The sled hissed over the wet turf, and Dominic felt the bar hard against his shoulder, felt the specific and separate weight of his own effort, which was all he had ever been able to feel of anyone's. When it crossed the twenty-yard mark, Coach said nothing, and Femi straightened up and looked back along the track of flattened grass.

"Again?" he said.

The sedan on the showroom floor was silver, or close to it, a shade the brochure called Lunar Mist, and Maria had circled it twice already without touching it, because touching things felt like a first step toward owning them. She had two thousand one hundred dollars in a savings account that her grandmother had started when Maria was nine, an account that had recently begun earning interest, small deposits of money the bank added just for letting it sit there. Forty-one cents last month. Fifty-three the month before. The growth was slow, but it ran in one direction, and she liked that about it.

Her mother was at the sales desk with a man named Duane, who kept sliding papers across the table like a card dealer who already knew the hand. Maria could hear the word "monthly" arriving again and again, a word that sounded small and manageable until you multiplied it by sixty. Sixty months. Five years. The loan on the used sedan, Duane said, could be theirs at seven percent, and he said it the way people say the weather is humid, a condition of the universe rather than a choice anyone had made.

Maria sat down in one of the waiting chairs, which was the exact chair from every dentist's office she had ever visited, and took out her phone. She had gotten her first credit card three weeks ago, a slim blue thing with a limit of five hundred dollars, because the online form had said she was pre-approved and she had wanted, for once, to be approved at something first. She had charged twenty-six dollars at the bookstore. The statement had arrived yesterday with two numbers on it: a minimum payment of twenty-five dollars and a full balance of twenty-six.

She opened the card's app and read the fine print, which was set in gray type on a gray field, evidently designed by someone who hoped she wouldn't. Somewhere in the third paragraph she found the phrase "grace period." It said that a grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, then held the phone away from her face as if distance would make it simpler.

"So if I pay all twenty-six dollars," she said to the empty chair beside her, "they charge me nothing extra."

The empty chair did not adjudicate the matter, but the sentence on the screen seemed to. Pay twenty-six, owe twenty-six. Pay twenty-five, the minimum, and the twenty-six would begin to grow, the way her savings grew but in reverse, in the wrong direction, compounding toward whoever held the debt. It occurred to her that the two systems were mirror images: interest could work for you or against you, and the only difference was which side of the ledger you were standing on. She had always assumed the sides were assigned. Now she suspected they were chosen, or at least drifted into, the way her mother was drifting toward the finance office.

Her mother had been an iconoclast about debt for as long as Maria could remember, the woman who paid cash for a lawnmower, who cut up a store card in the parking lot of the mall while Maria watched through the car window, mortified. And here was that same woman nodding at a payment schedule, because the old car had died on the interstate in February and the new job started Monday and the bus did not run to the office park. Principles, Maria was learning, were not abandoned so much as negotiated with, item by item, in rooms that smelled like new vinyl.

Duane came over with a clipboard and a smile calibrated to the wattage of a man about to save a family. "You're the daughter," he said. "Great. You want to take a look at the payment breakdown? It's a real education."

"I'm already getting one," Maria said, and held up the phone, screen toward him, the grace period sentence still open. She wanted to see whether he would flinch. He did not flinch. He squinted at it with the polite interest of a man being shown a photograph of someone else's children.

"That's a good card," he said. "You pay it off every month, it costs you nothing. More people should start that young." Then, without a seam: "Now, on the sedan, here's what the interest looks like over the life of the loan." He turned the clipboard toward her, and the number at the bottom of the column was larger than the price of the car itself. Not by a little. The car cost eleven thousand dollars, and the loan, over sixty months at seven percent, would cost more than thirteen, and Duane pointed at the monthly figure as though the other number were not also sitting right there, in plain view, waiting to be noticed.

Maria looked from the clipboard to her phone, from the turbid gray paragraph that had quietly told her the truth to the clean white column that was telling her a version of it, and back to her mother, who was signing something at the desk with the pen chained to it. There was a case for the loan; she could make it herself, in her own head, the way a lawyer argues for a client she half doubts. The car meant the job, the job meant the rent, the rent meant they did not move in with Aunt Carol. That was real. But the number at the bottom of the column was also real, and she could not make the two of them agree.

She paid the twenty-six dollars on her phone, the full balance, due date still nine days away, and watched the confirmation appear. Then she walked over to the desk and stood beside her mother, not saying anything yet, just reading the paper upside down, which she had taught herself to do in seventh grade out of boredom and which now, unexpectedly, felt like a kind of power.

"Mom," she said. "Before you sign that last page, can we read the bottom line together?"

On the third day of model parliament, Layla discovered that her bill was nonsense. She had written it in one evening, eight clauses about banning vending machines that sold energy drinks in schools, and she had been proud of its moral clarity. Now Mr. Osei had posted every submitted bill on the classroom wall, and hers was next to a bill by Priya Raman, and Priya's looked like a legal document while Layla's looked like a persuasive essay with numbered paragraphs.

"Who's going to enforce it?" Priya asked when Layla sat down beside her at the long table by the window. "Clause four says schools shall not permit the sale of noxious beverages. What counts as noxious? What counts as a school? Does a sixth-form college count?" Layla said she'd fix the definitions, but fixing definitions turned out to be its own kind of quicksand. If she named specific drinks, the bill went stale the moment a new brand launched. If she named caffeine thresholds, she needed numbers she didn't have. She spent a full study period drafting and redrafting clause two and ended up with something longer and less clear than what she'd started with.

The next morning she found Priya in the library with her laptop open to the UK Parliament website. "Look at this," Priya said. "In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament." She turned the screen so Layla could read it herself. "That's why theirs look like that. There's a whole office of lawyers whose job is the writing. We're doing their part and the MPs' part." Layla felt something between relief and irritation: relief that the difficulty wasn't her personal failing, irritation that the simulation had quietly handed them a task that actual professionals spent careers learning.

What she couldn't stop thinking about, though, was what the lawyers' involvement meant for the arguing. In her draft, every clause had been an argument wearing a costume; clause four had existed to say energy drink companies were behaving badly. A drafter's clause, she realized, reading Priya's version, was supposed to be neutral enough that even an opponent could apply it honestly. That was a different kind of writing, almost a different kind of honesty. She wasn't sure which she trusted more.

The committee session on Thursday put the question to a test she hadn't expected. Marcus, playing the industry backbencher, moved to amend her bill so that "the Secretary of State may issue guidance on permitted beverages" instead of the outright ban. It was, Layla had to admit, beautifully drafted; it sounded like action while doing almost nothing, and she suspected the subterfuge was deliberate. "So you want to replace a rule with a suggestion," she said. Marcus smiled. "I want to replace a rule the House will vote down with a suggestion it might pass. Your bill loses everything. Mine saves half."

Layla looked down at her clauses, at the margin notes Priya had penciled in, and tried to hold both thoughts at once. The ban was the right policy; she still believed that. But a law that failed in division was only a gesture, and Marcus's hollow amendment was at least a law. Her mother, who had grown up somewhere that government felt like a thing done to you rather than by you, had taught her that a perfect law nobody passed was worth less than a small one that restrained somebody's worst impulse. Priya, whose parents marched and wrote letters and believed compromise was how you got subjugated slowly, thought the opposite. Layla had spent two years assuming one of them was simply correct.

She stood to speak. "I'll accept the amendment," she said, and the room reacted before she'd finished, Marcus triumphant, Priya stiffening beside her. "But I want clause six changed. If the Secretary of State issues guidance, schools have to publish whether they're following it. If it's only guidance, then let everyone see who ignores it." The chair called for objections; Marcus studied her for a long moment, tapping his pen against the desk, trying to find the trap in it, and she waited, not sure herself whether there was one.

The amended bill went to debate on Friday, then to its vote, and passed on a division of nineteen to eleven, with four abstentions. It would go to the model House of Lords, then, if it survived, to their teacher-as-monarch for royal assent, a stamp and a bell. Priya walked out with her without speaking until they reached the lockers.

"Half a law," Priya said. "You're satisfied with that?"

"I'm not satisfied," Layla said. "I'm not sure what I am." She closed her locker and held the folder with the printed bill against her chest. "Ask me after the Lords."

The garden behind the food bank had been a parking lot two years ago, and it still looked like one trying to be forgiven. Xavier had signed up for the Saturday shift because his scholarship application wanted evidence of community engagement, forty hours minimum, and he had calculated that nine Saturdays at four hours each, plus travel, would preempt any awkward November scramble. He was good at that kind of arithmetic. His mother called it planning; his guidance counselor had used the word "extrinsic," in a tone that suggested she thought it was a diagnosis.

A woman named Ruth handed him gloves and a bucket and pointed at the raspberry canes along the fence. "Pick what's ripe. What's not ripe stays." Then she went inside to weigh people in at the desk, which was, Xavier gathered, where the real work happened. The garden was a sideline. Its produce went into the hampers as the fresh item, the single tomato taped to the top of the bag like a bow on a gift nobody had wanted to need.

He was not alone. A girl about his age was already halfway down the row, moving faster than him, her bucket ringing with fruit. "Dee," she said, without looking up. "You're the new one. Try to keep the canes from whipping back, they'll get you in the eye and then you'll be a liability, and Ruth makes you sign a form." She picked three berries to his one. She had, he learned by the third row, been coming since she was twelve, and she wanted, with a specificity that startled him, to run the whole operation someday. She'd drawn up a rotation schedule on graph paper. Ruth had said it was too complicated. Dee had not forgiven this.

Around ten, Ruth called them inside to pack hampers, because the Saturday line had backed up past the coat racks. The warehouse room smelled of cardboard and floor wax. Dee assigned him to the baby-food shelf without being asked to assign anyone anything, and he began assembling the small bright jars into groups of six, the way a laminated sheet instructed, then adding the juice boxes and the snack packs that went into any hamper flagged for kids.

He hadn't expected the flags. He'd imagined, he realized, a room of single men in windbreakers, the food-bank patron of the news segment, and instead the floor was loud with children doing the specific boredom of waiting, one boy conducting an invisible orchestra with a breadstick. He counted flags out of something to do with his hands while his mind idled. Nine hampers on the table. Six had the kid additions. He did it again on the next table. Eleven, seven.

"There's a thing," Dee said, not pausing, taping a tomato. "It was on the flyer from HungerCount, that's Food Banks Canada's report. In March 2025, in Canada, about a third of food bank visits were children. One in three." She said it flat, the way you'd say the mall closes at nine. She had clearly said it many times, to many new ones, and it had stopped being information to her and become something more like weather.

He kept packing. A woman at the desk argued gently with Ruth about the size of her family, and Ruth argued gently back, and the probity of the whole exchange sat strangely with him afterward, both of them so careful, as though honesty were a thing that had to be protected on both sides. He thought about his forty hours, the form in his backpack with its signature lines, and about Dee's graph paper, and he understood that he had walked in holding two completely different ideas of the same room. In one, the hours were the point and the garden was the setting. In the other, the tomato was the point and the hours were nothing. He was not sure the second idea, now that he had it, made the first one false. The scholarship was real. His mother's rent math was real. The forms existed whether or not he despised them.

But the flyer number was also real, and it was not going to be less real in November. He decided, sorting juice boxes, that he would come back after the forty hours were done, and that he was honest enough with himself to admit he did not yet know whether that was a promise or a prediction. Some things you couldn't know until Saturday came and you either showed up or didn't. He suspected that was the actual test, and that it was badly designed, and that it was still the test.

At noon the line thinned. Ruth gave them each a cheese sandwich and a peach, the excess of some donation, and Dee sat on the loading dock eating hers with her legs swinging, the rotation schedule sticking out of her back pocket where she'd shoved it. "You did okay," she said. "For a liability who hasn't signed the form." Xavier peeled his peach in one long strip, careful, the skin coming away whole, and set the bucket of raspberries down between them.

The screen door banged twice behind Ryder before it settled, and he carried his laptop out to the porch where the afternoon heat sat on the fields like a lid. His grandfather's farm occupied the flat alluvial bottomland along the river, soil so dark it looked wet even in August, and from the porch Ryder could see the water moving slow and brown between the levee and the treeline. He set the laptop on the rail, opened the message thread with Dex, and read what he had typed. You always mess this up. We lose because of you. He had written it at midnight and had not sent it, and now, in daylight, he couldn't decide whether it was honest or just mean.

Inside, his grandfather was drying dishes with his good hand. The stroke had debilitated his left side two winters ago, leaving the arm stiff in its socket, and he had learned to pin a plate against his body with his elbow while he wiped it. He had coached the high school debate team in this county for thirty-one years. Ryder had come for the weekend partly to see him and partly, though he hadn't said so, to be somewhere without cell service in the house, so he would have an excuse not to answer Dex.

"Still hiding from that boy's message," his grandfather said, not a question. He nodded toward the porch. Grandma had gone to town for groceries. "Come sit. Tell me what he did."

Ryder told him. Dex was his partner in team debate, the better researcher and the worse speaker, and at the district semifinal Dex had frozen during the rebuttal, lost the thread, and dropped their strongest argument. Worse, he'd missed two practices the week before and shown up late to the third. "I have to tell him he's costing us," Ryder said. "Coach says the team's mine to run next year. If I can't say it, I'm not actually running anything."

His grandfather set down the plate. He was quiet for a while, looking out at the river, and then he said one sentence, the way he said most things now, sparingly, as if speech were rationed. "There's a psychologist named Gottman. He separates a complaint, which names a specific behavior, from criticism, which goes after the person." Then he picked up the next plate and went back to drying.

Ryder sat with that. He thought of his own note, the words he'd typed at midnight. You always mess this up. Always. That wasn't a behavior, that was a verdict on Dex himself, a whole character in two words. He tried rebuilding the sentence in his head. You missed practice twice before districts, and in the rebuttal you dropped our strongest argument. It sounded smaller. It sounded like something that had happened rather than something Dex was. He wasn't sure it would land any softer. He wasn't sure, either, whether softness was even the point, or whether the point was that Dex could actually do something about two missed practices and nothing at all about being a person who always messed up.

He typed the new version on the porch, deleted it twice, and typed it again. "In the semifinal you dropped the school-funding argument in rebuttal, and you missed both practices that week. Those two things are why we lost, not anything about you. Can we fix them before state?" He read it aloud under his breath, hearing his grandmother's old elocution lessons in his own cadence, the way she'd made him say vowels around a pencil at the kitchen table. He walked to the end of the driveway where the signal lived, held the phone up like a lantern, and pressed send.

The reply came fast, which meant Dex had been staring at his phone too. Not a text. A voice note, forty seconds long. Ryder stood in the gravel and listened. "I've been waiting all week for somebody to say it to my face," Dex said. "Coach told me you were getting the team and I figured you'd just replace me." Then a pause, wind on his end. "I missed those practices because my mom had a biopsy Tuesday and I couldn't sit in a room with fourteen-year-olds arguing about school funding. But I should've told you. Look, I already asked Coach if we could run a full rebuttal drill on Monday. Two hours. If you're not tired of me."

Ryder started typing a joke about never being tired of anyone who did the evidence cards, then stopped, because there was something underneath the voice note he hadn't expected. Dex had been doing the same arithmetic Ryder had, the same weighing of honest against cruel, and had come out silent. Ryder had almost come out cruel. That the two of them could stand on opposite ends of the same fear and both be wrong about the other was not something he had a sentence for yet, and he let it stay unresolved, standing there in the gravel, the sun going low and gold across the bottomland.

His grandfather was on the porch when he came back, watching the river. "Sent it?"

"Sent it."

"Good." His grandfather turned the good side of his face toward him. "Your grandmother's going to want the whole thing at dinner. Word for word."

The party had moved to the backyard because the June wind had made the front steps impossible for photographs. Twice Amy's cap had lifted off her head while her uncle Marcus held his phone up and remonstrated with the sky as if weather could be argued into cooperation, and the second time it landed in the hydrangeas and came back with a smear of pollen across the tassel. She clamped it under her arm and carried it to the picnic table like something rescued.

"You could have worn it backward," said her cousin Devi, who was fifteen and had opinions about everything Amy wore. "Or pinned it. Everyone pins it."

"It's a borrowed cap," Amy said. "Nadia's. She graduates next year."

Inside, her grandmother was arranging the cake, a sheet cake with AMY in blue script that had begun to lean in the heat. Her grandmother was taciturn by nature and by long practice, and she communicated approval mostly through food, so the size of the cake, three layers of it, said more than most speeches. What she wanted, Amy had figured out years ago, was for Amy to take the scholarship to the state school, forty minutes away, close enough for Sunday dinners. She had never once said this. She said things like, "The dorms there, I hear the food is decent," and, "Your grandfather drove past it on Tuesday, said the campus looked tidy."

At the table Amy sat between her father and Devi, and the cap sat on the bench beside her, square and ridiculous, and she kept turning it over in her hands. Her father was telling the story of his own graduation, how his mother had cried into a paper napkin and then ironed it and kept it. Amy was only half listening. She had until Monday to commit, and the two letters were folded in the drawer upstairs, the state school and the one in Chicago, and every adult at this table had a vote they hadn't cast aloud.

"Why is it this shape?" Devi asked suddenly, reaching over and tipping the cap with one finger. "Honestly, it's the dumbest hat ever invented. It won't stay on. It's flat. It's a board."

Amy started to say she didn't know, and then stopped, because she did know, some stray fact from months ago surfacing. "It's called a mortarboard," she said. "Because it looks like the board bricklayers use to hold mortar."

"A bricklayer's hat," Devi said.

"Not the hat. The board. The flat thing they carry the mortar on." Amy set the cap upright on the table, its four points making a small square planet between the potato salad and the lemonade. "So it's a builder's tool. You graduate, and they put a bricklayer's board on your head."

Her grandmother looked at the cap for a long moment. "Your grandfather laid brick," she said. "Thirty years. He'd have liked that."

The table got quiet in the way it did when her grandfather came up. Amy's father passed the cake early, without ceremony, and slices went around, and Devi ate hers standing up, hovering near Amy's shoulder.

"Chicago has brick buildings," Devi said, too quietly for the adults. "That's not a sign, but it could be one."

"That's not how signs work."

"That's exactly how signs work."

Amy laughed before she could stop herself, and then her grandmother, who had heard everything, of course she had heard everything, set down her fork. "Your grandfather wanted Chicago," she said. "For himself. Never went further than Toledo." She looked at the cap again. "He sent money home instead. To his mother. For years. Called it reparation, though for what, he never said."

It was the longest sentence her grandmother had produced all afternoon, and afterward she went back to her cake, and everyone let her.

Amy picked up the cap and put it on, square and level, and walked to the middle of the yard where the wind could reach her. It caught the board immediately, tugged at it, and she held it down with one hand and turned to face the fence and the hydrangeas and the whole tilted, pollen-dusted afternoon. "Marcus," she called. "One more."

He came jogging with his phone already raised. Behind her, Devi shouted, "Smile like you've decided," and Amy stood there in the wind, hand flat on the mortarboard, and did not answer either way.

Evan arrived at the mall twenty minutes early, which he decided was worse than arriving late, because now he had to stand near the fountain and pretend to be interested in his phone while his heart did something arrhythmic and embarrassing. Priya had suggested they meet at the arcade at noon. In his pocket he had two rolls of quarters, a folding of cash he had earned bagging groceries, and a plan he had rehearsed so many times it had worn smooth and lost its edges.

She showed up in a yellow jacket, spotted him, and waved with the whole arm, not the small polite wrist-wave. "You beat me here," she said. "That's suspicious."

"I wanted to claim the good air hockey table," Evan said. "There is a good one. It's the one where the blower isn't capricious."

"Capricious."

"Sometimes the puck just stops. Like it's bored."

They played air hockey first, and she beat him twice, both times by one point, which felt like a mercy she was extending rather than luck. Then they moved to the bowling alley on the third floor, where the mall's carpet turned from gray to a bruised purple and the shoe rental guy didn't look up from his phone. Evan paid for both of them before Priya could reach for her wallet, and she said, "Okay, but I'm getting snacks," and he understood this as a small treaty being signed, a consonance between what he wanted to do and what she would allow, and it made him glad in a way he couldn't have explained to his brother, who would have said he was overthinking a pretzel.

The first game they were both terrible, laughing at gutter balls, and the second game tightened. Priya turned out to be the kind of person who narrated her own failures in a sportscaster voice. Somewhere in the third frame of the tiebreaker, Evan realized his hands were shaking, and not from the sixteen-pound ball. His pulse was doing the thing it did before exams, a fast shallow drumming, and Priya was standing close enough that he could smell the chlorine from her morning swim practice, and the two sensations braided together so thoroughly he couldn't tell which one belonged to which.

"You're pacing," she said. "You've walked past the ball return four times."

"I'm strategizing."

"You're vibrating."

He rolled a strike on the ninth frame purely by accident, and she rolled one back at him on purpose, and now they were tied going into the last ball, and the alley had gone quiet around them in the specific way arcades and alleys do, all noise receding to make room for one moment. He picked up his ball. His heart was slamming. He told himself it was the score, the tie, the fact that losing in front of her was suddenly unbearable and winning in front of her was somehow more so.

She won. Her last ball clipped the headpin at an angle that took down everything, and she didn't gloat, which was somehow worse than gloating, and they walked out past the snack counter where she bought him soft pretzel twists to expiate her victory, tearing one in half and handing him the bigger piece.

"It's a real thing," Evan said. They were sitting on a bench outside the arcade now, and the words came out before he could inspect them. "Misattribution of arousal. Psychologists call it that. A racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person standing nearby."

Priya stopped chewing. "Where did you read that?"

"My brother's psych textbook. I was looking for why I couldn't sleep last night." He turned the pretzel in his hands. "So here's my problem. My heart rate was completely abnormal for bowling. And I don't know if that means I like you, or if you just happened to be standing next to me during a tense tiebreaker, and my body filed the evidence wrong."

Priya looked at him for a long moment, and then at the fountain, where coins caught the light like small drowned constellations. "That is the most romantic terrible thing anyone has ever said to me," she said.

"I'm not done. The theory says I could test it. Bowling again, sometime, with the same stakes and no you. If my heart stays calm, it was you." He took a breath. "But if I'm being honest, I already know I'd rather not know than not see you again, which I recognize is not how experiments are supposed to work."

She finished her pretzel and dusted the salt off her fingers onto her jeans. "So we're skipping the control group."

"We're skipping the control group."

"That's bad science," Priya said. She stood up, zipped her yellow jacket to the chin, and held out her hand as if they were closing a business deal. "Same time next Saturday. Bring more quarters."

Evan took her hand, and his heart did the thing again, cause unknown, and he let it.

Dinner was late because Theo was late, and Theo was late because he had missed the bus. He came in with his jacket half off and his face set in that truculent way he had, daring anyone to mention it, so of course their father mentioned it within ten seconds.

"If you'd left five minutes earlier," their father said, spooning rice onto his plate, "you'd have been standing at that stop with time to spare. This is not advanced mathematics."

"Except you don't know that," Theo said, dropping into his chair. "If I'd left five minutes earlier, I'd have caught the bus. That's a fact."

"It's not a fact," Anna said. She hadn't meant to say anything. She was eighteen days from her own decision, the deposit envelope sitting upstairs under a lamp like something that might escape, and she was tired of hypotheticals, including her own. "You can never check it. You can't go back and leave five minutes earlier and see what happens. It sounds like a fact but there's no way to test it."

"Theo, pass the soy sauce," their mother said. "Anna, eat something before you litigate."

Anna speared a piece of broccoli mostly to be obedient, then kept going anyway. "It's called a counterfactual conditional," she said. "I found it last night. Counterfactual, meaning counter to the facts. It's a sentence about what would have been true if things had been different. Like, if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it. But the whole point is that Sally doesn't own a donkey. That's usually built in. The sentence kind of whispers that the if part is false."

"You looked this up," Theo said, "to win a fight I was having with Dad."

"I looked it up because of the deposit." That came out louder than she'd planned. Her father put his fork down. "I keep thinking, if I'd applied by the early deadline, I'd have gotten the bigger scholarship. And I say it to myself like it's evidence. Like it proves I should take the loans and go anyway, because the mistake was mine and now I have to pay for it forever. But it's a donkey sentence. I don't know what would have happened. Nobody does."

Her father was quiet for a moment, and Anna watched him decide not to be a magistrate about it, which she appreciated, because he could have been. "You know my position," he said instead. "Loans aren't a moral failure, they're a structure. You amortize them over twenty years, it's a monthly number, not a haunting. But I hear that your position isn't my position."

"Her position is Theo's position," Theo said, brightening. "You both missed a bus. Hers is just more expensive."

"That's not wrong," Anna admitted, and Theo looked so startled at being agreed with that he knocked over his water glass. Their mother caught it before it reached the rice, mostly.

While they mopped, Anna tried to say the thing she'd been assembling all week, the two halves of it. "Here's where I landed. Dad's right that the debt is a real number, knowable, monthly, concrete. And I'm right that the other path, the year off, the reapplication, whatever I imagine about it, is a donkey I don't own. So I can't weigh them against each other like they're the same kind of thing. One of them I can check. The other one I can only want." She paused. "The honest thing is to say I don't know what the deferral would have gotten me. I might be choosing the worse option. I can't rule that out."

"So what are you going to do?" her mother asked.

Anna looked at the envelope waiting upstairs, and then at Theo, who was still wet from his own missed bus, still convinced that five minutes would have saved him, still unable to prove it and still, somehow, okay at the table, eating.

"I'm going to mail it tomorrow," she said. "Not because it's the right choice. Because it's the checkable one. And I'm going to stop telling myself the early deadline story, because that donkey doesn't exist."

Theo raised his glass, which was empty. "To donkeys that don't exist," he said.

"To donkeys that don't exist," Anna said, and touched her water glass to his.

The game started at seven, but Nathan's grandfather had the television on by five, volume low, while he browned sausages in a pan that predated everyone in the room except himself. Family and neighbors folded into the sofas and folding chairs, plates balanced on knees, and Nathan sat on the floor near his grandfather's chair because the floor was where you sat when you were eighteen and the good seats went to aunts. The cup final was that night, and everyone in the house had picked a side except Nathan, who had picked neither and been teased for it twice before the anthem ended.

His cousin Marcus wanted the bet. He had twenty dollars riding on the game with a friend from his dispatcher job, and more than that he wanted Nathan to take a side, any side, so the room could divide properly and the shouting could mean something. "You can't just watch," Marcus said, leaning over the back of the couch. "That's like going to a wedding and not crying."

"I'm deciding," Nathan said.

"You've been deciding for three periods."

His grandfather laughed at that, a dry sound under the whistle of the crowd on the screen. Nathan had come to the house mostly for him, though he hadn't said so. In September Nathan would move six hours north for college, and his grandfather had been slow and then suddenly quick to mention it, asking about the dorms, the meal plan, whether Nathan would come back for deer season. Nathan wanted to leave something behind that wasn't just a duffel bag, some evening his grandfather would retell. An opinion felt like the cheapest available offering, so he decided to have one, and loudly.

Between the second and third period, with the score tied, the broadcast showed the trophy itself in its case, silver catching the arena lights. Marcus pointed at the screen and said the cup was older than anything else in sports, and Nathan, wanting his turn, said no, that baseball had older trophies, that everything in America was older than hockey. The room went quiet in the particular way a room goes quiet when a grandfather sets down his fork.

"Look it up," his grandfather said. "Not on my account. On yours."

Nathan pulled out his phone, half to end the conversation and half because he did not like being wrong in a house where being wrong had consequences. He found it, and then found it again on a second site to be sure. The cup had been donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, and first awarded in 1893, and it was the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America. Not baseball. Not anything. He read the words twice, and the second reading was slower, because the first had been about Marcus being wrong and the second was about him being wrong.

"Okay," Nathan said, and he said it out loud before he could decide whether to. "The cup. It's the oldest one there is. Donated in 1892, by a lord, Lord Stanley of Preston, and they first gave it out in 1893. For a pro team, in North America, nothing's older." Marcus spread his hands as if presenting a verdict. The aunts murmured. Nathan's grandfather nodded once and went back to his plate, but he was watching the screen now with a different posture, shoulders settled, like a man whose point had been made for him by someone he hadn't expected to make it.

Nathan sat with it through the third period. He cogitated, honestly, in the way he was learning to at eighteen, turning the thing over instead of shoving it away. He had wanted to win the argument, and he had lost it, and both of those were smaller than the fact itself: that a trophy could outlive its donor, its first winners, the entire league that first played for it, and still be handed over every spring like something new. His roommate-to-be, a law student's son, had once used the word jurisprudence at the dinner table to mean the whole slow accumulation of judgments, and Nathan understood it now in a way he hadn't then. Some things were valuable precisely because they kept being used. He also understood that this could be an excuse, that "old" was not the same as "good," and that he could not prove the cup mattered, only that it persisted. That part stayed unresolved, and he let it.

When the winning goal came, late, off a rebound through turbid traffic in front of the net, the room came apart. Marcus was on his feet with both fists up, twenty dollars richer on paper, and the aunts were shrieking, and the neighbor's dog started barking in the yard. Nathan stood too, and he was shouting, and he realized he had chosen the winner somewhere in the third period without marking the moment he'd done it. His grandfather reached down from the chair and gripped his shoulder, once, hard, and kept his eyes on the screen where the players were lining up to shake hands.

"September," his grandfather said, over the noise. "You'll write?"

"Every week," Nathan said. "First letter's about tonight."

"Make it good," his grandfather said, and pointed at the screen, at the silver being carried out under the lights. "You got the facts right. Now get the rest right."

Antoine had laced his skates twice before Dess arrived, once too tight and once too loose, and by the time she pushed through the rink doors in a green coat with frost still in her hair, he had convinced himself that neither configuration was right. She waved from across the rubber mats. She was in his stats class, the one who had corrected Mr. Halloran about a scatterplot in October and then apologized for correcting him, which was the combination that had made him ask her here in the first place.

"You came," she said, and then, as if that were too much, "I mean, obviously you came, you're wearing skates."

"I considered wearing shoes and standing tragically at the edge," Antoine said, "but that felt like it might portend the whole evening, so." She laughed, a short surprised sound, and he logged it as the best thing that had happened to him all month.

They went around the rink four times before she fell, and he fell with her on purpose, which she seemed to understand was on purpose, which was its own kind of conversation. On the fifth lap she took his hand and squeezed it, and then, when a cluster of little kids cut them off near the Zamboni door, she squeezed harder, her nails half-moons in the back of his wrist, and steered him sideways with a grip that stayed after the danger had passed. He noticed it the way you notice a door left open in winter, as a fact about the room.

Marcus worked the skate counter on Saturdays. When Antoine sat down to retie his left boot, Marcus drifted over with the unhurried, phlegmatic calm of someone who had watched a thousand first dates circle the ice and knew most of the ways they could go. "Your girl's got a grip on you," he said, not quite joking.

"She's steering. There were kids."

"There were kids ten minutes ago too. She's still got your arm." Marcus leaned on the rail. "My cousin does this thing where she talks about healthy relationships at schools. She's always saying this number. In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence." He said it flat, like a phone number he'd memorized for a reason. "Twelve to one. Sit with that a second."

Antoine looked at his own arm, where the red was already fading, and felt two arguments assemble themselves in him at once, like skaters approaching from opposite ends of the rink. The first said: it was nothing, a hand on an arm, a girl who didn't know her own strength, a night he didn't want to turn into a case study. The second said: Marcus had said the number for a reason, and the reason wasn't that Antoine was special enough to be the exception. The number didn't know Antoine. The number also didn't know Dess. It knew only that among people exactly like them, one in twelve had reported something, and reported was its own uncertain word, a floor beneath a floor.

"I don't think it's that," Antoine said, and heard how the sentence had a hinge in the middle, a place where it could swing either way.

"I don't think it's that either," Marcus said. "I think you should think about it anyway. That's all the number asks."

Back on the ice, Dess caught his hand again, gently this time, and pointed out the DJ booth with a story about her older brother's disastrous ninth-grade dance, and Antoine laughed in the right places while the two arguments went on trading the puck somewhere behind his sternum. He did not believe she was cruel. He also could not unknow that a grip can be a grip and still be a grip too hard, and that the difference between those things lived not in the hand but in what the hand felt entitled to. He decided, at the speed of a falling skater, that he could hold both ideas at once without dropping either, and that the honest part was admitting he couldn't yet tell which one was load-bearing.

They got hot chocolate at the counter, and when she reached to wipe a streak of it off his sleeve she paused, hand hovering, and asked, "Is this okay?" Antoine said yes, and the question sat between them like something she had been taught, or something she already knew. Maybe both. Maybe that was fine.

She kissed his cheek outside the rink, quick as a card trick, and walked to her mother's car with the frost coming back into her hair. Antoine stood under the sodium lights pulling at his laces, watching her go, watching Marcus stack rental skates with the erudition of a man who knew every size in the building by feel, and his wrist still faintly remembered itself. He took out his phone and typed "1 in 12" into his notes app, then deleted it, then typed it again, and left it there, unsigned, next to the word Dess and a question mark he did not fill in. Then he walked to the bus stop with one skate still half on.

Mia got to the coffee shop first and claimed the table by the window, the one where the afternoon light came in flat and steady across the wood. She put her notebook down, ordered a hot chocolate, and waited, because Theo and Priya were both coming, and both of them thought the other was wrong about something Mia had to write five hundred words on by Friday. The school paper wanted an opinion piece on media ownership, and she had told the editor she had a position. She did not, yet, have a position.

They arrived together, which was a bad sign. Theo dropped his bag on a chair and said, before anyone had sat down properly, "It's a conflict of interest, full stop. A politician shouldn't be allowed to own a TV network. That's not complicated." Priya pulled her scarf off slowly, the way she did when she wanted to seem unhurried. "It's not complicated for you," she said. "In Italy it actually happened and the republic survived. You want to ban things because they sound bad in a sentence."

Mia opened her notebook to a clean page. "Tell me the Italy part," she said. "The real part, not the slogan part." Priya leaned in. "Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, which owned three of Italy's main national TV channels, while he was serving as the country's prime minister. That's the fact. He had the state broadcaster on one side and his own channels on the other." Theo made a sound like a kettle starting. "So one man was the government and the competition. How is that not the whole argument right there?"

"Because people knew," Priya said. "They voted anyway, more than once. You're treating voters like they're being fooled, and maybe they just preferred him." Theo turned his cup in its saucer. "Or the coverage made them prefer him. You can know something is tilted and still drink from it every night." Mia wrote that down, then crossed it out, then wrote it again in the margin where she put things she couldn't yet place.

The shop had begun to fill. Behind the counter, the owner's son, who everyone said had been given the espresso machine job as a favor, pulled shots without much attention, and Priya, watching him, muttered that it was a sinecure, a position that existed because someone wanted him provided for. Mia found herself thinking that ownership and obligation ran along quieter lines than Theo's argument allowed. Whoever owned the shop owned the tone of the place, what got fixed, who got hired, what the regulars were allowed to feel at home saying out loud.

"I'll look it up," she said, and pulled her laptop over. The school database gave her the same fact Priya had recited, in flatter language, and then two historians arguing past each other about what it meant. One called the era's media landscape seismic, an upheaval that rearranged everything Italians understood about where their news came from. The other said the coverage had simply ossified, hardening over the years into a shape no one could remember being otherwise. Mia read both twice. Theo read over her shoulder. Priya read the opposing one, out of principle.

"See," Theo said. "Even the experts are only arguing from what they already believed." Priya closed her half of the screen with one finger. "Or they're describing a real thing from different sides. That's allowed." Mia turned the laptop toward herself again and began to write, slowly, crossing out the first sentence twice. What she settled on was this: it was possible to hold that a prime minister owning three of the main national channels was a genuine problem, and also to admit, honestly, that she could not prove from where she sat which votes that arrangement had moved and which it hadn't. Priya wanted a clean acquittal and Theo wanted a clean conviction, and the piece she was writing was going to disappoint both of them, which she suspected was the point of the assignment.

She read her draft out loud, the last paragraph, the one that ended on the sentence she was least sure of and refused to cut. When she finished, Theo said, "You're hedging." Priya said, "She's not, she's being accurate, there's a difference." Mia closed the laptop, finished the cold end of her hot chocolate, and said, "Both of you read it tonight and tell me which sentence you'd fight me on. That one's the one I care about."

The climbing gym sat at the back of a strip mall between a nail salon and a vacuum repair shop, and Ryan had worked its front desk since September, three evenings a week and Saturdays. His job was mostly ancillary: he rang up day passes, rented shoes, and made people sign the waiver before they touched a wall.
