The waiver lived on a clipboard, eight pages of small print that nobody read, and after four months Ryan had stopped watching people skim it. They signed where the arrow sticker pointed, the way he signed his own on the first day, back when his manager, Dahlia, told him everyone signs, even staff.

On a Tuesday in February a man named Kessler fell off the bouldering wall from about twelve feet up. Ryan heard the thud from the desk, then the quiet after it, which was worse. Kessler had climbed beyond the marked edge of a route where the padding had been rolled back for a floor cleaning that never got finished. An ambulance took him away with his wrist wrapped in a cold pack, and Dahlia spent the next hour on the phone in the office with the door shut.

The next shift, Dahlia called Ryan into the office before open. She had the incident report in front of her and the waiver behind it, Kessler's signature on the last page. "He signed," she said. "That's the whole point of the thing. Assumption of risk, release of liability. His signature says he knew bouldering is dangerous and he agreed not to come after us."

Ryan said nothing at first. He was thinking about the padding. He had rolled part of it back himself two weeks earlier because a mop bucket was in the way, and he could not remember rolling it all forward again. There was a note taped inside the supply closet that said PAD ROOM FLOOR IS PART OF THE JOB, in Dahlia's handwriting, which meant it had been part of nobody's job.

That night he looked it up on his phone, sitting on the floor of his room with his sneakers still on. Ryan was not a good student in the school sense, but he was an autodidact in the narrow sense that when a question got its hooks in him, he could not leave it alone until he had read everything free and legal to read. He read a law firm's page, then a second one, then a forum where climbers argued about waivers the way other people argued about referees. The rule that kept appearing was this: courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it. He read the sentence three times. A signature did not cover everything. There was a line, and the gym was on one side of it or the other, and where the padding had been rolled back was, he suspected, exactly the kind of thing that decided which.

He thought about it from both directions, because he was loyal to both. Dahlia had hired him without an interview, basically, had taught him to belay and let him climb for free after close. The gym was the only thing in town that hadn't tried to commodify his evenings; every other job he'd applied to wanted his Saturdays as inventory. At the same time Kessler had gone to the hospital, and Kessler had a daughter who came in with him sometimes, maybe nine years old, who wore a pink helmet and called the auto-belay "the robot." Ryan could hold both thoughts, but he could not make them into one comfortable thought.

On Saturday Dahlia asked him to pull Kessler's file, and she laid the signed waiver on the counter between them, turned so the signature faced Ryan. "If his lawyer calls," she said, "you're the one who checked him in, so you might have to say he signed it in front of you. That's all. He signed, that's the fact."

"He did sign it," Ryan said. "I watched him." He put his hand flat on the pages, not covering the signature, just resting there. "But the padding was rolled back past the edge of the route. I rolled part of it back, and I don't know if I put it all the way forward."

Dahlia looked at the note-in-progress in her own hand, a claim form she'd been filling out for the gym's insurer, and did not say anything for a long moment. The routes behind them were quiet before open, only the furnace ticking. Somewhere above, at the top of the lead wall, a carabiner swung on its cable and knocked, once, twice.

"We can write that down," she said finally. "Or we don't write anything."

Ryan took the clipboard off the counter and clipped the incident report on top of the waiver, padding note side up. "We can write it down," he said, and slid it toward her side.

Riley had exactly one appointment at Fennick & Associates, and he was eleven minutes early for it, which felt wrong, like arriving early to a punishment. The office smelled of toner and old carpet, and a vending machine in the corner hummed the way vending machines do when they are pretending to be refrigerators. He had brought a shoebox. In the shoebox were his T4 slip from the garden centre, a rubber-banded stack of receipts, and, underneath everything, the folded page of the bicycle ad he had been carrying since March. The bike cost four hundred and eighty dollars. His refund, according to the internet, could be "up to" some amount that the internet refused to specify.

"You're the student," said Mr. Fennick, who was small and precise and had the manner of an epicure tasting a wine he already suspected he would like. He took the shoebox the way other men took oysters. "First return. Wonderful. Everything is still honest."

Riley sat across the desk and watched receipts bloom into piles. His paycheques from the summer had already confused him once; he'd grossed eleven hundred in July and taken home less than a thousand, and when he'd asked his father about it, his father had said "that's just how it is" in the voice he used for weather. But the cheque stub was in the box, and Mr. Fennick tapped it. "See the line that says income tax deducted? That's the government taking its share before you ever see the money. Now we find out if they took too much."

"And then they give it back."

"If we're persuasive." Mr. Fennick held up a receipt for Riley's transit pass, all eight months of it, and then another for the steel-toed boots the garden centre had required but not paid for. He set them side by side like two witnesses. "One of these is a credit. One is a deduction. Do you know the difference, or would you like to guess badly first?"

Riley guessed badly first. He pointed at the boots, because the boots had cost more, a hundred and six dollars against ninety-two for the pass, and bigger numbers had never failed him in math class. "The boots. Obviously."

"Delightfully wrong." Mr. Fennick slid the transit pass forward. "A deduction lowers the income that your tax is calculated on. A credit subtracts directly from the tax you owe. So a credit is usually worth more than a deduction of the same size." He said it the way a man says checkmate, without gloating, because the position itself was the pleasure.

Riley did not understand it immediately, and he was truculent about not understanding immediately, which slowed everything down. He kept saying "but it's ninety-two dollars" and Mr. Fennick kept saying "it is ninety-two dollars against the tax, not against the income," until at some point the two sentences turned around in Riley's head and locked. The boots didn't erase a hundred and six dollars of tax. They shrank the income a little, and the tax on that smaller income came out a few dollars lighter. The pass, the smaller receipt, hit the tax itself. It was like the difference between paying for a meal before or after the discount, except that it was his money, in his life, and no one had mentioned it in any class he had ever sat through.

He tried to internalize it, testing the idea against other things he knew. His mother's receipts in the kitchen drawer, the stacks at garage sales, the way everyone talked about writing things off as if it were magic. None of it had ever been magic. It was arithmetic wearing a tie. He thought about the sales tax on the boots, thirteen percent, printed right there on the receipt, money that simply left and never came back, and he felt a brief irrational loyalty to the transit pass, which had at least fought for him.

"However," said Mr. Fennick, and here he spread both hands over the desk like a magician conceding that the trick also required a table, "you can have both. This is not a duel. Deduct the boots, claim the credit on the pass, and your refund comes to two hundred and sixty-one dollars. You are a very organized young man, which in this office is the highest compliment I am permitted to give."

It was not four hundred and eighty dollars. Riley did the subtraction in his head without wanting to. Two hundred and nineteen dollars short, and the bike in the ad was last year's model and would not sit in the shop window forever, waiting for his arithmetic to improve. He thought about saying something clever about a system that taxed a sixteen-year-old's boots before he'd even earned the money to buy them, but he looked at Mr. Fennick's calm, satisfied face and decided the man had heard every version of it. He was sixteen. There would be other refunds, other receipts, a whole life of shoeboxes ahead of him, and that thought was either comforting or terrible depending on the minute.

On the way out he stopped at the vending machine, fed it a toonie, and pressed the button for the coffee that had been steaming under the little light all afternoon. The cup dropped with a thud. It tasted like hot, polite nothing. He drank it standing up, reading his refund slip again, and then folded it once and put it in his back pocket, next to the ad.

The cemetery sat on a hill above the town, and Alexis climbed it with a bucket of water in each hand, her aunt carrying the flowers. The stones were small and close together, dark with rain, each family's plot delimited by a low curb of concrete so that the hill looked like a field of shallow rooms. Her grandfather's grave was near the top. She had never met him. He had died in March, in his sleep, and her mother had cried at the kitchen table in Ohio and then said, "You should go. You should know them." So here she was, sixteen and jet-lagged, at a grave that was supposed to mean something to her.

Her aunt knelt and began to wash the stone, pouring water over the carved characters with a small ladle. Alexis crouched beside her and copied the motion, careful, the water running off the granite and darkening the gravel. "Slower," her aunt said, in English, smiling a little. "Like you're cleaning his face." Alexis slowed down. It was strange to be gentle with someone who existed for her only as a voice on the phone twice a year, a man who always asked whether she was still studying.

That evening, back at the house, her cousin Natsumi pulled her toward the front step, where a small fire was burning in a clay bowl heaped with moss and twigs. "It's Obon," Natsumi said. "The spirits come home this time of year. The fire shows them the way." Their grandmother's face appeared in the doorway, and she set a plate of the grandfather's favorite sweet potatoes on the step beside the flame, as though he might actually sit down. Alexis watched the smoke rise past the lantern above the door. She did not believe spirits traveled anywhere. She believed in neurons stopping, in a body in a box, in the plain fact of absence. But the sweet potatoes sat there steaming, and nobody found it strange, and she began to feel that the strangeness might be hers.

For two days the house felt fuller than its rooms could explain. People who had known him told stories at dinner: his idiosyncrasy of folding maps into eighths so they fit his shirt pocket, his habit of naming every cat that wandered through the garden even when it never came back. Alexis listened hard, filing the details away like evidence. Each story seemed to delimit him further, and yet the shape they made was not a person she could see. It was a person she was constructing out of other people's love, and she could not tell whether that counted as knowing him or only as mourning a stranger politely.

On the last night of Obon, Natsumi woke her before dawn and they walked down to the river with the family, carrying a paper lantern with the grandfather's name brushed down its side in black ink. The bank was crowded. Dozens of lanterns already glowed on the dark water, drifting slowly downstream, each one carrying a spirit back to wherever spirits went when the festival ended. Alexis held their lantern while her uncle lit the small candle inside, shielding the flame with his cupped hands even though there was no wind.

"You set it on the water," Natsumi said. "Like this." She knelt at the edge and let the current take the first lantern, her grandmother's sister's. It spun once, steadied, and glided away.

Alexis knelt where Natsumi had been. The water was cold on her wrist. She thought of her mother across the ocean, asleep, and of the phone calls she had answered while doing homework, barely listening, saying yes, yes, still studying. That was all she had of him: eleven minutes a year of distracted affection. She could not make that into a grandfather. She could not pretend the lantern was going anywhere but down the river to the sea. And yet her hands were shaking slightly, and she did not want to let go.

She lowered the lantern onto the current, held the rim a moment longer, and released it. It joined the others, a small light among small lights, growing smaller. Her aunt put an arm around her shoulders. "He would have liked you," she said quietly. Alexis watched until the light was indistinguishable from the rest, and then kept watching anyway.

"Next summer," Natsumi said, "you light the fire yourself."

Leah had been coming to Mr. Okafor's office every Tuesday in February, and every Tuesday he asked the same question. "Still nothing from Harmon's?" Harmon's was the garden centre where she had spent the summer hauling flats of impatiens and running the register, and where she was owed a form she had been told to wait for. "They said it's coming," she said, setting her binder on his desk. Inside the binder were her pay stubs, every one kept in order, each showing her gross wages, the federal income tax withheld, the amounts for Social Security and Medicare, and the smaller number at the bottom that had actually landed in her account. She had wanted to file in January. She had wanted the refund by now.

The refund mattered. The community college in Midvale required a two-hundred-dollar deposit by the first week of March, and Leah's savings had been eaten by car repairs in November, when the Corolla's alternator died on the isthmus of highway between her town and the next one, that narrow stretch with water on both sides and no shoulder to speak of. Her mother had said she could help, but her mother's hours at the hospital had been cut, and Leah had watched her say it while refilling her coffee with the same grounds from that morning. So the deposit was Leah's to cover, and the refund was the only money she could see coming.

She understood her own pay stubs well enough. She could look at a stub from July, the one where she had worked fifty-one hours in two weeks, and see how income tax had been taken out of her wages before she ever touched the money. What she could not quite metabolize was the other half of the picture, the tax return itself, the form that would add up a whole year and compare what she had already paid against what she actually owed. That was the part Mr. Okafor did for people, and the part that required the paper from Harmon's.

"Every employer is supposed to give each employee a W-2 by the end of January," Leah said, reciting it the way she recited chemistry. "Showing last year's wages and the taxes they withheld." She had learned it from a government webpage at the library, printed it, and highlighted it in two colors.

"That's the rule," Mr. Okafor said. He was signing letters and did not look up. "Without it, we're guessing at numbers we shouldn't guess at."

She had tried being polite about it. Then she had tried being early, appearing at Harmon's at opening time, when Mr. Harmon's brother was unlocking the gate and the plants in the greenhouse aisle were still torpid from the cold night, leaves folded in on themselves like sleeping hands. He had told her the person who did the forms was "working on it." Today she decided to stop asking and start sitting. She brought a folding chair from the car, set it up beside the register where she used to work, opened her binder across her knees, and waited.

Sales tax came up while she waited, because a woman bought four bags of potting soil and complained at the total. "It's the sales tax," Leah said, pointing at the register screen, where the price of the soil appeared first and then the tax, added on top, a separate line before the sum. "Different thing from income tax. This one's on what you buy, not what you earn." The woman paid, still complaining, and Leah wrote nothing down, but she noticed that she had explained it without hesitation, and that noticing steadied her.

An hour in, Mr. Harmon himself came out from the back, saw her, and went into his office without speaking. Twenty minutes after that he came back holding an envelope. "This got sent to your old address," he said. "The one on your hiring paperwork. It came back to us." He held it out as though it were slightly her fault, and she took it before he could change his mind. The envelope had a green sticker and her handwriting from June on the back, her emergency contact, her mother's old apartment number. She did not open it there. She thanked him, folded the chair, and drove to Mr. Okafor's with the envelope unopened on the passenger seat because her hands were doing something strange and she didn't trust them at highway speed.

He opened it with a letter opener, angled so she could see. The form inside listed her wages for the year and, below that, the total federal income tax withheld, numbers she recognized from her own stubs, now gathered into one place. There were boxes for other things too, and Mr. Okafor said, "Now, do you have anything that might count as a deduction? Anything you kept receipts for?" and Leah said, slowly, that she had kept every receipt for the steel-toed boots and gloves she had been required to buy, somewhere in the same binder, and she started turning pages while he watched. Outside the window a man was salting the sidewalk, and the grains scattered white against the grey. She found the receipts, flattened them on the desk one by one, and slid them across to him.

Vincent had claimed the corner table at Marrow & Bean because it had the only outlet that worked, and he defended it the way you defend anything you can't legally own: with a bag on one chair, a jacket on the other, and a posture of permanent occupation. He was supposed to be drafting his deferral essay, the one explaining to the admissions office that a semester off was not the same thing as giving up, though so far he had produced a title and a bolded sentence he already hated.

Two tables over, a girl was talking to herself, or to her laptop, which amounted to the same thing. "The data's right there," she said, jabbing a finger at her screen. "I have eleven sources. Eleven." She caught Vincent looking and, instead of embarrassed, seemed relieved to have an audience. "Sorry. Persuasive essay. Due tomorrow. My professor is going to fail me."

"Eleven sources sounds like a lot," Vincent said.

"That's what I thought." She turned the laptop toward him like evidence at trial. Her claim, underlined twice, read: The city should not pathologize homelessness by treating it as a mental health crisis rather than a housing failure. Below it, a wall of statistics, studies, a citation from a philosopher named Toulmin. "But my professor wrote on the draft that I have a claim and I have grounds, whatever that means, and then just a question mark. A question mark. Like I'm supposed to know what's missing."

Vincent pulled his chair over, which felt like a decision, though it was really only two feet. The citation at the bottom of her bibliography caught his eye: The Uses of Argument, 1958, Stephen Toulmin. He'd scrolled past the same book the night before, hunting for structure words to steal for his deferral essay. "Can I see that page?" he asked, and she handed over the library copy she had wedged under her binder, its spine cracked at a chapter about an argument's backbone.

He read faster than he had all week. Claim, grounds, warrant. The claim was what you wanted to prove. The grounds were the data, her eleven sources. And the warrant was the thing explaining why those grounds actually supported the claim, the bridge between them. She had built two towers and assumed the river would cross itself.

"Okay," he said. "Say I told you my uncle got furloughed from the plant and his mental health went bad. You'd say that proves your claim, right?"

"Obviously. Housing and income instability, psychological decline."

"But my roommate would say the opposite. He'd say the mental health problem came first, that's why he lost the plant job, so it proves we need therapists, not apartments. Same story. Both of us have grounds. Neither of us has the thing that says which way the arrow points."

She stared at him. "The warrant."

"If I'm pronouncing it right."

She opened a new document and typed the word at the top of the page like a dare. Then she said, "So my warrant has to be something like: when cities treat a condition as medical, they fund clinics instead of housing, and the studies show the housing approach works better where it's been tried. Which means I have to actually say that. Out loud. In sentences."

"In sentences is the traditional method."

He watched her rebuild the essay in real time, and the strange part was that it was helping him too, though not about housing. His own essay had a claim, taking a semester off is responsible, and grounds, his father's recovery, the money, the hours at his uncle's shop. But he had never written the line that connected them, the line that said why the grounds proved anything. Maybe there wasn't one. Maybe the admissions office would read his eleven sources and draw the arrow however it liked. He could control the claim. He could control the grounds. The warrant was where he had to argue, in the open, where somebody could disagree.

"What's yours about?" the girl asked, nodding at his mostly blank screen.

"Me being scared and calling it a plan."

She laughed, a short, unguarded bark that made the barista look up. "Write that down," she said. "No, seriously. That's a claim about yourself. Grounds are easy. Warrant's the hard part, apparently." She copied the book's page number onto a napkin and slid it across to him. "Stephen Toulmin, 1958, The Uses of Argument. He's the reason you're about to fail your coffee."

"You're the reason," Vincent said. "Toulmin's just the alibi."

He opened a new document and typed the sentence he'd been avoiding: If a deferral is granted to students with clear obligations at home, then my situation qualifies because, and stopped. Because. He could hear the argument fork right there, the nascent disagreement waiting in the word, and for the first time all week he didn't mind it.

The girl had already written half a page, muttering, "Warrant, warrant," like a spell. Vincent leaned back, read his sentence again, and started typing.

The phone store smelled like new plastic and floor cleaner, and Dylan had been standing at the display case for twenty minutes, holding the putative object of all his summer savings in his hand. The phone was light in a way that felt like a trick. Behind the counter, a woman with a lanyard full of pins was explaining data plans to an old man who kept saying "but I just want to call my sister," and her voice stayed patient the whole time, which Dylan noted, because his mother would not have managed it.

"Good news," said Marcus, the sales guy who'd approached him ten minutes ago and then wisely backed off. "You're pre-approved for the store card. Zero percent interest for twelve months. You could walk out with it today."

Dylan looked at the price again. Seven hundred and forty-nine dollars. He had two hundred and eleven in his bank account, saved from mowing lawns since April, plus a birthday coming up that might bring fifty from his grandmother if she was feeling flush. The gap between those numbers had a physical weight, like the gap between the diving board and the water at the municipal pool.

"What happens after twelve months?" he asked.

"The standard rate kicks in. But you'd have it paid off by then, right?" Marcus smiled, and it was a real smile, not a sales smile, which somehow made it worse. "Most people just pay the minimum anyway. Keeps it easy on the budget."

Dylan's mother had a word for moments like this, borrowed from a documentary she'd watched about physics: determinism. Everything that came after was already contained in what came before, she liked to say at the kitchen table, and he'd always argued with her, because if that were true then choice was an illusion and arguing was pointless. Now, holding the phone, he felt the pull of it, the way the whole afternoon seemed to have been aimed at this counter since he'd first seen the commercial in June.

"Can I see the card agreement?" he asked.

Marcus blinked, then pulled a folded brochure from under the register. "Nobody reads these," he said, but he handed it over and didn't wander off. Dylan spread it on the counter, running his finger down the fine print while the old man behind him finally chose a plan and said thank you twice. There, in a box near the bottom, was a line that stopped his finger cold: a table showing that if he paid only the minimum payment each month, it would take him years to pay off the balance. Years, plural. The statement would have to show it to him every month, by law.

"Six years?" he said out loud.

"Minimum payments are small," Marcus said. "So it takes a long time. That's how it works." He said it without embarrassment, the way you'd report the weather.

Dylan did the arithmetic on the back of his hand with a pen from his backpack, badly, then again on a napkin the woman with the lanyard brought him without being asked. She'd seen him counting, apparently, and set down the napkin and a cup of water from the cooler and went back to her filing. If he saved what he could each month instead, the same two hundred and eleven would grow at the bank, his mother had shown him that once with a graph, little by little, without him lifting a finger after the deposit. The two ideas sat side by side in his head, not enemies exactly, more like two roads from the same trailhead, and he was surprised that nobody had ever put them next to each other for him before.

"I think I'll wait," he said.

"For the sale? The sale ends Saturday."

"For the phone." He set it back in the display cradle, and it clicked in like it had never left. The screen dimmed to its screensaver, a photo of a mountain lake at dawn. "My current one works. The battery's bad, but I can get a new battery."

Marcus shrugged, but the woman with the lanyard looked over from her filing and gave him a small nod, the kind you'd give someone for holding a door. On the bus home, Dylan took out the napkin and smoothed it on his knee. He still wasn't sure he'd decided rightly; maybe he was being cheap, maybe the twelve months of zero percent was a genuinely good deal he'd talked himself out of, maybe his mother's determinism was just an excuse people used when they wanted their choices to feel inevitable. He folded the napkin once, twice, and put it in his wallet behind his transit pass, where he'd find it again the next time he was in a store that smelled like new plastic and wanted something he couldn't quite afford.

When he got home, his brother was on the couch playing a game with the sound too high, and Dylan sat down next to him and said, "Hey. What do you actually know about savings accounts?"

Victoria was not, she would have told anyone who asked, the kind of person who got rattled by a poster contest. She simply wanted her design for the library's reading campaign to print properly, which was a reasonable want, and if she had stayed until five o'clock in the art room two days running, that was diligence, not panic. The deadline was Friday. Mr. Okafor had said, in his unhurried way, "A3 for the wall, A4 for the handouts," and left them to it, which Victoria took as a vote of confidence in her specifically, though he had probably said it to everyone.

The trouble began with her drawing. She had lettered the slogan by hand across an A4 sheet, a girl reading under a tree made of torn paper leaves, and it was good, she knew it was good. But when she photocopied it onto A3 at the public library printer down the street, the machine stretched the image to fill the page, and the tree's branches thinned into pale threads. On her second attempt the copier fit the whole design inside the larger sheet and left an ugly border, the girl marooned in white. Priya, working at the next table, kept glancing over, and Victoria kept her shoulders loose and her voice level, because she was not competing with Priya, whatever Dana thought. She wasn't.

"It's like the machine wants a number," Priya said, chewing her pen. "A scale percentage. But what?"

"That's what I'm going to find out," Victoria said, and she said it calmly, though she had already snapped one pencil clean in half, which she blamed on the pencil being cheap and ductile, bending before it broke, nothing to do with her grip.

She took the two sheets, A4 and A3, back to the art room and laid them side by side on the cutting mat. Dana leaned over her shoulder, smelling of turmeric from lunch, and said, "Hold them up to the window. Compare the shapes." Victoria did. The corners did not line up the way rectangles usually did when you enlarged them; the proportions matched somehow, angle for angle, which shouldn't have been possible. She measured. The A4 was 210 by 297 millimetres. The A3 was 297 by 420. The long side of the small sheet had become the short side of the large one.

"Look," she said, turning the A3 so its long edge ran vertical. "The A3 is the A4 with extra paper on one side. Same shape, just bigger." Dana squinted. Victoria took a fresh A3, the good heavy kind the school could apparently still afford, laid it flat, and cut it in half with the guillotine, one clean stroke. Two pieces fell apart on the mat. She set one against her original A4. It covered it exactly, corner to corner, like a shadow.

"That's not luck," Dana said.

"No." Victoria sat back on her stool. She remembered, distantly, a page from the library printer's manual she'd skimmed while waiting, a line about ISO 216, some standard, and she'd skipped it because it looked like fine print. "It's ISO 216," she said. "The paper sizes. A4's sides are in a ratio of one to the square root of two, so when you cut a sheet in half you get two sheets of the same shape. Every size in the set works that way." Dana repeated the ratio under her breath as if tasting it, and Victoria felt something loosen in her chest, the same feeling as when a proof closes in math class, every line accounted for. All afternoon the copier's refusals had incapacitated her, and the answer had been sitting in the paper itself, patient as furniture.

The scale was easy after that. If the shapes matched, the enlargement was just the ratio of the sides, and she found the percentage on her calculator and keyed it into the library machine the next day, one number, the machine humming, the image blooming onto A3 with every leaf intact. She printed the handouts at A4, and the two versions matched, exactly, the girl under her tree reading at two sizes like an echo. She held them up together and grinned at Priya, who grinned back, and it occurred to Victoria, briefly and uncomfortably, that she had spent most of the week treating Priya as a judge rather than a friend, which was probably not Priya's fault.

Still, one thing nagged at her, and she was honest enough, at least with the cutting mat at five o'clock, to admit it. She hadn't worked out why the ratio did what it did. She knew that it did, knew it the way she knew her bank balance after her grandmother's monthly remittance arrived, ten pounds for art supplies, no note, and she hadn't once spent it on anything as practical as pens. Was knowing that a thing worked the same as understanding it? She suspected not. She also suspected that the difference might not matter by Friday, and that this was the kind of question people asked to sound deep at parties, and both suspicions sat in her at once without settling.

On Thursday she pinned the A3 to the classroom wall and taped the A4 handouts in a fan below it. Mr. Okafor stopped, looked for a long moment, and said, "The proportions hold." Victoria nodded as though she had planned everything from the start, which was not quite true, and not quite false either, since the finished thing was hers whichever route it had taken. Dana came over with the two offcuts from her halved A3, holding them up like a magician about to reveal a card. "Same shape," Dana said. "Every single time you cut one." Victoria looked at the pair of them, then at her poster, then out the window where the real trees stood in the wind, none of them the same shape at all.

The line at the fire station moved in small, shuffling advances, and Mackenzie held her registration card the way she had once held a hall pass on the first day of school, as though the paper itself might not be enough. She had turned eighteen in March, registered in April, and read the sample ballot twice on the bus that morning, which had not stopped her from reading it a third time now, standing between a man in coveralls and a woman grading quizzes against her knee.

Ahead of her, a boy about her age was arguing with a poll worker in a low, tight voice. He wore a Grand Forks letter jacket, and his driver's license was out on the table like evidence. "I don't understand what you want from me," he was saying. "There's nothing to sign up for. I've voted with my mom, like, forever, back home."

"You have to be registered to vote here," the poll worker said, patient but firm, a querulous edge creeping in from someone farther back in line who had begun complaining about the wait. "This isn't North Dakota."

"What's North Dakota?" Mackenzie asked, before she could decide whether the question was too forward.

The boy turned, and she recognized him then, dimly, from a party in September, a friend of a friend who had transferred in. "Mackenzie, right? Devon's friend." He rubbed the back of his neck. "North Dakota is where I'm from. It's the only state without voter registration. They abolished it in 1951. You just show ID at the polls. That's it. That's the whole thing."

"That can't be right," said the woman with the quizzes, not unkindly, looking up. "Everywhere has registration."

"Not there," he said. "I promise you. My whole life, you show your license, they find your street in the book, you vote."

The poll worker consulted a binder, and a younger volunteer came over, and for a minute there was a low conference that Mackenzie couldn't hear. She thought about her own registration card, filled out at the kitchen table while her mother stirred soup and told her that voting was the family patrimony, handed down from grandmother to grandmother, which had struck Mackenzie as generous given that her great-grandmother had been turned away from more than one poll in her lifetime. Her mother meant well. Her mother mostly meant the soup.

"Provisional ballot," the younger volunteer announced. "You can vote provisionally, and you have some days to prove residency."

The boy's shoulders dropped an inch. "Okay. Yeah. Okay." He glanced at Mackenzie as though he owed the room an explanation, or owed it to himself. "I moved here in August. I didn't know I was supposed to do anything. Nobody said."

"That's not on you," Mackenzie said. "You didn't know." But even as she said it, she felt the two ideas grinding against each other: that people should be responsible for knowing the rules, and that the rules were different depending on which of fifty doors you'd walked out of. She had spent a semester in a government class arguing that registration was a reasonable safeguard. She had also spent that semester watching classmates who moved apartments mid-semester lose track of their own mail.

She voted twenty minutes later, in a booth with a curtain that smelled like a chalkboard. The pen dragged on the ovals. When she came out, the boy was sitting on the bench by the coats, filling out his provisional form in careful block letters, and the older poll worker was reading it over his shoulder, saying, "Write your dorm address exactly as it appears, now, no nicknames," and pointing at a line he'd skipped, and waiting while he fixed it.

That night she texted her mother: I voted. Took twenty minutes. A kid from North Dakota found out the hard way that everywhere else makes you register first; they got rid of it there before you were born. He still got to vote, kind of. Provisional. Nothing is provisional with you, Mom, so don't start.

Her mother replied with a photograph of the soup and a single line: "Proud of you. Bring the card home for the fridge."

Mackenzie set the phone face-down on her desk, then turned it back over and typed, "Tell Grandma hers counted twice, once for her and once for the one they wouldn't let her cast." Outside, a wind had come up that bent the streetlight reflections across the wet pavement, and she went to the window to watch the last voters hurrying toward the fire station doors, holding their papers against the cold.

The line outside the church hall on Delmore Street moved in short shuffles, and Brayden checked his wallet twice to be sure the voter information card was still there. His mother had worked polls for years and had habituated him to the ritual of elections, the sharpened pencils, the folded cardboard screens, but he had never been on this side of it. Today he was eighteen, registered, and carrying an argument he hadn't been able to settle in his own head all week.

Behind him, a girl about his age was talking to an older man in a quilted coat. "I thought you had to be twenty-one," she said. "My dad said he couldn't vote until he was older than us."

"Federal voting age," the man said. "Canada lowered it from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970." He said it the way people recite hockey stats, and then the line moved and he went back to his phone.

Brayden turned the number over. 1970. His grandfather would have been nineteen that year, suddenly eligible mid-decade, probably one of the first eighteen-year-olds in the family to mark a ballot. Brayden wished he could ask him, but his grandfather had been dead since Brayden was eleven, and the remaining memories were of a man who complained about taxes and grew dahlias, and who had once said, watching an election night on television, that young people vote like they're throwing rocks.

In front of him, two poll workers were laughing about someone's dog. One of them, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, noticed his card as he stepped up. "First time?" she said.

"Is it obvious?"

"You're holding it like a ticket that might not scan." She found his name on the list, folded the ballot into thirds without looking at it, and slid it across. "Straight to the box after."

The voting screen smelled of pencil shavings. Brayden stood there longer than he meant to. He had gone back and forth all week. His economics teacher, who liked to trace the etiology of every policy back to its first cause, had argued that the party promising lower costs would help his family most; his sister, home from university, had argued the opposite with equal force, and both of them had used numbers. The trouble was that he believed parts of each. He had started wondering whether a considered position was even possible, or whether everyone just picked a side first and built a bridge to it afterward.

His grandfather's line came back to him, throwing rocks. Maybe that was what 1970 had looked like to the people who already had the vote, a crowd of teenagers hurling something. Or maybe his grandfather had meant it as advice: don't vote to break things, vote to build one. Brayden noticed his own incipient bitterness, the itch to mark the ballot against whoever his father supported, purely because his father had been loud about it at dinner, and he recognized the feeling as not a reason. He put the pencil down for a second. Then he picked it up and marked the candidate he could actually defend out loud if someone asked him why, one whose platform he'd read twice and still had doubts about. The doubts were honest. He let them stand.

He fed the ballot into the box, and the poll worker with the glasses said, "There you go, citizen," in a tone that was half teasing and half not.

Outside, the girl from the line was waiting on the steps, scarf up to her chin. "Did you know it was only since 1970?" she said. "That people our age could vote. That's so recent. My dad voted at twenty-one and I voted at eighteen and nothing else changed."

"Something changed," Brayden said, though he wasn't sure what, exactly.

"Like what?"

He shrugged. "We're in the line now. We have to have an opinion even when we don't."

She laughed, a short sound that scattered into the cold. "I marked mine and I still don't know if it was right."

"That might be the whole thing," Brayden said. "Voting, I mean."

She pulled her scarf down so he could see her mouth. "You want to get coffee? There's a place on Delmore and I have forty minutes before my shift."

He looked back once at the church hall, at the box inside holding his folded answer, and then he zipped his coat. "Sure," he said. "I'm Brayden."

The garage smelled of dust and old grass clippings, and Logan had claimed it for the weekend because the kitchen table was no longer negotiable. He was painting his grandfather's old tackle box, transforming the rusted green steel into something covered in koi, orange and white fish curling around the latch. He had promised it to his sister Nora before she left for her first semester, which was now four days away, and the deadline had begun to feel like a held breath.

He had learned two ways of thinking about a project like this from two different people. His grandfather, a machinist, believed in doing the thing once, correctly, with cleanup as part of the work itself. His art teacher junior year, an ebullient woman named Ms. Okafor, believed in momentum, in following an impulse before it cooled, and she had once told the class that a finished imperfect thing beat a perfect thing unfinished. Logan had spent a year treating those ideas as rivals. Now, with the tackle box half covered and Nora's departure looming, he was not sure they were rivals at all.

The trouble began on Saturday afternoon. He had thinned his acrylics with water all morning, rinsing brushes in a jar between fish, marveling at how easily the paint moved while it was wet. Then Nora called from inside the house, asking for help carrying bins to her car, and he set his three best brushes on the bench and went in. They hauled dorm bedding and a fan and four boxes labeled in her careful handwriting, and she thanked him with a hug that lasted longer than her usual ones, and by the time he got back, the sun had moved across the garage floor and two hours had gone.

The brushes were ruined. He picked one up and the bristles held their shape like a tiny frozen fan, stiff as a toothbrush found behind a radiator. He ran it under the tap and the water beaded off. The paint had been water-based all morning, thinning and rinsing like ink, and now it simply refused the water entirely, as if the brush had decided to become something else while his back was turned.

"You left them out," Nora said from the doorway. She had followed him back out with two mugs of lemonade, and she stood there looking at the stiffened brushes with an expression that was half apology and half diagnosis. "That happened to half my brushes last spring. Acrylic cleans up with water while it's wet, but once it dries, it won't. It just won't."

"I thought I had more time," Logan said.

"You thought a lot of things were more forgiving than they are." She set down the lemonade and picked up the stiffest brush, turning it over. "So what now?"

He sat on the stool and considered. His grandfather would have thrown the brushes away and said the lesson was the point. Ms. Okafor would have said the lesson was nothing next to the koi, and would have handed him a palette knife. He tried, for a moment, to historicize the problem, to imagine how his grandfather's generation of careful men would have judged a boy who abandoned his tools for a hug and a box of sheets. Then he stopped, because the judgment felt borrowed and useless. The brushes were stiff. His sister was leaving. Both of those were true at once, and the second one mattered more, and he was not going to pretend otherwise, even to look disciplined.

He worked the rest of Saturday and most of Sunday with the brushes that remained and a cheap flat brush he found in a drawer, its synthetic bristles coarse enough to leave visible streaks. The streaks, it turned out, looked like water. Where he had planned smooth gradients of white belly into orange scale, the stiff-bristled strokes made ripples, and the koi seemed to be moving. Nora came out Sunday evening in her socks, saw the finished box under the work light, and did not say anything for a long moment.

"You did that with the ruined brush?" she asked finally.

"The ruined brush and one from the junk drawer."

She ran her thumb along the latch, over a fish's eye. "It's better than the other way would have been, isn't it."

He wanted to say yes. He had a whole argument ready about mistakes becoming texture, about how a revisionist reading of the afternoon might call it luck instead of carelessness. But he genuinely did not know whether the streaks were better or whether he was only making peace with what he could not undo, and he found he did not want to hand her a tidy answer on her last night home. "I don't know," he said. "I like it. I'm still annoyed about the brushes."

Nora laughed, a short surprised sound, and tucked the tackle box under her arm like something she intended to keep forever. "Good," she said. "Bring the lemonade in when you come."

Eva stood at her grandmother's sink washing the good teacups, the ones with hairline cracks that her mother always said should be thrown out and never were. The funeral had been four days ago. The kitchen smelled of lemon dish soap and the cold-cream soap that her grandmother had kept by the stove for reasons no one had ever impugned, because no one had ever wanted to argue with her about soap.

The problem was the movie. On Tuesday, two days after the burial, Eva had gone with her cousin Dara to see an action film, and she had laughed at it, really laughed, the loud kind, and then had sat in the theater afterward feeling like she had committed a crime. She had told no one. Now she was washing cups because her hands needed something to do, and her aunt Ruth was at the table behind her wrapping leftover casseroles in foil.

"You're scrubbing those like they owe you money," Ruth said.

"They're recalcitrant," Eva said, holding one up to the window. Tea stain, stubborn, along the rim. "Grandma's tea did that. She'd leave the bag in for ten minutes."

"Fifteen. She liked it bitter enough to stand a spoon in."

Eva dried the cup and set it on the rack. Then she said, without planning to, "Can I ask you something weird?"

"I sell insurance. Nothing is weird anymore."

"Tuesday I went to a movie. With Dara. And I liked it. Like, a lot. I laughed. And then I felt like garbage about it for two days, because how can I be laughing when she just, you know." She put the dish towel down and folded it into thirds, because folding was also something hands could do.

Ruth tore off a strip of foil and smoothed it over a dish with one long stroke. "Did you love her?"

"You know I did."

"Then let me tell you what a pamphlet from the bereavement group told me, because I read everything now, it's my new hobby." Ruth squared the foil edge against the counter. "There's these two researchers, Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, and they have a dual process model. It says grieving people go back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, instead of moving in one direction. So you're not supposed to just feel sad forever in a straight line. You oscillate. That's their word. You swing between the two."

Eva turned that over. "So the movie was the rebuilding part."

"Or maybe you just have bad taste in movies. Both things can be true." Ruth pointed at a casserole. "Hand me the tape."

Eva brought the tape, still thinking. The model made sense of something she hadn't known needed sense made of it: the way she had cried hard on Monday over a grocery list in her grandmother's handwriting, and on Wednesday had spent an hour comparing dorm prices online without crying at all, and had assumed the Wednesday version of herself was a fraud. If the model was right, neither day was a betrayal. She was just moving between the two, the way people apparently actually did, not the way movies about grief showed it, one long gray march toward acceptance.

But she didn't want to accept the whole idea too fast either. She had read enough in school to know that a tidy theory could be a way of not thinking. She sat down across from Ruth. "Okay, but here's what I can't figure out. How do you know when you're doing it right? Like, what if I'm just using the back and forth thing as an excuse? What if I use it to never really face anything?"

Ruth considered that while she wrote on a foil label. "That's a better question than my pamphlet answered."

"So you don't know either."

"Nobody knows, honey. You do the best swing you can."

That was not satisfying, and Eva respected it anyway. Her mother came in then with two bags of her grandmother's coffee mugs, the everyday ones, and a quiet detente settled over the kitchen, the kind where everyone agreed not to mention that the mugs should probably go to the church rummage sale and nobody said so out loud. Eva took the mugs one at a time and washed them, too, even though they had already been washed, because her grandmother had drunk out of them every morning for fifty years and that seemed worth one more rinse.

Dara texted her a picture from the theater lobby: the two of them Tuesday night, mid-laugh, blurry, terrible. Eva looked at it for a long moment, then turned her phone face down on the counter and picked up the last mug, the blue one with the chip on the handle.

"Want me to dry?" Ruth said.

"No," Eva said. "I've got this one."

The bowling alley smelled of rented shoes and cherry slushie, and Kaylee stood at the counter wondering whether she should pay for her own games before Dante arrived, or whether paying first would look like a statement. She had thought about it on the bus, weighing the two positions like a girl holding identical gifts in either hand. If she paid, she was independent, unbeholden; if she waited, she might seem to expect something. In the end she bought her shoes, rented two lanes by mistake, and had to ask for one lane back, which the clerk gave her with a look she chose not to interpret.

Dante came in at six exactly, which she liked, carrying nothing, wearing a jacket she had seen him in at school maybe four times and never once thought about until now. "You found it," she said, and he said, "I looked it up twice on the way," which she also liked, because it was an admission, and admissions were the currency she trusted.

He had asked her out on Tuesday, by the trophy case outside the gym, and she had said yes quickly, then spent the rest of the week deciding whether the quickness had been a mistake. Her mother, over dishes, had said only, "You don't owe anybody a second date, and you don't owe anybody a reason." Kaylee had rolled that around all week, and by Friday she had arrived somewhere adjacent to it: she didn't owe Dante a reason, but she might owe herself a fair look before making one up.

The first game, she won by nine pins. He laughed about it in a way that felt real, not performed, and she filed that away. On the second game, somewhere in the fourth frame, she noticed that they were both leaning on the ledge the same way, elbows down, chin on knuckles, watching her ball drift toward the gutter. She straightened up. A second later, so did he.

Her brother Will, home from his first semester of college, had told her about a study over winter break, in between complaints about his roommate. In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. Will had called it the chameleon effect, and Kaylee had filed that away too, the way she filed everything, in the drawer marked possibly useful, possibly nothing.

Now she watched. She crossed her ankles; two frames later his ankles crossed. She spun her cup in her hands; he got a cup of his own and spun it, laughing about something unrelated. And the strange thing was that she could not tell, watching him, whether it meant anything at all. If people liked a partner more when that partner mimicked them, then maybe he was doing it to be liked, which would be an affectation, a strategy, and she would have to decide how she felt about being managed. Or maybe it happened below everyone, some current neither of them steered, in which case there was no one to blame and nothing to decode.

"You're staring at your shoes," Dante said. "They're really something."

"They're size nines and they've been on four hundred feet."

"Mine have been on more," he said, and lifted one to show her, and she thought, without wanting to, he's matching me again, joking the way I joke.

By the eighth frame she had tried both ways of thinking and could not land on one. She tested him once more, deliberately, draping her arm along the ball return, and when his arm followed, thirty seconds later, she felt a small flat disappointment and a small warm spark at the same time, and could not have said which was the truer response. Maybe the study didn't cover this direction, her watching for it, both of them awake to the possibility. Maybe noticing ruined whatever the noticing was about.

She got a strike in the ninth, all ten pins folding sideways at once, and Dante stood up and held out his hand, palm up, noncommittal, offering the high five or something smaller, letting her choose. She looked at the hand. Her mother's rule said she owed him nothing; her own quieter rule said she owed him the truth of this moment, which was that she liked him and did not yet know why, and might not find out tonight.

She high-fived him, then kept her hand there a beat longer than the gesture required. "Overtime," she said. "Next game's mine to lose."

Ava spread the two pay stubs side by side on the kitchen table, the way her friend Priya had laid them out at lunch, and bent over them with her mother's reading glasses pushed up on her head. She had been trying since Tuesday to work out why the same eight dollars an hour had left her with more money than Priya, who made nine. Her mother set a mug of tea beside her without being asked, which was its own kind of kindness, and went back to peeling carrots at the counter.

"You're going to ruin your eyes," her mother said, not for the first time.

"One second." Ava ran her finger down the columns. Her own stub, from the bakery two streets over, listed the deductions in small grey print: income tax, then something called CPP, then EI. Beneath those, in plainer type, the amount that actually landed in her account every second Thursday. Priya's stub, photocopied on the school library machine so the edges were blurry, had different letters entirely. QPP, it said, and QPIP, and a parental insurance line that Ava's didn't have at all.

She pulled out her phone and typed the letters in. The first result made her sit back. Priya worked in Gatineau, just across the river, and Quebec ran its own pension and parental insurance plans instead of the Canada Pension Plan and Employment Insurance that showed up on Ava's paycheque. Outside Quebec, apparently, everyone's stub looked like hers. Ava read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed strange that two friends who could see each other's workplaces from the bridge would have such different pieces of paper.

Her mother came over, drying her hands, and looked at the stubs upside down. "That's a lot of tiny numbers."

"Mine's smaller," Priya had said at lunch, morose about it, turning her stub over as though the missing money might be hiding on the back. "Look, the deductions eat more of mine. And everything costs more there anyway." She had pulled a crumpled receipt from her jacket, from a coffee shop in Hull, and smoothed it out between them on the cafeteria table. GST and QST, the taxes stacked at the bottom, had pushed a four-dollar sandwich past five. Ava had found her own receipt from the bakery in her coat pocket that afternoon, and now she set it beside the stubs: HST, one line, thirteen percent, no fuss.

"Priya's trying to save for residence too," Ava said. Her mother made a sound that meant she was listening. "First deposit's due in March. She's got less left over every pay than I do and I can't tell if it's the wages or the deductions or the taxes on everything she buys." She paused. "I want to lend her some, toward the deposit. Not give, lend. She'd take a loan."

"You've thought about what happens if she can't pay it back?"

"I have." Ava lined up the receipts so their edges met. There was something she couldn't get past, though, and she said it slowly, because it felt like admitting a gap in her own argument. "I can't actually tell how much of the difference is because of where she works. Some of it's the taxes on purchases, some of it's the deductions, some of it's just that she buys lunch more than I do. So I can't say for sure how big the unfair part is, or whether it's unfair at all, or just different." She heard how uncertain it sounded and let it stand.

Her mother sat down across from her, which she almost never did mid-evening, and turned Priya's photocopy right side up to read it. "Your grandmother used to call the tax office an autocrat," she said. "Every April. Like it was a person who'd wronged her." She smiled at the memory, then tapped the deposit line on Priya's stub with one finger. "I never checked whether she was right. She usually wasn't, about people."

"I'll ask Priya to bring her return when she does it," Ava said. "Her mom's already filing, she said. I want to see what the whole year looks like, not just one pay. Then I'll know if I'm lending her money she needs or money she'll have by June anyway." It was a way of holding both things at once, she thought: the instinct to help immediately, and the patience to find out whether help was the right shape. She copied the three letters from Priya's stub, QPP, into her notebook, and under it wrote Priya's name and the word deposit, and drew a box around the amount she was prepared to offer.

"There's soup when you're done being an accountant," her mother said, standing, squeezing her shoulder once on the way to the stove.

Ava texted Priya a photo of the two stubs lying side by side, and underneath typed: bring your mom's filing stuff on Saturday, I'll make the good coffee.

Kyle had come to his grandmother's house for the weekend with one goal, which was to avoid thinking about Marcus, and so of course Marcus was all he could think about. Marcus had missed the Tuesday deadline for the robotics code again, the third time this season, and Kyle had told the group chat exactly what he thought of that: "you're lazy." Two words, sent at eleven at night, followed by an hour of nobody typing anything, which was somehow worse than an argument.

His grandfather found him on the porch Saturday morning, sulking over a bowl of cereal. "You look like a boy who lost a chess match to himself," his grandfather said, and disappeared inside before Kyle could protest that he didn't play chess. When Kyle followed him in, annoyed at being teased, he found the old man in the study, holding out a paperback with a cracked spine. "Take this. You have the face of someone about to write something he'll regret, and I've run out of porch to hide on."

The book was about leadership, which Kyle would normally have used as a coaster, but he was desperate enough to read anything. He sat on the kitchen floor between the radiator and the dog and read about the Situation-Behavior-Impact model, which came from a place called the Center for Creative Leadership. The idea was that you name when it happened, what the person actually did, and what effect it had. It sounded almost too simple to work, like being told the secret to juggling was to not drop anything. But there was a line in the book about how vague labels like "lazy" told a person nothing they could act on, and Kyle felt that line tap him on the shoulder like a teacher who had seen him passing notes.

"It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model," he told his grandmother at lunch, testing the words out, "and before you ask, no, I have not become a leadership dilettante overnight. I'm a dilettante of exactly one afternoon." His grandmother said she'd been a dilettante of marriage for fifty years and it had served her fine, and Kyle laughed so hard he had to put down his sandwich.

The problem was that when he pulled out his phone to fix things, "you're lazy" kept rewriting itself into other insults. "You're unreliable" was just the same word in a suit. He called his co-captain, Priya, hoping she'd do the hard part for him, but she refused on principle. "You lit it, you put it out," she said. "But if it helps, being specific isn't being mean. My mom does it to my dad about the dishwasher and he actually improved." Kyle said that was the least romantic thing he'd ever heard, and Priya said it was the most.

So he walked the backyard with the dog, muttering drafts. His putative apology, the one he'd been planning since Tuesday, turned out not to be an apology at all but a request that Marcus apologize to him, and Kyle had the honesty to recognize the difference and delete it. That was the strange part: the model wasn't just a format, it forced him to figure out what had actually happened instead of how he'd felt about it in the dark at eleven at night. When had it happened? Tuesday. What had Marcus done, in the world, in verifiable reality? He hadn't sent the navigation code by the deadline. What effect did it have? Kyle had stayed up until two rewriting it himself and had snapped at his little sister the next morning over nothing. He hadn't even connected those two things until he tried to write them down.

The message he finally sent was three sentences long and took him forty minutes. "On Tuesday, the code was due and I didn't get it from you until Friday. I rewrote the navigation myself that night and was a wreck the next day. Can we figure out what's going wrong before Thursday's build?" He read it eleven times, showed it to his grandmother, who said it was nicer than most things his grandfather had ever said to her, and sent it before he could turn it back into "you're lazy" with extra steps.

Marcus replied with a photo of his little brother in a hospital waiting room, then, a minute later: "sorry man. thursday for sure." Kyle sat down hard on the porch steps. He didn't know if the model had fixed anything, really; the code might still be late on Thursday, and "sorry" was doing a lot of work in that text. What he knew was that he hadn't known about the hospital, and that "you're lazy" would have made him the kind of person who'd said it anyway. His grandfather came out with two mugs of tea and sat down beside him without asking anything, which was its own kind of feedback, delivered with precision. "Well?" he said eventually. Kyle held up the phone. "Thursday," he said. "We'll see."

Zachary had signed up because the form was due Friday and the scholarship committee liked the word "service," a word he had until now associated mainly with tennis. The food bank occupied the basement of a church whose ceiling pipes sweated in the heat, and a woman named Ruth handed him a hairnet before he had finished saying good morning. "Canned goods on the left table," she said. "Anything opened or homemade comes to me. Not you. Me." She said this the way people say don't touch the stove, which made Zachary immediately curious about who had touched the stove.

He sorted cans for an hour, learning the taxonomy: soups with soups, beans with beans, a category Ruth called "mystery," which appeared to mean anything with a label in a language nobody at the table could read. A retired engineer named Desh worked beside him and held forth, in a pleasant drone, on the carbon footprint of tin. Zachary had expected the other volunteers to be like his mother, earnest and guilt-driven, or like his economics teacher, who believed charity was mostly signaling. Desh was neither. Desh was a polymath, or at least a man with an opinion about everything from soil depletion to the melting point of margarine, and he sorted beans while he talked, and the two activities seemed to have nothing to do with each other.

The trouble arrived at eleven, carried in a foil-covered dish by a woman in a rain jacket though it had not rained. She set it on the intake table with the confidence of someone delivering a solved problem. "Lasagna," she said. "For the families. I made it this morning, the good ricotta." Behind her, two children were attempting to climb the donation bin.

Zachary, being nearest, reached for it, because it was heavy and because reaching for heavy things was, so far, the entirety of his training. "Sir," the woman said, "you'll burn your hands," and she was right; the foil was still warm. He stood there holding a hot lasagna and no policy.

Ruth appeared from the back with the speed of someone who had done this before. "That smells incredible," she said, and she meant it; Zachary could tell because she closed her eyes for half a second. "But we can't take home-cooked food. We can't check how it was prepared or stored, so it can't go out to people." The woman's face did something complicated, a sort of settling, like a house deciding whether to shift. "It's a rule," Ruth added, softer, "and I didn't write it, and I've turned down my own sister's soup."

"That seems insane," Zachary said, later, in the loading area. He had been introspect-ing about it all through the lunch rush, if there was such a verb, and what he kept circling was this: the woman had made food for neighbors out of her own money and her own morning, and a system built to feed people had refused it. Desh wiped his hands on his jeans. "The rule protects the people eating, not the people giving," he said. "You can't verify her kitchen. You can verify a can." He tapped one, a dented thing labeled montane stew, which Zachary had earlier shelved under mystery. "Nobody cooked this in a bathtub."

"But she's right there," Zachary said. "We could just ask her about her kitchen." "And she'd say it was spotless," Desh said, "because everybody's kitchen is spotless when they're asked. The rule isn't about her. It's about the thousand people we don't know." Zachary thought about his economics teacher, who would have said the rule was institutional cowardice, trust replaced by paperwork. He thought about his mother, who would have said the rule was just common sense and the woman should take the lasagna to a shelter that took hot food, except he didn't know if such a shelter existed, which was its own problem.

He found he could hold both positions at once without either one winning. The rule was cold and the lasagna was warm and neither fact canceled the other. What he could not do was stand in the loading area holding nothing, which was what he was doing, so he went back inside.

The woman was still there, actually, sitting on a folding chair near the door while Ruth walked her through a printed list of places that accepted hot meals, underlining things in pencil with the gravity of a treaty. Zachary stopped at a respectful distance. "It smelled really good," he offered. The woman looked up. "It was," she said. "My mother's recipe. She'd have made me bring it somewhere anyway, she never let food sit." One of the children had surrendered the donation bin and was now reading a cereal box with total absorption, and Zachary thought, not for the first time that day, that children had the right relationship to everything.

Ruth finished underlining and handed over the list. "Next time," she said, "bring cans. Big ones. I'll put you on the good shelf." The woman laughed, a short surprised sound, and gathered her foil dish, which had gone from warm to merely heavy in the way of abandoned efforts. At the door she paused and looked back at Zachary specifically. "You'll be here next Saturday?" she asked. "I want someone to tell me if the cans taste any good."

The festival took up four blocks of Fremont Street, and by noon the asphalt smelled like fried dough and scorched sugar. Maelie walked behind her grandmother, carrying the box of oranges, while her father pushed through the crowd with the folding chairs. Somewhere ahead, her cousin Dax, who was nine, was already at the game booth spending quarters he did not have.

The red envelopes had been Maelie's job this year. Her grandmother had handed them over at the apartment that morning, eight crisp envelopes and a stack of new bills from the bank, and said only, "You're eighteen now. You do it." In the family it was the first year she had been trusted with the money instead of merely receiving it, and she had spent the train ride folding the bills lengthwise the way her grandmother did, creasing them with a thumbnail.

At the noodle stand she counted out the cash while her father ordered. Forty dollars for Dax, she decided. Round, substantial, a real gift from someone with a paycheck now, even if the paycheck came from shelving books at the library. She had just slid the second twenty into the envelope when Dax appeared at her elbow, saw the number, and grabbed her wrist.

"You can't give that," he said. "Four is death."

"Excuse me?"

"Four. You can't give four. Ask Grandma." He was already looking past her toward the booth with the goldfish, and she let him go because the line for noodles was moving.

Maelie stood there holding the envelope. Her father came back balancing two cartons and caught her expression. "What?"

"Dax says I can't give forty dollars. He says four means death." She said it flatly, testing it.

Her father set the cartons down on the rim of a trash barrel. "It sounds like death," he corrected. "The word. It's a homophone. It doesn't mean anything." He taught economics at a community college, and he liked to say that most of what people called culture was a series of unexamined externalities, costs pushed onto the future by people who never had to pay them. He said superstition was endemic to every market ever studied, and that the only rational response was benign neglect.

"Then why does everyone do it?"

"Because your grandmother's generation believed the sound mattered. And because it's easier to avoid a number than to argue with your mother." He handed her chopsticks. "Give him fifty. Give him thirty-eight. Nobody at that booth is checking your math against the afterlife."

Maelie ate standing up, watching her grandmother across the street. The old woman had wedged herself onto a folding chair near the stage, where a lion costume was being readied by two teenagers, and she was handing out envelopes to the children of strangers, pressing them into palms with a formality that made the kids straighten up. She had been doing this since before the neighborhood was called a neighborhood, since the festival was a single folding table of sesame balls outside the grocery that had long since closed, its awning bleached and desiccated in old photographs on the wall of the dim sum place.

Maelie took out the two twenties and looked at them. Her father was right that the sound meant nothing, in the way that a word on a page meant nothing until someone read it. But her grandmother had stood in a bank line to get fresh bills because creased ones were careless, had bought the oranges with stems and leaves intact because bare fruit looked stripped, had done a hundred small exact things all morning without once explaining them. The point was not that four could hurt Dax. The point was that Dax, at nine, already knew the rule, and would notice if she broke it, and would file it somewhere as evidence about what her love was worth.

Still, she could hear her father too, and she did not want to pretend she couldn't. A number did not carry death the way a live wire carries current. If she gave forty and said nothing, nothing would happen. She took out her phone and texted Dax: forty-five okay? and watched him across the street, waiting at the goldfish booth with a paper bag, until he pulled his phone from his jacket, read it, and gave her a thumbs up so large his whole arm moved.

She re-stuffed the envelope with two twenties, a ten, and five ones, then folded it lengthwise and creased it with her thumbnail.

Her grandmother waved her over when the drums started. "Come, the lion is beginning. Bring the envelopes." Maelie crossed the street with the box of oranges and the red stack in her hands, and her grandmother pulled her down into the chair beside her and said, "Hold the money like this, both hands, when you give it. Never one hand."

"Okay," Maelie said, and turned the envelope over twice so the characters faced out.

The studio smelled of resin and old radiator heat, and Mrs. Okoye's metronome sat on the piano lid like a small brass beetle that had wandered in from another century, anachronistic now that everyone kept time on their phones. Rachel unwrapped her cello on the second Tuesday of September, the same way she had every Tuesday for six years, and set the music on the stand: the Chopin polonaise she had taught herself over the summer, the piece she could play from memory with her eyes closed.

She got through the opening page before Mrs. Okoye raised one hand. Not the palm-out gesture of a conductor, just two fingers lifted off her knee, the way you would signal a waiter for the check.

"Play measures forty-one and forty-two," Mrs. Okoye said.

"They're awful," Rachel said. "That's why I skipped to the part I know."

"That's why we're playing them."

Rachel set her bow back on the string. The two bars contained a shift from third position to a harmonic she could not reliably find, followed by a string crossing her left hand wanted no part of. She missed the harmonic. She missed it again. On the fourth attempt she got it and then fumbled the crossing immediately after, which felt somehow worse, because it proved the problem was not one problem but two.

"Again," Mrs. Okoye said, and turned the metronome to sixty. "Just the shift. Nothing after it."

They spent the rest of the half hour on those two bars and a stretch in the slow movement that Rachel had been papering over since June. When the lesson ended, Mrs. Okoye wrote the measure numbers on a sticky note and pressed it to the inside of Rachel's folder like a prescription. "The polonaise can wait," she said. "It will still be there."

At home, Rachel did what she always did after a hard lesson: she played the polonaise from the top, the whole glorious run of it, fast enough that the hard passages blurred past on momentum. It felt wonderful. It felt like the summer itself, all that freedom she'd had before senior year started grinding. And then she recorded herself on her phone, because Mrs. Okoye had asked her to once, and listened back, and heard the truth. The shift was still a hole in the recording, a small swallowed silence exactly where the harmonic should have been. Playing the piece through had not fixed it. Playing the piece through had mostly let her practice not noticing.

That night she found the book. Her brother had left a stack of them in the garage when he moved out, and one was about how people get good at things. She read a chapter before bed, sitting on her floor with her back against the bed frame. The chapter had a phrase in it, deliberate practice, which it defined as working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, and it claimed this improved skill more than simply playing through pieces already known. She read the sentence twice. Then she thought about the sticky note in her folder, and the hole in the recording, and the fact that Mrs. Okoye had never once let her play a piece straight through in a lesson, and she understood that this was not cruelty or habit. It was policy. Her teacher had been running the experiment for six years and Rachel had only now read the results.

The next morning she tried it. She set her phone to record, picked a single goal, land the harmonic cleanly four times in a row, and played only the shift, nothing else, twenty times. Each time she listened back immediately. The misses sounded different once she could hear them: some were late fingers, some were a crooked thumb under the neck. She fixed one thing at a time. It was the least fun hour of cello she had ever spent, and at the end of it the harmonic was still not perfect, but it was honest. She could hear exactly how far off she was, which meant she knew exactly what to do Tuesday.

She kept at it for a week. On Thursday her friend Dana came over and asked why Rachel was playing the same three seconds of music over and over like a scratched CD, and Rachel tried to explain. Dana watched her miss the harmonic six consecutive times and said, "This looks miserable. Why not just play the fun part?"

"Because the fun part doesn't change anything," Rachel said. Dana shrugged and went to raid the kitchen, and Rachel went back to the shift, and she noticed she did not entirely disagree with Dana either. There was something in the repetition that closed the world down to a pinhole, and she missed the wide way the polonaise used to open up under her hands. She had not abrogated her right to enjoy it, she decided; she had only set it aside for a season, like a coat in summer.

There was also her mother to negotiate, because on Saturday her mother heard the same three seconds eleven times through the living room wall and came to the doorway with dish towel in hand. They reached a detente of sorts: Rachel would drill before noon, and after dinner she could play whatever she wanted, as loud as she wanted, and her mother would not say a word about the conservatory application sitting unfinished on the kitchen table.

Tuesday came. In the studio, Mrs. Okoye did not ask for the polonaise. She asked for measure forty-one, and Rachel set her bow and placed the shift, and the harmonic bloomed out clean and round, and then the crossing, which she had practiced separately all week, followed it like a sentence that had finally found its verb. She played the two bars again to be sure. The second time was clean too, though a little careful, and the third time, when Mrs. Okoye nodded once and turned the metronome up to sixty-six, was clean and not careful at all.

"Interesting week," Mrs. Okoye said, tapping the sticky note. "You found something."
