He was running the same sixteen bars over and over, and even through the half-open door she could tell it was the graduation march, the one that had been dragging behind her all week like a rope tied to her ankle.

"You know nobody actually likes that song," she said. "People like the idea of it. There's a difference."

Theo lowered the trumpet and looked at her the way he looked at slow wifi. "It's not a song, it's a march. Pomp and Circumstance. And it has history, actually." He said this with the smugness of a fifteen-year-old who had spent the afternoon on the internet instead of mowing the lawn. "It became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905. Edward Elgar was there getting an honorary doctorate of music. So every school that plays it is basically copying Yale."

"Copying Yale. That's the most American thing I've ever heard." Clara sat down on the workbench where their dad kept the antiquated paint cans he refused to throw out, cans labeled with colors the house hadn't been since before she was born. "We're in Ohio, Theo. We've never been to Yale. Nobody at my school has been to Yale."

"Everybody plays it, though. That's the point. It's a tradition."

"A tradition is just a mistake that's old enough to be forgiven," Clara said, and immediately regretted it, because it sounded like something she'd rehearsed, and she had rehearsed it, in the shower, for an argument with her father that hadn't happened yet.

The party started at four. By five the backyard had filled with relatives and classmates and Mr. Petrov from the bakery, and Clara moved through it all in her cotton dress with her diploma somewhere under a stack of cards, accepting congratulations the way you accept change from a cashier, automatically, without counting. Her father kept finding her with food. A plate of wings. A cup of punch. He was trying to allay something, she could tell, some worry he hadn't said out loud, and she let him do it because saying the actual thing out loud was her job, and she kept not doing it.

She had been accepted to a college in Boston with a good financial aid package and a name that made people at parties nod slowly, like a bell being struck. That was the story everyone knew. The other story, the one in the folder under her mattress, was a deferral form, one year, already signed by everyone except her. She wanted the year to work at Petrov's and save money and maybe just breathe, and her father had an adage for that kind of thing, the kind he deployed like a card game move: the early bird, the idle mind, the door that closes. She had counter-adages prepared. She had a whole arsenal. She was afraid that when the moment came, both arsenals would turn out to be made of paper.

The moment came at dusk, near the hors d'oeuvre table, when he said, "So, Boston in August," and handed her a cup of punch she already had.

"I need to tell you something," Clara said, and then heard herself say, "Did you know the march they played today became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905? Edward Elgar was getting an honorary doctorate of music there. Theo told me."

Her father blinked. "That's what you need to tell me?"

"No." She put the punch down on the table, next to the potato salad, which felt absurd, like setting a glass on a witness stand. "The thing is the deferral. The form's signed except for my line. I want to work this year and go next fall instead."

He was quiet long enough that she could hear Theo, inside, starting the march again, muffled through the screen door, sixteen bars looping like a conversation that kept circling back to its first sentence. She watched her father's face do the arithmetic she'd been dreading, watched the word "Petrov's" land in him somewhere, watched him decide, visibly, not to say any of his adages.

"Okay," he said finally. "Then you'll sign it, and we'll talk about money, and you'll still mow the lawn this summer."

"That's it?"

"You expected the firing squad? You saved a stranger from the firing squad, maybe, but not me." He smiled a small, tired smile that had her grandfather in it. "Your grandmother deferring anything? Impossible. But you, you were always going to do things in your own order. I've had seventeen years to get used to it."

Clara felt the gain and the cost arrive together, the way they apparently did: relief going in, and something like grief going out, grief for the girl in August walking a Boston sidewalk, the one who now would not exist, who had existed in her mind for months and now dissolved. She hugged her father, punch and all, and heard the trumpet stop.

Later, when the party had thinned to the loyalists and the fire pit was going, Theo came out and stood next to her with the trumpet under his arm, smug and sweaty from performing for the cousins. "I dedicate my next piece to the graduate," he announced. "It has history, actually. It became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music."

"You've said that four times today."

"Tradition," Theo said, and raised the trumpet.

"Play something else," she said. "Anything else. Please."

He thought about it, then put the trumpet to his lips anyway, and Clara, who had complained about that march all afternoon, stood there in the firelight and did not move until the last note of it faded over the fence and into the neighbors' yard.

Audrey had been at Dale's Auto for two hours, and the sedan she wanted had grown no cheaper in that time, only more familiar, like a dog at the shelter she was afraid someone else would take home. She ran her thumb along the hood's edge while Mr. Kessler, the salesman, talked about financing in a voice pitched to sound like a favor between friends. The price was eleven thousand dollars used, and she had nine saved from two summers bussing tables, plus what her grandmother had sent for graduation, which was supposed to be for textbooks.

Her phone buzzed against her hip. It was her friend Dev, and she stepped between a row of pickups to take it.

"I'm not quitting," Dev said before she'd finished saying hello. He worked at the pharmacy on Route 9, and he'd hated it since October, when they'd changed his schedule and stopped letting him sit down. "I already bought the uniform. Eighty bucks. Scrubs, the jacket, the shoes. If I quit now, that money's gone for nothing."

"That money's gone either way," Audrey said. "It's gone. You spent it in October."

"You don't get it. I have to stay long enough for it to be worth it."

She looked through the dealership window at the little sedan, silver, dented once near the back wheel, and something about the shape of Dev's argument bothered her the way a word bothers you when you've spelled it wrong. She told him she'd call back and walked inside to the coffee station, where a retired couple was arguing pleasantly about whether to trade in their truck.

Mr. Kessler found her there. "You've been circling that Camry all afternoon," he said. "You know what I see? I see a young person who wants to be responsible. Tell you what. We can do the paperwork tonight, get you a student rate."

If she bought the car tonight, the money her grandmother sent would go into the loan instead of the campus bookstore. Without a car, she'd take the bus home at Thanksgiving and Christmas, and her mother would drive the forty minutes to campus every other Sunday with groceries and whatever news had happened since the last visit. With the car, she could come home whenever she wanted, or never. She stood at the counter where the paperwork waited in a neat folder, and she understood that whichever way she chose, a whole version of her life was being quietly cancelled, the way they cancel a flight, apologetically, with a voucher.

"It's called opportunity cost," she said to Mr. Kessler, mostly to herself, but he nodded as though she'd complimented the coffee. "Whatever I pick, the next best thing is the price."

"You're a sharp one," he said, which absolved him of having to listen.

She called Dev back from the lot, between the used sedans and a populists billboard demanding lower gas taxes. "Listen," she said. "I learned about this once. The Concorde fallacy. It's named after the British and French governments. They kept funding the Concorde airliner even after they recognized there was no economic case for it anymore. They'd spent so much already that they kept spending. It has a name because everybody does it."

"So my scrubs are a supersonic jet."

"Your scrubs are a supersonic jet."

There was a pause, and she heard a register beep in the background, and then Dev said, "I'll think about it," which she recognized as an equivocal answer, the kind that lets a person keep the uniform in the closet a few more weeks.

Inside, the retired couple had signed for a smaller car than the truck, and the husband was explaining to Mr. Kessler that the truck money was going toward their granddaughter's tuition, and the wife was saying they'd miss the truck, and both things were true at once and neither was wrong.

Audrey sat down across from Mr. Kessler and slid the folder toward her, then didn't open it. "Not tonight," she said. "I want to think about the bus."

"The bus," he repeated, with a smile she could tell he'd use on the next kid.

Walking out, she passed the Camry one more time and patted its fender, feeling righteous, feeling like someone who had dodged a fallacy, someone who understood that money already spent could not be recovered and choices should be made forward, not backward. She was still feeling that way when she reached the road and checked her phone: a text from her mother, sent an hour before. She had taken a job in Phoenix. She'd been waiting until Audrey decided about the car to say it, because if Audrey bought the car, she wouldn't need rides anymore, and Phoenix was far, and the decision had been made, her mother wrote, for a while now.

Audrey stood in the parking lot with the dealership lights going out behind her, one by one, and the empty spot where the silver Camry had been.

The knife was dull again, and Charlotte had to force it through the onions, which was how people cut themselves, Denise always said, though Denise had been saying it for two years without anyone sharpening anything. Charlotte was sixteen and had the Saturday prep shift, six hours at minimum wage, no overtime because her hours never quite reached forty, a number the schedule seemed to avoid the way her hand avoided the hot flat-top. Taped inside her locker was her AP Bio study sheet, the phylogeny of land plants inked in green, because the walk-in had the best light for memorizing and the cooks didn't mind her muttering about mosses while she portioned chicken.

Renata, the kitchen manager, called her over during the lull. "I'm putting you on sauté next month," she said. "Marcus is leaving." Charlotte felt the sentence land in her chest like something warm. Line cook at sixteen. Her mother had worked restaurants her whole life and never got past the cold station, and here was the door opening early, if she was the kind of employee who deserved it, which meant the kind who didn't make trouble.

After the shift, three of them stayed behind the dumpster where the camera didn't reach: Denise from the salad station, Marco the dishwasher, and Priya who ran the grill. Marco had flyers, and he spoke about the union the way he spoke about everything, flat and doctrinaire, as if there were no honest position besides total commitment and anyone who hesitated was already a collaborator. "Signing cards is how we get the vote," he said. "Then we bargain. Wages, hours, conditions. That's collective bargaining. It's the law they have to come to the table." Charlotte stood with her backpack straps in both hands and said nothing, because a signed card was a name on a list, and lists had a way of being seen.

"Why the first of May, anyway?" Denise asked, rubbing sanitizer smell off her wrists. "My cousin marches every year in Manila and I never knew what for."

"Chicago," Marco said. "The Haymarket affair, May fourth, 1886. It grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday. That's why May first is International Workers' Day in so many countries."

"Eight hours," Denise said, looking back at the kitchen's lit windows, where the closers were still on hour ten.

Charlotte went home and lay on her bed doing the arithmetic she had been avoiding. Her scheduled hours had dropped from thirty-eight to thirty-one the same week she'd asked about overtime for a double she'd covered. Renata had smiled and said the payroll system rounded things differently, and Charlotte had let it go, because she was sixteen and the warm door of the sauté station was worth more than forty dollars. That was the deal she'd made without admitting it was a deal.

The next Saturday, Marco came in with his jaw set like a dropped hinge. "Renata has a card," he said quietly, at the pass. "Somebody's. She's got it in the office." He didn't know whose. Priya thought it was hers; Denise thought it was hers; the walk-in door kept opening and closing and nobody could finish a sentence. Charlotte kept chopping, and the pace of her knife gave nothing away, though her hands knew, before she let her mind know, exactly whose card it was. Three weeks ago, before Renata's promise, before the sauté station, she had signed it in the parking lot with Marco watching and Priya holding the flashlight. She had told herself since then that maybe it didn't count, that she'd been carried along, that a girl who wanted the line had every reason to stay quiet now.

Then the knife slipped on a wet onion and opened the base of her thumb, a clean diagonal welling fast. Denise wrapped it and said it didn't look deep enough for sutures, holding her hand tight above the sink while the blood thinned to pink in the running water. From the office doorway, Renata's voice carried across the kitchen, casual, asking Marco whether he wanted to pick up Sunday, and Charlotte understood that Renata was buying him too, the way she'd bought Charlotte, the way managers bought people in small denominations of hours and promises all the time, and that the card in the office was not an accusation yet but a weight, something Renata could hold until it was useful.

Charlotte dried her hands, walked past the pass, and knocked on the office door frame. Renata looked up from the desk, the card nowhere visible, her face arranged in friendly attention. "I need to put my cut on the incident log," Charlotte said, "and while I'm here, I want to say it's my card. I signed it. If you're going to hold it over anyone, hold it over me." The clock over Renata's shoulder read 9:40. Somewhere behind her the closers were starting hour ten.

Renata closed the log and slid it toward her. "That's a brave thing to say for someone who wants sauté."

Charlotte picked up the pen.

Kayla had counted the keys twice before Mrs. Okafor came back, and both times she got the same impossible answer: eighty-eight. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black, which meant the black keys outnumbered the whites by nothing and were outnumbered by sixteen, a piece of arithmetic she kept rechecking on the corner of her notebook as though the piano might have moved a key when she wasn't looking. The community center's practice room smelled like floor wax and old coffee, and the upright piano against the wall had a chip in the middle C sharp that she had already decided was a scar, not a flaw.

"You're counting again," said Desmond from the doorway. He was the only other Thursday student, seventeen, a saxophonist who treated every waiting room as his personal green room. "You know the piano doesn't change between lessons, right? It's not out here pulling pranks."

"Eighty-eight," Kayla said. "Fifty-two white, thirty-six black. Verify me."

"Verify yourself. I don't do math before six." But he came in and sat on the bench beside her anyway, and his finger hopped along the black keys like a man crossing stepping stones. "Huh. Okay, that's more than I would've guessed. All those little guys add up."

That was the thing she kept chewing on while Mrs. Okafor set up the metronome in the main room, its tick leaking under the door like a heartbeat the building had grown. Kayla had wanted to learn piano for exactly one reason, which she had told nobody: her grandmother had played, back when, and had died in the spring, leaving behind a cassette recording of something fast and bright that nobody in the family could name. Kayla's plan had been simple and, she now suspected, slightly foolish. Learn piano, learn the song, learn the grandmother. She had imagined it as a straight line, like a ladder.

The ladder, it turned out, was eighty-eight rungs wide. Mrs. Okafor had her doing five-finger positions and middle C until Kayla wanted to apologize personally to middle C for all the attention it was receiving. "You want the song," Mrs. Okafor had said last week, not unkindly, "but the song is at the top of the stairs, and you are on the second step, holding the railing, suspicious of the railing." Kayla had gone home and sulked productively, which was her specialty: she would cogitate on a problem until it surrendered or she fell asleep, whichever came first.

Tonight, though, sitting on the bench while the metronome ticked and Desmond hummed something ancillary and annoying behind her, she had a thought that felt less like surrendering and more like switching rivers. If fifty-two white keys and thirty-six black keys could add up to one instrument, then maybe her plan and the actual learning were not opponents. Maybe they were the white and black of the same thing. She didn't have to choose between the boring staircase and the grandmother's ghost of a melody; she had to notice that the staircase was made of the same wood as the song.

"Desmond," she said, "do you ever think about how your saxophone doesn't have a single visible note on it? You press buttons and blow and it just, like, happens."

"That's called skill, Kayla."

"It's called hiding the machinery." She spread her hands across the keys, all the way down, then all the way up, and the reach of it surprised her, shoulders and wrists complaining together. "I can see every note I'm ever going to play. They're all just sitting here waiting. That's either the most encouraging thing I've ever seen or a horror movie."

"A horror movie," Desmond said solemnly. "Definitely a horror movie."

Mrs. Okafor opened the door then, sheet music in hand, and Kayla closed the notebook where the arithmetic lived. She did not say anything about metaphysics or grandmothers or cassette tapes, because she wasn't sure yet whether the whole thought would hold its shape in daylight. What she knew was smaller and sturdier: fifty-two and thirty-six, and her hands resting on all of it.

"Same piece as last week," Mrs. Okafor said, settling into her chair, "but tonight, Kayla, I want you to make one mistake on purpose. Somewhere in the middle. Anywhere. A big, obvious, committed mistake."

"Why would I do that?"

"Because you play like someone standing guard over eighty-eight prisoners, and I want to see what happens when one of them escapes."

Kayla looked at the keys, all lined up and orderly, and started playing.

The printer at Grandma's house still used the old tray-feed paper, and Madison had to hold each sheet flat while it crawled out, warm and faintly chemical-smelling, like something developing. She had come here for the quiet, three days before the deadline, because at home her little brother debilitated any attempt at concentration by eleven a.m. and her mother treated every open laptop as an invitation to reminisce about her own college years. Here there was only the ticking kitchen clock and Grandma's rule of silence until noon, which Madison had once found oppressive and now found merciful.

The paper was supposed to argue something. Not summarize, her teacher had said, not report; argue. Ten pages, footnotes, a bibliography in Chicago style, which Madison had chosen because the sample page in the handbook looked the most organized, like a filing system for a mind. Her argument was that the federal highway projects of the 1950s had destroyed urban neighborhoods on purpose, not incidentally, and she had found a scholar named Rourke whose book said exactly that, in better sentences than she could write.

That was the problem, actually. Rourke wrote like someone who had walked the demolished streets himself. Madison had typed out one of his paragraphs on the neighborhood in Eastwick, then closed the book and retyped it from memory, changing the words as they came, the way she reworded song lyrics when she didn't want her friends to know what she'd been listening to. Her version was shorter and plainer. It felt like hers now. She moved on to the next section and didn't think about it again, which was either carelessness or a decision; she honestly couldn't have said which.

On the second morning Grandma set down a plate of toast and stood reading over her shoulder, which Madison normally hated. "You're awfully fast with that one book," Grandma said. "In my day we copied things out by hand and called it studying."

"Paraphrasing," Madison said. "It's not copying if you put it in your own words."

Grandma made a small sound, not quite agreement, and went back to the kitchen. Madison stared after her. There was something in the way Grandma had turned away, a haste in it, and it snagged on a memory from years ago: Grandma at the dining room table with her old college friend Helen, the two of them low-voiced over a scrapbook, and Helen saying, "They never proved anything, Ruth, you know that," and Grandma saying, "Everyone knew," and then silence when they noticed Madison in the doorway. Madison had been eight. She had thought they were talking about a man.

The clock ticked. Madison pulled the handbook back toward her and looked up plagiarism in the index, mostly to prove Grandma wrong, and the page said it plainly: plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording. Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation. She read it twice, then three times, the way you reread a sentence that has quietly rearranged the furniture of a room. Her Eastwick paragraph sat on the screen, plain and hers and not hers.

She went into the kitchen. Grandma was wiping a counter that was already clean, which she did when she wanted to seem occupied. "Did you ever get in trouble?" Madison asked. "At school. For something you wrote."

The cloth stopped. Grandma looked at the window above the sink, where the maple had gone yellow and was letting go of itself a leaf at a time, melancholic and unhurried, and Madison understood that her grandmother was deciding how much of the past was an encumbrance worth carrying into the light. "Helen and I wrote for the same magazine in sixty-one," Grandma said. "I used her research. Her idea about the textile mills. I didn't copy a word of it. I thought that made it mine." She folded the cloth into a perfect square. "She stopped speaking to me for two years. Longer, really. It was never the same after."

"I have to go fix something," Madison said, and her voice came out strange.

She went back and reread Rourke's paragraph against her own, side by side, and saw that she had kept his structure, his sequence of facts, his conclusion, and changed only the surface, like repainting a borrowed car. She typed a footnote number after the Eastwick paragraph, then sat with the cursor blinking in the footnote field, because the citation format wanted a page number and she had to go find it, which meant admitting, in the physical act of turning pages, what she had done. She turned the pages. Page 214. She wrote it down.

At lunch Grandma brought sandwiches without being asked and set one beside the laptop. "Fixed?" she said.

"Footnote four," Madison said, and pointed at the screen. Grandma leaned over, read it slowly, her lips moving a little, and then she straightened up and squeezed Madison's shoulder once, hard, the way she did when words would have been worse.

"Make it five while you're at it," she said. "I saw another one."

Nevaeh adjusted the mirror before her mother could tell her to, and the car seemed to settle around her, its smallness suddenly apparent, the roof close enough to touch. The parking lot of the community college was empty on a Saturday morning except for a groundskeeper pushing a cart along the far fence. She turned the key the way the manual had said, and the engine caught on the first try, which felt like a small mercy.

"Foot on the brake before you shift," her mother said, but Nevaeh had already done it, having read the chapter twice the night before, once at the kitchen table and once in bed with the flashlight her little brother used for reading comics under his blanket. She eased the car into drive. The lot's painted lines slid past the windshield, white and patient.

Her brother Marcus had gotten his permit two months before her, on the day he turned sixteen, and had spent that evening mapping out all the places he would take people. Lake behind the middle school, the taco truck on Fourth, his friend Dario's house out past the golf course. He had gone around the kitchen reciting names like a man distributing gifts. Then their mother had told him the sequence, and Nevaeh, thirteen then, had watched his face reorganize itself.

"It's called graduated licensing," Marcus had said that night, flat with disappointment, turning the laminated permit over in his hands. "First the permit, then a provisional license with restrictions, and only after that the full license." He had read it off the state website himself, slowly, as though saying it aloud might make it negotiable. It did not. He had sat in the driveway the next day anyway, in the driver's seat of the empty car, not driving anywhere, just holding the wheel with both hands.

In the lot, her mother said, "Signal, then check your mirror, then look over your shoulder. The signal doesn't replace the look." Nevaeh signaled, checked, looked. The empty lot offered no consequence for carelessness, which was somehow its own problem; she wanted the stakes to be real so that her attention would be real too. She pulled out onto the access road, and the first oncoming car passed close enough that she gripped the wheel tighter than she meant to.

"You're fine," her mother said. "He had the whole other lane."

They drove the loop around the college, past the gymnasium and the bus turn-around, and Nevaeh began to feel the pedal under her foot as a conversation rather than a command. Press, ease, press. When a bicyclist appeared ahead on the shoulder, she slowed early, well before she needed to, wanting to forestall any possibility of the woman on the bike having to make a decision about her. Her mother noticed. "That was good. Early is better than late."

At the stop sign at the edge of campus, Nevaeh braked fully and sat for a second with her hands at ten and two. "Can I ask you something?" she said.

"You just did."

"Mom."

"Ask."

"Do you think the rules are right? The ones Marcus hates. That you can't just get your license and drive whoever you want." She watched a sparrow cross in front of the hood and land on the sign itself, unbothered by the machinery idling below it.

Her mother was quiet long enough that Nevaeh thought she was composing something sagacious, the kind of thing adults kept in a drawer for occasions like this. Instead she said, "When I was seventeen I failed my first road test. Rolled a stop sign. My father said the examiner was too strict. I knew he was right and my father was being kind." She tapped the window with one finger. "I needed someone to not be kind about that particular thing."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the material for one. Go when you're ready."

Nevaeh went, turning left onto the busier road, and the traffic made everything she did meaningful. She held her speed. She thought about Marcus in the driveway, and about the bicyclist, and about the rolled stop sign from twenty years ago, and she understood that she was being asked to hold two things at once: that the restrictions were a shape imposed on her from outside, and that the shape was drawn around a real danger that she, personally, statistically, embodied. Sixteen-year-olds were not a phenotype you could select against, but they were, as a group, the thing the rule was drawn around. She was inside the group whether she drove well or badly, and the rule did not know her, and the rule might still be right. Both of those could be true. She wasn't sure yet how to live inside a rule that didn't know her, whether that was humility or erasure, and she decided she would have to keep driving long enough to find out.

"Turn here," her mother said, "and pull over where the curb is flat."

Nevaeh signaled, checked, looked over her shoulder, and brought the car to the curb in one smooth arc that surprised her with its competence. She set the brake and let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

"So can I drive us home?" she said.

"Permit," her mother said, and unclipped her seatbelt to slide over. "You drive, I ride, and neither of us tells Marcus you did better than him on day one."

"He already knows he was worse," Nevaeh said, and then, as she pulled back onto the road, "I'll drive him to the taco truck when I'm allowed. First thing."

Her mother was already halfway out the door and laughing. "Get your seatbelt," she said, "before I change my mind about everything."

Tristan had never been wrong about arithmetic, and he told himself this the way other people told themselves they were brave. So when he opened his first envelope from Halvorsen's Hardware and found sixty-eight dollars and change where seventy-three should have been, he assumed the fault lay with the envelope, or with Mr. Halvorsen, or with the wrinkled old man who did the books, and not with the only certainty he owned.

He had worked eleven hours at six sixty-five an hour. He had done the math twice on the walk home, once more at the kitchen table, and a fourth time in the margin of the flyer announcing the store's summer inventory sale, which started Saturday. Saturday was also the deadline to sign the rest of his hiring paperwork, the forms still folded in his backpack, and Mr. Halvorsen had said, in his flat way, that if the papers were not in by then, the job would go to the Rennick boy, who was fifteen and, according to everyone, unemployable.

Tristan's mother said eleven times six sixty-five was seventy-three fifteen, which settled nothing, since he already knew that. His sister said stores steal from kids, which he found too easy. Only Dee, who ran the register on weekends and had worked at Halvorsen's since she was fourteen herself, might know something, so Friday afternoon, with the paperwork deadline a day away and his suspicion calcifying into a grievance, he took his envelope to the register and laid it flat between them.

"Shorted," he said. He said it quietly, the way you say a word you have rehearsed. "Eleven hours. I counted."

Dee did not look impressed. She looked, if anything, tired, and she pulled her own check stub from under the register mat, where she kept it as though it were a bookmark for a book she had stopped reading. "Employers withhold part of your wages," she said. "Six point two percent, for Social Security tax. Up to a yearly wage limit, then it stops for the year."

Tristan looked at the stub, then at his own envelope, then at the ceiling fan turning its slow circles over aisle three. Six point two percent of seventy-three fifteen was four dollars and fifty-three cents, give or take a penny, and seventy-three fifteen minus four fifty-three was sixty-eight sixty-two, which was the number in the envelope down to the last digit. He had been shorted nothing. The ground he had stood on all week, the solid arithmetic ground, had been arithmetic about the wrong thing.

He thought about Mr. Halvorsen, whom he had privately cast as the villain, a man with detractors all over town who claimed he watered down the paint and fired boys for looking at their phones. Tristan had believed them, he realized, because the story fit the number, and the number fit the story, and neither had been checked against the other. It was a profligate way to spend a certainty, handing it out to anyone who would take it, and he had been doing it all week.

"You could have said something," he told Dee, though even as he said it he heard how it sounded, like a boy who wanted the world to apologize for arithmetic.

"You could have asked," Dee said. She rang up a woman buying curtain rods and did not look at him until the receipt was torn. "Most kids don't. They just quit and tell everyone they got robbed, and then the Rennick boy gets the job and the town gets another story about Halvorsen's." She slid the stub back under the mat. "I did that my first month. Told my dad the old man was a thief. He made me sit down with the numbers."

"Was he right to?"

"He made me figure it out myself. That part was right." She straightened the pens by the register, five of them, none of which wrote. "The part where I already knew he'd say I told you so, that part I made up. I'm still not sure which part was worse, what I got wrong or how sure I was while I was getting it wrong."

Tristan picked up his envelope. He did not feel corrected so much as rearranged, as though the store had shifted its aisles overnight and he was still navigating by the old map. Somewhere between his certainty and the town's stories about the old man was a version of things he could actually verify, and it was smaller than either, and slower, and it did not come with the satisfaction of knowing whom to blame.

He walked the three blocks home in the flattening light, took the forms from his backpack, and signed every page at the kitchen table. Then, before he could lose his nerve, he did the math on what Saturday's hours would come to, the gross and the withheld part, both numbers, in pencil, so he could change them.

At the store the next morning he handed the paperwork to Mr. Halvorsen, who looked at it longer than a stack of signatures seemed to require. "Sixty-eight sixty-two," Tristan said. "Last week. It checked out." The old man grunted and filed the papers in a drawer that stuck, and Dee, restocking near the register, said, "Told you nobody robbed him."

The scholarship application wanted two hundred volunteer hours, and Jackson had been counting his at St. Bridget's like a prisoner scratching tally marks on a wall. He had sixty-one. Today he was restocking the hydration station on the fourth floor, filling little green pitchers with ice and water, when he noticed that the family lounge outside Room 412 had gone quiet in the way rooms do when something heavy is being said.

"I want to be clear about the morphine," a doctor was saying through the half-open door. Jackson had seen her before, Dr. Reyes, the one with the gray braid who never used the elevators. "It will ease his breathing. That is what I intend. But at this dose, there is a chance it could shorten the time he has left. I want you to hear that from me and not from a nurse's note after the fact."

A woman's voice, thin and frayed: "So you're asking us to sign something that kills him faster."

"I'm asking you to let me treat his pain."

Jackson stood in the hallway with a pitcher sweating in both hands. He had assumed, without ever putting it into words, that doctors simply did good, the way furnaces simply produced heat. The idea that a good act could carry a foreseeable harm inside it, like a stone in a peach, was new, and he carried it with him down to the lounge where the patient's grandson sat hunched over an untouched coffee. Jackson only meant to be kind. He said that he'd overheard the doctors, that morphine could end things sooner, that maybe the family should fight it. The grandson's face changed, and he was through the door of 412 before Jackson had finished his sentence.

The charge nurse found him twenty minutes later and lambasted him in the supply alcice, her voice low and shaking, telling him that patient information was not his to repeat, that he had walked into the middle of a decision that had nothing to do with him. "The family's talking to a lawyer," she said. "If it goes anywhere, you could be part of a deposition. Sworn testimony, Jackson. About something you don't understand."

That night he sat on his bedroom floor with his phone and typed in what he remembered: harm you foresee but don't intend. The results led him to the doctrine of double effect, traced back to Thomas Aquinas, who had argued that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end. Jackson read it three times. Foresees, does not intend. The doctor hadn't been hiding anything from the family; she had been laying the whole trade on the table, the pain relief against the days it might cost, and asking them to weigh it. Jackson had taken the scale and thrown it at the grandson.

He asked to see the charge nurse before his next shift, and he told her he would say exactly what he had done, to the family, to a lawyer, to anyone, but that he had gotten the doctor's meaning wrong. Dr. Reyes was the one who came to find him instead, in the hallway by the ice machine. "I heard what you told them," she said. "You made it sound like we were choosing his death. What we were choosing was whether he spends his last days gasping or resting. Those are not the same conversation."

"I didn't know there was a difference," Jackson said.

"There is, and then there isn't," she said. "Aquinas gives you the frame, but the frame doesn't carry the weight for you. The family asked me yesterday whether the morphine was worth two days of his life. I said I couldn't answer that. Nobody can. We chose the morphine."

Mr. Okafor died four days later, on a Thursday morning, and the lawyer's letter never came, so there was no deposition, only a note in Jackson's file that his shifts would be supervised for the rest of the summer. His friend Diego texted him a picture from the lake, three girls on a dock, the caption calling it a hedonistic July, and Jackson typed "have one for me" and put the phone face down. On his last supervised shift, the grandson appeared at the fourth-floor desk, holding a paper bag of mangoes. "You stuck your nose where it didn't belong," he said, "but after you did, my mother finally asked the doctor the questions she'd been swallowing for a month. So." He set the bag on the counter. "He liked these cut into stars."

Jackson carried the mangoes to the break room, took out the little paring knife, and began cutting.

Jasmine had worked at the bookstore for three weeks, long enough to acclimate to the smell of old paper and the till that jammed on twenties, but not long enough to stop flinching when the receipt printer spat out a line she could not account for. On Friday her paycheque landed in her account, and she opened the portal on her phone behind the poetry shelf, where Mrs. Okafor never looked. Gross pay: 640.00. Net pay: 558.13. Somewhere between those numbers, eighty-one dollars and eighty-seven cents had gone missing, and she wanted it back.

"CPP, EI, and income tax," said Devi, the other part-timer, when Jasmine showed her the stub during their break. "It's on mine too. Deductions. Everyone gets them." Devi said it the way people said rain in April, as though the withholding were weather rather than a decision, and that was the part Jasmine could not accept. Somebody had chosen those lines. Somebody had a reason.

The same afternoon, a customer with a Manchester United scarf bought a stack of gardening books and asked, watching the register, what the tax was here. "Thirteen percent, HST," Jasmine said, because that was on the placard by the till. He laughed and said he was still converting everything in his head; he'd moved in February. "Our VAT's built into the price, so your tags look cheap and then the machine adds on." She rang him up, printed the receipt, and watched the 6.24 appear beneath the 48.00, that arithmetic of addition she had never thought about until a stranger found it strange.

That night she messaged her cousin Ade, who was doing a gap year in Leeds. Ade, you know tax stuff. UK sales tax, what's the rate? The reply came as a voice note, then a photo: a Boots receipt, tiny print at the bottom. "VAT's twenty percent," Ade's message read. "Has been since the fourth of January, 2011, back when we were kids. Standard rate. It's in the shelf price, you never see it added." Jasmine read it three times. Twenty percent, hidden inside the number on the tag; thirteen percent, bolted on at the register. She thought of arbitrage, a word from her economics unit, buying cheap in one market and selling dear in another, and wondered whether the same book cost the same soul in both countries or whether one of them was quietly more expensive than it looked.

She started keeping a page in the back of her notebook. Column one: the receipt from her own shift, coffee and a muffin, 9.85 total, 1.13 of it tax. Column two: the photo of Ade's receipt. Column three: her pay stub, the 640 shrunk to 558.13. She understood, slowly, that she was comparing unlike things, like weighing fruit against fish, and that the comparison was the point. The sales tax took from her as a buyer. The deductions took from her as a worker. Both took, and both bought something, though she could not yet say what.

On Tuesday she asked Mrs. Okafor for her tax slips, the ones for filing, and Mrs. Okafor printed them from the back office without ceremony. At home, Jasmine entered the numbers into the return and watched the software work a small reversal: her income was low enough, her tuition credit large enough, that the machine declared a refund. Not all of the eighty-one dollars and eighty-seven cents, but most of it, flowing back the other way, from the government to her. She sat very still with that, feeling something tectonic shift in her picture of the world, the deductions not theft but a loan she had not agreed to, or a membership fee for a club whose meetings she had never attended.

She wrote to Ade that night, a real letter, because Ade had complained that nobody wrote letters anymore. "Here's what I figured out. The money they took isn't gone, it's just early. I file and some comes back. The sales tax is different, that one's gone for good, or at least I can't find the door it went through. Yours is higher and invisible, mine is lower and visible, and I keep changing my mind about which I'd rather. At the store I watch people flinch at the add-on and I think, at least they see it. But then I think about the shelf price being a lie, sort of, and I don't know."

The last paragraph of the letter she crossed out and rewrote twice. In the end she kept it simple: "I still don't know if it's fair. I only know how it works, mostly." She sealed the envelope, stamped it, and left it on the hall table for the morning post. Then she set an alarm for her Saturday shift, took her notebook off the desk, and added one more line to the column that had no heading yet: 558.13, in ink, underlined once.

Levi had worked the front desk at Ridgeview Fitness for five weeks, long enough to learn the register, the towel count, and the laminated script for new members. The script was taped to the underside of the counter, and it used words he had never said out loud before his first shift: terms, conditions, liability waiver, monthly billing authorization. He said them forty times a week now. They had sensitized him to the paperwork everywhere else, too. He read his phone plan's renewal notice twice on the bus home, looking for the trap.

On a Tuesday evening in August, a boy came in with a duffel bag and a folded printout of the membership offer. His name was Marcus, he was seventeen, and he wanted the student rate before football conditioning started. He had a debit card in his hand and a school ID. Levi slid the contract across the counter and handed him the pen, and Marcus signed his name in careful block letters, and everything would have been fine except the form asked for his date of birth, and Marcus wrote it honestly.

"I need a parent's signature," Levi said. "It's the policy."

"Both my parents work nights," Marcus said. "I have the money. I have the card. What does it matter whose name is on the line?"

Levi did not have an answer. He looked at the script under the counter, but the script only covered pricing tiers and cancellation fees. He told Marcus he would ask his manager and hold the paperwork in the drawer, and Marcus said he would come back Thursday, and he took the pen with him by accident, a small theft neither of them noticed.

The manager, Ms. Okafor, was off until morning. Levi's coworker Danny was on the closing shift, and Danny was a dilettante who had opinions on contract law, real estate, sourdough starters, and the zoning dispute at the taco place across the street. "It's because he could cancel it," Danny said, spraying the treadmills. "A minor signs, a minor can walk away from it. That's the whole thing. It's voidable by the minor. Look it up if you don't believe me."

"I'm not looking up your theories."

"Look up whoever you want. It's common law, it's most of the country. The gym can't hold a kid to a contract. Kid can void it, gym can't. That's why they want the parent." Danny pointed the spray bottle at him. "There are exceptions. Necessities. Food, that kind of thing. A gym membership is not a necessity, no matter what Marcus's football coach thinks."

Levi did look it up, on his break, sitting on the stacked mats in the stretching corner with his phone. Danny had it right, which annoyed him. In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor was generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities. Levi read the sentence three times. It was not that Marcus could not sign. It was that his signature meant one thing for the gym and another thing for Marcus, and the gym had decided it did not like the arrangement.

The next morning Levi found the policy binder behind the desk, and in the membership section there was a memo in Ms. Okafor's florid handwriting, all loops and crossed sevens, dated three years back: No memberships to under-18s without parent or guardian signature. Refund if already billed. Levi read it and understood that the policy was not a rule about who could join. It was a rule about risk. The gym wanted a signature it could enforce, and Marcus's parents, working nights, were the enforceable ones.

When Ms. Okafor came in at ten, Levi asked her about it. "What if the parent can't come in? Can they mail it, or do it over the phone?"

"They can mail it, they can fax it if they find a fax machine, they can come in on a Sunday," she said. "Why, do you have one?"

"Kid came in last night. Football season. He's coming back Thursday."

"Then Thursday we get him the form to take home." She was restocking the protein bars and did not look up. "Or he waits until his birthday."

Levi spent Wednesday thinking about it during the slow hours, between checking people in and wiping down the key rack. He had assumed the policy was a wall. Now it looked more like a door with a particular handle, and the question was whether he was supposed to tell Marcus where the handle was. He could explain the whole thing: that Marcus's own signature was legal but fragile, voidable, that the gym wanted his parents because their signatures could not be taken back. He could also just say "policy" again, the way the script did, and let Marcus believe there was nothing on the other side.

Thursday evening Marcus came back, duffel over his shoulder, and put the stolen pen on the counter without comment. "My dad's asleep by the time I get home," he said. "He sleeps at four in the afternoon. Conditioning starts Monday. If I'm not there Monday, they give my spot to a junior."

Levi took the contract out of the drawer and laid it flat. He turned it so Marcus could read it, and put his finger under the line that said the agreement was voidable by any member under eighteen, that exceptions applied only to contracts for necessities. "That's why they need your dad," he said. "Not because you can't sign. Because you can sign and then cancel it whenever you want, and they can't stop you, and they hate that. Your dad's signature they can hold onto."

Marcus read the paragraph twice. "So if I sign it and they bill me, I can void it?"

"That's what it says. I looked it up. It's most of the country, the common-law places. I'm not a lawyer."

"And a gym isn't a necessity."

"That's the exception, apparently. Food, stuff like that. Not this." Levi slid the take-home form across the counter, the one with the second signature line, and set the pen on top of it. "You can take this for your dad, or you can sign yours and void it later if they mess up your billing, but I don't know what happens then. I've only been here five weeks."

Marcus picked up the pen and looked at the two lines, one under his own block letters from Tuesday, one blank. Behind them, someone dropped a weight plate, and the sound rang off the mirrors and faded. Marcus tapped the blank line with the pen clip, twice, and said, "My dad gets up at two. He's awake for like an hour before work."

The kiln had been broken since March, so the community studio smelled of acrylic and turpentine instead of fired clay, and Sarah had claimed the table by the window because its light came in flat and honest across the afternoon. Her portfolio was due in nine days. On the table lay her third attempt at the harbor piece: gray water, gray sky, a line of pilings marching out toward a buoy that refused to matter.

"You've got the horizon dead center," said Priya, leaning over from the easel she shared with two oil painters who never came on Saturdays. "Put it a third of the way down. Rule of thirds."

Sarah sat back. "Who made that a rule?"

Priya shrugged, already turning back to her canvas. "Some dead guy, probably."

That should have been the end of it. Instead Sarah found herself that evening in the college library, because the studio kept a shelf of donated art books and the shelf had failed her, and there was something in the question that wouldn't quiet down. She wasn't the kind of person who introspect her way into libraries, or at least she hadn't been; apparently she was now. She found it in a scanned copy of an old book, its pages photographed so carefully she could see the foxing: Remarks on Rural Scenery, by John Thomas Smith, 1797. He had written the phrase down first, "rule of thirds," in a book about rural scenery, of all things, two hundred and odd years before Priya told her to move her horizon. She copied the citation onto the back of a gas receipt and rode the late bus home holding it like a ticket.

The next Saturday she arrived first and redrew the harbor. Horizon a third of the way down, the pilings entering from the left, the buoy now sitting, not floating, at a point that felt almost unfairly deliberate. The painting looked better. That was the trouble with it. It looked like every photograph on every wall of every dentist's office she had ever sat in, a composition so absorbed into the world that using it felt like quoting without speech marks.

"See?" Priya said when she came in, coat still on, shaking rain off it. "Told you."

"It's from a book," Sarah said. "John Thomas Smith, 1797. Remarks on Rural Scenery. First wrote down the phrase 'rule of thirds.'"

"Okay," said Priya, delighted and uninterested at once, the way she was about most things that weren't paint. "So it's old. Old things work."

But Sarah had spent the week thinking about how a man looking at rural scenery in 1797 had casually set a boundary she was now standing inside, and how her grandmother's quilts ignored every such law and still stopped your breath, and how the pilings in the actual harbor at Revere Beach did not arrange themselves in thirds. The rain intensified against the window, streaking the light she had chosen the table for. She picked up a rag and wiped the buoy off. Then she wiped the horizon off, the whole careful line of it, and let the gray water and the gray sky bleed into each other at a height chosen by nothing but her own wrist.

Priya watched this with genuine alarm. "You're going to submit that?"

"I don't know what I'm going to submit," Sarah said, which was true, and which cost her something to say out loud, because the portfolio wanted confidence and she had been practicing confidence all autumn like a scale.

The afternoon organized itself around her not deciding. A retired man named Walter, loquacious after his second thermos of coffee, narrated his own progress on a lighthouse to anyone in range. Two kids from the high school argued about whether orange was a real color. Priya painted in her deliberate, stabbing way and did not mention the horizon again, though Sarah caught her looking, twice, at the place where water met nothing.

Near closing, Sarah did a small thing. In the lower third of the canvas, roughly, though she refused to measure, she set the buoy back in, small and black against the formless gray. Not at an intersection, not at a power point, whatever those were called. Just low and left of center, where a buoy would actually ride. The rest she left unresolved, water and sky agreeing to be the same color, the pilings dissolving at their tops like an archipelago seen through fog, half-real.

"That's it?" Priya said, packing her brushes.

"That's what I have," Sarah said.

Priya stood in front of it for longer than she stood in front of anything, head tilted, and Sarah understood that the verdict, whatever it was, would not be spoken tonight. Walter shut off the lights from the switch by the door, and the harbor went dark all at once, water, sky, and buoy together.

Jake found the card on the fridge on Monday morning, tucked under the sunflower magnet where the hydro bills usually lived. It was addressed to his father, Frank Dooley, and it named a polling place at the elementary school two blocks over. His own name was nowhere on it, which meant, Jake understood with a slow tightening in his stomach, that he had never sent in the registration he'd promised himself he would send in. He had turned eighteen in March, talked all spring about voting in his first federal election, and then finals had swallowed him whole and the form had stayed folded in his backpack like an apology he kept meaning to deliver.

"You're up early," his father said from the kitchen doorway, mug in hand, still in the shirt he'd slept in.

"I'm not on the list," Jake said. "I never registered. So I guess I'm done, right? You have to be on the list before election day."

His father took a slow sip, the way he did when he was deciding whether something was worth correcting. "Where'd you hear that?"

"Everybody knows that."

"Everybody's wrong, then." His father set the mug down. "In a Canadian federal election, if you're not on the voters list, you can register at your assigned polling place on election day."

"That's it? You just show up?"

"You just show up. With ID, proof of address. Don't make that face like I just performed a miracle."

Jake went upstairs not sure whether he felt relieved or cornered. He had wanted the excuse, he could admit that much. All through the spring his father and his grandfather had been conducting their long, cheerful war at the dinner table, his father arguing that the country needed a steady hand and his grandfather, who had voted the other way since before Jake was born, arguing with equal force that a steady hand was exactly the problem. Jake had listened the way he listened to weather reports, assuming it would all be decided somewhere above him. His grandfather called him a dilettante once, half teasing, and the word had stuck in his side all summer.

At the kitchen table he spread out his ID, his health card, a bank statement with the house address, and beside them the folded flyer he'd kept from the candidate who'd come to his school in April. She was young, unproven, from his grandfather's party, and she had talked about tuition in a way that sounded like she'd actually paid some. His father's party had been around long enough that its promises had a congenital caution to them, hedged and reasonable, careful not to promise too much to anyone. Jake had spent weeks telling himself the safe choice was the mature one.

He found his grandfather in the garage, sorting nails into jars with the concentration of a man who considered this a serious occupation. "You voting today?" Jake asked.

"At my age, voting and complaining are the only exercises I get." His grandfather held up a bent nail, judged it, threw it back. "You?"

"I wasn't registered. Dad says I can do it at the polling place." He watched the old man's eyebrows climb. "Today. On election day. He says you just register there."

"Well," his grandfather said, "then you're out of excuses. That must be uncomfortable."

"It is, a little." Jake turned a jar of screws a quarter turn, then back. "Grandpa, can I ask you something? Did you ever vote for a party you didn't agree with? Because it was the safe one?"

His grandfather laughed, a short bark that surprised a wren off the windowsill. "Once. Nineteen years old, scared of wasting my vote. Wasted it anyway, didn't I? Threw it at a man I didn't believe in because I believed in him a little less than I feared the other fellow." He pushed the jar aside and looked at Jake properly. "You're asking the wrong question, though. The question isn't safe or brave. The question is which one you'll still be able to look at in ten years."

Jake walked to the school with his father at ten, the morning bright and cold for April, election signs still standing in front lawns like a crop that had come up unevenly. Inside the gymnasium, the line moved in short shuffles between the floor tape and the folding tables. When his turn came, a poll worker with reading glasses asked for his ID, made a call, and printed something off; a few minutes later Jake was taking an oath and signing a form and being pointed toward a second table, where a ballot slid across to him in a folded square of heavy paper.

The screen was a cardboard tri-fold on a chair, and behind it the pencil felt smaller than he expected. He looked at the names for a long moment. Somewhere behind him his father was waiting, patient, certain of his own choice, and Jake understood that certainty wasn't something he could borrow, not from his father, not from his grandfather, not even from the candidate with the flyer. What he had instead was smaller and harder to hold: his own reading of the whole spring, both men's arguments still loud in his head, weighed once more in the privacy of the cardboard booth. He marked the ballot, folded it along its own creases, and slid it into the box.

Outside, his father asked him nothing, which Jake understood as a kind of respect. They walked home side by side, past the signs, and when they reached the driveway his father said only, "Proud of you for going."

"I almost didn't," Jake said. "I almost let the registration thing be my way out."

"I know." His father pocketed his keys. "Your grandfather's coming for dinner. You can fight about it then."

The notification buzzed against Abigail's thigh during third period, and by lunch the group chat had fifty-one unread messages. The thread was called "senior spring" and it existed mostly for memes and complaints about the calc teacher, but today Marcus had pasted a link to a Washington Post story about a warehouse somewhere in Ohio where drivers were suing over timed bathroom breaks. He had added a single line: "thoughts?"

Abigail read the story under her desk, then read it again at the picnic table outside the cafeteria, the screen glare making her squint. The reporting was detailed, almost gentle toward the drivers, and she found herself nodding along, feeling the small satisfaction of being informed. Then Priya replied to Marcus with a shrug emoji and the words "funny how they never say the quiet part," and when Abigail asked what the quiet part was, Priya sent a screenshot of a headline from a site Abigail had never heard of, one that called the Post "a billionaire's plaything."

"Bezos owns it," Priya typed, fast, the way she typed when she was winning an argument. "Jeff Bezos. Amazon founder. He bought the Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013 for two hundred fifty million dollars." Below it she added, "so yeah, do the math on why the coverage looks like that."

Abigail did not reply right away. She looked up from her phone at the actual picnic table, at Marcus pulling the tab off a can of soda and not drinking it, at Priya across from her wearing the lanyard from the journalism workshop she'd attended in February and hadn't taken off since. Priya wanted the editor-in-chief spot on the school paper next year, wanted it so badly that she had started calling other people's reporting biased the way other people called fouls in basketball, quickly and always in her own favor.

"It's a decent story, though," Abigail said out loud, because some things felt cheaper typed. "They quoted the drivers. They got the documents."

"They quoted the drivers they could afford to quote," Priya said. "That's what owning something means. You set the edges."

Abigail thought about the edges of things, about how her mother described her grandfather's farm and the way the river used to undulate through the low field before the county rerouted it, a slow silver muscle that belonged to no one and then, after the paperwork, to someone. Ownership was like that, she supposed: invisible until it moved.

That night she sat cross-legged on her bed with her laptop open and the group chat pinging on her phone like a small rain. She looked up the purchase herself, not because she doubted Priya, but because repeating a fact felt different from holding it. Two hundred fifty million dollars. It was a strange number, small for a man of that size and large for a newspaper, and she sat with the strangeness of it while her history textbook lay open and ignored beside her. Then she found a Post story about Amazon's working conditions from a few years back, a long investigation, unsparing, and she found another one, and another. She pasted three links into the chat without commentary and watched the typing indicator appear and disappear under Priya's name, appear and disappear, like something surfacing and thinking better of it.

"Fine," Priya finally sent. "They do hard stories on Amazon sometimes. That doesn't mean the ownership doesn't matter. It means we can't tell exactly how it matters."

Abigail read that twice. It was the most honest sentence anyone had typed all day, and it came from the person who had spent all day not being honest in exactly that way. She wanted to say so, but saying so would have cost her something, so instead she typed, "Agreed on the not-telling." Marcus sent a thumbs up, then a message that said he'd been the one who found the article because his cousin drove for the company over the summer and nobody believed him about the bathroom thing, and now a newspaper believed him, or half believed him, or believed him within certain edges.

The chat quieted around eleven. Abigail lay in the dark with her phone on her chest, feeling the day settle into some apportionment she couldn't quite perform, one part of her glad to know the fact about 2013 and the money and the family that sold, one part aware that knowing it hadn't told her what to do with any given headline, one part stubbornly impervious to Priya's certainty and to her own instinct to defend the paper just because Priya had attacked it. Tomorrow there would be another link, another argument, another version of this exact night. Her phone lit once more before she set it face down: Priya had added her to a new chat called "media literacy," created nine seconds ago, with two members and no messages yet.

The line at the former elementary school stretched past the doors marked gymnasium, and Aiden stood near the end with his hands in his jacket pockets. He had turned eighteen in March, three weeks before the registration deadline, and his father had driven him to the county office that same afternoon, saying little on the way. Now it was November, the gym smelled of floor wax and wet umbrellas, and Aiden advanced one folding-table-length at a time toward the clipboard where a woman with reading glasses checked names.

Ahead of him a boy from his economics class, Marcus, kept turning around to talk. "My mom's voting the other way from me," Marcus said. "She found out I registered and spent an hour trying to cajole me over dinner. Lasagna, garlic bread, the whole campaign."

"Did it work?"

"I told her she'd find out on Wednesday with everybody else." Marcus grinned, then the grin faded into something more serious. "Hey, actually. Nobody's allowed to watch you mark it, right? Like, they can't see how you vote at all?"

A woman in front of them, older, holding her ID ready in her hand, half turned. "It's called the Australian ballot," she said. "That's what the secret printed ballot is called." She faced forward again, as if she had spent her whole quota of conversation on it.

"The colonies there came up with it," Aiden said, mostly to himself, and then he realized he actually knew the rest. "Tasmania and Victoria, in 1856." He had read it in a library book in eighth grade, one he had pulled off the shelf because he liked the shape of the word ballot, and the fact had stuck the way certain useless facts stuck, lodged like a seed in a crack.

Marcus squinted at him. "Australia invented voting?"

"Secret voting. The ballot itself. Before that, people could watch you, or you said it out loud." Aiden was working it out as he spoke, the reason coming to him only now, in the line. If your vote was public, anyone could stand over you, an employer, a husband, a crowd outside the window. If it was secret, the lasagna and the garlic bread ended at the curtain. His mother's persuasion, Marcus's mother's persuasion, all of it stopped at the little canvas booth, which was, he thought, either a protection or a small entropy, opinions dissipating into silence where no one could trace them.

Two summers ago, before any of this mattered to him, Aiden had gone with his grandfather to vote in the midterms. The old man had parked badly, on a hill, and insisted on walking in without his arm. Inside, at the same folding tables, the same women with reading glasses, his grandfather had stood at the booth for a long time. Aiden, waiting by the door, had watched him hover over the paper with his pencil, and had wondered, without any real curiosity, what was taking so long. When they were back in the car his grandfather said, "Your grandmother and I cancel each other out, every single election, and we've never once discussed it. Fifty-one years." He had said it the way a man states the weather, and Aiden had filed it away with the Australian ballot and the other facts that belonged to adulthood.

Now the woman with the reading glasses called, "Next," and Marcus stepped up, gave his name, and was pointed toward the machines. Aiden followed. His name was on the list. He signed it and felt the pen snag slightly on the laminated page.

The booth was smaller than he expected, a canvas sleeve on three aluminum legs, and the ballot was a long sheet printed on both sides. In eighth grade he had imagined this moment as an ending, a door he would walk through and emerge from changed. Instead it was a man in a damp jacket holding a pen in a gymnasium, deciding. He thought of his grandfather's pencil hovering. He thought of the colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, someone in 1856 deciding that a vote should be a thing no one could see, and he thought, less comfortably, that he still wasn't sure whether that was mercy or just a very organized form of loneliness. The pen waited above the first contest.

Behind him, at the entrance, a poll worker was turning someone away, gently, for lack of ID, and the man's voice rose once, scathing, before it dropped and he left through the double doors into the rain.

Aiden marked the first box, then the second, then the races he had studied and the ones he had not. He fed the sheet into the scanner, which took it with a shudder and lit a small American flag on its face. Outside, Marcus was waiting under the awning with his hood up.

"So," Marcus said. "Wednesday?"

"Wednesday," Aiden said, and pulled his own hood over his head and stepped down into the puddled lot.

The auction barn smelled of wet straw and diesel, and Ava sat on a sawhorse with her phone in both hands, reading the same paragraph for the third time while her grandfather argued with a man from the bank at the folding table by the fence line. The man kept saying words like restructuring and opportunity, and her grandfather kept saying nothing at all, which Ava had learned was worse. Outside, the rain came down on two hundred acres of soybeans that had failed twice in three years, first under drought and then under a flood that shouldn't have come in June.

She was supposed to be rehearsing. On Thursday, in her last week of high school, her government class would debate whether countries could ever actually agree on an environmental problem, and her teacher had assigned Ava the yes side, which felt like a joke. Her grandfather read the farm reports out loud at breakfast, the ones about tariffs and commodity prices and the river sediment, and none of it suggested that anyone agreed about anything, ever.

Her cousin Dario came through the barn door shaking water off his jacket. "They still going?"

"Forty minutes," Ava said. "He won't look at the papers."

Dario sat on the hay bale across from her, took off his boot, and shook a pebble out of it. "Dad says the co-op's dropping another eight growers this fall. Says the buyers want the big consolidated lots now, the irrigated ones, out west where the water rights are." He said it flat, the way people around here said bad news, and Ava thought about how the drought out west and the flood here were both weather, both money, both somebody's decision at a desk far away. It was hard to say where one thing stopped and the next began.

She went back to her phone. She'd found a thread of sources the night before, chasing her debate topic out of stubbornness, and at two in the morning she'd hit something she hadn't expected. She read it aloud now, quietly, mostly to herself. "The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state."

Dario looked up. "Every one?"

"Every single one. Every country that was in the UN." She turned the phone toward him so he could see she wasn't inventing it, and he squinted at the small screen with his boot still in his hand.

"Huh," he said. "The ozone thing. The hole." He pointed at an aerosol can of fly spray sitting on the windowsill, half-empty, red. "That stuff they fixed?"

"That's how it worked with the chemicals, the sprays and the refrigerants, whatever was eating the ozone," she said. "They phased them out." She didn't say more than that, because she didn't know more than that yet, and there was something in not knowing that she wanted to keep honest. She had a night left to read, and a debate to lose or win, and a phone with a cracked screen and a battery at eleven percent.

Behind them, the bank man was packing his briefcase, and her grandfather crossed the barn in the direction of the feed room without a word to either of them. Ava followed him in. He stood with his hand on the lid of the grain bin, not opening it, and the rain on the tin roof was so loud she almost had to shout.

"You want me to say it went fine?" she asked.

"No," he said. "I want you to tell me what you were reading."

She told him about the treaty, every member state, the first one in UN history ever to get all of them, and he listened with his jaw working the way it did when he was deciding whether to spit or speak. "The whole world agreed on something," she finished. "I have to argue Thursday that they can."

He was quiet for a while. "Half this county can't agree on a drainage ditch," he said. But he opened the grain bin, and the smell of oats rose up, and he looked less lugubrious than he had at the table, almost as if the fact had sutured something in him, some torn place between what he believed about people and what he needed to believe to keep planting in the spring. Ava knew her own position was thinner than that. She believed the treaty happened, and she believed the droughts were getting worse, and she could not make those two facts hold hands yet, could not say whether agreement came easier when the sky itself was the patient or when the damage was slow and dispersed, when culpability spread out so wide that no one felt it in their own hands. Her grandfather's hands were cracked from rope and cold water. The bank man's hands were clean. Somewhere between those hands the whole system lay, weather and money and treaties, and she would stand up Thursday and speak for exactly six minutes about a world that had once, in one narrow instance, said yes together.

The rain kept on. Her grandfather scooped grain into the bucket, measure by measure, and carried it past her out into the dark of the barn, where the cattle had already begun to low.

"Come on," he said over his shoulder. "You can argue with the heifers first."

Carter had written three openings for the toast his grandmother expected at dinner, and he had torn up all of them. The first was a joke about finally being done with high school, the second was a thank-you list that read like an awards ceremony, and the third had tried to be serious and collapsed into greeting-card language he couldn't say out loud. He sat in his car outside his grandparents' house with his phone open to a draft, because Grandma June had cornered him last week and said, "You're the graduate, you're saying something, seven o'clock sharp, before the cake." It was six forty.

Inside, the dining room was loud with relatives he half knew. His diploma sat propped against the centerpiece, its seal catching the light, and every few minutes someone lifted a glass toward it. Carter's grandfather, Walt, sat at the far end, quieter than usual, turning his water glass in slow circles. Carter had always thought of the two of them as parallel cases: Walt had left school at seventeen, and Carter had just finished his, and the family treated both facts as different versions of the same thing, an unfinished story that had finally come out all right.

It was Aunt Rena who destabilized that, casually, while spooning potatoes. "Your grandfather has a diploma too, you know," she said. "Same one, basically. The GED." She said it like a footnote, but Carter put down his fork. He knew the letters, knew kids who had taken that route after leaving school early, but he had never once thought of them attached to Walt, who had run a hardware store for thirty years and could rewire anything in the house.

"Since when?" Carter asked.

"Nineteen forty-two, the tests started," Walt said, still turning the glass. "For service members. Fellows like me who'd left school and gone in. When I got out, I took it. Showed I had the schooling without the school." He shrugged, as if it were a minor clerical matter, but his voice had the careful flatness Carter recognized from when he was hiding something he actually felt.

Carter wanted to ask more, but the cake was already being lit in the kitchen, and his grandmother was mouthing seven o'clock at him across the table. He had maybe ten minutes. He pushed back his chair and followed Walt out onto the porch, where the old man had retreated with his coffee.

"You never told me that," Carter said.

"Never came up." Walt looked at the yard, where the neighbor's sprinkler ticked back and forth. "People get strange about it. Some cousin of mine, real ideologue about education, used to say the GED wasn't a real diploma. Man could turn any subject into an argument, that one. You learn not to hand people the opening." He sipped his coffee. "I passed it in an army office with a pencil that kept breaking. Hardest test I ever took. But nobody wants the story, they want the label."

Carter leaned on the railing, working through it. He had spent the spring arguing with a classmate, Marcus, who insisted that a diploma meant something only if you suffered through four full years to get it, that shortcuts cheapened the thing itself. Carter had half agreed, mostly because Marcus argued with such virulent certainty that disagreeing felt like picking a fight. Now, standing next to a man who had left school for a war and come back and proven himself on a single brutal exam, he wondered whether the paper or the proving was the point. Maybe both, he thought. Maybe the diploma was just a receipt, and the receipt mattered only because of what had been purchased.

"I have to give a toast," Carter said. "Right now, basically. Can I mention it? The GED, the test, all of it?"

Walt was quiet long enough that the sprinkler completed two passes. "You'd be telling my story in your toast," he said, which was not a no.

"That's the thing," Carter said. "It's not just my story without it. Mine's boring. I showed up and did the work. Yours is the interesting one." He hesitated, honest with himself at least: he still didn't know if he was asking permission or asking for material, and the difference bothered him. "I won't make it a speech about speeches. I'll just say what happened."

Walt set the coffee down. "Say the year right, then. Nineteen forty-two."

Through the screen door, Grandma June called his name in the tone that meant the last candle was being lit. Carter went in, stood at the head of the table with his glass raised, and felt every prepared sentence desert him except the true one.

"Sixty-three years before I got mine," he said, "the country invented a test so that service members who never finished school could prove they had the skills anyway. My grandfather took it. I got my diploma Saturday." He lifted the glass higher and looked down the table at Walt. "Same family, same receipt. To the graduate who earned it twice."

The restaurant had pushed four tables together under the big screen, and by the second quarter Sarah's uncle Theo had already lost a trivia bet to her cousin Marcus twice, which meant he owed him twenty dollars and a plate of nachos he kept trying to amortize by eating himself. Sarah sat between her grandmother and her best friend Priya, nominally watching the game, actually watching Marcus. He was the one who had told her, at the graduation party last month, that she argued like a lawyer and cared about nothing, and she had been carrying that sentence around ever since like a stone in her shoe.

"There's a trivia contest at halftime," Marcus announced, waving the paper flyer the waitress had left. "Winner gets fifty bucks off the bill. Sports and Olympics stuff, since the games start next month."

"I'll do it," Sarah said, before she could think better of it.

"You don't watch sports," her grandmother said, not unkindly.
