"I watch the Olympics. I like the opening ceremony. All the flags."

"Lugubrious music, everyone crying," Priya agreed, tearing a piece of napkin into small flags of her own. "It's the best thing on television."

The first half was a grinding, low-scoring affair that Uncle Theo narrated like a funeral oration, and by halftime Sarah had two of the three trivia questions right, tied with a man in a trucker hat from the bar who turned out to know an alarming amount about boxing. Then the waitress cleared her throat and read the tiebreaker: which colors appear in the five Olympic rings, and why those colors.

Sarah closed her eyes. The rings were blue, yellow, black, green, and red, she was sure of that. But the why escaped her, and she could feel Marcus across the table, grinning, waiting for her to fail so he could add it to his collection of evidence that she was all talk. She thought about the opening ceremonies she had actually watched, the part she liked best, the parade where every country came in behind its flag. She had once spent a whole afternoon as a kid hunting for her own country's colors in the rings on a poster in her grandfather's study, tracing them with her finger, and her grandfather had told her the answer then, and she had forgotten it, and now it came back the way forgotten things do, all at once and slightly sideways.

"They picked the colors so every national flag at the time had at least one of them," she said, opening her eyes. "That includes the white background of the rings." She paused. "And it was Pierre de Coubertin who designed them. Nineteen thirteen."

The waitress looked at her card. "That's... that's it exactly. Wow. Okay."

The trucker hat man raised his glass to her from the bar, which felt almost better than the fifty dollars. Almost, because the fifty dollars was real, and when Uncle Theo launched into a peroration about how they should put it toward his nachos debt to Marcus, Sarah held the flyer above her head out of his reach and said the money was going to dessert, split eight ways, and that his debts were his own affair.

"You knew that off the top of your head," Marcus said as the second half started and everyone leaned back toward the screen. "Sports trivia."

"It's not sports trivia. It's flags. There's a difference."

"There's really not."

"You said I care about nothing," Sarah said, keeping her voice light, because they were in public and because she was not sure she wanted the answer anyway. "I care about a French guy in 1913 who wanted every country to see itself in one symbol. That's something."

Marcus considered this while the crowd on screen and the crowd in the restaurant roared at a fumble. "So you're saying you care about, what, symbolism."

"I'm saying I care about the specific argument that you can make something universal without erasing anybody. He didn't pick colors for his country. He picked colors so nobody's country would be left out." She heard herself and laughed a little. "Which might be generous or might just be good design, I honestly can't tell, and I'm not sure it matters which."

"That's the most Sarah sentence ever spoken," Priya said, and stole the last tortilla chip.

The game tightened in the fourth quarter, and the restaurant rose and fell with it, and Sarah found she was standing too, shouting at the screen with her grandmother's hand gripping her arm. She still couldn't have named more than three players. She was still watching. On the wall above the screen somebody had taped up a paper promotion for the Olympics next month, five rings printed small in the corner, and every time the crowd noise dipped she found her eyes drifting to it, white showing between the colors.

With eleven seconds left and the score tied, Marcus leaned over and said, "Double or nothing on dessert. Field goal is good."

"Done," Sarah said, and did not look away from the ball.

Edouard found the letter in the mailbox on a Tuesday, folded into a rectangle and addressed in his sister's slanted handwriting. She was two hours away at college, and she wrote the way she talked, as if she were already halfway out the door. "I failed my first bio exam," the letter said. "Not badly, but enough. I have to retake it Friday and I still don't understand how DNA becomes protein. Mom says you're studying the same thing. Explain it to me in a letter, and don't copy the textbook. Explain it like a farm." She had signed it with the doodle of a crow she'd drawn since she was nine.

The problem was that Edouard did not entirely understand it either. He had a test of his own coming, and a week of August afternoons in which the only work was hauling hay and keeping the noxious ragweed out of the soybean rows before it went to seed. His father believed in learning by hand, and when Edouard complained at supper that he couldn't make the chapter stick, his father set down his fork and said, "Then build it where you can see it. Tomorrow, after the windrow's in, use the garden."

The next afternoon Edouard stood at the end of the vegetable rows with a roll of masking tape, a marker, and his cousin Maya, who had agreed to help because he'd promised her the last of the tomatoes. The garden was a square of tilled earth with stakes at each corner, and Edouard had torn the chapter into a plan the night before, writing things down to externalize what was still a fog in his head. First, he taped a long strip of paper along the fence and wrote on it a sequence of three-letter groups, A's and C's and G's and U's, six of them in a row. "That's the messenger RNA," he said. "The copy of one gene that came off the DNA. Each group of three letters is a codon."

Maya squinted at it. "You mean each little three-letter word matches something?"

"That's what I think. Now you're the other side." He handed her a stack of index cards. On each card he had copied a three-letter group of his own invention and, beneath it, a name: Leucine, Valine, Lysine, Arginine. "Each card is a transfer RNA," he said. "Look, I wrote the amino acid at the bottom. Each one carries exactly one amino acid, and the three letters on top, that's the anticodon." Maya turned a card over, checking for some hidden second amino acid, and found only the smell of marker.

She walked the fence line reading her cards against the taped sequence, trying to match each one. At the third codon she hesitated, holding out a card whose letters didn't line up. "This one has the right amino acid but the wrong letters," she said. "Can I just put it there anyway?"

Edouard started to say yes, because it would finish the row faster, and then stopped. He crouched in the dirt and looked at the two sequences, her card and the tape, letter against letter. "No," he said slowly. "That's the whole point. The anticodon has to pair with the codon, three bases to three bases, or the amino acid doesn't go there. The match is what decides the order." He took the card back and set it aside as a mistake he'd made, a card he'd mislabeled when he copied the chart by lamplight. Maya found the right one, matched it, and laid it under the fence strip, and they went on down the line, card by card, until six amino acids sat in the dust in an order that the tape had dictated and nothing else.

"So the long strip is like the order slip at the grain elevator," Maya said, brushing soil from her knees, "and you're the truck that brings one thing at a time."

"Except the truck checks the slip itself," Edouard said. "The matching is the truck's job, not somebody else's." He was quiet for a moment, watching a cabbage white drift over the kale. He knew the chapter left things out, that he had drawn the cell as a garden fence when it was nothing like a fence, and that somewhere between the letters and the living plant there was a distance he couldn't cross yet. What he had was a shape, honest as far as it went, and he decided he could say that much without pretending further.

That night he wrote back. He described the taped strip along the fence and Maya walking the line with her cards, and he told his sister to imagine the order slip at the elevator, the trucks each carrying one amino acid, each one reading the slip by its own three letters. He wrote that he still couldn't picture how the cell keeps the whole thing from tangling, that some of it stayed dark to him, and that he'd borrowed the garden for it because their father said the mind holds what the hands have walked through. At the bottom, before the crow he'd learned to copy from her letters, he wrote, "If you fail anyway, come home and we'll build it in the dirt together. The tomatoes are almost gone."

He walked out before bed to check the tape was still stapled down against the dew. The garden was silver and still, and the row of cards lay where Maya had left them, each one in its place along the fence, spelling out their small protein into the dark.

Victor had told Theo he was an excellent skater, which was true in the sense that he had once, in seventh grade, completed a full lap without touching the wall. The rink's fluorescent glare found him out within eleven seconds, when his feet performed a decision of their own and deposited him against the boards with a sound like a filing cabinet falling downstairs.

"You said intermediate," Priya said, gliding backward in front of him, hands in her coat pockets, entirely at ease on the ice in a way that seemed almost personal, as though the rink had taken her side.

"Intermediate is a spectrum," Victor said from the floor. "I'm on it."

"Where on it?"

"The floor part of it." He got up, and she laughed, and the laugh did something to his chest that he chose not to examine in front of witnesses.

She had asked him out, actually, which he kept forgetting to be honest with himself about. In his own telling, the whole thing had been his maneuver: the note in AP Gov about her locker sticker for a band he liked, the three days of strategic hovering. The truth, which he set aside the way one sets aside a bill, was that she had turned around in class and said, "You're the one who owns the same shirt as me in a worse color, we should skate sometime," and he had said "Obviously," and then gone into the hallway and stared at a fire extinguisher for a while.

They did laps, halting and smooth respectively. She coached him through crossovers; he expostulated that the wall was closer than it looked, and the wall, his true nemesis on the ice, proved his point by catching his elbow. At the snack bar they split a pretzel the size of a steering wheel and argued about whether the Zamboni driver had a favorite, the way teachers had favorites. "He resurfaces a lane of honor," Priya said. "For people he respects. You'll never see it." Victor said that was virulent propaganda against a man who drove a machine that was basically a giant iron, and she laughed again, and he began to hope the evening was something they would both want to remember in the same direction.

He was careful all night, and proud of the carefulness. He asked before taking her hand on the ice, and when they stood in the parking lot afterward, cold coming up through their shoes, he asked before anything else too, and she said yes, and kissed him briefly, and he floated approximately four inches off the asphalt.

Then, walking toward her car, she slowed. "Okay, so," she said. "I think I'd rather just say goodnight here. I'm kind of done with being touched tonight. Not a verdict on you."

His first impulse was to debate it, and he saw himself doing so, some version of him already opening his mouth to point out that she had kissed him, that the yes had happened, that in the court of Victor's feelings the evidence was overwhelming. He shut that version up. Somewhere in the fog of his own confidence, a fact surfaced from a health assembly he'd half ignored: consent to any intimate contact could be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given. Yes was not a contract. Yes was a weather report, good until it wasn't.

"That's completely fine," he said, and meant it, mostly, and the part of him that didn't was a part he could admit existed without letting it drive.

"You paused," she said, watching him. "That was a good pause. I've seen worse pauses. Some guys treat a kiss like a lease."

"A lease can't be revoked," Victor said. "Consent can. Any time, even after it was given. Which I definitely knew before tonight and did not just assemble from first principles in your parking lot."

"Smooth," she said. "Devastatingly smooth." She unlocked her car, then turned back, keys jingling against her palm. "Same time next week? You can fall down for me again."

"I'll bring a helmet," Victor said. "For the boards. They've been asking for a rematch."

She grinned and got in, and he stood in the cold until her taillights turned out of the lot, then skated the walk home on the frozen patches of sidewalk, badly, gloriously, without falling once.

Cameron sat on the hood of his mother's Corolla with his gown balled behind him like a dropped parachute, watching the lot fill. The ceremony started in forty minutes. Forty minutes, then his name, then a handshake he had been told to practice with a firm grip and a dry hand. He had the grip down. The dry hand was not cooperating.

Dewain came around the corner of the gymnasium at a half-jog, wearing his work polo from the car wash even though it was his day off, holding his phone out in front of him like a compass that had stopped pointing north. "Cam. Cam. You got a minute? Like a real minute."

"I got thirty-eight of them, roughly."

"Then stop looking at the gym." Dewain leaned against the fender, close enough that Cameron could smell the soap they used on the cars, some industrial lemon that never quite washed out of anyone. "I need you to read something. I applied to nineteen places since March. Nineteen. I got two interviews and one shift at the wash, and Marcus says I'm slow there." He pushed the phone into Cameron's hands. On the screen was a job application, half finished, the cursor blinking in an empty box where the highest level of education should go.

Cameron scrolled up. The application was for a warehouse position, full time, benefits after ninety days. "You've been filling these out at the shop?"

"On breaks. On my phone, on the bus, whatever." Dewain wiped his palms on the polo, which did nothing, since the polo was the thing making them damp. "Marcus found a site with the actual numbers. He was reading them off to everybody last week like it was the lottery. Three point nine percent unemployment for people twenty-five and up with a high school diploma. Five point six for people without one." He said it flat, the way you recite something you have checked twice. "So it's like one and a half times harder, roughly, before anybody even looks at what you can do."

"You're not twenty-five yet," Cameron said, because it was true and because he wanted to say something that was not the other thing, the thing about the empty box.

"No, but that's the road, right? That's where it goes." Dewain tapped the screen. "So the box. What do I put? I'm not a liar. I'm not going to write something I'm not."

The lot was filling with parents in ironed shirts, with toddlers in strollers being positioned for photos against the gym's brick wall. Somewhere inside, Cameron's row was forming, alphabetical, the C's near the front, near where his mother would be pointing her phone. He had wanted this morning to be clean. He had imagined it, in fact, the night before: him in line, everything decided, the next four years already paid for in deposits and orientation fees, a road with the guardrails installed. Dewain's road had no guardrails. Dewain's road was nineteen applications and a blinking cursor.

His grandfather had an adage about this, something about how you don't fix a man's roof while your own is leaking, but his grandfather had also skipped his own graduation to work a shift, and Cameron had never known what to do with that information except carry it.

"Okay," Cameron said. "Here's what I actually think. The diploma is worth something real, that's not a story people tell you, the numbers say it. But you're not standing at that fork. You're standing where you're standing." He typed the word Some into the box, deleted it, typed partial, deleted that too. "What if we do this. You put the truth in, but we make the rest of the thing so good they can't stop at the box. Every job you've actually done, every car you've detailed, the register you ran when Marcus was out sick. We write it like you mean it."

"You're going to miss your line-up."

"I've got thirty-one minutes." Cameron pulled out his own phone and opened a notes file, and for a while the two of them worked in the shade of the Corolla, Cameron typing while Dewain talked, suturing the pieces of the application together: the summer at his uncle's shop, the forklift video course he'd half finished, the two interviews, what they had asked, what he'd wished he'd said. A woman in heels hurried past and called something cheerful at them, and Dewain waved without looking up.

When they finished, Cameron read the whole application back to him out loud, and Dewain listened with his eyes closed like it was a letter from someone far away. "That sounds like a person," Dewain said. "That sounds like a person who does things."

"That's because it is one." Cameron pressed submit. The confirmation screen came up, gray and bureaucratic, and Dewain exhaled the way people exhale at the end of a held breath, long and involuntary.

A horn honked near the entrance. Cameron stood, pulled the gown from the hood, shook it out. "I have to go. But listen. That's one application done the way it should be done. There are going to be more, and they should all be like that."

"So you'll help me over the summer?"

Cameron looked at the gym doors, at the line of gowns disappearing inside them, and at Dewain, who was already gathering up both phones to sort which was whose. His roommate assignment came in August. His orientation was in July. The summer was a space he had been quietly planning to fill with things that had no room for the smell of industrial lemon, and he knew it, and Dewain probably knew it too.

"Send me the links," Cameron said. "Every one."

Dewain held up his phone and took a picture of him in the gown, the parking lot behind him full, the gym doors open. "Go on, then," he said. "Walk."

The presentation was due Thursday, and Maya still had not sent the slides. Jessica checked her phone under the lab table while Mr. Okafor wrote the phases of carbon on the board, and when she looked up, the word allotrope was circled twice. Graphite and diamond, same element, different arrangement. She copied it into her notes without thinking about it, then checked her phone again.

Maya sat two rows over, laughing at something Priya had whispered. That was the thing about Maya; she was easy to like and impossible to pin down. On Monday she had promised the slides by Tuesday night. On Tuesday she had promised them Wednesday morning. It was now Wednesday, fourth period, and Jessica had forty percent of a presentation and a stomach that felt like a clenched fist.

After class she cornered Maya by the water fountain. "The slides," she said.

"They're basically done," Maya said. "I just have to polish them."

"You said that yesterday."

"God. Relax." Maya filled her bottle and walked off, and Jessica stood there holding the sentence she had not said, the one that went you ruined the whole thing, which was not even true, and which she knew would make Maya defensive for the rest of the week.

That night Jessica did what she always did when she could not solve something: she searched it. Feedback without fighting. How to tell someone they let you down. She found a page about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon who had promoted something called I-messages back in the 1960s, a way to raise a problem without blaming. Instead of you ruined it, you said what happened to you. I felt stuck when the slides came in late. She read it twice, then opened her notebook and practiced, writing versions the way she would practice a French verb. I felt. When. Not you always, not you never. She felt ridiculous doing it, and she also noticed that the sentences she wrote were harder to argue with, because they were only about her.

The next morning she found Maya at her locker before first bell. "Can I say something?" Jessica asked. "I felt stuck when the slides came in late, because I couldn't practice my part, and the presentation is worth a quarter of our grade."

Maya shut her locker. For a second Jessica thought she was going to laugh, and the second stretched long enough that Jessica's ears went hot.

"I kept redoing the graphite part," Maya said finally. "It looked ugly. I didn't want to hand you something ugly." She pulled out her phone, opened the file, and turned the screen around. The slides were done, all twelve of them, and the graphite diagram was redrawn in colors Jessica hadn't known Maya could use. "I was going to send them tonight. After fixing one more thing."

"You could have sent the ugly version."

"I know." Maya zipped her bag. "I guess I thought you'd just think I was flaky."

Jessica recognized the logic, because she had a version of it herself. She tended to valorize effort that nobody could see, hoarding work until it was perfect and then presenting it as if it had cost nothing. Maya did the same thing with slides. Two allotropes of the same fear, she thought, and almost said it out loud, and decided Maya would just look at her blankly, so she kept it.

They presented on Thursday. Mr. Okafor, famously irascible about students who read off the screen, leaned back with his arms crossed and stayed that way through the first four slides, which Maya had built around images instead of paragraphs. When Jessica explained why the same carbon made both pencil lead and diamonds, he uncrossed his arms. Afterward he wrote something on his clipboard and did not tell either of them what.

In the hallway Maya said, "So that thing you did. At my locker. Did you rehearse that?"

"Maybe," Jessica said.

Weirdo," Maya said, and grinned, and pushed through the doors to the bus loop.

The community kitchen on Delancey smelled like Thursday, which meant day-old bread warming in the industrial ovens and bleach from the mop bucket someone had left in the corner. Cohen had the big stainless island to himself for once, six chicken thighs laid out on a cutting board, a pot of rice waiting, his mother's spice tin open beside the sink. She was working the late shift at the hospital, his father was two states away on a job, and so dinner for him and his sister had become his job, and he had decided, walking over, that he would do it properly.

He turned the tap on cold, the way his grandmother did every Sunday of his childhood, holding each thigh under the stream while the water hissed and jumped off the pink skin.

"Stop." Priya was eleven and standing on a milk crate to reach the counter, holding his phone out to him like evidence. "Stop, stop, stop."

"What."

"Mom texted." She read off the screen instead of handing it over. "Cohen. Do NOT rinse the chicken. I know Nani always did. CDC says no. Splashing water spreads bacteria all over the sink and counters. I mean it. Use paper towel." Priya looked up. "That was nine minutes ago. She saw your story about cooking tonight."

He kept his hands under the tap a second longer, out of some stubbornness he didn't have a better name for, then shut it off. The water had gone everywhere. He could see the fine spray on the faucet, on the rim of the spice tin, on the handle of the pot.

"How would she even know I was washing it."

"Because you always do. And she always yells. You just never did it where she could see."

He stood there with wet hands and thought about his grandmother, who had cooked for forty people at the temple without ever making anyone sick, as far as anyone said, and who had held chicken under running water with the certainty of a virtuoso, wrist turning each piece at exactly the right angle, no splash escaping her. She was not a careless woman. She had raised him half the time. And now a text message was telling him she'd been doing it wrong, or at least that the government thought so, which was not the same thing, and he couldn't ask her because she had been dead since March.

"Paper towel," he said, mostly to himself. He blotted the thighs dry, one by one, and the towel came away faintly pink, and he threw it in the trash and washed his hands with soap for as long as the hot water took to arrive.

Priya watched him wipe down the whole sink, the faucet, the spice tin, the pot handle, and then wipe the counter again because he had set the towel on it in between. "You're being weird," she said.

"I'm being careful. There's a difference."

"What's the difference."

He didn't answer right away. He salted the chicken, laid it skin-down in the pan his grandmother would have recognized, a wide black skillet that had come from her kitchen and still held a shadow of turmeric in its corners. The fat began to crackle. "The difference is," he said, "she was doing the best she knew how. And now I know something different. That doesn't make her stupid and it doesn't make the CDC stupid. It just means I do it this way now."

"So you're smarter than Nani."

"Nobody's smarter than Nani." He pointed the spatula at the crate. "Get down and make the salad."

She climbed down but didn't go to the fridge. She leaned on the island with her arms folded, the way she did when she was working something out and wanted company while doing it. "If she was wrong about the chicken, what else was she wrong about?"

The rice came to a boil behind him and he turned it down, slid the lid halfway, thought about the question while the steam sublimated off the edge of the pot in a thin white ribbon and vanished. His grandmother had also believed that you should never cook angry, that lentils needed a whisper of asafetida, that a guest who left hungry would carry your bad luck home. Some of that he kept and some of it he would probably let go without ever deciding to, the way you lose things you never meant to lose.

"I don't know," he said. "Some stuff, probably. I still think her chicken was the best chicken anybody ever made."

"So how come you're not washing it."

"Because the water splashes," he said. He flipped a thigh; the skin had gone gold and friable where it hit the pan, and it came up with a crisp sound that made Priya stop sulking and look over. "Because the CDC says not to, and splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and the counters, and I already did it, so now I get to clean everything twice. Because Mom's working a double and she still texted you about chicken, which means she's thinking about us at nine at night while somebody's vomiting in a bedpan." He heard his own voice get too loud on the last word and pulled it back. "Pick one. They're all true."

Priya went and got the lettuce. She tore it into the bowl the way their grandmother had taught her, no knife, hands only, and she didn't say anything else until the salad was done and the chicken was resting on a plate under foil and the rice had gone quiet.

At home they set the table with two plates and their mother's empty spot facing the door. Cohen texted her a picture of the pan. She replied with three thumbs-up and then, a minute later, a fourth one on its own.

"She's proud of you," Priya said, chewing.

"She's proud of chicken." He put the last thigh on his sister's plate, skin side up, where it gleamed.

"Nani would've washed it," Priya said.

"Yeah," Cohen said, and picked up his fork.

The elevator in the Blakely Arms smelled like wet cardboard and broke somewhere between the third and fourth floor every other day, so Audrey took the stairs, counting them out of habit, the way she used to count the steps to Marisol's porch. The movers had left her boxes in the living room in a tower that leaned slightly, and her mother was already at the new job, so it was Audrey alone who carried her desk lamp up six flights and set it on the windowsill facing the airshaft. From that window she could see a strip of the school three blocks off, the flagpole, the flat roof of the gymnasium. At the old house the window had faced Marisol's window, and they had signaled each other with flashlight beams after their mothers declared lights-out, one flash for hello, two for come outside.

School started on a Tuesday. In homeroom the teacher, a narrow man named Mr. Kestler whom the other students called a pedagogue in a tone that was not entirely affectionate, assigned Audrey a seat beside a girl named Priya Raghunathan. Priya lent her a pen without being asked and told her which stairwell avoided the crowd, and Audrey decided by Wednesday that Priya was the kind of person she would have been friends with already in the old town, which was a thought she kept to herself because it felt like a betrayal of somebody, though she could not have said of whom.

At night the apartment made noises the old house had not made. Pipes ticked, and a neighbor's television rose through the floor in muffled syllables. Audrey lay awake and found herself conducting an inventory she was ashamed of: the burr of her father's voice through the dining room wall, the lemon smell of Mrs. Ferreira's cleaning fluid on the shared stairwell, the particular slant of afternoon light across the biology lab where she and Marisol had dissected a fetal pig and laughed until Ms. Danner separated their stations. She was sixteen and in an apartment forty minutes from everything, and she missed a cleaning fluid. She resolved not to say this to anyone.

In the second week, in the cafeteria, Priya pushed her tray across from Audrey's without asking and sat down. Audrey had been looking at her phone, at a photograph Marisol had sent of the homecoming banner going up in the gymnasium, and she shut the screen off quickly, but Priya had seen it. "That's your old school," Priya said. It was not a question.

"My friend Marisol. They're decorating for homecoming." Audrey folded her napkin into smaller and smaller squares. "It's stupid. I've been here two weeks and I keep wanting to be back there, and it's only forty minutes. People commute farther than that for fun."

"Nobody talks about it here," Priya said, "but I looked it up when we moved, my sister's first year at college. The research on homesickness says nearly everyone who's away from home misses something about it. Almost everybody. Not just the weird kids. And it said around twenty percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of some severity scale." She stabbed a piece of broccoli. "So a fifth of them have it bad, and the rest still have it some. I found that out the week we moved here, and it made me feel less like a failure."

Audrey turned this over. She had been thinking of homesickness as a private defect, something to be subsumed under the general project of Starting Over, the way her mother had put it, new town, new chapter, as though the missing could be filed into a folder and the folder closed. If nearly everyone missed something, then the missing was not a failure of adaptation. It was closer to a tax everyone paid. But the severity scale bothered her, because twenty percent meant four out of five rated theirs below the midpoint, and Audrey had no idea where she fell on such a scale, and she suspected she fell higher than she wanted to admit.

That night she called Marisol. The connection was thin, and Marisol was halfway through a story about Danny Okafor and the banner committee, and Audrey listened and laughed in the right places, and when the story ended there was a pause in which the old signal system would have been useful, one flash for hello, two for come outside. "I miss it," Audrey said finally. "I miss you." Marisol said, "Obviously, you dork, it's been two weeks," and told her about the float, and the conversation moved on, and Audrey lay awake afterward and understood something she could not yet put in words: that missing was not the same as wanting to return, and that both were real, and that the two did not cancel out. She could be glad the apartment had a doorknob lock her mother let her use, and glad Priya existed, and still lie awake inventorying lemon smells. She did not know whether that was resilience or just confusion. She was honest with herself about not knowing.

The next Saturday the building had a tag sale in the courtyard, folding tables carried down by residents of all six floors. Audrey's mother contributed a lamp, a penurious contribution to the communal effort that the woman from 4C noted aloud with a short laugh, though the lamp sold within the hour for four dollars. Priya appeared with her younger brother and forty minutes of the afternoon to spend, and they walked the tables, and Audrey bought a chipped ceramic bowl with a blue rim for fifty cents because it was the exact blue of the old kitchen.

They took the bowl up the six flights, stopping on the third-floor landing where the afternoon light came through the stairwell window at a slant, and stood there a moment, both of them looking at it. "My sister says it gets quieter in your head after a month or two," Priya said. "Not gone. Just quieter."

"That's fine," Audrey said. "I don't need it gone."

She set the bowl on the windowsill beside the lamp, where it would catch whatever light the airshaft allowed, and went back down for the last box.

Charles set his work boots under his chair before he sat down, and his mother put the lasagna in the middle of the table without comment, which meant she had something to say and was waiting for an opening. He served himself first because his father always did, and because his father liked it when he did.

"Long shift," his father said. It was not a question.

"Nine and a half hours. We're stocking the new warehouse aisle before the Fourth sale." Charles cut into the lasagna. "Dana stayed late too. Rob left at five on the dot."

His mother passed the salad. "Are those the two you told your uncle about? The ones arguing?"

"Still arguing." Charles had described it to his uncle on the phone Sunday, and now the whole household treated it as a running story. "Dana transferred from Michigan in March. Rob's from Alabama. Dana fills out a dues card her first week, like it's nothing. Rob tells her she's crazy. Says nobody can make him pay a cent to the union if he doesn't want to."

"And can they?" his father asked. "Make him?"

"That's the fight." Charles pushed sauce around his plate. "Dana says yes, Rob says no, and the weird thing is they're both right. About themselves, I mean. Not about each other."

His father set down his fork. "How does that work?"

Charles had worked out how to explain it only on the drive home, talking to himself with the radio off, and he gave it in that order. "The union's still in. We voted it in two years ago, before I got hired. It's the local at the distribution center, everybody on the floor's under the contract. Wages, the overtime after eight hours, the breaks, all of that's in the contract. But the dues are the fight. Dana had to pay dues at her old job in Michigan, so she figures it's the same everywhere. Rob never paid dues in Alabama and figures Michigan people are suckers."

"So who's right?" his sister Ellen asked. She was fifteen and asked questions mostly to keep the table moving.

"Depends on the state." Charles had looked it up on his break, sitting on a stack of pallets with his phone, because he couldn't stand not knowing. "There's this federal law, the Taft-Hartley Act, 1947. Congress passed it over President Truman's veto. It let the states pass what they call right-to-work laws. Those ban contracts that make workers pay union fees."

"Michigan's not one of those states?" his father said.

"Michigan's not. Alabama is. So Dana's used to a contract where paying is required, and Rob's used to one where it isn't, and neither of them knows the state line is what changed." Charles took a bite. The lasagna was good and he had been hungry since four o'clock.

His mother reached for his plate and put more on it without asking. "And there," she said. "Which one is this?"

"Right-to-work." He said it plainly. "So Rob can't be forced to pay. But Dana's from a state where they can make you."

"Then why would anyone pay?" Ellen said.

"Dana says everybody benefits from the contract. The wage scale, the safety stuff, the overtime rules. Rob gets all that without paying, and he says that's the smart move. Dana calls it freeloading." Charles shrugged. "I listened to them for three days. Rob's not stupid. He's got a kid and a car payment, and fourteen dollars a month is fourteen dollars. Dana's not stupid either. She says the contract didn't fall out of the sky, that people before her paid in, and if everyone did what Rob does there'd be nothing left to freeload off of."

His father was quiet for a moment, working through it. "The breaks you get. The overtime after eight."

"I get them either way," Charles said. "That's the part that sits wrong with me, honestly. Rob and I do the same job. He keeps the extra fourteen dollars and I don't have to pay either, but if Dana's the only one paying, then she's carrying it. And if nobody pays, I don't know what happens to the contract. Nobody at the table knows."

"You could ask," his mother said.

"I did ask the steward today. He said the local's been losing checkoffs since the plant opened, people transferring in from right-to-work states who never sign. He didn't have a number. He just said it's slower than it used to be." Charles looked at his plate. He had signed nothing yet. The steward had left a card in his locker on Monday and it was still there, blank, under his jacket.

"Are you going to sign it?" Ellen asked.

"I don't know. Rob's right that the money's real. Dana's right that the contract's real. I keep going back and forth on the drive home." He picked up his fork. "Maybe I'll decide tomorrow."

His father poured more water into Charles's glass, as though filling it settled something, and the screen door banged in the kitchen where the dog had pushed through it.

The cursor blinked in the signature field, which was not really a field at all but a button that said "I Agree," and Audrey sat with her finger over the trackpad, not clicking it. The job was at Hollis Books, seasonal, twelve hours a week, and the agreement had scrolled past her in a gray column of text that she had, for the first time in her life, actually read. There were sections on liability and on non-solicitation of customers, which she gathered meant she could not open a competing bookstore out of her bedroom, and a paragraph about binding arbitration that she read three times and understood less each time.

Her mother came through the kitchen doorway with a towel over her shoulder. "You're not signing anything yet."

"It's a job, Mom. It's a good thing."

"On a screen? You click a button and that's a signature? That doesn't count. They need you to sign something. With a pen." Her mother said "pen" the way other people said "under oath."

Audrey rotated her chair. "I think it counts."

"You think."

"I'll check," Audrey said, which was, in her household, the polite form of "you're wrong," and she turned back to the screen and typed into the search bar: does clicking agree count as a signature. Her mother dried a plate with the slow deliberateness of someone waiting to be proven right.

The results came up in the usual jumble, law firm pages with stock photos of confident people shaking hands, and then a government page, plain and beige, about something called the ESIGN Act. Audrey read it twice. The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, said a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form. She sat back. Her mother had been assuming the opposite, that paper was the real thing and the screen was a toy, and the law had settled the question the other way before Audrey was old enough to have a question. She felt the incipient satisfaction of a person about to win an argument, and also, beneath it, something less comfortable, because if the click was real, then the gray column of text she had scrolled through was real too.

"Mom," she called. "The ESIGN Act. It says a signature can't be denied legal effect just because it's electronic. It's from 2000."

Her mother appeared in the doorway again, towel still on her shoulder. "So it counts."

"It counts."

"Huh." Her mother absorbed this with visible effort, the way she absorbed the fact that the car could parallel park itself. "So when you clicked accept on all those apps."

"I was twelve. Different problem."

Her mother went back to the dishes, and Audrey turned to the screen and did not click the button. That was the part her mother hadn't asked about and Audrey hadn't volunteered: the reading of it. Before, clicking "I Agree" had been a reflex, like blinking. Now she understood it as a signature, and a signature, her father liked to say, was an epigram you wrote with your name, a small compressed promise. His actual line was "a signature is the shortest essay you'll ever write," which Audrey had found embarrassing at eleven and accurate at seventeen. The arbitration clause bothered her. It said disputes would be resolved individually, not in court, and though she could not have explained the whole machinery of it, she understood that she was agreeing to give something up, silently, in advance.

She opened her email and wrote to the store's manager, a woman named Petra whose replies came in a bright green font. Audrey asked, in the most unhurried language she could manage, whether the arbitration provision was standard or negotiable, and whether she could be sent the terms as a document she could look at properly instead of scrolling through in a window designed, she suspected, to catalyze exactly the kind of skimming she had nearly done. She reread the email four times, deleted the word "superfluous," and sent it.

Petra answered within the hour, green font and all: totally fine, most people don't ask, here's a PDF, and also, if it helps, you can come in Saturday and sign the paper version, we keep copies in the back. Audrey printed the PDF, all nine pages, and spread them on the kitchen table, and her mother paused over them on her way with the laundry. "See," her mother said, tapping the signature line at the end. "Paper. Now it's real."

"It was already real, Mom. 2000."

Her mother frowned at the pages, then at Audrey, and seemed about to retreat, but instead she pulled out the chair across from her and sat down, which she almost never did in the middle of a chore. "What's all this then, if it was already real."

Audrey slid the arbitration section across the table. "That's the part I'm not sure about."

Her mother read it, lips moving slightly, a woman who signed things for a living, payroll forms and permission slips and the mortgage, and who had never once been asked what any of it meant. She looked up. "You're going in Saturday anyway?"

"To sign the paper one, yeah. Petra offered."

Her mother tapped the page once more, gently now, like patting something alive. "Take a pen from the drawer," she said. "The good one."

The pump at the community garden broke on the first Saturday of June, and by noon the okra leaves had gone soft at the edges, folding like hands. Jonathan had been coming since April to earn the last service hours his school required, but he kept coming after the hours ran out, and he could not have said exactly why. Maybe because Ms. Reyes, who ran the garden, had once let him take home a tomato still warm from the fence line, and the taste of it had enthralled him in a way that no grocery-store tomato ever had, a sweetness with something almost bitter underneath.

Now he stood at the pump with Ravi, a community college student who interned there on Saturdays, while the two of them listened to the motor grind and deliver nothing. "The city raised the water rate in March," Ravi said. "Half the gardens on this side of town turned their plots to gravel. Ms. Reyes is paying out of her own pocket." He wiped his hands on his jeans. "There's a meeting Thursday about a new hookup. Somebody's offering free water."

"Free water doesn't exist," Jonathan said, because his father said that about nothing being free, and his father was usually right in ways that took years to see.

The meeting was held under the tin-roofed pavilion, and it was there that Jonathan learned where the free water came from. A man in a golf shirt explained that a bottling company two blocks north was offering runoff from its filtration system, enough to fill the tanks twice a week, in exchange for a small thing: the garden would sign a letter supporting the company's permit application to take more water from the aquifer. "It's a win-win," the man said. "You get water. They get goodwill."

Ms. Reyes said nothing, which Jonathan had learned was her way of saying a great deal. An older man named Fitz, who grew collards on the corner plot, said the aquifer was already dropping; his well at home had gone sour with sulfur the summer before. The man in the golf shirt smiled and said the aquifer was a big system, complicated, and that one permit would hardly matter.

That night Jonathan typed "aquifer depletion" into his laptop and followed a thread he had not expected. It led him to the Aral Sea. He read the sentence three times: the Soviet Union had diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea had lost a fishing industry that had once employed about 40,000 people. Rivers sent elsewhere to grow one thing; a sea dying downstream; forty thousand people whose work simply evaporated. He thought about the bottling plant two blocks north, and the gardens south of it, and Fitz's sulfur well, and he understood that he was not reading history. He was reading a template.

The next Saturday, a group of tenth graders arrived for a field lesson, part of some school partnership, and Ravi put Jonathan in charge of the irrigation demo while he fixed the pump line. Jonathan showed them the drip tape, the timers, the rain barrels. Then a girl named Priya asked why the garden couldn't just take the free water, and Jonathan told them about the Aral Sea. "Somebody upstream got water for cotton," he said, "and the people downstream lost the sea." He pointed at the tanks. "The plant is upstream. We're downstream, until somebody else is downstream of us."

"Is that like a rule?" Priya asked.

"It's more like a heuristic," Jonathan said. "A shortcut for thinking. When somebody offers you water, ask who ends up with less."

Priya nodded slowly, and then she said the thing that turned the whole afternoon sideways. "My dad works at the plant," she said. "If they don't get the permit, he gets laid off in the fall. He told my mom last week." She looked at the okra, at the drip tape, at her shoes. "Forty thousand people somewhere. My dad here."

Jonathan had been building an argument all week, and now it stood in front of him in a polo shirt with a father. He thought of a day years ago, before the garden existed, when he and his own father had walked past this same corner and his father had called it a wasteland, and Jonathan, ten years old, had found a milkweed growing through the chain-link and had carried the seed pod home in his fist. Even then something in him had believed that a place could change. Now he was less sure whether belief was a heuristic too, and whether heuristics were honest or just comforting.

He thought about it the way his economics teacher had taught him to hold two ideas at once: the garden needed water to live; the plant's workers needed the permit to live; both of those things could be true, and the permit could still take water from someone further down the line whom no one at the meeting would ever meet. He could oppose the letter and feel clean, or support it and feel useful, and neither position covered the whole cost.

Thursday evening, at the second meeting, Ms. Reyes called for a vote. The pavilion was full, Fitz on one side and the man in the golf shirt on the other, and Priya's father stood quietly by the ice chest, a man with calluses Jonathan recognized because his own father had them too. Ms. Reyes looked around the circle and said, "Jonathan, you've been here every week. What do you think?"

Jonathan stood up. Outside, the drip tape he had repaired that morning was releasing its slow bright beads onto the okra, each one catching the last of the light before it disappeared into the dirt.

The folding chairs in the middle school gymnasium had been arranged in crooked rows, and Layla took one near the end, where she could see both the podium and the door. She had come because of the 6:40 bus, the one that had carried her brother Tariq to his job at the greenhouse until the transit authority cut the route in March. She had a speech drafted in her notebook, three paragraphs she had rewritten four times, and a plan to read it during public comment. What she did not have was any clear idea whether a speech at a town hall could become anything more than a speech.

The state senator, Marisol Reyes, opened with a recap of House Bill 214, which would fund rural and small-town transit by redirecting a slice of the state gas tax. She walked them through it the way a jeweler turns a stone. A constituent group had drafted the bill first, she said, with help from a legislative lawyer, and a sponsor had introduced it, and the transportation committee had held hearings in April, taking testimony from riders and drivers and county engineers. The committee had amended it twice, narrowing the funding formula, before voting it out on a nine-to-four tally. Then it had gone to the House floor, where members debated it for two days, and it had passed, barely, with the speaker gaveling through the last objection. Now it was in the Senate, where a committee had just begun its own review, and nothing was guaranteed, because each chamber worked from its own copy of the same bill.

A man in the front row, saturnine in a gray windbreaker, arms crossed the whole time, said the whole thing was theater. "You pass it, the governor line-item vetoes it, we're back at nothing," he said. Senator Reyes didn't flinch. She said the governor's office had signaled cautious openness, which wasn't assent but wasn't opposition either, and that if both chambers passed identical language the bill would reach the governor's desk by June. "After that, the governor signs it, or lets it become law without a signature, or vetoes it," she said. "That's the last gate, and I won't pretend I control it."

During the comment period, a senior from Layla's school named Priya stood up with her phone in her hand. She was there for a civics project, she admitted, and she said she had spent the weekend on a question she couldn't shake. "Last year in the U.S. Senate, a bill had fifty-five supporters, and it still failed," Priya said. "Fifty-five is more than half. It's a majority. Why did it die?"

The gym went quiet in the way rooms do when nobody wants to be the one who answers. Layla felt the question land in her own head and start turning. She knew there was such a thing as a filibuster, or thought she did, mostly from a movie her father liked where a senator talked all night. But the number fifty-five nagged at her. If it took a majority to pass a bill, and a majority wasn't enough to end debate, then debate was the thing that mattered. She pulled out her notebook and wrote, debate is separate from voting, then crossed out separate and wrote, before.

Beside her, an older woman wearing a transit union pin leaned over. "Cloture," the woman said quietly, as if confirming something Layla had nearly remembered. "That's what ending debate is called."

Layla wrote the word down. Ending debate required more than passing the bill did, and she worked the arithmetic in the margin the way she did stoichiometry, converting one thing into another. Fifty-five supporters out of a hundred was fifty-five percent. To end debate you needed more than that. She tried two-thirds and got sixty-seven, which seemed too high, and then she thought about three-fifths, which was sixty percent, which was sixty votes when all hundred seats were filled. Since 1975, the woman beside her murmured, checking her pin as if it held the date, cloture had required three-fifths. Layla looked at her notebook: fifty-five for the bill, sixty to end debate, five votes short of even being allowed to finish. The bill hadn't lost on substance. It had lost on a threshold.

When her turn came, she stood with the notebook shaking slightly in her hand. Her drafted speech suddenly seemed too small, a local complaint beside a national arithmetic. She read the first paragraph anyway, about Tariq walking four miles on Sundays because the replacement shuttle didn't run weekends, about the greenhouse manager saying she'd lost two workers to the cut. Then she set the notebook down on the chair. "I used to think a bill failed because people voted no," she said. "I learned tonight it can fail because it never got to a final vote. And I think HB 214 could fail that way too, in our Senate, if we assume a majority is enough. So I'm asking what the vote count actually is, and who the swing votes are, and what riders like my brother can do besides telling their stories."

Senator Reyes said the count was fluid, that the committee chairman was a farm-district senator whose district had lost two routes of its own, and that testimony like Layla's was exactly what made a chairman's mind fluid. "You've adumbrated the fight better than my caucus memo did," she said, and a few people laughed, warmly. She asked Layla to send the written version to her office so it could go into the committee record, which was, she noted, a thing that actually existed, a binder a senator could point to.

That night Layla sat on her bed and typed a message to Priya, then deleted it twice before sending the version she meant.

You asked the question that made this whole night make sense to me. I did the math: to end debate in the U.S. Senate you need three-fifths of senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled, and since 1975 that's been the rule. That's why 55 supporters wasn't enough, five votes short of even getting to a final vote. I used to think majority rules, period. Now I think majority rules sometimes, and other times you need a supermajority just to move. What I still don't know is whether that's a flaw or a feature, honestly, and I'm not going to pretend I settled it in a gymnasium. Come to the Senate committee hearing with me in May? We can count votes in person.

She attached the speech, addressed an email to the senator's office, and pressed send. Down the hall, Tariq's alarm went off for the early shift, and Layla heard him feel along the wall for the light switch.

Antoine arrived at the Gateway Cinema twenty minutes early, which he understood immediately to be a mistake, because it left him nothing to do but stand under the marquee rehearsing the opening line he'd already planned: something about how he'd never actually seen Jaws on a big screen. The showing had been Priya's suggestion, sent in a text he had read eleven times, and he had agreed with a speed he later regretted, since eagerness, his older sister insisted, was legible from across a room. He bought the tickets anyway, both of them, an act that felt munificent in the moment and miserly in retrospect, depending on which of his two competing theories of dating he let win.

The first theory he'd absorbed from his cousin Marcus, who held that a first date was a performance to be survived, every silence a deduction, every stumble a permanent record. The second theory he'd gotten from a podcast he'd half-listened to while mowing the lawn in June, something about a psychologist, Erica Boothby, who'd published a study in 2018 on what happened after people talked for the first time. The host had said the finding out loud and then laughed about it, and Antoine had laughed too, alone with the mower, and then forgotten it until this exact moment, standing under the marquee with two tickets going damp in his hand.

Priya arrived at four minutes past seven, waving from across the parking lot in a way that erased, temporarily, both theories. "I'm so sorry, my mom needed me to carry the recycling bins, and then she needed to tell me a whole story about the recycling bins," she said. "Did you already get tickets? You didn't have to do that."

"It was nothing," he said, which was casuistry of the most ordinary kind, since it had been something, and he had wanted it to be something, and he handed one over before she could reach for her wallet.

They found seats in the middle of the tenth row, and the pre-movie silence between them was not the silence he had feared. She asked whether he'd seen it before; he deployed his opening line about the big screen; she said she'd seen it exactly once, at her grandmother's house, with commercials, and that her grandmother had talked through the entire shark. "Like the shark could hear her," Priya said. "Like she was negotiating with it." Antoine laughed harder than the joke strictly required, and she looked pleased, or he thought she looked pleased, and there was the trouble, right there, the whole machinery of guessing.

The movie itself did the work for a while. He let himself watch her more than the screen, in glances he tried to make untraceable: how she leaned forward during the opening night swim, how she whispered "oh no" at the puppy on the beach, how she clutched the armrest during the Orca's descent and then, without ceremony, let her hand drift the last two inches until it rested beside his. He moved his own hand toward it the way you approach a horse. She did not withdraw. Their smallest fingers overlapped for the last forty minutes of the film, and neither of them said anything about it, and neither of them moved, and Antoine understood that this was the subtext doing what subtext does, carrying a conversation neither of them would risk out loud.

It was afterward, in the parking lot under the sodium lights, that the first theory staged its counterattack. She'd checked her phone twice during the credits. She'd said "that was so fun" in a tone he now replayed as obligatory. She'd hugged him quickly, a hug with air in it. Marcus's voice returned with a full inventory: the joke he'd fumbled about the mayor, the moment he'd talked too long about his community college schedule, the terrible stretch where he'd explained the ending of another movie she hadn't seen. Walking home along Center Street, he assembled the case against himself with a prosecutor's care, and by the time he reached the bridge over the creek he had almost convicted them both, himself for his performance and her for having to sit through it.

Then the podcast surfaced, whole this time, the way forgotten things do. A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and her colleagues. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. He stopped on the bridge and pulled out his phone and searched for it, because he no longer trusted his memory of a June afternoon, and there it was, the finding exactly as the host had said it, and it beguiled him, honestly, the idea that the ledger in his head might be wrong in one consistent direction, that everyone walking home from everyone else's first date was doing this same arithmetic and getting the same pessimistic answer. Not a guarantee about Priya. A tendency about people. He let the two theories stand side by side on the bridge and found, for once, that he didn't have to pick.

He typed and deleted three drafts of a text. The fourth was only: "hand was cold, that's my excuse, what's yours." He put the phone in his pocket and walked the last three blocks without checking it, which cost him something, and then stood in his driveway in the dark, where the phone buzzed once against his leg. He looked at the lit kitchen window, then down at his pocket, then at the window again, his thumb already moving.

Gavin crouched on the oil-stained concrete of his uncle's garage, holding a stopwatch he had won at a yard sale and did not entirely trust. The ball launcher, built from PVC pipe and a garage-door spring, pointed at the far wall, where he had taped a measuring tape along the baseboard.

"We need thirty feet by Saturday," Priya said from the workbench, where she was stripping wire with her teeth because the pliers had vanished two weeks ago and neither of them would admit to losing them. "Marcus's team hit twenty-eight on Monday."

"Then we angle it higher." Gavin cranked the barrel up to sixty degrees. "More height, more hang time, more distance."

"That's not how it works."

"It's how it feels like it works."

She came over and stood beside him with her arms crossed, radiating the particular patience of someone who had already done the reading. He fired anyway. The ball climbed, hung, and dropped eleven feet short of his last attempt. The garage smelled like rubber and cold coffee, and somewhere behind the water heater a cricket had been living rent-free since August.

"Congratulations," Priya said. "You've incapacitated your own launcher. It can only go up now. You've turned artillery into a fountain."

He lowered the barrel in increments, firing after each change, and the numbers on the tape told a story his intuition had refused to write. At sixty degrees the ball landed at nineteen feet. At fifty-five, twenty-two. At fifty, twenty-five and change. He kept going, expecting the pattern to collapse, and at forty-five degrees the ball sailed past all its predecessors and bounced off the far wall with a sound like a knuckle on a door. Twenty-nine feet, and that was with the wall in the way.

"Forty-five," he said, mostly to himself.

"Forty-five," she agreed, and wrote it on the back of her hand. "On level ground. Which the gym floor will be, thank God, because if Mr. Okafor made us launch off the bleachers I'd transfer schools."

Gavin sat back on his heels and looked at the tape measure, then at the barrel, then at the notebook where he'd been scribbling. The physics textbook was open on the workbench to a page he'd read four times, the one about splitting a launch into horizontal and vertical components, treating each as its own little problem. He'd understood the words separately the way you can know every ingredient of a cake and still burn it. Now the tape measure had done something the page hadn't. The ball's speed got divided between going far and going high, and every degree past forty-five bought height it paid for out of distance, while every degree below bought speed it paid for out of flight time. Forty-five was the split where neither account was robbed.

"It's not that complicated," Priya said, watching his face. "You're making the face you make when you think you've discovered fire."

"I'm making the face of a putative genius who has just learned he's three hundred and seventy years late." He tapped the textbook. "It was in the assigned reading. I read it. It didn't take."

"So the lesson is do the homework."

"The lesson is fire the homework and measure everything." He stood, brushed concrete dust off his knees, and reset the angle to forty-five exactly, checking it twice against the protractor taped to the hinge. "Saturday we launch at forty-five and we win."

Priya didn't answer right away. She was looking at the garage door, which stood open a hand's width to the October air, and beyond it the driveway where a breeze had just skittered a dry leaf across the chalk mark he used for alignment. "That's outside," she said.

"What's outside?"

"The air. The contest is in the parking lot. All this is clean numbers, no air resistance, perfectly flat ground, the world as physics wishes it were." She shrugged. "There'll be wind."

Gavin looked at his beautiful forty-five degrees, then at the leaf, which had already reached the gutter. He thought about arguing that the breeze was nothing, that twenty-nine feet of margin didn't care about a leaf, and he thought about the sixty-degree shot that had felt so right and landed so wrong. He picked up the notebook instead.

"Then we test outside," he said. "Right now. You hold the tape."

He hauled the launcher to the driveway by himself, wheels squealing, and pointed it down the long flat stretch of cul-de-sac where, he was almost certain, the ground was level and the wind, for the moment, was holding its breath. "Mark where it lands," he called, and pulled the trigger.

The menorah stood on the sideboard between the kugel and a platter of rugelach, and Alex's grandmother had handed him the matches before he could invent an excuse. Four nights already, and every night an uncle or a cousin had supervised the lighting, but tonight the aunts were arguing about the brisket and his father was showing someone a video on his phone, and the silver candelabrum was just waiting there, winking under the dining room light.

He had agreed to it in August, in the parking lot of the community college, when his roommate-to-be, Dev, asked if he was "religious" and Alex had said "not really, cultural, I guess," and then spent the whole drive home wondering what he had meant. His grandmother's Hebrew was better than his. His father's was worse. Somewhere between them was Alex, holding matches and trying to remember which candles went where.

He set the box down and counted the branches of the menorah with his eyes. Nine. Eight in a row, all the same height, and one standing apart, a little taller, set off to the side or raised above the rest. Four nights, he thought. So four candles, but he had a handful of them out of the box already and had lost track of how many he'd actually set in the holders, because his little cousin Rosie had been counting out loud along with him and then had started counting the rugelach instead.

"Five," Rosie announced from the table, mouth full.

"Four," Alex said. "It's the fourth night."

"Five rugelach."

He looked at the menorah. One of the holders had a candle in it, and he couldn't remember putting it there, or whether Rosie had reached up while he was answering a question about his major. If he lit five tonight, his grandmother would notice tomorrow, and his uncle Izzy would make it a joke at the table, the way he made everything a joke, and Alex would smile and feel like a fraud in his own grandmother's dining room.

His grandmother drifted over, drying her hands on a dish towel. She didn't say anything. She watched him count the branches again, tapping the air above each one with a knuckle, like a pianist finding middle C.

"That one," she said at last, nodding at the taller candle, the one set apart. "That's the shamash, the helper."

"The helper," Alex repeated. He'd heard the word his whole life, in songs, in his grandfather's gravelly transliteration, and never once thought about it. He took the extra candle out of the holder and set it in the shamash's place instead, and suddenly the arithmetic was simple: four for the four nights, one helper to light them, five flames in total once it was done, and all eight standing in a straight line waiting for the nights still to come. The ninth candle wasn't part of the count at all. It was how you counted.

He struck the match. The room smelled of onion and burnt sulfur and his aunt's perfume, and under that, faintly, the furniture polish his grandmother used to burnish the sideboard every Friday, rubbing the dark wood until it gave back the light of the chandelier. He lit the shamash, and the shamash lit the others, right to left, the way his grandfather had done it, though Alex only knew the direction because Dev had asked him once and he'd had to look it up, embarrassed, at one in the morning.

They sang. Alex knew maybe sixty percent of the words and mouthed the rest, and Rosie banged her spoon, and his uncle's voice slid a third below everyone else's in a way that should have been ugly and somehow wasn't, a consonance Alex felt in his sternum more than heard. His grandmother watched the flames with her hands folded, and when the song ended she didn't say good singing or well done. She said, "Your grandfather did it exactly like that. Sloppy on the words."

Later, at the table, Uncle Izzy piled a second helping of everything onto Alex's plate with an epicurean seriousness, as though the brisket were a matter of principle, and asked him what he was going to study. Undeclared, Alex said, and waited for the joke. Izzy just nodded and said that was honest, that most people lied and picked something.

Alex thought about the helper candle on the way out to the car, holding the tin of leftovers his grandmother had pressed on him. He still couldn't read Hebrew. He still wasn't sure what he believed, or whether Dev's question had a real answer, or whether cultural and religious were two different things or one thing badly divided. But he could count the branches now, and he knew which candle did the lighting, and tomorrow night there would be five in the row and one apart, and he wanted to be the one to set them.

"Next year you do all eight," his grandmother called from the porch.

"Nine," Alex said, and got in the car smiling.

Jordyn arrived at the community garden at eight with a biology textbook, a spiral notebook, and forty dollars of her mother's money for a plot fee. The plot was hers on one condition: she had to run the Saturday morning table where neighborhood kids could ask questions about the science wall, a poster the garden committee had put up next to the tomato beds. The committee chair, Ms. Okafor, had read the poster aloud at the last meeting, stumbling over the words transcription and translation, and had looked straight at Jordyn when she said the senior member usually handles it.

The problem was that Jordyn did not fully understand the poster. She could recite the steps for her exam, DNA to RNA to protein, but on Wednesday her study partner Dev had asked her why the process worked that way, and she had opened her mouth and produced nothing. She got a 74 on the quiz. Her mother said a 74 was fine; the committee said the table started Saturday. So Jordyn brought the textbook to the garden and spread it on the bench beside the basil, determined to build the explanation from the ground up before ten o'clock, when the kids came.

At nine-forty a man in a wheelbarrow shirt, one of the volunteer composters, stopped at the poster and read it frowning. "Copied DNA," he said. "So when a cell copies its DNA, the new molecule is all new material. Like a photocopy."

Standing beside him, a teenager from the apartment on Cypress, maybe thirteen, shook his head. "My brother says it's half old. He says one strand is the original and the other one is new." The two of them looked at Jordyn, because she was the one at the table with the book.

"All new," the man said. "A copy is a copy."

"Half old," the boy said. "He showed me a picture."

Jordyn's first instinct was to say she didn't know and refer them to the poster, but the poster didn't cover it. She turned to the diagram in her textbook, the wide double ladder with the rungs split down the middle, and worked outward from what she could see. If the two strands separated, each old strand could serve as a pattern for a new partner. She traced the arrows with her pen. The daughter molecule on the left held one dark strand and one light one. The daughter on the right held the same. She looked up and said, "It's semiconservative."

"What's that mean," the man said, not unkindly.

She kept her eyes on the diagram so she would not lose the thread. "Each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand. So you're both right. It's not all new and it's not all old. Half of each."

The boy leaned over the bench. "Okay, but then what's the poster about? The transcription thing."

That was the part she had faked on Wednesday. She had been treating the whole process as a heuristic, a shortcut, a chant to get through the quiz: DNA to RNA to protein, three words, no meaning. The chant had carried her to a 74 and then failed her in front of Dev, and standing here with two people waiting, she understood that she needed the other way of thinking, the slow one, the one where you look at the picture until the picture tells you something. The garden had taught her that already, in a different register. You could memorize a seed packet, or you could watch a bean split open in the soil over six days, which her plot neighbor Ruth had made her do in June.

So she walked it through on the bench like a garden row. The old strand stays; a working copy gets made off it, and that copying is what the poster calls transcription. The copy goes out, and translation reads it, three letters at a time, and builds a chain of amino acids, which folds into a protein. The man said, "Like a recipe copied out of the safe and taken to the kitchen." Jordyn said that was closer than anything her teacher had said all spring. The boy copied the words semiconservative and transcription into his phone.

Then came the twist. The boy turned the textbook around and pointed at the top of the page, at the diagram number. "This is from chapter sixteen," he said. "My brother's book has the same picture but the labels are different. Why does yours say the old strand is the dark one and his says the light one?" Jordyn looked and found he was right in a way that mattered and didn't matter: the colors were arbitrary, chosen by the artist, while the relationship, one strand old, one strand new, was the fixed thing underneath. She said so, and heard herself say it, and understood that this was the difference between memorizing colors and understanding structure, between the chant and the picture. Whether she could hold onto that way of thinking next Tuesday, in a silent exam room, with no man in a wheelbarrow shirt to explain things to, she genuinely did not know.

At noon she watered the tomatoes and thought about her plot, how every seed she had planted had come from last year's plants, which had come from the year before, a line running back unbroken, and yet nothing in the bed was the same plant. Nothing was entirely new either. The soil had been turned and the stakes repositioned; the whole bed had shifted since June in small, tectonic ways she noticed only in the before-and-after photographs she took each week. Whether the mind worked like that, keeping one strand and building the other, she couldn't prove, and she wasn't going to pretend she could.

Ms. Okafor came by at one with the sign-up sheet for next month's table. "You'll do it again?" she asked. Jordyn was still holding the pen she'd used to trace the diagram. "Let me check something first," she said, and turned the textbook back to chapter sixteen.

Lucas had claimed the kitchen the way his mother claimed a sale rack, decisively and with both arms, and now the counter at his grandmother's house looked like the aftermath of a small pastry tornado. He was making dinner for the whole family, his th announcement of departure for college having prompted, somewhere in the organizational machinery of the household, the idea of a send-off meal cooked by the departing person himself. Breaded chicken, a green salad, and, because he had read three articles about it at two in the morning, homemade mayonnaise. His grandmother, Nonna Rosa, sat at the table shelling peas and narrating his technique in a tone she usually reserved for weather.

"You are adding the oil like it owes you money," she observed. "Slow. Slow, like a scandal developing."

"I'm going slow."

"That is not slow. That is a skirmish."

He was, in fairness, going slowly enough. He had learned the method from a video in which a calm man with excellent forearms whisked oil into a yolk drop by drop, and the mixture had thickened, glossy and obliging, for nearly a minute. Lucas felt the particular pride of a person doing something his phone had promised was possible. Then, somewhere between confident and cocky, he added a glug rather than a drip, and the bowl curdled into something shameful: a oily lake with a sad yellow puddle in the middle, exactly the substance the video had warned him about and exactly the substance he had made.

"It broke," he said. "It split. It's ruined."

Nonna Rosa set down her peas and came over with the unhurried authority of a woman who had survived worse in bowls. She peered in. "Hm. The oil went on strike."

"Do I start over?"

"You never start over. Starting over is for people with no history." She took a fresh egg from the carton, cracked it, separated the yolk into a clean bowl with one hand, a gesture so casual it was almost rude. "Whisk the new yolk. Now, slowly, you put the broken one in, spoon by spoon." She tapped the bowl. "The lecithin and the proteins in the yolk, those are emulsifiers. They hold the little oil drops in the water so it doesn't separate."

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"That is the whole trick of many things," she said, which Lucas felt was either profound or an evasion, and possibly both.

He whisked the new yolk pale, then added the curdled mess a spoonful at a time, and it was, he had to admit, a little bit magical: the ruined lake folded in and became sauce again, thicker even than before, holding together with what he could only describe as commitment. In chemistry class last spring, Mr. Okonkwo had covered solutions and suspensions and had once, in a digression about carbon, called graphite and diamond allotropes of the same element, which had bothered Lucas for a week: same thing, utterly different arrangement, utterly different result. This felt like the reverse. Different things, whisked into one arrangement, behaving as a single substance. He mentioned this to his grandmother, who considered it while eating a pea raw.

"So the diamond is the good mayonnaise," she said.

"Basically."

"And the graphite?"

"The broken one. Still carbon. Still egg and oil."

"You think too much," she said, but she said it warmly, the way you'd tell someone they wore too much cologne, and she stole a fingertip of the sauce to taste. She nodded once, which from her was equivalent to applause.

The rest of it came together, more or less. The chicken burned on one edge and was fine everywhere else; the salad required no chemistry beyond ambition. When the family sat down, his uncle asked where the jar of mayonnaise was, and Lucas, with tremendous dignity, indicated the bowl. There was the tasting, the pause, the verdict. His little cousin declared it "yellow and perfect," his father said it was better than the store kind, and Lucas suspected both statements of diplomacy but chose not to investigate, since some suspensions, once questioned, fall apart.

Later, alone in the kitchen with the washing up, he held the last spoonful of sauce over the sink and watched it cling, refusing to drip, an evanescent little structure that would be gone by tomorrow and that he had, twice now, brought into existence. He turned off the tap and called into the dining room, "Nonna, can I take the whisk to college?"

"Take the whisk," she called back. "Leave the bowl. The bowl stays with me."
