It didn't tell you whether you were in the half that survived or the half that didn't, and it didn't tell you whether the belt itself was freedom or leash, or whether those were even different things.

Afterward, in the strip mall parking lot, Mr. Okafor filled out her progress sheet. "Control is good," he said. "Confidence will come." He tore off her copy and held it out, and as she took it he added, "Same time next week," in a tone that assumed she would say yes.

Her grandmother was idling at the curb in her enormous Buick, and Samantha got in, and reached, out of habit older than memory, for the seat belt. The buckle hung up halfway down the door pillar, the old fabric gone stiff, and she had to feed it back through with two hands while her grandmother watched with an expression that was not quite disapproval and not quite its opposite.

"Your father never wore his," her grandmother said, pulling out into traffic.

Natalie had carried the fragments to school in a shoebox lined with a dish towel, and through first period the box sat in her locker like something breathing. In the art room, fourth period, she finally opened it on the counter near the window: seven pieces of her grandmother's rice bowl, the celadon glaze catching the light along edges sharp enough to matter. Mr. Ferreira wandered past, glanced in, and said nothing, which was the reason she had chosen his room and not the ceramics studio, where Ms. Okoye would have asked questions.

The bowl had broken on Tuesday. Her grandmother had been napping, the apartment warm and smelling of barley tea, and Natalie had reached over it for the good brushes her grandmother kept in a jar behind the stove, the ones she never used anymore because her hands shook. The bowl had been under a cloth. That was all. It had not even made much of a sound, just a settling, and Natalie had stood there with her grandmother's brushes and her grandmother's broken bowl, sixty years of a life in pieces on a linoleum floor.

Her first plan had been glue and paint. There was a kit in her backpack, cyanoacrylate and a tiny bottle of green acrylic she had mixed to match the glaze, because her grandmother's eyes were going but not that gone. The plan was simple and it was a lie, and both of those things had recommended it. She had even rehearsed the sentence: I found it like that. She laid the pieces out now in their rough circle, and the jagged lines between them adumbrated a shape she couldn't name, a map of the moment her hand had knocked against cloth.

Priya leaned over from the next table, brush in her teeth, hands black with ink. "Whose is it?"

"My grandmother's. Was." Natalie turned one piece over. "I'm fixing it before Sunday. She's making rice for the equinox thing and she'll want it."

"You're going to fake it." Priya said it without judgment, the way she said everything, and set her brush down. "You could fake it. Nobody would know."

"I would know." Natalie heard how it sounded, like a line from a movie, and hated it, and meant it anyway. She had spent two days weighing the truth against her grandmother's face when she saw the bowl, and the truth kept losing. Her grandmother had come to this country with two suitcases and a sister, had been impecunious for decades in a way Natalie only understood in fragments, stories about washing dishes in a restaurant that served food from home. The bowl was from home. It had crossed an ocean in a rolled sweater. It was the only object in the apartment her grandmother had ever called by a name.

Priya pulled out her phone, typed, scrolled, and turned the screen around. Natalie read it twice. A photograph of a mended bowl, black seams running through it like rivers drawn in ink, and every seam blazing with gold, so that the breaks were the most alive part of the thing, more visible than they would ever have been unbroken.

"Kintsugi," Priya read. "It's a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold." She looked up. "It treats the break as part of the object's history instead of hiding it."

Natalie took the phone and read further, past the bright photographs, into the practice of it: the lacquer, the curing, the weeks it took. Real gold, real urushi lacquer that could blister her skin, patience measured in months. She thought of her cheap kit, the acrylic paint, the rehearsed sentence, the whole small hegemony of pretending nothing had happened, and she understood that she had been weighing the wrong things. She wasn't choosing between truth and her grandmother's face. She was choosing what the bowl would be for the rest of its life: an object with a scar, or an object with a secret.

"It takes months to cure," she said. "Properly. I have five days." Mr. Ferreira, watering the paint sinks like a man tending a garden, said from across the room, "Some things you can't speed up," and nothing else. Priya was already scrolling again, muttering about mica powder and epoxy and a craft store two bus transfers away, and whether a girl on a babysitting income could afford even the fake gold. Natalie swept the fragments gently back into the towel, folding it over them the way her grandmother folded wrappers, corners first.

At the craft store she stood a long time in front of two options: gold leaf she could not afford and a small jar of mica powder the color of a struck match. She bought the mica. On Sunday she would set the bowl on the table, seams rough and glittering where they should have been lacquered and smooth, and she would not say I found it like that. She would say something else, though she did not yet know what, and she practiced nothing on the bus ride home, only held the shoebox on her lap with both hands and watched the mica gold shine through the cloth every time the doors opened and the light came in.

Raphael's grandfather had a desktop computer in the room that used to be an office, and that was where Raphael sat on Saturday morning with his project due Monday. The assignment was to overlay a flood risk map and a housing map of the city on one screen and write about what the overlap meant. The teacher had given them a trial version of the software and a folder of files, and Raphael had assumed the hard part would be the writing. It was not.

The housing map loaded first: parcels of land drawn as clean outlined shapes, thousands of them, each one clickable, each one carrying an address and a year built. When he dragged it around, the parcels undulated across the screen in a slow ripple as the software redrew them, thin blue boundaries breathing over the gray background. Then he opened the flood map and something entirely different appeared. It looked like a photograph, like weather radar on the news, a smear of colors from pale yellow to deep red, soft-edged and grainy when he zoomed in until he could see the individual squares of it, one blocky cell at a time.

He tried to put one on top of the other and the software refused. A gray box told him the layers did not match. He clicked through three menus, closed the box, opened it again, and went to find his grandfather, who was sorting seed packets at the kitchen table with the radio murmuring ball scores.

"Can I ask you something about maps?"

His grandfather set down a packet of marigolds. "I drew maps for the county for thirty-one years. Ask."

"On the computer. One of my files looks like shapes, outlines you can click, and the other one looks like pixels. Like a photo. They won't stack."

His grandfather was quiet for a moment, the way he was quiet before he answered anything worth answering. "The pixel one," he said. "That's raster." He turned another seed packet over in his hands. "The shapes are the other kind. Look it up, kiddo. I only ever drew the lines."

Raphael looked it up. It took him twenty minutes of reading and another twenty of squinting at the software's help pages, and then he sat back in the stiff office chair with the strange satisfaction of a door swinging open. The shapes were vector data, built from points, lines and polygons, and that was why each parcel could carry its own record, its own little encapsulation of address and age and owner. The pixel map was raster data, a grid of cells, each cell holding exactly one value, which in this case was a flood risk score. One value per square. That was why zooming in showed him blocks instead of boundaries. The two maps weren't broken; they were two different languages describing the same city.

The problem of stacking them turned out to be a problem of translation. He found a tool that converted his vector parcels into the same grid as the flood map, and watched the tidy polygons dissolve into squares. Something was lost, he could see that immediately. Two narrow lots became one fat cell. A sliver of park disappeared entirely, too thin to claim its own square. He sat with his hand on the mouse, circumspect now in a way he hadn't been an hour ago, because he understood that every choice about how to merge the maps was also a quiet claim about what mattered. If he made the cells smaller, he kept the slivers, but the flood map's cells were the size they were, and he couldn't invent precision that wasn't in the source.

He ran it anyway. The overlay bloomed on the screen, and there it was: a band of red and orange running through the east side where the housing grid was densest, block after block of cells sitting squarely on top of parcels built in the forties and fifties. He printed it on his grandfather's old printer, which groaned like it disagreed, and carried the warm page to the kitchen.

"This is it," he said. "This whole neighborhood. High flood risk, and it's the most crowded part of the map." He laid the page on the table between the marigolds and the tomatoes.

His grandfather put on his glasses and leaned close, tracing the red band with one finger. "Your great-aunt lived right there," he said. "Water came to her porch steps in '77. Twice since." He tapped the dense grid of squares. "You know what I can't tell from this, though?"

"What?"

"Which of those squares is a family that can absorb a flood, and which is a family that can't." He handed the page back. "That's not in anybody's data."

Raphael stood there holding the map. He had a page due Monday, eight hundred words, and now he knew what at least the first paragraph would say: that the grid could tell you where the water went, and the shapes could tell you who lived there, and both of them together still left the most important thing unnamed. He didn't know yet how to write that without it sounding like giving up. He went back to the office, set the printed map beside the keyboard, and opened a blank document. On screen, behind the cursor, the city's parcels still rippled in a slow wave, red squares holding their ground beneath them.

Aiden had until midnight, and the kitchen clock kept proving it. The portfolio submission closed at eleven fifty-nine, and the piece he wanted to send, a drawing of the river by his grandmother's old house, existed only as a photograph in his phone and forty loose squares of paper on the table. The idea had come to him in fragments all week: draw the river small, many times, on separate scraps, and then assemble them so the water broke apart and reassembled like memory does. Now the scraps were spread across the table like silt, an alluvial fan of graphite and eraser dust, and he had to decide how they fit before he could photograph the whole thing and upload it.

He picked up two squares, held them side by side, and put them down again. His grandmother had taught him one way of drawing, which was patience: build the tone slowly, one faint layer after another, until the paper held the light. His art teacher had taught him another way, which was risk: make the thing wrong on purpose, tear it, collage it, let the seams show. For months he had been pretending those were two different careers, as if he had to pick a life the way you pick a major. Tonight the deadline made pretending expensive.

Maya padded into the kitchen in her pajamas, holding a pencil with a wet, splintered end. She was seven, and she had been sent to bed an hour ago, and she was crying in the quiet, hiccupping way that meant the fear had been building in the dark by itself. "I ate some," she said. "The paint part and some of the lead. I was chewing it and I swallowed."

"You swallowed the lead?" Aiden pulled her onto the chair beside him.

"The gray part. Lead is poison. Marcus at school said lead gets in your bones and you get sick." She held the pencil out like evidence at a trial, and her hand was shaking a little.

Aiden turned the broken end toward the light. He remembered his father saying something once, offhand, over homework, and he reached for his phone to check it before he promised anything, because Maya took promises literally. He read, then read again, and put the phone down. "It's not lead," he said. "It's called graphite. Pencil lead has never actually been made of lead, not ever. They only call it lead because back in the sixteenth century people thought graphite was a kind of lead ore. It isn't. It's just graphite and clay."

Maya looked at the wet gray end. "So I'm not poisoned?"

"You're not poisoned. You're just gross." He wiped the pencil on a napkin, which made her laugh, and the laugh broke the fear open and let it drain. She leaned her chin on the table to watch him work, and after a while she began sliding squares toward him, playing advisor, and he let her, because her eye was untrained and therefore strange.

"Those two go together," she said, pushing a dark square and a pale one. "The dark part is where the water's deep."

He would not have put them together. The pale square was one of his best, the river at noon, and gluing it next to the heavy one would make both harder to read. But he tried it, holding them at the joint, and something happened that hadn't happened in three hours of arranging: the river had a bottom and a surface at once. The two ways of drawing, the patient and the torn, met in the seam and neither one lost. He thought of how his father talked about their mortgage, how they'd amortize the cost of the roof over years, spreading one impossible number into many survivable ones, and he understood that he was doing the same thing with the drawing, spreading one impossible river into forty small decisions. Some of them could fail and the whole thing would still hold.

He worked while Maya drifted asleep against his arm, which cost him his right elbow and slowed every stroke. He gained the seam and lost the hour. At eleven he had the full assembly on a sheet of cardboard, and he saw immediately that it was too big to photograph well in the kitchen light, and that the two squares he loved most, the noon square among them, caught glare no matter how he angled the lamp. He tried the porch light, the stove light, the flashlight propped in a bowl. Each version flattened some part of what the piece actually was, and there was no time to solve it, only time to choose which failure to send.

At eleven forty he set the phone on a stack of cookbooks, framed the whole piece with the noon square blazing out one blank corner of it, and pressed record. The file uploaded slowly, the progress bar crawling while the clock in the other room struck the quarter hour. He thought about how his teacher would see the glare and call it sloppy, and how his grandmother, if she were still alive to see it, would have known instantly that the glare was the water. Both of those readings were true, and he could not make them be the same one, and he submitted anyway at eleven fifty-three with Maya asleep on his shoulder and his arm gone completely numb beneath her weight.

The confirmation page loaded. He sat still, listening to Maya breathe, looking at the forty squares drying on the cardboard, the seams already beginning to curl.

"Aiden," Maya said, not waking up, "the dark part is where it's deep."

The funeral was at eleven, and Colton arrived at ten because his mother said the family should be there early, though nobody explained what they would do with the extra hour. The sanctuary smelled of lilies and furniture polish. His grandfather's photograph stood on a table beside the casket, a picture from twenty years ago: Grandpa Walt in a linen shirt, squinting into what had to be bright sun, standing somewhere in Kenya where he had taught school for two years before Colton was born. Behind him in the photo stretched the savanna, gold grass running out to a flat horizon, a lone acacia throwing a shadow like a sundial.

Colton's mother hugged people near the doorway. His father talked quietly with the pastor, a tall woman named Reverend Okafor who had only met Walt once, at a hospital, which struck Colton as a strange qualification for delivering a eulogy. Colton walked down the center aisle and stopped at the photograph. He had come here wanting something, though he had not let himself name it. He wanted to be sure he was grieving correctly. That was the want, and it embarrassed him.

Three days before, cleaning out his grandfather's apartment, he had found a book on the nightstand with a bookmark still in it. Continuing Bonds, it was called, published in 1996, by three authors whose names he had copied into his phone because they sounded like a law firm: Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman, Steven Nickman. He had read the bookmarked chapter late that night with his desk lamp on, and it had said something he kept turning over. It argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on. Colton had always assumed the opposite, that the whole point was to let go, that the healthy people were the ones who packed the apartment in two days and did not cry at the leasing office.

"You're the grandson," said a voice behind him. A woman in her seventies, small, wearing a green coat, held out her hand. "I'm Phyllis's friend. No, not that Phyllis. I'm Ruth. I played chess with your grandfather on Thursdays."

"He mentioned you," Colton said, and it was true, though it had sounded like a small thing at the time, chess on Thursdays, two old people in a library meeting room.

"He said you argued with him about everything," Ruth said. "He was proud of that. He said you enunciated your positions like a lawyer." She smiled at the photograph. "He told me you'd want to say something today and wouldn't know if you were allowed."

Colton felt his face go warm. "How did he know that?"

"Because you argued about everything and then asked whether it counted." She patted his arm once, the way you close a book you intend to reopen, and went to find a seat.

The service began. There were hymns, and Colton held the hymnal with its vestigial ribbon marker, faded red, hanging loose from a spine nobody had opened in years, and he sang where he knew the words. Reverend Okafor read a psalm and then spoke about Walt's life, the teaching in Kenya, the forty years at the public library, the wife who had died before Colton could remember her. She said the word "loss" eleven times. Colton counted without meaning to. She never said the word for what he actually had, which was not an absence but a presence with nowhere to go.

When she opened the floor for remembrances, three people stood. A cousin told a story about a fishing trip. Ruth did not stand; she only looked at Colton across two rows of folded hands. The organist began the closing music before he had decided anything.

Afterward, in the fellowship hall with its folding tables and coffee urns, Colton's mother pressed a plate of cookies into his hands and he carried it around like a task. He found Ruth by the window. "I read a book of his," he said. "Continuing Bonds. He had it marked."

"Ah," Ruth said. "He bought that after Miriam died. He said it gave him permission."

"Permission for what?"

"To keep her. He'd talk to her while he cooked. Terrible cook. He'd say, Miriam, how much salt, and she never answered, and he said that was still her doing, in a way." Ruth sipped her coffee. "I told him he was being morbid. He said the book said otherwise. He lent it to me. I never gave it back."

Colton set the cookie plate down on the sill. "So it's normal. That's what the book says. Keeping the connection. Not a failure to move on." He heard his own voice enunciate it, lawyer-like, and almost laughed.

"That's what he took from it," Ruth said. "I took something smaller. I took that grief is not one size."

The afternoon light moved across the parking lot. His mother was at the door, hugging the last guests, and his father was loading lilies into the trunk with the careful concentration of a man avoiding his own thoughts. Colton understood, standing there, that he could hold both ideas without choosing: the book's claim, which felt like a hand on his shoulder, and the honest uncertainty underneath it, the question of whether talking to someone who cannot answer is connection or only rehearsal. He did not know. He was sixteen, and he had never grieved before, and nobody had taught him the rules because there might not be rules.

At the apartment the next weekend, his mother handed him a box. "These are yours if you want them," she said. Inside were the chess set, a small carved elephant from Kenya, and the book. He took the book out and put the bookmark back where his grandfather had left it, page one hundred and twelve.

That night he set up the board in his bedroom, the way Walt always did, white toward himself because Colton was learning. He moved a pawn to e4, Grandpa's favorite opening, the one he called "honest chess."

"Your move," Colton said.

Chloe's father had volunteered to teach her, twice, and twice she had said no, and the second time she had heard him go quiet on the other end of the phone in a way that made her stomach drop. So now it was Dana, an instructor with a lanyard and a clipboard, sitting in the passenger seat of a car with dual brakes, and Chloe was adjusting a mirror that didn't need adjusting.

"Pull out when you're ready," Dana said. "Easy does it."

The driveway emptied onto a quiet street of lampposts and parked sedans. Chloe turned the wheel too early, corrected, and heard a tire kiss the curb. Her hands were sweating through the gloves she had bought for this, which now seemed like an encumbrance, a costume for a person who knew what she was doing. She pulled them off and dropped them in the cup holder.

The first ten minutes went tolerably until they reached the road with traffic. A silver hatchback sat ahead of her at the speed limit, and Chloe, without deciding to, drifted closer. And closer. Dana said nothing. Chloe watched the hatchback's bumper fill the windshield, felt the visceral pull of it, the strange certainty that being near the car in front meant being safe, meant moving, meant keeping pace with everything. Her father used to tailgate on the highway, one hand loose on the wheel, and her mother would say his name in a flat voice and he would ease off without answering. Chloe had always sat in the back and counted the seconds between her own breaths.

"You're crowding that car," Dana said finally. "Pick a fixed point. A sign, a lamppost, anything that isn't moving. When the car ahead passes it, start counting. One-thousand-one, one-thousand-two. If you reach that same point before you finish counting, you're too close. It's called the two-second rule."

Chloe glanced at her, then back at the road. "A lamppost?"

"Any fixed point works."

The next lamppost came up on the right, tall and pale. The hatchback passed it, and Chloe began counting, silently at first, then aloud, because the silence made her rush. One-thousand-one, one-thousand-two. She reached the lamppost before she finished. Her mouth went dry. She eased off the gas and watched the gap widen, silver and ordinary in the morning light.

They drove to the end of the street and back, and Chloe ran the count at every lamppost, every mailbox, once at a faded stop sign whose paint had gone the color of chalk. Some counts she passed easily, and some she barely made, and twice she caught herself drifting forward again, thinking about her phone in her bag, thinking about the form due for housing, thinking about anything except the road. She was beginning to internalize it, the way the counting reached her before the worry did, the way the lamppost arrived as a question rather than a blur. At a red light Dana asked how it was going, and Chloe said, "I keep failing it and fixing it," and Dana laughed and said that was the whole job.

At the far end of the route, Dana told her to pull into a driveway, some stranger's driveway with a basketball hoop and a sprinkler ticking across the grass, and put the car in park. "That's enough for today," she said. "You did fine." Chloe kept her hands on the wheel. She was thinking about her father, about the third time she hadn't called him, about whether a person could be sorry for a choice and still certain it was right, and she could not make those two things sit together no matter how she turned them. Maybe the counting worked like that too: you watched something pass a fixed point, and you measured yourself against it, and the answer told you only whether you were too close, never whether you were where you belonged.

She turned the key and the engine died. "Can we do one more loop?" she asked. "I want to try the lampposts without you telling me."

Dana clicked her pen and wrote something on the clipboard. "Back out when you're ready," she said.

The camera above the pastry case was small and matte black, and Arianna had worked at Corvo's for five weeks before she noticed it at all. She noticed it on a Tuesday because Dev, the closing manager, paused behind the register and tilted his head toward it. "Corporate installed those last month," he said. "They say it's for training. It records us making drinks, and some software scores the shots we pull." He said this without heat, the way he reported the weather, and moved on to restacking cups.

After that she could not stop noticing it. Her hands felt slower over the portafilter, though she had measured the same dose a hundred times. When she dropped a stir stick she looked up first, checking whether the little lens had registered the fault. By Thursday she was wiping the counter in long, even strokes even when no one was sitting at it, and she understood, in a sidelong way, that the camera had changed her without ever speaking.

A regular named Marcus came in at four, as he always did, with a battered paperback and an order he never varied. He was a philosophy student at the community college, reticent about most things, though he liked to argue gently with whoever worked the counter. That afternoon Arianna asked him, almost against her will, whether a camera could make you a different person just by existing. "That's an old question," Marcus said, pleased. "Look up Jeremy Bentham's panopticon. His 1791 prison design. A central tower in the middle, and the inmates can be watched at any time without ever knowing whether they actually are." He stirred his americano. "The point isn't the guard. The point is the not knowing."

She looked it up on her break, hunched over her phone at the corner table. The drawings were clean and terrible, a ring of cells around one bright circle of tower. She read that prisoners, unable to tell when eyes were on them, came to police themselves, and she thought of her own even, performative counter wipes, and felt a small cold recognition settle in her chest. Not shame exactly. Something more like being caught in an argument she hadn't known she was having.

That same week the new scheduling system arrived. Corporate had rolled out software that built the rota automatically, taking in availability, sales data, and something the memo called "team performance metrics," whose provenance no one at the store could explain. Dev's hours were cut first. He was thirty-one and had been at Corvo's six years, and the software had, as far as anyone could tell, weighted the camera scores. "I train the new hires," he told Arianna on Friday, counting out change. "A machine watched me make a cappuccino and decided I'm bad at my job. And nobody can tell me what I did wrong, because nobody knows what it was watching for."

Arianna had a physics test the next morning, but she stayed an hour past her shift, sitting with Dev while he closed. They pulled up the scheduling dashboard on the store laptop and clicked into every menu. The system offered no reasons, only rankings. She understood, dimly, that an algorithm's judgment could be as unanswerable as Bentham's tower, except that this one also signed the paychecks. She kept thinking she ought to be able to predicate an appeal on some fact, some number she could point to, and kept finding that the facts had dissolved into the software's opinion of them.

That night she wrote an email to the regional manager, drafting it twice before sending. "I've worked here since September," she wrote, "and I've never been told what the camera measures or how the schedule is made. Mr. Okafor has trained every barista in this store. If the system disagrees, I'd like to see the reasons. If there are no reasons, I'd like to know why we're pretending there are." She read it over, wondered if it was too sharp, and sent it before she could soften it. Then she went back to her physics, and the equations came slowly.

On Sunday the reply came, short and corporate, thanking her for her engagement and noting that the metrics were proprietary. But Monday's schedule posted with Dev's hours restored, unexplained, and when he saw it he stood very still in front of the sheet for a moment before saying, "Huh." He didn't thank her. He made her a drink off the menu, something with cinnamon he'd invented years ago, and set it on the counter in front of her.

Arianna took it to the corner table, under the camera she still couldn't tell was on. Marcus came in at four and asked how the panopticon research was going. "It wasn't research," she said. "It was just my job." He laughed and opened his paperback, and she sat with the cooling drink, still unsure whether she'd won anything or only been handed a quieter version of the same arrangement. The lens sat above the pastry case, small and matte black, watching or not. She picked up the cup and took a long sip.

The festival on Carroll Street smelled of honey and frying dough, and Madeline had exactly one hour before her grandmother's bus arrived from the church on Fifth Avenue. One hour, and she still hadn't found the gift. Her family had celebrated Christmas on December 25 like everyone else on their block, with the plastic tree and the socks, but her grandmother kept the old date, and this year she had asked, almost shyly, whether Madeline might come to the street festival with her afterward. Madeline had said yes before she understood what she was agreeing to.

The cold seemed to invigorate the crowd rather than thin it. Women in headscarves sold pirozhki from folding tables, a man in a fur hat argued cheerfully with a teenager over the price of painted wooden ornaments, and somewhere behind the stalls a choir was warming up, the basses humming low enough that Madeline felt it in her ribs. She moved through it all with her hands in her pockets, noticing how the whole street had decided that Christmas was still coming, that the neighbors' discarded trees lying frozen at the curb meant nothing here.

"You look lost," said a girl behind a table of jam jars, maybe nineteen, with mittens that had lost their fingers. "Lost people always walk in circles. You've passed my table three times."

"I'm trying to find a present for my grandmother before her bus gets here. Fifty-one minutes." Madeline said it and heard how ridiculous it sounded, and the girl laughed, which made it sound even more ridiculous.

"Sit," the girl said, pointing at a milk crate. "Tell me about her."

So Madeline told her: that Babushka Vera had been married in a church with towers like upturned onions, that she still crossed herself in a way that made Madeline think of water, that last week she'd said something Madeline couldn't stop turning over. She'd said, "We have Christmas on January 7, because our church keeps December 25 on the old Julian calendar, two weeks behind yours." Madeline had assumed, all her life, that the family was simply late, or disorganized, or stubborn. "I never asked why two Christmases exist in one family," she said now. "I just got used to opening my stocking while she was still fasting."

The jam girl, whose name turned out to be Anya, nodded without surprise. "My mother does the same thing. In January the stores put everything on sale, so we eat better than the December people." She leaned across the jars. "But you said your grandmother is coming from Fifth Avenue. That bus stops running early on festival days. Check."

Madeline checked. The bus, according to a schedule taped inside a festival booth, would stop at the corner at six o'clock, not seven, because the street was closing for the procession. Which meant she had eleven minutes, not fifty-one, and her grandmother would arrive at a corner with no one standing on it. She stood up so fast she knocked over the milk crate.

"Go," Anya said, but then, as Madeline turned, "wait," and pressed something into her hand. A small jar, dark, unlabeled. "Rowanberry. My grandmother's recipe. Tell yours a girl at the festival gave it to you, and she'll know exactly what that means." Madeline ran the six blocks with the jar cupped against her stomach like a small heart, past the choir now singing in full voice, past a man selling candles who called out "Almost too late!" in a tone of such theatrical grief that she laughed out loud while running, which hurt her throat in the cold air.

She reached the corner as the bus hissed open its doors, and there was Babushka Vera in her gray coat, looking small and certain, the kind of stoicism that Madeline understood now was not hardness but a way of carrying things. "You came," her grandmother said, as if Madeline had done something remarkable by standing on a cold corner. Madeline held out the jar, and her grandmother took off one glove to touch the glass, reading the jam's color like a language Madeline didn't speak yet. "Rowanberry," Vera said softly. "In January, always rowanberry." Behind them the procession was beginning, and Anya, Madeline realized, would be closing her table now, stacking her obsolescent milk crates for another year. "Tell me about this girl," her grandmother said, tucking the jar inside her coat, right against her heart, and taking Madeline's arm.

Justin had been borrowing Mrs. Okonkwo's cello for three weeks, and every Tuesday the A string went flat on him as if it had opinions. He tightened the peg, plucked the string, and watched the clip-on tuner blink red. He wanted, more than he could reasonably explain to anyone at school, to play the Bach minuet his grandfather used to hum while fixing things in the garage, and he wanted it before winter, though nobody had set that deadline but him.

"The A is still low," Mrs. Okonkwo said from the kitchen doorway, holding two mugs. She had the insouciant habit of delivering corrections as if they were weather reports, which made them easier to hear and somehow harder to fix. "But your bow arm is better. You've stopped strangling the frog."

"That sounds like a compliment with a crime in it."

"Drink your tea and tune."

He plucked the A again and the tuner settled at 437, its needle sulking left of center. He eased the peg up until the screen flashed 440 and green. Then, because he was sixteen and curious and Mrs. Okonkwo had gone back to the kettle, he slid his first finger down the string and played the A an octave higher, just to hear it ring.

The tuner read 880.

He stared at it. He plucked the low A, then the high A, then the low again, like a magician checking his own trick. The numbers doubled, exactly, every time. He said it out loud, quietly, because saying things out loud made them real: "A note one octave higher vibrates at exactly twice its frequency." He looked toward the kitchen to see whether anyone would catch him talking to a tuner, but the kettle was shrieking and Mrs. Okonkwo was arguing with it in Igbo.

When she came back, he showed her. "Watch. Low A, 440. High A, 880. The octave is just... double."

She set the mugs down and watched the screen, and something in her face shifted from teacher to player, which he had learned was the better of her two faces. "You found that yourself?"

"The tuner told on the string. I just listened."

For a second he thought she would launch into one of her lectures, the kind his father called "the professor voice," but instead she picked up her own cello and played the two As herself, slow, the low one humming under his collarbone and the high one arriving like a smaller, brighter version of the same voice. Same note, doubled. He heard it differently now that he knew the arithmetic underneath, and that bothered him a little, the way knowing a magic trick's mechanism can bother you.

Here was the problem he chewed on all through the C major scale she made him play twice: his grandfather, who had been dead since Justin was eleven, had hummed that minuet without knowing a single number. To him the octave had been a feeling, a place in the air you could reach. Justin had the tuner and the doubling and the green blinking light, and he had the feeling too, sometimes, late at night, when the string rang and something in his chest rang after it. He was not sure the two ways of knowing could live in the same person, or whether one of them made the other smaller. His friend Dez, an ideologue about analog everything, had told him last week that tuners "kill music," and Justin had defended the tuner without quite believing his own defense.

"Mrs. Okonkwo," he said, setting the bow down. "Did you know about the doubling when you started?"

"Of course. Conservatory makes you memorize frequencies like a drill sergeant."

"Does knowing it ever ruin it?"

She sipped her tea and let the question sit there, and he could see her deciding against an easy answer, the shadows of three different lectures seeming to adumbrate behind her eyes before she chose none of them. "I forget it when I play," she said. "I remember it when I teach. You'll find your own arrangement." Then she tapped the minuet book on the stand. "Again. From the third measure, and this time let the octave at the end open up. Don't press it. Just double it."

He set his fingers, drew the bow, and the low A hummed out at 440, and when he reached up for the octave, he didn't look at the tuner at all.

The radiator under Nadia's window made a sound like a spoon in a kettle, and Laura had stopped noticing it until Nadia's brother Samir came in from the balcony with a stack of papers and dropped them on the table between the cereal bowls.

"They want it in writing by Friday," he said. He was twenty-four, three years into a job at the hospital, and he was trying to buy a flat. "The bank's agreed in principle. It's real, more or less."

Nadia picked up a page and turned it sideways. "More or less is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

Laura had come over to work on their presentation for English, a comparison of two war poets that neither of them had started, and the folder of poems was still zipped in her bag. But the papers had a gravity to them, columns of figures and a stamp in the corner, and she found herself leaning across the table before she'd decided to.

"The whole thing's four hundred and twenty," Samir said, tapping a number. "I've got sixty saved. That sixty is the down payment, the part I pay upfront so I borrow less. The loan covers the rest, and then it's mine, in theory, in twenty-five years."

"It'll never be yours, you'll be paying the interest forever," Nadia said, in the jaundiced way she said everything about money, as though the whole economy had personally disappointed her. "You should just rent like Mum does. Renting's simpler. One deposit at the start, that's it."

The word snagged somewhere in Laura's head. "Wait," she said. "Deposit. Like the deposit we paid on this flat? The one you get back when you leave?"

Samir looked at her for a second, and then he laughed, not unkindly. "No, different thing entirely. Same word. When I was in Manchester the adviser kept saying deposit, and I thought he meant my renter's deposit from the old place, like I'd somehow use that. Took me half the meeting to work out we were talking about two different things." He pulled a pen from behind the radiator, where Nadia stored everything, and wrote on the back of an envelope. "Here. Down payment. That's what we call it. A deposit's the British word for the same thing. The part of the home's price the buyer pays upfront, so less must be borrowed."

"That's a terrible system," Laura said. "Two meanings of one word for the two biggest payments of your life."

"It's the phonetics that get you," Samir said, pleased with himself. "Same sounds, same stress, and your brain just files it under the first thing you ever learned the word for. I sat there nodding along like I understood."

Nadia went to the kitchen for tea, and Laura read the papers more slowly than she'd read anything in weeks. There was a line for the mortgage, which she'd always thought of as one thing and now saw was a loan like any other, something a bank gave you and then watched you repay with an expression of professional patience. There was a line for the survey, the legal fees, the insurance. There was the sixty thousand, marked as the buyer's own contribution, and beside it the borrowing, which was three hundred and sixty, and she did the subtraction twice because the number seemed too large to be a subtraction a person could live inside of.

Her parents rented. She had watched her mother photograph every scuff on every wall the day they moved into their house, because the deposit came back only if the walls matched the photographs, and she had understood, at thirteen, that a certain amount of money belonged to her family only in the sense that it was being held somewhere, waiting, possibly forever. She had thought that was what money did when it came to housing. It waited. Now she saw there was another whole architecture underneath it, one where money went in first and bought a share of something, and the waiting happened afterward, for decades, in monthly pieces.

Samir was on the phone now by the window, saying "yes, I can transfer it Monday" in a voice pitched lower than his normal one, and Nadia came back with two mugs and set one down in front of Laura without asking.

"Don't let him make it sound heroic," Nadia said quietly. "Mum says the bank owns it till the end. He says he owns it from the start. They've been arguing about it since Easter."

"They're both right, maybe," Laura said. "Or it's both at once, and which one you are depends on which month you ask." She turned the envelope over, where Samir had written the two words side by side, down payment, deposit, and then a small arrow between them. She took out her phone and photographed it, telling herself it was for the presentation folder, knowing it wasn't.

"Whose are you?" Nadia asked. "The renters or the buyers?"

"I don't know yet. I don't even know what I'll be earning." Laura said it plainly, because it was true, and because around Nadia she could say true things without dressing them up. "I like that he's paying toward something. I like that Mum can leave any year she wants. I can't get both."

Samir hung up and turned around, holding the envelope. "You took a photo of my handwriting?"

"It was good handwriting," Laura said, and pulled the poetry folder out of her bag at last, and unzipped it on top of the mortgage papers. "Now explain to us what a war poet and a bank have in common, because we have six hours and no thesis."

Samir sat down and stole a spoonful of Nadia's cereal. "They both know exactly how much everything costs," he said, "and neither of them ever says it out loud."

Hudson had never once been wrong about a number, which was the kind of thing he told people at parties, or would have, if he went to parties. Instead he told Priya Nair, third row, business class, Tuesday morning, that the GST on her calculator receipt was seven percent. He knew this the way he knew his own birthday. The GST, he said, had been seven percent since it started, and anyone who thought otherwise was confusing it with something provincial.

Priya held up the receipt. She had bought a coffee and a muffin at the place across from the school, and the tax line read something smaller than seven percent of the total. She did not say anything. She just turned the paper toward him and let the number sit there in the fluorescent light, and Mr. Okonkwo, who had a rule about never settling an argument for them, wrote "verify" on the board and kept taking attendance.

Hudson worked Thursdays and Saturdays at Frayne's Hardware, where his job was mostly restocking and occasionally the register when Doreen took her break. His paycheque had arrived Monday, and he had stared at it longer than he'd ever stared at any document in his life. The top number, the gross pay, was generous, heroic, a number you could build a summer on. Then came the column beneath it, and the summer shrank. Income tax, it said, in a small black abbreviation. CPP. EI. Deductions, plural, each one taking its share before the money ever reached his hands. He had folded the cheque stub into his wallet like evidence in a case he hadn't decided to bring yet.

That Thursday, a man bought a socket set and a roll of duct tape, and while the receipt printed, Hudson, still stinging from Tuesday, found himself narrating. "See that tax line," he said, pointing. "GST. Seven percent, federally. Hasn't changed." The man said "huh" in the tone of someone buying duct tape, and left, and Hudson looked at the receipt still curling out of the printer and did the arithmetic in his head. Five. The line was five percent of the subtotal, exactly, the way a thing is exactly what it is when you finally bother to look.

He should say something to Priya. He metabolized this over the shift, turning it over the way Doreen turned the CLOSED sign at closing, slowly, and with some resistance. It wasn't that admitting error was impossible; it was that his error had been so confident, so birthday-certain, and he could feel the difference between being right and merely never having been checked.

Friday he looked it up on his phone behind the paint aisle. The GST had come in on January 1, 1991, at seven percent. Since January 1, 2008, it had been five. Both facts sat side by side on the screen, and Hudson had the strange sensation of having been half-right, of holding one true thing from one decade and one true thing from another and having glued them together wrong. His father, he remembered now, had complained about the tax when it arrived, back when complaining was seven-percent sized. That was probably where Hudson's certainty had come from: inherited grievance, passed down like a watch.

In class on Monday, Mr. Okonkwo had them filling out a practice return, the T1 kind, the real shape of the thing. Hudson entered his wages from Frayne's, subtracted his deductions, watched his taxable income become a smaller and more honest number. Priya, beside him, was faster at it. "So the GST," she said, not looking up from her form. "It was seven when it started in ninety-one. Five since the start of 2008. I looked it up." Hudson said, "I know. I found out Thursday." It came out flatter than he intended, and she glanced over, waiting for the rest.

Here was what he hadn't figured out yet, and what he turned over on the walk home: whether a country that keeps a ledger on every coffee, that skims its share off the top of every seventeen-year-old's paycheque before the money is even money, is a technocracy or just a very patient kind of agreement. Maybe both. Maybe the GST at five percent was the government being generous, or being clever, or being tired of arguing at seven. He didn't know, and he noticed that not knowing felt different now, less like a gap and more like a door. He stopped at the coffee place, ordered a muffin, epicurean choice, blueberry, and stood over the receipt doing the math slowly, twice.

"You're blocking the counter," the barista said.

"Five percent," Hudson said, and stepped aside, still holding the receipt.

Grandpa's house smelled of cedar and old vinyl, and in the back room stood a violin that had belonged to Great-Uncle Theodore, who had, according to family legend, once played for a room of unimpressed chickens. Ryan had inherited the instrument in June, along with a beginner's book and a standing invitation to practice there on Saturdays, because his apartment had thin walls and a neighbor who referred to herself, without apparent irony, as a connoisseur of silence.

On the third Saturday, his nine-year-old cousin Priya showed up with her own violin, half-sized and sparkly at the chin rest. She had a lesson nearby and their grandfather had offered to keep her for the afternoon. While Ryan wrestled through a page of quarter notes, chin cramped, eyes pinned to the staff, Priya wandered to the piano in the hallway and picked out, plink by plink, the melody of a commercial she liked. Then she did the same thing on her violin, from memory, in tune.

"How," Ryan said, not as a question so much as an accusation.

"I just hear it," Priya said, shrugging, as if he had asked how she breathed. "Can you play the ice cream song?" She hummed it. He could not. His fingers knew where to go only when the notes were printed in front of him, marching in orderly black ranks. Take the paper away and he had nothing, which was galling in a way he couldn't quite articulate to a fourth grader.

He thought of the autumn audition, back before he owned a violin at all, when the middle school orchestra teacher had asked him to echo three notes on the piano and he had laughed nervously and said, "I'm more of a reader." He hadn't gotten the seat. Mr. Kessler hadn't even looked up from his clipboard, just said "Mm," in a tone Ryan still remembered with a small internal wince. Priya would have echoed those notes and then harmonized with them out of pure boredom.

"What does your teacher do," he asked, "in lessons? Do you get books?" Priya said yes, actually, a red one, but they mostly copied her teacher first, listening and repeating, and they didn't read the notes yet, even though she'd been playing two years. Ryan frowned at that. Two years without reading seemed, at first glance, like a scam, or at minimum a doctrinaire way of doing things, some rigid philosophy imposed on small children. He was halfway into composing a lecture about it when Priya said, "It's the Suzuki method. My mom says it's how you learn to talk first, before you read."

He opened his mouth to argue and then closed it, because the comparison landed before he could get defensive. Nobody handed a baby a phonics workbook. Babies heard, imitated, garbled, improved. Priya's fingers had a vocabulary his didn't, though he could decode anything on the page, name the key, count the rhythm. She spoke; he read aloud, slowly. Neither was worse, exactly. They were just built in a different order, and the uncomfortable, interesting truth was that he would need both, and Priya would too, eventually, when the red book gave way to actual notation.

Their grandfather appeared in the doorway holding two glasses of lemonade and his own want, which he had been carrying around all summer: he wanted to hear Theodore's violin play "Shenandoah" just once before he stopped being able to say the sentence casually. He had assumed Ryan would learn it from sheet music, properly, the way their family did things. Now he looked between the two of them, and Priya, who loved an audience more than she loved dessert, offered to learn it by ear if he would hum it. "You hum terribly," Ryan told him. "Debatable," said Grandpa, and hummed anyway, wavering on the high part.

Priya got the phrase in four tries. Grandpa acceded to her rhythm, slowing his humming to her tempo rather than the reverse, which Ryan understood was a kind of surrender for a man who conducted from his armchair. Then Priya taught the phrase to Ryan, note by note, no paper, and he got it wrong, and wrong, and then, suddenly, right, and the sound of it coming out of Theodore's old violin made all three of them go quiet. "Again," Grandpa said, and set down his lemonade.

The folding chairs had been set in rows across the basketball court, and the banners from conference championships hung motionless in the heat, and John stood in the hallway outside the gymnasium with a cardboard cap sliding down his forehead and an envelope folded into his gown's inner pocket. The envelope held his father's handwriting on one side: open after. He had carried it for eleven days without opening it, a feat he managed mostly by not being home.

"You're humming," said Priya beside him, adjusting her tassel for the fourth time. "You always hum when you're nervous. It's your mannerism, like cracking knuckles." John stopped, then started again, softer. The tune was the one everyone knew, the one that walked brides of learning down gymnasium aisles across the continent, and he realized he had no idea where it had come from. It felt older than the building. It felt like it had always been here, the way the pledge of allegiance felt like it had always been in classrooms, which he knew was wrong, because everything came from somewhere.

"Do you know what this song even is?" he asked. Priya shrugged. Behind them, Mr. Okafor, who taught shop and had agreed to marshal the line, checked his watch and told them they had six minutes. John pulled out his phone, shielded it against his gown, and searched. The first result made him laugh out loud, a short bark that turned heads down the line. "It's Elgar," he said. "Pomp and Circumstance March Number One. It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool." He said it again in his head, letting the facts settle. Liverpool, not Boston, not Toronto. A march written by an Englishman a hundred and twenty some years before this gymnasium was even a twinkle in a school board's eye, and now it belonged to every graduate in North America by pure accumulation. Things traveled. Things got adopted and worn smooth and nobody asked anymore.

Priya peered at his screen. "So we're walking in to a Liverpool march." "We're walking in to a Liverpool march," John said, and pocketed the phone as the double doors swung open and the band, eleven students who had learned the piece in three weeks, struck up the first chords.

The problem was not the march. The problem was that in the envelope his father had written something, and John had a suspicion, and the suspicion had kept him from sleeping properly for a week. He was supposed to leave for State in August. He had already paid the housing deposit with money from two summers at Delgado's garage, where his father had gotten him the job, where his father had worked since before John could read. Then in April his father's shoulder had gone bad, the real kind of bad, surgical, and Delgado had said, carefully, in the tangential way men said important things, that the shop could use a steady pair of hands through the fall. Nobody had asked John anything. His father had simply stopped discussing the fall entirely, which was itself an answer.

They processed in. John found his row, sat, folded his hands, watched the principal shake hands with the school board president. The speeches began. The salutatorian talked about roads and journeys. John's mind kept circling back, and he tried to forestall the spiral by counting the ceiling tiles, but the counting turned into a rhythm and the rhythm turned back into Elgar, who had written a march for a city in England and could not have imagined this: eight hundred folding chairs, a boy in a rented gown deciding two lives in one afternoon.

When they stood to cross the stage, row by row, the line moved faster than he expected. Priya went before him, pumping her fist, and then there was a gap, and a woman with the name cards said "John," and he walked. The handshake, the scroll, the flash of his mother's camera from the bleachers, his father beside her with his arm in a sling, standing anyway, mouth open in a shout John couldn't hear. And it was on the way back down the stairs that he understood what he had been refusing to understand for eleven days: his father had not written open after so that John would make a decision. He had written it so that John would know that his father had already made one, whatever it was, and that John could stop carrying the weight of guessing. The envelope was not a demand. It was a hand letting go, or reaching out, and John would not know which until he read it.

Afterward, in the parking lot, caps and gowns already peeling off in the heat, John sat on the tailgate of his father's truck and opened the envelope. Inside was a single sheet and a photograph of the two of them outside Delgado's, John fourteen, holding a wrench too big for his hand. The sheet said: Go. We'll figure the shop out. Your mother says to tell you she's proud. P.S. Elgar, right? Looked it up. English fellow. Funny that we all march to it. John laughed, folded the letter along its creases, and put it in his wallet behind his driver's license.

His father came across the lot, sling swinging, keys jingling. "You opened it." "I opened it." "And?" John slid off the tailgate and stood. "And I'll call Delgado tonight. Tell him thanks, and that I'll be back Christmas break if he still wants hands." His father looked at him a long moment, then nodded once, the way he did when an engine turned over clean. He tossed John the keys. "You drive," he said.

Hunter got to the counter at 7:52, eight minutes before the manager locked the door and turned the sign, and ordered the largest black coffee they would sell him. The mug warmed his hands while his phone sat face down on the table like a card he was refusing to turn over. Maya and Devon were already wedged into the corner booth, arguing the way they argued about everything, which is to say loudly enough that the last barista kept glancing over.

"It's simple," Devon said. "You get the grades, you get in. Dana had a 4.0 and she's at Ridgemont. Case closed."

"That is not what happened to Dana." Maya peeled the sleeve off her cup in one long strip. "My cousin had a 4.0 and got flat rejected from three schools. Grades don't guarantee anything."

"Then what's the point of working for them?"

Hunter turned his phone over, then face down again. He had been turning it over for two days, since the email from Weldon had arrived with a subject line he still hadn't opened. The deposit deadline was midnight tonight. His mother had already filled out the forms for Hartley, the safety school, the one with the good program and the wrong everything else, and she'd said, gently, that they couldn't hold both checks past Friday.

"Guys," he said. "You're arguing past each other."

"Nobody asked, Hunter."

"I know nobody asked." He pulled a napkin toward him and borrowed Maya's pen. "Look. Devon says grades get you in. Maya says grades don't get you in. Both of you have examples. So maybe the truth is weirder than either of you is saying."

Devon leaned back with the particular boredom of a boy who had heard Hunter do this before. Maya, at least, leaned in, because Maya liked an argument the way some people liked storms, and watching her follow a line of reasoning had a way of enrupturing a whole table, even strangers two booths over.

"Think about the sun," Hunter said. "Direct sunlight. For it to hit you, the sun has to be above the horizon. No sun above the horizon, no direct sunlight, period."

"Obviously," Devon said.

"But the sun can be above the horizon and you still don't get direct sunlight, because you're standing in a shadow. Something's in the way. So the sun being up is necessary but it's not sufficient." He wrote the two words on the napkin and underlined them. "Necessary means it has to hold for the thing to happen. Sufficient means it's enough by itself. Grades are like the sun. If you don't have them, you're out. But having them doesn't mean you're in. Something else can cast a shadow."

The barista began stacking chairs somewhere behind them. Maya was quiet for a second, which for Maya was a tectonic event, a whole continent of argument shifting before it settled. "So Dana and your cousin both had the sun," she said slowly. "And your cousin was standing in a shadow."

"Something like that. Maybe the essay. Maybe nothing he could see."

"That's depressing," Devon said.

"It's not." Hunter found he actually meant this. "It just means the argument changes. Stop arguing whether grades are enough. Start arguing what the shadows are, and which ones you can move out of."

It was Maya who noticed his phone, who reached over and flipped it before he could stop her, and who read the subject line out loud with her eyebrows already climbing. Weldon Admissions Decision. Sent forty-nine hours ago. The whole booth went still, and the espresso machine hissed into the silence like it had opinions.

"You haven't opened it," she said.

"The deposit's due at midnight. If it's a no, I send Hartley's check tonight and it's done. If I open it and it's a no, it's still done, just sooner." He picked the phone up. It was heavier than a phone should be. "If it's a yes, then I have to figure out money in three hours, and my mom already signed the other forms, and I don't even know which of those is the shadow and which is the sun."

"Open it," Devon said.

"Hunter," Maya said, quieter, "the sun being up doesn't mean you get the light. But you're never going to know what's in the way from under this table."

The barista called last call from the counter with her keys already in her hand. Hunter pressed his thumb to the screen, watched the blur of the loading circle, and pulled the phone close so only he could see it, while Maya and Devon leaned in on either side of him and the first chairs went up on the far tables, one by one, like a count reaching zero.

The line outside the fire station moved in short, patient shuffles, and Sophia stood in it with her registration card going soft at the edges in her hand. Behind her, Marcus was still talking about the poll from Tuesday, the one he had screenshotted and sent to the group chat at midnight.

"Four-point lead," he said now, tapping her shoulder as if the number itself needed emphasis. "Margin of error is three. So even at the worst case, it's still a lead. It's basically over."

"It's not basically over," Sophia said. The man in front of them, older, in a coat too warm for November, glanced back and then returned to his newspaper.

"Three from four is one," Marcus said. "One is still bigger than zero. That's arithmetic, Sophia."

She had done that same arithmetic herself on Tuesday night, lying on her bed with her phone held above her face, and it had felt airtight, almost like a proof. She remembered the satisfaction of it, the way certainty had settled over her like a warm blanket. She had even typed a message to the chat saying the race was decided and it was pointless to argue about it anymore. She had never sent it. Something about the typing had slowed her down, the way copying a sentence slowly can transcribe doubt into a person, and she had deleted it instead and lain in the dark listening to the radiator tick.

The line advanced. Inside the station, the smell changed to floor wax and burnt coffee, and volunteers at folding tables called out street names in flat, unhurried voices. A woman with a lanyard checked Sophia's card, circled something, and pointed her toward a machine she didn't recognize from the diagrams she'd studied.

"First time?" the woman asked.

"First time."

The woman's smile was brief and genuine. "It goes faster than you think."

While Sophia waited for the machine, an argument caught her attention from the far table, where a younger poll worker in a hoodie was talking with a man holding a printed page. "You can't read it like that," the poll worker was saying. "The margin of error applies to each candidate's share, not to the gap. The margin of error for the lead is about twice as large."

Sophia stood very still. The words arranged themselves in her mind next to Marcus's arithmetic, and the arithmetic came apart. A four-point lead with a three-point margin of error was not a floor of one. Each share could move; the lead itself could move by more. She turned the idea over and could not make it sit still. Six, roughly, was the number for the gap, and six swallowed four whole.

"Marcus," she said quietly, when she was back beside him in the line for the stickers, "I think we had it wrong. The three points, it applies to each candidate's share. Not to the lead. The lead's margin is about twice as large."

He frowned at her, then at the gymnasium floor, the scuffed lanes of a basketball court visible under the folding tables. "Who told you that?"

"I heard it. Just now. And it makes sense of why I couldn't sleep Tuesday."

"You couldn't sleep over a poll?"

"I couldn't sleep because I was sure, and being sure felt too easy."

He didn't answer right away. A volunteer handed them stickers, the cheap kind, the adhesive already evanescent against her jacket sleeve, and Marcus pressed his onto his notebook like it was something to keep. She thought of her mother, who had once admitted, over dishes, that she hadn't voted in her first eligible election because the polls had said it was a landslide anyway, and who had refused, ever after, to tell anyone which election it was. The memory had always seemed like a small shame in the family. Now it seemed like something more complicated, a whole vote surrendered to a number that could not carry the weight assigned to it.

At the machine, Sophia made her choices. Her hand hovered longer than she had expected it to, not from indecision about the candidates but from the strangeness of the act itself, this private, unprovable moment that no poll had ever measured and no margin could contain. In her biology class they had spent October building a phylogeny of the hominids, tracing which fragments of skull descended from which, and she had learned that a tree of life is only as honest as its uncertainty, that scientists draw some branches with solid lines and some with dotted ones. The poll's dotted line had been the gap all along, and she had traced it solid.

When she came out, Marcus was waiting under the bare maple by the curb, breath fogging.

"So it could be losing," he said. It wasn't quite a question.

"It could be a lot of things. That's what the number actually says."

"It says less than I thought it did."

"Everybody says it says more than it does," Sophia said. She looked back at the fire station, at the line still stretching out the door into the gray afternoon, people waiting on the strength of numbers they mostly hadn't examined. Somewhere in that line was someone deciding not to bother, the way her mother once had. Somewhere in it was someone sure of an outcome the way she had been sure on Tuesday night.

"Then what's the point of polls?" Marcus asked.

She zipped her jacket higher. "They tell you where the fog is," she said. "They don't tell you what's inside it."

She started walking toward the bus stop, and after a moment, she heard his footsteps behind her.

The gymnasium had been arranged into rows of folding tables facing a raised platform, and by eight forty-five the Grade Eleven model parliament was already arguing about whether the Speaker's coffee counted as a recess privilege. Brandon sat in the third row for the government side with his bill clipped to a binder, the pages soft from being thumbed through all week. It was called the School Food Disclosure Act, and it required the cafeteria to post where its produce came from. He had drafted it alone at his kitchen table on a Tuesday night, folding in a clause his older sister suggested about allergen labels, because she said a bill with two ideas in it was harder to dismiss.

The clerk read the title for first reading, and Brandon rose to move that the bill be read a first time and printed. It passed without debate, which he had learned was the custom, bills being introduced like strangers at a door. Then came the part he had not prepared for. The Speaker assigned the bill to committee, six members drawn from both sides, and for two days they took it apart in a corner classroom with a whiteboard that still bore the ghost of a chemistry diagram, some igneous rock cycle half-erased behind the chair's head.

The committee was where his bill changed. A girl named Priya from the opposition moved an amendment that would exempt the cafeteria's outside vendors from the disclosure rule, on the argument that the school couldn't compel businesses it only rented space to. Brandon resisted it at first, and then, listening to the committee chair read the amendment aloud a second time, he heard the logic of it sitting there plainly, like a coin on a table. He voted with the amendment. One of his own caucus members called him a pragmatist in a tone that made it sound like a diagnosis, and another, later, in the hallway, called him an egoist who just wanted the bill to pass with his name on it. He carried both words around for an evening before deciding they were not the same accusation, and that only the second one was unfair.

Second reading was the debate on principle, and it went longer than anyone expected. Brandon spoke for four minutes on the idea that students deserved to know what they were eating, and an opposition member named Theo spent six minutes on the cost of signage and the burden on the cafeteria manager, who, he pointed out, was one woman with a laminator. The chamber divided, and the tellers counted raised hands. The bill passed second reading by a margin of three, which felt to Brandon like walking across a frozen creek and hearing one small crack beneath his left boot.

Between readings, Theo found him at the water fountain. Brandon expected a fight and got something else, a quiet question about whether the committee's amendment had actually weakened the bill's purpose, since the vendors supplied nearly half the food. Brandon said he had thought about that too. He said the amended bill covered less ground but stood on firmer ground, and he admitted he was not certain the trade was worth it. Theo said he wasn't certain either, which was, in its way, the most honest exchange of the whole conference.

On the final morning the Speaker called the bill for its last stage. "We now proceed to third reading," she said, "the final debate and vote on the bill as amended, after its details have been examined in committee." Brandon wrote the words in the margin of his copy, not because he would forget them but because he wanted the sentence to exist in his handwriting. Everything the committee had done, the amendment, the clause on allergens, the exemption Priya had argued for, all of it was now fused into the text he was standing to defend, and this was the last door it had to pass through.

Debate was brief and almost gentle. Theo rose to speak against the bill one more time, but he did not proselytize about cafeteria freedom the way he had on second reading; he simply restated the cost concern, said the amended version had addressed most of his objection, and sat down. Priya spoke in favour. Brandon closed for the government with a short speech he had rewritten at midnight, saying the bill was smaller than the one he had drafted and better than the one he had imagined, and that he had learned the difference between those two things in a corner classroom with a half-erased rock cycle on the board.

The chamber divided. The tellers counted. The Speaker announced that the bill had passed third reading and declared, "I do assent to this bill," tapping the gavel once, and the clerk recorded the assent in the minutes of the day. Under the rules of the model parliament, the Food Disclosure Act was now law, binding in theory on a cafeteria that would never hear of it. Brandon looked down at his binder, at the sentence he had written in the margin, and then across the chamber at Theo, who caught his eye and gave a small shrug, palms up. Brandon shrugged back, picked up his pen, and drew a thin line under the words on the page.

The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Brody stood in the middle of the living room where the previous family had left faint rectangles on the carpet, and the movers had set his boxes along one wall in a line that looked like a small city seen from a plane. Somewhere outside, a sprinkler ticked across a lawn that didn't know him yet.

He found his phone in his back pocket and texted Marcus first, because Marcus would be awake even at ten in the morning on a Tuesday. "Landed. House is empty." Then he took a photo of the boxes and sent that too, because Marcus liked evidence.

The reply came in pieces, the way Marcus always texted, a thought arriving and then being corrected. "looks like a prison." Then, "of boxes." Then, "you find the kitchen yet."

Brody walked through the rooms to check. Kitchen: white counters, a window over the sink facing a backyard with one tree. He opened the fridge, which hummed at him like it was clearing its throat, and found nothing inside but a roll of quarters his mother must have left for the moving truck guys. He took two quarters and put them back. Even the small kindnesses in this house belonged to someone else's plan.

Upstairs, in what would be his room, he sat on the floor between two boxes and did the thing he'd been avoiding for the whole drive, which was to look at how many days of summer were left before school started. Twenty-six. Under that calculation sat a heavier one, the thing he'd read three nights ago at two in the morning in his old room with the walls already stripped of posters. He'd gone down a rabbit hole about making friends after a move, and one page had stopped him cold: a researcher named Jeffrey Hall, in a 2018 study, had estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together. Ninety hours. He'd lain there doing the arithmetic against the ceiling. If school was seven hours a day and you counted every minute, it would take almost thirteen school days, and nobody counted every minute, because most minutes you were just sitting near people, which didn't count, or did it, he didn't know, nobody had defined near.

He'd tried it out on Marcus before he left, sitting on the tailgate of Mr. Alvarez's truck while they loaded the last of the stereo equipment.

"Guess how long it takes to make a real friend," Brody had said. "Guess the hours."

"From nothing? Or from like, knowing the guy?"

"That's the thing, there's a difference. Casual friend to actual friend. This study says about 90 hours together."

Marcus had whistled, low, the way he did when a price came back higher than expected. "How long did we take?"

Brody had done that math too, lying awake. Six years of lunch periods, but you couldn't just multiply, because the first two years they'd barely spoken, and then the camping trip, and then junior year when Marcus's parents split and Brody had come over every day for a month without being asked. Whatever the real number was, it was enormous, and it was already spent, and that was what made it valuable and what made leaving feel like theft.

In the new room, he texted: "90 hours to make a real friend. im doing the math and its brutal."

"so skip casual. go straight to loyal," Marcus wrote back. Then: "join a club. same faces every week, it compounds."

Brody almost laughed at the idea of Marcus giving him advice, since Marcus's usual strategy in any new group was to become a sycophant to whoever seemed in charge, complimenting shoes and laughing at jokes that hadn't earned it, until he'd secured a position and could relax into being himself. It had worked, more or less, for years. Brody had watched it work and had never once considered it tenable for himself, not because he was nobler but because he couldn't act that well. The two of them had built their friendship on the difference, on Brody saying the flat thing and Marcus saying the smooth one.

The trouble was that now, in a town where he knew nobody, the flat thing felt like a luxury. You needed standing before bluntness read as honesty instead of hostility.

He got up and went downstairs, where his mother was taping labels onto cabinet doors so the unpacking wouldn't incapacitate her tomorrow, she said, when the fatigue hit. She had a system for everything. She looked up when he came in, and he could see her doing her own arithmetic, counting his silence like a bill coming due.

"There's a bike shop on Marsh Road," she said. "The sign said they're hiring. I know you didn't ask."

"I didn't ask."

"I know." She went back to her labels, then stopped, tape hanging off her thumb. "There's also a flyer at the grocery store. Some astronomy club, meets at the community college Thursdays. I took a picture of it, but I didn't sign you up for anything, I just. Took the picture."

He looked at the photo when she sent it to him, standing in the empty kitchen with the fridge humming behind him. Meets weekly, all levels, beginners welcome. Thursday nights from now until the school year ended. He counted the Thursdays out of habit, then counted the hours, three per night, and found the number was big enough to be a promise even though it was only arithmetic, and only about being in the same room.

He texted Marcus the flyer photo. Under it he wrote, "same faces every week."

He pulled his shoes back on, found his bike leaning against the garage wall where the movers had left it, and rode toward Marsh Road to see what a town he'd never chosen looked like at street level, the sun hot on the back of his neck, the flyer's picture still open on his phone in his pocket.

Hayden had waited until eighteen to learn to drive, which his mother said was sensible and his uncle said was cowardly, and the truth was neither, or both. He had put it off the way he put off dentist appointments, and then the summer before college had arrived with no more excuses in it. Now he sat in the driver's seat of the family Corolla in the empty lot behind the church on Delmar, his hands at ten and two, his mother in the passenger seat with her coffee held between her knees like something fragile.

"Foot on the brake, then start it," she said. He did, and the engine came alive under him, a vibration he felt in his teeth. He had imagined this moment for years, and in the imagining it had always felt like freedom, but the actual feeling was closer to being handed something heavy and breakable in a crowded room.

He let the car creep forward in the lot, turning wide, careful circles around the light poles. His mother adjusted the mirror on her side without comment, which he understood as a comment. When he braked too hard the second time, she set her coffee in the cup holder and said, "Smoother. Like you're setting it down, not catching it." He tried again and the car settled without lurching, and something in him loosened, and then immediately tightened again, because loosening was exactly what he could not afford.
