Then he picked up his pencil and worked the derivative, and after that the next one, while behind him the machine hissed on.

Laura had signed up because her guidance counselor said forty hours of volunteering would look good on applications, and because her mother had said, more quietly, that it would be good for her in other ways she'd have to figure out herself. The food bank ran out of the basement of the seniors' residence on Ashrow Street, folding tables stacked with pasta and tins, and on her first Saturday the coordinator handed her a clipboard and a hairnet and told her to greet people at the door.

That was where she met Mrs. Okonjo, who came down from the third floor in a green housecoat and slippers and looked at the tables with an expression Laura couldn't read at first. Not embarrassment, she decided. Something more like appraisal. "You're new," Mrs. Okonjo said. "The last girl stood by the elevator like a security guard. You don't have to do that. Nobody here is going to steal a can of peaches."

Laura laughed, and then a man in a windbreaker took a numbered card from her clipboard and she forgot about the conversation for a while, because there was an actual line, actual people, an old fellow who wanted only soup and a young mother who asked whether the baby formula had an expiry date and Laura had to go check. It had not occurred to her, before Saturday, that a food bank line would contain people who lived in the building itself, upstairs, above the very tables they were queuing for.

During the lull, Mrs. Okonjo settled into a folding chair beside her and asked how old the food bank was. Laura said she didn't know, probably pretty old, and Mrs. Okonjo snorted. "You think so? I remember when there weren't any." She counted on her fingers. "Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981. I was a grown woman already." Laura did the arithmetic twice, because it couldn't be right, and Mrs. Okonjo watched her do it and smiled the way people smile when they've won a small argument with the whole idea of a country.

"Less than fifty years," Laura said. "But before that, what did people do?" Mrs. Okonjo shrugged. "Neighbours, mostly. Or they went hungry quietly." She nodded toward the tables. "My mother would rather have starved than stand in a line where her friends could see her. It stigmatized you, that was the word for it, being known as someone who needed." She said it flatly, a fact about the past rather than a complaint, and then she added that none of this was germane to whether the peaches were good, and demanded Laura open a can for her.

While they ate peaches with plastic forks, a volunteer named Dev, a college student with a laminated map of Canada on the wall, overheard them and admitted he'd assumed food banks had existed since the war. "Some kind of permanent thing," he said. "Like libraries." Mrs. Okonjo said, "We invented libraries before we invented hunger lines, dear. Draw your own conclusions." Laura wrote the date in the margin of her clipboard so she wouldn't lose it, January 16, 1981, and found herself thinking that a thing could be temporary and permanent at once, an emergency that had lasted her whole life and most of her mother's.

At the end of the shift, Dev found a note that had slipped between two crates of juice, and handed it to Laura because she was nearest. It was written in blue ballpoint on the back of a hydro bill envelope, in careful capital letters: "TO WHOEVER RUNS THIS. LAST MONTH I ONLY TOOK HALF MY SHARE BECAUSE A MAN I WENT TO SCHOOL WITH WAS BEHIND ME AND I DIDN'T WANT HIM TO KNOW HOW LITTLE I HAD. THIS MONTH HE WAS NOT THERE SO I TOOK THE REST. PLEASE DON'T PUT THE BEANS IN THE SAME BOX AS THE PET FOOD, IT IS DEPRESSING. THANK YOU FOR THE RICE. IT WAS GOOD RICE."

Laura read it twice, and her eyes were hot by the end of the second reading, and she couldn't have explained why, exactly, except that the good rice part undid her. She looked up at the ceiling, then at the folding tables, then at Mrs. Okonjo, who was back in her chair waiting for someone to walk her to the elevator. Laura crossed the room, took her arm, and pressed the button for three. "It was the middle door," Mrs. Okonjo said, "the good rice. You put it behind the beans where nobody sees it." Laura said she'd move it to the front table, first thing next Saturday, and Mrs. Okonjo said, "Put the peaches beside it."

Eva had the museum map folded into her back pocket and fifteen minutes before the placement review session started, which was not enough time and was exactly the time she had. She took the escalator two steps at a time to the third floor, where the Hall of Human Biology kept its dim, blue-lit corridor, and found the mitochondria exhibit at the far end, past the plastic brain and the giant walk-in ear.

She had gotten the question wrong on Tuesday. On the practice exam, question forty-one had asked what happens in muscle cells when oxygen runs low, and she had written that lactate builds up as a waste product and shuts the cell down. Her mark came back with a red line through it and a note in the margin: reread fermentation. Daniel, who sat beside her in the review session and had gotten it right, had offered to explain, and she had said no thank you, which had come out colder than she meant. Now it was Saturday, and she was standing in front of a wall display with her phone in her hand, determined to disabuse herself of her own answer before Monday's exam.

The display was called Inside the Powerhouse. A transparent model of a cell the size of a car occupied the middle of the room, its mitochondria picked out in orange. Along the left wall ran a sequence of panels: glucose, glycolysis, pyruvate, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, ATP. She read them in order, resting her fingertips on the railing in front of each one. Glucose split into two molecules of pyruvate, yielding a small payout of ATP. If oxygen was plentiful, the pyruvate went into the mitochondria and the payout grew enormous. If oxygen ran low, the sequence stopped partway, and she stood at that panel for a long time, because the panel stopped partway too. A piece of the interactive screen had gone dark, a recalcitrant gray rectangle where the words about what happened next should have been.

"Are you here for the review session?" a voice asked. A girl of about ten stood beside her, holding a clipboard, a junior docent by her badge. Her badge said Priya.

"No," Eva said. "I'm here to fix my own head. Do you know what this panel says? The one that's out."

Priya looked at the dead rectangle and then at her clipboard. "It's been broken since Thursday. But I know the piece, I had to memorize the script." She read from her clipboard in a flat, rehearsed voice: "When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose."

"Say that again," Eva said. Priya said it again, slower, and Eva typed it into her phone, then deleted it, because typing it was not the same as having it. "So the lactate isn't the poison. It's the fix."

"It's the trade," Priya said, as though correcting a customer who had misread a price. "You get less ATP that way. Two per glucose. But you keep getting it."

Eva walked to the far wall, where a stationary bike sat in front of a heart-rate monitor, part of an exhibit on exertion. She pedaled hard for ninety seconds, watching her pulse climb and feeling the familiar burn arrive in her thighs, the same burn she had felt in August sprinting across her uncle's farm field to beat a storm to the barn. She had thought then that the burn was the moment her legs gave up. She pedaled and understood that it was the moment her cells improvised. Her legs had kept moving through the whole field, which meant the glycolysis had kept going, which meant the NAD+ had kept coming back, which meant the lactate had been on her side the entire time. She slowed the pedals. A woman waiting behind her with a toddler asked if she was done, and Eva got off, still breathing hard.

She took out her phone to text Daniel. She wrote, I was wrong about forty-one. When muscle cells run low on oxygen they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis keeps making 2 ATP per glucose. The lactate isn't what stops you. She looked at the message. It read like the docent's clipboard, flat and complete, and she decided that was fine, because completeness was what she had come for. She sent it.

Daniel replied almost immediately, and his reply was a voice message. She stood under the blue lights with the phone against her ear, sweat cooling on the back of her neck. "Hey," he said. "So first, that's the whole thing, you basically just recited the model answer, nice. Second, I have to tell you something. Professor Ayeni posted an announcement an hour ago. Monday's exam got moved to Friday. Some scheduling thing with the gymnasium." There was a pause with wind in it; he was outside somewhere. "So you spent your Saturday learning this for nothing, kind of."

Eva looked at the broken panel, the gray rectangle that had made her pedal a museum bicycle in front of a toddler to understand a sentence she could have read off a working screen. She thought about the denouement she had been picturing all week: the exam, question forty-one, her pen moving without hesitation, the small private vindication of it. That denouement was gone, or postponed, and the knowledge was still here, sitting in her legs and her phone and her memory, arriving five days early for a party that had been rescheduled.

She put the phone in her pocket and turned back toward the model cell. Priya was leading a family toward the giant ear, clipboard tucked under her arm. Eva caught up with them at the mouth of the walk-in cochlea and tapped the girl on the shoulder.

"Your script," Eva said. "The broken panel. Somebody should tell the front desk it worked anyway."

Mr. Okafor had taped a sample ballot to the whiteboard on Monday, and by Wednesday it was still there, curling at the corners like a leaf deciding whether to fall. He would not tell them how to vote, he said, but he would not let them treat the election as weather, something that simply happened to the country. "You want to historicize it," he said, tapping the board with a knuckle. "Place it. Ask what came before, what forces arranged it. Then you walk in and pull a lever like you mean it." Mason had written the word in his notebook, historicize, and underlined it twice, though mostly he was thinking about the fact that in nine days he would be eighteen, and in eleven days he would vote.

He had registered in September at the DMV, a trip his grandfather had insisted on driving him to even though the office was four blocks from the school and the weather was still warm. In the car afterward, his grandfather had done the thing he always did at moments he considered ceremonial, turning his wedding ring with his thumb, a mannerism Mason had noticed since he was small and had never asked about. "Nobody in my family voted before 1965," his grandfather said at a red light. "Legally, I mean." He didn't say anything else, and Mason hadn't needed him to.

The morning of the election, Mason woke before his alarm. He ate cereal standing up. He took the sample ballot his teacher had photocopied, folded twice, and put it in his jacket pocket along with his driver's license, and he walked the six blocks to the community hall with his breath showing white in front of him and his stomach doing something complicated that was not quite fear.

The line moved slowly, and he spent it listening to two women behind him argue about a school levy in the polite, murderous way of neighbors. When his turn came, he gave his name to a poll worker with reading glasses on a beaded chain, a woman whose son had been in Mason's chemistry class last year. She ran her finger down the list. Ran it again. Flipped a page, then flipped it back, and Mason felt the paper-thin confidence of the morning begin to go out of him like heat from a cracked window.

"I don't see you here, honey," she said. "Are you sure you're at the right precinct?"

He was sure. He had checked twice. He gave his address, his birthday, the September date of the DMV visit, and she shook her head with real regret, and behind him the line shifted its weight, and Mason's face went hot. He thought of the folded sample ballot in his pocket, of the underlined word in his notebook, of his grandfather turning the ring in a stopped car. He was about to ask whether he could just fill something out, some form, when the woman raised a hand toward a younger poll worker at a side table.

"He can do a provisional ballot," the younger woman said.

"What's that mean," Mason asked, and heard how young his voice came out.

"It's under the Help America Vote Act of 2002," she said. "A voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot. It only counts once officials confirm your eligibility." She handed him a form on a clipboard. "You fill this out, your ballot goes in a special envelope, and if they confirm you're registered, it gets counted."

He filled out the form at the side table, his handwriting smaller and more careful than usual, and fed his ballot into its envelope, and the envelope into a folder, and then there was nothing left to do but thank them and walk out. He told no one at school. When Mr. Okafor asked the class, at the end of fourth period, who had voted that morning, Mason raised his hand, and it did not feel like a lie, exactly, but it did not feel entirely like the truth either, and he held both of those feelings at once without deciding between them, the way you hold two books you intend to read.

The twist came nine days later, in the same classroom, during the same period. Mr. Okafor was collecting essays when the front office called down, and a runner brought Mason a sealed envelope, county stationery, and everyone watched him open it because everyone always watches. The letter said his eligibility had been confirmed. His provisional ballot had been counted. The DMV clerk had simply failed to transmit his registration on time, an oversight, no one's malice, a snag in the nascent machinery of his civic life, now repaired.

That night his grandfather called. "So it counted," he said. "So your vote counted."

"It counted," Mason said. "It just counted late." He was quiet a moment, and then, because his grandfather would understand it in a way no one else would, he added, "The election was called before mine counted. It didn't matter."

"Everything matters," his grandfather said, and Mason heard the ring turn against the phone, a small metallic whisper, once, twice.

Violet told herself she had taken the junior counselor job for the experience, and for most of June this was almost true. She liked the mornings at Lakeview Day Camp, the way the five-year-olds arrived with their backpacks still bobbing above their shoulders, the smell of sunscreen and cut grass outside the arts shed. She told her mother she was practically volunteering, since eight dollars an hour was hardly money at all. She did not mention that she had been keeping a tally in the back of her notebook since the first week, a column of hours with small sums beside it, because the tally was just for practice, the way one might practice budgeting.

In the third week of July, Deenie, who ran the oldest campers' group, wrenched her ankle on the dock steps and went home for the summer. The director, Ms. Amara, stood at the picnic table with her clipboard and asked who could cover Deenie's afternoons, the extended-care block that ran until six. Several hands went down again as fast as they had gone up. Violet raised hers and kept it there. By Friday she had worked the morning block, the afternoon block, and two extra days covering the front desk while the receptionist was out, and when she added the column in her notebook she counted fifty-one hours in one week.

She was not counting the money, she reminded herself. She was being useful, which was different. Rosa, her best friend at camp, had a theory about this. "You proselytize about not caring," Rosa said, peeling the label off her water bottle in one long strip. "You convert people to it. That's how much you care about not caring." Violet laughed and said Rosa should have been a lawyer, which was what Rosa's mother was and what Rosa was tired of hearing about.

The paycheck came on the second of August, a thin envelope with a stub inside. Violet read it in the supply closet where the extra life vests hung, because that was the only quiet place at two o'clock. The stub listed her regular hours at eight dollars. Then there was a second line, hours at twelve dollars an hour, eleven of them. Twelve was not a number she had earned anywhere. Eleven was a number she recognized, the amount past forty. She stood there doing arithmetic on the paint-spattered counter, and the total matched exactly, and she felt a small unearned glow, as though she had gotten away with something she had not even attempted.

She decided not to ask about it. If the camp wanted to overpay her, that was the camp's problem, and mentioning it might make someone realize a mistake and take the money back. She rehearsed several versions of this reasoning on the bus home and found all of them convincing. Rosa, when told, was less convinced. "You're being an apologist for your own greed," Rosa said, "and not even greed for money. Greed for being the girl who doesn't ask." Violet said that was the most convoluted compliment she had ever received, and also that Rosa should return the orange crayon she had borrowed in April.

But the twelve dollars sat in her mind the way a pulled thread sits in a sweater. On Monday she went to the office during nap block and found Ms. Amara laminating name tags. Violet put the stub on the desk, faceup, and tapped the second line. "I didn't work any senior hours," she said. "Why are eleven of my hours at twelve dollars?"

Ms. Amara looked at the stub, then at Violet, and something in her expression shifted, a loosening, as if she had been braced for a complaint and received a question instead. "That's not a mistake," she said. "It's the law. Non-exempt employees get one and a half times their regular rate for every hour past forty in a workweek. Eight times one and a half is twelve." She slid the stub back across the desk. "You crossed forty last week, so your last eleven hours paid at twelve. Most of your hours this summer won't, since you're usually under. But when you cover for someone, they can add up fast."

Violet said, mostly to the laminator, "I thought that was only for real jobs." Ms. Amara said the law did not distinguish, not in the way Violet meant, and turned the machine off between name tags. "Half the counselors never read their stubs," she added. "You read yours." She said it without particular praise, as a fact she had observed, and somehow that landed heavier than praise would have.

On the bus home, Violet took out her notebook and, next to her column of hours, wrote a second column, rate, and a third, earned, and filled them in for every week so far. The numbers were smaller than her old estimates, because her old estimates had quietly rounded up. She noticed this about herself and did not entirely know what to do with it, that her careful tally had been careful the way a funhouse mirror is careful. She was, she concluded, a person who liked to seem unconcerned with money while being extremely concerned with it, and she could admit that now without deciding yet whether to change it. Rosa would say this was progress. Rosa would also say the orange crayon thing again.

In August she signed up for two more of Deenie's afternoon blocks, telling Rosa it was for the experience. Rosa raised an eyebrow and said nothing sagacious, which in Rosa's mouth was practically a standing ovation. On the last Friday of the summer, Violet bought two ice creams with her own money from the truck by the lake, and handed one to Rosa, and said, "I'm only letting you think I'm generous. My hours past forty pay time and a half, and I checked the schedule." Rosa took the cone and bit the top off. "Fifty-one hours next week?" she asked, and Violet, watching the older campers tip their canoe in the shallows, said, "Fifty-two."

The field behind the middle school had been Victor's home for eleven summers, and this was the last one. In the fall he'd be two states away, in a dorm, and the league would go on without him, and he found he cared about that more than he'd expected to care about anything all year.

Dex had hit three home runs in the game against Fairlawn, and in the two games after that he'd hit two more, and by Thursday's practice the whole team had organized itself around him. Reyes stood at the cage and called pitches down the middle so Dex could extend. Kirby gave up his spot in the order. When Victor lined into a double play, Dex put a hand on his shoulder in the dugout and said, "Get on for me and I'll cash you in," and it wasn't cruel, which somehow made it worse.

Victor had found the study the way he found most things, chasing a thread past midnight. A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky had concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance. Five makes in a row were exactly what you'd expect from a decent shooter rolling dice. The authors had called the hot hand a fallacy. Victor read it twice, then a third time, feeling something in him go quiet and stubborn. He didn't want it to be true. He wanted Dex to be a machine for one more month, wanted the season to have a shape, a hero, an ending you could narrate. But wanting wasn't evidence, and the paper sat in his browser tab all week like a signed affidavit against the thing the team had decided to believe.

He brought it up wrong, of course. He brought it up in the dugout with Dex six feet away, sweat still on his neck from his third homer in four days.

"Did you know there was a study," Victor said, "1985, Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky? They looked at pro basketball shooters and the streaks were no more common than chance. The hot hand is a fallacy."

Dex looked at him. "I play baseball."

"It's the same idea. Streaks. I'm not saying you're bad. I'm saying the streak doesn't predict the next pitch."

"So pitch me like normal," Dex said, "and watch."

Reyes laughed from the end of the bench. Kirby said something about spreadsheets that made everyone laugh except Victor, and except Dex, who hadn't actually smiled at all.

The coach pulled Victor aside by the fence. He was a good coach, mostly, a plumber who'd aged out of catching and never stopped squinting at the field like it owed him something. "You want to be right," he said, "or you want to win Saturday?" He didn't wait for an answer, which told Victor the coach thought those were the same thing, or that rightness was some obsolescent luxury the moment had outgrown. Victor said nothing. The conversation had a smell he recognized from arguments with his father: both sides talking about the future, neither saying which future.

Saturday they trailed 2-1 in the sixth. Victor led off with a clean single, and the sign came down from the third base box, small and unmistakable: take. Take until Reyes walked or struck out, take the whole at bat, because if Victor was erased on a bunt the inning belonged to Dex three batters later, and Dex was hot. Victor stood in and let a fastball sail over the inner half, a pitch he could have fouled off or driven. He took it. The crowd made its small approving noise. He took the next one, outside, and the one after, thigh-high, and the count ran to 2-2 before Reyes chopped into a force play that put Victor out at second by four steps. He walked back to the dugout through his own breath. He had done what the fallacy asked of him, or what its refutation asked, and it had cost exactly nothing that a bunt wouldn't have. That was the part nobody had prepared him for, that the evidence didn't portend anything in particular, that it sat there being true while the game ignored it.

Dex came up in the seventh with Kirby on first and the outfield playing shallow, and Victor caught himself leaning forward, wanting it, the same wanting as everybody else. Dex worked the count full and struck out on a slider in the dirt. He came back and sat at the far end of the bench and pulled his helmet down over his eyes. Nobody said anything. In the ninth, with two out and the tying run on third, he singled off the wall to tie it, and the team poured off the bench like something breaking open, and Victor was among them, shouting, pounding Dex's back, and honest enough in the noise to admit he had no idea what any of it proved.

They lost in the tenth on a wild pitch. Afterward, packing the gear bag by himself while the lights hummed and moths bounced off the poles, Victor found Dex sitting against the backstop, cleats off, socks in his hand.

"Three for five," Victor said.

"One for nothing, until I wasn't," Dex said. He looked out at the infield. "That study. It's real?"

"It's real."

Dex nodded slowly, working a knot of clay out of his cleat with his thumb. "Next game, swing when they give you something," he said. "Stop taking pitches for me."

Victor slung the bag over his shoulder. The last light was going off beyond the outfield, and the two of them sat there a moment longer, neither one of them sure.

The box had been under the bed in Gran's spare room for as long as Addison could remember, and she had never once been allowed to open it. Tonight Gran had said, almost offhandedly, that she could, which was how Addison knew something had changed, though she did not ask what.

"You're doing that college essay," Gran said from the doorway, hands folded over her cardigan. "The one about family. Take it, then. But read it carefully, not fast."

The box smelled of coal smoke and old paper. Inside were a christening gown gone brown at the hem, a ration book, and a bundle of letters tied with shoelace. Addison untied it on the bed while the light outside went crepuscular and the radiator ticked. The topmost letter was dated 1842, written in a hand so cramped she had to sound the words aloud. A man named Joseph Lockwood, her great-great-great-grandfather, wrote to his sister about shifts at the mill, about the dust that got into his lungs, about being turned off for asking his wage in full. She read it twice. She had expected soldiers or farmers in her family, people who turned up in textbooks. Joseph turned up nowhere.

She carried the letter downstairs. Gran was peeling potatoes at the sink, and the window behind her had gone to purple. Addison read a line aloud, about the foreman docking him a shilling, and Gran set the knife down.

"Your grandfather spent years on that lot," she said. "Before he got ill. He wanted to write it all down, our Joseph and the rest of them, and nobody would take it. Said the library wasn't interested in mill hands." She dried her hands slowly. "There's his study, you know where."

The study still smelled of him, pipe tobacco gone stale in the carpet. Addison found his notebooks first, then, behind them on the low shelf, a battered paperback with a spine cracked white. The Making of the English Working Class. 1963, said the title page, and E. P. Thompson. In the margin, in her grandfather's pencil, a line was underlined twice: he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from, and then in quotes, the enormous condescension of posterity. She did not know the word posterity at first, then she did: everyone who came after, everyone like her. She sat down on the floor with the book in her lap and the notebook open beside her and did not notice the room going dark.

Her grandfather's notes were the problem. In one notebook he had written that Joseph was out on strike in 1842, standing with the hands. In the other, later notebook, the claim had a question mark beside it, and a page reference to a newspaper of the time that listed Joseph Lockwood among the men who went back in on the third day. Addison went back and forth between the two notebooks, then to the letters, then to the book. The newspaper was a partial thing, she understood; its owner hated the strikers, and a list in such a paper could be wrong, or vindictive. But the first notebook rested on a story Joseph's daughter had told sixty years after the fact, which was partial too, the apportionment of blame smoothed by family love. She could not predicate Joseph's loyalty on either source alone, and she could not stop wanting to know it.

She carried both notebooks down to the kitchen. "Gran, which one is true? Was he out on strike or wasn't he?"

Gran looked at the pencil question mark for a long moment. "I never asked him," she said. "He'd sit there with his papers and I'd think, there's tea to be made. I never asked what he'd found." She tapped the page. "Maybe he couldn't decide either. That's why the question mark."

The potatoes were boiling over. Gran lifted the pan and Addison found herself holding both notebooks against her chest, the way you hold something you're afraid of being asked to put down. She thought about her grandfather, alone in this room, wanting to rescue a man no book had room for, and ending on a question mark anyway. She would write the essay with both versions in it. She would say what she could not settle.

"The enormous condescension of posterity," she said aloud, testing it.

"What's that, love?"

"Nothing. Something Grandad underlined." She set the notebooks on the table, side by side, question mark facing up, and reached for a plate.

The library had kept its evening habits even in June: the radiators ticking though the heat was off, the tall windows going from gold to gray, the math club occupying the carrels nearest the atlas shelf because nobody else wanted them. Keira spread her worksheet against the wood grain and weighted the corners with two pencils and her calculator. At the next carrel, Deshawn was muttering at his own paper, and Priya had already finished and was reading a novel with the worksheet face down beside her, which was a kind of showing off Keira chose not to impute to arrogance. Priya was probably just fast.

The problem was the last one on the sheet. Find the area enclosed between the line y equals x plus two and the parabola y equals x squared, between the points where they crossed. Keira had found the crossing points first, setting the two expressions equal and getting x equals negative one and x equals two, and she had drawn the picture carefully, ruler and all. In her sketch the line rode above the curve the whole way across, a chord drawn tight over a sagging bow.

Deshawn leaned over the gap between the carrels. "What did you get?"

"Six." She turned her paper so he could see the columns of algebra.

He frowned at his own result. "I got four and a half. Same interval. Same curves." He slid his work toward her, and she read it the way she read proofs, line by line, expecting to find a dropped sign. There was no dropped sign. He had integrated the parabola and subtracted the integral of the line, top to bottom as it were, and the arithmetic underneath was flawless.

"You subtracted in the wrong order," she said.

"That can't matter."

She looked at her own sketch again. Somewhere in the back of her mind was an inchoate idea about negative area, something a substitute teacher had once said in the fall and she had filed without examining. She didn't want to lean on half a memory, and she didn't want to simply assert that order mattered, because Deshawn was the kind of person who needed to see a thing break before he believed it was fragile. She took a fresh sheet and wrote it out twice: once the line's integral minus the parabola's, once the parabola's minus the line's. Six, then negative six. Same magnitude, opposite sign.

"So one of them is wrong," Deshawn said.

"Or one of them is upside down." She set the two sheets side by side. "On our interval the line is the upper function and the parabola is the lower one. If you subtract the other way, you get the negative of the area. You have to take the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they're ordered that way."

Deshawn turned back to his diagram, the one he had drawn without a ruler, quick and confident, and looked at it for a long moment. Keira watched him retrace it with his pen, following the line with its steady climb, then the curve hanging beneath it between the crossing points. Down at the reference desk, Ms. Okafor was logging the day's disbursement of loaned calculators into a green ledger, her pencil moving in small unhurried strokes, and the ordinary sound of it made the carrels feel less like a contest and more like a workshop.

"The whole interval, though," Deshawn said. "What if they crossed in the middle somewhere? What if the line went under?"

"Then you'd have to split it." Keira drew a second sketch, a line and a curve braiding through each other, and divided it at the crossing with a dotted vertical. "Upper minus lower on each piece, where they're ordered that way on that piece."

"So the order isn't a rule you memorize. It's just which one's on top."

"That's how it looks to me." She said it plainly, because she was aware of what she hadn't verified. Somewhere past the crossing points, if you extended the interval, the parabola would climb above the line, and she had only checked the ordering between negative one and two, by eye, on a hand-drawn figure. Her certainty was local, and she was willing to say so. "I checked it on the picture. I haven't proved it algebraically for every point between."

Deshawn pulled his worksheet back and began crossing out with single clean strokes, the way he did everything, and Priya lowered her novel to watch the correction travel down his page. "Six," he said, when he reached the bottom.

"Six," Keira agreed. She folded the two comparison sheets together and slid them into her folder, along with the sketch of the braided curves, though nothing on the worksheet had asked for it. Outside the tall windows the streetlights had come on, and the yellow squares lay across the atlas shelf in long parallelograms. Deshawn clicked his pen twice and wrote at the top of his page, in the margin where the teacher would see it, upper minus lower.

The restaurant smelled like burnt coffee and maple syrup, a combination Samuel would later associate with the entire summer he turned sixteen. He sat at the corner table of the Ridgeview Diner with his hands folded, the way his mother had told him to, while the manager, a reticent man named Delgado who spoke mostly in short declarative sentences, looked over his one-page application.

"You're sixteen," Delgado said. It wasn't a question, so Samuel didn't answer it. "Weekends, bussing tables, clearing plates, restocking. Seven twenty-five an hour." He said the number the way he said everything, flat, as though it had been posted on the wall for years, which in a sense it had.

Samuel had prepared a few things to say, mostly about his work ethic, but the number caught him off guard. It sounded small. It sounded like the price of two and a half milkshakes at the restaurant he was sitting in. He said yes anyway, because a job was a job, and because his friend Marcus had been teasing him for weeks about being the last of their group without one.

That evening Marcus came over, and they sat on the porch steps while the sprinklers hissed across the lawn. Marcus had started two weeks earlier at a burger place one town over, and he was still in the flush of it, showing Samuel his first paycheck like a winning lottery ticket. Then he paused, squinting at it. "Wait. Yours will be seven twenty-five? I make more than that. Like, more per hour."

"How much more?" Samuel asked.

"Enough that it's weird. We do the same stuff. You're not worse at carrying plates than I am at carrying trays." Marcus turned the stub over as though the explanation might be printed on the back. "It's not like you're worse at anything."

Samuel thought of his geometry teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, who had a habit of saying that before you solve a problem you have to agree on what kind of problem it is. Some things were exercises, some were theorems, and some were what he called lemmas, smaller results you needed first, the scaffolding under the real proof. Samuel had liked that idea, the notion that you could be honest about not yet knowing something, that uncertainty was a station you could work from rather than a failure.

He looked it up on his phone while Marcus ate the last of the pretzels. The federal minimum wage was $7.25 an hour, and it had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, which meant it had been the same number since Samuel was in preschool. But many states and cities set a higher minimum, and Marcus's burger place sat just across the state line, in a state that had done exactly that. Samuel read the dates twice. He thought about 2009, about how his parents talked about that year, and about how a number could sit still for so long while everything around it moved.

"So it's not the boss being cheap," Marcus said, leaning over to see the screen. "It's the law. Different law here."

"Here it's the federal one. There it's the state one." Samuel turned the phone off and set it face down on the step, the way Mr. Okonkwo did when he wanted a class to think instead of read.

Marcus left after that, satisfied, but Samuel stayed on the steps until the sprinklers shut off. He found himself weighing something he couldn't quite name. Part of him thought he should quit before he started and apply across the line, where the same hours would add up to more, and part of him thought that was a cowardly way to think about the diner, about Delgado, about the town he'd grown up in. His grandfather had worked at the hardware store on Miller Road for forty-one years and had never once, as far as Samuel knew, compared his pay to anyone else's. Samuel admired that and also suspected it was a kind of surrender, a willingness to let habit subjugate ambition and call the result loyalty. He could not decide which interpretation was fair, or whether fairness had anything to do with it.

The next morning, a Saturday, he took the bus to the diner for his first shift. Delgado handed him a tan apron and a rag and pointed at table eleven, where a family of five had just left a wreckage of napkins and half-eaten pancakes. Samuel tied the apron, gathered the plates with the careful stacking motion he'd practiced in his mirror at home, and carried them toward the kitchen. Behind him he heard Delgado say, without looking up from the register, "Bus fourteen next. And smile at the door when you pass it."

Samuel adjusted his grip on the plates, caught his own reflection in the chrome panel by the pass-through window, and smiled.

The group chat had forty-three unread messages by the time Naomi sat down at her kitchen table, and most of them were about Marcus. Someone had posted a screenshot of the school's new attendance system, which scanned faces in the hallway, and someone else had noticed that it had marked Marcus absent three days in a row, which was impossible, because Marcus was in her second period and had lent her a green highlighter only that morning. "The camera doesn't like me," Marcus had written, followed by the shrugging emoji, and then a wall of replies arguing about whether that was even possible.

Naomi typed, "It's a program. Programs don't like or dislike." She deleted it before sending. It sounded like something her father would say about the dishwasher.

"It's not that deep," Priya wrote. "So a computer glitches sometimes. Teachers make mistakes too."

"Yeah but teachers' mistakes are random," Marcus answered. "This thing's mistakes are all in one direction. Ask around. Who else is getting flagged?" Over the next hour, a pattern assembled itself out of scattered complaints: Marcus, who was Black; Ana, whose face the system seemed to read as male half the time; Jaylen, who wore a hoodie that flattened him into shadow. Not one of the flagged kids was white. Not one of them had thought to compare notes before.

Naomi scrolled back through the thread with her chin on her fist. In her civics class they had spent two weeks on the Constitution, and she had done her presentation on the Fourth Amendment, and she had felt virtuosic about it, standing at the front of the room with her index cards, laying out the logic of warrants and probable cause like a solved proof. She had not once, she realized now, connected any of it to the camera above the gym door.

Priya was still going. "Honestly who cares, I have nothing to hide. They can scan my boring face all day."

Naomi's thumbs hovered. She typed slowly. "Would you let me read your phone? Like all of it. Every text, every number you've called, how long you talked."

"That's different, you're a person."

"Okay, would you let a company you've never heard of read it?"

Priya sent the eye-roll emoji, but she didn't answer right away, and in the pause Theo jumped in with a link. "This actually happened," he wrote. "In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers."

"Not the calls?" Naomi asked, reading the article on her laptop while the chat blinked. "Just the records. Who you called and for how long."

"Millions of them," Theo confirmed. "Ordinary customers."

Priya came back online twenty minutes later. "Okay so I asked my mom and she said the government can't just do that, there are laws." Her next message took longer to appear, the typing indicator pulsing on and off. "But I looked it up and it happened anyway. So the laws and the doing are two different things."

Naomi leaned back and looked at the ceiling, which was her thinking posture, inherited from her mother. The scale of the leak felt tectonic to her, something enormous shifting beneath ordinary life without making a sound, and yet Priya's reaction had been a shrug until the shrugging got hard. Meanwhile the hallway camera was tiny, one bad system in one bad school, and it was ruining Marcus's attendance record in real time. Maybe that was the trick of it, she thought, that the enormous thing was easy to ignore and the small thing was fixable. She didn't type that. She wasn't sure it was true.

She opened a new message to Marcus directly. "Do you have the three absence emails?" He sent screenshots, timestamped, with the subject line ATTENDANCE ALERT in gray capitals. She forwarded them to the vice principal with a short paragraph asking whether the system had been tested across different skin tones, then copied the paragraph into the group chat so everyone could see what she'd asked and how. Theo immediately added that there were researchers who audited this kind of software professionally. Ana said her cousin had gotten a similar flag last year and nobody had believed her, and that seeing the pattern laid out in the thread made her feel less crazy, which was not a feeling Naomi had anticipated.

The vice principal replied the next morning: the vendor would be contacted, the flagged records held in suspense pending review, the attendance office instructed to accept manual corrections. It was not an apology and it was not a fix. Marcus reposted it with "small victories," and Priya, who had started the whole argument with "not that deep," wrote, "I still think most surveillance is boring people watching boring people. But I don't think the boring people all get watched the same."

Naomi read that twice. She wanted to tell Priya that she had just stated the entire problem in one sentence, but she suspected that saying so would make Priya retreat. Instead she wrote, "Meeting before school Monday, room 114, we're drafting what we want them to change. Bring the screenshots."

Twelve people clicked the little thumbs-up, including Marcus, including Ana, including Priya, last of all, at 11:42 that night.

The fourth floor vending machine took Sadie's dollar and gave nothing back, which felt like the whole week in miniature. She had spent Tuesday in Mr. Okafor's seminar arguing about a pesticide called Kelvar with a boy named Dmitri, and she was still losing the argument in her head three days later, on the teal upholstered chair outside room 412, where she was supposed to be delivering a water pitcher.

Dmitri had leaned back and said the burden of proof lay with the people claiming harm, that you waited for evidence before you banned something, because bans cost jobs. Sadie had wanted to argue and found she couldn't, not cleanly, not the way she could argue about things she'd actually read. So she'd gone home and typed serious irreversible damage into the library search bar at midnight, and the phrase had surfaced a document she'd never heard of, and now she had it screenshotted on her phone like a stone in her pocket.

The water pitcher was for Mr. Ahmadi, who had a liver thing nobody on the floor said out loud and a daughter named Layla who came every evening at six with a canvas bag of hospital-inappropriate food. Sadie had learned the shift's geography in three weeks: which nurses wanted silence, which families wanted talking, which rooms you knocked on twice and which you passed quickly. The Ahmadi room was a talking room. Layla was maybe twenty-five, worked in county public health, and treated Sadie like a person rather than a polo shirt.

"You look like you're studying for something," Layla said today, catching her refilling the pitcher. "Or against something."

"A debate I already lost." Sadie set the pitcher down. "There's this pesticide they want to use near the river, and I said we should hold off, and this guy said, wait for proof it actually hurts people. And I didn't have an answer. I had a feeling and no answer."

Mr. Ahmadi turned his head toward the window. Layla smiled at him, then back at Sadie. "My whole job is that argument. Do you know the Rio Declaration?"

Sadie shook her head, feeling the screenshot grow warm in her pocket.

"Nineteen ninety-two, big UN environment meeting. Principle fifteen." Layla pulled a tab on her coffee lid, unhurried. "It says where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures. People call it the precautionary principle."

"That's a mouthful."

"It's a leash," Layla said. "It keeps 'we're not sure yet' from becoming 'never.'"

Sadie took out her phone and found the screenshot and held it up, and Layla laughed, short and surprised, and said, "You already had it. Why are you losing to this boy?"

Because, Sadie admitted, it felt like the principle cut both ways, and she said so, pulling the visitor chair closer. If you acted without certainty, you could ruin livelihoods over nothing; if you waited, you ruined a river you couldn't un-ruin. Irreversible was doing a lot of work in that sentence, and so was cost-effective, and she suspected Dmitri would grab both words and pull. Layla listened with her chin on her fist and offered nothing, which Sadie was beginning to understand was how Layla talked best.

"There was a case in my office," Layla said finally, quietly, glancing at her father. "A well near a plant. Kids with the same bloodwork, more or less. The company's experts said causality was equivocal, too many other explanations, no proof the plant did it. And they were right, technically. Proof takes years. The families had months." She straightened the blanket edge without seeming to notice she'd done it. "The county couldn't make the plant close on suspicion. But they could require testing the town had to pay for, and they did, and the testing came back worse than anyone guessed. Nobody was absolved, exactly. Everyone had done the defensible thing."

"And the kids?"

"Some of them are fine. It's not a story with a shape." Layla gathered her canvas bag, checking the time. "Tell your Dmitri the principle doesn't say who's right. It says who has to move first."

Sadie walked the empty pitcher back down the corridor, past the vending machine she now forgave, past a nurse dictating notes in a low monotone, and thought about the word defensible, which she hadn't used before tonight and which she disliked on contact. Outside room 409 an old woman waved her over to fix a window blind that had stuck halfway, admitting gray evening light at a crooked angle, and Sadie stood on a chair and worked the mechanism until it gave. The blind snapped down all the way, darker than the room needed, and the old woman said, "Oh, well, now I can't see the parking lot at all," and laughed, and Sadie stood there with her hand still on the cord, deciding whether to raise it again.

The rink smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee, and the party had taken over the benches behind the boards, where Loic's aunts had laid out a table of noodle boxes that were going lukewarm while everyone watched the screen above the skate rental counter. On the ice, his little cousin's skating lesson was winding down, but nobody was watching the ice. The big screen was showing the World Cup match, and the sound was off, which somehow made everyone louder.

"Forty-eight," said Théo, Loic's cousin, holding a fork like a gavel. "I'm telling you, this one has forty-eight teams. It's the first time ever."

"It's thirty-two," said Uncle Marcel. "It's always been thirty-two. You're inventing things." He reached across Loic for a spring roll. "More teams means worse teams. Dilution. Like adding water to good soup."

Loic had been quiet, working through his own disagreement with himself. He liked Uncle Marcel's argument; it had the shape of something true, a preference for excellence over inclusion. But he also remembered something Théo's numbers were brushing against, something about the tournament being different this time, bigger, stranger. He couldn't place where he'd learned it, which bothered him, because a fact you can't place is a fact you shouldn't use.

"You're both guessing," he said, and pulled out his phone.

"Look at this," Uncle Marcel said, gesturing at the screen with his fork. "The match is in Toronto. The next one, my friend at work says, is in Mexico City. How does a tournament travel like that? It's absurd. A proper tournament has one host, one crowd, one heartbeat."

Loic scrolled. The wifi at the rink was friable, thin as old ice, and the page loaded in pieces: first the year, 2026, then a headline, then the sentence he'd been half-remembering. He read it twice, feeling the small satisfaction of a thing settling into place.

"It's forty-eight," he said. "This World Cup, 2026. First one ever with forty-eight teams. And it's hosted by three countries." He looked up. "Canada, Mexico, and the United States. That's the whole thing. First with forty-eight, first with three hosts."

Théo put down his fork with the gravity of a judge. "I said forty-eight."

"You said forty-eight and invented a reason," Loic said. "Different crime."

The aunts laughed. Uncle Marcel waved him off, but he leaned in to see the screen, and Loic let him read it himself rather than disabusing him out loud, because a man who finds his own error keeps more dignity than one who is corrected in front of spring rolls.

"But Marcel has a point," Loic went on, surprising himself by saying it, since he'd spent most of the argument against him. "Sort of. I think." Everyone turned back to him, and he felt the pressure of having to sound surer than he was. "More teams probably means more bad matches early on. That's just arithmetic. But it also means more countries get to be in it, whole places that never qualified before, kids watching who've never seen their flag in a tournament. That's worth something. I don't know which thing matters more. Maybe they both do."

"That's not a position," Théo said. "That's a shrug with vocabulary."

"It's a position with an asterisk," Loic said. "I'm allowed the asterisk."

Down the glass, the birthday girl came off the ice, blades hissing on the last dry strip before the door, cheeks red as stop signs, helmet crooked. She barrelled into the row of coats and Loic caught her, mostly, one skate blade scraping his shin on the way past. On the screen above them, the muted crowd in Toronto rose as one, a wave of blue and green, and here in the rink the whole family rose with it, shouting at a television with no sound, and Uncle Marcel was shouting loudest of all.

"See," he said, pointing at the screen as the ball hit the net. "Forty-eight teams and still only one can win it. That part I like."

Loic's little cousin tugged his sleeve and asked him who he was cheering for, and he honestly did not know yet. "The host countries," he said. "All three. It's their party." She considered this, and skated a slow circle around the bench to show it was acceptable.

Behind the counter, the rental clerk turned the volume up, and the noise of the crowd came through at last, and it was louder than all of them.

Morgan had opened the coffee shop at five, and by seven the morning light was coming through the front windows in long stripes across the counter, catching the steam off the espresso machine so that the whole room looked faintly theatrical. Her phone sat face down beside the register, but she had already seen the message that morning, before the alarm even finished: a photograph from her aunt Meera in Bangalore, holding up one finger stained a deep, unapologetic purple. Beneath it, in her aunt's brisk style, no greeting, no punctuation: "voted. no one can vote twice. they mark us with silver nitrate ink. since the 1962 general election. always indelible."

The customers that morning were divided into two camps, which Morgan found funny in a distant way, since the election itself seemed to divide everyone into the same two camps. There were the people who ordered quickly and left quickly, wearing their seriousness like a coat, and there were the people who lingered and wanted to talk. A man in a rain jacket, waiting on a cortado, told her he had voted at six a.m. because delay was deleterious to resolve; he said it smiling, but he meant it. Morgan was an epicure of the slow morning herself, and she liked him anyway.

Her father had called the night before while she was closing out the register. His position was arithmetic: you vote for the candidate who can actually win, because a vote is not a diary entry, it is an instrument, and you do not use a fine instrument to make yourself feel interesting. Her roommate Jules held the opposite conviction and did not merely hold it but proselytized, in the kitchen, on the stairs, over the last of the yogurt: that a vote spent on the lesser evil was still spent on evil, and the only honest ballot was the one that could embarrass you at dinner. Morgan had listened to both of them with the sensation of holding two magnets the wrong way around.

Between orders she turned her aunt's photograph over in her mind. Meera was seventy-one and had stood in a queue since before dawn, and she was proud of the stain on her finger, proud enough to send it across an ocean to a niece she'd met three times. Morgan kept thinking that the ink made something visible that her own ballot would not. In this country her vote would leave no mark on her at all; she would walk out of the gymnasium looking exactly like a person who had not voted, and no one, including herself, would be able to tell the difference afterward.

At two o'clock her shift ended and Jules came in, ordered a large coffee with an excess of ceremony, and slid into the chair opposite Morgan's spot at the corner table. "You're going at five, right?" Jules said. "Polls close at seven. I already went. I voted my conscience and I have never felt so clean, except morally I mean, I still haven't showered." Morgan laughed and wrapped her hands around her cup. She laid out the two arguments the way she laid out the pastry case in the morning, each item in its place, and found that neither of them, laid out side by side, actually canceled the other. Her father was right that a vote was an instrument. Jules was right that instruments were all anyone ever hid behind. What Morgan settled on, slowly, watching a busker outside tune a guitar badly, was a position with a splinter in it: she would vote for the winnable candidate she distrusted less, and she would not pretend the splinter wasn't there.

"You're sure?" Jules said. "Because if you're not, the clean thing is right there."

"I'm not sure," Morgan said. "I'm decided. It's a different thing."

At the gymnasium the line moved in a shuffle, past folding tables, past a woman with a clipboard who found Morgan's name and pronounced it correctly, which almost nobody did. The ballot was longer than she had expected, full of judges and school board members and a referendum about storm drains, and she stood in the booth longer than she meant to, reading everything twice. When she finally fed the sheet into the scanner, it made a sound like a printer accepting its fate, and a poll worker peeled a sticker off a roll and handed it over with the solemnity of a medal.

Outside, in the long light, she took a photograph of her own hand, sticker stuck to one finger, and sent it to Meera with the caption "mine." Then, because her pen had leaked on the walk over, there was a small blue smudge along the side of her index finger, and she photographed that too and sent it as well, holding the finger up exactly the way her aunt had. The reply came while she was still standing on the corner: "very good. but yours washes off. vote harder next time."

Parker arrived at the mall eleven minutes early, which he decided was six minutes too many, so he walked twice around the fountain near the east entrance and then stood where he could see both escalators. Marisol had said two o'clock by the pretzel stand, and it was 1:54. A rope and a line of plastic plants delimit the seating area there, and he stood just outside it, holding the second button of his shirt closed between two fingers, a habit he had not noticed until his brother pointed it out in a scathing text that morning: "Unbutton the collar, you look like you're being buried in it."

They had met at a party neither of them wanted to be at, in a kitchen, where she had argued that the movie everyone loved was actually badly paced and he had agreed too quickly and then, correcting himself, argued the opposite until she laughed. Now she came down the escalator with her hands in her jacket pockets, and he took his hand off the button.

"I was thinking bowling," she said. "There's lanes in the basement level."

The bowling alley was loud in a way that made talking easier, because nothing either of them said was required to be important. She bowled straight and fast; he bowled with a strange three-step approach he'd invented at a birthday party in seventh grade and never fixed. Through two games they were close enough that the machine put them into a tiebreaker frame, and in that frame she threw three strikes in a row, arms up, spinning to face him with her chin out, and he got the last two he needed by a margin of four pins.

His heart was going hard enough that he could feel it in his ears. She sat down next to him on the bench, still warm from the game, still grinning, and said, "You want to know a gross fact about this exact moment?"

"Always."

"Okay, so. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal." She picked up a napkin and folded it into a smaller square. "It's when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby."

"Where did you read that?"

"Psych class. There's a study where they had guys cross a scary bridge and meet a woman on the other side, and way more of them called her afterward than the guys on the boring bridge." She set the napkin down. "So I don't trust anything I feel in the ten minutes after a tiebreaker."

He laughed, and then did not, because he had been about to say something and the fact arrived in front of it like a car pulling out. All evening, under the arcade's strobing lights and the noise of the lanes, he had been reading his own pulse as evidence about her, and it might have been, and it might have been the escalators and the tiebreaker and the fact that he had rehearsed this date out loud in his car.

"So what do you do," he said, "if you can't tell the difference?"

"You wait for a boring minute. And then you see what's still there."

They left the bowling alley and drifted past a travel agency with a wall-sized photo of a fjord, a sheer black wall of rock dropping into still water, with a single white ferry making a wake across it. Marisol stopped. "My grandmother grew up on one of those. She says Americans photograph them because we don't have anything that old and quiet."

"We have malls," Parker said, and she laughed in the exact way she had in the kitchen, quick and then covered, like she was rationing it.

They walked the length of the second floor, past the phone cases and the candle store, and he noticed that his heart had gone back to its normal work and that the quiet it left was not empty. He still wanted to sit near her. He also understood, honestly, that wanting something in a quiet minute and wanting it in a loud one were different tests, and that he had only passed one of them so far, and that she might be running the same experiment on him.

At the fountain they stopped without deciding to. The coins on the bottom had gone green except one, near the center, that was still bright.

"Boring minute," Marisol said, checking her phone. "It's 4:12. Nothing is happening."

"Right," he said. "Nothing."

She put the phone away and looked at the water. He looked at it too. Then she said, "I get frozen yogurt with people I don't like. Just so the data's clean."

"Is that an offer?"

"It's a methodology," she said, and started walking toward the food court without checking whether he followed.

Nicole had circled the psychology building twice before going in, because the boy handing out maps had a clipboard and a lanyard and the confident posture of someone who intended to eviscerate her with friendliness if she gave him the chance. Inside, the hallway smelled like floor wax and cut fruit from the welcome table. A banner read DISCOVER YOUR FUTURE, which seemed like a lot to ask of a folding table and a bowl of orange slices.

She was here for one reason: the department had a research lab that studied adolescent decision-making, and Nicole had spent most of senior year convinced that decisions were the only currency she had. Which college, which major, which city, whether to say yes to Danny Merck before graduation or after, whether after even meant anything. Her mother said she overthought. Her mother said this while weighing two brands of olive oil for ten minutes at the grocery store, so Nicole took it as a compliment.

The lab table was staffed by a graduate student named Priya, who wanted, visibly and urgently, for someone, anyone, to sign the interest sheet, because the department chair counted signatures and Priya had exactly four. "You can put your email," Priya said, sliding the clipboard closer before Nicole had spoken. "There's no commitment. It's just interest. Hypothetical interest is also fine."

"Tell me about the research first," Nicole said.

"Self-control," Priya said. "How people choose between something now and something later. We run versions of the delay task with adolescents."

Nicole's mother appeared beside her, holding a coffee she had not paid for, from a table marked FOR ADMITTED STUDENTS ONLY. "Oh, the marshmallow study," her mother said. "I know that one."

"You do not," Nicole said.

"I do. They gave little kids one marshmallow and told them if they didn't eat it, they'd get a second one later. A 1990 follow-up of those preschoolers found the kids who waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers." Her mother sipped the stolen coffee, pleased with herself. "You would have eaten it immediately. You ate a whole birthday cake at four. I have photographs."

A father hovering nearby with his own prospective student laughed. "So one afternoon with a marshmallow decides your whole life," he said. "Great. My son waited an hour once for a video game and now he can't wait five minutes for anything."

The son, arms crossed, said, "That's not what it means."

"It tends," Priya said carefully, glancing at the chair's office down the hall. "It's a tendency. Not a destiny." She rotated the clipboard so the blank lines faced them all.

Nicole looked at the sheet. She thought of Danny, who wanted an answer before September, and of the gap between the two of them, which was mostly a gap between how they each thought about later. He thought later was a place you arrived at by accident. She thought later was a place you built on purpose, brick by tedious brick, and she had always privately considered this a moral distinction, hers the altruistic one, his the selfish. She was starting to suspect that was unfair. He was generous in the present, actually, in ways she never was because she was too busy preparing for the future. Two temperaments, not two ethics. The marshmallow kids weren't better children. They were just children whose waiting happened to be measured.

Still. The study tracked something real, or the numbers wouldn't have moved. A tendency was a counterpoint to a destiny, not a refutation of it, and Nicole could hold both at once without pretending either one was the whole song.

"I'm not saying it's destiny," the father was saying to his son, in the tone of a man saying it was destiny.

"I'll sign," Nicole said. She wrote her name, then her email, then, after a pause, her phone number, which was more than the form asked for. Priya beamed as though Nicole had donated an organ.

"That's five," Priya whispered, mostly to herself.

Her mother linked arms with her as they walked out past the orange slices and the banner. "So did you learn your future?"

"I learned that a four-year-old with a birthday cake doesn't decide anything," Nicole said. "And that I still would have eaten it."

Outside, the map boy had abandoned his post and was giving directions to a lost family anyway, pointing with his whole arm, unbothered by the fact that he was pointing the wrong way.

Carter had promised himself he would finish the physics problem set before dinner, and now the sun was going down over the fence and he had finished exactly one problem, which he had finished wrong. He sat at the picnic table with the textbook propped against a jar of nails, his pencil chewed to splinters, and tried again to make the numbers behave. The problem was about a ball launched off a table at some horizontal speed, and the book kept insisting, in its bland way, that he separate the motion into components, as if velocity were a bag of mixed nuts he could sort into bowls.

He understood the idea and did not believe it. That was the uncomfortable part. The equations said that the ball's sideways speed had nothing to do with how fast it fell, that the vertical part went about its business as if the horizontal part didn't exist, and every instinct he had said a ball thrown hard ought to hang in the air longer than a ball simply tipped off the edge. His uncle, a man who could fix a transmission and quote Kierkegaard in the same breath and called himself a polymath mostly at cookouts, had told him once that physics was mostly learning to distrust your eyes. Carter had thought that sounded profound at the time. Now it sounded like an excuse.

Priya came through the back gate carrying two tennis balls and a bag of chips she had clearly already started, because she was loquacious when she was eating and she was already talking. "Your mom said you were being tragic back here. I brought props."

"I'm not tragic. I'm stuck."

She dropped onto the bench across from him and read the problem upside down, which she claimed she was good at and was not. "A ball rolls off a table at four meters per second. Blah blah. Where does it land." She tossed one tennis ball in the air and caught it. "You know what I think? I think you're overcomplicating it because it feels too easy."

"That's the thing. It doesn't feel easy. It feels wrong."

"Then don't feel it. Test it." She stood up and put one ball on the table's edge, holding it with one finger, and held the other in her other hand. "Okay. Bet. This one I just drop. This one I throw straight out, level, as hard as I can. Same height, same second. Which one hits the grass first?"

"The dropped one," Carter said immediately. "The thrown one's in the air longer. It's traveling farther, so it takes longer to come down."

"Fifty cents."

"You're on."

Here is what Priya would remember about it afterward: the way he said it, absolutely certain, like a man announcing his own birthday. She counted down from three, dropped the one finger and snapped the other wrist at the same instant, and both of them froze, heads tilted, listening. The two sounds came so close together that she honestly could not have sworn to the order, so they did it again, and then a third time, and on the third time she made him be the one to throw so she could only listen, eyes shut, chips forgotten in her hand.

"They hit together," Carter said.

"Say it properly."

"One sound. They hit the grass at the same time." He said it twice more, as though the sentence might change under repetition. The thrown ball had sailed a good four meters and the dropped one had landed practically at the table's leg, and they had landed together, and somewhere in his chest a door swung open onto a room he hadn't known was there. The book wasn't sorting mixed nuts. The book was saying you could let two things be true at once, that the fall and the flight were separate and simultaneous, that the problem had two lives running side by side and you were allowed to look at them one at a time.

He went back to the picnic table and did the problem in four minutes. The horizontal part was just distance equals rate times time, a thing he had known since seventh grade. The vertical part was free fall, which he had done last week. What had seemed like one impossible braided thing turned out to be two easy things refusing to touch each other, and he wondered whether that was a trick of physics or a way of seeing you could subsume other problems under, though he wasn't sure yet and wasn't going to pretend to be. Some problems probably really were braided all the way through. This one, gloriously, was not.

"Four point two meters," he said.

"From the table?"

"From the table's edge. Four point two meters out." He held up the paper. "And I only believe it because of your fifty cents, which you still owe me, by the way, since I lost the bet and you never actually paid up either direction."

Priya dug in her pocket, produced two quarters, and set them on the table next to the jar of nails, where they sat catching the last of the light. "For the record," she said, "I only bet against you because you sounded too sure." She tossed him the second tennis ball. "Throw it again. I want to hear it one more time."

The summer league practiced on the ragged field behind the community center, where the goals had holes and the water fountain only worked if you hit it on its left side. Alexia had joined because her roommate at State had said it would be easy, and it was, at first. Nobody counted anything. The team lost 4-1, then 6-2, and at practice on Thursday half the girls walked through the shuttle drill while Coach Reyes stacked cones with the resignation of a woman who had seen this before.

"Can I try something?" Alexia asked her afterward, while the others filed toward the parking lot. She'd found a stopwatch app on her phone during her statistics lecture that spring, half-listening, and the idea had sat in her since. "If we timed everyone's sprints separately. Like, each person gets her own number, posted on the fence."

Coach Reyes looked at her for a long moment. "You want to be the one holding the stopwatch? That's a popularity contest you'll lose."

"I know," Alexia said. "But everybody walking isn't working either."

The stopwatch came out on Monday. She called out times as each girl finished the forty-yard sprint, and Priya, who played midfield and never lifted above a jog in drills, glanced at the fence where Alexia had taped a sheet of paper with everyone's name on it. Priya's time was second-worst. On the second sprint she beat two people. By the third round, girls who usually saved themselves for games were spitting into the grass and putting hands on knees, and the sheet of paper on the fence had numbers nobody wanted next to their name.

"You know there's a name for this," Priya said afterward, wringing out her shirt. "My brother's taking psych at City. He says it's called social loafing. People slack in groups, and the slacking shrinks when each person's contribution can be identified." She shrugged. "I didn't believe him until I saw my own time up there."

Alexia wrote the times down every practice after that, and the team's losses narrowed. But it wasn't clean. Dana, their sweeper, who had organized carpools all June and once drove forty minutes to bring Cleo shin guards she'd forgotten, stopped carpooling. She'd pulled a hamstring in the third timed session and played through it badly rather than have a slow number posted, and when Alexia asked if she was okay, Dana said, "You'd write it down, wouldn't you," and walked to her car alone.

Alexia sat on the bleachers that night trying to interpolate between two things she believed. If she charted the averages, effort had clearly risen across the squad; the numbers were unambiguous. What the numbers didn't capture was Dana driving alone, or the way girls now paired off for water breaks instead of collapsing in one sweating heap the way they had in June. She kept running the comparison and it kept sliding: more effort, less team, and no stopwatch in the world that measured the second thing.

She brought it to Priya during a scrimmage break, both of them lying in the shade of the one good tree. "I don't think the times are the point anymore," Alexia said. "I think the point is that we're fifteen individuals now. We happen to wear the same shirt."

"Individuals who run hard," Priya said. "In June we were a group that jogged."

"That's the whole trade, though. That's it, exactly. Group and slow, or separate and fast."

Priya picked at the grass. "My brother would say you can't have it both ways. Accountability breaks the loafing apart, and it breaks other stuff apart too."

The semifinal was the following Saturday, and Alexia made a decision she couldn't fully defend. She timed the sprints as always, but after practice she pulled Dana aside by the fountain, smacked its left side with the heel of her hand, and said, "You don't go on the sheet till the hamstring's healed. Your time stays whatever it was before." Dana studied her, waiting for the catch. "That's not fair to everyone else," Dana said finally, and Alexia said, "I know. I can't tell if it's the right kind of unfair." She meant it. The sprint numbers had risen the whole season and she could not prove that the numbers had caused it, that it wasn't August pride or Dana's bad example or just girls getting fit; and now she was carving an exception out of the one system that had worked, on a hunch that a team was a thing the numbers could kill.

They lost the semifinal 2-1, on a goal that slid through the exact gap Dana would have closed. She'd played the whole second half on the bad leg, refusing to come off, and afterward she sat with her shin packed in ice while the others gathered around the schedule to see when the third-place game was.

Dana waved Alexia over. "My time tomorrow," she said. "Put it on the sheet."

The temple basement smelled of ghee and wet cardboard, and Maya's grandmother had already claimed the long table by the time Maya came down with the second box of lamps. There were three hundred of them, unlit, each a small clay cup with a cotton wick curled inside like a sleeping question. Outside, above the door, the committee had strung electric fairy lights that blinked in a rhythm no one had chosen, and Maya thought they looked anachronistic against the carved wooden lintel, like ringtones in a library.

"You're late," her grandmother said, without looking up.

"The bus was late." Maya sat down and began filling the cups from a plastic jug of oil, tilting each one so the wick drank. She had done this since she was seven, first at home, then here, her hands steadier every year while the occasion itself grew more complicated inside her.

Her grandmother worked faster, lining the finished lamps along the edge of the table in rows of ten, counting under her breath in Hindi. Around them the hall filled: her uncle expatiating to two new volunteers about the correct width between rows, her little cousin dragging a chair to reach the windowsills. Maya's phone buzzed in her pocket. She oiled four more lamps before she let herself look.

The message was from Priya, her roommate assignment at the college she'd be moving into in January, mid-year admission, which Maya had told her family about last week and her grandmother had not mentioned since. Priya had sent a photo of a snow-dusted quad that stretched flat to the horizon, treeless, like a steppe, with the words: come early. theres a thing jan 4. you could stay w me before classes.

Her grandmother's hand appeared over her cup, waiting. Maya passed her the jug.

"Nani," her cousin shouted from the windowsill, "why do we put them everywhere?"

"Diyas," her grandmother said, setting a lamp down with the care of someone placing a chess piece. "Everywhere, so the whole place is lit. That's the whole point."

Maya knew the point. Light over darkness, the lamps in homes and temples, rows of them along walkways and sills, the story her grandmother told every year about returning royalty and lamps guiding them home. What Maya had never managed to explain, at dinner or in the car, was that she still loved the story while no longer being sure she believed anything behind it, and that leaving felt less like escape and more like taking the lamps out of the temple to see if they burned anywhere else. She had tried to say some version of this once and her uncle had laughed and said she'd be back by Easter, which wasn't even their holiday.

She filled lamps and thought about January 4th. The temple celebration went until midnight; the bus to the airport left at six the next morning; she had already bought the ticket. The ticket was in her phone, and the phone was in her hand, and her grandmother was watching the hand.

"Who is texting you during Diwali?"

"Roommate. From school."

Her grandmother went back to the lamps. Maya counted the silence in rows. Nine, ten.

Later, when the first guests came up the stairs and the uncle on ladder duty set the fairy lights to steady on, Maya found her grandmother alone in the basement hallway, closing the empty oil jug. The hallway had one bulb and a long sill, and on the sill her grandmother had placed a single row of diyas, unlit, wicks dark with oil.

"I want to tell you something," Maya said. "January fourth. There's a program at the school. I'd leave the morning after Diwali."
