LEMONADE, TWO DOLLARS. They were raising money for the robotics club, and they had eleven days to make four hundred dollars.

"Where'd you get the lemons?" William asked.

"Foodtown," Dan said. "Three dollars a bag."

"There's a produce market on Delancey," Priya said. "Eighty cents a bag. My aunt shops there. But it's across town."

William did the arithmetic out loud, half to them and half to himself. Three dollars against eighty cents. Two dollars and twenty cents saved on every bag. Then he asked how they would get there, and Dan said the bus, and the bus was two seventy-five each way, and Priya said that didn't matter because they'd buy a whole crate, enough for the whole week.

At the Foodtown they squeezed a bag of lemons into maybe fourteen cups, which at two dollars a cup meant each bag brought in twenty-eight dollars against three spent. On Delancey, Priya's aunt had said, the same bag cost eighty cents. William wrote the numbers in the margin of his quiz, below the red circle, and drew a line between them. One person was better at making lemonade cheaply and one place was better at making lemons cheaply, and the gap between them was where the money lived. He felt a small exhilaration, the kind that came with seeing a shape inside a shape, and he almost said something about how this was exactly the thing on his quiz.

Then he tried to parametrize it, the way Mr. Okafor was always telling them to do, put the numbers in a general form and see what held. Let the bus fare climb. Let the gap shrink. He ran his pencil down the page and stopped. If it cost one person more to carry the lemons across town than the difference between what lemons cost in the two places, the whole arrangement collapsed. Two seventy-five times two was five fifty in bus fare, against two twenty saved per bag. They would need to buy three bags just to break even, and they didn't have a way to carry three bags, and they didn't have a fridge to keep them in.

"So it's not worth it," Priya said when he showed her.

"It's worth it if we buy enough," Dan said.

"We can't buy enough. That's the point. The bus eats it."

William sat back. Here was the thing, he realized, that question four had been circling. Both sides still gained from trading, that part was true, he could feel it was true, the Delancey grower and the robotics club both came out ahead if the goods moved. But the gains were not a fixed prize. They shrank as the carrying got expensive, and somewhere past a line, the trade simply stopped paying. His first answer hadn't been wrong so much as incomplete, and Mr. Okafor's "closer" now looked less like a rebuke than a map.

He took the retake on Thursday and wrote it plainly: each one gains by making the thing it gives up least to make, and both sides gain even if one is better at everything, but only so long as the cost of moving the goods doesn't exceed the difference in what they cost to make. Mr. Okafor read it while William stood there, then looked up.

"Where'd you finally get it?"

"Lemonade stand," William said. "Bus fare across town."

Mr. Okafor laughed once and wrote something at the top of the page. He turned it around so William could see the check mark, and beside it, underlined: comparative advantage.

Priya texted him that afternoon. Sold out at lunch, she wrote. Still buying lemons at Foodtown. William slid the phone into his pocket and walked out past the folding table, where Dan was stacking the last cups into a pyramid, two dollars at a time.

Brayden's board was titled "Pushed Around: Equilibrium Under Temperature Stress," and the second word had been misspelled on the bus, corrected in the parking lot, and now sat slightly crooked above two beakers of pink solution. The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and someone else's vinegar volcano, which had already erupted twice at table nine. He had chosen cobalt chloride because it changed color, pink when the equilibrium favored the hydrated form, blue when it tipped the other way, and because color was the kind of thing a judge could see from three feet away without reading a single paragraph of his abstract.

Priya Fernando was two tables down with a wind tunnel and a laser. She wanted the regional slot, the one that came with a banner and a photograph in the local paper, and she had told him so in October with the courtesy of someone announcing weather. They had been friendly in the way of two people who keep score. She came over now with her badge already pinned straight and studied his beakers.

"Which one is hot?" she said.

"This one. The pink turns blue when I warm it, and back when it cools." He lifted the hot beaker by its rim, set it in the ice bath he had rigged from a cooler and a bag of pellets, and they both watched the blue creep back toward rose along the bottom of the glass. It looked, he thought, like a tide deciding against the shore.

Priya frowned at it. "That's not a fair test. You're changing two things."

"I'm changing one thing."

"You're changing temperature and color."

"The color is the measurement. The temperature is the cause." He heard his own voice get defensive and adjusted it. "The reaction sits at an equilibrium, and when you heat it, the system shifts to use up the added heat. Cool it, and it shifts back the other way. It pushes against whatever you do to it."

"So it's stubborn."

"It's more like it's balanced and trying to stay that way."

Priya picked up his reference list, which was half a page, typed the night before. "Who's Chatelier?"

"Le Chatelier." He had typed the name from the panel that morning. The chemistry department had borrowed three displays from the science museum in the city, and one of them stood at the end of their aisle, a tall panel about equilibrium with a portrait of a bearded man. Brayden had looked him up on his phone in the hallway. "The principle is named after Henry Louis Le Chatelier," he said. "He was a French chemist. He stated it in 1884." The date had stuck with him, the way certain dates do, because it meant the idea was older than the gymnasium, older than the town, and had been waiting patiently all that time for him to misuse it.

He had misused it once already, that morning, in practice. He had put a beaker in the warm bath and declared, to his lab partner Marcus, that the reaction would speed up. Marcus, who considered himself a connoisseur of Brayden's failures and kept a private catalogue of them, had pointed out that speed and direction were different claims. Brayden had started to remonstrate, saying that obviously heat did both, and then stopped, because it obviously did both, and the interesting question was which part the principle was actually about. It was about the shift. Not faster, but elsewhere. He had rewritten his conclusion twice on the bus.

A judge arrived at eleven, a woman with a lanyard and an Igneous Rock Club tote bag, which Brayden noticed and decided not to mention. She dipped a thermometer into his warm bath, asked him to run the cold trial again, and watched the color turn without expression. Then she asked him something he had not prepared for: whether the principle told him anything about the world outside the beakers. She said it lightly, the way judges ask impossible questions when they are deciding between two good projects.

Brayden looked down the aisle at the museum panel, at the Frenchman's photograph with its fixed, patient stare. "It tells you systems push back," he said. "But it doesn't tell you how far, or how fast, or when you've pushed too hard and broken something instead of shifting it. I don't know where that line is." The judge wrote something. She might have been writing "honest." She might have been writing "should have had a second trial."

Priya came back during cleanup, while he was dumping the pink solution into the waste jug and the ice had melted into gray water. "They took my wind tunnel data to ask about turbulence models," she said. "Your beakers turned a nice color." She paused, straightening a poster corner that did not need straightening. "I still want the banner, though."

"I know," Brayden said. He held up the last beaker, still faintly blue at the rim where his hands had warmed it, and set it down in the ice water to watch it change.

The radiator in Room 214 clanked all through sixth period, and Violet had stopped hearing it until the question on the board made her hear it again. Predict the effect of an increase in temperature on the reaction below, Ms. Okafor had written, and beneath it, N2 + 3H2 goes to 2NH3, with a note in parentheses: exothermic. Violet's pencil hovered. She could do pressure shifts, concentration shifts, the whole tidy logic of Le Chatelier, the system pushed one way and pushing back. But temperature had always slid past her. Temperature was not a substance you could add. It was everywhere at once, like weather, like her mood since March.

Around her, pens moved. Marcus, two seats over, was already underlining something with the flat certainty he brought to every answer, right or wrong. Priya had her hand half raised, then lowered it, then raised it again, and Ms. Okafor said, "Hold your thoughts, everyone. Lab partners, compare. I want arguments, not answers." Violet turned to the boy beside her, Daniel, who was re-copying the equation as though neatness might make it confess.

"It shifts left," Daniel said. "Heat speeds things up, so it makes more product, but then it makes less, but the forward reaction is exothermic so..." He trailed off into the shape of his own confusion, and Violet felt a small, unwelcome warmth toward him for being honest about it. She had spent most of the semester protecting the opposite impression, that she understood everything, which had disenfranchised her from the one thing she actually needed: the right to ask a dumb question.

"If you can't add it," she said slowly, "then what does 'adding temperature' even mean." The radiator clanked. She thought, without warning, of her grandmother's kitchen in February, the stove going all afternoon, and of the evening she had sat there with this same textbook and no Wi-Fi, snow sealing the road, her grandmother humming over a pot of something that needed to simmer. She had been so bored that week, a damp, subterranean ennui, that she had resorted to the homework she'd brought to avoid doing. Same chapter. Same equation. And she remembered what she had done, because it had felt almost criminal at the time.

"Give me your pencil," she told Daniel, and he surrendered it warily. On his paper, beneath the equation, she wrote: N2 + 3H2 goes to 2NH3 + heat. Daniel frowned. "You can't just add heat to the equation." "Watch me," she said. "It's exothermic. So heat is a product. It's like the ammonia, it comes out of the reaction." She held the pencil still, testing the idea against the week in her grandmother's kitchen, where it had first appeared to her as a way of making an unsolvable problem solvable, a trick she had trusted only because nothing else had worked. "And if a reaction is endothermic instead, heat is a reactant. It goes on the left. It goes in."

"Okay," Daniel said, but his voice was careful, the voice of someone deciding whether to be convinced or embarrassed. "So if heat is a product and you raise the temperature." "You're adding product," Violet said. "The system shifts away from it. Left, toward the reactants." She looked at what she had written and felt the ground of it, solid in the way her grandmother's kitchen floor had been solid, tile warmed all afternoon by the stove. Heat as a product, heat as a reactant; the whole slippery question of temperature suddenly had handles.

Ms. Okafor drifted past their desk and paused at the penciled equation. Violet braced for correction, for the eraser, for the phrase "you can't just." Instead Ms. Okafor read it twice and said only, "Say that to the class, Violet," and moved on, which was its own kind of verdict, though Violet noticed she did not say whether the trick was a real method or a useful lie, a model that happened to work, and that question stayed with Violet longer than the answer did. She had lived inside models before. Last spring she had modeled herself as fine, cheerful, recovered, and the model had worked right up until the day it didn't, which was March, which was why her mood was weather now. She knew better than to trust a model completely. She also knew that a model that got her through the problem was not nothing.

When Ms. Okafor called on her, Violet stood with Daniel's paper still in her hand, its rewritten equation facing her like a small window. "Exothermic means heat is a product," she said to the class, her voice steadier than she expected. "Endothermic means it's a reactant. So raising the temperature is adding it, and the system pushes the other way." Marcus looked up from his underlining with an expression she couldn't read, possibly defeat, possibly interest, possibly the recalculation of everything he'd written. Ms. Okafor wrote "shifts left" on the board and then, beneath it, drew a long arrow pointing to the right.

"What's the arrow for?" Priya asked.

"That," Ms. Okafor said, capping her marker, "is next semester."

The hostel's courtyard smelled of orange peel and rain, and Brayden had exactly four days to become someone who could argue about climate policy in Spanish for five minutes. His sister, Maya, had signed them both up for the intercambio night at the cultural center without asking, the way she did most things, and when he'd protested she'd said, "You took four years of Spanish, Brayden. Use it or it dies." Now he sat with a laminated list of energy vocabulary, repeating transición, renovable, impuesto, while she fed crumbs to the courtyard's putative cat, an animal that belonged to no one and everyone.

His partner for the debate was a local student named Teo, who was seventeen and spoke English only when he wanted to be funny. "Tu acento," Teo said on the second evening, tilting his head, "es como un gringo cantando." Brayden laughed, but the laugh sat wrong in his chest afterward, and he lay awake composing sentences he would never have the nerve to say. Their opponent, according to the sign-up sheet, was a university student named Rocío, who had won the regional competition in the spring. Teo delivered this information with the flatness that seemed to portend disaster.

On the third day they practiced in the plaza, under the plane trees, and Brayden discovered that his problem was not vocabulary but structure. In English he could argue circles around anyone; his father called it the family disease. In Spanish, each sentence cost him something, and halfway through a point he would forget the clause he'd begun. "Empieza otra vez," Teo kept saying, "pero más simple," and Brayden resisted this, because simple felt like surrender, until Maya, watering the plants beside them, said quietly, "Simple isn't dumb. It's clear." He watched her steady the small pot she'd bought the hostel's owner that morning, the woman whose knees had been aching on the stairs, and he let the sentence go and started over with three plain words instead of twelve.

Rocío turned out to be formidable in a way he hadn't imagined. At the informal session on Thursday she spoke on carbon taxation with such fluency that he understood maybe two-thirds and felt the shape of the rest, the way you feel a wave through a boat's hull. Afterward she approached their table, and Teo, nervous, made a joke of it. "Él va a debatir contigo," he said, and then, in English, with a grin that didn't quite reach his eyes, "Good luck understanding him." Rocío looked at Brayden and waited. Brayden understood the joke, and understood also that it had been aimed somewhere uncomfortable inside him. "Vamos a ver," he said, and was pleased at how steady it came out.

The debate was Saturday evening, folding chairs in a room with tall windows, maybe thirty people. Brayden opened with the argument he'd rebuilt a dozen times, that a carbon tax works fastest when its revenue returns to households, and he got through ninety seconds before his grammar began to fray. He slowed down. He let the pauses exist. Somewhere in the fourth minute, when he'd said that the tax without rebates punishes the people with the fewest choices, Rocío responded, and he understood every word: she didn't answer the point. She said, smiling at the audience, that it was charming to hear a foreigner pronounce economía that way, and the room laughed, a small warm ripple at his expense.

For a moment the laughter filled his ears and he nearly lost the thread of everything, the Spanish, the argument, the room. Then he remembered a term from Mr. Alvarez's class junior year, surfacing the way forgotten things do, whole and intact. He raised his hand for the moderator. "Un momento," he said. "Eso es un ad hominem. Ataca a la persona, no al argumento." His accent made the Latin words sound strange, but the moderator, an older man in a gray cardigan, nodded slowly, and some murmur went through the chairs, and Brayden realized he had just done, out loud and in two languages, the thing the whole fallacy meant: he had named the attack on the person instead of the claim, and named it as a fallacy, the way it is treated in formal debate. Rocío's smile thinned. She returned to the rebates, and they fought over the actual point, and it was hard, and he lost the thread twice and found it twice.

When the five minutes ended he was sweating through his shirt. He couldn't tell who had won, and the moderator, when asked, said only that the audience would decide what it had heard. Brayden found this unsatisfying and then, walking out, less so. He had walked in with an argument he'd sanded down to what he could actually defend, and he'd discovered, mid-sentence, a distinction he'd previously known only as a vocabulary word: attacking a person is not answering them, and it doesn't count as answering them here, either. Whether his own position survived the evening was another question, one he turned over on the walk back, and he noticed he liked the turning.

Teo bought churros from the cart by the fountain and handed Brayden the first one without comment. Rocío appeared at the edge of the lamplight, backpack over one shoulder, hesitating. She came over and said, in Spanish, that his pronunciation of impuesto had been wrong all night, and that his argument about the rebates had been, if he wanted honesty, half right. "Which half?" Brayden asked. She tore a piece off her own churro and considered him. "Come back Tuesday," she said, "and lose to me properly, and maybe you find out."

The kitchen table had disappeared under Mia's science fair supplies by four o'clock: agar plates, a borrowed scale, a box of cotton swabs, and a two-pound bag of table salt with a nutrition label she had read four times without understanding. Her project was supposed to answer whether salt slowed the growth of bacteria she'd swabbed from the kitchen counter, and the article Mrs. Okafor had printed for her kept using the word epidemiology, describing researchers who tracked illness through populations the way Mia was tracking colonies across a grid of plates. She liked that idea, that a kitchen counter could be a small country and she its mapmaker.

The trouble was her procedure sheet. At the bottom, in Mrs. Okafor's tidy handwriting, it said: convert your salt masses to moles before you record them. Mia had read the sentence so many times it had gone smooth and meaningless, like a stone handled all winter.

"You're going to need the good scale, not the kitchen one," her brother Danny said, sliding onto the chair across from her with a granola bar. He was twelve and considered himself her lab assistant by right of proximity.

"The kitchen one measures grams. That's fine." She tore a paper towel, set it on the scale, and zeroed it. Then she poured salt until the display read 175.0. The plan called for three concentrations, and this was the first. She copied the number onto her data sheet and then sat staring at the blank column beside it, the one labeled moles.

"Like the animal," Danny said, mouth full.

"No." She pulled her chemistry textbook toward her, flipped through the chapter on quantities in reactions, and found the periodic table with the atomic masses printed beneath each element's name. Sodium, 22.99. Chlorine, 35.45. She added them on her calculator twice because the first answer seemed too plain: 58.44. She checked the textbook's example and saw the same number there, printed beside the formula NaCl. Sodium chloride, table salt, molar mass 58.44 grams per mole.

"Say that again?" Danny leaned over the book.

"Sodium chloride. Fifty-eight point four four grams per mole." She wrote it at the top of her notes in capital letters so she would not lose it, and then did what she always did with a number she did not trust: she asked it a question. If one mole weighed 58.44 grams, then 175 grams was not one mole, and it was not two. She divided, 175.0 by 58.44, and got 2.99. Almost exactly three. She stared at that small, unlikely neatness, then divided again and got 2.9946, which was less neat and somehow more believable.

Her mother came through with groceries and paused at the table. "How much did that kit cost?"

"Twenty dollars. But the plates are sterile and the swabs are reusable, so I can amortize it," Mia said. "Danny can use the leftovers next year for his mold bread thing."

"I will not be doing mold bread," Danny said, with dignity.

Mia weighed the second sample, 58.4 grams, and wrote one mole beside it, checking her own confidence like a loose tooth. She was honest enough with herself to know the conversion was arithmetic, not understanding; she could not yet say why chemists wanted moles at all, only that they counted substances by weight and that this was how. Somewhere between the bag of salt and the textbook there had been a small tectonic shift in her thinking, the plate of it moving quietly, and she could feel that something had resettled even if she could not name the new terrain.

She weighed the smallest sample last, 29.2 grams, and wrote half a mole, then sat back. On the counter beside the stove, the first agar plate waited with its lid on, and the article on epidemiology lay folded to a page about rates and populations, and outside the window the light was going the color of weak tea. Mia picked up the cotton swab, rubbed it once along the cutting board, and lifted the lid of the plate.

"Ready?" she said.

Danny leaned in, granola bar forgotten.

Daniel had spread the textbook across the picnic table so that both pages faced the sky, and he was copying the diagram onto a paper bag because he had left his notebook in Marcus's car. The diagram showed glucose being broken down, first in the cytoplasm, then inside the mitochondria, where the carbon pieces spun through a circle of arrows that fed electrons into a chain and pushed protons across a membrane. ATP came out at the end like water from a tap. Marcus sat on the table's edge, half on and half off, the way he sat when he wanted to seem like he wasn't really studying.

"You actually want to do this?" Marcus said. "It's Saturday. It's June. We graduated."

"I failed the exam," Daniel said. "I want to understand it before I have to take it again in the fall."

Marcus rolled a bottle cap along the boards with his thumb. He had passed, barely, and the difference between them had become a thing neither of them named out loud. Daniel drew the circle of arrows again, slower this time, and noticed that the first compound in the circle wasn't glucose or anything shaped like it. It was citrate. A six-carbon acid, like the sour stuff in lemons.

"Why is it called the citric acid cycle?" Marcus asked, leaning over. "It's in a textbook. Shouldn't it be called something about energy or cells?"

Daniel didn't know. He flipped back through the chapter and found a name in the caption, small print under the diagram. Hans Krebs. He read it aloud. "Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937." Below it, in even smaller print, something about a prize. "And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it."

"So a guy just found it and got his name on it," Marcus said. "Like a planet."

"It's not his name on it, though. It's the acid. His name is in the caption." Daniel thought about that for a moment. Somewhere in England, in 1937, a man had watched carbon atoms move in a circle and understood what nobody else had understood, and then a committee in Stockholm, sixteen years later, had decided it mattered enough to hang a medal on. Daniel felt the gravitas of it, the weight of a whole life spent on one wheel of reactions, and it made his paper bag diagram seem either ridiculous or connected to something enormous. He couldn't decide which.

He tried tracing the steps out loud. Glucose splits in the cytoplasm, two smaller pieces slip into the mitochondria, the pieces lose their carbons one at a time around the circle, and every turn hands electrons to the chain, which uses them to build ATP. It came out flat, like reciting a pledge. Marcus frowned at the drawing and pointed at the circle. "So the pieces go around once and they're done?"

"They go around and they're gone. Each turn eats one piece." Daniel stopped. That was the part he'd gotten wrong on the exam, or one of the parts. He had written that glucose itself entered the cycle directly, that the whole sugar spun around, and the grader's red line had cut through his answer like a fence. He could still feel the peevish little jolt he'd had reading that mark, the impulse to argue with the paper itself. Now, in the backyard, with the wasps circling the lemonade and Marcus's knee bouncing against the table leg, he saw his error plainly. Glucose never entered the circle. It was taken apart on the doorstep and handed in piece by piece.

"Okay," Marcus said, "but who cares about the names? The exam's not going to ask who Krebs is."

"That's not why I'm reading it." Daniel tapped the caption. "Somebody had to figure this out. It wasn't just sitting in a textbook waiting. He described it in 1937, with Johnson, and then the prize didn't come until 1953. Sixteen years later. Sixteen years of doing the work before anyone decided it counted." He wasn't sure why that steadied him, but it did. His own failure was two weeks old and already felt permanent; here was a man who had needed sixteen years for the world to catch up to what he already knew.

Marcus turned the bottle cap over with his finger. "So you're saying fail slow."

"I'm saying I don't know yet." Daniel picked up the pencil again. "I understand the steps now, mostly. I still don't really get how moving protons makes ATP, and I can't tell if I'm getting it or just memorizing it again in a prettier order. That's the part I can't fix by tonight." He said it without the shame he'd expected to feel, and that absence assuaged something in him more thoroughly than any pep talk from his mother had managed.

He redrew the circle one last time, then wrote the date 1937 next to it in the margin, small, where a grader wouldn't see it but he would. Then he folded the paper bag along its creases, the way it had been before, glucose to citrate to the little turbine of the membrane, and pressed it flat under his hand.

"Quiz me," Marcus said.

I did not care about the showcase, which is why I stayed up past lights-out rewriting my critique for the third time. The art shed at Camp Wanoka had one good lamp and a wasp nest above the door, and I claimed the desk every night that last week of July because it was quiet, not because I wanted to win. That's what I told Marisol, anyway, and she rolled her eyes at me, which I chose to ignore.

The workshop was Ms. Petro's idea, though she mostly sat by the fan and let us fight. Twelve of us, reproduction prints taped to the plywood tables, learning to say why a painting worked instead of just whether we liked it. I had always been a liker. I liked sunsets, I liked dogs, and by Wednesday I understood that none of that counted as thinking. Marisol, who was doctrinaire about formal analysis in a way that made her insufferable and right, kept saying, "Colour first, then composition, then symbolism. In that order. Feelings last, if there's room." I thought that order was a cage until I got inside it and found it was actually a ladder.

My print was The Broken Column. I'd picked it because everyone else wanted the one with the monkeys, and because on the first day I'd looked at it for ten seconds and had to look away, which I did not admit to anyone, including myself. I told the table I picked it for the palette. The desert greens, the cracked earth, the grey of the corset. "Good," Marisol said, without looking up. "Say something about the nails."

There were nails in the painting, driven into the figure's face and body, and tears running down her cheeks. That much I could catalog. What I couldn't catalog, what kept sending me out to the wasp nest for air, was that despite all of it she looks straight at the viewer. The eyes don't ask for anything. They don't even accuse. They just meet yours, and then you're the one who has to decide what to do with your own face. I wrote three paragraphs trying to explain my discomfort and deleted all three, because they were about me, and the assignment, annoyingly, was about her.

Thursday night Marisol found me in the shed at eleven. "Petro says you're folding," she said, dropping onto the stool. "She said you called your draft garbage."

"I called it garbage because it is garbage. It's a list. The tears symbolize pain, the column symbolizes her spine, it reads like a fortune cookie."

"So stop maligning your own draft and fix it. You have the whole fact on the page and you're hiding behind it." She tapped my notebook. "Nails through the face and body, tears on the cheeks, and she's looking straight out at us. You wrote that like it's the setup. It's the whole thing. The discomfort you keep not admitting is data."

"That's not data, that's me being weird."

"Then be weird on purpose." She stole my grape soda and left, which is how you know she cares.

So Friday, at the showcase, when Petro called my name, I stood in front of everyone with my notecards and did not use them. I talked about the green of the valley against the dry pale sky, how the vertical split of the body pulls your eye down the way the column does, how the corset straps cut the canvas into bands. I talked about the tears and the nails as symbols you could name without explaining away, the way you can name a wound without knowing who struck it. And then I said the true part, the part I'd decided to keep. "Every critique I wrote before this one tried to figure out why her gaze is unbearable, and I don't think that's a question with an answer. She's pierced everywhere, she's crying, and she still looks straight out at you. When you meet her eyes, the painting stops being about her pain and becomes about your looking. You want to glance away and there's nowhere to glance. I'm telling you I don't know what to do with that, and I don't think a formal analysis is supposed to solve it. I think it's supposed to stand there, the way she does."

The applause was thin, because it was 90 degrees and half the camp was asleep, but Marisol nodded once, hard, like a referee calling a point. Petro did not pick my critique for the yearbook page, the thing I supposedly did not care about; she picked a boy named Devon's essay on the monkeys, which was tidy and had a thesis. Marisol was furious on my behalf, which was more satisfying than winning would have been, though I planned to keep pretending otherwise.

After the showcase I walked down to the lake with the last grape soda and sat on the dock. Marisol came and sat beside me and didn't say anything for a while, which for her was practically a sacrament. Somewhere behind us a counselor was rounding up stragglers, and I felt the particular ennui of the last night of anything, when you're too tired for what's ending and it hasn't ended yet.

"Devon's essay was better organized," I said.

"Devon's essay would've been fine about a shoe ad." She nudged my elbow. "You going to do this in college? The whole looking-at-things-till-it-hurts thing?"

"Undecided," I said, and she laughed, and out on the water a fish rose and fell, one silver circle widening and then gone.

Austin had chosen the back corner of the library because it was the only place where talking was permitted, though barely, and because the shelves there formed a kind of booth that hid him from anyone who might wander past. On the table in front of him lay a photocopied Spanish news article, three short paragraphs about a flood, and beside it a sign-up sheet with his name written in the second slot. The oral reassessment was in twenty minutes. If he summarised the article aloud without mistakes, the department would let him skip the intro language course in the fall and go straight into the intermediate one, which mattered to him more than he had admitted to anyone, including himself.

Priya sat across from him with her own copy, the same flood, the same three paragraphs. She had already done her reassessment that morning, fourth slot, and she had come back to the library with an expression he could not read, which frightened him. He had asked how it went. She had said, "Fine, mostly," and turned a page. That equivocal answer had been sitting in his chest ever since, because Priya was better at Spanish than he was. She had taken it since middle school. If the assessment had gone badly for her, it could go badly for anyone.

"Read it again," she said, "out loud, all the way through, then close your eyes and give me the summary."

He read. The Spanish came slowly at first, the consonants bunching up in his mouth, and then it smoothed out the way a path smooths out when you walk it twice. A river had risen. Roads were closed. Hundreds of people had left their homes. When he finished, he closed his eyes and began, in Spanish, "The article reports that heavy rain caused flooding in," and then he stopped, because he could not remember the name of the town.

"It says it right at the top," Priya said.

"There's no town in the first paragraph. It starts with the rain."

"No. Before the first sentence. Those two words in capitals at the very beginning, before anything else starts. Didn't you look at those?"

He opened his eyes. There, ahead of the first sentence, in capitals, sat the name of a city, followed by a dash and then the article's opening words. He had read straight past it a dozen times, treating it like a stain on the page, decoration, part of the newspaper's furniture. He had been so careful with the verbs that he had never once asked what that fragment was doing there.

"That's where the story was reported from," Priya said. "That's what my guy called the dateline, when he marked my sheet."

"My guy," Austin said. "What did he mark?"

She turned her paper toward him. In red at the top, beside a score that was lower than she needed, the grader had written a single line: wrong country in summary. She had told the assessor the flood had happened in the capital, because the capital was the only place name she could find in the text, mentioned once, deep in the third paragraph, as the destination of some displaced families. She had skipped the two words in capitals at the top and invented a geography the article never claimed. Austin stared at the red ink and felt his whole understanding of the task rearrange itself, quietly and completely. All the vocabulary he had drilled, all the physiology of reading, his eyes trained to leap from verb to verb, had trained him to leap right over the one detail that anchored everything else.

"So it's not decoration," he said.

"It's the ground floor, apparently," Priya said. "And I built the whole house in the wrong yard."

He worked through it again, this time reading the way a stranger would, letting the capitals come first. The city in the dateline was not the capital; it was a mid-sized river town he had never heard of, and once he held it in mind, the article's shape changed. The rain was local. The closed roads were those roads. The families moving to the capital were leaving that place, not stranded in it. His summary, when he tried it aloud again, came out steadier than any version he had produced all week, because it finally stood on something. What he still could not tell, and said so, was whether the reassessment would want the dateline spoken in Spanish or left as a proper noun, and Priya shrugged, because she did not know either, and her grader had not thought to say.

The clock over the reference desk showed five minutes to the hour. Austin picked up the article, folded it along the third paragraph so only the top was visible, and stood. He walked toward the front of the library with the folded page in his hand, mouthing the name of the city once more under his breath, and at the door he turned back to Priya and pointed at the capitals.

"Watch the top," he said.

The machine arrived in a box that had clearly been opened and resealed, because Dad never ordered anything he didn't research first, and this one he had researched for two weeks. He set it on the kitchen table next to the salt shaker he was trying to ignore, and Tyler watched him slide his arm into the cuff the way the pamphlet showed, quiet and almost formal, like a man being fitted for something.

"You do it," Dad said. "I keep flinching when it squeezes."

Tyler pressed the button and the cuff hissed and tightened and then let go, and the screen showed two numbers, one over the other. 148 over 94. Dad looked at the ceiling and did the thing he did when he was deciding whether to be worried or just tired, and Tyler, who wanted to help but didn't know how yet, said, "Is that bad?" which was not a useful question and Dad didn't answer it, which was its own kind of answer.

The doctor's office was where Tyler went looking, or rather the folder from the doctor's office, which Dad had left on the counter with his reading glasses on top like a paperweight. Inside was a printout with the 2017 guideline from the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association on it. Tyler read it twice, because the first time the numbers didn't mean anything to him. Normal, it said, for an adult, is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. He said the words out loud to the empty kitchen to make them stick. "Normal is below 120 over 80." Below both. He copied it into his phone.

He started reading at the table that night, while Dad watched a game with the sound low. There was a lot about systolic and diastolic, the top number and the bottom number, and a lot less about what to actually do, which was mostly the same sentence wearing different coats: move more, eat differently, cut the sodium. Tyler had assumed, before this, that blood pressure was the kind of thing you either had or didn't have, like a limp. Reading disabused him of that by the second page. It was more like a bank account, and Dad had been making small withdrawals for years without the balance ever being called in.

The trouble was Dad himself, who treated every change like an accusation. When Tyler came home with a bag of unsalted almonds and left it on the counter, Dad ate a handful out of spite and then said they tasted like drywall. When Tyler suggested a walk after dinner, Dad said his knees were between him and the sidewalk, which was true about the knees and not true about the reason.

Tyler tried another way, which was to stop presenting solutions and start asking questions. He showed Dad the guideline printout and pointed at the line he'd copied into his phone. "Under 120 and under 80," he said. "That's the whole target. Both numbers."

"That's for normal people," Dad said, but he looked at the numbers longer than he needed to, and later that week he let Tyler take his reading before the game instead of after, and it was 141 over 89, and Dad said, "Lower than Tuesday," with the careful flatness of a man trying not to be pleased.

The garden was where they ended up, because it was movement that didn't announce itself as movement. Dad had let the tomato bed go weedy since August, and the soil had gone friable and soft with rot under the leaves, crumbling when Tyler dug his fingers in, and the two of them spent a Saturday pulling it apart and turning it over. Dad's knees complained and Dad complained, and Tyler carried the heavy bag of compost without being asked. It wasn't restitution exactly, though Tyler thought of it that way, the way he thought of the almonds and the walks, small deposits against a debt he hadn't incurred, being paid anyway because that was how family worked, or how he wanted it to.

Afterward they sat on the back steps with their elbows on their knees, and Dad's face was flushed and his breathing was loud, and Tyler took the machine outside and cuffed Dad's arm right there on the steps. The cuff squeezed in the cold air, and the screen blinked while it thought, and Dad watched it over Tyler's shoulder, and neither of them said anything until the numbers came up.

The farmers' market opened at eight, and by half past Tristan had sold four jars of his mother's plum jam and memorized none of the vocabulary spread across his lap. He was supposed to be watching the cash box while his mother fetched change from the car, but the exam was Monday, and Monday did not care that Saturdays belonged to the stall.

"Portugal and wine," he said under his breath, tracing a column of his notes with one finger. "Or was it Portugal and cloth." He had written Ricardo's example down twice in class and both times the countries had swapped goods on him, the waydreams rearranged rooms.

"You're muttering at jam," said Priya, sliding around the corner of the stall with two coffees. She handed him one without being asked, which was the kind of thing she did, and which he had never properly thanked her for. She was in the same class, bound for the same exam, and she had a way of standing beside him on Saturday mornings as if it were coincidence.

"It's Ricardo," Tristan said. "There's this original example, England and Portugal, cloth and wine, from 1817, and I keep getting which country had which good backwards. I think Portugal made the wine. That part at least feels safe. England making cloth."

"Feels safe," Priya repeated, and her mouth did the thing it did when she knew something he didn't. She sat down on the overturned crate they used for the honey display and sipped her coffee, unhurried, letting him stew.

He thought of his uncle last spring, before any of this, standing in this same spot and arguing with a man selling goat cheese. Tristan had been fourteen and had asked, later, why his uncle bothered, since the cheese man clearly wasn't going to change his mind about the parking situation downtown. His uncle had said that arguing with someone you'll see every week isn't about winning, it's about keeping the argument alive so the relationship doesn't die of politeness. Tristan hadn't understood it then. He thought of Priya on the crate now, keeping something alive, and understood it a little.

"Fine," he said. "Tell me."

"I'm not telling you. That's not learning, that's copying." She set her cup down. "But I'll trade you. You explain comparative advantage to me, out loud, like I'm a customer, and I'll tell you if you've got the countries wrong."

So he stood up behind the stall, in the same spot his uncle had argued from, and did it as a pitch. Suppose, he said, two countries, and one of them is better at making everything, absolutely better, both goods, and the other one is worse at both. His hands moved over the jam jars like they were England and Portugal. Everyone assumes the strong country has nothing to gain, he said, but the point of comparative advantage was that trade isn't about who's best, it's about what each side gives up least to get what it wants. Even the weaker country has something worth trading, because the strong country's talent is wasted on the thing it's only slightly better at. Both sides walk away ahead. Nobody loses.

"Both sides," Priya said slowly, and he could see her testing it, turning it over the way he had at midnight with the textbook open and the lamp too bright. "That's the part I keep refusing to believe. It sounds like symbiosis, but between countries, like neither one has to lose for the other to gain." She frowned at the jam. "Okay. Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. England and Portugal. Cloth and wine. And you have it right, Portugal is wine, England is cloth." She pointed her cup at him. "You had it right the whole time. You just didn't trust it."

At that moment an obstreperous toddler two stalls down lunged at a display of peaches, and his mother, rushing past with the cash bag, detoured to catch the basket before it fell, and the peach farmer called out his thanks, and for a second the whole market seemed to be a web of small rescues nobody had planned. Tristan looked at all of it, the trades and the rescues and Priya deciding not to simply tell him the answer, and felt the idea settle somewhere deeper than his notes.

"I was going to fail that question," he said.

"No, you weren't," Priya said. "You were going to get it right and then panic and change it." She picked up his textbook, closed it, and slid it under the cash box, out of reach. "That's why I came over. Your mom texted me." She stood and brushed off her jeans, then paused. "Also, I got the countries backwards on Thursday's quiz, so this was for me too."

"You let me do the whole speech."

"Both sides walk away ahead," she said, and held out her hand for his coffee.

The quarry had filled with spring rain until it was a rectangle of green-black water, and Cameron stood at its edge holding his phone like a man holding a bird he meant to keep from flying. On the screen was the graph he had been assigned to explain, the one from the observatory on Mauna Loa, carbon dioxide rising and rising across sixty years in a line that climbed like a staircase made of teeth. On Monday he would have to stand up in earth science and explain it, and the graph, and the whole business of greenhouse gases, to a room that included Priya Rao, who had already corrected him twice this semester in a voice that was never unkind and never soft.

Marcus had chosen the quarry for the study session, and Marcus's idea of studying was swimming. He was already treading water ten feet out, calling Cameron's name in the bellicose way of boys who want company more than they want to admit it. Dana sat on a flat rock with her sneakers off, and Tess, who was Dana's cousin and in the same class, crouched at the edge dragging a stick through the pale quarry dust.

"I don't get the sawtooth part," Tess said, before Cameron had even sat down. She drew in the dust, and her drawing did look like the graph, a long jagged climb. "The line goes up, and up, and it wiggles the whole way. If the instruments were any good, wouldn't it be smooth?"

"Probably measurement error," Cameron said. "Old machines, right? Like static." He said it with confidence he did not feel, because he had thought the same thing at midnight, leaning over his phone in bed, and the wiggles had looked like noise to him too. He had a page of notes about greenhouse gases, though, and he started there, because that part he actually understood. Sunlight comes through the air, he said, and the ground warms up and gives off heat of its own, and carbon dioxide and the other gases let the sunlight in but hold some of that heat on its way back out, like a blanket that only works in one direction. Dana nodded along. Tess kept drawing teeth in the dust.

Marcus climbed out, dripping, and shook water off like a dog, and Cameron moved the phone fast to the middle of the rock, out of the splash radius. This turned out to be the first good decision of the afternoon, though he did not know it yet.

"Wiggle, wiggle, wiggle," Marcus said, reading over Cameron's shoulder, because of course he would not go get his towel first. "Why does it do that? Is the carbon dioxide, like, breathing?"

Cameron almost said he didn't know, and that would have been honest, but something about the way Tess was carving the little dips into the dust stopped him. The dips came every year. That was the thing he kept sliding past. Not random static, not old machines. Regular as anything. He held the phone flat on the rock so all four of them could see it, and dragged two fingers apart to enlarge the last ten years, and there it was again, the same tooth shape repeating and repeating, springing down and climbing back, springing down and climbing back. Measurement error did not keep a schedule.

"The wiggles aren't mistakes," he said slowly, still testing it as he said it. "Look how even they are. Same size, every single year, for sixty years."

"Then what makes them?" Tess said.

He stared at the dust where she had drawn her teeth, and then at the trees on the far rim of the quarry, the whole green band of them, oaks and brush running along the limestone edge, and then at his own hands, which had gone cold in a way that had nothing to do with the water. Somewhere in his notes from Monday's class there had been a phrase about plants. He had written it down without reading it, the way you write things at the end of a long class period.

"The Northern Hemisphere," he said. "Think about all the plants up here. All of it, everything that leafs out." He pointed at the tree line above the water. "In spring and summer, when everything's growing, the plants take in carbon dioxide. The whole hemisphere's plants, pulling it in. Then in autumn and winter, when the leaves die and decay, they release it back." He looked at the graph again, checking his own logic against the line. Down in the northern summer, up in the northern winter, down and up, and underneath it all the slow climb that never stopped. "The plants are the wiggle. That's why it's so regular. The graph is breathing."

Nobody said anything for a second. Then Tess dragged her stick through her drawing and made it again, slower, and drew little leaf shapes at the bottom of each dip, and Dana said, in the voice of someone deciding whether to believe a thing, "So the zigzag is real. The line is doing two things at once."

"Two things at once," Cameron said. "That's actually the whole assignment." He was talking faster now, the words assembling themselves. "The plants take the carbon dioxide back every year and give it back every year, and they've done that the whole century, and the line climbs anyway. It's like, the breathing is steady, and something else is climbing on top of the breathing." He stopped there, because past that point he wasn't sure yet. He did not know how much of the climb was what, and his notes had numbers he hadn't finished checking, and Monday was coming either way. He said so, out loud, because it seemed better to say it than to have Priya say it for him. Dana nodded like that was the right kind of answer, though with Priya he couldn't be sure.

Marcus, still wet, reached over to point at the top of the curve, and his hand dripped, and the drop landed a half inch from the phone, and Cameron slid the phone into his back pocket, dry, and stood up, and Tess was still drawing leaves at the bottom of every dip, one for every year.

The cuff hissed and tightened around Grandpa Sal's arm until his fingers went blotchy, and Isabella watched the digital display climb, stall, and settle. One sixty-eight over ninety-four. She wrote it in the notebook she'd bought for her pharmacy tech course, and under it she wrote his pulse, and under that she drew a small frowning face, which she immediately crossed out because professionals did not draw frowning faces.

"You look like your mother when she's about to tell me the mower is broken," Grandpa Sal said.

"The mower is broken," Isabella said. "I heard it wheezing from the porch. Kind of like you on the stairs."

He laughed, which turned into a cough, which turned into him waving her off toward the kitchen for a glass of water. This was the third reading she'd taken that week, at his request, after his own doctor had said a number at him and then gotten called away, and he'd come home knowing only that the number had been "not wonderful." Isabella had made a chart. She was a person who made charts. The chart had a row for morning readings, a row for evening, and a column she'd labeled "variables," where she tracked whether he'd had coffee, salt, or an argument with his neighbor about the fence line, which was chronologically reliable, occurring roughly every other day. The chronology of it all was the only tidy thing in the house.

The numbers were not tidy. They sat high across the whole week, and when she flipped back through the pharmacy course module on blood pressure, she found that a reading consistently that high had a name. She read it twice to be sure.

"Grandpa," she said at dinner, spooning sauce onto his plate before her own, "it's called hypertension. That's what the module says. Persistent high readings like yours."

"Hypertension," he repeated, testing it. "Sounds like a Greek philosopher. Sounds like something that should be wearing a toga and judging me."

"It kind of is." She turned her fork over. "The module also says regular aerobic exercise, brisk walking or cycling, on most days, lowers blood pressure in a lot of people. Even people who already have hypertension." She said it carefully, the way she'd say a word she'd just learned in Spanish, half expecting him to correct her pronunciation.

He pushed a meatball around his plate. "I walk. I walk to the mailbox."

"The mailbox is forty feet from the door."

"It's uphill both ways if you're committed."

Isabella put her fork down. She thought about her accounting elective, where the teacher had made them amortize a loan across five years so they could see how a big intimidating number became small survivable payments. The word had stuck with her because it felt like a general principle of the universe, or at least of Tuesdays. She drew a line down a fresh notebook page and wrote "week 1" at the top of the first narrow column, then "week 2," then enough weeks to reach September. Under week one she wrote "20 minutes, easy pace, after dinner." Under week two, "25 minutes." The plan was deliberately parsimonious, nothing fancy, no gym, no equipment, just him and the road past the cemetery, which he claimed had the best sunset in the county and which she suspected he'd avoided for six years, since Grandma Rosa.

"Every evening," she said, sliding the notebook across the table. "Most days, the module said. You pick the nights off. Two a week, maximum."

He looked at the schedule for a long time. "And you'll be where during this?"

"Walking with you," she said. "Obviously. Somebody has to carry you home."

He snorted. He signed the bottom of the page the way he signed contracts with the fence guy, with a flourish and a mutter. That night she took his reading again, out of curiosity, and wrote it down without comment: 166 over 92, which she already understood proved nothing, one way or the other, and which she wrote down anyway.

They started the next evening. He set the pace, which was slower than her brisk and faster than his mailbox, and he talked the whole first mile, mostly about the fence, some about the mower, once about a girl he'd known before Rosa and immediately retracted. On Thursday it rained and he wanted to skip, and she stood in the doorway holding both jackets until he surrendered. On Saturday they went twice as far as planned because the sunset was, in fact, ridiculous over the cemetery, and he stood at the gate a while, not saying anything, and she looked at the road instead of at him.

At the end of the second week she pumped up the cuff again in his kitchen, the chart open beside the machine. The display thought about it, the way it did, then gave its verdict. She looked at the number, then at the week's column, then back.

"Sixteen points down," she said. "If that's right."

"It's right enough," Grandpa Sal said, and held out his arm. "Again. I want to watch it happen."

The robotics lab smelled like solder and cold pizza, and Ryder had been staring at the same line of code for ten minutes when Devon kicked the leg of the workbench and said, "This is garbage, by the way. Your whole teleop branch is garbage."

Ryder looked up. Devon was holding the printout of the drive-team roster, but he wasn't looking at it; he was looking at Marcus, who sat in the corner soldering a motor mount with the resigned posture of someone who had learned not to argue back. Marcus had missed the build deadline on Saturday. He'd said he'd have the arm assembly done and he hadn't, and now Devon was orbiting the lab saying things like "some people just don't care" and "I guess we'll lose at regionals, whatever," loud enough that everyone metabolized the resentment slowly, all afternoon, without anyone naming it.

"That's not helping," Ryder said, finally.

"I'm being honest," Devon said. "You want me to lie?"

Ryder wanted a lot of things. He wanted the arm assembly finished. He wanted Devon to stop doing this corrosive loop every time something went wrong, because the vitriolic version of honesty, he was beginning to suspect, wasn't honesty at all, it was just anger wearing honesty's clothes. But mostly he wanted Marcus to still want to be on the team in three weeks, and that seemed, at the moment, genuinely in doubt.

That night he lay on his bed with his phone and searched, half embarrassed, "how to give feedback without being a jerk." Most of it was junk. One page, though, was from something called the Center for Creative Leadership, and it laid out a model: situation, behavior, impact. You named when it happened, what the person actually did, and what effect it had. No verdicts on character. No "you're lazy." Just "Saturday, the arm assembly didn't arrive, and we lost the practice day." It felt almost too simple, like a recipe with three ingredients, and Ryder distrested how clean it was. But it also reminded him of something from programming, the modularity of good code, each function doing one thing, taking clear inputs, returning clear outputs. Maybe feedback could work like that too. He wasn't sure. He turned the idea over for another hour before he slept.

The next day he caught Marcus in the hallway outside the cafeteria, before he could talk himself out of it. "Can I say something about Saturday?"

Marcus shifted his backpack. "Devon already said plenty."

"I'm not Devon." Ryder's palms were damp, which seemed absurd, since he was about to say something reasonable to a person he liked. "It's this thing I found. It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model. You just say when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had." He heard his own voice, flat, reciting, and winced. "Okay, that sounded like a worksheet. But here. On Saturday, the arm assembly wasn't finished when the build day ended, and we lost our only practice window before regionals. That's it. That's all I wanted to say."

Marcus was quiet long enough that Ryder began composing his apology. Then Marcus said, "My mom was in the hospital Friday night. I didn't tell anyone because I didn't want it to be an excuse."

"I'm sorry. Is she okay?"

"She's home now." Marcus looked at the floor. "I should have texted somebody. I just went quiet instead."

"You could tell the team that," Ryder said. "Not as an excuse. Just so we know." And then, because the model had one thing it couldn't do, he added, "I don't actually know if saying it the clean way makes it easier to hear. You tell me."

Marcus half smiled. "It was easier than 'some people don't care.'"

At the afternoon build session, Ryder watched Devon launch into his orbit again, and he cut across it, voice steadier than he felt. "Devon. Situation, behavior, impact. Try it." Devon stared at him like he'd started speaking Icelandic, so Ryder said the whole thing himself, the Saturday, the assembly, the lost practice, and then Marcus, unprompted, said, "My mom was in the hospital. I should have told someone. I'll have the arm done by Thursday." The lab went still in a different way than usual, the absence of the low static everyone had gotten used to.

Devon picked up a wrench and didn't say sorry, but he also didn't say "whatever," and when Marcus's soldering iron slipped a few minutes later, Devon just steadied the motor mount with two fingers and held it there until the joint cooled. Ryder still didn't know if three clean sentences could survive a whole season, or whether Devon would ever learn to say them himself, but Thursday was two days away and the arm was half-built and everyone was still in the room.

"Hand me the wire strippers," Marcus said.

The gym smelled of floor wax and old sweat, and the twelve eleven-year-olds in front of Brianna were already obstreperous, bouncing balls off each other's backs while she tried to pin her practice plan to the clipboard. She had drawn the drills the night before at her kitchen table: three-line passing, weave, chest pass to the target. Her problem was specific and she could name it. These kids telegraphed everything and threw passes that arrived at chests, at elbows, at the backs of heads. Nobody caught anything cleanly.

"Lines," she called. "Five passes down, five back."

It went badly. Every time a pass sailed wide, she corrected the thrower the way her own coaches had corrected her: "Bend your wrists." "Follow through." "Square your hips." The words came out of her mouth like an inheritance, a patrimony of commands she had never thought to question, and the kids' shoulders got stiffer with each one. By the second drill, Marisol, their best player, was staring at her own hands before every pass as if they belonged to a stranger.

Brianna called water and stood alone at the free throw line. She was flashing back, without meaning to, to her junior year, the state semifinal, when Coach Ruiz had told her during a timeout to stop thinking about her elbow. "Stop aiming your elbow," he'd said, exasperated, "aim at the rim." She had made the next shot and the one after that. At the time she'd thought he was just fed up with her. She'd never wondered whether the words themselves had done something.

While the kids drank, she scrolled her phone one-handed, because she had a term paper due on motor learning and a half-formed suspicion. She found the study she'd skimmed a week ago, work by a researcher named Gabriele Wulf, and read it properly this time standing on the line with her thumb moving fast. Learners usually improved faster when they were told to focus on the effect of a movement, on the target, rather than on their own body parts. She read it twice. Her whole coaching vocabulary, it turned out, had been pointed the wrong direction, at wrists and hips instead of at the thing the wrists and hips were for.

She set the phone down on the bleachers. It could exhilarate a person, this feeling of a door swinging open, and it could also sting, because every correction she'd given tonight had made somebody worse.

"New rule," she said when they came back. "I'm not going to talk about your bodies anymore. Not your wrists, not your feet. Listen for what the pass does, not what you do."

Marisol squinted at her. "Then what do we think about?"

"Hit your teammate's hands," Brianna said. "That's it. The pass has to arrive at their hands. Don't think about how."

They ran it. The first five minutes were chaos, because the kids kept glancing at her for the old instructions, and Brianna had to bite down on every correction that rose in her throat. When Devone's pass smacked Marcus in the shoulder, she said only, "Hands, Devone," and stepped back. The second five minutes were different. Passes began to arrive where hands were waiting. Marisol caught three in a row without looking down, and Marcus, the worst passer on the team, threw one that hit Marisol's palm so cleanly that she gasped.

"Again," Brianna said, and they went again.

At the end of practice she had them run the weave one last time, and it was better, it was unmistakably better, balls snapping hand to hand down the floor. But it wasn't fixed. Devone still threw high when he got excited, and half of them would probably forget by Thursday, and Brianna understood that she'd traded something away, too. The old commands had made her feel like a coach, somebody with technical authority; this new way made her more like a witness, standing quiet at the edge while they found the target themselves. She wasn't sure yet which of those she was supposed to be.

The last kids filed out. Marisol lingered by the door with a ball under her arm.

"Same thing Thursday?" she asked.

"Same thing," Brianna said, and began collecting the cones.

The kettle had just begun to sigh when Isabelle spread the printout across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the curling corners with a salt cellar and a jar of marmalade. The graph showed carbon dioxide climbing in a jagged line from the 1960s to now, and beside it, in her own handwriting, the notes from the online course she had started two weeks ago: parts per million, Keeling curve, wavelength. Her grandfather set down two cups and looked at the paper the way he looked at weather coming in over the ridge, without comment.

"Can I ask you something," she said. "About the graph."

He sat, folded his hands, and waited. He was a laconic man, her grandfather; whole visits could pass on a dozen words, and Isabelle had learned that his silences were not indifference but attention, held open like a door.

She traced the line with one finger. "So this is carbon dioxide, measured every year, and it goes up and up. It never dips, not really. Even the little wiggles are just seasons." She glanced up. "That's what I'm supposed to be able to explain by Friday. How the gases trap heat. How to read this."

"There were men who worked the quarry," he said at last. "My father among them. They'd have looked at that and seen their livings in it, one way or another." He tapped the paper's edge, where she had written the source in small print. "Who made this?"

"Some observatory. I wrote it down. Mauna Loa, and then ice cores for the older part." She was proud of having recorded the provenance of every number, because her teacher had drilled it into them that a graph without a source was just a shape. "That part I understand. What I don't understand is the argument I got into yesterday."

There was a knock at the back door and Theo let himself in, as he always did, shaking rain off his jacket. Theo lived three farms over and had driven Isabelle's mother crazy since they were both seven. He pulled out a chair without being asked and read the graph upside down with the ease of someone who did everything sideways.

"Still fighting with Dev," Isabelle said, "from chemistry."

"The quarry kid," Theo said. He grinned. "You know what's funny, people stigmatize the kids whose dads work there, like they personally dug the hole in the sky. Dev's dad hauls stone, that's all." He reached for a biscuit. "What's the fight?"

"He says if you want to slow warming in the next few years, you go after methane leaks first, not carbon dioxide. I said that's backwards, because everyone says carbon dioxide is the main problem, it's the one in all the graphs, it's the one we measure at Mauna Loa." She flattened the paper. "He got mad. I got madder."

Her grandfather sipped his tea and said nothing, which Isabelle had come to understand as permission to keep going.

"So last night I looked up methane, and here's the thing." She pulled a second sheet from her folder, covered in her cramped notes. "A methane molecule traps far more heat than a carbon dioxide molecule. Way more, per molecule. I thought Dev had that wrong and he didn't." She paused. "But it only stays up there about a decade on average. Carbon dioxide stays much, much longer. Centuries, some of it."

"So who wins the argument?" Theo asked.

"That's what I couldn't figure out. Both, I think. Or neither." She turned her cup slowly on its saucer. "If a gas disappears in ten years and a different one stays for centuries, then cutting the short-lived one changes things faster, but cutting the long-lived one matters more for, like, everything after us. Dev was arguing about the next few years and I was arguing about the whole century, and we were both talking as if it was one question."

Her grandfather rose, refilled the kettle, and set it back on the stove. When he turned around he said, "Your grandmother settled arguments like that by feeding people."

"I'm not wrong, though," Isabelle said. "Am I? About carbon dioxide being the long one?"

"You're not wrong," he said. "That's not the same as winning."

Theo snorted into his tea. Isabelle looked at the two graphs side by side, the century's slow climb and the methane notes beneath it, and something settled in her, not a conclusion exactly but a willingness to hold both lines at once. She took out her phone and typed a message to Dev: "You were right about methane being stronger per molecule and shorter lived, about a decade. I was arguing a different timescale. Talk tomorrow?" She set the phone face down before the reply could come or not come, because she wasn't ready to know which.

The kettle began to whistle. Her grandfather lifted it off and poured, and Isabelle moved the marmalade jar so the steam wouldn't wrinkle the paper, pressing the graph flat with the heel of her hand as though she could keep the line from climbing any further tonight.

The trail behind the community college cut through oaks and then opened onto a mown field, and Clara had chosen it because the placement exam was in six days and her bedroom had begun to feel like a held breath. She carried a binder of flashcards and a water bottle and the particular stubbornness of someone who had tested into the lowest tier of everything and was tired of it. Biochemistry was the section she feared most. The words themselves seemed recalcitrant, refusing to arrange themselves into anything she could hold onto: glycolysis, pyruvate, NAD+, the electron transport chain, as if the cell were a factory built in a language she had never been offered.

Her friend Priya had come along, ostensibly to sketch, actually because Priya never believed anyone should study alone. They stopped where the trail widened near the field's edge, and Clara sat on a flat rock and shuffled the cards without looking at them.

"Say one," Clara said.

Priya took the deck. "Okay. Where does glycolysis happen, and what does it start with?"

"Outside the mitochondria. In the cytoplasm. It starts with glucose, one six-carbon sugar, and it breaks it down to pyruvate." She said it fast, the way you say a phone number before you forget it. "And it makes a little ATP. Two net. That's the part I keep losing. Everything after that needs oxygen, but glycolysis doesn't."

"Correct," Priya said, and drew an oak leaf in the margin of her sketchbook.

The problem, as Clara understood it, was that she could memorize the sequence but not the reason anyone should care. The steps enraptured her when she read about them late at night, this tiny combustion happening in every cell of her body, but by morning the enchantment faded and she was left with the same blank page. Her mother said she thought too much and too separately. Her brother said she should just get the tutor the college offered for free. Clara had refused the tutor with a pride she couldn't entirely justify, some conviction that if she couldn't build it herself, in her own head, on her own walk, then it wasn't really hers.

"Last card," Priya said. "What happens to pyruvate when there's no oxygen?"

"I don't know that one yet." Clara stood. "Ask me tomorrow."

"You have six days."

"Then don't waste today's oxygen on worrying." She started across the field at an easy jog, just to move, and Priya's laugh followed her and then thinned out behind her, and then there was only her own breathing.

She sprinted. She didn't plan to; her legs simply wanted to, the way legs do when the grass is short and the far fence is measurable and the afternoon has been sitting too long. Halfway across, her thighs began to burn, a heat that climbed from muscle into certainty, and by the time she reached the fence her legs were shaking and she had to grip the wire and stand there with her head down, gasping. Her lungs felt too small for the request her body was making.

And standing there, bent over, she thought about oxygen. Not in the abstract way of the flashcards but as a shortage, an actual deficit in actual muscle, and she thought: my cells are running low on oxygen right now. This is the scenario. This is the card.

She walked back slowly, turning it over. Glycolysis didn't need oxygen, that much she had. Glycolysis took glucose to pyruvate and made two ATP per glucose, small change but fast, and it needed something else, some partner molecule, NAD+, that had to be there or the whole thing stopped. She remembered the phrase from the textbook, NAD+ regenerated, and she had underlined it twice because the sentence had felt like a lock without a key. The cell, starved of oxygen, still wanted its two ATP. It still wanted glycolysis. So what did it do with the pyruvate?

Her legs ached, and the ache had a name she had heard in gym class years ago without anyone explaining it, lactic acid, and the ache was saying something. Lactate. The muscle made lactate. From what? From pyruvate. When muscle cells run low on oxygen, she thought, they convert pyruvate into lactate.

She stopped in the middle of the field. But why would a cell bother? Making lactate had to cost something, and then the cost resolved itself the way a word resolves itself when you finally hear it spoken: the conversion put NAD+ back. It regenerated NAD+. That was the point. The cell burned pyruvate into lactate not as a failure but as a trade, sacrificing the pyruvate so that NAD+ existed again, so glycolysis could keep running, so the two ATP per glucose kept coming even while she stood here starving every cell of oxygen. Her legs weren't just tired. They were rationing.

She was laughing by the time she reached the rock, breathless and half-doubtful, because she had assembled the whole thing from a burn in her thighs and two underlined sentences, and half-doubtful was a familiar country for her.

"Ask me the last card," she said.

Priya looked up, pencil still. "What happens to pyruvate when there's no oxygen?"

"When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate," Clara said. "And that regenerates NAD+, so glycolysis can continue, making two ATP per glucose." She said it slowly, and then, quieter, testing it: "That's why my legs are burning right now. I sprinted the field to check."

Priya lowered the sketchbook. "You sprinted a field to study?"

"I sprinted a field because I wanted to, and then it turned into studying." Clara sat down on the grass, still catching her breath. "I don't know if I have it exactly right. I don't know everything about it, just that one piece. But I know it from the inside now, from my own legs, and that feels different."

Priya was quiet for a moment, in the way she was quiet when she was deciding whether to say the subtext out loud. "You know the tutor's still there," she said. "If you wanted."

"I know." Clara pulled a blank card from the binder and wrote on it, then turned it so Priya could see: low oxygen, pyruvate, lactate, NAD+, 2 ATP. "But this one's mine. I earned it in the grass."

Priya took the card and added a small drawing in the corner, a stick figure running with burning legs, and handed it back. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Same trail," Clara said, and put the card on top of the deck.

Jordan had told his mother, twice, that explaining things was basically his gift, which was why he had volunteered to make a five-minute video for the college's incoming-freshman science page on how greenhouse gases trap heat. He regretted this. He regretted it most at his grandfather's house, where he'd been sent for the weekend with a printed graph of carbon dioxide over the last century and a phone camera he hadn't turned on once.

The graph lay on the kitchen table beside a bowl of pistachios. Jordan squinted at the jagged line, which rose overall but undulated as it climbed, small teeth inside a long slope, and he could not for the life of him say why it wiggled. His grandfather drifted past in slippers, glanced at the paper, and said, "That looks like my heartbeat monitor. Am I dying?" Jordan said he was not dying, probably, and Grandpa took a pistachio and drifted out to the sun porch to listen to a baseball game with the sound off.

Jordan's cousin Priya arrived around noon, ostensibly to return a casserole dish but actually, as she admitted within ninety seconds, because her mother had heard Jordan was making a fool of himself with a camera and wanted to watch. "You said you'd start filming at ten," she said, settling into the chair across from him. "It's twelve forty. That's not a filming schedule, that's a hostage situation."

"The problem," Jordan said, "is the wiggle. If I can't explain the wiggle, the whole thing looks like chicanery. Like somebody drew a scary line on purpose." He traced the little rising teeth with his finger. "People will think it's a trick."

"People think everything's a trick," Priya said. "My chemistry teacher says you could show some people a sunrise and they'd ask who painted it." She pulled the graph closer. "Also, and I say this with love, what are greenhouse gases even for? Aren't they just bad? That's the whole assignment, right? Gases bad, planet sad, the end."

That was, in fact, more or less the script Jordan had drafted in his head the night before, and hearing it out loud he found he didn't like the sound of it. It had the shape of a slogan, not an explanation. He went looking for something better, which in this house meant the sun porch, where his grandfather kept forty years of old astronomy magazines in unstable towers. Grandpa watched him dig without comment except to say, "Don't topple the one with the eclipses," and Jordan, sneezing twice, found a tattered issue with a sidebar about Earth's heat balance. He read it standing up, one hand on a tower of magazines to keep it from avalanching.

"Okay," he said, coming back in with the magazine open like a waiter with a menu. "So. Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius." Priya mouthed the numbers back at him slowly. "Fourteen is what we actually have. Minus eighteen is the version with no greenhouse effect at all."

Priya frowned at the magazine, then at the window, where the February yard sat brown and thawed. "So it's not bad. It's the reason I'm not wearing a spacesuit right now." Jordan said the natural effect was the reason, yes, and what he had to figure out was how to hold both things at once, that it kept the planet livable and that the line on the graph kept climbing, and he'd have to be honest in the video about which parts he understood cold and which parts he was still shaky on. The wiggle, for instance. He was still shaky on the wiggle.
