At the butcher's trailer she asked for a pound and a half of ground pork, and the butcher asked her what she was making, and when she said rice bowls and soup and a chili she was mostly inventing, he nodded as though she had said something wise.

The problem revealed itself slowly, over the course of the afternoon, in her own kitchen. She cooked the rice in the biggest pot, all four cups of it, and browned the pork, and roasted the sweet potatoes on one sheet pan while the kale wilted in a skillet. By five o'clock the counter held six containers, labeled in her careful hand, and she felt something close to triumph. Then, spooning a test bowl for herself, she stopped. The rice had been sitting in the pot, then in a container, then in the microwave, and somewhere in the back of her mind was a fragment from a food-safety unit in eighth grade, half remembered and shaped like a warning. She had read, too, in one of the batch-cooking articles, that a thermometer was not optional equipment. Her mother owned one. It lived, she discovered, in the drawer with the dead batteries and the birthday candles, a thin metal probe with a small dial.

She had never used it. She microwaved her test bowl again, longer this time, until the edges of the rice scalded her thumb, then pushed the probe into the center of the pile and watched the needle crawl. It stopped at what looked like a hundred and forty. She pulled the phone from her back pocket and searched, and there it was, plain as a bus schedule: the USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which was 74 degrees Celsius. She looked at the dial, which had both scales printed on its face, the Celsius numbers smaller, inside. A hundred and forty was nowhere near. She had been about to eat it.

"Fine," she said out loud to the empty kitchen, feeling both foolish and, strangely, more competent than she had all day. She stirred the bowl so the cold center and the scalded edges traded places, put it back in the microwave for another minute, and probed it again. This time the needle eased past the mark, 74 on the inner ring, 165 on the outer. She held it there a moment to be sure the number stayed. Then she ate her dinner standing at the counter, rice and pork and a fried egg she had added because she deserved it, and it was good, and hot all the way through in a way she could now feel as a fact rather than a guess.

She texted her friend Priya, who had laughed at her earlier in the week for the eggs-and-peas dinners. Making real food now, she wrote. Reheated rice at 74 Celsius, verified. Priya sent back a thumbs up and a question mark, and Annabelle did not explain, because explaining would have turned it into something smaller than it was.

On Monday she carried a container to her mother's room, reheated in the kitchen first, probe through the center before she would let herself climb the stairs. Her mother was propped against pillows, gray faced but hungry, and she ate half the bowl while Annabelle sat on the end of the bed and pretended not to watch.

"It's good," her mother said. "When did you learn to cook?"

Annabelle considered the truthful answer, which was two days ago, in a kitchen full of steam and a drawer full of dead batteries, and the other truthful answer, which was that she hadn't learned yet, not really, that Thursday's chili was still an open question and Wednesday's might be a disaster. "I'm working on it," she said, and took the empty bowl back down to wash.

Luca had claimed his grandmother's parlor for the whole of Saturday, and the parlor, which had hosted forty years of church meetings and one memorable divorce announcement, seemed willing. Six chairs faced a strip of Persian rug that he had decided was the stage. The one-act was called The Littoral Road, twenty pages about two lighthouse keepers who may or may not be brothers, and his drama teacher had assigned it to him with the words "Direct something small and don't be precious about it," which Luca had already failed at, twice, by Wednesday.

"You moved on the wrong line," he said to Priya, who played the younger keeper. "You cross downstage when she says the thing about the tide. Not before."

"I felt it before," Priya said. "The line was coming toward me and my feet went with it."

"That's not how it works. The blocking is fixed. Stage left, four steps, turn, sit." He had drawn it that morning in his notebook, numbered arrows marching across a sketch of the rug, and he believed in those arrows with the whole of his chest.

His grandmother drifted through with a tray of lemonade and stayed to watch, which everyone pretended not to mind. "When your grandfather did am-dram," she said, "the director was a tyrant about where people stood. He called the little diagrams in his book a puppet show for actors." She sipped. "Then the actors moved anyway, and he sulked, and then they got married. Him and the tyrant, I mean. Different story."

The problem arrived on Sunday and looked like Marcus. Marcus played the older keeper and had opinions, which he shared while eating a biscuit: that fixed blocking was a cage, that blocking should breathe, that theatre was "really a hermeneutics of the body," which he said in a way that suggested he had read it on a poster. Luca argued back with his arrows. Priya, sensing blood, argued for feeling. Two rehearsals collapsed into a debate that Marcus won mostly by being taller.

Luca sat on the porch steps afterward with the notebook, maligning actors in general under his breath, and then stopped, because his grandmother was right there handing him lemonade and because maligning people was less interesting than the thing he was circling. Marcus's way and his way were both about the same worry: that the show would be different every night, and one of those nights would be bad. Fixed blocking was his answer to the worry. Freedom was Marcus's answer to a different worry, that the show would be the same every night, and dead. Both of them wanted the thing on the rug to be alive. He did not know yet how to hold both, so he did the practical thing first: he called Devi.

Devi was stage managing, which so far had meant texting everyone the schedule. Luca asked her what a stage manager actually did besides that, and she said, "In a real house, everything. In ours, mostly the book." She showed up Monday with a fat binder she'd assembled from templates online. "This is the prompt book," she said, tapping it. "I record the blocking in it, so it can be repeated the same way at every performance."

"So it's my arrows," Luca said.

"It's your arrows after I've argued with them," Devi said. "Sit down."

What he proposed to the cast on Tuesday was a trade, and he was honest about the parts of it he hadn't worked out. "Every cross we set, Devi writes down, and that's the cross forever. But for anything we haven't set, you can move where the scene asks you to, and if it works twice, we set that too and it's forever." Marcus asked who decided if it worked. "I do," Luca said, "unless I'm wrong, then Devi's book decides, because her book outranks all of us. Even me." Marcus considered this with the gravity of a man weighing a treaty. "The hermeneutics of the body," he said, "accepts these terms." Priya said, "He read that on a poster," and rehearsal started four minutes late because nobody could stop laughing.

They performed in the parlor for eleven people, including Luca's grandmother in the good chair and his drama teacher by the window, arms folded like a customs officer. Eight minutes in, Priya stood up to cross and then didn't, and stood there in the lamplight with her mouth slightly open, and from the hallway Devi's voice came quiet and level: "Your cross is downstage on the tide line. You're waiting for it." Priya waited, the tide line came, and she moved, four steps, turn, sit, and the room breathed again.

Afterward Marcus found Luca by the lemonade. "The book outranks the director," he said. "I want that on a T-shirt." Luca said the book was the director, mostly, and Marcus laughed and said that was the saddest true thing anyone had said all night, and then Luca's grandmother raised her glass and said, "To the tyrant's puppet show," and everyone drank to that.

The photocopy of the diagram had been taped to the lab window so long that the sun had bleached it pale, and Maelie had to squint to make out the two helices drawn side by side. One was labeled with solid lines, the other with a mix of solid and dashed. Ms. Ferreira had written a single question beneath it in red marker: after one round of copying, how much of the new DNA is old? The class had until the end of the period to commit to an answer, in writing, and the answers would be read aloud.

Maelie wanted the answer to be hers, not borrowed. That was the whole problem. Priya had already finished and sat back with her arms crossed, radiating the calm of someone who had looked it up the night before. Deon was scribbling something that involved a lot of arrows. Maelie had read the chapter twice and understood, in a loose way, how the code became protein, how the cell transcribed a message and then translated it, but the copying question felt like a different order of thing, a question about inheritance rather than instruction. She wrote in the margin of her notebook: am I reasoning or remembering?

"You're staring at the wall," Priya said.

"I'm thinking about thinking," Maelie said. "Ms. Ferreira calls it metacognition. She says if you can watch your own mind work, you catch the places where you're just reciting."

"So watch it," Priya said. "What does it tell you?"

Maelie told her the memory from the science museum instead of answering. She had been fourteen, at the genetics exhibit with her cousin, and two older students had been arguing in front of the rotating model of the double helix. One insisted that when DNA copies itself, the copy is entirely new, a fresh molecule built from scratch, the old one left intact like an original photograph. The other said no, it's half and half, each copy carries something of the parent in it. They had gone back and forth until a docent arrived, and Maelie and her cousin had drifted off toward the bubble exhibit without hearing the verdict. For three years the question had sat in her like a stone under a rug. She had never looked it up on purpose, which now struck her as strange, almost superstitious.

"The half-and-half one said something," Deon said, not looking up from his arrows. "He had a word for it. Semiconservative. I remember because it sounded like a political party."

Priya rolled her eyes. "That's not evidence."

"It's not evidence," Maelie said slowly, "but it's a hypothesis. Two hypotheses, actually, and only one of them can be parsimonious with what a cell would actually want." She was following something now, the feeling of a thought catalyzing into an argument she could test against herself. "If the copy were all new, the original would have to stay whole. Two separate molecules, one old, one new. But then every time a cell divided, one daughter cell would get the original and one would get the copy, and the copies of copies of copies would drift." She drew it quickly, a line splitting into two lines, one solid, one dashed, and then those splitting again. "But if each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand, then every copy is anchored. Half of it is always old. Every cell in your body is carrying a strand that has been handed down, split and paired, split and paired, since the first copying."

The room had gone quiet around her. She hadn't noticed.

"That's not proof," Priya said. "That's an argument from elegance."

"Cells don't care about elegance."

"Then what do they care about?"

"I don't know," Maelie said, and the honesty of it surprised her. "That's the part I can't get from reasoning alone. It could still be all-new copying with some repair step I don't know about. Or the half-and-half version could be right for reasons that have nothing to do with why I like it. I can hold both in my head and I still can't tell you which one the world actually does. I just know which one I'd bet on, and I know that betting isn't knowing."

Deon turned his paper around. His arrows formed a branching tree, the same shape as hers, but he had drawn it without the dashes, both lines solid at every generation. "I was arguing the other way," he said. "I thought, if the old molecule stays whole, you always have a backup. That's parsimonious too, isn't it? One perfect original, forever."

"Unless the original gets damaged," Priya said. "Then you have one perfect thing and everything else is secondhand."

"Or unless the original isn't perfect to begin with," Maelie said.

Ms. Ferreira began collecting the papers, moving down the rows. When she reached their bench she paused over Maelie's page, where the answer sat in a shaky box: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original, paired with one newly built strand. The teacher read it, then read the paragraph beneath it, the one that ended I believe this but I have not earned the belief yet.

"Would you read yours aloud?" Ms. Ferreira asked.

Maelie stood. The class turned, forty minutes spent, the bleached diagram glowing faintly in the window behind her. "Half of every copy is old," she said. "It's called semiconservative. And I want to say I'm sure, but the honest version is that I want it to be true more than I know it is."

Nobody laughed. Deon looked down at his all-solid tree, crossed it out, and drew the dashes in.

The waiting room had a fish tank with one moribund beta lying sideways near the plastic castle, and Ella decided that if she were going to be a peer health educator, she would first have to survive her own appointment. She was there for a training physical, the last hoop before the county clinic let juniors and seniors talk to freshmen about consent, contraception, and where to get tested. Her folder of pamphlets sat on her lap like a credential, though she had read none of it closely enough to say anything out loud.

A nurse named Dora called her back, took her blood pressure, and asked the usual questions in the usual flat music. Then, without changing tone, she asked whether Ella wanted an HIV test today.

Ella blinked. "I didn't do anything," she said, and immediately heard how it came out, like a confession of the opposite.

"It's routine," Dora said. "The CDC recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once, as part of regular health care. Like a cholesterol check." She clicked her pen. "So. Today?"

Ella said yes, mostly because saying no would have meant explaining what she'd meant, and while the swab and paperwork happened she did the arithmetic she hated doing: thirteen to sixty-four. Not risk groups. Not behaviors. Everyone, folded into ordinary maintenance, the same way the clinic folded her height and weight into a chart nobody blushed over. It was either bureaucratic laziness or an actual philosophy, and she suspected the second.

The hard part came in the parking lot, where her friend Priya was waiting in her brother's rusted Civic because Ella had promised to practice on her. Priya's whole position, delivered with great erudition for someone eating gas station licorice, was that the peer program was embarrassing. "You're going to stand in a gym class and say words like condom," she said, "in front of Tanner Booth."

"That's the point of the words," Ella said. "Tanner Booth should be uncomfortable." She arranged her pamphlets on the hood of the car and started over, the way she wanted to do it in the gym: consent first, because it was the thing you could practice before anything else happened, a yes that could be taken back, a no that needed no excuse. Then contraception, the clinic's sliding scale, the fact that you could walk in without a parent in this state. Then testing, and here she stumbled, and here she landed on the thing Dora had told her, saying it almost the way Dora had said it, everyone thirteen to sixty-four, at least once, routine.

Dora, meanwhile, had gone to the front desk expecting a quiet afternoon. She had been at the clinic eleven years, long enough to have watched three separate youth education programs bloom, get defunded, and die, and she had assumed this one was moribund too, kept alive by a grant nobody wanted to cancel. She watched through the window as the girl from room four stood by a beat-up car, waving pamphlets at a skeptical audience of one, repeating the testing line word for word the way kids memorize things they intend to keep. Dora had offered the test to a thousand teenagers precisely so that one of them might do exactly this, carry it out the door like contraband. She had nearly given up on it working. She found she was smiling at the fish tank, which was more than the fish could manage.

Priya, for her part, had stopped chewing. "Thirteen," she said. "That's, like, everyone at the middle school."

"That's the point I'm making," Ella said. "It's not a punishment you earn by doing something. It's just maintenance. Like the dentist."

"I have never once thought of the dentist as not a punishment."

"You're proving why my job exists."

Priya considered this, then took a pamphlet, then took four more, ostensibly for her brother, though Dora, still watching from the window, would have bet her coffee that the pamphlets were for Priya, and that within a month Priya would be standing next to Ella in the gym with her own lanyard, claiming she'd invented the whole program. The beta fish chose that moment to right itself and swim one slow lap around the castle, and Dora knocked on the glass and said, "Same to you, buddy."

Mr. Okonkwo handed the essays back on Tuesday, third period, and Cohen found a red circle around one phrase on his first page: "unreliable narrator." In the margin, in small careful handwriting, stood a single question: Where does this term come from?

He had written it because it was the obvious thing to say about Holden in The Catcher in the Rye, the book the whole eleventh grade had slogged through in October. Holden said one thing and did another; he called everyone a phony while performing his own phoniness; he insisted he wouldn't tell you his life story and then told it for two hundred pages. Cohen had typed the phrase at eleven the night before, half asleep, because it sounded like something an essay should say. He had not thought about where it came from. He had not thought it came from anywhere. Words like that, he had assumed, were just in the air.

At lunch he found Priya at the long table by the windows, because Priya read everything and remembered worse things than this. She was working on an economics worksheet, muttering about a question on stagflation, which she defined for Dessie across the table as the miserable combo of rising prices and a stagnant economy, no growth, nothing to do but endure it. Cohen slid his essay in front of her, finger on the circle.

"Where does what come from?" she said.

"The phrase. Unreliable narrator. Like, who decided that's a thing."

Priya frowned at the margin. "I mean, it's a thing because books do it. Somebody had to notice it first, I guess." She pushed the essay back. "Look it up, obviously."

He did not want to look it up, exactly, because looking it up felt like the difference between knowing something and performing knowing something, and the red circle had already made him unsure which one he'd done. But the library had a shelf of criticism behind the study carrels, dusty books nobody touched, and Thursday was a free period, so he went.

The first book he pulled was useless, all about symbolism. The second was worse. On the third shelf down, spine cracked, he found a dark blue cover: The Rhetoric of Fiction. He carried it to a carrel near the window and started flipping, not sure what he was looking for, and then there it was in the index, narrator, unreliable, and a page number.

The book was by a critic named Wayne C. Booth. Cohen checked the copyright page, twice, because it seemed strange that something so ordinary could have a birthday. Nineteen sixty-one. So for most of the history of novels there had been no name for this, no way to point at it, and then one critic wrote one book and gave readers a handle to grip. He read the surrounding pages slowly. Booth's point, as far as Cohen could follow it, was about distance: the author places you at a certain angle from the narrator's mind, and from that angle you can see what the narrator cannot.

Cohen sat with that for a while. It bothered him a little, the idea that trust could be engineered, that someone had built the gap between him and Holden on purpose and he had walked into it. But it also gave him something he couldn't quite put down: if the angle was deliberate, then his own arguments with Holden, all those moments of shouting at the page, were part of the design. The book had wanted him to argue.

He went to find Mr. Okonkwo on Friday morning, before the first bell, holding the blue book against his chest.

"So I looked it up," he said. "The term unreliable narrator was coined by Wayne C. Booth. Nineteen sixty-one, The Rhetoric of Fiction."

Mr. Okonkwo leaned back in his chair. "Coined. That's the right word for it."

"I used it without knowing that. I don't think I even knew I was borrowing it from somebody." Cohen shifted his weight. "I want to rewrite the paragraph. Not just add a citation. I think I can make a better argument now, because Booth's whole thing is that the author sets the distance, and Holden's distance is weird, he's lying to us and telling us he's lying, and I don't fully know yet what that does to the reader. That's the part I'm still figuring out."

Mr. Okonkwo was quiet for a moment, the way he was when a student said something he actually wanted to hear.

"Rewrite it," he said. "Tell me what you figure out." Then he gesticulate-d toward the shelf above his desk, that small circular motion he made when he meant keep going, and turned back to his coffee.

Chase sat at the kitchen table with his chemistry notebook open, a calculator warm in his hand, and the strong suspicion that his answer was ridiculous. The problem wanted grams of ammonia from 51 grams of hydrogen reacting with nitrogen, and his result, 289 grams of product, sat on the page like an accusation. Nothing weighs more coming out than going in, not when the other reactant was a gas in the same tank. He checked his work three times and kept arriving at the same number, which was either a sign of consistency or of a single error faithfully repeated.

His mother set a cup of tea beside his elbow without asking whether he wanted one, which was her way of noticing a boy who had been staring at the same page since dinner. "Bad homework or bad day?" she said.

"Bad homework." He turned the notebook toward her, knowing she'd look anyway. "I'm supposed to figure out how much product I get from a starting amount, and my number's impossible."

She tapped the balanced equation he'd copied from the board. N2 plus 3 H2, arrow, 2 NH3. "That part looks tidy. That's as far as my chemistry goes." She squeezed his shoulder and went back to the sink, leaving him with the tea and the puzzle.

He texted Priya, who was doing the same assignment across town. Her answer came back in a photo of her page: 289 grams, identical to his, with a triumphant little star beside it. Chase frowned at it, then at his own paper, and did not feel triumphant at all. Two wrongs arriving together was not verification; it was a conspiracy. He texted back, doesn't that seem high? She replied with a shrugging emoji and went quiet, presumably to finish the rest of the set.

His little sister Nora wandered through the kitchen hunting for the good scissors, found them in the drawer where they always were, and paused at his elbow long enough to read his equation aloud in a dramatic voice. "En-aitch-three. It's the smelly one, right?"

"Ammonia. Yes." He was about to wave her off when he stopped, because she had read the equation as if it were a sentence, and it was a sentence, and he had been reading it wrong. The big 3 in front of the hydrogen and the 2 in front of the ammonia were speaking in a language he hadn't bothered to translate. He had taken 51 grams, divided by the mass of one hydrogen molecule, and then multiplied by the 2 over the 3 straight from the equation as though those numbers were talking about amounts of stuff, grams of stuff, the stuff you could weigh on a scale.

"What?" said Nora, who could sense when someone stopped listening.

"Nothing. You actually helped." He pulled the calculator closer. "Hey, do me a favor. If I tell you the numbers in the front of a recipe mean batches, not cups, what would you do first?"

"Convert to cups," she said, in the tone of someone humoring the slow. "Obviously. Batches and cups aren't the same thing." She took the scissors and left, and Chase sat very still, because that was it, that was the whole error, sitting in the open where a nine-year-old had stepped over it. The coefficients in the balanced equation were a ratio of moles that reacted, not a ratio of masses, and he had been dividing grams by grams while pretending the numbers meant what he needed them to mean. It was a kind of casuistry, honestly, an argument that sounded rigorous all the way down to the last digit while resting on a quietly swapped premise.

He started over. Molar mass of hydrogen first, grams converted into moles, and only then the 2 over 3 applied, and then back out through the molar mass of ammonia into grams. The answer came out to 289, and his stomach dropped, and then he saw the dropped digit in his long division and corrected it and got 289 anyway, which sent him hunting through the arithmetic until he found the place where he had divided by 2 instead of multiplying by it. On the third pass the answer settled at 289 grams, unchanged, immovable, and he put his head in his hands.

Then he laughed, because the number was fine and the number had never been the problem. He texted Priya again: our answers are wrong the same way. The coefficients are moles, not grams. You have to convert first. The reply came in bursts: a string of exclamation points, a photograph of her crossed-out work, and finally, wait, so the whole class got this wrong? Chase looked at the time, weighed the judicious option of waiting for morning against the small cruelty of letting thirty people turn in a shared error, and opened a group chat for the class, typing before he could talk himself into caution.

Nora came back through with her scissors and a half-finished paper snowflake, watched him type, and asked what he was doing. "Sharing a correction," he said. "Somebody might still be up." The message sent. Somewhere across town a phone on a bedside table lit up, and Chase, still not certain whether anyone would thank him in the morning, closed the notebook and took his cold tea upstairs.

Brandon had shared the video at 7:42 in the morning, before his toast was even cool, and by lunch it had gone everywhere. It showed a shelf of canned goods collapsing onto a clerk, the caption claiming it happened yesterday at a supermarket two towns over, and the comments were full of people vowing never to shop there again, calling for boycotts, calling the manager a name Brandon would not repeat at his grandmother's table. Forty people he knew had shared it, including his lab partner Daisy, who had captioned hers "this is why I do my own shopping, folks."

By afternoon the supermarket had issued a statement denying the incident, which only made half the internet angrier, because denial, as Brandon's grandfather liked to say over his third coffee, is what guilty people do first. Brandon wanted it to be true, in the small way you want a story to be true when you have already passed it along. He was the one who had found it, screen-shotted it, fired it into the group chat. If it was fake, then he had helped denigrate a business that might be run by somebody's aunt.

The public library smelled like lamination and old carpet, and the computers near the window were always free because the screens faced the sun and only the desperate used them. Brandon took one, put his hood up against the glare, and started typing. He found the store's local news archive. He found a Reddit thread calling the video a repost. None of it felt like proof, just noise in different directions, and his search history was starting to look like a cry for help.

Then he remembered Theo. Theo was a college kid who interned at Brandon's dad's office over the summer, and Brandon had visited once in July because Dad wanted to show off the new espresso machine. In the cubicle next to Theo's, a colleague had been clicking through something on her screen and called Theo over, laughing, to look at a video she wasn't sure about. "Just run it through this," she'd said, tilting her monitor. "The InVID-WeVerify plugin." Brandon had mostly been thinking about whether the espresso machine did hot chocolate. He remembered her saying it came out of a European Union-funded project, and something about how it handled video, but he'd been twelve feet away and deeply invested in a ham sandwich.

He found it now, in the library's patchy wifi, and installed it. It took a video and split it into key frames, stills you could reverse-search, which meant you could take each frozen moment and hunt for where it had appeared before. Brandon fed it the supermarket clip and watched the frames scroll out in a grid, like a comic book version of the collapse. He reverse-searched the clearest one, a frame where a can of pears hung mid-air over the clerk's shoulder, and the results loaded slowly, one grainy thumbnail at a time.

The video was three years old. It had happened in a different country. The "clerk" was a performer in a staged sketch that had gone viral, died, and been resurrected this week with a new caption and a new grocery store pasted into its history. Brandon sat back. The sun had moved, and his hood was now purely decorative. He felt the specific vertigo of having been useful to a lie.

Daisy texted him a screenshot of her own post, which had sixty likes, with the message "I'm famous." He typed back a link to the original video, then deleted it, then typed it again, then deleted it again, because there was a version of the afternoon where he just let the whole thing rot quietly and nobody checked his timeline. But the store's reviews were already sliding downward, one star at a time, and the owner had posted something about the deleterious rumors cutting into a week's takings, in wording that suggested a man googling "how to sound official" while panicking. One more bad month, a comment under that post said, and it's insolvency for them, laughing-crying emoji. People were rooting for the collapse like it was a sport.

He sent the link. Then, because a bare link looked like an accusation, he sent the frame grid too, the pears frozen mid-air, and the caption "three years old, different country, staged." Daisy replied with a single "?" and then, after a minute, "oh no." Then "OH NO." Then, "okay I'm deleting, you have to help me write the correction, mine has sixty likes, I can't just post 'my bad.'"

They worked on it in the library's silent section, passing his phone back and forth under the table like contraband, arguing over tone. Daisy wanted to open with "As some of you may have noticed" and Brandon wanted to open with "I helped spread a fake video, here's the receipt." A librarian drifted past once, clocked the phone, and kept walking with the weary mercy of someone who had seen worse. Sixty likes became forty as the correction climbed, and somebody in the comments called Daisy a hero and somebody else called her a coward for deleting, which Brandon figured was the internet keeping its books balanced.

He stayed after Daisy left, ran the plugin on one more video, an older one, just to see. The key frames came up clean, and he sat there a moment, unsure whether clean meant true or only unfindable, and then the librarian began stacking chairs, so he logged off and carried his hood out into the evening.

The library at four o'clock had a crepuscular quality even in spring, the light giving up somewhere past the tall windows and the lamps taking over in patches, so that the book club's table looked like an island that nobody had fully committed to inhabiting. Xavier arrived with a paperback copy of Great Expectations and a borrowed stack of photocopies about critical theory, which he had told Ms. Okafor were for an essay he had no intention of starting. The essay was real. His intention was the questionable part.

"We're doing lenses today," Priya announced, because she had appointed herself facilitator in September and no one had contested it since. "Feminist first, then Marxist. Xavier, you brought the passages?"

He had. He'd chosen the scene where Pip first comes to Satis House, because it was short, and because when he'd read it at midnight it had seemed to have something underneath it that he couldn't name, which was either literary depth or the fact that he'd read it at midnight.

Dani read the excerpt aloud anyway, slowly, the way she read when she suspected people weren't listening. Estella calling Pip coarse and common. Miss Havisham in her yellowed wedding dress. Pip deciding, by the end of it, that he was inadequate and that Estella was the measure of all things.

"So," Priya said. "Feminist lens. Go."

"They're both stuck," Xavier said. "Miss Havisham stopped her own clock and now she's running the house like a museum of the day she got hurt. And Estella's not actually judging Pip, she's doing what she was built to do." He paused. "Also she's literally named Star. Like she's a decoration."

"Okay, that's the lens," said Dani. "Now the other one."

Here Xavier consulted his photocopies, which he had annotated in three colors of highlighter, an effort that had lasted four pages and then been abandoned. "For the Marxist part," he said, "we're supposed to look at who has money and who doesn't, and how the scene makes that feel natural instead of constructed. Pip's a blacksmith's apprentice. Miss Havisham has a decaying mansion. Estella calls him coarse, and coarse is a class word, not a personality word."

Dani had gone quiet in a way Xavier had learned to be suspicious of. She slid a thin pamphlet out of her bag, a battered little edition of something, and put her finger on a page like she'd been waiting all afternoon for this.

"This is from the Communist Manifesto, 1848," she said. "The first section opens like this: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.'" She looked up. "Does that fit the novel?"

The table went quiet except for the radiator, which ticked with the effort of an institution from another century. Xavier turned the question over and found it heavier than expected. "It fits Pip," he said slowly. "His whole plot is wanting to climb, and every character is either above him or below him and the ones above get to decide what's refined. That's a struggle, class-shaped."

"And Miss Havisham?" Priya asked.

"Miss Havisham breaks it," Xavier said, and heard himself say it before he'd finished thinking it, which was usually how his worst ideas arrived, though occasionally his best. "She has the money and none of the power that's supposed to come with it. She's aristocracy running on fumes. If it's all class struggle, she's a struggle that already happened, and the loser just hasn't been told."

Dani tilted her head. "So the Manifesto fits?"

"Both," he said. "It fits and it doesn't. Pip's story is class all the way down. But Estella gets used as an instrument, and that's a different engine wearing the same clothes. I think you can read it through both lenses at once and they argue with each other." He frowned at his highlighter colors, all three of which now meant nothing. "I can't titrate which one is more true. I don't think there's a scale for it."

"You could just say you don't know," Dani said.

"I'm saying I don't know with vocabulary."

Priya started packing up her bag, since the library closed at five and the librarian had begun her slow orbit of the shelves, retrieving strays. Dani was still holding the Manifesto open, and Xavier noticed she had highlighted the same line in yellow, ages ago by the faded look of it, and had written one word in the margin in tiny letters.

"What's the note?" he asked.

She closed the pamphlet. "Ask me in September."

"Why September?"

"Because that's when you'll have an opinion worth arguing with." She dropped it into her bag, and the librarian arrived to take the chair next to Xavier's, and the lamp above them went out on its timer before either of them moved.

Jade had been at the kitchen table since seven, and by nine the two articles had stopped being articles and become adversaries. One, by a Dr. Okafor, claimed that a summer reading program improved test scores; the other, by a Dr. Renner, looked at the same program, the same question, and found almost nothing. The assignment was to compare them, to render a verdict, and Jade had written a verdict she was proud of: a paragraph calling Okafor's study "95 percent likely to be right," since that was the number in the results section, and a number felt like armor.

She texted a photo of the paragraph to Priya, who lived three streets over and never let anything go. The reply came in under a minute. "are you sure that's what the number means." Jade typed "it says .05" and then deleted it, because she wasn't sure what she was asserting, only that she had copied it faithfully. Priya's next message said she was coming over, and Jade's heart began to palpitate in that specific way it did before she found out she was wrong about something she'd already handed in, or almost handed in, or was about to.

Priya arrived in sock feet, carrying a bag of clementines, and sat down across from Jade without taking her coat off, which meant she considered this urgent. She picked up Jade's draft and read the paragraph aloud, slowly, in a lugubrious voice she reserved for ceremonial mockery. "Ninety-five percent likely to be right," she repeated. "So if Okafor ran the study, there's a ninety-five percent chance the reading program works."

"That's what significant means," Jade said, but her voice went up at the end, and Priya heard it.

They pulled up the results section on Jade's laptop. The sentence was there, plain as a door: the difference between groups was significant, p = .05. Jade had read past it a dozen times. Now she read it aloud, twice, and something about it refused to close. Priya peeled a clementine and said, "Significant to whom. Of what." Jade told her to shut up, kindly, and turned to the methods section, looking for the sentence that would translate the number, and it wasn't there, and it wasn't in the discussion either, and Okafor used the word "confirms" four times in a way that suddenly seemed like a person talking too loudly in a quiet room.

The Renner article had been sitting under Jade's elbow all night, and she had treated it as the dull one, the naysayer, the article whose job was to be wrong. She opened it to the section she'd skimmed, a paragraph near the end that read like a footnote and now read like the hinge of the whole assignment. Renner laid out the definition in a single unadorned sentence, and Jade read it out loud so that both of them had to hear it at the same speed: the p-value was the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect. It was not, Renner went on to complain, the probability that the hypothesis was true, a mistake Renner called common enough to be almost traditional.

The kitchen was quiet except for the refrigerator. Jade wrote the sentence down on a napkin, then on paper, then in the margin of her draft, where her old claim sat under it like a confession. "So Okafor's number means if the program did nothing, there'd still be a five percent chance of seeing results this big," she said. "It's backwards from what I wrote. I said the study was probably right. It's more like, if the study were wrong, the data would probably look different than this." Priya considered, ate a segment of clementine, and said, "So which article is right?"

That was the question, and it was Jade's question too, the one the whole review was supposed to answer, and she understood at the table that it might not have the kind of answer she'd been trying to manufacture. Okafor had a small sample, schools in one district, and a result that sat exactly at the threshold. Renner had more students, more places, and a result that was smaller and less certain in the direction Jade had assumed was safe. But Renner's design had its own soft spot, a way of measuring the reading program that Jade had underlined earlier and then ignored, because it was easier to pick a winner than to weigh two imperfect instruments against each other.

She started the paragraph again from scratch, and this time she didn't write like a judge banging a gavel. She wrote that Okafor's evidence was real but fragile, that Renner's was broader but blunter, that the honest position was somewhere Renner would call skeptical and Okafor would call premature, and that she couldn't yet say which label fit better. It was strange, she thought, deleting her old confident sentences, how much harder the honest version was to write, how the confident one had flowed and this one kept catching, like every clause had to be tested before it could be trusted. In math class they called a proven statement you used to prove something else a lemma, a stepping stone, and she thought of her first draft that way now, not waste but scaffolding, something she had needed to stand on in order to see why it wouldn't hold.

Priya read the new paragraph over her shoulder, coat finally off, clementine reduced to peel coiled on the table. "You still don't say who's right," she said.

"No," Jade said. "I say what we'd need to find out." She highlighted the last sentence, saved the file, and turned the laptop so Priya could see the whole screen at once.

Elijah had agreed to meet Marisol at the community garden because her mother said the house was too loud for studying, which was a subterfuge, since the real reason was that the tomatoes needed watering and Marisol's court-ordered community service had somehow become everyone's habit. She sat on an overturned bucket with a biology textbook open on her knees, glaring at a diagram the way she usually glared at the kale.

"Look at this," she said, jabbing the page. "They change one letter in the DNA. One. And then they say, and I quote, 'the resulting protein is unchanged.' Unchanged? How? If I change a letter in a recipe from 'bake' to 'cake,' I get a different sentence. If I change one brick in a wall, it's a different wall."

"Maybe it's a typo," Elijah offered, dragging a second bucket over. He was supposed to be learning this material himself, for a test on Monday, and being asked to explain it felt like being asked to juggle while drowning.

"It's in the textbook. Textbooks don't do typos, they do tragedy." She flipped the diagram toward him. "See? The codon went from one thing to another thing, and the amino acid is the same one. Same one, Elijah."

He leaned in. The garden hummed around them, somebody's wind chime doing its thin silver business, and for a moment he almost said he had no idea, which would have been honest but useless. Instead he said, "Okay, wait. Let me tell you the whole pipeline first, because I think the answer's in there somewhere, and if I get it wrong we can blame the textbook anyway."

"Proceed," said Marisol, saturnine as a gargoyle, arms folded over the bucket.

"So DNA gets copied into RNA. That's transcription. It's like, okay, this is going to sound dumb." He picked up a dry leaf and held it like a card. "DNA is the master recipe written in ink, and you don't want to get marinara on your only copy, so you photocopy it. The photocopy is RNA. Except the copier can't read one of the letters, so everywhere the DNA says T, the copy says U. It's not translating, exactly. It's more like transliterating, letter by letter, same words, different alphabet, like writing your name in Greek letters."

"Elijah becomes E-lambda-iota-alpha," Marisol said. "Still you, worse font."

"Exactly. Then translation, which is different. That's where the cell actually reads the RNA in groups of three letters, and every three-letter group is a codon, and every codon means one amino acid. Amino acids get chained together in order, and the chain folds up, and that's the protein. So the recipe metaphor kind of breaks, because it's less like baking and more like ordering at a restaurant in a language where some words are synonyms."

Marisol stopped glaring. "Synonyms."

"Wait," Elijah said, and the wait was real; he was flipping backward through his own memory of Monday's lecture, the codon chart the teacher had projected in colors like a plumbing diagram. "Wait, wait. Because several codons can code for the same amino acid." He said it slowly, testing the floorboards before putting his weight on them. "So if a mutation changes one base, one letter, sometimes the new codon still means the same amino acid as the old one. Same amino acid, same protein. Nothing changes."

Marisol looked at her diagram again, and her whole face did something complicated, like a door unlocking and a burglar alarm going off at the same time. "So it's a mutation that doesn't matter?"

"It matters and it doesn't," Elijah said. "The DNA changed, the RNA changed, but the finished protein comes out exactly the same. Those are called silent mutations."

"That's the most biologically dramatic term for 'no visible effect' I've ever heard," Marisol said. "Like a tree falling in a forest where all the trees are secretly the same tree."

"It's very quiet drama," Elijah agreed. "Meanwhile other mutations, the ones that do change the amino acid, those are loud. Those are the ones the test wants you to find."

They worked through her problem set in the smell of wet basil, Marisol reading codons aloud like lottery numbers, Elijah hovering over the chart. She got one wrong on purpose, he was almost sure, just to see if he'd catch it. He caught it. She grinned and gave him a tomato, the small ugly one, still warm.

"For the tutor," she said. "Silently accepted."

He turned it in his hand and said, "That's a subterfuge, that's a bribe," and ate it anyway, standing up, watering can already in the other hand, marching toward the kale.

Seth had been staring at the same two tables for forty minutes when Marcus finally looked over his shoulder and said, "You're overcomplicating it. Just find the customers with orders and subtract everybody else."

It was a fair suggestion, and Seth hated it. The tables sat side by side on Marcus's kitchen laptop, one listing customers with their IDs and names, the other listing orders with customer IDs and products. The assignment, from the online course they were both taking to pad their college applications, asked for something that sounded simple: which customers had never ordered anything. Mr. Alvarez, the instructor, had hinted that the answer involved a join, which was the whole point of the lesson, and Seth had decided he was not going to cheat the lesson by inventing a workaround.

"That's like finding everyone who didn't come to the party by counting who did," Seth said. "It works, but it isn't what he's asking."

Marcus rolled his eyes with theatrical patience. "It works, and it's eleven at night, and my mom's going to make us sequester ourselves in the basement if we keep arguing up here."

They had been friends since seventh grade, when Marcus had been the pugnacious kid who picked fights at recess and Seth had been the kid who watched him do it, cataloging the outcomes. Somewhere along the way Marcus had softened into a person who argued for sport rather than for blood, and Seth had discovered he liked being argued with, the way a musician likes a counterpoint, a second line running against his own that made both of them sharper. Tonight the counterpoint was getting on his nerves.

"Say it out loud," Marcus said. "Sometimes it helps. Say what you want the computer to do."

Seth rubbed his eyes and tried. "I want every customer from the customers table, and then, next to each one, their orders if they have any, and if they don't have any, I still want the customer. I just want the order columns to be empty."

He stopped. The sentence hung in the air between them, and something in it snagged. If he still wanted the customer even when there were no orders, then it wasn't the ordinary kind of join, the kind that matched rows and threw away the unmatched ones. It was a join that kept one side whole and let the other side go blank. He scrolled through the lesson notes until he found the phrase LEFT JOIN and read its description twice.

"Wait," he said. "I think the join itself can do the subtraction. You join everything, and then you look for the rows where the order side came back empty. The nothing shows up as an actual row instead of an absence."

Marcus leaned in, which he only did when something genuinely surprised him. "So the empty thing is a thing."

"The empty thing is a thing," Seth said, and typed it: a left join, then a condition checking whether the order's ID was null. He ran it. Two names came back, customers who had been sitting in the first table all along, quiet and orderless, invisible to the ordinary join. Seth felt a small, disproportionate thrill, the kind he associated with taking apart a clock as a kid and finding that one gear had been doing all the work.

He thought of that clock now, of the summer he was eleven and his grandfather had let him disassemble it on the porch, all the brass wheels laid out in a row on a towel, and had said only, "Notice which one isn't moving when it stops." He hadn't understood then that absence could be information. It seemed strange that a database language built by strangers decades before he was born should be teaching him the same lesson his grandfather had, but there it was.

Actually, that raised a question. "How do you even say it?" Seth asked. "S-Q-L, spelled out? Or sequel, like the movie?"

"Sequel," Marcus said immediately. "Definitely sequel."

"It's spelled S-Q-L."

"Doesn't matter. Everyone says sequel."

"Then why isn't it spelled that way?" Seth pulled out his phone and searched, and started laughing before he finished the first paragraph. "Because it was. It was first called SEQUEL. They developed it at IBM in the early 1970s. Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce."

Marcus took the phone and read it himself, frowning like a man being asked to concede a point he'd won by accident. "So I was right."

"You were right for no reason. That's not the same as being right."

Marcus held the phone a moment longer, then handed it back. Outside, a car swept past the kitchen window, its headlights dragging a slow rectangle of light across the ceiling. Seth looked at his two query results glowing on the screen, the two customers who had ordered nothing, and caught himself wondering what else he'd been passing over because it wasn't listed anywhere, what other absences were sitting in rows he'd never thought to join.

"Run it again," Marcus said. "I want to watch it work this time."

The laundromat closed at ten, and after the last customer left with her damp shirts over one arm, Audrey carried the traffic cones from behind the dryer and set them up in the parking lot. Her mother had bought the cones at a police auction, three dollars each, the same week Audrey turned fifteen and a half. Since then, three nights a week, while the final load of towels fermented in its own dampness because someone always forgot a load at closing, Audrey practiced parallel parking between the cones in her mother's Corolla.

The trouble was the angle. She kept finishing crooked, the rear of the car close to the curb and the front swinging wide, so that an imaginary car would have scraped its fender against the bumper of the imaginary car in front. Tonight she had done it five times, and each time she climbed out and looked at the geometry of her failure with her hands on her hips.

"You're turning too late," her mother said from the plastic chair by the door, where she sat counting the coin rolls. Her mother had driven delivery trucks for eleven years before the laundromat, and she did not rise from the chair to demonstrate anything. She believed, or said she believed, that Audrey should work it out herself, that driving was one of the few remaining meritocracies where the examiner didn't care how much money your family had or didn't have. Audrey thought this was partly a way of not admitting her mother couldn't afford actual lessons.

Audrey pulled forward alongside the front cone, the way the handbook showed, close and parallel, until her rear bumper sat just past it. She reversed, and this time she turned the wheel toward the curb immediately, watching the mirror. The car's nose swung out over the lane as the rear end came around. Then, when the cone appeared in the side window at the angle her mother had once marked with a piece of masking tape, she turned the wheel back the other way, away from the curb, and the car swung level into the space, straight, both cones still upright.

"Now that," her mother said, not looking up from the coins, "is how you do it."

She had been doing it backward without knowing. You went in from alongside the car in front, you turned toward the curb first, and then away, and the whole thing worked because of the order. Audrey sat in the parked car with her hands on the wheel and thought about how she had spent weeks trying to fix the angle by adjusting the second turn, when the problem had been the first one all along. Some errors you could only see from outside the mistake.

The highway was harder. On Saturday mornings they drove out to the ring road early, before traffic, and Audrey merged at sixty kilometers an hour with her jaw set. Her mother's method was to say nothing at all, which Audrey had learned to read as its own kind of instruction. The first time, she slowed at the end of the ramp and a delivery van honked. The second time she held her speed, found the gap, and slid into it, and her mother exhaled once, quietly, like a valve releasing.

The test was on a Tuesday. Audrey took the morning off school, which her history teacher would note, and which would cost her the extension on the essay she had already needed every day of. The examiner was a man with a clipboard and a gray mustache, and when he said "Parallel park at the next available space," her stomach dropped, because the space was small, smaller than the cones, and there was a real car in front of it with a bumper sticker about fishing.

She pulled alongside the car in front. She reversed, turning toward the curb, and when she judged the moment, she turned back away, and the car settled straight into the space with a hand's width on either side. The examiner made a mark on his clipboard and did not say anything, which she chose to believe was good.

She failed anyway, on the highway portion, for slowing below the flow of traffic during her second merge. The examiner said it kindly. In the parking lot afterward, her mother was leaning against the Corolla with her arms crossed, and when Audrey got in the passenger side and closed the door, neither of them spoke for a moment.

"Next month," her mother said, starting the engine. "The parallel parking was perfect."

"Small mercies," Audrey said, and watched the cones of the driving school lot across the street, where somebody else was setting up for the afternoon, sliding by the window as they pulled out.

Nicole had taped a grid of masking tape across the living room carpet, one square per meter of the imaginary stage, and by Tuesday evening the squares were already peeling at the corners. Her cousin Tasha and a boy from her chemistry class, Marcus, stood on the two downstage squares holding their scripts like shields. "From the top," Nicole said, sitting backward on the piano bench she'd dragged in as a director's chair. "You enter left, Marcus, you cross to her, and Tasha, you turn away before he finishes the line."

They moved like people wading through shallow water. Marcus read his lines with his eyes down, his feet planted as if the tape had glued him there, and Tasha kept drifting off her mark to glance at her script on the arm of the couch. Nicole stopped them four times in ten minutes. She had read that a director's real work was blocking, the architecture of movement, and she had believed it in the way you believe something you read at two in the morning: completely, and without any idea what it cost.

She had wanted this job since September, when the drama teacher announced that students could direct the winter one-acts and Nicole had raised her hand before she finished weighing it. Her mother had said, at the time, that directing was just telling people what to do with more politeness. Her father, who was impecunious that month and apologizing for it, had offered to buy her a director's megaphone as a joke, and she had laughed and not corrected him, because the truth was she didn't know yet what a director actually did.

"Tomorrow," she announced, when they had run the first scene six times, "is off-book." Tasha's head came up sharply. "What's that mean?" Marcus answered before Nicole could, because he had looked it up the night before, hoping to be spared. "An off-book rehearsal is one where we perform without scripts. Everything memorized." Tasha said nothing, but her thumb went to the corner of her pages and began worrying the paper, and Nicole pretended not to see it because she did not yet know what to do with what she was seeing.

That night she sat on the peeling tape grid alone and tried to introspect, which was a word her therapist used and which Nicole privately thought sounded like a machine part. What she found was not complicated: she had set the off-book date because a website said directors should, and she had enjoyed setting it, the small authority of the deadline, and she had never once asked whether Tasha could actually meet it. In chemistry that week they had started polymers, how a monomer was a single small unit that mattered only when it linked with others, in chains, and Nicole thought about how each rehearsal was supposed to work that way, each small unit clicking onto the next until the thing had shape. Her rehearsals were not linking. They were separate evenings of standing on tape.

The next evening Tasha made it through eleven lines and then stopped, mid-sentence, her face going stiff and remote, and said she was sorry, twice, and then a third time in a voice that made Marcus look at the carpet. Nicole felt the two directions pull at her like the tape pulling loose from the carpet in opposite corners. One was the deadline, the discipline, the argument that an audience would not hold scripts for anybody. The other was Tasha's thumb worrying the page corners last night, the apology now stacking up like something with weight.

"Okay," Nicole said. "New plan. Marcus, you're off-book, you stay off-book, you're ready. Tasha, we put the script on the chair. You can go to it when you need to, but every time you don't, we mark it, and Friday the chair moves to the hallway." Tasha looked at the chair, then at her. "That's still a deadline." "That's a staircase," Nicole said, though she was not sure it was, not sure it wasn't just a slower way to arrive at the same failure, and she let her face show that she wasn't sure, because hiding it felt like another thing she'd be directing rather than doing.

They ran the scene again. Marcus crossed to his mark, and this time he took Tasha's elbow as he spoke, a gesture Nicole had never given him, something he had found on his own, and Tasha turned away from him exactly on the beat, empty-handed, six lines before she needed the chair. They stood in the middle of the taped grid, both of them breathing a little hard, waiting to find out what came next. Nicole reached down and pressed one of the peeling corners flat against the carpet with the heel of her hand. "Again," she said. "From the top."

The garage smelled of WD-40 and old sweat, and Devin had cleared a space on the workbench between a coffee can of screws and a bike wheel with no tire. He set down a battered notebook, open to a page of his own handwriting, and tapped it twice.

"Same problem as last night," Devin said. "Skater comes off the ledge at the park, going horizontal, four meters a second. Ledge is a meter and a quarter up. Where does he land?"

"In the gravel, probably," Nolan said. "That's where I landed."

"Nolan."

"I'm kidding. Sort of. I still have gravel in my elbow."

Devin was sixteen months older and phlegmatic about almost everything, including, apparently, his brother's failings. He slid the notebook across. Nolan looked at the page. There was a drawing of the ledge, an arrow, and then a long vertical drop of equations he did not follow.

"Here's what you told me yesterday," Nolan said. "You said split the velocity into pieces. Horizontal piece, vertical piece. And then what, they never talk to each other again?"

"They talk at the end. To get distance you need time of flight, and to get time of flight you use the vertical piece. But the whole flight, the horizontal piece just keeps going. Four meters a second at the lip, four meters a second when he lands."

"Nothing slows it down?"

Devin shook his head. "If you ignore air resistance, the horizontal velocity stays constant the whole flight, because no horizontal force is acting on it. Nothing's pushing it sideways. So it just goes."

"Gravity's not touching it?"

"Gravity pulls straight down. That's the vertical piece's problem."

Nolan sat down on an overturned milk crate and thought about that. It had a strange cleanliness to it. Down in the garage, with the door half open and the October light coming in flat and gray across the concrete, he could almost see the skater's arc, the horizontal arrow riding along it unchanged, calm, indifferent, while the vertical arrow stretched and stretched underneath.

"Okay," he said. "So how long is he in the air?"

"You did falling bodies three weeks ago."

"I did them badly."

"Do them well now."

Nolan took the pencil. He wrote one point two five equals one half g t squared, and then, because Devin was watching with the patience of a man waiting for a bus, he solved it. Half of nine point eight was four point nine. One point two five divided by four point nine, then the square root. He got about half a second. He said so.

"Okay," Devin said. "So how far does he go?"

Nolan's pencil stopped. The two halves of the problem sat there in front of him, the falling part and the going part, and for a moment he was back at the park, standing on that ledge in June, looking at the gravel and the board beneath his feet, and he had pushed off thinking about everything at once, speed and height and landing, and the thinking had gotten tangled and he had gone into the gravel with his arms out. He came out of the little reverie and found Devin waving a hand in front of his face.

"Hello."

"I'm computing."

"You're staring at a coffee can."

"They're the same thing." Nolan put the pencil down on the horizontal arrow. Four meters a second, the whole flight, because nothing horizontal was acting on it. Half a second in the air. "Four times half a second," he said. "Two meters. He lands two meters out."

"Which is?"

"Where I landed. Almost exactly. There's a scuff mark on the curb there, I've seen it."

"Congratulations," Devin said. "You can now predict your own injuries retroactively."

"Better than predicting them in advance, like you do."

Devin smiled at that, which for Devin was practically applause. He flipped to a fresh page and drew a new ledge, higher this time, with the takeoff at an angle, and Nolan's stomach dropped slightly, because an angle meant sines and cosines, meant the two pieces were tangled at the start even if they flew apart afterward.

"Angle of thirty degrees," Devin said. "Speed eight meters a second off the lip."

"So I have to split it first."

"You have to split it first."

Nolan wrote the sine and the cosine, and it occurred to him, halfway through, that he didn't actually know why the split worked, why the world was arranged so you could take one motion apart into two and then put them back together. He asked. Devin shrugged and said the man on the video said it does, and Nolan laughed, and wrote the numbers down anyway.

"Also," Devin said, "next time don't put your arms out when you fall. That's how wrists happen."

"You could have told me that in June."

"I was in Ohio in June."

"You could have sent a postcard. 'Dear Nolan, gravity pulls straight down. Love, Devin.'"

"Write the problem," Devin said, and stole the pencil back to underline the thirty degrees, twice, hard enough to dent the page.

The kitchen table at Priya's house had been commandeer ed by four laptops, two bags of chips, and a poster board that was supposed to explain the immune response by Sunday. Jason set down his phone and looked at the diagram Dante had spent all Thursday night making, the one Dante was clearly proud of, the one with the arrows drawn in three colors and the title in bubble letters. It was also wrong. The diagram showed antibodies attacking the antigen directly, swallowing it like a Pac-Man, when what actually happened was that antibodies tagged the antigen so other cells could find it. It was the difference between a B and an A, maybe the difference between passing the unit at all.

"Pretty sick, right?" Dante said. He spun the marker between his fingers.

Nobody said anything. Priya was suddenly very interested in formatting the works cited page. Marcus opened his laptop wider, hiding half his face behind the screen.

"It's good," Priya said. "The colors are good."

Jason knew why nobody was saying it. He had almost said it himself, three weeks ago, when he'd messed up the solubility calculations in chem lab and Marcus had caught it but told him privately, later, in the hallway, in a voice like he was delivering bad news about a pet. Jason had spent the rest of that week feeling like the group's weakest link. But he'd also fixed the calculations, and the lab had come out fine, and somewhere in there he'd read something for his psych elective, a paragraph he'd screenshotted and never deleted. A researcher named Amy Edmondson, in 1999, had described something she called psychological safety: a team's shared belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. He'd thought it sounded soft at the time, a management word, the kind of thing adults put on posters. Now he wasn't sure it was soft at all. Their group had none of it, and here was the proof: four people sitting around a table, all seeing the same error, all pretending not to.

"It's good," Jason said, "but." Dante's shoulders went up half an inch. Jason kept going anyway. "The part where the antibody eats the antigen. That's not how it works. The antibody binds to it, like a tag. Then the macrophages come in. The rest of it, the layout, the color coding, that's the best thing anyone's made for this project."

Dante put the marker down. "You could've just said it looks good."

"I did say that. I also said the true part."

"Are you being facetious right now?" Dante said. "Because it's hard to tell."

"No. I mean the layout. I'd have done the whole thing in one color and it would've looked like a ransom note."

Marcus lowered his laptop a few degrees. "The binding thing is right," he said quietly. "I checked it too. I just didn't want to be the one."

"Didn't want to be the one to what?" Dante said.

"To make it a thing," Marcus said.

Priya pushed the works cited aside. "You mean like how nobody told me my slides had the wrong due date for two weeks."

"Nobody noticed," Jason said.

"Marcus noticed," Priya said. "He told me after."

Dante was quiet for a second, tapping the marker against the table. "So we all just do this. We all sit on it."

Jason pulled the screenshot up on his phone and slid it across the table. "Read this. I've had it saved for like a month." Dante read it, then read it again, then passed it to Priya without a word.

"Okay," Dante said finally. "Okay. So I fix the arrow." He uncapped the marker, hesitated over the diagram, and looked up. "But you're telling me how. Not just that it's wrong. Because I swear I read that section."

"The antibody's the label, not the teeth," Jason said. "Draw it like a flag stuck on the antigen, and the macrophage as the guy who follows the flag."

"A flag," Dante repeated. He drew it. It took him forty seconds, and it was obvious now, and it looked better than the original. He turned the board around. "Like that?"

"Exactly like that," Jason said.

Priya wrote something in the margin of her notes, and when Jason leaned over he saw it was just the date, 1999, circled twice, like a thing worth remembering. Marcus finally closed the laptop all the way.

"So the deal is," Dante said, capping the marker, "next time one of us screws up, we just say it. Out loud. At the table."

"Out loud," Priya said. "At the table."

"Even me," Marcus said.

Dante pointed the marker at him. "Especially you."

"Pass the chips," Jason said, and Marcus threw the bag across the table without looking up.

Matthew got the assignment on a Tuesday, fourth period, in the drama room that smelled like dust and the glue from last semester's set pieces. Write a ten-minute play about a moment from your own life, the handout said. Stage it. He had never written a play, only short stories for English, and even those had mostly been about characters he invented so that no one could ask him whether any of it was true.

He wrote about the afternoon his sister Beatrice had her allergy testing, because it was the one afternoon he could remember in detail: the waiting room, the numbered grid drawn in pen on her back, the doctor saying the word antigen as though it explained something, and their mother texting their father, who did not answer. Matthew put the unanswered text in the play as a real letter, because the teacher had said plays are spoken things and a phone screen is hard to stage. So the mother writes a letter in scene one and sets it on the table, and in the rest of the play nobody mentions it again.

On Thursday there was a table read in the library at lunch. Daniel read the father, Priya read the mother, and a girl named Oyelaran who Matthew barely knew read Beatrice, pronouncing the medical vocabulary better than anyone. They went through it once, and then Daniel leaned back in his chair and tapped the page.

"Okay, but the letter," Daniel said. "You spend like half a page on her writing it in scene one. And then nothing. Why is it there?"

"Because that's what happened. She wrote to him and he didn't answer."

"Sure, but on a stage it reads like a clue. Like it's going to come back." Priya nodded at that. Daniel shrugged. "There's a principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play." He said it the way he said most things, as though quoting something he'd read on his phone at two in the morning.

Matthew argued for a minute. The silence was the point, he said. The father's absence wasn't a prop; putting a payoff in would reify it into a plot device, an object with a function, when in real life the letter just sat there useless. Priya said that might be true in life but an audience watches a stage, and a stage is not life, it's a small bright box where everything visible is a promise. Matthew said that sounded like a poster. Daniel ate his sandwich.

He went home and thought about it while doing his biology homework, which that week was about immune response, and he noticed that he liked the word antigen because it named a thing by what it provoked rather than what it was. Then he noticed he was avoiding the actual problem by finding it interesting. He sat at the kitchen table until eleven and rewrote the ending twice. In the first version, the father arrives in the last scene and reads the letter aloud. That felt false, a machine for delivering feeling. In the second version, Beatrice, waiting for her results, folds the letter into a paper boat and sails it on the sink in the exam room's bathroom, and the mother watches from the door and doesn't stop her. That felt closer to the actual afternoon, which Matthew now admitted he had been tidying.

But he kept the second version for a doctrinaire reason, he told himself, not just an emotional one: the letter now mattered later without explaining itself. The promise got paid without being cashed. He could defend it to Daniel. He practiced defending it to Daniel in the shower.

At the performance, in the black box theater with folding chairs and a card table borrowed from the front office, Oyelaran was very good. When she sailed the boat, somebody in the second row made a small sound, and the room went quiet in a way that felt like the play had landed. Afterward the teacher took him aside in the corridor and said the ending worked, that the paper boat had earned its moment.

Daniel found him by the water fountain. "So you fixed the letter," he said.

"I made it matter later," Matthew said. "It comes back as the boat."

"Right," Daniel said. "Only now the boat's the thing that doesn't come back." He was grinning a little. "You spend the whole last scene on it and then it's gone. Tomorrow someone's going to ask you what happened to the boat."

Behind them, the stage manager was striking the set, and Matthew watched her pick up the paper boat from the sink prop, flatten it with one hand, and drop it into the recycling bin with the programs.

The community garden on Fell Street had gone to half weeds by August, and Robert had taken the onion bed because nobody else wanted it. He knelt there on Saturdays not because he loved onions but because the plot was quiet, and quiet places to study were scarce in his house, where his younger brothers treated every hallway as a racetrack. That Saturday he had his biology textbook open on the flattened cardboard between the rows, and he was losing an argument with a diagram that showed a long ladder curling like a ribbon.

The problem was simple and enormous. On Monday he had to explain, out loud, in front of the whole senior class, how DNA gets copied and how it becomes protein, and the textbook kept dissolving into arrows and labels the moment he looked away from them. RNA polymerase, messenger RNA, ribosomes, codons. He could recite the words. He could not make them mean anything, and Mrs. Okafor had been clear that reciting would not pass.

A shadow fell across the page. Dana from the next plot stood at the fence with a watering can, watching him with the particular amusement of someone who has caught a neighbor talking to an onion. Dana was garrulous in a way that filled whole afternoons, and Robert usually enjoyed it, but today he braced for a monologue about tomatoes.

"You look like the book insulted you," Dana said.

"It did." He turned the diagram toward her. "I have to explain this Monday. Transcription and translation. How DNA becomes protein. And I understand exactly none of it."

Dana set the can down and climbed the low fence, which was against the posted rules, and settled onto the cardboard beside him. She was studying to be a nurse, and had failed chemistry once before passing it, a fact she mentioned often and without shame. "Explain it to me, then. I'll tell you when you lose me."

He started, badly, with the ladder again. "So this is DNA, the double helix. Two strands, and the rungs are base pairs. And to copy it..." He stopped. The arrows on the page pointed at a blobby shape labeled helicase, but the blob told him nothing.

Dana was quiet for a moment, which was unusual. Then she reached for the zipper of her jacket and pulled it down slowly, the teeth separating two by two, a small sound like tearing paper. The jacket fell open into two halves.

"Okay," she said. "Do that with your hands. Show me."

Robert put the book down. He held his two hands flat together, fingers interlaced, then slid them apart like the jacket opening. "Before DNA can be copied," he said, mostly to himself, "it has to open. Something has to unzip it." He looked at the diagram again, at the blob, at the little marks where the rungs came apart. The label read helicase. He found it in the text, and there it was, in one sentence he had read four times without seeing: helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.

"That," he said. "That's the zipper. Helicase. It breaks the hydrogen bonds, the little things holding the base pairs together, and the two strands come apart." He pulled his hands apart again, farther this time, and something in his chest loosened the same way. "It's not magic. It's a jacket."

"Congratulations," Dana said. "You have now explained one percent of it."

"One percent that the rest hangs on." He was already moving, talking faster, pointing at each strand of his open hands in turn. "Because now you've got two single strands, and each one is a template. Free nucleotides, the little monomers, float in and pair up along each strand, and you get two copies." He paused. "I think that part is copying, actually, replication, which is separate from what I have to present. But it's the same opening move."

Dana pulled her jacket closed again, zipping it slowly, and he laughed, because that was the copy, two halves sealed into two wholes. He found the RNA polymerase arrow next, and now that the zipper was in his head, the rest began to arrange itself. The DNA opens the same way, one short stretch, and RNA polymerase reads along one strand, building a messenger RNA copy, a transcript, which then travels out of the nucleus to a ribosome, where the sequence gets read in threes and each three-letter word calls in a specific amino acid, and the amino acids link into a chain that folds into a protein. He stumbled at the ribosome, tried again, used the garden itself: the transcript was like a recipe card carried from the kitchen to the potting shed, and the ribosome was the gardener who read it and assembled the plants, one monomer at a time, until a whole protein stood where there had been only instructions.

"That last part was bad," Dana said, "but I followed it anyway."

He wrote it out in the dirt with a stick, the four steps, then wiped it clean with his palm and did it again from memory. Twice the order scrambled, and he sat back on his heels and stared at the onions until it unscrambled. He was aware that he did not fully understand it, that somewhere under the words were machines he could not picture, and that on Monday someone might ask why the hydrogen bonds specifically, and he would have to say he didn't know yet. That was tolerable in a way it had not been that morning. Not knowing had a shape now, and a place in the sequence, like a weed in a bed that had been mapped.

Mrs. Okafor's rubric wanted diagrams.
