The twist arrived with the dinner bell. Ruiz came down the path carrying two paper cups of lemonade and set one in front of Elijah without comment, which from Ruiz was practically a speech. He looked at the print, then at Elijah's notes, then at the print again. "You've been at this four hours," he said.

"Is that wrong?"

"It's the most anyone's given it." Ruiz sat down, uninvited, and waited. That was his method, Elijah had heard: he waited until you talked yourself into a corner or out of one.

So Elijah talked. He laid out the composition, the funnel of foliage, the framing necklace, the distributed reds. He said the cat peered over her shoulder and that everyone read it as bad luck and death, and that the reading was right but incomplete, because placement was meaning too: the symbol sat where she couldn't see it, in the viewer's sightline, so the bad omen belonged less to her than to the one looking. He heard himself say "belonged less to her than to the one looking" and felt the small electric shock of a sentence he hadn't planned.

Ruiz drank his lemonade. "And which do you believe?"

"Both," Elijah said, and then, because honesty was all he had left after four hours, "I can't tell yet whether holding both is insight or cowardice."

Ruiz almost smiled, a movement of one corner of his mouth that appeared and was withdrawn. "Tonight, tell them both, and tell them you don't know. Then next year, or the year after, tell them which one won." He stood, took his cup, and walked back up the path toward the lodge, where the fire was already being built, the smoke standing straight up in the windless dusk.

Priya came back with a stolen cookie and read the draft over his shoulder. "It's good," she said. "It's better than good. You know he's going to push on the cat part."

Elijah looked at the print one more time, at the animal's yellow eyes fixed on him from behind the painter's shoulder, patient, unhurried, keeping its own counsel about whether it meant anything at all. He folded his notes once along the middle and put them in his jacket. "Then I'll let him," he said, and they walked up toward the fire.

The whiteboard in the library's small study room still carried the ghost of yesterday's tutoring session, half-erased equations, and Brianna had to commandeer a rag from the front desk before she could use it. She wrote Pride and Prejudice across the top in tall letters, then drew a line down the middle. On the left she wrote OWNS, on the right, WORKS.

"You're doing it wrong," said Priya, who had claimed the room first and was only tolerating Brianna because they had the same seminar on Thursday. "There's no such thing in that book. Nobody works. That's the whole point of it."

"That's what I thought too." Brianna uncapped a marker. "But the Marxist thing isn't only about jobs. My dad explained it once. In Marxist terms the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, like factories and land, and the proletariat owns only its labour, so it has to sell that for wages. Owners on one side, workers on the other."

"Your dad reads Marx?"

"He drives a delivery truck. He reads everything." Last spring, when her father was recovering from the knee surgery and could not climb into the cab for six weeks, he had sat at the kitchen table with a paperback of Das Kapital so old its spine had gone soft, and he'd read passages aloud to her while she washed dishes, not teaching, just wanting the words in the air of the house. She remembered him laughing at one part and saying, "We're the ones with nothing but our hours to sell, Bri. Might as well know the name for it." She had gone back to her chemistry homework that night. Now she wished she had pulled a chair over and stayed.

She wrote Darcy under OWNS. Then Pemberley, then his aunt's estate, then Bingley. Priya, despite herself, came to stand at the board. "So the working side is," she began, and then they both saw the problem at the same time. The gardeners. The housemaids. The servants who carried letters between houses so that Elizabeth and Darcy could fall in love at a distance. None of them had names. Brianna wrote servants? on the worker side and looked at it.

"They're in the book the way weather is in the book," Priya said, which was more literary criticism than either of them had managed all afternoon, and Brianna copied it into her notebook before she could lose it. She tried the feminist lens next, the way the seminar packet suggested, and that one fit almost too easily: Charlotte Lucas marrying Mr. Collins to secure a roof over her head. Charlotte, twenty-seven, plain, no inheritance, choosing a sullen little fool because the alternative was depending on her brothers. Was that oppression or was it judgment? Brianna wrote both and circled neither.

Then the two lenses collided, and that was the part she had not expected. Charlotte selling herself into marriage looked, suddenly, like her father's description of the proletariat: a person with nothing but herself to sell. Elizabeth, meanwhile, could refuse Darcy twice, could afford the luxury of a self, because her family still had land and a house and a father with an income. The feminist reading said Charlotte lacked choice; the Marxist reading said nobody in her position had choice, that choice itself was something the owning side got to have. Brianna stood at the whiteboard with the marker going dry in her hand and thought that she had come here to apply a lens and instead the lenses were applying each other.

What she could not decide, and wrote in the margin in small letters, was whether Austen had known she was doing this. Maybe the author was simply describing her world, the way a camera describes a room, and the criticism was the part where you looked at what the camera refused to turn toward. Maybe every classic was two books: the one about people and the one about money, and you only ever got both by reading twice.

A librarian knocked softly and pointed at the clock; the study room was reserved for a GED class at four. Brianna began erasing, and Priya, who had not even brought that book, who had come only to do calculus and stayed for two hours, picked up the second rag and started on the other half of the board without being asked. "You know the sad part?" Priya said as the servants disappeared first, the question mark lasting a second longer than the word. "The only person in that whole novel who works for wages is the one nobody remembers. And they made a movie of it, and my mum watched it four times."

"She did?"

"Four times. Cried every time at the wedding."

Brianna capped the marker and looked at the clean white board, which was now exactly as blank as it had been before she knew anything.

Chase spread the two notebooks across his grandfather's kitchen table, one labeled Congress in his own handwriting, the other labeled Bundestag in Mrs. Okonkwo's. The house smelled like coffee and old newspapers, and his grandfather had claimed the armchair by the window an hour ago and hadn't moved since, which meant he was watching. On Thursday Chase had to open the mock parliament session by demonstrating how a head of government is chosen and removed in two different systems, and the only thing he knew for certain was that he currently knew almost nothing.

The American half came fast. He wrote: elected separately, fixed term, removed by impeachment, vote in House then trial in Senate. It felt solid, architectural, like the beams in this house. The German half kept collapsing. He had a page on coalition talks, a page on the chancellor's election by the Bundestag, and then a paragraph from a classmate named Dara that said only, "no confidence, look it up properly." He'd been in a group chat fight about it since Monday.

She knocked at the screen door at four, holding her own binder and a bag of apricots from the tree down her street. "You said your grandfather had wifi that actually works."

"He has a kitchen that actually works. Sit."

They staged it right there. Dara pushed the fruit bowl to the center of the table and called it the chamber. Chase was chancellor, because he was the one who'd argued removal should be simple. She read from her binder, playing the opposition, and moved that he be removed. He stood up, joking, and she told him to sit back down. "You don't get to leave yet."

"Then I'm removed. Motion passes, I'm out."

"Nope. That's the whole thing. Germany uses a constructive vote of no confidence. The Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote."

"So there's no vote of no confidence."

"There is, but it's constructive. You have to name who comes next. In the same vote. You can't just clear the chair and walk away."

Chase pulled the laptop over and typed while she ate an apricot. The screen confirmed her, in the flat tone of an encyclopedia, and he sat back. "Okay. So I was wrong all week in the chat."

"You were loud, too."

"Both are curable." He read it twice more, then looked at the fruit bowl, the chamber, and tried to see the whole design at once. In the American system the removal was slow and split between two chambers, but it could leave the office empty and hand it down a list. In the German system removal could be fast but never left a vacancy, because the successor was chosen in the very act of removing you. He liked, briefly, the clean audacity of that, and then he liked the American friction, and then he stopped trying to pick a favorite and wrote at the bottom of the page: two different bets on what you fear more, a vacant office or a rash one.

His grandfather crossed to the table, coffee cup in hand, and squinted at the notes. He was a retired county clerk who claimed he could prognosticate election results from the number of yard signs on Route 9, and he was right just often enough to be unbearable about it. "What's this for?"

"Model parliament. Thursday," Chase said. "We compare how two systems pick and fire the head of government."

"Fire. Hm." He tapped the Bundestag page. "That one keeps the lights on."

"That's not the point, Grandpa."

"It never is, at your age."

After he went back to the armchair, Dara said, "He's not wrong, though."

"That's what's annoying." Chase flipped to his Congress notes and then back. He had wanted one system to be the answer, the way kids in the chat wanted one to be the villain. The zeitgeist of the whole argument online was certainty, everyone certain that one design was obviously sane and the other obviously a trap, and he'd caught the contagion himself. He'd even drafted, on Tuesday night, a nascent manifesto about how parliamentary systems were cleaner by nature. He scrolled to it now and deleted it without ceremony.

They ran the exercise again. Dara moved to remove him, and this time he demanded to hear the successor's name before he'd yield the fruit bowl. She named her choice, Marco from third period, and the apricot pit stood in for the vote tally. "Passed," she said. "You're out."

Chase picked up the pit and turned it over once in his fingers. "Thursday I open with this. But I'm going to say I don't know which is better. I know how each one works and I know what each one's afraid of, and that's it."

"That's it?"

"That's it."

Dara reached across and took the pit back. "Then you'd better stand up when I move against you."

Thomas had one interview suit, borrowed from his cousin Marcus, and it hung on him at the shoulders like a coat rack wearing a coat. The career center at school was running mock interviews all week, and Thursday at 2:15 was his slot, with a real manager from the Home Depot on Route 9 sitting behind a folding table. The job was stocking shelves nights and weekends, eighteen hours a week, and Thomas wanted it the way you want something you have not yet ruined by imagining.

The trouble had started at Sunday dinner, when his mother laid out her instructions like surgical instruments. "You keep your eyes down," she said, spooning kimchi onto his plate whether he wanted it or not. "When Mr. Yamashita interviewed your uncle, your uncle looked at the table the whole time and got the position. Looking straight at a senior person that long, it is rude. Like staring down a judge." His mother had spent her first nineteen years in Busan and her next twenty-five in New Jersey, and she could hold both opinions about anything, sometimes in one sentence.

Then on Tuesday the career center coach, a man named Mr. Delgado who owned four identical blue ties, had said almost the opposite. "In a North American interview, steady eye contact reads as confidence. Drop your gaze every time you answer and they'll think you're hiding something." He had made Thomas practice saying "I'm a reliable team member" while holding eye contact for a full six seconds, which Thomas managed for four and a half before laughing. Priya, practicing in the next chair, laughed at everything, including her own handshake.

Priya wanted the interviewer job, not the hardware job. She had decided in tenth grade that she would run human resources somewhere, and she treated the mock interviews as auditions for a future that had not been invented yet. She had already made Mr. Delgado promise she could run the camera that recorded everyone. "You're lucky," she told Thomas in the hallway. "You get a real manager. I get a tripod and Kevin from third period forgetting his own name."

Thomas sat in the library Wednesday night with both instructions in front of him, written on separate index cards, and could not make them into one instruction. His grandmother had emailed him too, a single line in Korean he had to photograph and translate on his phone: "A senior can look at you. You look at the floor and answer well." He tried to imagine the Home Depot manager, a man named Rick according to the sign-up sheet, and could not decide whether Rick was more like Mr. Yamashita or more like Mr. Delgado, or whether those two men would even have agreed on what a floor was for.

What he settled on was a rule that felt less like courage and more like arithmetic. He would hold eye contact while Rick asked the question, because a person deserved to know he was listening, and then let his eyes rest somewhere near the name tag while he answered, looking up again at the end. It was a compromise, which is a word people use when they mean they could not decide. He could not verbalize why it felt right, only that both his mother and Mr. Delgado were describing real rooms, and he happened to be standing in a doorway between them.

Thursday, 2:15. Priya behind the camera, mouthing "shoulders back." Rick turned out to be a heavyset man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead. He asked the first question off a laminated sheet: "Tell me about a time you solved a problem." Thomas gave his answer about the time he and Marcus unclogged the storm drain on Delancey Street using a coat hanger and a garbage bag, eyes steady on Rick during the question, drifting to the laminated sheet during the middle, returning at the end. Rick nodded along and wrote something down. At the second question Rick looked up sharply and said, "You can look at me, kid, I don't bite," and Thomas held the gaze for a full six seconds, and something in his chest unlocked, and he said, "My mother says it depends where you're from," and Rick laughed, a real laugh, and said, "Fair enough," and Priya, behind the tripod, gave him a thumbs-up that only he could see.

He did not know if he had passed. The results came in sealed envelopes on Friday. But that night his mother asked how it went, and Thomas said, "I looked at him when he spoke and looked away when I did," and his mother considered this, then took his plate to the sink and said, "That is what your grandfather did with the bank manager in 1988." He took the envelope out of his backpack and set it on the table between them, still sealed.

The test came back on Thursday with a red circle around the last line of his work, and beside the circle, in Mr. Okoye's small square handwriting, the words "no plus C on a definite integral" and a deduction of two marks. Andrew had written the antiderivative, added the constant, evaluated at the top limit and the bottom limit, and subtracted. He folded the paper into his back pocket and carried it to his shift at Dettmer's Corner Store, where he worked the register on Friday and Sunday afternoons.

Dettmer's sat at the intersection of two streets that nobody drove down quickly. Andrew stocked the cooler in the afternoon lull, and when no one came in for twenty minutes he took the test out of his pocket and flattened it against the counter beside the lottery machine. His boss, Mrs. Dettmer, was in the back room arguing with a bread supplier on the phone, so he had the front to himself, the hum of the coolers, the smell of floor wax and newsprint.

The function on the test had been an ordinary polynomial, and the antiderivative had been easy. What he could not see was why the constant mattered so little in one kind of problem and so much in another. In his notes from Tuesday there were indefinite integrals everywhere with plus C written after them, sometimes circled twice. He had a vague memory of Mr. Okoye saying the constant stood for a whole family of functions, all of them shifted vertically, all of them with the same slope at every point. For the definite integral, though, the answer had been a number, and the number had not changed whether he wrote the constant or not. Two marks gone anyway, for a symbol that did nothing.

The bell over the door rang. A girl from his calculus class, Priya, came in for a bottle of juice, and she saw the paper on the counter before he could slide it under the register.

"What'd you get?" she said.

"Ninety-two. I lost marks on the last one for plus C."

"On the definite one?" She set her juice down and pulled the paper toward her across the counter. "Yeah, you can't put it there. It cancels out. You add the constant when you plug in the top limit, and you add the same constant when you plug in the bottom limit, and then you subtract, so it just goes away." She tapped the two lines of his work where he had written C both times. "It doesn't change the answer. It just doesn't belong."

Andrew looked at his own handwriting. There it was twice, once in each evaluation, and then the subtraction line where one C met the other and neither survived. He had done the arithmetic correctly and had never once noticed what he was carrying through it. "So it's not wrong exactly," he said. "It's useless."

"It's a habit," Priya said. "You write it so many times on the indefinite ones that your hand does it automatically." She paid for the juice, and the register drawer stuck the way it always did when the twenties sat crooked, and Andrew thumped the side of the till until it opened.

After she left he thought about it between customers, ringing up cigarettes for a man in a Transit van and a quart of milk for the woman from the apartment above the laundromat. Mr. Okoye's little bromide from the first week of the unit came back to him, that integration and differentiation were inverse operations, and for once the phrase seemed less like a poster on a classroom wall and more like something he could hold up to his own work and see through. The constant made sense to him now in both directions. In an indefinite integral you kept it because you honestly did not know which function you had started from. In a definite integral you kept getting the same number no matter which one you had, and now he could see the mechanism in his own hand, plain as a receipt. The whole subject had begun to enthrall him in a way that surprised him, not because it was beautiful, though the textbook insisted it was, but because it kept turning claims he had accepted on faith into things he could check line by line.

He was honest with himself about what he still did not understand. He did not know why the area under a curve should be connected to an antiderivative at all; that had been stated in class and demonstrated with rectangles whose widths shrank to nothing, and he had followed the demonstration without feeling its necessity. Maybe it would resolve the way the constant had, some afternoon when he was not looking for it. He had also heard that in physics the constant was sometimes the whole point, carrying an initial condition, a starting place, and that what vanished in one setting mattered in another. He did not yet know how both could be true of the same symbol.

At closing time Mrs. Dettmer came out of the back room, still holding the phone, and told him to sweep. He pushed the test paper to the end of the counter, took the broom from behind the ice machine, and started at the door. Midway through the aisle with the canned soup he stopped, held the broom still, and said quietly to the empty store, "It cancels because you add it to both and then subtract it away." Then he finished sweeping, collected the test paper, and put it in his shirt pocket instead of his back one, where he would not sit on it and crease the line where the two constants met.

The binder had been Emilie's idea, back in August, when Coach Reyes told the seniors that whoever organized the off-season program would get a say in the spring lineup. She'd spent two weekends on it already: a Monday session, a Wednesday session, hard Friday, and two rest days circled in pencil because she'd read that recovery was when the body actually adapted. The problem was Saturday, the day of the park meet, the day she couldn't figure out how to fill.

"Show me the warm-up page," Dana said, dropping onto the bench beside her and reaching for the binder before Emilie could answer. Grass undulated down the slope in front of them, cut into long stripes by the mower, and at the bottom of the hill the sprinters were already laying out cones.

"Page four," Emilie said.

Dana read it, then looked up. "Dynamic drills. Leg swings, skips. That's it? Where's the stretching?"

"I moved it to after."

"After." Dana set the binder down with exaggerated care. "I've held my hamstring stretch on every start line since freshman year. Sixty seconds, sometimes longer. You're telling me I've been wasting my time."

The first race was the 200, and Dana ignored her. Emilie watched from the fence as her friend folded over her leg at the blocks, holding the stretch the way she always did, minute after minute, then stood, shook out, and settled into her stance. When the gun went, Dana ran flat. She didn't tie up, didn't strain; she simply had nothing in the first fifty meters, and the girl from Central pulled away like Dana was running through deep water. Fourth place. Dana didn't look at Emilie on the walk back up the hill.

They sat through two heats without speaking. A little kid chased pigeons near the water fountain. Emilie turned to the notes section of her binder, where she'd copied the findings from three coaching manuals, and slid it across the bench.

Dana read for a long moment. "Sixty seconds or more, right before explosive activity, can briefly reduce strength and power," she read aloud, slowly, as if testing each word. "So the long holds are why I feel empty at the gun."

"That's what it says. That's why the programs warm up with dynamic movement instead."

"You could have said that louder in August."

"You called my program a coloring book."

The corner of Dana's mouth moved, not quite a smile. She flipped back to page four, ran her finger down the drill list, then closed the binder and held it out. "Then it's your program. Fix Saturday. I'll do whatever's on the page, all of it, even the rest days. Especially the rest days, after that."

The next race went off without them. Emilie took the binder down to the empty end of the track and tried to build the session there, on her feet, the way her inchoate plan kept refusing to become anything she could defend. She marked a drill distance, watched joggers round the far curve, and thought about what she actually believed: that the stretching she'd grown up with wasn't wrong, only wrongly timed, and that sorting that out required more discernment than she'd expected, the kind that came from watching Dana die at fifty meters and knowing she'd had the fix in her bag the whole time. That part she hadn't said out loud, and wasn't sure she would. It would sit in her like a stone either way.

Dana came down the hill and stood beside her. "So what do I do at the blocks?"

"Leg swings. A few short lunges. Keep moving."

"And the long holds?"

"After. Or on the rest days, when there's nothing explosive coming."

Dana rolled her shoulders, spat into the grass, and stepped onto the track. "Count me through it, then. And Emilie, next time a coloring book beats my legs, say so at full volume."

Emilie clicked her pen and wrote dynamic, six drills, ten minutes, across the top of the Saturday page.

Thomas found the notice taped to the gym door on a Tuesday morning, folded once, his name printed in block capitals above the word UNFORTUNATELY. His science fair entry, the model of mitochondrial ATP synthesis he had spent six weeks building out of resin and copper wire, had not made the regional shortlist. He read the letter twice, then put it in his backpack between his calculus folder and a half-eaten granola bar, and went to homeroom without telling anyone.

By lunch he had told exactly one person, Dara, who sat across from him in the cafeteria peeling an orange with surgical care. "Unfortunate," she said, sardonic in the way she allowed herself only about institutions, never about people. "That's the word they chose. Not rejected. Unfortunate."

"I knew the model was ugly," Thomas said. "I thought the ugly part wouldn't matter if the science was right."

"Was it right?"

He pushed his tray a centimeter toward the center of the table. "The sequence was right. Glucose gets broken down, the carbons go through the cycle, and the mitochondria make ATP. I could trace every step from memory. I wanted them to see that." He looked at the window, at the parking lot, at anything. "They didn't even open the display case, I think. The latch was still dusty."

That afternoon he had study hall in the library, fourth period, and instead of doing his chemistry homework he pulled a biology textbook from the shelf and opened it to the chapter he thought he knew. The diagrams were cleaner than his model, which stung, and the cycle had a name attached, Krebs, with a small biographical note at the bottom of the page. He read it, then read it again, then carried the book to the photocopier that only the librarian was supposed to use and copied the page for ten cents.

He found Dara at her locker before last period. "The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's nineteen thirty-seven paper on the citric acid cycle," he said. "He published it in Enzymologia instead."

She closed her locker slowly, watching him. "And?"

"And the cycle is in every textbook now. It's got his name on it." He held up the photocopy. "I'm not saying I'm Krebs. I'm saying rejection isn't a verdict. It's just what happened first."

Dara took the photocopy from him and read it, her lips moving slightly, the way she read when she was checking whether someone was exaggerating. "You found this in twenty minutes," she said. "In a school library. After one rejection letter."

"I know how it sounds."

"Do you?" She handed it back. "You're treating it like proof. One case. It's a story people tell because it feels good, not because it's common."

He walked home holding both thoughts at once, the letter and the photocopy folded together in his jacket pocket, and he could feel them disagreeing through the paper. His uncle had once called him an autodidact, mostly as an accusation, meaning he learned what he wanted and skipped the rest, and Thomas had never decided whether it was a flaw or just a description. What he did know, sitting at his desk that evening with the model dismantled in front of him, copper wire coiled loose like something that had atrophied out of usefulness, was that he still wanted to understand the cycle better than the judges had. That want had not been rejected. Only the display had.

So he rebuilt it. Not prettier, but truer: he added the steps he had fudged, marked where each carbon left, and wrote the ATP yields in the margins where a judge would have to look. It took him four days. On Friday he brought it to Mr. Okafor's classroom after last bell and set it on the lab bench, and Mr. Okafor walked around it twice with his hands behind his back.

"Regional's over," Mr. Okafor said. "You know that."

"I'm not entering anything. I just wanted to show somebody who'd actually trace it."

Mr. Okafor leaned in, followed the wire from glucose through the turns of the cycle, and nodded slowly at the point where Thomas had marked the payoff. "This part's better," he said. "You fixed it."

"Krebs got rejected by Nature and published in Enzymologia," Thomas said. "I looked it up."

"Good for Krebs," said Mr. Okafor, straightening. "There's also a district showcase in March. No prizes. Just tables in the gym and people who walk past." He picked up his keys. "I could get you a table."

Thomas looked at his model, sitting on the lab bench under the fluorescent light, complete and unjudged, and heard himself say, before he had fully weighed it, "Can Dara have the next table over? She wants to display her orchid data."

"She can have whatever table she wants," Mr. Okafor said, and turned off the lights.

Faith spread the two articles across the library table like cards she had been dealt and did not want. Both were about pension trustees and whether their fiduciary duty, the legal obligation to act in beneficiaries' interests, should include considering climate risk in investment decisions. The assignment sheet, folded into quarters beside her, asked for a critical review comparing the two, and Mr. Okonkwo had written at the bottom, in his pithy way, "A comparison is not a summary of two summaries." She had read that line eleven times since Tuesday and still did not entirely know what it meant.

The first article was beautiful. A researcher had interviewed thirty trustees, deep in their own words, about duty and risk, and Faith had underlined so many sentences that the pages looked wounded. The second article was ugly by comparison, all tables and coefficients, a survey of thirty thousand plan participants asked whether they wanted their retirement money managed with climate risk in mind. Its prose was the color of concrete, but the finding was striking: a substantial majority said yes.

She had written a draft that praised the first for its depth and the second for its reach, treating them like two witnesses who happened to agree. She was copying it out in neater handwriting, because the draft was due Friday, when Devon sat down across from her with his own stack of papers and a granola bar he began eating with terrible slowness.

"Same assignment?" he said. She nodded. "Which ones did you get?" She slid him the titles, and he grimaced at the survey. "I had that one first. My whole first draft was about how the interviews one was obviously better written."

Faith bristled, because that was more or less her draft. "It is better written."

"Sure," Devon said. "But here's the thing. My cousin does polling for a living, and when I told her both articles found the same thing, she laughed. She said a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one. That's why the big survey cost somebody a fortune to run." He shrugged and went back to his granola bar, as though he had mentioned the weather.

Faith looked at her draft. She had written that the two articles "converged on a similar conclusion," and she had meant it as a strength of the case, evidence accumulating. She turned back to the survey article and found the table she had skipped, the one reporting the margin of error, and then flipped to the interview study and found nothing like it at all. Thirty people. Thirty thousand people. The word "converged" sat on her page like a coin she had mistaken for two coins.

She pulled the draft toward her and, in the margin, wrote "converged?" and then crossed out the question mark and left the word alone with its scar. All year she had trusted the article that read well. In history class she had chosen the elegant source over the tedious one twice, and once, on a paper about the Marshall Plan, Mr. Okonkwo had circled a quotation and written, "Lovely. Is it representative?" She had not known what to do with that question in October. She thought she might know now.

"So what did you argue?" she asked Devon.

"That the interview study tells you why trustees think what they think, and the survey tells you how many people actually think it, and the second one is the one you can build a rule on." He crumpled the wrapper. "But I couldn't figure out whether the why matters more than the how many. My cousin said I was overthinking it. She interposed between me and my panic with a bag of chips."

Faith laughed, then looked down at her page again. She did not think he was overthinking. She thought the trouble was that both arguments were partly right, and that a review, whatever Mr. Okonkwo wanted, was not a courtroom where one article won. She began a new paragraph. The interviews revealed the reasoning of trustees, she wrote, but thirty voices could not speak for a profession, while the survey's thirty thousand participants gave the finding its weight and its margin, and the margin was the honest part, the acknowledgment of how far the number could drift.

She stopped writing and read the sentence back. It was true, as far as she could tell, and it did not resolve anything, because she still did not know whether a trustee's private reasoning or a beneficiary's stated preference should govern a fiduciary's choices, and she suspected the two articles had been assigned together precisely because nobody in the field had settled it either. She wrote that, too, more carefully, and then sat looking at the two stacks of pages, one bleeding underlines, one gray with tables, neither one willing to interpose itself and settle the question for her.

The library lights dimmed for the closing announcement. Devon gathered his papers and held up the survey article between two fingers, like something found at the bottom of a pool. "Concrete," he said. "But concrete is what holds things up." Faith slid both articles into her folder, the new draft clipped on top, and followed him out past the front desk, where the librarian was already switching off the copier.

Makayla found the broken axle at 4:37, ten minutes before Coach Dan locked the gym, and by the time she'd carried the robot to the bench everyone else had packed up except Priya, who was still coiling extension cords with the slow precision of someone avoiding a conversation.

The robot was for Saturday. The drive base had failed twice during the scrimmage run, both times on Priya's new mounting bracket, and Makayla had spent the whole practice biting down on the sentence she actually wanted to say, which was some version of you ruined the drive base and now we have three days. She set the robot down on the bench between them.

"I'm not mad," Priya said, which was the wrong opening, because it meant she thought Makayla might be.

"I'm not either." That was mostly true. What Makayla felt was closer to foreboding, a tightening behind her ribs every time she pictured Saturday's first match and the robot tipping over on the ramp in front of two hundred people. She could say that. She was less sure she should.

Priya finished the last cord and sat on her heels. "The bracket was too heavy. I knew when I printed it."

"Then why'd you put it on?"

"Because everyone was so excited that it fit." Priya looked at the floor. "I thought I could fix it during the scrimmage."

There it was, the actual problem, sitting out in the open, and Makayla understood that whatever she said in the next thirty seconds would either make Priya defensive or make her a teammate Makayla could count on in three days. She had watched it go both ways on this team. Last season Dominic had told a freshman his code "was a disaster," honest and specific and completely useless, because the freshman had stopped volunteering for anything after that. Honesty without care had effectively incapacitated him; he'd sat at the parts table for the rest of the season sorting screws. Makayla did not want to do that to Priya. She also did not want to say "it's fine," because it wasn't, and Priya would know she was being managed.

Her psych binder was in her bag, and she remembered the page from Monday, the one she'd half-read while eating lunch. She dug it out and found the heading while Priya watched her, puzzled. The notes said that I-messages, statements like "I felt stuck when the parts came in late," were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise a problem without blaming. She'd written it down thinking it was a worksheet answer, nothing to do with her life.

"I-messages," she said, half to herself, tapping the page. "Gordon, sixties."

"What?"

"Nothing. Give me a second." She tried, silently, the sentence she'd been holding. You put a bad bracket on and now we might lose. She rebuilt it. "I panicked during the scrimmage when the base tipped, because I couldn't tell if it was the bracket or my driving, and I felt like I couldn't say anything without it coming out wrong."

Priya blinked. "It was the bracket. Not your driving. I checked the weight after."

"Okay. Then here's what I need." Makayla pointed at the broken axle. "A bracket under forty grams by Friday, and I'd like to test it with you before we mount it, instead of after. Not because I don't trust you. Because I drive better when I'm not guessing."

"That's fair." Priya picked up the robot and turned it over, studying the mounting plate the way she studied everything, like it owed her an explanation. "I have filament for a lighter print. I can run it tonight."

They walked out together, and in the parking lot Priya stopped by the chain-link gate. "You could have just yelled at me. It would've been faster."

"Probably." Makayla shifted her bag on her shoulder. "But then Friday would be us being weird at each other, and Saturday we'd still have a heavy bracket." She wasn't entirely sure that was true, that kindness had bought them anything besides time. Maybe Priya's new print would fail too. Maybe being this careful was just a slower way of being dishonest, postponing the real conversation until it exploded on the bus to the competition. She held both possibilities at once, and let them stand next to each other, the way the robot and the toolbox stood next to each other in the back of her car.

"Text you when the print's done," Priya said. "Come by at nine if you're awake."

"I'll be awake," Makayla said, and clicked the hatch shut on the robot, the axle, and all three days they had left.

Elliot had promised his grandfather he would explain the greenhouse effect by Sunday, and by Thursday he still could not do it without his sentences collapsing into a shrug. He sat in the back row of his environmental science class with the textbook open to a diagram he had traced twice: arrows bouncing off the earth's surface, arrows sliding past a layer of gases, arrows caught and thrown back down. The picture made sense until he tried to say it out loud. Ms. Ferreira had given them a week to prepare a short talk for a family member, someone outside the class, and she had been clear about the point of the assignment. Teaching it, she said, is how you find out whether you know it.

At lunch he spread his notes across the table in the courtyard, and Dana sat down across from him without asking. She was the kind of person who read the assigned chapters in one sitting and then complained that they were too short. "That diagram is lying to you," she said, tapping the little arrows. "It makes it look like a mirror. It's not a mirror."

"Then what is it?" Elliot asked, and he was not being rhetorical; he genuinely wanted to know, and the wanting surprised him a little. He had signed up for the class mostly because it fit his schedule, and he had expected to be bored by it. Instead he found himself enthralled by the strange fact that invisible gases could be doing something enormous, continuously, everywhere, all the time, and that he had walked around inside that fact for eighteen years without once thinking about it.

Dana leaned over his notes. "The energy comes in as light and leaves as heat, and some of the heat can't get out as easily." She squinted at what he had written. "That's not a mirror, it's a blanket with holes in it. Or a parking garage where some cars can't find the exit." She sat back. "Pick whichever one your grandfather would like better."

He tried both versions on his walk home, muttering at the sidewalk. The parking garage made him laugh, which felt wrong for the subject, though Dana had argued that wrongness. "People don't listen to things that sound like a funeral," she had said. "They listen to things that make them curious." He was not sure he agreed. He had watched his grandfather's face at Christmas when someone mentioned the news, the way it closed like a book, and he suspected that the whole thing already felt like a lecture to him, like something the culture kept pushing at him from every direction. Elliot wondered whether there was a way to talk about it that didn't feel like being recruited into somebody's zeitgeist, and whether honesty could survive that softening.

Sunday afternoon, at his grandfather's kitchen table, the moment came. His grandfather had pulled a folded graph from under a stack of gardening catalogs, the same one Elliot had printed for him months ago and assumed had been thrown away. The line on it climbed in a long, wobbling sawtooth up the page, decade by decade. "You said you'd explain this," his grandfather said, not unkindly, and set his coffee down on the corner so the paper would not slide.

Elliot began with the arrows, then abandoned them. "Okay, light comes in from the sun and the ground heats up," he said. "The earth tries to send that energy back out as heat, and some gases in the air, water vapor, carbon dioxide, they absorb the heat on its way out and send part of it back down. So the planet ends up warmer than it would be with nothing catching anything." He paused. "It's not that heat gets trapped and stays there forever. It's that the escape gets slower, and the level fills higher."

His grandfather turned the graph toward himself and traced the climbing line with one finger, the way he checked a saw for a dull tooth. "So when does it cross that dashed line?" he asked, tapping the 400 marked along the side. "The one they printed in bold." Elliot knew this one, because Ms. Ferreira had made them memorize it as a milestone, and because he had looked it up twice to be sure. "At Mauna Loa, the observatory in Hawaii where they measure it, the daily average carbon dioxide passed four hundred parts per million for the first time in the record on May ninth, twenty thirteen." His grandfather nodded slowly and said nothing for a while, and the refrigerator hummed in the quiet.

"I turned eighty in March of that year," he said finally. "I was complaining about my hip and somebody was writing that number down." He looked at Elliot with an expression that was not closed at all, but open in a way Elliot hadn't prepared for. "So it's not a prediction, then. It's a receipt."

Elliot said yes, that was exactly what it was, and felt the parking garage and the blanket both dissolve, because the graph was doing the work now, and it needed no metaphor at all. His grandfather folded the paper along its old creases and stood to put it on top of the refrigerator, under the magnet shaped like a lemon. "Come back next Sunday," he said. "You can tell me what the sawtooth parts mean. I noticed the little teeth in the line, and I want to know what makes them."

The ice was bad at Practice Palace on Tuesday nights, chewed up by the afternoon public skate, and Alyssa dragged a puck through the ruts at center while twelve twelve-year-olds banged their sticks against the boards. She was eighteen, three weeks out of high school, and the association had given her the Bantam house team because nobody else wanted Tuesday nights. Her problem was simple and specific: in Saturday's game, forty-one pass attempts, seventeen completed, and every failed one she had watched on her phone in the bleachers afterward had died the same way, on the blade of a defender's stick laid flat across the passing lane.

She blew the whistle and set up the first drill before the kids could start maligning each other's mothers. Three lines, a cone, a coach standing in the lane with her stick on the ice, a rule that the pass had to get through or the whole line restarted. "It's a game condition," she told them. "That's Maya. Maya is the other team." Maya, who was fifteen and helping for service hours, took her role seriously and tipped the first four passes away.

"Make it harder," Maya called after the tenth failure, peevish now, or pretending to be, because the kids were getting loud about it. "Coach, this is impossible."

Alyssa stood at the blue line with her clipboard and watched Devon, her smallest winger, try the same flat pass for the fifth time. Sweep the puck, watch it clip Maya's blade, skate to the back of the line with his chin down. The drill was hers, designed by her, and it wasn't fixing anything. She had planned it like she planned everything now, with spreadsheets, with completion percentages, with a laminated periodization chart she'd made at two in the morning because planning was the only part of coaching that felt like something she could actually control. Her father called her system a technocracy, half admiring and half worried, and she'd laughed, but the word had stuck to her.

Flashback: her own last season, the semifinal, and she remembered it not as a whole but as one shift. Two-one, four minutes left, her on the wall with the puck and a defender's stick stretched across the lane like a toll gate, and she had tried to force the pass through anyway because forcing it through was what she knew. Turnover, goal against, season over. In the handshake line the other coach, an old man with a scratched whistle, had said something to her she hadn't understood until later. "You tried to go through the stick. There's another direction." She'd thought he meant around the stick. She'd spent a year thinking he meant around it.

Now, on the bad Tuesday ice, she pulled a puck from the bucket and walked it out to the faceoff dot. She'd been watching NHL clips on her laptop since Sunday, looping the same three seconds, and there was a pass she'd seen a hundred times without seeing. She rolled her wrists, opened the blade, and floated the puck off the ice, not high, just off it, so it skimmed flat over the stick she'd laid down as a test and dropped onto the concrete beyond. She did it again. Again it lifted, sailed level, and settled flat on the other side.

"Everyone in," she said.

They gathered at the dot, breathing hard, and she demonstrated at half speed. "You see how it lifts it just off the ice? Watch." She rolled the pass over Maya's stick, and it landed flat, wobbling, on the tape of Devon's blade where he'd parked it as a target. "It's called a saucer pass," she said. "It flies over their stick and it lands on your blade. That's the whole point of it. It lands on the blade, not the ice."

She didn't fully understand the mechanics, wouldn't have claimed to. What she understood was the geometry, and geometry was enough: a lane that was closed at ice level was open two inches above it. She rebuilt the drill on the spot, crossing out her laminated sheet in green marker, and had Maya raise her stick blade flat and low like a real defender, and made each kid attempt five saucers before the line could move. Devon's first three went end over end and one nearly cleared the boards. His fourth skimmed over cleanly and died perfectly on the tape, and he made a sound like a kettle.

"They'll get it by Saturday," Maya said during the water break, which was less a prediction than a question.

"Maybe." Alyssa watched Devon trying to teach the wrist roll to a teammate who wasn't listening. "Or maybe it takes a month and we lose three more games learning it. I honestly don't know which."

"That bother you?"

"A little. It's not in the spreadsheet."

Maya laughed. The whistle was cold in Alyssa's hand. She looked at the clock, at the twelve kids, at the ruts and the buckets and the crossing-out on her clipboard, all of it hers. Then she raised the whistle toward her mouth and skated to the dot, dragging the puck with her, blade open.

Alexandre had claimed the corner table by the periodicals at ten in the morning, and by noon he had spread three books on comparative government across it, a stack of printed articles, and a legal pad with two columns ruled down the middle. At the top of the left column he had written parliamentary. At the top of the right, presidential. In eight days he would sit an entrance interview for a politics program in Montreal, and the interviewer, according to the program's website, liked to ask first-year applicants one question: which system would you rather live under, and why. Alexandre did not yet have an answer, and the not having felt like a debt accruing interest.

The parliamentary column filled quickly. He wrote that the head of government was the prime minister, chosen by the legislature itself, and that the same majority could withdraw its confidence and force a resignation or an election. One column of power, flowing in one direction. It was tidy. It made removal almost arithmetic: lose the numbers, lose the office.

The presidential column went worse. He wrote that the president was elected separately from the legislature, for a fixed term, and then he stopped, because he could not remember how such a president was removed, only that there was a word for it, and that the word was used loosely by people on television. He left a blank space and underlined it twice.

A girl about his age slid into the chair across from him without asking. She had a canvas bag with a broken zipper and a paperback of poems held together with a rubber band. "You have the whole table," she said. "The study rooms are booked until four. I need somewhere to rehearse."

"Rehearse what?"

"A reading. Saturday. I'm sharing the bill with two other people and one of them is very loud, so I need to be louder in a different way." She set the paperback down. "I'm Priya. I'll be quiet. Quieter than the loud one, anyway."

He moved two books to make room. She began mouthing her poem, occasionally whispering a line, while he went back to the blank space. On his phone he pulled up the transcript of a courthouse tour he had attended the previous spring with his civics class. He had recorded it because the teacher offered extra credit, and he had never once played it back. He skipped forward through the guide's voice until he reached a question from a student named Elliott, who had asked what happened when a president got impeached. "So when they impeach him, he's out," Elliott had said, "right? Impeachment means he's removed."

Alexandre remembered the moment, because the guide had paused with her hand on the railing of the staircase. "No," she had said. "Impeachment is the accusation. In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them." Elliott had looked briefly belligerent, as though the distinction had been invented on the spot to embarrass him, and then he had written it down.

Alexandre wrote it down now, in the right column, word for word as the recording gave it to him. Then he sat back and looked at the two columns together for the first time. The parliamentary side was a door that opened with one push. The presidential side was a door with two locks, and the second lock needed a much larger key. Two separate bodies, two different thresholds, one for accusing and one for removing. He drew an arrow between the columns and wrote, near it, "stability or accountability?" and immediately crossed out the question mark and wrote the word "tradeoff" instead, because he suspected the interviewer would like that word, and then felt faintly dishonest for suspecting it.

"It's not a poem about government," Priya said, watching him. "In case you're wondering about the overlap."

"Sorry. What's it about?"

"A fish. A fish that might be able to feel everything, and a person who has to decide whether to cook it. There's a word for whether something can feel, did you know that? Sentience. Whether there's somebody home in there." She tapped the paperback. "That's the whole problem of the poem. You can't get an answer out of a fish."

"You ask it a question and it just sits there," Alexandre said.

"Exactly. And you still have to decide about the pan." She went back to whispering, and he went back to his columns, and the parallel of it did not strike him until later, when he was packing up.

He had wanted the blank filled. It was filled now, and the filling had made the whole question harder rather than easier, because he could see the argument on both sides and could not find a lever that tipped one over the other. The parliamentary system removed a head of government whenever a majority lost faith, quick and blunt. The presidential system made removal deliberately difficult, one chamber to accuse by simple majority, another to actually remove, and only with two-thirds willing. He trusted neither absolutely. He wrote a final line on the legal pad, under both columns: "I would rather live where the prime minister answers every day, but I would rather be accused where two chambers have to agree, most of the way, twice." He read it over and could not tell whether it was a position or a hedge, and left it on the page anyway.

At four o'clock Priya closed her paperback and recited the fish poem once at full voice, quietly loud, watching the reference desk to see if the librarian would look up. She didn't. Priya grinned and began restretching the rubber band.

"What's your interview question," she said, "the one you've been fighting all day?"

"Which system I'd rather live under."

"And?"

"I think I'll tell them I know how each one fires its leader, and that I'm still deciding what that's worth."

"Good," Priya said. "Say it exactly like that, and then don't recuperate." She wound the rubber band tight around the book. "The deciding is the good part."

The packet was on Sara's desk before the bell finished ringing: five pages in Spanish, a rubric, and a note in Ms. Ferrán's looping hand that said only "Sara, día jueves." Thursday. Five minutes, in front of everyone, arguing a current issue entirely in Spanish. She flipped to the rubric and found a row labeled Nivel objetivo: B2. No translation. No mercy.

At lunch she took the packet to Tomás, who had lived in Seville until he was eleven and now ate his sandwiches like a man being timed. "B2," she said, pointing at the row. "What is that?"

"It's from the Common European Framework," he said, mouth full. "It describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options." He swallowed. "So basically you. Supposedly."

"So it's not just talk. It's argue, then admit the other side exists." She said it flatly, testing it.

"That's the whole thing, sí." He went back to his sandwich.

That night her topic sat on the screen of her laptop like a dare: whether the school should switch to a four-day week. She had opinions. She had, in fact, too many opinions, all of them in English, all of them arriving at her tongue at once and dying there. She wrote "recuperar" at the top of her notes, because Tomás had told her that the Spanish for the lost sleep she'd recuperate on a free Friday was recuperar, and she liked the shape of it. Then she wrote nothing else for forty minutes. Her desk lamp buzzed. Her father knocked once, saw her face, and slid a plate of toast through the door without comment, which was its own kind of language.

Wednesday after school she commandeered the empty chemistry lab, which smelled of chalk and something faintly citrus from the janitor's mop bucket, and she made Ana listen. Ana sat on a counter swinging her feet, playing the role of skeptic with an ascetic's discipline: no encouragement, no smiles, just "otra vez" every time Sara stalled. The first run lasted ninety seconds. The second, two minutes. On the third attempt Sara got out "los estudiantes podrían... podrían..." and stopped so long that Ana finally offered, "¿Recuperar el sueño?" like handing her a rope.

"No. Don't rescue me." Sara said it in English, then again in Spanish, slower. "Si me rescátas, nunca aprendo." That was the moment it shifted, though she couldn't have said why. Not fluency. Something more like agreeing to walk out onto a plank in public. She stopped trying to sound like a textbook and started sounding like herself with fewer words, which turned out to be a different self, one who had to choose. In English she could hedge forever. In Spanish she had to pick a side and stand there, holding the disadvantages in her other hand where everyone could see them, because that was the level. That was, she understood now, what B2 meant, not charm but structure: a viewpoint, and the honest weight against it.

Thursday came. Room 114, afternoon light lying in long bars across the linoleum, the radiator ticking like something vestigial from a century that still believed in winter. Ms. Ferrán checked her watch and said "Sara, cuando quieras." Sara stood. The first sentence came out too fast. The second came out right. Somewhere in the third minute she heard herself say that a four-day week would let students recuperar real rest, and then, in the fourth minute, say the thing she'd been afraid of: "Pero existe una desventaja seria," and lay it out, the working parents, the younger kids, the hours that had to come from somewhere. Her hands were shaking. Her voice wasn't.

At four minutes fifty she stopped, one option still unexplained, one advantage she'd planned and never reached. Silence. Ms. Ferrán made a small mark on her clipboard and said, "Bien. ¿Preguntas?" and Rodrigo, from the back, who had spent the whole five minutes slouched like a dismissed hypothesis, raised his hand and asked, in Spanish, what she would say to a student whose parents worked Fridays.

Sara looked at the clock. Six seconds gone already. "Diría que tiene razón," she said, and reached for the next word.

Sophie had told the health science teacher, Ms. Okafor, that she wasn't nervous about the practical exam, and she had told herself the same thing on the bus, and again in the hallway, which was already twice more than a person usually needs to repeat something true. The exam was simple on paper: take a classmate's blood pressure, get an accurate number, then explain in plain language how diet and exercise could change it over time. Sophie had practiced the cuff until she could wrap it in her sleep. What she hadn't practiced was what happened when the numbers came out wrong.

Her partner was Priya, who wanted the certification for a lifeguarding job that started in June and had already bought the whistle. Priya ran to fourth period from the far portables every day, and today was no different. She dropped into the chair, held out her arm while still catching her breath, and Sophie pumped the cuff the way she'd been taught. The screen flashed a number that made both of them lean closer, a top number high enough that Ms. Okafor would have to note it on the skills sheet.

"That's not me," Priya said. "I mean, that can't be me."

Sophie wrote it down anyway, because the sheet demanded a number, and the number was the number. But she kept looking at Priya's sneakers, one heel tapping the floor, the other tucked under the chair, and at her arm dangling loose in her lap instead of resting on the desk. Something about the posture bothered her, though she couldn't have said why, and she was fairly sure the machines in the nurse's office were too antiquated to trust anyway. She'd half convinced herself the equipment was the whole problem by the time Ms. Okafor paused beside their desk.

"Read it again," Ms. Okafor said, which wasn't an explanation, only an instruction, and then she moved on to the next pair.

Priya complained that she didn't want a number like that in her file, that a bad reading would follow her to the lifeguard job, that people would stigmatize her as the one with the high blood pressure. Sophie said nobody's file said anything of the kind, and privately thought Priya was being dramatic, which was a thought she would later have to revise.

After school they stopped at the pharmacy on Alder Street because Priya wanted a second opinion from the machine by the pharmacy counter, the kind with its own chair and its own printed slip. A man hurried in ahead of them, dropped his bag, sat down and jammed his arm in immediately, still muttering into his phone, and got a number that made him frown and do the whole thing over again. This time he put the phone away, sat back, planted both feet flat on the floor, and set his arm on the machine's rest so it sat level with his heart. He waited. The second slip printed, and the top number was much lower than the first, low enough that he folded both slips together, pocketed them, and left looking relieved.

Sophie read the instruction card mounted beside the machine, the one nobody ever read, including the man, who had done it by second nature. For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers. She stood there holding the card's edge while Priya paid for lip balm.

"You ran to class," Sophie said. "You were still breathing hard. And your arm wasn't supported, and your feet weren't flat, and we didn't wait." She said it slowly, testing each part against what she'd seen. "Posture and activity change the numbers. So we measured the run, not you."

Priya sat down in the machine's chair, put her phone in her pocket, and set a timer for five minutes. She kept her feet flat and her arm on the rest at heart level, and for the whole five minutes she was quiet, which Sophie had never once witnessed before. The machine inflated, deflated, printed. The number was lower, ordinary, unremarkable. Priya tore off the slip and held it up to the light like a ticket she'd won.

The next morning Sophie asked Ms. Okafor to recheck the practical. She took Priya's reading after a quiet stretch of the period, feet flat, arm supported, and then talked her way through the second half of the exam, how weeks of walking and a diet lower in salt could bring the numbers down over time, how the reading was a snapshot and not a verdict. Ms. Okafor made a small mark on the sheet and said the retake would be Monday. Sophie walked out to the portables telling herself she had never been nervous in the first place, and rehearsing, under her breath, "five minutes, feet flat, arm at heart level," as Priya jogged past her toward class.

The training binder had a sticker of a cartoon condom on the front, which Amelia took as the program's first statement of philosophy: if you could survive the embarrassment of the sticker, you could survive anything. She had signed up to be a peer health educator mostly because the alternative was study hall, but by the third Tuesday session she had found that she liked the material, liked the strange dignity of words like "contraception" spoken out loud in a classroom, liked the way her grandmother's brisk caution and the nurse practitioner's unhurried factuality could both be true at once. Her grandmother believed knowledge of such things invited trouble; the trainer believed ignorance invited it faster. Amelia had not yet decided which half of her inheritance to amortize over the rest of her life, so for now she paid attention to both.

The trouble, when it arrived, arrived by text. Priya, from her chemistry class, sent a single message at 9:47 on a Thursday night: can i call. Not a question mark in sight, which was how Amelia knew it was serious.

Priya's voice on the phone was querulous in a way Priya never was, all edges and small grievances stacked on top of one larger unspoken thing. The condom broke. It had broken Saturday night, which Amelia made her say twice, because her first instinct was to believe she had misheard the timeline. Saturday. Five days ago. Priya had spent the intervening days telling herself that stress had delayed her period, that the odds were small, that waiting was the mature option, that a pharmacy would judge her, that she would figure it out tomorrow.

"Okay," Amelia said, pulling on shoes with the phone wedged against her shoulder. "We're going to find a pharmacy that's open late. Right now. I'm looking."

"Do you actually know anything about this," Priya said, "or are you just being brave at me?"

"Both are happening simultaneously."

The pharmacist was a compact woman named Dora who looked up from a stack of insurance forms and did not blink at the two of them, one still in pajama pants, whispering at the shelf of cold medicine as cover. Amelia did the talking at first, haltingly, testing the phrases from her training like new shoes. Emergency contraception. Unprotected sex, five days ago. Dora nodded and slid a small box across the counter, and then she said the thing that rearranged the whole night.

"The sooner you take it, the better it works," Dora said. "It works mainly by delaying ovulation, so once the egg is already released, you've missed the window. Five days is really pushing it."

Priya stared at the box. "You mean waiting was the mistake."

"Waiting is always the mistake," Dora said, with the mild cheer of someone who has said this four hundred times. She rang it up without ceremony, mentioned that it didn't protect against infections, and told them the clinic on Delancey Street did testing on walk-in afternoons, no appointment, bring a book because the waiting room was slow. Then she said, "Next time, you come in the next morning," and turned back to her insurance forms as though the whole transaction had been about vitamins.

They sat on the curb outside the closed bakery next door while Priya swallowed the pill with warm water from Amelia's bottle, because Priya had refused to do it inside, in case the pharmacist watched, in case the pharmacist thought something. "She was thinking about her forms," Amelia said. "You could have juggled the box and she'd have stayed neutral."

"She was kind, though."

"She was kind, though," Amelia agreed. Priya leaned back on her hands and finally exhaled, and Amelia found herself doing the arithmetic she could not do out loud: that the pill might work and might not, that five days was five days, that neither of them would know anything for weeks. She had a training session on Saturday about exactly this, about how to tell a frightened freshman the same things Dora had said, and she realized she had learned more in twelve minutes at a pharmacy counter than in three Tuesdays with the binder. There was something funny about that, and also something that made her jaw tighten.

"So the clinic," Priya said. "Testing, Saturday, she said?"

"Walk-in afternoons. Bring a book."

Priya nudged her with an elbow. "You'll come with me. You can practice your whole peer educator machination on the receptionist."

"It's not a machination, it's a public service."

"With a sticker on the binder."

They walked toward the bus stop, and Amelia texted her grandmother that she'd be late, offering no explanation at all.

Victoria had promised her cousin Dana the last of the lemon cake, and Dana arrived with the tin still warm from her own oven, so there were now two cakes on the kitchen table and one novel between them. The novel was Gone Girl, which Victoria had finished at one in the morning three days earlier, and which Dana had finished an hour before walking over. They had decided this in July, when the pool was still open and the plan had seemed far away: a book club with a membership of two, meeting at whichever house had the kitchen to itself.

"I feel stupid," Dana said, cutting the cake with more force than it needed. "I believed her. The whole diary part, I believed every word." She set the knife down and looked at Victoria the way she looked at referees who had made a bad call. "That's not fair. You can't just lie to the reader like that."

Victoria pulled two mugs from the cabinet and filled the kettle. "I believed it too," she said. "Until the middle."

"You didn't." Dana's voice went peevish, the tone she used when losing at cards. "You never believe anybody. You didn't believe Mrs. Halloran when she said the field trip money was going to buses."

"That was different. That was adults and money." Victoria carried the mugs to the table. "This was a diary. Diaries are supposed to be where you tell the truth when nobody's watching. That's the whole point of them."

She had been thinking about this since three in the morning, lying awake with the window cracked, listening to the neighbor's wind chimes. The book alternated between two narrators, husband and wife, and one of them, Amy, had kept a diary that turned out to be false, written deliberately to mislead the police. The novel had come out in 2012, four years before either of them could read it, and Victoria had found herself wondering how many readers across all those years had sat exactly here, in kitchens like this one, feeling exactly this betrayal.

Here was the question she could not let go of: had the author tricked Dana, or had Dana tricked herself? Because the diary chapters were not exactly lies. They were a performance of a person, the way Dana performed confidence at tryouts, or the way Victoria performed indifference when her essays came back with comments. The words on the page were true to something, just not to what they claimed to be true to.

"Okay," Victoria said, turning her mug a quarter turn on the table, a habit her mother called fidgeting and she called thinking. "When you read the husband's chapters, did you trust him?"

Dana considered, stealing the larger slice of cake for herself. "Halfway. He was hiding something about her, but I thought it was guilt, not, you know." She waved the fork. "So no. I didn't trust either of them, really. But the diary felt different."

"Why?"

"Because it was private. Because nobody writes lies in their own diary for themselves."

Victoria felt the small exhilaration of a door swinging open. "Except she wasn't writing it for herself. Once you know the diary is aimed at the police, it's not a diary anymore, it's evidence dressed up as a diary. It's wearing a costume." She reached across the table and slid the book toward Dana, open to the page she had dog-eared at two in the morning. "Look at this entry. She mentions the date, the weather, what he said. All checkable things. The lie isn't in the facts, it's in what the facts are arranged to make you feel."

Dana read the page with her fork suspended in the air. The kettle climbed toward a whistle behind them and Victoria got up to lift it off the burner before it sounded, because her father was asleep after a night shift and the house ran on small accommodations like that. She poured the water slowly, watching it steam.

"So the trick," Dana said slowly, "is that we trust the form, not the person. A diary gets trust just by being a diary."

"Or," Victoria said, sitting back down, "the narrator gets trust by borrowing it from the form. I can't decide which way to say it. Both feel true." She wrapped both hands around her mug. "And I don't know if that makes the book unfair or if it makes it honest, because people do walk around constructing themselves like that. I do it. You do it at tryouts."

Dana was quiet for a moment, chewing. "Then how am I supposed to know who to trust in a book? Or anywhere?"

"I don't think you're supposed to know," Victoria said. "I think you're supposed to notice why you trusted them in the first place." She took a bite of the cake Dana had baked, which was better than her own, and said so. Dana took the compliment with visible satisfaction, then closed the book and pushed it back across the table, cover up, the two faces on the jacket staring at the ceiling.

"We're reading something happy next," Dana said. "I mean it. Something with a dog in it."

The marble stairs of city hall were slick from rain, and Keira took them carefully, the binder of her case pressed flat against her chest. Inside, the hallway smelled of floor wax and old paper. A security guard pointed her toward the council chamber, where the mock court would sit, and where her coach, Ms. Okafor, had already arranged the chairs into a semicircle.

"You're arguing both sides today," Ms. Okafor said, not looking up from her clipboard. "Petitioner first, then respondent. Twenty minutes to prepare the second after you finish the first."

Keira had known this was coming. Still, hearing it said plainly made her stomach tighten. The case was fictional but modeled on a real dispute: a student suspended for a speech delivered off campus that the school claimed disrupted the learning environment. Keira had spent three weeks building the petitioner's case, that the suspension violated the student's rights, and she had built it well. She had quotes, precedents, a closing line about the marketplace of ideas that always drew nods.

She set her bag down at the petitioner's table and began unpacking. Across the aisle, Tobias from Lincoln Prep spread out his own materials, glancing at her with the flat confidence of someone who had only ever argued one side of anything.

"Both sides," he said. "Rough."

"I asked for it," Keira said, which was mostly true.

The panel filed in: three lawyers from downtown firms, volunteers for the day, plus a judge from the county court who would preside. The judge called the session to order and invited the petitioner to begin. Keira stood, straightened her notes, and started the argument she had rehearsed until it ran without her.

"The First Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified in 1791, says that Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech," she said. "A public school is an arm of the state, and punishing a student for words spoken off campus is abridging that freedom in everything but name."

The middle panelist leaned forward. "Congress, counsel. The amendment says Congress. Does it reach a school principal at all?"

Keira had an answer ready, about incorporation, about the Fourteenth Amendment carrying the prohibition against the states. She gave it cleanly, and the panelist nodded, though not as if he were convinced. More as if he were filing her answer away for later, and that unsettled her more than a challenge would have.

She finished strong. The judge called a recess, and Keira sat at the respondent's table with twenty minutes to become her own opponent.

Here was the problem she had been avoiding for three weeks: she did not believe the school was right. Or she believed it was wrong about this student, in this case, but she had begun to suspect it was not wrong in principle, that a school might sometimes have to silence speech to keep other students able to learn at all. She had shoved the suspicion aside as a contrivance of the assignment, something invented to make her argue badly on purpose. Now the invention was the assignment, and she had to make it honest or fail at it.

She turned to a clean page. Congress shall make no law. The words were absolute in form, and yet everyone in that chamber, including her, accepted that they were not absolute in practice. The petitioner's case rested on that gap being small. The respondent's case had to rest on it being, in some places, unavoidable. She began writing the suspension rationale not as a defense of the principal's judgment but as the narrow question of who decides: a principal who sees the hallway the next morning, or a court that never will. It was not an argument that the speech deserved punishment. It was an argument about institutional competence, and it problematized her own earlier claim in a way she thought might actually be true.

The recess ended too fast. She stood for the respondent and heard herself begin, "The school's obligation runs to all of its students, including the ones the petitioner's client targeted." Her voice steadied as the structure held. The judge probed; the middle panelist asked whether her position made the First Amendment a dead letter in schools. She said no, that it meant schools had to justify themselves, that the amendment existed precisely to make justification necessary, and that this principal had done so. She believed the last part less than she said it, and she let the panel see the hesitation rather than bury it, because a lawyer who never hesitated sounded specious, and she had decided, somewhere in the twenty minutes, that sounding right was worth less than being careful.

Tobias argued a brief rebuttal, and then the panel withdrew to deliberate. Keira sat with her hands folded, listening to the radiator tick. She had argued that the school was wrong and that the school had the right to decide, and she could not yet say which claim was the floor of her actual belief and which was the argument built on top of it. Perhaps both. Perhaps the amendment's flat certainty and the school's messy morning-after could only be held together by accepting that they pulled against each other, permanently.

The panel returned. The judge announced that the panel had split, that on balance they scored the respondent's argument higher, and that Ms. Okafor would want to discuss what that meant. Keira gathered her papers, both sets of them, and slid them into one side of the binder. The judge stepped down from the bench on his way out and paused beside her table.

"Which one did you believe?" he asked.

"Both," Keira said. "Ask me again in four years."

Sienna had been maligning the tutoring centre for three weeks before she set foot inside it, mostly to her brother, who had suggested it. "It smells like dry-erase markers and defeat," she told him, and he said, "You've never been in it," and she said that was exactly the point of having opinions. But here she was on a Tuesday evening at the long table by the window, homework spread in front of her like evidence, while a boy named Theo from her calculus class worked two seats down, ostentatiously not looking at her.

The problem on her sheet was a polynomial on a closed interval, and she was supposed to find where it reached its largest value. She had learned to take the derivative that afternoon from a worksheet, a strange little machine of a process: bring the power down, subtract one, repeat. She could do it now without her pen trembling. She set the derivative equal to zero, found a tidy critical point inside the interval, circled it, and sat back.

"I got 2.4 seconds," she announced, because her problem was about a thrown ball and its height, which the textbook insisted on calling h of t.
