It bent away toward the northeast, out across the whole Atlantic. That was the part she couldn't make sense of. Why here? Why not keep hugging the coast toward Virginia, toward New York? She traced it with her finger and the laminate was gritty with sand under her fingertip, and the arrow went on and on until it pointed at the British Isles like a road with a destination.

She had told her lab partner, Dara, that she already understood currents, which was not true, and Dara had said good, because she wanted to do the conclusion slide. Sophie had agreed to that before she understood what the conclusion would need to say. So there was the problem: she wanted to walk into Monday knowing what she was talking about, and she didn't, and her only resources were the map, her phone with one bar of signal, and the ocean itself, gray-green and turbid where the waves stirred up the sand, going about its business without caring whether she understood it.

A boy of about twelve was digging near the dune line with a plastic shovel, and a woman who was probably his mother sat in a folding chair with a book, recuperating from something, maybe a night shift, maybe nothing Sophie could name. Sophie walked down to the waterline with the map rolled under her arm. The water was warmer than she expected for October, warmer than the air, and she remembered her mother once saying that the beaches here stayed swimmable later than the beaches up north where her cousins lived, and that this was "because of that current." Her mother was vague about most science but certain about this.

Back at the hood of the car she opened her notebook and wrote the fact as she now believed it: the Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic. She had put the pieces together from the map's own labels, from a paragraph in her phone's cached pages, and from where the arrow bent, which was under her own two feet. That much she was sure of. What she was less sure of was the rest of the assignment, the part where the warm water's heat somehow ended up responsible for mild winters in London, a city at the same latitude as Newfoundland, which was not mild at all. The map showed the red arrow reaching Europe, and it showed the prevailing winds, and she could see that warmth could travel in water the way it travels in a radiator, but the "somehow" was doing a lot of work in her notes.

Her ethics teacher had spent October on utilitarianism, the idea that you judge an action by its consequences for everyone affected, and Sophie caught herself applying it to her own presentation. If she presented the parts she knew and skipped the parts she didn't, the class would be fine, Dara would get her slide, the grade would come. If she admitted the gaps, the presentation would be messier. She sat on the bumper and let the wind snap the map and thought that Dara deserved better than a conclusion built on a "somehow," and that she herself deserved to actually know the thing rather than to have performed knowing it. Those two wants were not the same want, and she could not fully reconcile them, and she wrote in her notebook, honest as far as it went: I know where it turns. I know it carries heat. I do not know yet how the heat gets from the water to the winters, and I will not pretend I do.

Later, walking the beach with her shoes tied together over her shoulder, she tried to explain the current out loud, as rehearsal, to nobody. "It leaves the coast here," she said, "near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and it turns northeast across the Atlantic." The sentence came out clean. The rest of it, the warming of northern Europe, came out in pieces, and some of the pieces contradicted each other, and she stopped talking when she noticed the boy with the shovel watching her from the dune.

"Are you talking to the ocean?" he asked.

"I'm talking to my homework," Sophie said.

"Does it answer?"

She looked at the water, the long rollers coming in from the southeast, which was, she realized, the direction the red arrow went. "Not in words," she said. She rolled up the map and carried it back toward the car, and the boy went back to digging, and the tide kept coming in over the hole he'd made.

The flyer went up on Monday morning outside the cafeteria: club sweatshirts, eighteen dollars each, and Peyton, who as treasurer of the junior class had argued for the price in a meeting she now wished she could forget, stood in front of it with her backpack sliding off one shoulder. Eighteen dollars was what the senior class had charged last year, and last year the seniors had sold forty-two. So far this week the juniors had sold nine.

"Lower it," said Marcus, who was class president and had wanted twelve dollars from the start. He was eating a bag of chips at the bench behind her, and the cafeteria noise around them undulated as third period let out, a wave of voices rising and breaking against the walls. "Twelve dollars, sell more, done."

"That's not how it works," Peyton said, though she was not entirely sure how it worked, which was the problem. "If we sell more at twelve but make less per shirt, we could still lose money. There has to be a middle somewhere."

Marcus crumpled the chip bag and tossed it toward the recycling can, missing. "So find the middle. You're the one taking calculus."

She had walked into fifth period already annoyed, because being told to use calculus was like being told to use a language she had been studying for exactly six weeks. On the board, Ms. Rojas had written a function, then its derivative, then a number line with plus signs to the left of a point and minus signs to the right, and Peyton had copied it without feeling anything land. She understood the algebra. What she did not understand was why anyone cared which way the signs pointed, and Ms. Rojas, who was cheerful to the point of being choleric in reverse, had a habit of saying "you'll see" that Peyton found less than comforting. Today's quiz had a problem exactly like the board work, and Peyton had gotten it right, she thought, but the rightness felt borrowed, like wearing someone else's coat.

After school she went looking for her grandfather, who was already in his usual spot in the corner of the family center, where he sat on Tuesdays waiting for her while her mother finished her shift. He had driven a delivery truck for thirty-one years and done the dispatch math in his head, and he was the only person Peyton knew who thought numbers were something you could argue with. When she laid out the sweatshirt problem, the nine sold, the seniors' forty-two, the deadline on Friday, he pulled a napkin from the dispenser and smoothed it flat with the side of his hand.

"Suppose we pretend people buy fewer shirts every time the price goes up," he said. "Some steady drop. What's that called in your class?"

"A linear model," Peyton said. "If it drops off at a constant rate." She wrote revenue equals price times the number sold, and below it she substituted what she actually wanted: price times some starting quantity minus a rate times the price, all of it multiplied out into a polynomial, an x squared with a negative coefficient out front. Then she took the derivative the way Ms. Rojas had drilled them, the power rule falling out of her pencil almost without her deciding anything.

"Those signs again," her grandfather said, tapping the derivative she'd set beside a rough number line she'd drawn to test it.

"It's the first derivative test," Peyton said, mostly to hear whether the words still belonged to someone else. She marked a plus sign to the left of the critical point and a minus sign to the right, and then she stopped, because she saw it: where the signs went from positive to negative, the function had to be rising and then falling, which meant that point was a local maximum. Not a guess for the middle. The actual top of the hill, at least as far as the model went. She checked the arithmetic twice and got fifteen dollars, and under it, a revenue that beat both eighteen and twelve by a margin she made herself recalculate a third time before she would say it out loud.

"Of course," her grandfather said, "people aren't a formula."

"I know." And she did know, which was the part she couldn't put on the napkin. Maybe the drop-off wasn't steady. Maybe eighteen dollars worked as a disincentive for freshmen in a way it wasn't for seniors with jobs, or maybe this year's juniors were just slower to buy and the nine would become thirty by Friday regardless of anything she did. The model said fifteen; the world might say otherwise. She folded the napkin into her pocket anyway.

At Thursday's meeting she put the napkin, unfolded and flattened, in the middle of the table, and Marcus leaned over it with his arms crossed. "You're telling me the answer's fifteen."

"I'm telling you the model says fifteen," Peyton said. "We can test it. One day, one price, and if it's wrong, we'll know the model's wrong, not just me." Marcus looked at the napkin for a long moment, then at the sign chart with its plus and minus, and pulled out his phone to change the flyer.

By Friday afternoon they had sold eleven more, and Peyton stood by the cash box counting singles, watching the line of students at the table stretch past the water fountain and wondering whether to trust the number in her notebook or the evidence of her own eyes, and deciding, for now, to hold both.

The computer lab at Camp Wrenhaven smelled of pine sap and warm plastic, and Ashley had claimed the terminal by the window because it was the only one where the fan didn't rattle. Her assignment, due before the campfire at eight, was to build a class in Java with private fields, getter methods, and a test that proved the whole thing worked. She had written the fields already, three of them, and she kept staring at the word private like it was a locked door she herself had installed.

"You're glaring at it," said Devon from two seats over. He was a connoisseur of other people's screens; he wandered the lab every evening, sampling code the way some people sampled the snack table. "What did your class do to you?"

"Nothing yet. That's the problem." She turned so he could see. "I made the fields private, and now my test can't touch them. I can't even check if I set the student's name right."

Devon pulled a chair over, taciturn for once, and read the whole file top to bottom before saying anything. He was the sort of person who seemed to believe silence was a form of respect. "So write a getter," he said finally.

"A what?"

"A method that hands the value back. getName. One line, returns the field." He tapped the screen. "Private fields, methods in front. That's the whole architecture."

Ashley typed it, a small method called getName that did nothing but return the value, and ran her test, and the test passed, and she felt something she couldn't quite name, a kind of smallness and a kind of power at once. She had hidden the data and then built a doorway to it. Why bother hiding something you were going to hand out anyway? She asked Devon, and he only shrugged, which she was beginning to understand was his way of saying the question was better than he could answer.

Across the lab, Priya Ranganathan sat with her laptop angled away from everyone, as she had all week. Ashley had inured herself to Priya's silence, mostly, the way camp inures you to cold showers and bug bites; it stopped being an insult and became weather. Priya was the best programmer in the cabin and had never once said so, which somehow made it more true. That evening, though, Priya's screen kept flashing red with errors, and her pencil tapped the table in a rhythm that meant trouble.

From Priya's side of the lab, the evening looked different than Ashley could have known. Priya had watched Ashley build her class piece by piece all week, and she had noticed, with an interest she concealed out of long habit, that Ashley wrote things the slow way on purpose, taking apart what worked just to see the gears. Priya's own code was breaking for the opposite reason: she had let her main program reach directly into the fields of her camper class, reading and rewriting them wherever it pleased, and now she wanted to change how one of those fields was stored, from a plain string to something else, and forty lines elsewhere in her program immediately screamed. She knew she could undo the change and patch each error by hand. She also suspected there was a principle she was missing, one everyone else seemed to have absorbed without ever saying aloud.

She carried her laptop across the lab and set it down beside Ashley's. "Can I show you something?" It came out flatter than she meant, and Ashley blinked at her, then pulled over a third chair.

"Here's my class," Priya said. "Camper. And my program reaches into it everywhere, like this, changing the field directly. I wanted to change how the field is stored. When I did, everything using it broke." She scrolled through a wreckage of red. "Yours wouldn't do that, would it? Yours has the methods in front."

Ashley looked at her own screen, then at Priya's, and the two ways of seeing the class slid together with an almost audible click. "Private fields, methods in front," she said slowly. "That's the whole architecture. My test doesn't know how the object stores its data. It just asks. So if I changed how it's stored, my test wouldn't even notice."

"Encapsulation," Priya said.

"Is that what it's called?"

"That's what it's called." Priya was already dragging her chair closer, her screen beside Ashley's, two programs open at once. "Other code uses the object without depending on how it stores its data. I read that in the chapter and it went in one ear." She began, methodically, to make her fields private, one by one, and Ashley watched the errors bloom and then, as each getter took its place, go quiet.

By the time the counselor leaned in to say the fire was being lit, Priya's program ran clean, and Ashley's test suite printed eleven green lines. But Ashley kept one tab open, her cursor blinking after the last getter, because something still bothered her and she wanted to be honest with herself about it. The doorway she had built handed out the name to anyone who asked, no questions, which meant the hiding was thin, a curtain rather than a wall. What was privacy that gave everything away on request? Maybe the point wasn't secrecy. Maybe it was something else, control, or the freedom to change her mind later without breaking anyone who trusted her. She didn't know yet, and she liked not knowing, the way she liked a problem with room left in it.

Devon drifted past on his way out and read the green lines over her shoulder. "Done, then," he said.

"Done enough." Ashley saved the file, closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again to look at the word private one more time. Priya stood in the doorway with her laptop under her arm, waiting, and outside the window the first sparks of the campfire went up. "Coming?" Priya asked.

The library closed at nine, but the study room was reserved until eight, and Laura had arranged her materials on the long table with the ceremony of someone who intended to use every minute: two legal pads, a photocopy of the case, a bottle of water she kept forgetting to open. Mr. Reyes had assigned each of them a Supreme Court case and, worse, both sides of it. "You will argue for the government on Tuesday," he had said, "and for Schenck on Thursday. If you find yourself agreeing with one side, you haven't done the work."

Sitting across from her, Marcus snapped a rubber band around his wrist. He had been her debate partner since sophomore year, and he had the infuriating habit of playing devil's advocate even when no devil was required. "Start with your strongest line," he said. "Government side. Go."

Laura squared the legal pad in front of her. "During wartime, speech that creates a clear and present danger can be punished. The defendants mailed leaflets urging men to resist the draft. That's not abstract argument, that's interference with military operations." She heard her own voice go flat and official, the way it did when she was reciting rather than believing.

"Fine. Now the other side. Say it like you mean it, or I'll believe you don't."

She looked down at the words she'd written three days earlier and hadn't reread since. That was the trouble with arguing both sides. Her positions had started to calcify the moment she committed them to paper, the first draft hardening into something she defended instead of reconsidered. She remembered, briefly, her sister's graduation two years ago, when their father had given a toast about standing up for what you believe in, and how even at fourteen Laura had wondered what you were supposed to do when two things you believed in were pointed at each other.

"The leaflets went to men who had already been drafted," she said slowly. "They were mailed, privately, to named recipients. The government wants to punish words on paper, mailed through the post, that changed nothing. Nobody rioted. Nobody deserted. If the First Amendment means anything, it has to mean the government can't jail you for being unpersuasive."

Marcus raised his eyebrows, and she flushed, because it had come out better than anything on her pad. "Where was that Tuesday version of you?" he said. "Okay. Counter. The famous line. You know the one everybody quotes."

"Falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic." She said it without checking her notes. "The point is that free speech doesn't protect that."

"Who wrote it?"

Laura opened her mouth and then stopped, because she suddenly wasn't sure she had ever known, or whether she had known and let it go the way you let go of a fact that's inconvenient to the sentence you're building. She flipped to the photocopy. "Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes. Nineteen nineteen. It's in the Schenck opinion itself."

"So the same man who wrote the theatre line wrote the opinion you're attacking Thursday." Marcus leaned back until the chair creaked. "Your strongest argument against the government side is a sentence the government side wrote."

She read the line again, the whole fact of it sitting there in Holmes's own words: free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic, written in 1919, in this very case. She had been wielding the fire line for years without ever asking whose hand it came from. In eighth grade she'd used it in a class discussion about a kid who got suspended for a parody account, and she'd felt so right, so adult, invoking the theatre. She hadn't known then that the words came from the opinion that sent men to prison for leaflets. Maybe it didn't change whether the words were true. Maybe it changed something else.

"Maybe it's both," she said. "The line is good. The application is terrible. He wrote a principle I agree with and then used it to uphold a conviction I think was wrong."

"That's not an argument, that's a headache."

"That's the argument." She was writing now, fast, the pen skipping. "Thursday I say: the theatre analogy came from the same pen that jailed Schenck, and that should make us careful with it. Tuesday I say: even Holmes thought there were limits, and the fire example still holds." She stopped. "Except that's not really careful. That's just convenient. I'm picking up the line when it helps and putting it down when it doesn't."

Marcus pulled the rubber band and let it go. "So pick. Which side do you actually believe?"

The radiator under the window ticked, the room's own stubborn homeostasis, holding its temperature against whatever was happening to hers. Outside, a security guard was pushing a cart of returns toward the front desk. Laura thought about being parsimonious with her principles, saving them up and spending them only where they'd buy the most, and how that wasn't the same as having principles at all. But she also thought that a person who could see both sides wasn't weaker than a person who saw one. She just hadn't figured out yet what seeing both sides was for.

"I don't know," she said. "Ask me Tuesday."

"Tuesday you're the government."

"Then ask me Thursday." She closed the legal pad and slid the photocopy of the opinion into her folder, the theatre line face down. "I want to get the dates exactly right in my notes before I say any of it out loud again."

Marcus stood and stretched. "The room's ours for twenty more minutes."

Laura opened the folder back up, found Holmes's sentence, and began, slowly, to copy it out by hand.

Jade had agreed to debug Rohan's code over the phone, which turned out to mean listening to him panic while she sat on her grandmother's porch with a glass of sweet tea going warm beside her. The club's new membership roster had two hundred and six names in it, and their little program was supposed to find any one of them. It kept coming back with nothing found, even for names everyone knew were in there, like Okafor, which was the whole reason the program existed.

"It's a binary search," Rohan said, as though saying it again would make it work. "I read about it last night. It's supposed to be faster than checking every single name one at a time."

"Than a linear search," Jade said, mostly to show she'd been listening. She didn't actually know yet what made the two different, beyond a vague sense that one was a plodder and the other was supposed to be clever. That was the embarrassing part. She'd told the club she could fix it. She'd said it in the confident voice she used when she hadn't yet looked at the problem, a voice she was starting to suspect she used to externalize an optimism she didn't really hold.

Her grandmother came out with the newspaper folded under her arm and settled into the other rocker. She had been a county clerk for thirty-one years and regarded computers the way she regarded weather, as something that happened to other people. "Who are you arguing with?" she asked.

"Nobody. A program. It keeps missing names that are definitely there."

Her grandmother made a small sound, the sound of a woman who had filed a great many things. "Come inside when you're done shouting. I'll show you something."

What she showed Jade was the old phone book she still kept in the drawer by the refrigerator, because she didn't trust the internet to be up when she needed it. "You city children search like this," she said, and turned to the front of the book, and ran her finger down the first page, one name at a time, mouthing them. "Aardvark Removal. Abel. Abelard." She glanced up. "How long do you think I'd be at it before I reach Whitfield?"

"Forever."

"Now." She opened the book wide, found the exact middle, and put her finger there. "I look at the name in the middle and I think, is the name I want before this or after it?" Her finger rested on a name somewhere around Morgan. "Whitfield comes after. So I take the front half and I throw it away." She let the pages flop forward, half the book gone in one motion, and Jade felt something rearrange itself in her head. "Then I find the middle of what's left and do it again. Whitfield. After. Throw away the front half. Two hundred pages, then a hundred, then fifty."

"It works because it's sorted," Jade said slowly. "Because the names are in order, you know which half can't have it."

Her grandmother shrugged. "I'd be a fool to throw away half the book if I didn't know what order it was in."

Jade was already dialing. "Rohan. Is the roster sorted?"

There was a silence long enough to hold a whole confession. "Sorted how?"

"Alphabetically, Rohan. Is it alphabetical." She could hear him scrolling. The club had entered members in the order they paid dues, which was the order they'd walked into the gym on sign-up day, which was the order of nothing at all. The list was two hundred and six names of pure chronological accident, and Rohan's program had been cheerfully discarding the half that contained Okafor every single time, because a binary search on unsorted data was just a machine that threw away the right answer with great efficiency.

She stayed three more days at her grandmother's, and each morning she sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open, sorting the roster and rewriting the search with a note tacked to the top of her screen in her own handwriting: check the middle, then throw away the half that can't hold the target. It felt strange to be learning the cleverest thing she knew from a woman who called the laptop "the television with keys," but there was something fitting in it too. Her grandmother had spent three decades believing that how you organized information was a moral question, that an unsorted file was a small act of chaos, and Jade had spent the summer believing the opposite, that structure was something the machine would supply on its own. She wasn't sure yet how to hold both ideas, whether her grandmother's whole ontology of careful record-keeping and her own faith in fast code were rivals or just two halves of one job. The club members back home, disaffected after weeks of a search tool that couldn't find their own names, would take some winning back either way.

On the last evening she ran the finished program. She typed Okafor and hit enter and the result appeared in less time than it took her to exhale. Her grandmother looked over her shoulder at the glowing screen and rocked back on her heels.

"Faster than reading every name," Jade said.

"Of course it is," her grandmother said. "Now close that thing and help me shell these peas."

Samuel spread the flashcards across the kitchen table like a man laying out evidence for a trial he was not sure he could win. Tomorrow at four he had to pass the peer health facilitator check, fifteen minutes in front of the coordinator, explaining consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the county clinic. Tonight the kitchen was his, his mother on shift until eleven, and the only witness was the dishwasher's low hum.

He started with consent, saying it out loud to the refrigerator. "Consent is a clear, freely given yes. Not silence, not maybe, not a yes you talked someone into." It sounded rehearsed, because it was. He had written the sentences on the bus, on his hand, on the back of a chemistry worksheet, until the words had lost their edges. That was the problem. He could recite them and not believe a single one in a specific situation, and Mrs. Okonkwo, the coordinator, would smell that hollowness the way a substitute teacher smells fear.

Nadia came in for cereal at nine, barefoot, fifteen, skeptical by constitution. "You're talking to the fridge again."

"I'm practicing. Ask me something. Anything. Hard questions."

She leaned on the counter, spoon in hand, and obliged. "Okay. If someone's on the pill, they don't need a condom, right?"

Samuel opened his mouth and then closed it, because the honest answer required a story, and the story was three weeks old. He had been at Duval's Pharmacy waiting for his mother's blood pressure medication when a girl from his grade, Marta, stood at the counter with a paper bag and a question she asked too quietly. "Does this, like, cover infections too? The birth control?" The pharmacist had shaken her head, kind and unhurried. "It prevents pregnancy. It doesn't protect against infections. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections." Marta had nodded, paid, and gone out into the March drizzle with her bag clutched like contraband, and Samuel had stood there realizing he'd had it wrong too, in some dim, unexamined way, assuming that one protection was protection.

"So?" Nadia said now, dragging him back. "Was I right?"

"No. That's the thing. The pill prevents pregnancy, but it doesn't protect against infections. Only condoms do both. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of STIs." He said it and heard the pharmacist's cadence in his own voice, borrowed but true.

"Then why doesn't everyone just use both?"

"Because people make tradeoffs. Because nobody taught them. Because it's awkward to talk about, and this whole thing I'm doing tomorrow is trying to make it less awkward." He heard his own earnestness and let it stand there, unfashionable and exposed.

There was a second voice in his head, older than the pharmacist's. His mother, the previous Sunday, chopping onions, when he'd told her about the facilitator program. "You're seventeen," she'd said. "What do you know to teach anybody?" Not an accusation exactly, more a genuine question, the kind she asked while doing something else so that he could pretend not to answer if he chose. And beneath it, unspoken, the whole grammar of how she'd been raised, in a house where such things were managed by silence and luck. He had not argued with her. He had thought about her cousin Adaeze, whose story the family told in fragments and never in full, and he had decided that silence was a tradition you could decline to inherit without despising the people who'd kept it. Still, he couldn't fully dismiss her point either. He was seventeen. Tomorrow he would stand in a church basement with a laminated diagram and more confidence than his experience could strictly support, and that gap was real.

"Okay," Nadia said, setting down her bowl. "Role-play me. I'll be some random person at your thing. Do the consent part."

He straightened. "Imagine you're with someone, and things are moving, and you're not sure if they want to keep going. What do you do?"

"I ask."

"How?"

"What do you mean, how? Do you want to? That's how."

"And if they say nothing?"

"Then I stop." She said it so plainly that he almost laughed, not at her but at the fifteen minutes of jargon he'd been rehearsing for a thing she'd compressed into four words. Except it wasn't that simple, and he knew it, and it was his job tomorrow to say why: that stopping can feel enormous in the moment, that people say yes to avoid disappointing, that consent can be withdrawn after it's given and the withdrawing must be honored the same as the first no.

"That's right," he said. "That's the whole center of it. Everything else is plumbing."

"What about the clinic stuff? Where do people even go?"

He pulled the county health department's printout from under a flashcard, a page he'd annotated in three colors like scripture requiring its own hermeneutics. "Here. Testing is free, you can walk in, and it's confidential, which means they don't tell your parents. You can call ahead, or just show up." He traced the hours with his finger. "Results take about a week. If something shows up, most of it's treatable."

Nadia studied the page with an interest she tried to disguise. "Is it scary? The test?"

"I haven't done it," he admitted. "So I don't know. I shouldn't pretend I do." He slid the page toward her. "But I'm going to find out, before summer. Then I can say it from the inside."

The dishwasher clicked off, leaving the kitchen quieter than he'd noticed it being. His mother would be home in twenty minutes, tired, penurious with her energy at that hour, saving her words for the morning. He gathered the flashcards into a stack, then stopped, and left the clinic page out on the table where she would see it, face up, when she came in.

Nadia took her bowl to the sink. "You'll pass," she said. "Even though you talk to appliances."

"Thanks," Samuel said, and turned the flashcards facedown.

The cuff hissed and tightened around her grandmother's arm until the fingers went dull, and Sienna watched the screen blink up its verdict: 148 over 91. She had bought the monitor with her first paycheck from the garden center, partly because her grandmother kept saying the machine at the pharmacy had called her numbers "high" and she refused to believe a machine that also sold lottery tickets.

"Two numbers," her grandmother said, peering at the display over her glasses. "Which one is the bad one?"

"That's not how it works," Sienna said, and then caught herself, because three weeks ago she hadn't known either. She'd stood in aisle four at Duane's Pharmacy waiting for a prescription, and the free machine had sat there with its molded plastic seat, and she'd tried it on a whim. 112 over 74, the screen had said, and she'd stared at it feeling like she'd been handed someone else's homework to grade. She'd taken a photo of the screen with her phone and, over three evenings of searching and squinting at diagrams, had pieced together what the numbers were. The top number was called systolic, the pressure when the heart beats; the bottom was diastolic, the pressure when the heart relaxes between beats. Both measured in millimeters of mercury, a phrase she loved for its sheer strangeness, blood translated into the language of old thermometers.

"The top one is the systolic," she told her grandmother now, unstrapping the cuff. "That's when your heart beats. The bottom one's the diastolic, when it relaxes between beats. They measure it in millimeters of mercury."

"Mercury," her grandmother repeated, as though Sienna had announced the reading in runes. "So which one is bad?"

"Both of them matter." She said it carefully, not like a verdict but like a door she was still pushing open. She'd read about sodium and arteries and walking, though the deeper mechanisms stayed foggy to her, honest fog, the kind she could admit to. What she trusted was the pattern she kept finding: the numbers moved with how people lived, and they moved back when the living changed.

Her grandmother was not, by any standard, an epicurean woman; she ate canned soup standing at the counter and considered salt a birthright. But she had been a nurse's aide for thirty years in a milieu where nobody explained anything to anybody, where doctors wrote things on charts and the charts went into drawers. Sienna wondered sometimes whether that was where her grandmother's suspicion came from, all those years of being handed outcomes without reasons.

"Grandma, sit down. I want to try something." She got the notepad from the kitchen drawer, the one with the hummingbird on the cover, and drew a wobbly heart with an arrow through it. "Okay. So the top number is the heart beating. Pushing." She tapped the drawing. "The bottom number is it resting. In between beats." She wrote 148 and 91 beside each other and circled them. "The doctor said to walk. If you walk, and ease up on the salt, these could come down. Not in a day. But they can move."

Her grandmother looked at the notepad for a long moment. Outside, the October light was doing its slow business on the hydrangeas, which had desiccated over the past month into papery brown skulls, still upright, still holding their shape. "You sound like your mother," she said finally.

"Mom's a dental hygienist."

"Your mother explains things anyway."

Sienna laughed, then made her grandmother hold out her arm and took the reading again, mostly because she wanted to see whether the numbers would sit exactly where they'd sat before. 147 over 92. Almost the same, close enough that she couldn't tell if the difference was real or just the machine breathing. She wrote both readings down in the hummingbird notepad and dated them, because that seemed like the right instinct even if she couldn't have defended it.

"So we walk," her grandmother said. It came out somewhere between a question and a dare. "Tomorrow morning. Around the block. And I'm not giving up the soup."

"Half the salt," Sienna said. "That's my offer."

They shook on it over the kitchen table, her grandmother's hand dry and light in hers, and then her grandmother picked up the notepad and read the numbers aloud again, slow, like she was memorizing a phone number from a country she was planning to visit. "Systolic," she said. "Systolic, diastolic. Fine. Write it here so I don't forget which is which."

The blood pressure cuff hissed and Aiden watched the needle settle on the dial, one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four, which meant nothing to him yet. Marisol, his partner in the health aide track at Camp Wanocksett, unwound the cuff from his arm and wrote the numbers on her clipboard with an air of ceremony, as if the gesture itself were the skill. Their instructor had given them a handbook, a box of practice cuffs, and almost no direction, saying only that by Friday each of them had to take a reading, interpret it, and explain it aloud to the group. Aiden flipped through the handbook that evening on the dock, the lake going copper behind him, and found a page he had skimmed past the first time. Under the 2017 American guideline, it said, stage 1 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139, or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.

He read the line three times, then set the book on his knees and looked at the water. His grandfather had mailed him a photograph last month, before camp started: the little log the old man kept beside his armchair, columns of numbers in his careful draftsman's handwriting, taken every morning with the home monitor Aunt Renata had insisted on. Grandpa had written something insouciant on the back, "Still alive, see you in August," which was his way of refusing to take any of it seriously. Aiden had looked at the numbers then and felt only a vague unease, the kind you get from a receipt you can't quite read. Now he pulled the photo up on his phone, zoomed until the columns blurred, and found the entry from the second week of June: 136 over 85.

There was a kid at camp named Derek who wore a stethoscope around his neck between sessions, which everyone agreed was an affectation, since they were nowhere near the simulation where stethoscopes were actually issued. Derek had done a first aid certification the year before and liked to hold court at the picnic tables. "Stage one hypertension," he announced the next morning, when Aiden mentioned what he'd found in the handbook, tapping his own neck where the stethoscope hung. "That's what those numbers are called. My mom's a nurse." Aiden asked him what a person was supposed to do about it, and Derek shrugged, said something about salt, and drifted off toward the boathouse, apparently satisfied to have named the thing without ever wondering what the naming was for.

Aiden wasn't satisfied. He carried the question through the afternoon like a stone in his shoe. During free swim he sat on the dock again with Marisol, who was teaching herself to interpret readings by inventing patients. "This one," she said, pointing at a made-up 148 over 92, "that's past your range, right? So that's stage two, or worse." She said it lightly, burnishing her own competence a little, but she was the only one taking the arithmetic seriously, and Aiden found he trusted her more than Derek for exactly that reason. He showed her his grandfather's log. She went quiet over it, scrolling, then said, "He wrote you this and didn't take it to anybody?"

"I don't think he looked at it that way," Aiden said. "He thinks of it like checking the oil. Numbers in a notebook, job done." He was remembering now the summer he was twelve, when Grandpa had ignored a splinter in his palm until the whole hand swelled, and Grandma had driven him to the clinic herself, furious, while Aiden sat in the back seat watching the fields go by. She had died the following spring. There was no one left to do the driving now, and no one left to be furious, which Aiden understood, in a way he couldn't articulate, was the actual problem.

Marisol said, "So call him." It was that simple for her, and he envied the simplicity. He thought about it through dinner, through the evening campfire, through the walk back to his cabin under a sky gone loud with cicadas. If he called and said the words, stage 1 hypertension, his grandfather would hear a lecture, would hear Aunt Renata, would go amiable and dismissive and promise to mention it at some appointment he would not schedule. If he said nothing, the log would keep filling up with numbers in that steady hand, and Aiden would carry the June entry around like a folded map to a place he'd never been.

The next morning was interpretation day. When his turn came, Aiden took Marisol's reading, one hundred and twenty-six over seventy-eight, and stood in front of the group and worked through it aloud, systolic and diastolic, below 130 and below 80, within the normal range under the 2017 American guideline, not hypertension, not even stage one. He heard his own voice steady on the terms, and he heard, underneath it, the sentence he was not saying to anyone. Derek, mercifully, kept quiet. The instructor marked something on her clipboard and called the next pair up.

That night Aiden walked out past the flagpole to where the camp's one payphone hung on the wall of the mess hall, a relic nobody used. He fed in the quarters he'd been carrying since Monday and dialed the number he knew by heart. It rang twice, three times, and he watched a moth circle the bare bulb above the phone while he decided, one more ring at a time, exactly what he was going to say. Then his grandfather's voice came on the line, cheerful and unhurried, and said, "Well, this is a surprise."

The lab smelled like chalk dust and the faint vinegar of old agar, and Jessica had copied the same DNA sequence onto her worksheet three times before she trusted her hand. Mr. Reyes had left a strand on the board, AGCTTAG, and told them to write the RNA it would produce. She wrote it out letter by letter, then checked it against her notes, then sat back with the particular hollowness that comes from realizing you do not know how to check something you have just done.

"You're stuck too?" Devon leaned over from the next stool, holding his pencil like a dart.

"I'm not stuck. I'm thinking."

"Same thing in this class." He was being facetious, but only halfway, the way people are when the joke is a shelter. "I got TCGAATC for mine, but I don't know if that's RNA or just DNA wearing a costume."

Jessica looked at his paper. At the bottom, in his cramped left-handed scrawl, he had written TCGAATC and then, in the margin, the word RNA with a question mark after it. She looked at her own answer. AGCUUAC. She had copied the strand faithfully, flipped the letters to their partners, and there, sitting in the middle of the third position, was a T. She had put it there herself, five minutes earlier, without noticing.

"Wait," she said.

"That's encouraging."

"No, really. Look." She turned her worksheet so he could see it. "In the DNA, adenine goes with thymine and guanine goes with cytosine. That part I know cold, I made flashcards in September. But when you write the RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine. So adenine still pairs with adenine's partner, but it's U, not T. There shouldn't be any T in mine at all."

Devon squinted at her paper, then at his own. "So I've got two problems."

"You've got at least two problems." She took his pencil out of his hand and crossed out the second letter. "If the DNA you started with had adenine there, you write U."

"You're sure?"

She was not sure. That was the thing she could feel pressing at her from underneath the certainty of her voice: she had said it with confidence because saying it with confidence was how you found out whether you believed it. The rule felt right, the way a key feels right before you turn it. She pulled her binder toward her and found the page from the unit on RNA, the diagram with the two strands and the letters floating between them, and there it was in the print, the same pairing she had just said, the U standing where she expected a T.

"Okay," she said. "Okay, it's right."

"You didn't know?"

"I knew it the way you know someone's phone number. You have to say it out loud before you know if it's in there."

Down the row, Priya was erasing something with such force that her whole worksheet buckled. Jessica watched her do it, then watched her write the same wrong letter again. Priya was the one who had explained mitosis to the whole table last month, drawing circles on the desk with a wet finger, and Jessica had privately considered her the standard, the person whose understanding indemnified the rest of them against their own confusion. It had never occurred to her that Priya could also sit in this room at 2:15 on a Tuesday with an answer she could not defend.

"Hey," Jessica said, not loudly. "Check your T's."

Priya looked up. "What?"

"In your RNA. If you were copying from DNA, adenine pairs with thymine in the DNA itself, but in RNA it's uracil instead of thymine. If you've got T's in there, they came over from the DNA side."

Priya looked down at her paper for a long moment. "I have four of them."

"I had one. It's like the T is a stowaway."

The three of them worked through their sequences together after that, calling out letters, arguing briefly about whether guanine went with cytosine or the other way around, which was an argument that resolved itself the moment they realized it was symmetrical and therefore not an argument. Devon kept saying that if he had to choose, he would rather be graded on the DNA, since at least DNA kept its letters in one place, and Jessica told him that was exactly backwards, that the copying was the point, the whole reason any of it counted as a mechanism rather than a word game. Language, her philosophy teacher had said that morning, works because the sign stays put while the meaning moves. Here the letters had to move so the meaning could stay. She did not say this out loud. She thought it and then, because thinking it felt like showboating, she let it go and wrote U where U belonged.

The bell rang while Priya was still recopying her sequence, and Mr. Reyes came down the row collecting worksheets without looking at them, which meant the checking would happen later, elsewhere, by someone they would never see. Jessica handed hers over with the corner folded where she had pressed too hard.

"Read the board on your way out," Reyes said. "Homework's changed."

She looked. The assignment now read: explain, in one paragraph, what you would tell someone who insisted RNA and DNA were the same molecule. Devon groaned beside her.

"Great," he said. "Now we have to explain the thing we just barely stopped getting wrong."

"We're the experts," Jessica said, and swung her bag over her shoulder. "We know exactly which mistakes get made."

The tournament had thirty-two schools in it and one empty chorus room behind the cafeteria, and Mya had been promised both. Her debate rounds were on the second floor, the one-act rehearsals were wherever she could find walls, and her partner, Dev, had handed her a battered binder before the bus left with the words "you're the director now" and an expression that suggested he had just converted his obligations into an annuity, paying himself out over time in free afternoons.

She had compartmentalized, in theory. Rounds until noon, rehearsal at noon, lunch eaten while walking. In practice the compartments leaked. During her second cross-examination she caught herself thinking about whether Jonah should enter left or right, and she asked a question about trade deficits that her opponent answered in a tone of genuine confusion, since it had nothing to do with her case.

At noon she herded four actors into the chorus room, where the risers made a shallow stage. They were doing the scene where the sister returns after seven years, and it kept going wrong in a way Mya couldn't name. Jonah, playing the brother, would cross toward Priya, playing the sister, and Priya would end up behind him, half invisible to the imaginary audience, her big line delivered to the back of his shoulder.

"Move when he moves," Mya said. "Just, like, drift."

Priya drifted. Jonah crossed faster. She ended up in the same pocket of invisibility, only now she looked like she was hiding on purpose, which was a different and worse choice.

"I feel like furniture," Priya said. "Furniture with lines."

Mya stood on a riser and looked at the shape they made, the two of them lumped on one side of the stage like a pile of coats. She had spent three years of debate learning that positioning was argument, that where you stood determined what the judges could see, and it occurred to her, slowly and with some embarrassment, that a stage worked the same way and nobody had ever needed to tell her. She got the binder out. Between a page on "spike marks" and a page on "cheating out" there was a paragraph with a word underlined twice in pencil by some previous director whose name was water-damaged into illegibility.

"It's called countering," Mya said. "When one actor crosses, the other one shifts to balance the stage, so the audience can still see both."

"Shift where?" Jonah asked.

"Wherever isn't behind you. Opposite direction, kind of."

They ran it again. Jonah crossed toward Priya with his speech about the money, and Priya took two quiet steps downstage and to the side, and suddenly there were two people on the stage instead of one person and a shadow. The line she'd been muffling all morning landed flat and clean: "You can't buy back a year, Marcus." Mya, standing on the riser with her phone out to time the scene, forgot to start the timer.

She texted Dev between rounds, sitting on the floor outside the auditorium with her laptop open to a case she was supposed to be reordering.

The countering thing worked. Priya stopped being a coat rack. Also I think I'm going to lose round three, I spent all of prep writing "DOWNSTAGE LEFT" on notecards. Do not say I told you so. You may think it very loudly.

His reply came during her opponent's first speech, a single thumbs-up, which she felt was obdurate in its cheerfulness, though she had to admit she'd trained him to be that way about her.

In round four she argued that certainty was a luxury of people who hadn't read the evidence, and she meant it more than she usually did. Directing had made debate feel suddenly transparent, both of them just ways of deciding where people should stand so the audience could see them. But that wasn't quite right either, and she couldn't have said which one had gotten clearer. She won the round on a 2-1 and the judge's reason made sense only in the way that judges' reasons sometimes did.

The final rehearsal was at five, in the actual black box theater, borrowed for twenty minutes because a teacher had liked her when she'd asked nicely. The actors ran the scene with the real lights, and Priya's counter was so smooth now that Mya almost didn't see it happen, Jonah crossing, Priya answering, the two of them keeping the stage balanced between them like a scale that wanted to stay level.

When they finished, nobody said anything for a second. Priya was still standing in her spot, breathing like someone who'd just landed something, and Jonah was looking at Mya with his eyebrows up, waiting.

"Once more," Mya said, and climbed off the stage to watch from the back of the house, where the audience would be.

The skate park sat behind the middle school like a bowl carved out of the afternoon, and James had been standing at the top of the quarter pipe for ten minutes without dropping in. He was not afraid of the drop itself. What bothered him was his physics worksheet, folded into his back pocket, which he had taken out four times already. His tutor had said the words to him last night, separate the velocity into components, and James had nodded the way you nod when the words mean nothing yet. Below him, his friend Ravi was carving the shallow end with his arms loose, tracing long curves on the concrete, and James watched the board leave the coping and fall, and fall, and land, and thought: everything here is falling. The only question is what it does while it falls.

"Are you skating or doing your taxes?" Ravi called up.

"Homework," James said. He sat down on the coping and unfolded the worksheet against his knee. A ball launched at twelve meters per second at thirty degrees, and the problem wanted the range. "I keep setting it up as one motion. One speed, one angle, one straight push. And I keep getting answers that are wrong."

Ravi skated over, kicked his board up into his hand, and climbed the ramp to sit beside him. He read the problem upside down. "So split it."

"I don't know what that means." James said it flatly, without embarrassment, because Ravi had watched him fail a math test in eighth grade and had lent him notes ever since. "He said something about the horizontal part and the vertical part being separate. I wrote it down and then I lost the sentence."

Below them the drinking fountain by the chain-link fence was running, because some kid had jammed the button with a pebble, and the water rose in a silver rope and bent over itself and fell. Ravi noticed it first. He pointed with his chin. "Doesn't that look like your graph?"

It did, in a way James could not immediately name. He stared at the water while it held its shape, the same shape, rising less and less steeply, hanging for an instant, then steepening downward, and the word arrived before the reasoning did: parabola. The graph from algebra class, y equals x squared, drawn in water. He took out his phone and searched, mostly to prove himself wrong.

Ravi leaned over to read the screen while the wheels of somebody's board rattled across the far side of the bowl. He read aloud, half to himself, the way he read everything. "Galileo showed that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola. Two New Sciences, published in 1638." He scrolled. "That's a real book. He was old when he wrote it." It seemed strange to Ravi that a shape could have a lineage, that some old man watching cannonballs had handed this curve down through almost four centuries to a kid on a quarter pipe, and he said so, and James only half heard him.

Because something had come apart in James's mind, the way the water had come apart in the air, into a sideways piece and a falling piece. The horizontal motion had no reason to change; nothing pushed against it if you ignored the air, which felt like cheating until he considered that the air was extrinsic, a local annoyance, not part of what the ball was doing. The vertical motion was just falling, the falling he already knew. Two clean straight things crossed over each other, and where they crossed, the curve appeared, the same curve as the fountain. He took out a pencil, drew the axes on the back of the worksheet, split twelve into its sideways part and its upward part, and the numbers came out obedient for the first time all week. He did not trust it entirely. He still did not understand why the world would keep those two motions separate, only that it seemed to, and that a man dead for centuries had said it did.

"Drop in with me," Ravi said, standing, stamping his board down onto the coping beside James's sneakers. "Then throw something."

James folded the worksheet into his pocket and set his board on the metal edge. He looked down the curve of the ramp, at the water still arcing silver over the drain across the park, and wondered whether he would feel the separation, the sideways push and the fall, or whether it would only ever be one motion from inside. He pushed off.

Ravi watched him drop in, low and committed, and when James shot out the far side and flung the board up into the air, both of them tracked it against the sky.

"Parabola," Ravi called out, catching it as it came down.

The basement smelled like dryer sheets and cold pizza, and Marcus's laptop sat open on the pool table because the actual desk was buried under model airplane parts. Jaxon pulled a folding chair up beside him and unfolded his notebook to the page where he'd copied the assignment: build a class in Java, keep the fields private, write getter methods, write tests. He had wanted this for weeks, ever since Marcus had shown him a program that tracked every guitar pedal he owned, and Jaxon had understood, with a small clean shock, that software was something a person could just make.

"Private fields first," Marcus said, tapping the screen. "That's the whole religion of it. Nobody reaches in and grabs your data. They have to knock." He typed `private String playerName;` and `private int score;` and then, beneath them, the getters, small polite doors into the class: `public String getPlayerName() { return playerName; }`. Jaxon copied the shape of it into his notebook, not the words exactly but the architecture, the idea that a thing could hold its facts close and still let you look.

He built his own class on the second laptop, a `Song` class, because he wanted a program that remembered what he'd been learning on guitar. Title and artist private, getters below, and then a test that created a `Song`, called the getters, and checked what came back. It ran. Green bar. He leaned back and let himself feel it for exactly four seconds before Marcus said, "Now make it useful. Add a constructor so you can't build a song with nothing in it."

So Jaxon wrote `public Song(String title, String artist)` and set the fields inside it, and then ran the test again, and the green bar was gone. The compiler refused to compile his old test, and the error pointed at the line where the test did `new Song()`, empty parentheses, no arguments, and said it couldn't find that constructor. Jaxon read it three times. "I didn't delete anything," he said. "It's right there. The class. I just added a constructor."

"Then it should work," Marcus said, in the tone of somebody reciting a maxim he didn't fully trust: when in doubt, blame the machine. He took the laptop, scrolled, gave it back. "Nope, that's real."

Jaxon sat with it. Before he'd written any constructor, `new Song()` had worked; he had run that test himself, watched it pass. After he added one constructor with parameters, the empty version stopped existing. He said it out loud slowly, testing it: "If a class defines no constructor at all, the compiler adds a default no-argument one. But once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added." It was like the compiler had been holding the door open for him out of courtesy, and the moment he built his own door, courtesy withdrew. He wasn't sure yet whether that felt like a trap or like being taken seriously.

"Message Deja," Marcus said. "She broke her whole project over this last month and she'll pretend she didn't." Jaxon texted her, and while they waited he fixed the test the honest way, giving `new Song()` real arguments, real title, real artist. His phone buzzed with her reply: "lol welcome. my old test broke the second i added a constructor with parameters. i sat there for an hour thinking my laptop was moribund. it was fine. i was the problem. you have to write the no-arg one yourself now if you still want it." Jaxon read it twice, then typed back, "But you don't have to want it. That's the part I like."

Because he did like it, and he could admit that it was a strange thing to like. His father's whole approach to problems was to get in there and fix them with his hands, wires and wrenches, no layers between you and the thing; Marcus's approach was to paste the error into a search box and interpolate an answer from whatever strangers had said. Jaxon was discovering he wanted both, the grease-under-the-fingernails reading of the error line by line and the borrowed experience of somebody who'd already been stuck here. Maybe a considered position was just knowing when to do which, though he was honest enough with himself not to be sure he'd know when that was.

He ran the test again. Green bar. Marcus peered over, mock solemn, and said, "Your getters work. Your fields are locked up like a museum. I'm proud of you and I want royalties." Jaxon laughed and started typing a second test, because one green bar was a fact and two was starting to be a pattern, and at the top of the file he wrote a comment for his future self: this is the one that bit you.

The paper was due in nine days, and Ava had spread it across her grandmother's dining room table like a field surgeon laying out instruments: the draft, the sources, the teacher's comments sheet with its red marginalia, and her laptop balanced on a stack of National Geographics from 1984. Mrs. Perrine had written "Footnotes need work. See me" on page six, which was the kind of note that cauterized all her confidence in a single stroke, leaving nothing but the sore awareness that she did not know what she didn't know.

"You're biting that pencil like it owes you money," her grandmother said, setting down a mug of tea that Ava hadn't asked for and would drink anyway.

"It's the citations. She marked half of them wrong and I don't know why. I did exactly what the guide in the library said."

Her grandmother disappeared into the study and returned cradling a fat orange book with a cracked spine, dust fanning off it in the lamplight. "Your grandfather's. Chicago Manual of Style. He footnoted everything, even letters to the editor. Swore by it." She set it down with the ceremony of someone delivering a family relic, and Ava, charmed despite herself, opened it to the chapter on notes.

There it was, an example with the word ibid. marching down the page after a full citation, ibid., ibid., ibid., a little stutter of Latin that looked efficient and scholarly and exactly like what she had done. She had used it eleven times in her paper on the Peloponnesian War, because it saved her typing Thucydides over and over, and because it looked the way footnotes were supposed to look, the way they looked in her grandfather's generation.

"Grandpa used this?" she asked.

"Underlined the whole section. He said an oligarchy of editors in Chicago decided how the rest of us should cite, and he'd be damned if he'd argue with them." Her grandmother laughed at the memory, then squinted at the page. "Is that what's wrong? You didn't use the ibid.?"

"I did use it. That might be what's wrong."

She pulled the laptop closer and searched, half to defend herself and half to prove the manual right, because it would have been a nice thing, to have inherited a correct grandfather. What she found instead sat there on the screen while her grandmother read over her shoulder. The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, had begun discouraging ibid. in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title. She read it twice, and something in her chest performed a small, complicated maneuver that was half relief and half loss.

"So my way is outdated," she said slowly. "Not wrong, exactly. Outdated."

"Seventeen editions," her grandmother said. "That book of his is the fourteenth." She touched the orange spine the way you'd touch a photograph of someone gone. "He'd have called that specious, you know. Changing a perfectly good Latin word because some committee got restless. He liked things that stayed put."

Ava laughed, a real one that surprised her. "He sounds like half the guys in Thucydides, honestly. Complaining that Athens isn't what it was while Athens sails off without them." She was already scrolling back through her draft, finding the eleven ibids., deciding which ones would become Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 3.82 and which ones could just go, because half of them, she could see now, had been propping up sentences she hadn't actually earned. That was the uncomfortable part. The ibids. had let her hide, a little, behind the look of rigor. Shortening each citation meant naming, every single time, exactly what she was leaning on.

She began to type. The room went quiet except for the keys and the tick of the kitchen clock, and after a while her grandmother pulled out the other chair and sat down across from her with a crossword, not helping, just present. Twice Ava started to ask whether she should really trust a 2017 rule over fifty years of her grandfather's practice, and twice she decided the question answered itself, which did not stop it from circling back. She kept working anyway. Certainty about the rule didn't require certainty about everything, and maybe, she thought, deleting the last ibid., that was the whole difference between a draft and an argument: you committed to what you could verify and you were honest about the rest.

"Tea's gone cold," her grandmother said around midnight, standing, collecting the mug. She paused at the door with the orange manual under her arm, and Ava looked up from her bibliography, twenty-three entries now, alphabetized, formatted, repeatable by anyone who cared to check.

"Keep the book anyway," her grandmother said. "The old rules are in there too, if you ever need to know how he thought."

Ava set it on the table beside her laptop, spine cracked to the chapter on notes, and went back to typing Thucydides one more time.

Andrew arrived at the community art studio on the first Tuesday of October with a cardboard box of drawings he had made over three years, and the box was heavier than it looked. He set it on the long table near the window, where the afternoon light fell across the scarred wood in pale rectangles, and began lifting out the pieces one at a time. There were charcoal hands, a watercolor of the drainage ditch behind his house, four pen-and-ink moths pinned to imagined boards. The studio smelled of turpentine and old coffee, and someone's radio was playing low in the back room.

The portfolio course met twice a week for six sessions, and the teacher, a quiet woman named Ruth who wore paint under her fingernails the way other people wore rings, had said on the first day that they would each build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme. Ten, she had repeated, holding up both hands with the fingers spread. And with it, an artist's statement. Andrew had written the number in the margin of his notebook and underlined it twice.

His problem was the theme. Everything he had made was competent and nothing was connected. Priya, the girl across the table who worked in ink and spoke in short, definite sentences, suggested water, since two of his drawings involved rain. His mother, when he described the assignment at dinner, suggested family. Neither felt right, and he spent the second session pushing drawings around the table like a man trying to solve a puzzle with pieces from different boxes.

It was Priya who broke first. On the Thursday of the third week she slid a single sheet toward Ruth, a paragraph of careful cursive, and Ruth read it and passed it back with a small smile. "This is good," Ruth said, "but you keep calling yourself 'the artist.' The statement is written in the first person by the artist. Say 'I.'" Priya looked down at the page, at the phrase the artist chose to render, and began crossing out words with her pen. Andrew, watching from across the table, felt something shift in his understanding of the assignment, though he could not yet say what.

That night he sat at his desk at home and tried to write his own statement, and the same instinct took him. The artist explores themes of containment, he typed, and stopped. It sounded like a wall text from a museum, like a voice announcing him from a distance. He deleted it and tried again. I explore, he wrote, and the sentence immediately felt more exposed, more like a confession than a description. He closed the laptop and went to bed without finishing.

On Saturday he found his theme by accident. He had taken the bus to the studio early, before anyone else arrived, and was sorting through the box again when he noticed how many of his drawings were of things held inside other things: moths under glass, a fish in the drainage ditch's concrete channel, his grandmother's hands folded one inside the other in the last drawing he had made of her. He laid six pieces along the window ledge and saw the thread he had been sewing without knowing it. Containment, he wrote in his notebook. Places that hold things.

Ruth arrived while he was counting. "How many?" she asked, counting with her eyes. "Six that work," he said. "I need ten." She nodded and said the four he made next would be better than the six he already had, because now he would be making them on purpose. He thought about arguing, about defending the older pieces, but she was already moving on to the kiln room, and he let it go.

He worked through the next two sessions making four new pieces, and Priya stood over his shoulder once and said, "The moth one is scathing, in a quiet way." He wasn't sure that was what he meant, but he didn't dislike it. When Marcus, the oldest student in the class, told him the theme was brilliant in a voice that wanted complimenting back, Andrew only said thanks, because he had learned that year to recognize a sycophant and to give him nothing to feed on.

On the last Tuesday, Ruth read his statement aloud to herself while the class packed up. She paused at one line, where Andrew had written I am drawn to containers because I cannot decide whether they protect what is inside them or disenfranchise it from the world outside, and she read it twice. "That's the true sentence," she said. "The whole portfolio is the argument around that sentence, and you don't have to win it." Andrew looked at his ten pieces lined up on the wall, the moths and the ditch and his grandmother's folded hands, and then at the page in Ruth's hand where every sentence began with I.

He picked up his pencil and added, at the bottom of the statement, one more line: I still don't know. Then he carried the box to the window, where the light was already thinning, and began to photograph each piece in order.

The problem had followed Naomi home from robotics, and now it sat at the dinner table beside her, unnoticed by everyone else. Across the table her brother Theo was telling their parents about his group project, laughing a little as he described how his lab partner had mislabeled an entire data set and nobody had said anything until the grade came back. "We didn't want to make it weird," Theo said, spooning more rice. "So we all just let it ride."

Naomi put down her fork. "That's exactly what happened with us." She told them about Marisol, who had built the drive-train mount off spec twice, and how the whole team had praised her effort in the meeting afterward and said nothing about the spec. Then the mount failed the drop test on Thursday, in front of the judges, and Marisol had stood there red-faced while everyone pretended it was bad luck. "I said it was the plywood," Naomi said. "It wasn't the plywood."

Her mother tilted her head. "So why didn't anyone tell her?"

"Because she's my friend," Naomi said, and heard how thin it sounded the moment she said it. "Because she works harder than anyone and it felt like kicking her."

Theo, who was seventeen minutes older than Naomi and never let her forget it, was quiet for once. He pushed edamame around his plate. Their father launched into one of his garrulous stories about a colleague who had been "brutally honest" at work and made enemies for a decade, a story that circled the airport without landing, and Naomi stopped listening halfway through. She was thinking about Priya, the team captain, who had stayed after the meeting last week and said, quietly, "Somebody has to talk to her before regionals," and then looked at Naomi and left it there.

After dinner she went up to her room and called Priya. "I'll do it," Naomi said. "But I don't know how to say it without it being either nothing or cruel." Priya said she'd been reading something her mom left on the coffee table, a book from 2017 called Radical Candor, and that the whole idea was that good feedback meant caring personally about someone and challenging them directly, both at once, not one or the other. "That's it," Naomi said slowly. "That's the part I kept missing. I thought I had to choose."

She thought about it while she drafted a message and deleted it, then drafted again. Her old instinct, the nice one, would have produced some version of "the mount was so close, you tried so hard," which would instantiate exactly the silence that had already cost them one competition. The other extreme, the one her father's colleague practiced, was just an insult wearing a virtue costume. Somewhere between silence and insult there was a narrow path, and she couldn't quite see it, only feel where it wasn't.

Saturday morning she found Marisol in the shop before anyone else arrived, already sanding the new mount. Naomi's hands were cold. "Can I show you something before you cut that?" She laid the old mount on the bench next to the drawings. "See where the holes are a quarter inch off the spec line? That's what failed Thursday. Not the plywood, like I said. I lied about that, and I'm sorry." Marisol's jaw went tight, and Naomi kept going because stopping now would be its own kind of lie. "I'm telling you because you're the best builder we have and we need you at regionals, and because I should have said something three weeks ago instead of letting you walk into the drop test."

Marisol looked at the holes for a long time. Then she picked up the drawing and held it against the failed mount, and Naomi watched her see it, the small drift she must have measured around without noticing. "Why didn't anyone say anything," Marisol said, not quite a question. "I don't know," Naomi said. "I think we thought we were being kind." Marisol snorted, and marked the drawing with a pencil, twice. "Okay," she said. "Next time tell me the day I do it, not the day it breaks."

They cut the new mount together, both of them checking the spec line out loud before each pass of the saw, an arrangement so obvious in hindsight that Naomi almost laughed. It wasn't fixed, exactly; she could still feel a thin place in the air between them, and she didn't know whether it would close or harden by regionals. But when Marisol clamped the piece down and said "measure it again, and I mean actually say the number this time," Naomi read the dial and said, "Quarter inch on the line," and Marisol nodded once, like it was a kind of thanks.

The branch on Carling Avenue had a shelf of deposit slips, a bowl of stale mints, and a desk at the back where Landon sat every Tuesday and Thursday after school, opening mail for the assistant manager and shredding what she told him to shred. He had taken the placement through his school's co-op program because his mother said a bank would look better on a university application than the grocery store, though the work itself mostly involved a letter opener. On the Thursday in question he had spread two leases across the desk beside the shredder, and he was reading them for the third time.

The first lease was for a one-bedroom above a hardware store on Bank Street. Rent was fourteen hundred a month, and the tenant paid electricity and heat separately. The second was a basement unit near Lansdowne, fifteen hundred and sixty, with heat included but electricity and water billed to the tenant. His friend Dev wanted him to decide by Saturday, because Dev's cousin had already offered to drive the boxes.

"Those aren't bank documents," said Mrs. Okonjo, passing with a stack of cheques.

"They're mine," Landon said. "Sort of. Mine and Dev's."

She looked at the pages for a moment, said "carry on," and continued toward the vault.

Landon made a column on the back of an envelope. He wrote the fourteen hundred, then underneath it the words hydro, heat, water, each with a blank. The landlord above the hardware store had sent him a note saying the one-year term would begin June first and that they should come in Friday to sign. There was something in the landlord's tone, a briskness, that made Landon feel the deadline was firmer than it probably was. His grandfather would have called the tone a peccadillo, a small fault hardly worth naming, and would have said so while reaching for a coffee.

His grandfather did in fact arrive at eleven, as he did most Thursdays, to deposit the proceeds of a small business repairing violins. He was a compact man who wore the same grey jacket in all seasons and who regarded the bank as a place one visited with the same regularity as a barbershop. He took a number even though Landon was visibly alone at the desk.

"Grandpa," Landon said, "do you know anything about leases?"

"I know mine." His grandfather lowered himself into the chair across the desk. "Twelve years in the same apartment on Byron. The term ended years ago and I never signed another thing."

"You never signed? Aren't you, like, squatting?"

"I'm a tenant, not a squatter. In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, you don't have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month on the same terms, automatically." He said it the way he said most things, as though reporting the weather.

Landon wrote this down on the envelope, under the column of blanks. "So the landlord can't just kick you out for not signing?"

"I said it continues. Don't add to what I said."

Mrs. Okonjo called a number, and a woman with a stroller went forward. Landon looked at the hardware store lease again. Section 4 gave the term as one year, beginning June first. If the term simply ended and the tenancy carried on, then the pressure he had felt about Friday was not pressure at all, or was pressure of a different kind, the kind that worked only on people who hadn't asked. He did not say this aloud, because saying it aloud would have transmuted a hunch into a plan, and he wasn't sure yet it was a plan.

"Which one are you leaning toward?" his grandfather asked, nodding at the pages.

"I don't know. The cheaper one isn't cheaper if the utilities are huge, and I can't find out what the utilities are without living there."

"Estimate."

"That's not knowing."

"Nothing is knowing. You repair a crack in a violin belly knowing the wood will move anyway. You still glue it."

His number was called. He stood, buttoned the grey jacket, and added, "Bring the numbers to Sunday dinner. Your aunt moved apartments four times; she made every mistake available." Then he went to the counter and counted out his cheques.

Landon spent his lunch break at the desk with the envelope. He found an old hydro bill in his email from his mother's house and scaled it for one bedroom instead of four: maybe sixty a month for electricity. Heat was harder, since the hardware store unit had baseboard heaters and the basement was partly underground. He called the utility from the branch phone, and a recorded voice gave him an average winter cost for a similar unit, which he wrote down and then rounded up, because averages were made of people who had survived. Water, the city website said, ran about forty. He added the column twice. The Bank Street unit came to roughly sixteen eighty a month all in. The basement, even with heat included, came to about the same, within twenty dollars either way, depending on a winter he could not predict.

The margin was so small that the choice stopped being about money and became about the lease terms themselves, and about which landlord had tried to make him feel a deadline that the law did not require him to feel. That was a reason, but it was not a clean one, and he could admit that his own certainty had shifted twice since morning, once when his grandfather spoke and once when the numbers came out even. Some things would stay uncertain: the winter, the neighbours, whether Dev would actually help carry boxes. He folded the two leases together, put them in his backpack, and left the envelope with the arithmetic on it squared on the desk.

On his way out he passed the phones for sale on the wall by the door. He called the hardware store landlord, and a man answered on the second ring.
