By closing time she had two openings written, one for each side, and both of them were good. That was the part she hadn't expected, that she could hold both and not feel split down the middle. She believed the student had the better case. She also believed a principal standing in a hallway at 7:40 in the morning, watching a disruption build, had a real problem that the law hadn't fully solved, and she couldn't say where the line fell between them. She could only say where it had fallen once, in 1969, by a vote of 7-2, and that the line had been argued about every year since.

On the night of the competition, the courtroom was fuller than she'd expected, and the panel turned out to be three attorneys and a sitting judge with a reputation for being merciless. Laura argued the student's side first, and the Tinker line landed exactly the way she'd practiced, the schoolhouse gate, the 7-2 ruling, constitutional rights that students carry with them through the door, and she watched one of the attorneys nod.

Then she switched to the school's side, took a breath, and began the argument she had built with Marcus at the library table, and somewhere in the middle of the captive-audience point she realized she was winning, genuinely winning, panel leaning forward, judge's pen moving.

When the scores came back, the student side had taken second. The school's side, the one she'd fought against for weeks, had taken first.

Her mother found her afterward by the water fountain. "So which one did you actually believe?" she asked.

Laura looked past her at the judge gathering his papers, and said, "Ask me tomorrow."

The retake notice arrived on a Tuesday, folded into Eva's locker like a threat. Sixty-one percent. She had one week to learn transcription and translation properly, or the biology mark would follow her into her college applications the way a smell follows a coat.

Her uncle's farm was forty minutes away by the school's activity bus, and her cousin Daisy, twelve, lived there with a workbook full of questions Daisy claimed were pointless. Eva's mother had suggested the visit before the retake notice existed, and now Eva packed her biology text along with the sleeping bag, thinking she could read in the evenings. She read the same paragraph four times on the bus and could not have repeated it after the fourth.

The paragraph was the problem. It described DNA being copied into RNA and RNA being turned into protein, and it used eleven terms per sentence, each one leaning on the others like drunks at a bus stop. She understood, in a vague way, that there was a cell and that something happened inside it. Beyond that, nothing. On Wednesday she sat on the farmhouse porch with the book open and her highlighter dying, and Daisy came out eating toast.

"You look like the toast," Daisy said, sitting down on the step.

"Thanks."

"What's that?"

"A book that hates me."

Daisy leaned over. There was a diagram, all curling lines and arrows, and Eva realized she could not even say which part was which. She snapped the book shut, which augured nothing good for the evening.

Thursday morning they were in the milking parlour waiting for Daisy's father, and Daisy was drawing on the concrete floor with a piece of chalk she kept in her jacket for reasons she did not explain. Eva, without planning to, asked whether Daisy knew why the cows were brown.

"Genes," Daisy said promptly. "It's in their, the thing. The DNA."

"Where is the DNA?"

Daisy pointed at a cow, generally. Eva looked at the cow, which stood chewing, and thought about her own cells, and thought about the fact that the instructions were all shut away in there, in the middle, in some protected inner room, and that the cow was brown anyway, out here, in its hair and its skin and its milk. The instructions never left the room. Something else must do the travelling.

"Okay," Eva said. "Watch." She took the chalk. "Say this square is the cell. And this little circle in the middle, that's where the DNA lives. The plans for brown, everything, all in there. Does the DNA come out here to the hair to tell it what to do?"

Daisy considered. "It'd get wrecked. It's the only copy, right? You don't send your only copy out in the rain."

Eva's hand stopped. Something in her chest went quiet and then loud. "Right," she said. "You don't send the original. You make a working copy."

She drew an arrow from the circle toward the edge of the square. On Friday she verified it against the book and found that her guess had the shape of the truth and the details wrong. The cell did make a working copy, and the copy was called messenger RNA. An enzyme did the copying. It was called RNA polymerase, and it read one strand of the DNA, and built a matching strand of messenger RNA to match it, and the messenger RNA carried the gene's instructions out, away from the original, toward whatever needed building. The copy then got read, three letters at a time, and each three-letter group told the cell which amino acid to add next, and the chain of amino acids folded up into a protein, and the protein did the actual work of being brown, or digesting milk, or anything else. Eva wrote none of this down the first time. She just sat with it.

She did write it down, later, in the hayloft, on the back of a feed invoice, in her own words, and then she made Daisy repeat it back, and Daisy, bored, made it a song. "Polymerase, polymerase, reads one strand," Daisy sang, tunelessly, to a cow named Verity, "builds the copy with its hands." The hands part was a travesty of the actual mechanism, and Eva said so, and Daisy sang the verse again, louder, directed now at Eva personally, and the cow swung its head toward them as if to register a complaint.

At the retake on Monday, Eva drew the square and the circle and the arrow in the margin before answering a single question, the way a pianist touches middle C. She filled nine pages. Some of it, she knew when she handed it in, was probably still wrong, probably in the parts about how the code was read, which she could describe but had never quite reconciled with how a cell could possibly know where to start. She was honest on the last page, in a sentence she added and then almost crossed out: that she could follow the process step by step and still could not say she understood it, only that she could now explain it.

She got an eighty-four. She texted Daisy a photograph of the mark, and Daisy texted back a voice note, four seconds long, of the song.

The fluorescent lights above aisle six made everything look slightly ill, the oranges especially, and Nevaeh stood under them with two folded lease agreements in the front pocket of her hoodie, waiting for her mother to finish arguing with the coupon machine. The machine had eaten another quarter. This was the third time. Her mother slapped its side with the flat of her hand the way she slapped the dryer at home, and Nevaeh looked away, because looking away was easier than watching.

The leases belonged to her brother, Dorian, who was twenty and moving out of Aunt Cece's basement in eleven days. But Dorian worked nights stocking the same warehouse where their mother worked days, and he had handed the papers to Nevaeh at breakfast with a shrug that meant you do the math, you're the smart one. She had accepted the shrug the way she accepted most things from Dorian, silently, and then spent two evenings with a calculator and a growing suspicion that neither apartment was possible.

The first apartment, on Peralta Street, rented for nine hundred and forty a month, utilities not included. The second, out past the community college, was eleven hundred and twenty, utilities included. It had taken her most of one evening just to find out what utilities meant in practice, because the Peralta landlord's listing said "tenant pays all utilities," which turned out to mean electric, gas, water, trash, and internet, each billed separately, each with its own deposit. She had called the water company pretending to be a tenant and written the numbers on the back of a receipt.

At the store she pushed the cart while her mother dropped in the cheap peanut butter, the dented cans, the bread that was two days from expiring and therefore forty percent off. Nevaeh had been reading the backs of her mother's choices for years, the way other kids read cereal boxes, and she could metabolize a unit price in seconds now, cost per ounce, cost per sheet, cost per calorie. It was the same skill, she realized, standing in front of the rice, that she was applying to the apartments. What she had never done was apply it to their own household, and the realization had a seismic quality, a slow shifting under what she had assumed was solid ground.

"You're quiet," her mother said at the meat counter, where she bought one package of chicken thighs and put back a second.

"I'm doing Dorian's math. The apartments."

Her mother made a sound that could have meant anything. Nevaeh laid it out anyway, in the checkout line, on top of the moving belt. Peralta came to roughly eleven hundred a month once she added the utility estimates. The other place was eleven twenty flat. Nearly identical. "So it's not even a choice," she said. "The second one's better. Everything's included, nothing can jump up on him."

Her mother fed the coupon machine one last quarter, won, and exhaled. "What does he make? At the warehouse."

"About nineteen hundred a month. If the hours hold."

Her mother did not say anything for the length of the belt, the scanner beeping, the total climbing. Then she said, "There's a word for that, you know. More than thirty percent of income on housing. They call it cost-burdened. It's a government thing. Your aunt told me when we were looking for this place." She took the bags in both arms. "He'd be paying more than half."

Nevaeh stood there while the numbers rearranged themselves. She had been comparing the two leases as though they were two brands of rice, cheaper against cheaper, but the real comparison was between either lease and her brother's paycheck, and on that scale both failed, badly, identically. Sixty percent. She said the percentage out loud in the parking lot, holding the cart while her mother loaded the trunk, and heard how it sounded, and stopped saying it.

In the car, the phonetics of it stayed with her, the word her mother had used, burden, how blunt it was, no softer syllable in it anywhere. She watched the store shrink in the side mirror and understood something she could not yet put into a sentence: that she had learned to compare two things and discovered that the comparison was beside the point. Dorian needed a third option that did not exist in his folder, or a raise, or a roommate, and she did not know how to calculate any of those. At home she found him awake in the kitchen, and she put both leases on the table in front of him, and said, "Before you sign either one, sit down with me and bring your last three pay stubs."

The laundromat on Marsh Lane had a broken change machine and a bulletin board layered so thick with old flyers that archaeology students could probably have dated it, and Naomi had claimed the folding table as her desk because home was too loud and the library closed at nine. Two leases lay side by side among the warm towels: the studio above the chip shop, and the one-bedroom out past the canal with a landlord named Terence who wrote in green ink. She was seventeen, starting at Sheffield in September, and her mother had said, in the tone she reserved for unwelcome news, that Naomi could sign but she would be the one paying if it went wrong. So the numbers had to be right.

The dryer buzzed. She fished out her sheets, folded them badly, and went back to the studio's page of "additional costs": water included, electricity capped at forty a month, internet not provided, council tax exempt for full-time students but only if she sent the exemption form, which the lease mentioned once, in a footnote, as if embarrassed by it. The one-bedroom out past the canal was cheaper by twenty-five a month on rent, but electricity was unmetered and shared, whatever that meant, and there was a "communal maintenance contribution" of fifteen pounds that Terence had underlined in green ink like it was a treat.

A woman came in with a duvet stuffed into a pillowcase, nodded at the table of paper, and said, "Doing your homework in here takes commitment."

"Comparing flats," Naomi said. "I'm trying to work out which one actually costs less, which turns out to be a scam designed by whoever invented utilities."

The woman laughed and fed coins into the washer. "My daughter just signed a lease in Leeds. Landlord wanted a fortune up front."

That word, up front, sat in Naomi's head while the drums turned. Because Terence's lease had a deposit line too, and she'd been so circumspect about the monthly figures that she hadn't done the one-time ones. Terence wanted eleven hundred and forty. The chip shop studio wanted only five hundred and ten, which she'd thought meant the chip shop landlord was nicer, or that Terence's flat was more precious somehow.

She flipped to the front page of Terence's lease. Rent: one hundred and ninety a week. She did what she'd learned to do with weekly rents, multiplied by fifty-two, divided by twelve, got around eight hundred and twenty a month, and wrote it down. Then she sat with the deposit figure and the weekly figure and thought about her economics teacher, who liked to say that a rule you can't test is just an opinion. There was a rule about deposits, she was almost sure, something her cousin had mentioned at Christmas over the pudding. She looked it up on her phone with one bar of signal: in England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is fifty thousand or more.

Terence's annual rent was well under fifty thousand, so the cap was five weeks. Five times one hundred and ninety was nine hundred and fifty. Terence wanted eleven hundred and forty, which was six weeks exactly, as if he'd looked at a rule meant for much richer flats and decided it suited his. Or as if he'd never read past the first number. She couldn't know which, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that the difference between greedy and lazy mattered to her more than it probably should.

When the woman came back for her duvet, Naomi showed her the arithmetic, weeks times rent, cap of five under fifty thousand, six at fifty thousand or more. "So he's a hundred and ninety over," she said, "if I've got this right. Which I might not."

"Message him," the woman said, hoisting the pillowcase. "The worst he says is no."

Naomi texted Terence, circumspect even in typing, deleting the word "illegal" and settling on "I believe the deposit is capped at five weeks for this rent." Then she did the true totals on the back of a warm pillowcase tag, because the dryer had eaten her last clean page. The chip shop studio came to more each month once electricity was counted; the canal flat was cheaper to live in but demanded more to enter, even corrected. Her mother would predicate the whole decision on the monthly figure, because her mother counted what recurred; Naomi found she was starting to count what recurred too, and it felt like a small death of something she couldn't name.

The phone buzzed against the table. Terence, in green-ink punctuation: "Fine. 950. View it Saturday?" She looked at the two leases, the chip shop grease she could already smell through the page, the canal she'd never walked along, and did not answer yet. She put the last towel in the basket, still warm, and carried everything out into the dark.

Ava was hiding in the surgery prep room again, flashcards fanned across the counter beside a bottle of betadine, when Dr. Okafor's dog started coding in kennel four. She was supposed to be studying for her cell bio placement exam, the one that would decide whether she could skip the intro lecture and take the smaller seminar in her first semester, and instead she was listening to the clock by the gurney and mouthing the steps of cellular respiration like a prayer she half remembered. Glycolysis. The link reaction. The citric acid cycle. Then the part she could never keep straight, the electron transport chain, which her textbook had drawn as a row of lumps in a membrane like stones in a stream.

The dog was old, a settershepherd mix named Biscuit with a heart that had been failing since spring, and the technicians moved around Ava as though she were a piece of equipment. She watched them bag him, watched the monitor stutter, and she thought about her father, who had sat in this same clinic two years ago with their cat Mango's carrier on his knees while the vet explained what a peaceful end looked like. Ava had been sixteen then, and she had said yes to the euthanasia without letting her father finish the sentence, because she could not stand the silence where the explanation was supposed to go. She had wondered since whether she'd agreed too fast, whether deciding quickly was mercy or just cowardice wearing mercy's coat.

"Glucose to pyruvate," she whispered, shuffling cards. "Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA." One of the techs, Marisol, backed through the door with a bag of fluids and said, "If you're going to mutter, mutter something useful, like my ex-husband's address." Ava laughed, and the laugh loosened something, and she said the next step out loud: electrons.

Here was her problem, the actual problem, the one underneath the exam. Her textbook and her flashcards disagreed. The cards, which she'd bought secondhand from a girl in a cosmopolitan study group who had covered them in annotations, said the oxygen you breathed became energy. The book said no such thing. It said the oxygen sat at the end of the electron transport chain, in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and accepted electrons, and combined with protons, and became water. Ava had read that sentence nine times. It refused to become intuitive. Energy felt like fire, like fuel burning; water felt like a byproduct, something you expelled. The two frameworks sat in her like two people at a party pretending not to know each other.

She had tried to force it earlier that week by transliterating her notes into what she called "kitchen language": glucose was the dough, ATP was the finished bread, the mitochondria were the oven. That worked until she hit oxygen, because oxygen wasn't an ingredient you could taste in the bread; it was something about the oven itself, the draft, the flame under the coils. She'd gotten tangled and angry and had written, in the margin, "ASK SOMEONE WHO ISN'T MAKING THIS UP." But there was no one to ask. Her mother was a nurse who understood patients, not membranes. Her father still couldn't say the word euthanasia out loud.

In kennel four, the monitor steadied. Biscuit was going to live through the afternoon at least, and Dr. Okafor came out pulling off her gloves and saw the flashcards and said, "Electron transport chain? God, I haven't thought about that since 1994." She leaned on the counter, tired in a satisfied way, and looked at Ava's margin note and raised an eyebrow.

Ava explained, feeling like a fraud, that she couldn't make the oxygen make sense, that her cards said oxygen became energy and the book said something about water. Dr. Okafor did not lecture. She only tapped Biscuit's chart, where a fluid bag was noted, where a nasal cannula had been noted, and said, "What's in that fluid bag, mostly?"

"Water," Ava said.

"And what was on his face?"

"Oxygen."

Dr. Okafor went back to her patient, and Ava stood there with her mouth slightly open, because she could see it suddenly, not as a diagram but as a fact inside a body: the oxygen Biscuit had breathed in had ended up as water inside him, inside his cells, in the inner mitochondrial membrane where the chain ended and the oxygen took the electrons and took the protons and made water. The oxygen she herself was breathing, the oxygen her father had breathed in the waiting room while Mango's heart slowed, all of it destined for the same quiet conversion. It was not fuel. It was a place where something was received. She did not yet fully understand the difference between those two ideas, but she understood that the difference mattered, and she wrote on a fresh card, in her own handwriting this time, "O2 is the final electron acceptor. It combines with H+ to form water. Breathe in, become part of yourself."

She thought about enthalpy for half a second, the word from her chemistry teacher, energy contained and released, and about whether her quick yes two years ago had released something for her father or only contained it. She could not decide, and she noticed that she did not need to decide tonight, that some judgments could be carried like flashcards in a back pocket, worn soft from handling, answers still pending. She squared the deck, put it in her scrubs, and went to help Marisol carry Biscuit, breathing and heavy and wet-nosed, out to the car.

The smell of the clinic was antiseptic underneath and dog on top, and Alexis had stopped noticing either by her second Saturday of volunteering. What she noticed now was the waiting room's plastic chairs, where she had spread her biology notes across three of them, and the diagram of a mitochondrion she had drawn twice already because the first one looked like a jelly bean with regrets.

"You're off duty until the Pattersons get here," said Rosa, the technician with the gray braid, passing through with a stack of towels. "So be off duty somewhere less visible."

Alexis gathered her things into the exam room where the kennels were, where it was warm and the beagles snored in stacked cages. Her test was Monday. Cellular respiration, glycolysis to ATP, the whole winding road of it, and she still could not keep the order straight. Last night the group chat had collapsed into an argument. Devon insisted the first carbon dioxide came out of the Krebs cycle. Priya said no, it was earlier, it was when pyruvate got processed, though she couldn't say where that happened, and Devon had typed three laughing emojis and the word "guessing," which Priya did not deserve. Priya had been the one who stayed late after the last test to help Alexis with enzymes, and Alexis had watched her get vilified in the chat for a half-remembered answer, and said nothing. She had typed "lol" and closed the app. That was Friday. It sat in her like a swallowed stone.

She read the chapter again, slowly this time, the way Priya read, one finger under each line. Glycolysis happened in the cytoplasm, outside, and it split glucose into two pyruvates, and no carbon dioxide left anything. That much she was sure of. So Devon's claim depended on the Krebs cycle being the first place carbon left the molecule. She turned the page.

The beagle in cage four lifted its head, yawned, and settled again, phlegmatic about everything, including its overnight stay. Down the hall a door opened, and Rosa's voice rose with it, then another voice, higher, cracked at the edges.

"His name is Biscuit," the woman was saying when Alexis leaned out. "He's breathing funny. He was fine this morning."

Rosa took the little dog, a dachshund with a barrel chest and rapid, shallow breaths, and carried him past. Alexis caught the vet, Dr. Okafor, already in scrubs though it was her day off, and then the door of the back room swung shut and there was nothing to do but go back to her chair. Her phone buzzed. Priya: did you figure out the co2 thing? devon is still being devon.

She typed and deleted three replies. She didn't want to answer until she was sure, and she was aware that this was a decision too, that waiting could look like loyalty or like cowardice depending on how the answer landed. She went back to the diagram.

The chapter moved the pyruvate out of the cytoplasm and into the mitochondrion, into the matrix, which she made herself label on her drawing, the innermost space, past both membranes. And there it was, a sentence she must have skimmed three times without seeing: in the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide. Before the Krebs cycle ever began. Before Devon's answer. She read it again, then a third time, then looked up Krebs in the index just to confirm the order of operations, that the cycle took acetyl-CoA as its starting material, which meant the conversion had to come first, which meant Priya was right and had been right while being laughed at.

"In the mitochondrial matrix," she said out loud, to the beagle, to the warm room. "Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, and one carbon dioxide comes off right there."

The beagle thumped its tail once against the cage floor, which she chose to take as corroboration.

She thought about how sure Devon had sounded. That was the thing about him, the erudition was real, mostly, but the confidence ran ahead of it, and the rest of them followed the confidence. She had followed it herself, on the enzymes question, and had gotten it wrong on paper and worse than wrong in the chat. She pulled the phone toward her and then pushed it back, because there was still the question of how to say it. Not whether to say it. She'd settled that, or mostly settled it; the part she hadn't settled was whether she was doing this for Priya or for the pleasure of being right at Devon's expense, and she suspected it was some of each and that the mixture mattered.

The back-room door opened. Rosa came out with her braid coming loose and her face tired in a way Alexis hadn't seen on her before. "The dog's staying," she said. "Oxygen cage, overnight watch. He's stable."

"What was wrong with him?" Alexis asked.

Rosa rubbed the back of her neck. "We'll know more after bloodwork. Right now it's breathing and watching." She looked at the notes spread across the chair, the jelly bean mitochondrion, the arrows. "Any of that make sense yet?"

"Part of it," Alexis said. "The part where the cell breaks things down and gets energy back out. It's all steps. You can't skip one or the whole thing stalls."

"Like a clinic," Rosa said, and went to call the owners.

Alexis picked up the phone. She typed: it's not the krebs cycle. it happens before, when pyruvate turns into acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, and one CO2 comes off right there. i checked the book. she hovered, then added: sorry i didn't say anything last night. She sent it before she could weigh it further, and the weighing kept going anyway, the way Biscuit's breathing had gone on in the back room, quick and small and unobservable from here.

Then she began drawing the matrix again, this time careful, both membranes labeled, and wrote pyruvate at the border with an arrow going in, and beside it, small and exact, one CO2 going out.

Sebastian had been sitting in the waiting room of the student health clinic for eleven minutes when he realized he was still holding the folded paper against his chest like a hall pass. The paper was his script, or the beginning of one: six lines about consent, contraception, and testing that he was supposed to deliver tomorrow at the orientation workshop for first-years. Ms. Okafor had asked him on Tuesday because, she said, he was good at saying uncomfortable things in a normal voice. He wasn't sure that was a compliment. The deadline was 9 a.m., and he had until this appointment at 4:40 to turn six vague lines into something a person could actually use.

The nurse practitioner, a compact woman named Angela with a lanyard full of enamel pins, called him back and asked what he needed. He hadn't come for anything medical. He'd come because the script had a hole in it, and the hole was shaped like a question he couldn't answer: why did every pamphlet about the pill nag about setting a daily phone reminder, as if forgetting one small tablet were some catastrophe? He had a girlfriend, Priya, and they had talked about her starting the pill next month, and he wanted to know what he was signing up for as the other half of that arrangement.

Angela didn't lecture him. She spun her chair to the screen, typed something, and turned it toward him with her chin propped on her fist. With typical use, she said, about seven in one hundred people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. She let that sit while he read it twice. "Seven out of a hundred," Sebastian said slowly, "not out of a thousand." She nodded and asked what he thought typical use meant, and he guessed: real people, real mornings, real forgetting. Perfect use was the lab version; typical use was his version, was Priya's version, was everyone who ever slept through an alarm.

That was the moment the script stopped being homework. He asked about reminders, and she showed him the app the clinic recommended, the one that buzzed and kept escalating until you tapped it. He asked what happened if a dose was missed anyway, and she slid a chart across the desk, told him the pharmacist could walk him through the specifics, and said the important thing was not to panic or to disappear. He thought of his brother, who at seventeen had vanished for a whole summer rather than tell anyone anything, and how their mother still spoke of that summer in a careful, flat voice. Nobody in their house had ever stigmatized the clinic itself, exactly, but silence had done quieter work.

Then he asked the question he'd been circling since Tuesday: how would a person actually get tested here, if the person were scared. Angela stood up, which he hadn't expected, and walked him back out through the waiting room to a door marked LAB, nodding at it the way you'd nod at a neighbor. "You check in at that front desk, you don't need a parent, you don't need a reason you can defend in court," she said. "The form takes four minutes. That's it." He wrote "four minutes" on his script, under the part about consent, and realized the two things belonged on the same page even though he'd drafted them as separate worlds: the part where you ask, and the part where you act on what you've asked.

The consent section was the part he'd been avoiding, because the workshop's official definition felt like something printed on a laminated card, and laminated cards made eighteen-year-olds stop listening. He'd been to a party in March where a friend, drunk and earnest, had kept steering a girl toward the stairs after she'd said maybe twice, and Sebastian had said something, one sentence, and the friend had laughed at him, and the girl had left, and Sebastian had spent the rest of the spring unable to decide whether he'd done enough. The chronology of that night was fixed forever in his memory, unchangeable: maybe, then his sentence, then the laugh, then the door. What stayed changeable was the meaning, and he could feel it shifting as he sat here, from a story about his own discomfort toward something more like a responsibility he hadn't asked for and still carried.

He asked Angela, as a test run, how he'd explain consent to a room of strangers without sounding like a compliance officer. She said, "Try saying what you'd want someone to say to you when you were eighteen," and he understood that his drafts had all been written in the voice of a person forty years old, and that the turbid, tangled feeling in his chest whenever he thought about that March night was actually the correct starting material, not an obstacle to be routed around.

On the bus back to campus, he rewrote the whole script in pen, in the margins of a chemistry handout. Consent as a question you keep asking. The pill at its real numbers, seven in a hundred with typical use, and a reminder set not as nagging but as the difference between the number you get and the number you don't. Testing as a door he had now physically stood beside. He left one line at the bottom unfinished, the one about what you do when you've said the sentence and your friend laughs anyway, because he did not know the answer and suspected there wasn't a clean one, and he thought eighteen-year-olds deserved to hear that out loud.

At nine the next morning he stood in front of forty first-years with their orientation lanyards still stiff, and he told them about the seven, and the reminder, and the door marked LAB, and then he said, "There's a part of this I still got wrong once, and I'll tell you about it if you want," and forty faces looked up.

The shop smelled of isopropyl alcohol and burnt coffee, and Alyssa had decided she loved that smell, though honestly she had decided a lot of things lately. She was spending her last summer before college not at the lake with Dana and Priya, the way they'd planned since eighth grade, but behind the counter of iPhix on Route 9, learning SQL from Marcus the owner because he'd mentioned once, in an offhand way she'd probably inflated in memory, that data analysis paid real money. Her mother said she was hiding. Alyssa said she was building her resume. Both could be true, but she preferred the second version, so that was the one she told.

Marcus wanted a list of customers who had never brought in a device, dead weight in his mailing list, so he could decide whether to cut them. He'd shown her the customers table and the orders table on the ancient laptop by the register, and she'd spent two evenings getting comfortable with joins. She'd even started feeling a flicker of pride, an inchoate sense that she might actually be good at this, the way she'd once thought she might be good at the violin, an episode nobody in the family mentioned anymore.

On Thursday she wrote her first version and it worked. LEFT JOIN customers to orders, and the customers with nothing came back with empty slots where their orders should have been, holes in the rows like missing teeth. Eleven names. Mrs. Okafor. The Hendersons. A guy named Ted V. with a gmail address from 2009. She printed the list, which was a mistake, because the warm paper in her hand made the names feel like more than names.

But Marcus, leaning over the register counting receipt rolls, said he only wanted the ones worth keeping, so could she narrow it to customers whose orders, if any, totaled more than zero, so he'd know who the real dead weight was versus who just hadn't come in yet this year. Sure, she said, easy. She added WHERE orders.total > 0 and ran it again.

The list shrank. Then she counted, and counted again, and the empty rows were gone. Ted V., Mrs. Okafor, the Hendersons, all eleven of them had vanished, and instead she was looking at sixty-some customers who had ordered plenty. The exact people she wasn't looking for. She said a word she'd picked up from Priya, whom she hadn't called in three weeks, or maybe it was four, the days at the shop ran together when you weren't counting them.

She stared at the query until the screen went swimmy. Somewhere in that staring, the shape of it came to her, and later she would explain it to Dana over the phone with more confidence than she'd earned: putting a condition like total > 0 on the right table in the WHERE clause took out the NULL rows, the empty ones, and once they were gone the join was acting like an inner join, which she'd learned was the plain kind, the kind that only kept matches. The quiet customers had no total at all, so the filter swallowed them along with the zeros. She moved the condition up into the ON clause instead, reran it, and the eleven names came back. She may have said "yes" out loud, alone in the shop, though in her retelling she was very cool about it.

When Marcus came back from the stockroom, she showed him both lists and told him the trick, quickly, before her nerve failed, and he nodded slowly and said, "So which ones do I cut." She looked at Ted V.'s 2009 email and thought about how a person could exist for fifteen years in a database as nothing but absence, and how the query couldn't tell you whether that absence was poverty or a move or a phone that just never broke. Maybe she was being sentimental. Maybe working with data all day was starting to desensitize her in the other direction, toward seeing people as rows, and this small resistance in her chest was the last of something worth keeping. She didn't say any of that. She had never been the eloquent one; that was Dana, whose erudition used to make teachers sit up straighter, and whom Alyssa was suddenly, specifically homesick for.

"Cut the ones with old emails," Marcus said. "Keep the rest for one more year." Alyssa saved both queries, the working one and the broken one, in a file she labeled plainly, because she wanted to remember which was which. Then she took out her phone, and before she could talk herself out of it, she dialed. Dana picked up on the second ring, and Alyssa heard lake water in the background, someone laughing, and she said, "Hey. So I did a thing today."

The portfolio workshop met in the art barn at four o'clock, when the sun came through the gaps in the wall boards and laid stripes across the concrete floor. Morgan set her sketchbook on the long table and opened it to the page she had been avoiding all week: the assignment sheet. Ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement by the end of August. The instructor, Ruth, had said the theme could be anything, as long as it was a lens and not a label, and Morgan had spent three days deciding that this sentence meant nothing.

Her problem was simpler than philosophy. She wanted to do self-portraits, because faces were the only thing she could draw with any confidence, but she had tried four already and they all looked like the same girl in the same hoodie, slightly annoyed, staring out of the page. She spread the four portraits across the table and looked at them in a row, and beside her, Dev, who was building a portfolio of etchings of drowned cities, leaned over.

"They're good," he said. "But it's like the same picture four times."

"I know."

"There's this photographer," he said, pulling out his phone. "Cindy Sherman. She did Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. Seventy black-and-white photographs, all of herself, posed as characters from movies that don't exist. Imaginary ones." He turned the screen toward her: a woman in a maid's uniform looking over her shoulder, a woman in a headscarf on a lonely road, a woman in an office dress caught mid-phone-call, each one grainy and strange, like a still pulled from a film nobody had ever made.

Morgan held the phone a long time. Seventy, from one face, and none of them repeated, because each one was answering a different question about who the face belonged to. She handed it back. "The movies aren't real?"

"That's the whole thing. She made them up."

That evening, after dinner, Morgan went back to the barn alone. The screen door complained, then settled. She found a box of costumes in the prop closet from some long-ago camp musical: a raincoat, a feathered hat, a plaid scarf, a pair of white gloves gone gray at the fingertips. She carried them to the mirror by the sinks and started trying things on, and what she saw was not a costume but a story, each one suggesting a person who might have existed, a detective's assistant, a widow, a runaway with somebody's peccadilloes written all over her suitcase. She taped a sheet of tracing paper to the window and sketched the mirror instead of herself, so that the reflection was the subject and she was only the occasion.

The next two days she drew fast. A self-portrait as an astronaut, using the white gloves and a colander. A self-portrait as a stranger on a bus, done from an angle where her own chin became somebody else's jawline. She began to think the theme was identity, and wrote "IDENTITY" at the top of a planning page, and then crossed it out, because identity was the label Ruth had warned about, the kind of word that sat on a portfolio like a tarp. The lens, she decided, was closer to pretending: not who she was but how many people one face could be persuaded to become. She was still not sure whether that was the same thing as lying. Some of the drawings felt honest and some felt like a peccadillo, a small vanity, and she could not always tell which were which.

On Thursday the whole workshop did crits. Morgan tacked her five finished pieces to the corkboard wall in a row and stood back, and the other campers went quiet in a way that could portend admiration or the opposite. A girl named Priya, whose landscapes were so precise people had accused her of tracing, pointed at the bus portrait.

"Who is that?"

"Me," Morgan said. "As somebody else."

"It doesn't look like you at all."

"It's me in the mirror," Morgan said. "I just drew the reflection."

Priya frowned, then leaned close, and her frown turned into something else. "Wait. The mirror's not flat. That's why the jaw is wrong. You didn't change it. The mirror changed it."

Morgan came forward and looked, and it was true: the old mirror in the barn was warped along one edge, and every portrait she had done at that sink carried the same small distortion, a jaw pulled subtly out of true, and she had spent two days thinking she was inventing people when the glass had been inventing them with her. She laughed, and then stopped, because the question she had been carrying all week turned over and showed its other side.

"So the series is a collaboration," Dev said from the back. "You and a warped mirror."

"Then that's the statement," Morgan said, and pulled the fifth drawing off the wall and held it up to the light, running her thumb along the bent jaw. "I did all this work pretending to be other people, and the whole time the mirror was doing the pretending for me." She looked at the glass by the sinks, which gave back her own face, slightly and faithfully wrong.

The article arrived on Tuesday, one photocopied page per student, warm from the machine. Ms. Reyes wrote "Resumen oral, jueves" on the board and said nothing else about it, which was her way of making the silence do the work. Payton looked down at a wall of Spanish print and felt the familiar vertigo of realizing how much of the world she could not access.

She had wanted this, though. That was the part she kept returning to. In March she had watched her older cousin translate for a family at the clinic where she volunteered, moving between two languages like someone carrying water between two houses, and Payton had signed up for Spanish Three with a private ambition she had told no one. Two semesters later she could conjugate anything and read almost nothing, and the gap between those two abilities had begun to feel parochial, a limit she had drawn around herself without noticing.

At lunch she took the article to the library and started at the end. The final paragraph was shortest, and she had a theory that endings would be easiest, the way songs trail off into repeated words. She worked the dictionary. "El agricultor." The farmer. "La sequía." She flipped pages. Drought. The farmer was quoted saying something about praying for rain, and Payton copied the sentence out phonetically, pleased with herself, then realized she had spent twenty minutes and had no idea what the article was actually about. It was like being handed a photograph of someone's foot and asked to describe the whole person.

Ana found her there, backpack sliding off one shoulder. Ana was the one who had grown up in two languages and treated the second one like a bicycle she no longer remembered learning to ride. She looked at the page upside down and then at Payton's notebook, where the farmer's prayer sat in careful phonetics.

"You started with the last paragraph," Ana said. It wasn't a question.

"It was short."

Ana tapped the top of the page, the first dense block under the headline. "Read this one first. The important stuff is at the beginning. They call it the inverted pyramid." She pulled out the chair across from Payton and sat, which meant she had decided to stay, which meant Payton had approximately forty minutes before sixth period to recalibrate her entire approach.

The first paragraph, it turned out, was harder than the last, longer and faster, but it carried the freight. She and Ana went word by word, and the story assembled itself with strange efficiency: a region in northern Mexico, a declining aquifer, new limits on how much water could be pumped, announced by officials on Monday. Everything Payton needed was in that opening block. The middle paragraphs added quotes and numbers and context, and the ending, she now saw, was decoration, the farmer's prayer trailing off like a song. She had spent Tuesday's lunch hour decoding the decoration.

Thursday came. Ms. Reyes drew names from a coffee mug, and Payton sat with her palms flat on her desk, watching the names accumulate on the board, none of them hers, and then hers. The walk to the front of the room took four steps and felt considerably longer.

She had prepared a summary in Spanish, seven sentences, memorized, and she began it in a voice that came out a half-octave high. Then something happened that she had not planned. Between her third and fourth sentences she stopped looking at the back wall and started looking at Marco, who sat in the second row and whose grandmother, he'd once mentioned, lived somewhere with water problems, and Payton changed what she was going to say. She dropped a sentence about the officials and added one about the farmers instead, in slower, plainer Spanish, the farmer's sentence, the prayer for rain, the thing she had learned first because she had read the article backwards.

Marco nodded. Someone behind him nodded. Ms. Reyes did not write anything down, which Payton had learned was either very good or very bad.

Afterward, at her desk, Payton looked at the photocopied page again. Ana's method had worked, and she would use it again, starting at the top where the weight was, but she noticed she couldn't dismiss her own stupid route either. Reading the last paragraph first had been inefficient, and it had also made her care about the article in a way the opening block alone might not have. The inverted pyramid told you what happened. It did not tell you why it mattered. She could hold both of those ideas at once without pretending they added up neatly, and she was aware that this was the kind of thing people said when they wanted to feel sophisticated about their mistakes.

Ana passed her a folded note on the way out. Payton opened it at her locker. "You slowed down at the good part," it read. "Also, aquifer means what you think it means. I checked."

Payton laughed once, out loud, alone in the hallway, and slid the note into the front pocket of her binder, next to the phonetic farmer and his prayer.

Megan arrived at the science museum an hour before the fair opened, carrying her capacitor in a shoebox lined with paper towels. The grand hall smelled like floor wax and old rain, and above the admissions desk a suspended skeleton of a blue whale hung so low she could see the seams in its fiberglass ribs. Her table was number fourteen, between a boy with a model aquifer and a girl who had grown moss on a corkboard.

She set the plates upright on their wooden stand, twelve centimeters apart, checked the wire to the hand-crank generator, and then read the message her lab partner, Dana, had sent the night before. "Good luck today. My mom says I have to visit my aunt, so don't set anything on fire." Megan read it twice. There was no mention of coming late, or of the argument they'd had on Tuesday about whose name went first on the display card, and the absence of any mention felt louder than an apology would have. She typed "we'll be fine," deleted "we," typed "I'll be fine," deleted the whole thing, and put the phone in her pocket.

The judges came through at ten, lanyards swinging. The first one was a woman with reading glasses on a chain, who looked at the two aluminum plates and said, "Tell me what's happening in there."

Megan had rehearsed this part. "When I crank the generator, it puts a voltage across the plates," she said. "The field between them is uniform, which means it has the same strength everywhere in the middle. The electric field strength equals the voltage across the plates divided by the distance between them, E equals V over d." She pointed at the meter clipped to the stand. "Right now it reads ninety volts, and the plates are twelve centimeters apart, so the field strength is ninety divided by twelve."

"Seven point five," the judge said. "Volts per centimeter."

"Per centimeter, yes." Megan felt her ears go hot, not from embarrassment but from the small clean click of it. She had gotten the formula wrong for two weeks, multiplying instead of dividing, and had only caught it when she noticed her answers made no sense, fields getting stronger as she pulled the plates apart, which contradicted everything the museum's electrostatics exhibit downstairs had shown her, the one with the buzzing metal sphere and the girl's hair lifting off her shoulders like slow seaweed.

"So if I move the plates closer together," the judge said, "same voltage?"

"The field gets stronger. V over d, and d is smaller." Megan slid the adjustable stand until the plates were six centimeters apart, cranked until the needle settled at ninety again, and watched the woman's eyebrows rise slightly at the meter. "Fifteen now," Megan said. "Half the distance, twice the field strength."

The judge made a note on her clipboard. "You're not going to expatiate on the health effects of electric fields, are you? The last table lectured me for ten minutes."

"No," Megan said. "I looked that up. Between plates like these, at these voltages, nothing deleterious happens to you. The dangerous thing would be the discharge if I shorted it, which is why the resistor is there." She touched the small cylinder soldered across the terminals. "It drains the charge slowly."

The judge smiled at that, the way people smile when someone has answered the question behind the question, and moved on to the aquifer boy.

The hall filled slowly with families, and by noon Megan had explained the plates nineteen times. A small boy asked her whether the field was the blue stuff, and she said no, there wasn't blue stuff, the field was the name for how the space between the plates had changed, and he looked unconvinced and went to find the dinosaurs.

At one o'clock she sat behind her table and ate the sandwich she'd brought, and her phone buzzed. Dana again. "How'd it go. Are we winning." Not a question mark anywhere, Megan noticed, and no mention of the name order either, though the display card still read DANA KOWALSKI AND MEGAN PRIETO, which Megan had printed on Tuesday before the argument, in a moment of generosity she now regarded as a heuristic that had failed her, the general rule being that yielding early prevents fights, evidence here being that it hadn't.

She typed, "Judge liked it. Plates closer means stronger field, same voltage. You would've been good at the judge part." She looked at the whale ribs, at the light coming down through the glass roof in long dusty columns. Then she added, "We can talk about the card when you're back," and sent it, because she had decided during the nineteen explanations that the order of names on a card was a thing she could hold loosely, though she was not entirely sure she'd still feel that way on Monday, and she was honest enough with herself to leave that open.

Dana replied with a single thumb.

Megan put the phone face down, wiped the aluminum with her sleeve, and waited for the next family to stop.

Nathaniel had told his mother he was meeting a study group, which was true in the sense that Priya was technically a group of one, and that they would technically study, provided the museum café sold coffee strong enough to sustain the pretense. The biology placement exam was Monday. If he passed it, he'd skip the introductory lecture course and start the second-semester sequence, which mattered for reasons he hadn't explained to anyone, least of all himself.

The museum was nearly empty this late in the afternoon. Light came slantwise through the atrium glass, turning the hall crepuscular, the exhibits glowing in their cases like things underwater. Priya walked ahead of him past the dinosaur cast, past the pendulum knocking down its little pins, and stopped at a doorway marked Cells and Energy.

"Two hours," she said. "Then dinner. I'm not imputing any nobility to this. You just want to skip a class."

"I want to start where I actually am," Nathaniel said. "Not where the registrar thinks I am."

Inside, the room was dim and blue, mitochondria enlarged to the size of rowboats lining the walls. He'd read the chapter three times the night before. Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain: he could recite the order, could name glucose and pyruvate and the carbon dioxide that left at the end like steam from a train. What he couldn't have done, if someone put a gun to his head, was say how any of it made ATP. The textbook kept using the word "coupled," and the word sat there doing nothing, a platitude of biochemistry, as if naming a connection were the same as having one.

Priya found the interactive first. "Come look at this."

It was a model, waist-high, a housing shaped like a mushroom cap with a stalk descending into a cutaway membrane. A handle made the stalk turn. When you cranked it, three knobs at the top opened and closed like mouths, and a counter on the side tallied glowing pellets. The label read: ATP SYNTHASE. Nathaniel read the smaller text twice. Protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP. That was all. No explanation, just the sentence, and the machine waiting for him to crank it.

"It's a motor," Priya said. "Look, you turn the bottom and the top does the work."

"No," Nathaniel said slowly, and then stopped, because he wasn't sure yet what the no was doing. He'd been turning it in his head since the label. The protons weren't food or fuel the way glucose was. They were stacked up behind the membrane like water behind a dam, all those electrons from the transport chain pumping them across, and the only place they could flow back was through this one enzyme. Through it. And flowing through it made part of the enzyme spin. The spinning was the whole point. The motion itself built the ATP. He cranked the handle and watched the knobs open, close, open, each cycle adding to the counter, and something in his chest turned over with it.

"The glucose doesn't make ATP," he said. "Not directly. The glucose pays to stack the protons up. Then the protons fall through this thing and it spins and the spin makes the ATP. It's a rotary motor. Like a mill wheel, except it's making molecules."

"You just figured that out from a handle and a sign?"

He was still cranking. The counter climbed. Somewhere upstream of him, in every cell of his arms, this was happening constantly, billions of tiny motors, and he had gone eighteen years without knowing. "The chapter never said it like that. It kept saying coupled, coupled. Nobody said spin."

"Maybe that's why you failed the practice test," Priya said, and there it was, the thing he hadn't told her. She said it lightly, but she'd been carrying it all afternoon; he could hear the care under the lightness. He'd told her he'd done fine on the practice exam. He'd told his mother the same thing on the phone, standing in the kitchen with his back to her, and his mother had said that's wonderful, honey, and gone to bed early.

He let the handle slow. The counter stopped.

"I got a fifty-two," he said. "The practice test. I got a fifty-two and I told my mom I did fine."

Priya didn't answer right away. Around them the blue light pulsed in a slow rhythm, like something breathing. "Why lie to her?" she said finally. "She's not going to take the exam for you."

"Because if she thinks I'm fine, I can still decide whether I'm fine. If she knows, it becomes a thing. It becomes her worrying at the kitchen table while I'm trying to read about protons." He heard how it sounded even as he said it. He was trying to keep a version of himself intact, and the cost was that his mother was holding a fact that wasn't a fact.

"And now?"

"Now I don't know. Maybe I tell her tonight. Maybe I tell her after Monday, when I can tell her the real result instead of the practice one." He looked at the model, at the three patient mouths still half-open where he'd left them. "That's still lying by omission, isn't it."

"That's your call," Priya said. "But if you're asking me, the spin makes the ATP. The worrying doesn't make anything." She checked her phone. "Dinner. You have until the museum closes to decide."

The guard was already walking the far hall, keys sounding against his thigh. Nathaniel gave the handle one more full turn, watched the counter tick up, and let it go.

On Monday, he thought, he'd write the whole pathway out from the top: glucose, glycolysis, the cycle, the chain, the dam of protons, the motor. And tonight, probably, he'd call his mother. Probably. He took a last look at the spinning thing going still and followed Priya out through the blue room's doors.

"Order me the thing with the noodles," he called to her back. "I'll be there in a second."

He stood a moment longer in the emptying hallway, then went.

"Okay," Anna said, spreading the two leases across the cafeteria table like a dealer laying out cards. "You are about to witness adulting."

Priya set down her milk carton. "Those are from your mom?"

"My mom photocopied them at work and left them on my bed with a sticky note that said, in all caps, YOU DECIDE." Anna smoothed the first page. "So now I decide. Apparently."

The plan was this: Anna and her mother were moving in June, and two buildings had openings. The one on Fenwick Street wanted twelve hundred dollars a month, but it was running a move-in special, one month of free rent on a twelve-month lease. The one on Corliss Avenue wanted eleven fifty, no special, no fanfare. For a week Anna had assumed Corliss was obviously cheaper, the way she assumed a lot of things, and then she'd started doing arithmetic on the back of her chemistry homework and gotten a feeling like the floor tilting.

"Utilities," Priya said, tapping the Fenwick lease. "It says here water and trash are included. That's like fifty bucks you're not paying."

"Which sounds generous until you see the Corliss one." Anna pulled the second lease forward. "Corliss includes water, trash, and gas. Fenwick makes you pay your own gas, which, in winter, ugh."

"How much is gas?"

"No idea. That's the noxious part. Not the gas itself, the not knowing. Dad says I should call the utility company and ask for an average, but calling people is my least favorite sport."

Priya grinned. "You could email."

"They don't email. They have a phone number from 1987." Anna pulled out her notebook, where she'd already started a grid in purple pen. Across the top she'd written FENWICK and CORLISS and, underneath, in smaller letters, ECON BOX, because the whole thing had started as extra credit for her economics unit. The teacher had said bring in a real-world comparison, and Anna had thought, real world? I live in the real world, my house has a for-sale sign in the yard. Now the extra credit had turned into her actual life, which felt like bringing your homework on vacation.

She wrote the Fenwick numbers first. Twelve months at twelve hundred, but one of those months was free, so eleven months actually paid. Eleven times twelve hundred. She did it twice because the first answer seemed too polite. Thirteen thousand two hundred for the whole year. Divided by twelve months, because that was the fair way to look at it, the way you'd actually live it. Eleven hundred a month. She sat back.

"That can't be right."

"What?" Priya leaned over. "What can't be right?"

"Fenwick. The expensive one. With the free month it works out to eleven hundred a month. Effective rent, it's called." Anna stared at her purple grid. "That's fifty dollars less than Corliss."

"Wait, so the move-in special beats the cheaper building?"

"By fifty dollars." Anna recalibrate d nothing, at first, because the tilting-floor feeling got worse. She had spent a week saying the Fenwick building was for people who liked flashy lobbies and overpaid for them. She'd said this out loud, at dinner, twice. "I told my mom Fenwick was a trap."

Priya was already laughing. "You told your mom. To her face."

"I used the word trap, Priya. I used the word trap."

"So you have to tell her she was right to look at it."

"No, worse. I have to tell her I was wrong, which is different, and worse." Anna flipped to the utilities section of both leases again, because there had to be a catch, and there it was, kind of: Fenwick's electric wasn't included either, and neither was Corliss's, so that was a wash, but the gas question still hung over everything like weather. If gas at Fenwick ran more than fifty dollars a month over what Corliss's included gas would have cost, then Corliss won again, and Anna was back where she started, only now she had a purple grid to prove it.

"Can I use this?" Priya pulled the notebook closer, squinting at the ECON BOX header. "My econ thing is due Friday and I was going to write about stagflation, which I do not understand even slightly."

"Stagflation is when everything costs more and nobody has jobs. Take the grid, it's yours." Anna pulled out her phone and found the utility company's ancient phone number. She looked at it for a second, the way you look at a diving board. Then Priya reached over and pressed dial.

"Hello?" Anna said, when a voice answered. "Hi. I have a question about average gas bills. It's for a very important homework assignment. And also my whole life."

The trouble began on the first evening of the arts intensive, when the director announced that each camper would deliver a formal critique of a single painting at Saturday's exhibition, and Nathaniel understood that he did not know what the word "formal" was supposed to mean in that sentence. He had applied to the program in the Valle de Bravo because his portfolio needed figure drawings and because his mother had said a month away would be good for him. He had expected sketchbooks and canoes. He had not expected a lecture hall above the boathouse, whiteboards covered in terms like "chromatic weight" and "negative space," and a girl named Priya who took notes in two colors of ink and asked questions even the instructor paused before answering.

Priya had claimed The Two Fridas before anyone else could. She said it plainly, over rice at dinner, the way you might claim a window seat. "I'm doing the Kahlo. It's in the Museo de Arte Moderno in the city, and we see it Thursday." Nathaniel had been half in love with the painting since tenth grade, when he'd found a poster of it in a used bookstore and taped it above his desk without fully knowing why. He said none of this. He said, "That's a hard one," and Priya said, "That's why I picked it," and he spent the rest of the meal drawing tines on his fork with a thumbnail.

He chose a de Chirico instead, shadowy arcades and a distant train, and for three days he buried himself in vocabulary. He learned to describe how a composition divides the rectangle, how color advances or recedes, how an object repeated twice forces the eye to compare. The knowledge felt like a new grammar, and he liked grammar, liked the way rules could make a sentence carry more. But at night, in the bunkroom, listening to the lake water slap the dock pilings, he kept thinking of the poster above his desk, and of how none of his new words seemed to touch what the poster had done to him when he was fifteen.

There was a memory he kept circling. His grandfather, the summer before he died, had taken Nathaniel to a museum in Chicago, and they had stood in front of a Pollock for a long time while his grandfather, who repaired irrigation pumps for a living, said nothing. Finally the old man said, "I could do that," and then, after a silence, "No, I couldn't," and he had laughed, and Nathaniel had laughed, and neither of them had needed to say anything else about it. His grandfather had looked at the painting the way he looked at a broken engine, patiently, with his whole body, until it gave up what it was.

On Thursday the camp bused into the city, and the valley fell away behind them, the fields spread out on the alluvial flat where the river had spent centuries laying down its soil, and Nathaniel watched it all through the window without sketching any of it. In the museum the group moved through rooms of Orozco and Siqueiros, and Priya walked fast, ahead of everyone, a small determined figure with her notebook already open. When they turned the corner into the Kahlo room, Nathaniel felt something in his chest adjust, the way ears do when a plane descends.

He had never known the painting's size. On the poster, on his wall, it had always been intimate, the way a diary page is intimate. Here it was enormous, nearly square, about 173 centimeters on each side, he heard Priya telling a counselor, and the two seated self-portraits sat side by side filling it, dominating the whole wall. Priya kept stepping backward, back and back, nearly into a bench, to see how the two figures used the full square of the canvas, and other visitors had to part around her, and she did not appear to notice or care.

Nathaniel stood closer than she did. He looked at the hearts, at the artery that ran between the two women like a bridge or a leash, at the white dress and the Tehuana dress, at the storm sky behind them. He heard one of the other campers, Marco, who all week had been flattering every instructor within earshot, telling the counselor that the brushwork here was the finest in Mexican painting, and the counselor nodded along, and Priya, without turning, said, "He's such a sycophant," quietly, to her notebook.

She found him afterward in the courtyard, by the reflecting pool where the heat made the air undulate above the water so that the museum seemed to waver at its edges. "You've been staring at my painting all afternoon," she said, and it wasn't hostile, exactly. He said, "It was mine first. Sort of. In a way that doesn't count." She sat down on the wall beside him and said, "Then tell me one thing about it that isn't from a study guide."

He told her about his grandfather and the Pollock. He told her that the longer he studied formal analysis, the more it seemed like the grammar of a language he had been speaking without knowing it, and that he was afraid of what happened when you learned the grammar, which was that you could no longer say a sentence the old way. Priya was quiet for a moment, the pool trembling between them. "You could do the critique with me," she said. "Two people, two Fridas. The director said pairs were allowed if neither one was lazy." He said, "Which one am I?" and she said, "The one on the right, obviously," and he laughed, though he wasn't sure the joke had a floor to it.

They worked on it that night at a table in the boathouse, the lake black beyond the windows, the lamp making two shadows of each of them on the wall. They built the analysis together: the square format and how its stability argued against the violence of the exposed hearts; the way the left Frida's white dress bled into the ground while the right one's colors held; the storm sky as a field of feeling rather than weather. Priya argued the symbolism was about the divorce, about Diego cut out of the locket, and Nathaniel said maybe, but he thought the painting was also doing something the biography couldn't reach, something about watching yourself, and he couldn't yet say what. Priya wrote both positions down, side by side, in her two colors of ink, and underlined neither of them.

Saturday morning, before the room filled, they stood at the front with the projected image behind them, the double self-portrait looming square and enormous even flattened onto a screen. Priya nudged him and whispered, "You start," and Nathaniel turned to the painting instead of the audience, looked at the two women holding hands in the storm, and began.

Maria spread the practice test across the kitchen table, third cup of coffee going cold beside her, and read the same line for the fifth time: estimate the area under the curve between x equals zero and x equals four. Monday was the placement exam that would decide whether she started college calculus in the fall or spent a semester repeating what she should already know. She had drawn the curve twice, a gentle parabola rising like a hillside, and under it she had sketched rectangles, ten of them, then twenty, watching the gaps shrink.

Her younger brother Danny leaned over her shoulder on his way to the refrigerator. "What's with the jail bars."

"They're rectangles," she said. "The curve is like a roof and the rectangles are rooms underneath it. If I make enough rooms, the wasted space gets small."

"So it's never exact."

She tapped the pencil against the page. "That's the part I can't tell." The method was named for somebody, she knew that much, some dead mathematician, and the study guide mentioned him only in passing, as if everyone already knew. She copied the name onto the back of a receipt: Riemann.

At the kitchen computer, sticky with orange juice residue along the trackpad, she searched for him. The first solid result was a scan of an old textbook chapter with the sentence underlined in blue by some previous reader. She read it aloud mostly to make it real: "Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen."

"That's it?" Danny said, peeling an orange at the counter.

"That's the whole fact. A qualification paper. Not some grandiose manifesto." She liked that, actually. He had been applying for a job, more or less, and the way he chose to prove himself was to say what everyone had been doing loosely and make it precise. There was something almost humble in it, rectangles under a roof, and then a single clean claim about what happens when you let the number of rooms go on and on. She couldn't have explained the proof, but she could feel its shape, the way the answer stopped wobbling once the rectangles got thin enough.

She went back to the table and tried it herself with the parabola. Sixty rectangles took forever by hand, so she built a spreadsheet, one column for widths, one for heights, a sum at the bottom. Each time she doubled the count, the sum moved less. Two hundred rectangles. Four hundred. The number settled toward something like twenty-one and a third and then simply stopped arguing with itself. Danny drifted back over and watched the screen scroll.

"So it is exact," he said.

"It converges," she said, then heard how that sounded and laughed. "It settles down. The gaps stop mattering." She wrote the settled number at the top of her practice test and boxed it. Somewhere at the end of a long argument she couldn't follow yet, in a language she hadn't learned, that number had been waiting, and Riemann had drawn the map. She thought about texting her father, who believed any tuition money spent on pure math was evidence of a coming plutocracy where only people who could compute would eat. He would want her in something practical. She decided not to text him tonight. She would accede to one of his practical majors eventually, probably, but not before she had finished arguing with this.

The overhead light buzzed and she got up to find a quieter lamp. In the living room, her mother was half asleep in front of the news, a blanket over her knees, the same channel she left on every night like a companion. Maria stood in the doorway a moment. On Monday she would sit in a fluorescent room and shade little boxes under little hills, and somewhere behind the exam there would be a paper from 1854, a man standing before the University of Göttingen hoping to be allowed to lecture, offering rectangles as his life's evidence. She didn't know yet whether she was good at this or only stubborn. Both had gotten her this far.

She carried the lamp back to the kitchen and clipped it to the shelf above the table. Danny had left half his orange, the segments pulled apart in a fan. She ate one, wiped her fingers on her jeans, and started the next problem: a different curve this time, dipping below the axis, where the rectangles would have to mean something else.

Lea sat on a swing that didn't swing, one sneaker hooked in the wood chips, her physics workbook balanced on her knees. The formula for the field between two charged plates glared up at her, E equals V over d, and beneath it a problem asking for the field strength at a point between plates held at 340 volts, separated by 2.0 centimeters. Around her the playground did its afternoon business: a man commodifying his own patience by letting a toddler decide, at length, which slide to reject, and two women arguing near the water fountain about whether juice was basically soda.

"Seventeen thousand," she said aloud, dividing before she had fully decided to. Volts per meter. The number sat there looking both exact and completely unreal. She was supposed to imagine a field strong enough to matter, and she could not. Numbers like that came out of her pencil the way coins come out of a vending machine, and she was beginning to suspect she'd been vending nothing.

Her little brother, Theo, eleven and magnetically attached to the monkey bars, dropped into the chips beside her. "What's seventeen thousand?"

"Units I can't picture. It's the electric field between two plates."

"Plates like dinner plates?"

"Like metal plates, charged, facing each other." She paused, and then the science museum came back to her, the field trip in October, the jaundiced fluorescent lighting in the Hall of Measurement, everything the color of old paper. There had been a glass case with a replica inside: a squat brass chamber, and two horizontal metal plates, one above the other, with a little window and a sprayer. She'd stood in front of it for ten minutes because a card beside it said Robert Millikan, oil drops, and she'd thought at first it was an exhibit about cooking.

"Theo, remember the museum. The brass thing with the plates." He shrugged, so she kept going. "Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron with that. He sprayed tiny charged oil drops between two horizontal charged plates, and the electric field held them still against gravity."

"Oil? Like for a bike chain?"

"Like for a bike chain," she said. "Tiny drops, so small you'd need the microscope they had on it. Gravity pulls them down and the field holds them up, and when a drop just hangs there, not falling, that's the moment. That's what he watched for."

Theo considered this with the seriousness he usually reserved for referee calls. "So the drop's like on an invisible shelf."

She had written E equals V over d with the confidence of someone copying a recipe. Now she looked at the same letters and saw the drop, hanging in the brass chamber, gravity on one side of the ledger and the field on the other, the whole apparatus built to catch a single instant of stillness. Two ways of holding the same thing, she thought: the equation, which was clean and told her nothing, and the chamber, which was grimy with history and told her everything except the number. Somewhere between them was an understanding she could actually keep. What she couldn't yet do was say what a field was, only what it did, and she decided, provisionally, that this might be the honest position.

"It's not a shelf," she said. "A shelf would be easier. It's more like the drop is falling and being pushed up at the same time and the two exactly cancel. Nobody's holding it. That's the strange part. It looks held."

"You could do that to me," Theo said. "Charge me up and stick me between plates."

"You'd need a bigger power source than the playground has."

"Then jump off the monkey bars and I'll hover."

"You'd fall," she said, "and I'd be responsible, and Mom would have questions."

He went back to the bars. Lea turned to the blank back page of the workbook and drew two horizontal lines with a dot between them, suspended. Under the dot she wrote mg, because gravity pulls down; above it she wrote qE, and made them equal. The whole genealogy of her homework problem was suddenly visible to her, one line of it anyway: her exercise, then textbooks, then a man in a room watching oil not fall, and somewhere at the root a question about the smallest piece of charge there is. She didn't know the whole lineage and suspected it was messier than any diagram, papers she'd never read, arguments she'd never heard. She underlined qE equals mg and left the underline crooked.

She tried to get from her drawing back to her number. If the drop hung still, then the field had to be exactly as strong as her seventeen thousand volts per meter claimed, at least for whatever drop and whatever charge Millikan had used, which she hadn't been given and couldn't reconstruct. The problem in the book wanted only the arithmetic. The chamber in the museum wanted the world. She sat on the dead swing with both of them, unwilling to give up either, and no way yet to prove they were the same thing.

Then she got up, workbook under her arm, and walked over to the monkey bars, where Theo was hanging by his knees with his arms out, holding himself against gravity in the only way available to an eleven-year-old.

The argument started over the potato kugel, which was where most arguments started at Aunt Rivka's table, because that was where Uncle Marco stationed himself, kugel in one hand and an audience in the other. Marco was the family raconteur, a man who could stretch the story of a parking ticket into twenty minutes, and by the time dessert came around he had already begun on this year's target: Liam's grandmother's rule that no one worked on Saturdays, not even to drive, and how it was, in Marco's opinion, a beautiful antique that sensible people kept in a display case and never actually used.

"Then don't use it," Liam said, and then, because he had been arguing with Marco since he was nine and losing since he was nine, he added, "but you can't say the rule itself expired. You'd have to show that from the text."

Marco set down his fork. Around the long table, the younger cousins resumed chewing, the way crowds settle in for a show. "From the text," Marco repeated, delighted. "The college man wants sources." He was still calling Liam that even though Liam had only been accepted, not enrolled, and the letter was sitting in a drawer at home partly because Liam was not sure he wanted the label confirmed.

The trouble was that Liam had a real stake in this, one he had not announced. On Monday, his senior seminar was holding its last graded debate of the year, and the assigned question was whether ancient religious rules still bound modern life, and the teacher had required every argument to come from the primary text, no outside authorities, no vibes. Liam had drawn the affirmative, the side he privately half-believed and half-didn't, and he had until Monday to find out which half was which. He had spent two evenings with a borrowed chumash and a legal pad that now had more crossed-out lines than written ones, and the only thing he knew for certain was that his strongest verse, the one about the Sabbath being a sign forever, was the same verse Marco would quote and then swat away.
