"Do you know what exegesis is?" said his cousin Deborah, from across the table. She was home from her second year at a seminary in Baltimore and had been silent all dinner, which everyone had wrongly attributed to shyness. "It means drawing a text's meaning out of its words and context," she said. "The opposite is eisegesis, reading your own ideas into it. Our rebbe accuses everyone of it, mostly us."

"Meaning what," Marco said, though he clearly meant, give me the weapon.

"Meaning the kid's right so far," Deborah said. "You can't say a rule expired just because you find it inconvenient, Uncle Marco. That's not interpretation, that's preference. You looked in the verse and found only what you already believed."

Marco turned this over with visible pleasure, the way he turned over a good line he intended to keep. "So you're saying the Sabbath binds me. My phone, my car, my hedonistic Sunday brunch, all of it."

"I'm saying you haven't earned your no," Deborah said, and went back to her tea, and Liam understood that Deborah had her own argument happening, some old one with Marco about her year in Baltimore that he had called, at last Passover, "a waste of a bright girl," and that she was using Liam's debate to win something she hadn't been able to win as herself.

Liam's grandmother, from the head of the table, said that in her day debates happened after the dishes, and a deadline descended in the form of cousins already stacking plates. So Liam did what he had planned all along, which was to walk Marco to the front hall, where Marco always retreated to smoke by the door, and lay out the affirmative as best he could while Marco pulled on his coat. The words in the verse matter, Liam said. The context, the generation it addressed, the fact that the text itself contains its own mechanisms for interpretation, its arguments with itself. He said that some of the rabbis had read "an eye for an eye" as monetary compensation, from the text, not from comfort with it, and that this was drawing meaning out rather than stuffing meaning in.

"You sound like Deborah," Marco said, halfway out the door, which was both an insult and a concession. "All right. Monday, you tell them the rule applies, and then you tell them why you still drove here today, and you don't skip the second part, because that's the part where you'd be reading yourself into the text." He tapped ash into the planter by the door, an ancient transgression in his own right. "Texts don't disenfranchise anybody, kid. People do that all on their own, and then blame the book."

Liam stood in the doorway after the last cars pulled out, holding his legal pad, the crossed-out lines still visible in the porch light. Monday was two days away, and somewhere between his affirmative and his grandmother's keys was a position he could actually defend, though he could not yet say what it was. He wrote at the bottom of the page: ask Deborah what her rebbe got wrong. Then, underneath: ask Marco the same thing.

The lab smelled of wet chalk and something faintly chemical that no one could ever identify, and Maika sat at the third bench with a worksheet that had defeated her twice already. At the top, in her physics teacher's cramped hand, was the problem: a ball launched at twelve meters per second at thirty degrees, would it clear a fence three meters high? Beside her, Deniz was already on the last question, his pencil moving with the indifference of someone who had understood this weeks ago.

She had tried it the night before by treating the velocity as one thing, one arrow, one number, and the answer had come out absurd: the ball sailing over eight meters of fence or smashing into it halfway up, depending on which mistake she made. Both answers had felt wrong without her being able to say why, which was the worst kind of wrong. Now she spread the worksheet flat and started over, and Deniz glanced at her blank second page without comment, which was somehow kinder than commenting.

"The trick," he said finally, when she dropped her pencil for the third time, "is that nothing up and down ever talks to anything side to side. They're two separate problems wearing one ball."

She almost argued. It was one ball, one throw, one arc drawn on the whiteboard in the teacher's blue marker, and the whole point of the arc was that it was one continuous thing. But she copied his first line anyway: split the velocity. The vertical part was twelve times the sine of thirty degrees, which was six. Six meters per second, straight up, as if the sideways motion had never existed.

Then she stalled again, because knowing how fast it went up did not tell her how high it went, and the fence was three meters and her mother's car was parked on the other side of it, which mattered because if the ball cleared the fence it would land on the car and Maika would be paying for a windshield until graduation. She had actually volunteered to test the throw after class, since the seniors had been arguing about it since Monday, and only now did it occur to her that volunteering before solving the problem had been backwards.

She found the formula in her notes, half-buried between a failed quiz and a schedule for the debate tournament: ignoring air resistance, maximum height equals the square of the initial vertical velocity divided by twice g. Six squared was thirty-six. Twice nine point eight was nineteen point six. Thirty-six over nineteen point six. Her calculator said 1.84, and she wrote it down and then sat very still.

The fence was three meters. One point eight four was not three meters.

"So it hits the fence," Deniz said, reading her page upside down, and Maika felt a strange double reaction: the small satisfaction of the thing actually working, and the larger embarrassment of having promised a throw that physics had just quietly cancelled. She checked it again, the way she checked everything now, ever since the debate coach had told her that a position you only examined once was not a position, it was a preference. The math held. The ball would crest at one point eight four meters and come down against the chain-link like a deposition against her own confidence, a written record of the gap between what she'd assumed and what was true.

She walked to the window anyway. The fence stood out in the yard, and the seniors had left the ball on the bench outside, orange and half-deflated. Her first thought was that she could still try the throw and let everyone see the ball bounce off, which would at least be honest; her second thought was that there was no dignity in demonstrating a failure you'd already predicted on paper. Neither thought felt entirely tenable. What she actually wanted was for the answer to be wrong, and she knew that wanting was not evidence.

She went back to the bench and resuscitated her first attempt, the one from last night, turning the page over. There it was: she had used the full velocity, twelve, instead of the vertical part, as though the sideways motion could help lift the ball over. It couldn't. That was the thing she was slowly willing to accept, that the horizontal and vertical were separate the whole way up, separate the whole way down, and only ever met in the single object they jointly carried.

Then she looked at the problem line again. Twelve meters per second at thirty degrees. The launch angle wasn't fixed, she realized; the problem stated it, but the yard didn't. She pulled a fresh sheet toward her and tried forty degrees, then forty-five, and at forty-five the vertical component was eight and a half, and eight and a half squared over nineteen point six was three point six seven, which cleared three meters with room to spare. It wasn't the problem she'd been asked to solve. It was the problem she actually had.

At the window she pushed the latch and leaned out into the cold. The seniors were drifting toward the yard for the last ten minutes of lunch, and one of them, sensing something, picked up the orange ball.

"Forty-five degrees," Maika called down. "Throw it at forty-five."

"Or what?"

"Or it hits the fence." She watched him weigh the ball, step back from the chain-link, and raise his arm.

The overhead projector hummed above the third-row sinks, throwing a yellowed diagram of a mitochondrion across the whiteboard, and Tyson copied it for the third time because his first two attempts had collapsed into arrows pointing nowhere. Glycolysis he could manage: glucose splitting in the cytoplasm, a small profit of ATP, pyruvate drifting toward the mitochondrial membrane like a commuter catching the last train. After that the diagram turned into a spiral of names, citrate to isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate, and somewhere in the spiral, electrons were supposed to start their descent. He set his pencil down and rubbed the graphite smudge on the heel of his hand.

His lab partner, Priya, had already filled two pages and was now drawing little stars next to the steps she was sure would be on the exam. Her want was simple and she had announced it at nine o'clock that morning: finish the review sheet before lunch, leave school at noon, and get to the community college gym before the open tryouts closed. She had been practicing her jump shot in the parking lot before first period, and the ball was still in her backpack, wedged beside her binder so it wouldn't roll.

"You're on the Krebs cycle," she said, tapping his page. "You've drawn the same arrow four times."

"It's a cycle," Tyson said. "It goes around. I don't see how you draw something that has no beginning."

"It has a beginning. Acetyl-CoA comes in, citrate comes out."

"But why is it called the Krebs cycle? Half the words on this sheet are just people's names. Who decided a piece of your cells gets somebody's name on it?"

Priya looked at the clock, then at her stars, then at him, and he could see her weighing whether his question was worth the minutes. She flipped to the back of the textbook anyway, which surprised him. "It says here Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937," she read. "And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it."

"Shared," Tyson repeated. "With who?"

She ran her finger down the column. "Somebody else, for something else. It doesn't say." She closed the book on her thumb. "There. Can we finish?"

He didn't answer right away. He was looking at the diagram again, at the little wheel turning in the middle of the mitochondrion, and something about the date had snagged on him. Nineteen thirty-seven. His grandfather hadn't been born yet, and yet the wheel had been turning in every person who was alive then, every person before them, back through all of it, unnamed and unexamined until two men sat down and worked out what it was doing. The cycle hadn't needed a name to run. Only to be understood.

"I always thought of it the other way," he said slowly. "Like science invents things. Vaccines, plastics. But Krebs didn't invent this. It was already in him. In us. He just found the words for it."

"You're romanticizing," Priya said, but without much force, because she was watching his pencil start to move again, tracing glucose down through glycolysis, through the membrane, into the wheel, out along the electron transport chain to ATP. "It's a metabolic pathway. It's chemistry."

"It's both, though." He drew the spiral tighter this time, and it held. "It's chemistry that we found by asking questions, and the questions come from somewhere that isn't chemistry. Wondering isn't in the textbook." He paused, unsure of that, and said so. "Or maybe it is and I just haven't read far enough."

Mrs. Okoye passed behind them on her rounds, and Priya tried to remonstrate with her about the review sheet's length, saying it was unfair to assign twelve steps on a game day, that expecting concentration under such duress was unreasonable. Mrs. Okoye was obdurate about deadlines but not unkind; she only smiled and said the mitochondria had been working without complaint for a few billion years, which was not, Tyson thought, actually a counterargument, but which he liked anyway.

Priya finished her stars at eleven-forty and left with the ball under her arm, pausing at the door to say she hoped his wheel worked out. Tyson stayed another ten minutes, alone at the sink, redrawing the cycle one last time from memory. When he got to citrate, he wrote Krebs beside it in small letters, then Johnson under it, smaller, then sat back and looked at the two names turning inside his diagram like spokes. Somewhere across town a ball was bouncing on a gym floor, and somewhere inside his own forearm, billions of wheels were spinning without his attention, and he picked up his pencil and added the last arrow, completing the loop.

The county grant application closed at five o'clock, and by three fifteen Eve still had no list. Ms. Okafor had given her the library's member table and the checkout table that morning, along with one instruction: tell the county how many members never borrow anything, so the outreach money has a number behind it. Eve had assumed the hard part would be typing the query. She had not assumed the answer would be zero.

"Zero is wrong," said Marcus, dropping into the chair across from her at the back computer bay, near the atlases nobody touched. "Look around. Half those people are asleep. Nobody's checking anything out."

She turned the screen toward him. Her query joined members to checkouts and filtered for members whose checkout count was zero, and it returned nothing, a clean and empty grid, which was somehow worse than an error. Marcus leaned in with the confidence of someone who had finished a coding camp the previous summer and forgotten most of it.

"Your join eats them," he said, mostly to himself, scrolling through her SQL. "Before your filter even runs."

"That's not how it works," Eve said, though a cold feeling suggested otherwise. "A join just connects the tables."

They argued about it in whispers for ten minutes, the way they had argued since seventh grade, while a man at the next station asked them twice to lower their voices. The deadline sat in the corner of Eve's mind the way a test sat at the front of a classroom. She thought about the members in the database who had cards and had never once borrowed a book. Somewhere in the join, she realized, they were simply gone, and she could not say where.

"Run it without the filter," Marcus said finally. She deleted the WHERE clause, executed, and the grid filled with four hundred rows of members who had checkouts attached. She scrolled and scrolled. Her list had every active borrower in it, and none of the others. The join itself was the filter. It returned only rows that had a match in both tables, so the members with no checkouts disappeared from its results entirely, before any condition she wrote could ever find them. She sat back. All morning she had trusted the empty result as an answer instead of asking what question it was actually answering.

"LEFT JOIN," Marcus said, and she typed it before he finished the word, keeping every member from the left table whether or not a match existed, then filtering for nulls. The query ran. The number that came back was two hundred and eleven, and beneath it the names: people who had signed up at the summer fair, people who had moved, people who had apparently wanted only the quiet.

Ms. Okafor arrived at the reference desk at four forty with a folder and a pen she kept clicking. Eve printed the list and carried it over, conscious of her heartbeat, and explained what she had found: not that the library had no inactive members, but that her first query had been built in a way that could never see them. Ms. Okafor read the first page slowly. She read the second page more slowly.

"You're on here," she said.

Eve leaned over the desk. There was her own name, her own card number, in the column of members who had never borrowed anything. She had signed the form in September, the week she started volunteering, thinking she would use the library constantly. Since then she had come every Tuesday, sat at the back bay, taught herself queries, argued with Marcus, and carried every fact she needed in on her own two feet.

"Fix it," Ms. Okafor said, clicking the pen once and handing it to her. "Cross your name off. Then we'll talk about the two hundred and ten."

Nathaniel had been at his grandmother's house for three days, and the ten-minute play was due in nine, and so far he had produced a title ("The Fight") and a stage direction ("A kitchen. Evening."). His grandmother, who had spent forty years in community theater and referred to her own retirement as "between engagements," had converted the dining room table into a writer's desk by putting a vase of dandelions on it, which she called his muse.

The problem was the scene itself. It was about the night his sister Priya came home two hours late and he told their mother before she got to tell her herself, and how she'd stood in the doorway of his room afterward and said, "Nice, Nathaniel. Really nice." He had written it out faithfully, and read it back, and it was terrible. Everyone said exactly what they felt. His mother said, "I'm very angry and also worried." Priya said, "I feel betrayed by you." On the page they sounded like robots filing complaints.

His grandmother drifted past with a watering can and peered over his shoulder. "Everyone is announcing things," she said. "People don't announce. People conceal." She watered a fern that had clearly been dead since spring, then set the can down and delivered a line with sudden, alarming tenderness: "Lovely weather we're having." Then, in the same breath, flatly: "That's what I said to your grandfather the day the bank called." She picked up the can and left, which Nathaniel was beginning to understand was her version of a master class.

He sat with that. He tried writing a scene where two characters talked about the weather while meaning something else entirely, and it was worse, because he had no idea what they meant. He was a virtuoso of saying nothing, apparently, but he had no talent for meaning something. He crossed out four pages. He ate a granola bar his grandmother had bought in bulk in 2019, because she was penurious in the specific way of a person who had once been genuinely poor and now simply distrusted expiration dates.

That evening she cornered him after dinner. "Read it to me," she said, arranging herself on the sofa like a panel of judges. "All of it. Don't forestall me with excuses about drafts. A play exists when someone listens."

He read. When he got to the robot mother saying she was very angry and also worried, his grandmother winced so theatrically he worried for her face. But when he got to Priya's "Nice, Nathaniel. Really nice," she held up one hand.

"That one's real," she said. "Why?"

"Because that's what she actually said."

"And what did she mean by it?"

He thought about the doorway, the way Priya had looked at his shoes instead of his face. "Not nice things."

"So write the scene again, but take out everything they mean, and keep only what they say."

He started the rewrite that night at the kitchen table. The mother didn't say she was angry. She said, "There's leftover pasta," and put a plate in front of Priya, and stood there while Priya didn't eat it. Priya didn't say she felt betrayed. She asked Nathaniel how his history paper was going, in the tone of someone offering him one last chance to say the right thing, and he said it was going fine. Ten minutes, he realized, was almost too much time for how little people would say to each other in that kitchen. The whole fight was going to happen underneath.

The next morning he read the new version aloud to his grandmother, doing all the parts, holding the pasta plate for the mother. When he finished, she was quiet for a moment, which frightened him more than any wince.

"Say it," he said. "What's wrong with it."

"Nothing's wrong with it. I want to know what you'd call what you did. You wrote all the feeling, and then you buried it."

"Subtext," he said, surprising himself with how quickly the word arrived. "Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say. The anger and the love that the lines never name out loud." It was from a book he'd skimmed in the school library in April, a whole chapter he'd skipped because it had seemed abstract, and here it was, sitting in his grandmother's parlor in the shape of a plate of uneaten pasta.

"Love?" she said, cocking her head. "Where's the love in this scene? Nobody loves anybody in this scene."

He looked at his pages. The mother making pasta nobody asked for. Priya asking about his paper at all instead of walking past his door. Him saying "it's going fine" when the right answer, the one that might have fixed things, was "I shouldn't have told her before you could." Everyone in the scene was angry, and everyone was doing something kind, and nobody would admit either one.

"I don't know if it ends right," he said. "The real night didn't end right. Priya just went to her room."

"So let your play do the same thing," his grandmother said. "We are not in the business of fixing kitchens, dear. We're in the business of standing in the doorway."

For the staged reading, she insisted on full ceremony. She dragged the armchair to center parlor for the mother, positioned the coffee table as the counter, and cast herself as director with a pencil for a baton. "Places," she called, though the cast was one seventeen-year-old boy and a teapot. Nathaniel picked up the pasta plate, faced the armchair, and delivered his first line, which was no line at all, just a silence in which somebody, somewhere under the words, hoped to be forgiven.

His grandmother tapped the pencil against her knee. "Again," she said. "But this time, be sorrier."

The bus from campus dropped them at the edge of the memorial park just after ten, and Addison unfolded the paper her professor had photocopied for anyone who wanted the extra trip: two pages from a 1965 book called Atomic Diplomacy, by Gar Alperovitz, and beside it a paragraph from a textbook that disagreed with him. Her roommate, Priya, had come along mostly for the autumn air and the bakery near the visitors' center, and she was already eating a maple scone as they walked toward the low granite wall where the names began.

"So which one are we supposed to believe," Priya asked, brushing crumbs from her jacket, "the book or the book?"

"That's the assignment. Weigh them against the evidence." Addison had said it lightly, but she had been carrying the two excerpts around for a week like a stone in her pocket, reading them on the bus, in line at the dining hall, in bed before the lamp went off. Alperovitz argued that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. The textbook called that overreach, an argument stretched past what the documents could hold.

They stopped where the wall turned a corner and a small bronze plaque mapped the Pacific theater. An older man in a veterans' cap was standing there, squinting at it, and when Priya leaned in to look he shifted half a step aside to give them room without being asked. Addison noticed that. She noticed, too, that his hands were unsteady on his cane, and before she thought about it she said, "There's a bench in the shade, if you want it," and he thanked her in a voice like dry paper but stayed standing.

"My grandfather was on a ship headed for Japan in August of forty-five," Priya said quietly, once the man had drifted toward the wall of names. "The invasion fleet. He always said the bombs were the last act of the Second World War. They saved him."

"Alperovitz would say they were the first act of the Cold War," Addison said. "Gar Alperovitz, in Atomic Diplomacy, 1965. He argued the bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union. Partly. Not only."

Priya demurred, holding up one crumb-dusted finger. "Partly is a slippery word. It lets him claim everything and prove only something."

"I know." Addison sat down on the bench after all, and Priya sat beside her and split the second scone in half without comment, handing half over. The kindness of it steadied her more than she admitted. "That's actually what I keep circling. The textbook says the timing was military, that Japan was already collapsing but not surrendering, that the invasion plans were real and enormous. Alperovitz says look at who the diplomats were watching. Neither of them shows you the whole board."

The veterans' cap moved slowly along the wall, pausing at certain names. Addison watched him and found she could not summon the mild ennui that had been sitting on her all semester, that grey flattening of everything lectures had begun to produce. This was different. Two explanations, both speaking to the same August, and the evidence thin and contested and mostly locked in the heads of men who were now leaving, one by one, like the man in the cap, whose hand rose once to touch the granite and then fell back to the cane.

"You're doing the thing," Priya said. "The thing where you argue with yourself out loud and expect me to keep score."

"Keep score, then. My grandfather figure, your grandfather, the invasion fleet. That's evidence the bombings belong to the Second World War. The Soviet warning, the timing, that's evidence for Alperovitz's reading, the Cold War already starting inside the ending. Both can be true at once. A decision can have more than one reason." She turned the photocopied pages over, as if the backs might confess something, and found only library stamps.

Priya was quiet for a moment, which for her was nearly unheard. "My grandfather never talked about it like history," she said finally. "He talked about it like weather. Something that happened to him. Maybe that's the part your two historians can't get at. They're both writing about the century, and he was just standing under it."

The man in the cap had reached the end of the wall. Addison stood, gathered the papers, and walked over to ask him, before she could lose her nerve, whether he had been in the Pacific. He said he had been a radio operator, that he was seventeen then, younger than she was now, and that he did not care what the books said because he had carried the codebooks and the codebooks did not care either. Then he looked at her more closely and asked, "So what do your books say, anyway?" and Addison heard herself answer, "I don't know yet. That's what I'm trying to figure out," and he laughed, a small dry sound, and said, "Good. Keep it that way," and tapped the wall once with his cane.

Justin had been told twice that the marble slab was cold, and twice he had still pressed his palm flat against it to check, as though Chef Rios might have been exaggerating. The kitchen at Merle's ran its ovens all afternoon, so the corner by the pastry station stayed steamy and bright, and the marble, hauled out of the fridge an hour early, sweated under the lights like everything else in the room.

He had the bowl of melted chocolate at ninety-two degrees and the spatula in his right hand, and the whole business was supposed to be simple. Move the chocolate across the marble, spread it thin, scrape it back, cool it down to eighty-one, warm it back to eighty-eight, and it would set shiny and snap clean when you broke it. That was tempering. Justin had watched four videos on his phone in the break room, and in every one the chocolate behaved like a contrivance, obedient and glossy, gliding wherever the demo cook pushed it. His first attempt that morning had gone dull and streaky, and the batch after that had set soft, bending instead of snapping, like a crayon left in a car.

"You're beating air into it," Dess said from the dish pit, not unkindly. Dess was the senior line cook, laconic by nature, and Justin had learned in two weeks that when Dess offered more than five words, the situation was serious. Dess had also, on Justin's first day, made him taste a strawberry that had been dipped in badly tempered chocolate, and the wax had clung to the roof of his mouth for an hour. Justin took that as a kind of inculcation, the way this kitchen taught things: not by lecture but by consequence.

The problem, as Justin saw it, was that the videos treated the chocolate like a machine with settings, and the kitchen treated it like an animal with moods. He had spent most of his senior year studying chemistry the first way, believing that if you knew the numbers, you controlled the outcome. His father, a carpenter, had always insisted the opposite, that you learned material by ruining some of it first. Justin had argued with him about it at graduation, in a half-regretted exchange over cake, and he had meant to prove the numbers method worked here, in his first real kitchen job, before college started in the fall.

So he worked the batch again, checking the thermometer like scripture, and this time it came out right: a thin stripe on the tip of a knife, set in the fridge's back shelf for two minutes, hard and glassy. He pulled it out into the humid kitchen to test the snap, and it broke with a sound like a small icicle. Then he watched the surface change. Within a minute, a dry, gritty white film crept across the top of the test piece, powdery where it had been mirror-smooth. He touched it with one fingertip and it felt like sand.

"That's sugar bloom," Dess said, coming over with a stack of plates. "Cold out of the fridge, humid in here. Moisture gets on the surface, the sugar dissolves, then the sugar recrystallizes as it dries. Dries gritty."

Justin looked at the ruined stripe, then at the fridge, then at his thermometer, which still read exactly what it was supposed to read. "So the tempering was right," he said slowly, "and I wrecked it afterward."

"Chocolate you made perfect thirty seconds ago." Dess stacked the plates on the shelf and went back to the pit.

Justin stood there with the grit on his finger. His instinct was to argue that the method had not failed, only the conditions, but he could hear his father in that distinction and had to admit it was a thin wall to hide behind. The numbers were necessary; he had needed the thermometer to get anywhere at all. They were just not sufficient, because the chocolate also lived in a humid room, on a sweating slab, in the hands of somebody who had never done this before. He set the bloomed stripe aside, wiped the marble dry with a fresh towel, and started a third batch, but this time he moved the testing to the doorway of the walk-in, where he could cool the sample and break it without carrying it through the steam. He also wiped the knife blade dry first, which the videos had never mentioned and which felt, in his hands, like the beginning of actual knowledge.

The third batch tempered clean, and he broke the test piece in the doorway's cold breath, and it snapped. He held the two halves up and looked at them, shiny as tar, no bloom yet, and he did not know whether one good batch meant anything. It might be luck. It might be the towel, the doorway, the temperature, or some alignment he could not name, and he would not know until he ruined another one tomorrow. Dess drifted past with a bus tub and glanced at the pieces without stopping.

"Same time tomorrow," Dess said. "Bring a dry towel."

Justin wrote "DRY TOWEL" on the corner of his prep list, underlined it twice, and pocketed the two halves of chocolate still shining under the pass's heat lamp.

I was not nervous about the placement exam, and I had not spent three days pretending to study while actually scrolling through my phone, which is what my sister claimed. What I had done was spread my materials across the kitchen table in an orderly fashion: the review packet, graph paper, a borrowed calculator, and a wooden ruler that belonged to my father's old drafting kit. The packet said a passing score would let me skip introductory calculus in the fall, which mattered to me only because Priya Nair had already tested out, and I mention that as context, not as a motive.

Priya herself was at my kitchen table, because our mothers had arranged it, not because I asked. She had founded the math club at our school and had a way of proselytizing about calculus that made you feel like a person who simply hadn't heard the good news yet. "It's not about the formulas," she said, arranging her pencils. "It's about seeing what a function is doing." I said I could see what a function was doing fine, which was true in the sense that I could look at a parabola and tell which end was up.

The problem she wrote out was a polynomial, some cubic with a coefficient I'd have to check against my memory later, and the question was to find its maximum on a given stretch of the graph. "You differentiate," she said, "and then you look for where the derivative is zero." I nodded as though this was a formality. I differentiated on my own paper, in pencil, and got something, and she leaned over and said, "You dropped a sign," and I said I hadn't, and then I looked and I had. I told her the pencil had smeared. She let that go, which I took as generosity at the time.

Here is the part I got wrong first, and I'm stating it plainly because there's no other honest way to state it. She said, "The derivative at a point equals the slope of the tangent line there." I wrote down the number I'd computed, set it against the graph, and declared that the maximum was at a spot that was, in fact, not the maximum. I was not embarrassed. I remember being entirely calm, though my sister, passing through for a glass of juice, later said I had said "whatever" four times in one minute.

Priya did not argue with me. She took my ruler instead and laid it along the curve on the graph paper, tilting it until it touched the curve at exactly one point near where I'd claimed the maximum was. "Tangent," she said. "Look at the ruler. It's climbing." The ruler was, visibly, tilted upward, climbing, and a line that is climbing has a positive slope, and she said, "Your derivative here should be positive. If you got zero, something's off." Then she slid the ruler along the curve, small movement by small movement, until the tilt flattened, until the ruler lay level, touching the curve at the true peak, and the slope of that tangent line was zero. My computed derivative at that same point was zero. The two agreed. The maximum sat right where the ruler said it did.

I checked the arithmetic and found the dropped sign had migrated, or a new one had appeared, and after correcting it my numbers matched the ruler's verdict at every point we tested. I said, "I basically had it," and Priya said nothing, and I want to be accurate: she was not effusive, she was not even particularly warm about it, and I preferred that to the alternative, though at the time I told her I appreciated her enthusiasm.

We worked through two more problems. Somewhere in the second one she mentioned that half the math club had quit by October last year, that the attrition was brutal, and that the ones who stayed were the ones who stopped trying to be right on the first try. I said the club sounded like it had a retention problem, not a math problem. She said, "Sure," and squared her graph paper against the table's edge.

What stays uncertain for me is whether I could have found the error without the ruler. I believe I would have, eventually, by checking the function's values on either side of my supposed maximum, the way the packet's second method suggested. But I had declared the wrong answer with complete confidence, and the ruler had disagreed with me, and the ruler had been right. That is a fact about the ruler and about the slope and about the tangent line, and I am leaving it as that.

Priya packed up at nine. She left the graph paper with the flattened ruler-line penciled faintly across the peak, and at the door she said, "Same time Thursday." I said I'd check my calendar, and then I sat back down and wrote Thursday on the back of the placement packet, twice, and circled one of them.

The office smelled like toner and the faint sweetness of someone's birthday cake, three cubicles over, already reduced to crumbs on a paper plate. Faith sat at her mother's desk while her mother was in a meeting, a database textbook open beside her, because she had asked for exactly this: something to do over spring break that wasn't homework. Her mother, in a fit of either generosity or desperation, had also given her a copy of the customer orders report and said, "See if you can figure out who never ordered anything. The report says nobody. The report is wrong."

Faith liked that sentence. The report is wrong. It sounded like the beginning of a detective story, or at least the middle of one, the part where the detective already knows something the report writer doesn't. She typed her first query into the practice window, joining customers to orders, and the machine answered her in the only way it ever would: with a table, silent and certain, every customer showing a count of at least one.

She sat back. Maybe the report was right and her mother was wrong, which happened, occasionally, though never about spreadsheets. But her mother had printed a highlighted list of names, hand-verified, customers whose accounts had gone quiet for a year and who should therefore have shown nothing. Should a person be able to show nothing? Faith wondered. It seemed like the kind of thing a system ought to be able to say, and yet the query kept insisting otherwise, cheerfully, a witness with no memory of the crime.

She reread the chapter on joins, which she had skimmed the night before in an embryonic way, the way you read anything at eleven at night, understanding arriving and departing like tides. A LEFT JOIN, she gathered, kept all the customers even when there were no orders to match them. So far so good. The mystery wasn't the join. The mystery was the counting. Her report counted rows after the join, and after a LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders still got a row, a row the join had filled with blanks. If you counted that row, everyone had something. Her mother's highlighted names were drowning in blankness being counted as substance.

Faith tried the other count. She wrote it carefully, counting the order number column instead of counting everything, and ran it again. The table redraw itself. There, near the top, was Alderman Papers, count of zero. Then Corbett, zero. Then four more names she recognized from her mother's highlighter. The blanks, when you counted only the real order numbers, added up to nothing, which was, she thought, what nothing was supposed to do. It felt almost like a trick of grammar, like the difference between "everyone said something" and "everyone spoke," a distinction so small it could hide an entire mistaken report inside it.

Her mother came back with a paper cup of coffee and stood behind her, reading over her shoulder the way mothers do, one hand on the chair back. "So what was it?"

"After a LEFT JOIN, counting the orders column gives zero for customers without orders, but counting everything gives one, because of the blank-filled row," Faith said. "I was counting everything."

Her mother made a small sound, half laugh, half sigh of a person who had spent a morning suspecting the universe and could now go back to suspecting only software. "That's the whole report, then. That's three days of arguing with accounting." She set the coffee down without drinking it, which Faith understood to be the highest compliment available. "Can you fix the real one?"

"Probably," Faith said, though she was already less sure than the word implied. She had made one query work. She did not yet know what else the report assumed, what other quiet blanks were being counted as facts, whether the same error lived in the quarterly numbers or only here. The fix was easy; the trust was harder. She copied her query into a new file, typed her initials at the top, and paused with her fingers over the keys, wondering how many true things in the world looked exactly like this, one small counting decision, invisible until somebody asked to see the zeros.

She ran it once more before changing anything, just to watch the zeros appear again, six small integers standing in a column like evidence. Behind her, someone finally threw away the paper plate.

The community centre had the smell of floor wax and instant coffee, and the room they'd been given was spartan enough that every voice carried: folding chairs in a horseshoe, a whiteboard with half a ghosted diagram still on it, a table of borrowed civics textbooks nobody touched. Avery arrived early because the sheet she'd printed said arrive early, though it didn't say much else. Model Parliament Workshop, Tuesdays, Room B. She'd told her mother it would look good on her application. She'd told herself it would be easy, since she'd done the reading, sort of, in the car.

There were nine of them. The facilitator, a second-year university student named Priya with a clipboard and a lanyard, wrote two columns on the whiteboard and said almost nothing else, which Avery found either brilliant or negligent. The columns were headed PARLIAMENTARY and PRESIDENTIAL, and the group's job, apparently, was to fill them. A boy called Marcus, who'd introduced himself by saying he'd argued with his grandfather about this for an hour at Thanksgiving, went first. "Nobody even voted for our prime minister," he said. "I asked my grandma at her place, like, why does he get to be in charge, and she said that's just how it works. That can't be how it works."

Avery, who wanted the room to know she had prepared, sort of, said the prime minister was chosen the same way a president was, basically, except without the big national race. She heard the sentence leave her mouth and immediately disliked it, the way you dislike a text the second after you send it. Priya didn't correct her. She wrote nothing in either column and moved on, and the absence of correction was worse than correction, because now Avery couldn't tell whether she'd been right or merely ignored.

The exercise turned into an argument about removal. Marcus insisted a president could only be forced out through impeachment, which he described with more confidence than detail, and a girl in a lacrosse hoodie said no, the whole thing was that you could just vote the leader out. "You can't just vote a prime minister out," Avery said, "there's no election to lose." And then she stopped, because she was no longer sure which column she was defending, or whether the thing she'd said an hour ago in the car, underlining lines with a dying pen, had been the same thing. She could feel the two columns pulling in different directions on the whiteboard and she did not know which one she had been reading from.

During the break she went to the textbook table after all. She found the page by accident, or by something adjacent to accident, since she'd been avoiding it on purpose. The passage was short. It said that in a parliamentary system, the head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election. She read it three times. Nobody voted directly for the prime minister at all, that was the whole point; the job lasted exactly as long as the legislature's confidence did, and not a day past it. Marcus had been right at his grandmother's kitchen table and hadn't known why. Avery had been wrong in a folding chair and now did. She looked up and Priya was watching her from across the room, marker uncapped, waiting to see what she'd do with it.

When they reconvened, Avery asked to go back to the whiteboard. "I got it backwards before," she said. "There's no separate popular election for the prime minister at all. The office stands or falls on the legislature's confidence. That's the difference. That's the whole difference, or the first difference, anyway." Marcus said, quietly, "So my grandma wasn't dodging the question." Priya wrote it in the parliamentary column, the exact sentence, and for the first time that afternoon the room had something on the board that was true.

Then Priya turned the clipboard around, and Avery learned what the workshop actually was. Two spots, for the provincial model parliament in the spring, chosen by the end of tonight; the rest of the Tuesdays were for the two who made it. She had prepared for a class and had been auditioning the whole time. Every confident wrong thing she'd said was on somebody's scorecard. Priya asked each of them one final question, going around the horseshoe, and when she reached Avery the question was not the one Avery had braced for. "Now that you know you were wrong," Priya said, "argue the side you argued against."

Avery stood up. The room was quiet in the way rooms get when everyone has decided at once to pay attention, and outside, someone dragged chairs across the gym floor, a long scrape that slowed and stopped. She thought of the two columns, of her grandmother's kitchen where Marcus had asked a better question than any she had asked all day, of how little she still understood about what confidence actually meant when it broke. "A prime minister never faces the voters alone," she said. "So I'll start there."

The library had that smell of carpet cleaner and old glue, and Kate had claimed the carrel by the window before anyone else could, spreading out her laptop, two printed articles, and a highlighter she immediately lost in her sleeve. The assignment was due Friday: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles that answered the same question. Her question, chosen three weeks ago with more confidence than she now felt, was whether reading disability was mostly inherited or mostly made by environment. The two articles disagreed completely, which was the point of the assignment, and which was also the problem.

The first article, by a researcher named Okafor, argued from twin studies that reading disability was substantially genetic. Kate had understood about two-thirds of it, and the part she had understood had mesmerized her: identical twins raised apart, turning out to struggle with print in eerily similar ways, their vocabularies and decoding speeds tracking each other across different countries and different schools. The tables of correlations looked like weather maps of a single climate.

The second article, by a Dr. Lindqvist, was leaner and angrier. It claimed that the genetic studies overreached, that what looked heritable in childhood was largely a function of schools sorting kids into book-rich and book-poor worlds. One line had stuck with her all week: calling genetics "the last refuge of those who would rather not fund libraries."

She was stuck between them the way you get stuck between two people at a party who are both right about the other and wrong about themselves. She wrote a sentence, deleted it, wrote it again. Her friend Priya slid into the opposite chair and peered at the pages.

"Which one are you arguing for?"

"That's the thing," Kate said. "I keep flip-flopping. Okafor has the better data. Lindqvist has the better conscience."

Priya snorted. "That's a whole essay right there."

But it wasn't, and Kate knew it. A review that said "both sides have merit" was a bromide, the intellectual equivalent of a fortune cookie, and her teacher had explicitly banned the phrase "more research is needed" in any conclusion. She needed something true to say, and she didn't have it.

Priya left for class. Kate sat turning her highlighter over and over, watching the two stacks of pages as if they might speak to each other. What did researchers do, she wondered, when two studies pointed in opposite directions? Did they just take sides forever? It seemed like an obvious question, and the obviousness of it made her suspicious that someone had already asked it. She opened the library database and typed, feeling slightly absurd, reading disability genetics versus environment pooled studies.

The result that came up made her sit forward. Its title named decades of twin studies, dozens of them, and the word in the method line was one she didn't know. Meta-analysis. She read the abstract twice. Instead of one study with one sample, this paper had gathered every qualifying study on the question, dozens of separate samples, and pooled their results to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could on its own. The estimates that had looked so solid in each individual paper wobbled when set beside their neighbors. Okafor's headline number sat at the low end of the pooled range. Lindqvist's dismissal sat outside it entirely.

She found the full text through the library's journal portal and skimmed to the results, and that was when she stopped, hand still on the trackpad. The author list had three names. The second one was Okafor. The third was Lindqvist.

Kate read the acknowledgments, the author notes, the conflict-of-interest statement, anything that would explain it. There was nothing dramatic, just the ordinary machinery of scholarship: these two people who had written what looked like warring articles had, some years later, combined their data with everyone else's and written a quieter paper together saying, in effect, that the truth was smaller and harder to pin down than either of them had claimed. The pooled estimate landed between their positions, with wide uncertainty around the heritable share, and a paragraph noting that phenotypic measures of reading, the actual observed skills, couldn't cleanly separate inherited potential from accumulated environment over ten years of a child's life.

She turned in her chair and looked out the window at the parking lot, the row of scraggly birches, a bus idling. The two loud articles were still loud. The quiet one, the one that had done the boring work of gathering everything, was the one telling the truth, or something closer to it, and nobody had assigned it, and it had shown up in no one's syllabus. She wondered how often that was the shape of things: the argument you notice, and the pooling nobody notices.

She opened a new document and typed a first sentence she actually believed. "Okafor and Lindqvist disagree more with each other than either disagrees with the combined evidence." Then she paused, cursor blinking, because she had to be honest about what stayed uncertain. She didn't delete it. She wrote underneath: "The pooled estimate narrows the question without settling it."

At the next carrel over, a boy dropped an entire stack of books, and Kate looked up and laughed before she could stop herself.

"What?" he said, gathering them.

"Nothing. I just found out two people who fight about everything wrote a paper together."

"Huh," he said, and sat back down. Kate turned to her screen and began the second paragraph.

Sophie had chosen her grandmother's house because it was quiet, and quiet was what she needed, because tomorrow morning at nine she had to stand in front of a examiner she had never met and debate immigration policy for five minutes, entirely in Spanish. She had three arguments about border policy and a stack of note cards, and she had told her grandmother she was here to study, which was true in the way most convenient statements are true.

She set up at the kitchen table while her grandmother shelled peas on the porch, the screen door half-open between them. Sophie had a year of Spanish behind her, a good grade in it, and a fluency in English that she could wield like a scalpel. At school she had been the one classmates half-annoyedly lionized before debates, the girl who could take either side of an argument and win both. She had assumed, in the casual way of people who have never been tested, that the ideas would carry her through, that Spanish was just a costume her arguments could wear.

She stood up, phone timer set to five minutes, and began. "La política de inmigración debe ser más humana," she said, and then hit the first gap almost immediately. She wanted to say that the system punished people for circumstances they couldn't control. She had the word for punish. She did not have the word for circumstances, or control, or, she realized with a slow cold feeling, system.

She sat back down. She tried again, and again the sentence collapsed somewhere in the middle, this time when she reached for the idea of causality, the whole spine of her argument, the reason she could claim that policy caused suffering rather than merely coinciding with it. She knew the concept cold in English. In Spanish it simply was not there. She had read a thing on her study app last week, a linguist named Merrill Swain, something called the output hypothesis, the idea that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn. At the time she had scrolled past it, because it had seemed abstract, and now she thought: this is what it means. She had felt fluent, and fluency had been a room she'd only seen with the lights off. Every time she opened her mouth she found another wall.

There were four hours until dark, and dark was when she had promised her mother she would drive home, which made this less a study session than a countdown. She changed tactics. Instead of translating her three arguments, she rebuilt them from the Spanish she actually had, shorter sentences, simpler nouns, and where the language ran out she rerouted. She couldn't say circumstances, so she said vidas, lives, and pointed the argument at lives instead. It was clumsier. It was also, she noticed, harder to hide behind. The clause that had sounded sophisticated in English now had to earn its place or get cut.

She was halfway through a run-through, gesturing at the window, when the screen door opened and her grandmother came in with the bowl of peas and said, in Spanish, calm and unhurried, "Do you really believe that, or is it just what's easy to argue?"

Sophie's mouth stayed open. Her grandmother had lived in El Paso for forty years and had, as far as Sophie knew, a vocabulary of kitchen words and pleasantries, honed at church and the tortillería, never once deployed on her granddaughter. It had never occurred to Sophie to wonder why that was.

"Abuela. You speak it. You've been listening the whole time."

"Only some of it. The parts through the door." Her grandmother sat down across from her and pushed the bowl aside. "Again, from the top. Five minutes. And this time, when you don't know a word, don't stop. Say it wrong and keep going. That's how you find the holes."

"Para eso sirve," Sophie said slowly, half to herself, meaning that was the point of it, and then she began again, watching her grandmother's face for the flinches that would mark the gaps, because those flinches, she understood now, were a map. Two minutes in, her grandmother raised one finger at a verb Sophie had mangled, and Sophie noted it and kept moving, and when she reached the part about which arguments were truly germane to policy and which were only sentiment dressed up as reason, her grandmother nodded, once, without smiling.

"Better," her grandmother said, when the timer sounded. Then she stood, lifted the bowl of peas, and added, in English, as though it cost her nothing: "Tomorrow, after your exam, you'll call me and tell me how it went. In Spanish."

Hunter spread the two books across the kitchen table at ten o'clock on a Tuesday, one propped against the fruit bowl, the other flat under the lamp. One was by a historian named Reisman, the other by a woman named Kovac, and between them they disagreed about nearly everything, which was the whole problem, because Friday's essay asked him to decide who was right.

The disagreement itself was simple enough to state. Reisman argued that the United States had exaggerated the Soviet threat, that domestic politics and a fondness for enemies explained the Red Scare better than any real danger did. Kovac argued the danger had been real, the spy networks real, the paranoia ugly but grounded. Each had footnotes. Each had conviction. Hunter had a stack of index cards and a bag of pretzels and no idea which way to lean.

His mother came through the kitchen, still in her scrubs from a double shift, looking for the yogurt she'd hidden behind the orange juice. She taught nursing, not history, but she had opinions about essays anyway. "You're supposed to pick a side," she said, spoon in hand. "That's what the rubric wants. A thesis." What she wanted, Hunter had learned, was for him to stop worrying things past the point of usefulness, which was a habit she blamed on his father and his father blamed on her.

"I don't have a side yet. I have two books and they don't even agree on the facts."

"Then find the facts." She pointed her spoon at the library stack by the window, five more books he'd dragged home because one of his teachers had said, once, that real research meant reading against your own first impression. Hunter had been trying to do that all week, and mostly it felt like being handed two maps of the same city drawn by people who hated each other.

He went back to it after she went upstairs. Reisman's prose was turgid in places, paragraphs that circled the same claim three times before landing on it, and Hunter found himself skimming, then feeling guilty about skimming, then reading the footnotes anyway. That was where he noticed the dates. Reisman's book had come out in 1989. Kovac's had come out in 2001. He sat with that for a moment, pretzel halfway to his mouth, because it seemed to matter, though he couldn't yet say why.

He pulled the laptop over and searched. What he found sent him back to the kitchen for a legal pad, because this was the thing: the Venona decrypts, Soviet intelligence messages the US government had decrypted and finally released in 1995, had confirmed that Soviet spy networks really had operated inside the United States. Reisman had written six years before that release. He could not have seen the decrypted messages; no one outside a small circle could have. Kovac had written after, and her footnotes cited the decrypts directly, page after page of them. Hunter wrote it all down, the dates lined up in his terrible handwriting, and felt something shift that wasn't yet a conclusion but was close to one. Evidence had arrived in the middle of the argument, like a witness walking into the courtroom after the lawyers had already begun.

But it didn't settle everything, and Hunter was honest enough with himself to know it. He read Kovac's chapters again, looking for places where she leaned too hard on the new material, places where she seemed to valorize the American intelligence apparatus because it had turned out to be right about the spying. And he found a few. She had a paragraph on the Rosenbergs that read more like a verdict than an argument. Reisman, for all his blindness, had been good on the ugliness of the loyalty boards, good on careers ended by rumor, and Hunter couldn't make that disappear just because the decrypts had proven one of his premises wrong. One man being mistaken about the spy networks didn't make him mistaken about the hearings.

His father called at eleven, as he sometimes did, from his apartment across town, and Hunter told him about the essay because there was nothing else to tell him. His father wanted him to visit the following weekend, wanted it in the careful sideways way he always asked, and Hunter said maybe, and meant it, and changed the subject back to history because history was easier. He explained the problem, the two books, the release of the documents in 1995, the way the whole field had to be rewritten in the middle of some people's careers. His father said, "That's quite a bind," and then, quieter, "Some choices you make without the whole picture. Doesn't always mean you chose wrong." Hunter wasn't sure his father was talking about historians anymore. He wasn't sure he was supposed to ask.

He wrote until one in the morning, filling a page and a half with a position he could actually stand behind: that Kovac was more persuasive about the reality of the espionage and less persuasive about its meaning, that Reisman had been working blind but not dishonest, and that the part he couldn't resolve, how much fear was justified once the fear had already done its damage, he would leave unresolved in the essay and take the grade that came. It was the kind of answer that wouldn't fit neatly on a rubric. His mother would say he was overthinking it. His father would say he was thinking it exactly the right amount.

In the morning he found his mother at the table with his legal pad, reading his notes over her coffee. She didn't look up when he came in. "You didn't pick a side," she said.

"I picked what I could defend."

The synagogue's social hall smelled of coffee and floor wax when Sienna arrived with three grocery bags and her grandmother's Haggadah boxed under one arm. Rabbi Fox had given her the key that afternoon, along with a clipboard listing what the families had signed up to bring, and Sienna had spent the drive rehearsing the order of the blessing over the candles, which she had only ever watched her grandfather recite. He was in hospice now, his voice down to a ribbon, and at Purim he had pressed the old book into her hands and said only, "You know more than you think."

She began by requisitioning the long folding tables from the storage closet, startling Mr. Adler, who was arranging chairs and who insisted on carrying the heavy ends himself. By six the hall had filled. Her parents came with her little brother, and her aunt and uncle, and then, hovering near the sign that said FIRST NIGHT SEDER, WELCOME, came a girl from Sienna's chem class named Priya, who had texted that morning asking if she could come because her roommate was away and the dorm was too quiet.

Sienna poured grape juice into the silver Kiddush cup and its paper-cup companions, and began. She stumbled on the second blessing, recovered, and felt her ears burn, but nobody laughed. Her little brother asked the Four Questions in a monotone that made Priya smile into her sleeve. When they reached the plate at the center of the table, Priya leaned toward it, curious and a little wary of the horseradish root and the shank bone and the pastel heap of charoset.

"That's maror," Sienna said. "Bitter herbs. Horseradish, usually. We eat them on purpose, to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt."

Priya looked at the root, then at the faces around the table. "You eat something bitter deliberately. At a party."

"At the exact opposite of a party," Sienna said. "Or the exact same thing. I've been arguing with myself about it all week." She held up the Haggadah, its spine cracked to softness. "My grandfather says the whole night is hermeneutics, that every generation has to read itself into the story, and for years I thought that was just something old men say to sound important. But tonight I keep catching myself doing it."

She distributed the maror, and Priya took her piece with the others, and Sienna watched her cousin Daniel, home from his first year of college and freshly bellicose about every tradition he'd grown up with, glare at the horseradish like it had personally insulted him. "This is performative suffering," he announced. "You can't taste someone else's slavery."

"You're not supposed to taste theirs," Sienna said. "You're supposed to notice what bitterness does in your own mouth, and then notice how fast you want it gone." She hadn't planned to say that. It came out of the week of reading, of the notes her grandfather had left in the margins in his cramped hand, and it landed in the room and sat there.

Daniel chewed his maror with theatrical resentment, eyes watering, and then said, unexpectedly, "Okay. That's actually not stupid." Priya's eyes were watering too, and she laughed while she cried, and Sienna's mother passed the charoset quickly down the table like a rescue line.

Later, after the meal, after the front door had been opened for Elijah and the night air had come in cold and smelling of rain, Sienna stood to lead the grace after the meal and found that her hands were steady. Daniel was humming along with the Chad Gadya under his breath, having declared it capitalist propaganda and then learned all six verses anyway. Priya had taken one of the extra Haggadot and was reading ahead, mouthing the words.

At the sink in the kitchen, washing the silver cup, Sienna thought about texting her grandfather a photo of the table. She typed and deleted three drafts. She didn't know yet whether she believed the way he believed, or whether the bitterness and the sweetness sat in any kind of order she could name, and she suspected she wouldn't know for years. What she knew was the cup in her hands and the sound of her family's voices carrying the last verses from the hall, and that seemed like enough to hold for one night.

She dried the cup, set it upright on the towel, and walked back in as they reached the final line, and she sang it louder than anyone.

The cones in the church parking lot had been Grandpa's idea, set out with a tape measure to the exact length of the testing space, fourteen paces he counted aloud each morning as though the number might change overnight. Michael had failed the test once already, in March, for a parallel park so crooked the examiner had leaned out the window to check whether the tires were still touching the curb's country. His father's response had been a lecture about humility and practice, delivered across the dinner table with the flat certainty of a man who had not sat behind a wheel of any kind since selling the station wagon. His grandfather's response was the cones.

"Hands at nine and three," Grandpa said from the passenger seat, one hand braced on the dash, the other resting on the cane he now carried even to the mailbox. "Back in until you can see the cone in your rear window at the corner. Then turn the other way. It's geometry, not luck."

Michael did it, clipped a cone, did it again, and on the fourth attempt slid between the markers with a margin he could measure in inches. He sat there with the engine idling, pleased in a way he tried to keep off his face, because Grandpa distrusted visible pride almost as much as he distrusted broccoli.

"The highway tomorrow, then," Grandpa said. "Route 9. You can't pass the test without the merge, and you can't merge in a parking lot."

Here was where the two voices in Michael's life diverged. His father believed speed was the enemy, that caution was a virtue that could never be excessive, that the safest car was a slow car. His grandfather had driven trucks for thirty years and held the opposite conviction with the same certainty: that on a highway, hesitation was the danger. For a week Michael had carried both opinions without trying to reconcile them, the way he carried his father's worry and his grandfather's calm, as if he had to choose a side eventually.

Route 9's on-ramp was short and curved uphill, and the first time Michael reached it he did what his father would have wanted. He eased off, hovered at forty, waited for a gap so enormous that no car would ever need to acknowledge him. Behind him a pickup closed fast, its driver's hand appearing on the horn, and Michael watched the traffic ahead brake, one car after another, ripple after ripple, a chain of red he seemed to have caused from a lane where he technically hadn't been driving yet. He aborted onto the shoulder, heart drumming, and put on his hazards.

"That's the fear talking," Grandpa said. Not unkindly.

"I was being careful."

"You were being slow, and everyone had to brake for you." Grandpa looked at the mirror, then at Michael. "The ramp gives you the acceleration lane so you can come up to the speed of the traffic before you move over. You weren't careful. You were a rock in a stream."

Michael sat with that. It ran against everything his father had said, and yet the braking cars were a fact, visible and unarguable, still unwinding down the highway ahead of them. He thought of how his father called defensive driving a tautological thing, safe driving is driving safely, as if the phrase closed the argument by itself. But the stream had shown him otherwise. He breathed out, checked the mirror, and pulled back onto the ramp.

The second merge was not graceful. He accelerated hard, harder than felt polite, watching the speedometer climb toward sixty while his instincts shouted that this was recklessness, that his father would have closed his eyes. Then he signaled, glanced, and slid into the stream of traffic at nearly its own speed, and nothing braked. Nothing honked. The cars simply continued, and he was among them, moving with them, one pulse in a larger rhythm. It captivated him, that sudden harmony, the way thirty strangers accommodated him without a single one of them having to slow down. Being safe, he understood now, was not the same as being slow; sometimes the careful thing and the fast thing were the same thing. His father would not agree, and Michael could not say which of them was more right, only that the braking cars had been real and so was this.

"That's it," Grandpa said quietly. "That's the whole thing."

They drove ten miles north, past the quarry and the orchards, and Grandpa talked about hauling produce on this road when the orchards were twice the size, pointing out a diner that had burned down in 1987 and a hillside where, he said, he'd once seen a mountain lion, though he then admitted he might be thinking of a different hillside, or possibly a different state. It was like this more often now, Michael had noticed, small slips in the weave, a name reached for and recovered a beat late. Some synchronicity of memory and road, both wearing down together, and Michael drove carefully in both senses, steering around the potholes and around the gaps.

Back home, the parallel park between the cones was clean on the first try, and Michael left the engine running while Grandpa worked his cane out the door. "Test is Tuesday," Michael called after him. "Want me to drive you to your appointment Thursday?"

Grandpa paused on the sidewalk, weighing it, the way he weighed everything now. "All right," he said. "But take Route 9. I like the merge."

Matthew had taped the inflation graph to the refrigerator because the kitchen was the one room where he could not escape it. The line crawled upward through the seventies, then stood at its summit, then plunged, and next to the plunge he had written, in pencil, "why?" His study partner, Priya, was coming over at seven, and their economics teacher had promised that whoever could explain that steep drop would not have to take Friday's quiz.

Priya arrived with her own agenda, which she announced before her coat was off. "I need this quiz exemption," she said. "Not want. Need. If I ace this unit, Ms. Ferrar writes my recommendation letter, and if she writes it, I'm applying early decision, and if I'm applying early decision, I need October free for essays." She spread her notes on the kitchen table and began to collate them, matching the pages from the textbook with the pages from her own binder, tapping each pair into a neat stack. "So. The line. Tell me about the line."

He sat across from her and made himself trace it out loud. "Inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980," he said, running his finger along the summit. "And by 1983 it was below 3 percent. Same country, same people, same stores. Three years, and the thing just falls." He looked at her. "Doesn't that seem fast? Like a fever breaking overnight."

"Explain it, then. That's the assignment."

He had a half-answer, the one the textbook kept circling. "The Federal Reserve raised interest rates. Sharply." He said the words and watched her face to see whether they landed as explanation or as incantation. She waited, chin on her fist, which meant they had not landed.

In the doorway his mother appeared, still in her lab coat, holding a mug. She was a geneticist and had a habit of listening to whatever crossed the kitchen whether or not it concerned her. "Sorry," she said. "Carry on. I'm just curious." She stayed, and Matthew found that this helped, in a strange way, because explaining to two people forced him to be slower.

He tried it as a story about restraint. "Imagine money as something that can be cheap or expensive," he said. "If the Fed makes it expensive, that changes what people do." But even as he said it, he heard the softness of it. Expensive money changing behavior was not the same as showing Priya the mechanism, and he did not actually have the mechanism. He had a fact and a sequence: rates went up sharply, and inflation, which had peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980, was below 3 percent by 1983. He had the before and the after, and a gap in the middle shaped like the word "because."

"Is that enough?" Priya asked. "Rates up, inflation down, three years. Maybe that's all the assignment wants."

"I don't think it's all I want," Matthew said. "The two things happened in that order, but I can't see the wire between them. It's like," and he looked at the graph, at the scatter of small quarterly points around the main line, "like an archipelago. You can hop from island to island and it looks like a path, but underneath there might be one landmass or there might be nothing connected at all."

His mother set down her mug. "We argue about that constantly in my field," she said. "Two populations look different, and everyone wants to say the difference is genetic, but half the time the phenotypic variation is mostly environment, and you can't tell which from looking." She smiled at their expressions. "Carry on. I just like hearing you two argue."

Priya had stopped taking notes. "So we present it as what we know and what we don't?"

Matthew pulled the graph off the refrigerator and laid it flat between them, the pencil "why?" still visible beside the drop. "We present the whole thing. Rates up sharply, then the fall. Fourteen point eight in March 1980, under three by 1983. And then we say the part everyone skips: here is the order of events, and here is where our seeing ends." He tapped the empty space under the line. "Ms. Ferrar said the exemption was for whoever could explain the drop. Maybe the honest version is the better explanation. Or maybe we lose the exemption to somebody with a smoother story."

Priya picked up her pen and wrote across the top of her collated stack: known, sequence, unknown. "Fine," she said. "But if you're wrong and I have to take Friday's quiz, you're quizzing me Thursday night."

Let me be clear from the start: I was not failing chemistry. I had a 71, which on my scale is a work in progress, and anyway Mr. Kwan never called home, so the whole thing with my mother was an overreaction. That is the version I intend to defend, and I am aware that Priya would roll her eyes at it, since she was there.

The lab had that afternoon smell of alcohol lamps and somebody's burned pretzel from the vending machine. We were doing stoichiometry, which Priya kept pronouncing like it was a town in Romania. The problem on the board gave us a mass of reactant and asked for the moles of product, and the path ran through molar mass, which is where I always stumbled. You divide the grams by the grams-per-mole and get moles, and then you can climb the balanced equation like a ladder, and I could do each rung alone but not in sequence. That day it mattered, because the unit test was Friday, and because Priya had said, in the parking lot, "If you fail this I'm not tutoring you again," and I had laughed like it was funny.

Mr. Kwan, who does not explain things so much as scatter clues, wrote a number on the board and drew a box around it: 22.4. "You'll want this for the gas questions," he said, and moved on to take attendance, which is very like him.

"Twenty-two point four what?" I asked Priya.

"Litres. For a mole of gas." She was already three steps ahead in her notebook. "One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure. It's on the reference sheet, you don't even have to memorize it."

I said "obviously" and wrote it down, and here is the first place I have to be honest: it meant nothing to me. It sat on my page like a phone number for a person I would never call. I did the practice problem, got the moles, then multiplied by 22.4 like she did, and produced some litres of carbon dioxide, and Mr. Kwan put a check next to my name, and I felt like a fraud, because the check had no idea I was copying a rhythm without hearing the song.

That night I decided to prove something, though at the time I told myself I was just studying. I found a cardboard box in the garage, the kind my father's parts come in, and I did the arithmetic: if one mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere, then a box that size was one mole of gas, sitting there, invisible. Twenty-two point four litres. I measured it out with the kitchen measuring cup and a marking pen, cut nothing, taped nothing, just drew the volume on the cardboard's inside walls, and then I sat inside the box. My knees didn't fit. A mole of nitrogen, a mole of oxygen, the whole sky's smallest unit of it, was smaller than my folded legs.

My older sister Dana found me there and stood in the doorway with her cereal. "Are you eulogizing a box?" she asked.

"I'm learning chemistry."

"You're doing existentialism in a box." She sat down on the concrete, though, which for Dana is a compliment. "So how much air is that?"

"One mole. Of an ideal gas. At zero degrees and one atmosphere." I said it the way you recite an address until it belongs to you, and I watched her nod slowly, and something in me turned over. The number had been quiescent all day, folded up on my page, and now it was the size of a box I was physically sitting in. A mole wasn't a number anymore. It was a thing you could occupy.

Which brings me to the twist, and the part I have been arranging carefully all along. On Friday I got an 88, and I told everyone the box did it, and that is mostly true. But here is what I left out: Thursday night I redid every practice problem from the beginning, and I found that on Wednesday's quiz I had used the molar mass backwards, multiplying when I should have divided, and that my 71 had been riding on that one flipped operation the whole time. Mr. Kwan had written "see me" on it in red, and I had told everyone he wrote "nice work." So no, I was not failing, and no, I was not fine. Both had been true, which is the part I'm still working on.

In the lab on Monday, Priya slid my quiz across the table and pointed at the last question, the gas one. "Explain it," she said. Not asked. Demanded, in the way she does, chin on her fist.

I took out a scrap paper and drew a box, labeled it 22.4 litres, wrote "one mole, 0 degrees, 1 atmosphere" underneath, and turned it toward her. "The grams of the reactant, divided by the molar mass, that's your moles. Then the moles of gas, that's just boxes. This many boxes' worth of gas." I tapped the drawing. "That's the whole problem. It's boxes."

Priya looked at the box for a long second, then at me, then started copying it into her notes.

The studio smelled of rosin and radiator dust, and the photocopy of Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, lay on the music rack with its margins already crowded.
