By Thursday I had four pieces: two thresholds, a doorway, and a collage I told myself was about liminality. Nobody in the studio was impressed, least of all Theo, who was seventeen and painting, with total confidence, a series about his grandfather's hands. Ten pieces on hands. He already had eight. His family had a lineage of carpenters, he told me, three generations, and he said "lineage" the way other people say "inheritance," like it came with papers.

The problem started on Friday, when Priya, who was doing a portfolio on water in some form I couldn't quite identify, asked Miriam whether she should wait to post her pieces online. Her cousin had told her that once something was on the internet, anyone could use it, and she'd spent the whole afternoon photographing her work in bad light instead of posting it. "So posting it means I lose it," she said.

"You don't lose it," I said, before Miriam could, because I had looked this up in April for reasons I'll get to. "It's protected by copyright automatically, the moment you make it. Fixed form, like on paper. It's yours." Priya said that couldn't be right. I said it was, mostly. "Registration is voluntary," I added, and then, because she was looking at me like I was the camp brochure, "but you'd need it before you could sue over a US work." She wrote this on her forearm in gel pen, which I chose not to interpret as an evaluation of my teaching.

The reasons I'd looked it up in April: my aunt runs a shop that prints tote bags, and in March she printed one with a drawing of mine on it, a heron I'd done junior year, and sold forty of them at a craft fair without asking me, on the theory that she'd bought the drawing, framed it, hung it in her kitchen, and therefore owned it. I'd wanted to know if I had any standing to be angry, legally speaking. It turned out I owned the drawing the whole time, which did not settle the question of whether I had any standing to be angry in the family sense. I did not sue my aunt. We ate Easter dinner across from each other and discussed her hydrangeas.

I told none of this to Priya. What I told her was that she should post her work, and what I thought, in the privacy of my own skull, was that ownership is a cleaner idea on paper than at a table with your aunt passing the potatoes. The heron existed. It was mine the moment I fixed it. It was also on forty tote bags in a county I could drive through in an hour. Both of these things are true, and I have not found a way to make them into one thing.

That night I couldn't sleep, so I went to the studio, where Theo was also not sleeping, adding a ninth hand. I told him about the heron, because at one in the morning the heron felt like a confession I owed somebody. He listened, which I hadn't expected, and then he said, "So your theme isn't thresholds." I said it absolutely was, and he pointed his brush at my collage, the one about liminality, and said, "That's a heron." It was, in fact, a heron. I had cut it out of a magazine in April and kept moving it around the page for two weeks without asking myself why.

Here is where I admit I've been unreliable. The portfolio I'm building is not about doors or thresholds. It's about the heron, and my aunt's shop, and the forty tote bags, and what it means to own a thing that other people carry around a county without knowing your name. I'd been avoiding the theme because it was embarrassing and because it required calling my aunt, which I did Saturday morning from the payphone by the lodge, the one nobody under thirty knows how to use. I told her I wanted to talk about the bags. She said, "Abby, sweetheart, I sold out of those in May. I was going to print more."

There are eight pieces now, and Miriam says the statement is the strongest thing I've written, though she said it in a way that suggested my draft about thresholds had been, in her words, "in the process of ossifying into something careful." Priya photographed my ninth piece for me, in good light, and then photographed hers. When she asked where I was posting mine, I said I hadn't decided yet.

"Wait," she said, gel pen already out, "so even if you post it, you still own it, right? Automatically?"

"That's the deal," I said, and held still for the shutter.

The email arrived on a Tuesday: the black box theater had flooded, and the fall one-acts would move to the multipurpose room, where chairs would surround the playing space on all four sides. Grace read it three times at the kitchen table while her mother browned onions behind her, and by the third reading she understood that the blocking she had spent two weeks marking into her script was finished.

She had wanted this play since March, when she first read Devon's script, twelve pages about two sisters dividing their dead mother's phonetics records, old tapes of vowel sounds and word lists. Grace loved the strangeness of it, the pithy arguments the sisters had about which of them the mother had been recording all those years. She had told Devon she would protect the script from actors who wanted to make it sentimental. That was the promise she kept thinking about now, because a room with audience on every side had a way of exposing everything.

Devon arrived first on Thursday, carrying a bag of cassette tapes he wanted as props. "I want them real," he said, setting them in a careful row on the floor. "If the sisters are fighting over her actual voice, the objects can't be fake." Grace said she would try, though the tapes were heavy in a way that complicated everything, and he heard the hedge in her voice and looked at her for a long moment before going to arrange them again.

The actors came at six. Priya, who played the older sister, had wanted the role badly enough that she had auditioned twice, and she had opinions about everything, entrances, pauses, the second-act turn. "In the black box I entered downstage left," she said, standing where the doorway used to be. "Where do I even come from now?" Grace looked at the chairs pushed against every wall, the square of open floor in the middle, and admitted she did not know yet.

They tried the first scene with the old blocking. Within thirty seconds Grace saw the problem: the sisters faced each other in a fixed line, and the two full rows of chairs behind them were looking at nothing but backs. A woman in the corner, a janitor who had stayed to sweep, actually stood and moved her folding chair to a diagonal so she could see a face. Grace called a halt. "We can't stand still," she said. "If the audience sits on all sides, then no matter where we stop, somebody's staring at our backs. We have to keep you moving, so every section gets faces for a while."

Priya resisted. "Moving for the audience's sake is dishonest," she said. "My character would plant herself and refuse to leave." Devon, from his row of tapes, said that was exactly what her character would do, and Priya turned on him, pleased to be defended and suspicious of why. Grace stood in the middle of the square and felt the two arguments pull at her, truth of character against truth of the room, and could not find the sentence that held them both.

She tried again on Saturday, alone except for Devon, walking the sisters' lines herself with the script under her arm. She let Priya have her planted moment, the refusal, ten seconds of stillness with her back to the east rows, and then built the scene so the younger sister circled her, so the movement came from conflict instead of furniture. She telephoned Priya that night and said, "Your character digs in, and the digging in is what sets the other one orbiting. You never move. She never stops." Priya was quiet, then said she would try it, which from Priya was nearly a surrender.

The Sunday run-through half worked. The orbit held through the first scene, and the janitor, who had come back with coffee to watch, called out that she could see someone's face at all times, which Grace chose to take as a review. But the tapes were a disaster. Devon had arranged them in a straight row against the north chairs, and when Priya turned to them in the final scene, she turned her back to the entire south side, and the moment the play had been building toward was delivered to a wall of empty vinyl seats. Devon sat very still afterward, then began gathering the cassettes into his bag, one at a time, as if they might abscond if he hurried. "We can fix the turn," Grace said. He zipped the bag and said, "She should face the tapes. That's the whole scene." Grace looked at the square of floor, at the chairs waiting on every side, and did not answer him yet.

The waiting room smelled of hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Claire kept her peer-educator notebook flat on her knees so the title page wouldn't show. She had volunteered to run the health table at the fall club fair, which meant she had until September to learn how to explain things she had only ever whispered about: consent, contraception, where a person actually goes to get tested. Her aunt, a nurse, had arranged for her to shadow a morning at the Riverside clinic, and the first thing they'd done was put her in a paper gown so she could understand what a patient feels before she ever tried to explain anything to one.

"It's just your checkup," Dr. Okafor said, washing her hands. "Same as anyone's."

Claire had assumed she would spend the morning observing. Instead the doctor talked to her as though she were any sixteen-year-old patient, which, in the examining room, she was. Then came the question that startled her, offered as casually as asking about allergies: would she like an HIV test today?

"Is that something I need?" Claire asked. "I'm not, I mean, I haven't." Her ears went hot.

"It's routine," Dr. Okafor said. She said it the way she'd said the blood pressure cuff would squeeze, a fact of the room rather than a judgment in it. "The CDC recommends everyone aged 13 to 64 get tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care."

Claire wrote it down on the exam table paper, ballpoint tearing slightly. Thirteen to sixty-four. She turned the numbers over, testing them. She had walked into this room thinking a test was something you asked for because of a reason, a specific night, a specific person, and the doctor was talking as though it belonged to a checkup like a reflex hammer did.

Last spring, in Marisol's basement with the space heater ticking, her friends had played a game of what they'd all admit to, and Claire had stayed quiet while the others talked around the subject of tests as if it were a word too heavy to lift. Marisol had finally said she wouldn't know where to go, wouldn't know what to say at the desk, wouldn't want her mother's doctor knowing. Claire had said, glibly, that she'd find out, and had then not found out. The notebook in her lap was the shape of that promise, and until this morning it had been mostly blank.

"Can I ask how it works?" she said. "The test. And what you'd say to someone scared of it."

Dr. Okafor pulled the stool closer and went through it briskly, the way a person explains something for the hundredth time without letting it sound mechanical. Consent first: nothing happened without a yes, the yes could be taken back, a yes to one thing wasn't a yes to everything. Then the swab, the twenty minutes, what a negative meant and what a preliminary positive would mean, that confirmation existed. Claire's pen moved. She asked how a doctor would explain contraception options to someone, and Dr. Okafor described a conversation that started with questions instead of a lecture, then asked Claire to try one back at her, patient to doctor, and listened while Claire stumbled through the difference between a condom and a prescription method, correcting only once.

Some of it Claire could hold onto firmly, like the idea that consent had to be freely given or it wasn't consent, which struck her as almost axiomatic once stated, so obvious it was strange anyone had to state it. Other parts slid around like the kelp she'd seen undulating off the pier at her grandmother's town, visible and then not, and she didn't pretend otherwise. She understood that a virus could be detected in the body, and that Dr. Okafor had used the word genotype once about how some infections were typed, and Claire had underlined it twice because she didn't yet know what she'd need. There were gaps. She wrote the gaps down too, a column of things to look up before September.

She held out her arm for the blood draw without being asked twice. The nurse hummed along to the radio while the vial filled, and Claire watched the dark thread of it and thought about Marisol, about the club fair, about the kids who would walk past her table the way she had walked past tables her whole life, looking away.

"So it's negative," the nurse said, snapping off her gloves. "You'll get a card to keep, proves today's result."

Claire folded the card into her notebook, between the page on consent and the blank page after it. On the walk out she texted Marisol: you free saturday? I found some stuff out. Then, before she could second-guess the wording, she added, there's a test that's just routine now. everyone 13 to 64. Marisol's reply took eleven minutes, long enough for Claire to buy a coffee she didn't want, and when the phone finally buzzed in her hand she stopped under the clinic awning to read it.

"ok but you're buying the fries," it said, and Claire started typing back before she'd decided what to tell her first.

The training manual called it "peer health leadership," but Rosalie's mother called it "the birds and the bees with a laminated poster," and Rosalie privately called it Tuesday. Every morning that last week of camp, while the younger campers made friendship bracelets on the porch of the craft shed, she and five other junior counselors sat in the infirmary with Nurse Quill, practicing how to say words out loud without turning the color of the camp's famous raspberry lemonade. Consent, she learned, was mostly about asking and then actually listening to the answer, which sounded easy until you practiced it with a partner staring at you. Contraception was a chart. Testing was a clinic two towns over, where you could walk in, ask for a screen, and walk out with a phone number to call in a week.

She had volunteered because the college application essay practically wrote itself, and because she genuinely could not explain a condom to her little brother without him hiding under the table, which seemed like a failure of citizenship somehow. But on Thursday night the essay stopped mattering. Maren found her at the washhouse, stood too close, and said, in a voice like a dropped plate, "Can I talk to you? Not here."

They sat on the sullen gray rocks behind the boathouse, the ones the counselors called the whales because they held the heat of the sun long after dark. Maren wrapped her arms around her knees. "So there's a boy from Lakeview," she said. "There was a, a thing. Tonight. And we didn't, like, plan anything." She stared at the water. "I don't know what to do and I can't call my mom, obviously, and you're doing that nurse training thing, so you're basically the closest thing I have to a professional."

"I'm the closest thing you have to a laminated poster," Rosalie said, and Maren laughed, wetly, which was the point. "The poster says there's a pharmacy in Millbrook. And there's a bus at seven tomorrow. The poster also says I'm supposed to go with people, so, you know. I'm contractually obligated."

"Shut up," Maren said. "Thank you. Shut up and thank you."

In Millbrook the pharmacy smelled of floor wax and limes, and the pharmacist was a small man with reading glasses pushed up into gray curls. He listened to Maren stammer through the situation, then to Rosalie, who found herself saying the words clearly for the first time, like she'd been practicing all week for an audience of one. The pharmacist nodded and slid a small box across the counter.

He said, "The emergency pill works mainly by delaying ovulation, so the sooner you take it after unprotected sex, the more effective it is. Waiting a few days would be a mistake." He tapped the box. "Take it today."

"Today today?" Maren said.

"Today today," he said. "Some people put it off because they're hoping they won't need it. It doesn't work that way. The clock runs one direction."

From where Maren stood, the whole transaction looked strangely ordinary, like buying stamps. She had expected fluorescent lights and a lecture, maybe a form with her mother's name on it. Instead there was just this man with lime-smelling shelves behind him, saying numbers and words with the same calm he probably used for cough syrup. She took the box. She took the water bottle Rosalie had already uncapped for her, because Rosalie was like that, always half a step ahead with the logistics. Outside, on the bench by the bus stop, she swallowed the pill and then said, "Okay. That's done. Now I'm terrified about the other thing."

"The test thing?" Rosalie said. "The clinic in Harwick does walk-ins. Tuesday's my day off. We could take the eleven o'clock bus, be back by dinner."

"You'd come with me?"

"I told you. Contractually obligated. It's in the laminated bylaws."

Maren leaned her head on Rosalie's shoulder, then straightened up fast, because there was a limit to how much sentimentality she could tolerate before lunch. "What are you going to put in that essay of yours?" she asked. "'This one time at summer camp'?"

Rosalie considered it. She had started the week thinking the point of the training was knowing the right answer, the way she knew that enthalpy was the heat content of a system, a number you could look up and be done with. But sitting on the bench, watching Maren peel the label off the water bottle in one long, mesmerized strip, she understood that knowing was only the smaller half. The larger half was the seven o'clock bus, the uncapped water, the seat saved on the eleven o'clock Tuesday. She couldn't quite put the two halves together yet, and she suspected the essay would be worse and truer for it.

"I'll write about posters," she said. "I'll figure the rest out later."

The bus pulled in, brakes gasping, and Maren stood and held out her hand to pull Rosalie up. "Tuesday," she said. "Eleven o'clock. Bring the water bottle."

Emily's grandfather backed the Buick out of his narrow garage in one motion, his hands barely turning the wheel, as if the car knew where to go and he was only agreeing with it. He drove them to the empty stretch behind the supermarket, where faded yellow lines marked two imaginary cars, and told her the test was tomorrow at nine, so today was the last chance to get the parallel parking right. She had failed once already, in March, on a hill in the rain, and the examiner had written something in her clipboard that Emily had not been allowed to see.

"You're too far out," her grandfather said from the passenger seat, his loquacious mood from breakfast replaced by something quieter and more watchful. "Line up your back bumper with his front, then turn the wheel all the way."

She tried it. The Buick swung wide, then corrected, and settled eleven inches from the curb, which her grandfather measured with his thumb and a squint and pronounced "close enough for government work." She did it again, and again, until her neck ached from twisting backward, and each time the distance shrank until it was eight inches, then six. Somewhere in the fourth attempt she stopped thinking of the wheel and the curb as separate problems and began to feel the whole arc of the car as one motion, the way she had once, at nine years old, finally stopped reading notes and just played the piano line.

She remembered that afternoon with sudden clarity: her grandmother sitting on the porch with a glass of iced tea, applauding with two fingers against her palm when Emily got through the whole song, the summer the garden still had the roses in it. Her grandmother had been dead for two autumns now, and the roses were gone, but the porch chairs were still out there, facing each other, waiting for nobody.

"Now the highway," her grandfather said, and Emily's stomach dropped, because the test route ended with a short merge onto Route 9, and in March she had messed it up, though not the way everyone assumed. She had checked the mirror, seen nothing, begun to drift over, and then a horn had sounded so close it seemed to come from inside the car. A gray sedan sat in the lane beside her, close enough that she could see the driver's mouth moving. The examiner had gripped the wheel and steered her back and written something long.

"You know what went wrong," her grandfather said. It was not a question. On the entrance ramp he let her build speed, and when the mirror showed only empty road he said nothing, and Emily, remembering the horn, remembered also what a boy in her driver's ed class had said afterward, the only useful thing anyone said that whole semester: "Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind the car. You have to look over your shoulder." She turned her chin fast, and there in the space the mirror had called empty was a white pickup, patient and close, its driver holding a steady distance as though he had been watching her learn.

She stayed in her lane until the truck passed, then looked again, found the gap, and moved over smooth as water finding a channel. Her grandfather made a small sound, not quite approval, more like relief escaping.

Back at the house, dusk coming on over the fence, Emily began to remonstrate with herself out loud, listing all the ways tomorrow could go wrong, the hill start, the three-point turn, the examiner's clipboard. Her grandfather laughed, a short bark, and said she argued with herself like her grandmother used to, with great rectitude, as though losing an argument to herself was a moral failing she could be forgiven for. Then he said, "You looked over your shoulder. You looked before you decided. That's most of driving, and it isn't a bad habit for anything else either."

He was trying to say something larger, she could tell, and she was too old to be told things larger, but she let it stand because it was nearly dark and the porch chairs were out there and the test was in fourteen hours. She would either pass or fail, and the blind spot would still be beside the car either way, invisible and ordinary, waiting for her to turn her head. She went inside and set two alarms, one for six and one for six fifteen, and stood at the window looking out at the Buick in the driveway, silver under the streetlight, trustworthy now, or nearly.

"Keys on the hook," her grandfather called from the kitchen. "We'll leave at eight."

Wyatt counted the trash bags before he zipped them. Two bags of gone-off peppers, a slime of spring onions, half a block of cheddar gone grey at the edges, and a carton of eggs three weeks past their date. He and his father had been at the campsite since the start of July, and the cooler and the trunk of the car had become a kind of landfill with a lid. His father handed him forty dollars for the next run to the store and said, "Maybe buy less this time."

At the picnic table that evening, Wyatt looked up food waste on his phone, mostly because the wasted cheddar bothered him in a way he couldn't have explained to anyone. He read it twice. A UN Environment Programme report had found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, and about 60 percent of that waste happened in households. He said the numbers out loud to hear them.

"Say what?" his father said from the fire pit.

"A billion point oh five tonnes. Wasted. In one year. And most of it, sixty percent, came from houses. People like us." He turned the phone face down on the table. "Not restaurants. Not farms. Kitchens."

His father poked at the coals and didn't answer, which Wyatt took as agreement or at least as surrender. The next morning he sat at the table with a notebook and did something he had never done before: he wrote down seven dinners, in order, with the ingredients listed under each one, and then crossed out every duplicate so that each item appeared once with a total beside it. Chicken twice, because a whole roasted chicken could become tacos two nights later. Rice in three of the meals. One bag of carrots, counted out by meal. He left the page with the eggs half blank, since his father's schedule kept shifting, and drove to the store with the list folded into his back pocket.

The shopping took longer than buying whatever looked good had ever taken. He stood in the sauce aisle doing arithmetic on the back of the list, working out whether a jar of pasta sauce used across two meals cost less per serving than two jars used once each. At the meat counter he asked for exactly one and a half pounds of ground beef, and when the butcher raised an eyebrow, Wyatt said, "It's planned. Three meals, half a pound each." He felt slightly ridiculous saying it and also, quietly, like someone who had his life in order.

Back at the campsite he cooked in batches, because the camp stove had exactly one burner and reheating was easier than cooking twice. He browned all the beef at once with onions, split it into three portions in the cooler, and boiled a full pot of rice that would underpin the rest of the week: fried rice on Wednesday, burrito bowls on Friday, something with the leftover chicken on Saturday. The table, which had been a scatter of crumbs and unpeeled vegetables all month, became for an afternoon an organised surface, containers labelled in his handwriting with masking tape.

His friend Dele drove out on Thursday to swim at the lake and stayed for dinner. He watched Wyatt reheat a portion of the batch from Tuesday and plate it with the last of the spinach before it turned.

"You're like a meal service now," Dele said. "Since when do you plan anything?"

"Since I threw out two bags of food and read that a UN report found 1.05 billion tonnes got wasted in 2022, and about sixty percent of that came from households. Household kitchens. Us." Wyatt handed him a fork. "It's not metaphysics. It's just a list."

Dele ate, said it was good, and asked what was for the rest of the week, and Wyatt showed him the page with the crossings-out. Friday's burrito bowls went as planned. Saturday went wrong in a small way: the chicken had gone off a day early, the ice in the cooler having melted faster in the heat, and Wyatt stood over it deciding whether the smell was bad or only suspicious. He threw it out, changed the plan, and stretched the last portion of beef with an extra can of beans. The system held, mostly. Sunday he sat at the table revising the notebook for the coming week, and what stayed uncertain he wrote in the margin: how much ice, how fast the chicken turned, whether his father would eat the leftovers or let them sit quiescent in the cooler until they became next month's trash bag. He underlined "check cooler twice a day" and got up to start the water for rice.

The essay was due at eight the next morning, and Charlie had written the same sentence four times. Her laptop sat open on her grandmother's kitchen table, beside a bowl of shelled pecans and a stack of unopened mail that had been requisitioned as a paperweight. The prompt was simple enough: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She understood the mechanics, roughly, the way she understood photosynthesis, as a diagram she could recite without quite believing in.

"Still fighting with it?" her grandfather asked. He was garrulous by nature and doubly so after dinner, and he lowered himself into the chair across from her with the air of a man settling in for a long campaign.

"Every time I get to the part about why two percent inflation counts as success, it falls apart," Charlie said. "If rising prices are bad, shouldn't the goal be zero? I can't explain a target I don't understand." She pushed the laptop toward him as if the problem were visible on the screen. "The whole second half depends on it."

Her grandfather chewed a pecan and looked at the ceiling, which was what he did when he was consulting some interior archive. "Your grandmother kept everything," he said finally. "Down in the sunroom. The biomes of old paper. She filed by decade, more or less. If a fact ever lived in a newspaper, it lives in that room."

The sunroom smelled of dust and lavender sachet. Boxes labeled in her grandmother's cramped hand filled the shelves, and Charlie worked through them under the small lamp, sneezing, moving fast because it was already past ten. Her grandmother had been a teller for thirty-one years and had clipped anything that touched money, which turned out to be nearly everything. Charlie found mortgage announcements, grocery price comparisons, a 2011 piece about groceries costing more than the year before, and then, in a folder marked MISCELLANEOUS FINANCIAL, a front page from the business section dated January 25, 2012. The headline said the Federal Reserve had adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent.

She read it twice, kneeling on the floor with the paper flat in front of her. The article said the target was measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, a phrase so long it wrapped to a second line. Two percent, measured that way, made official on that specific day. That was the fact she'd been missing, and it changed the shape of her second half. The Fed hadn't always had a number. Someone had chosen one, on a date, and chosen a yardstick to measure it with, and every argument about whether two percent was success or compromise came after that choice. She could write that. She could even argue it.

She carried the paper back to the kitchen to show him, but it was her grandmother who was sitting there now, in the chair her grandfather had warmed, reading his abandoned crossword. Charlie had thought she was asleep by nine, always. "Grandpa said you kept everything," Charlie said, and spread the page on the table. "This is what I needed. For why the number is two percent at all."

Her grandmother put down the crossword and pulled the page closer, and something moved across her face that Charlie couldn't name. "I remember that day," she said. "It was the first week at my new desk. We watched the wire." She tapped the fold of the paper, not the headline but a smaller line beneath it, and Charlie leaned in to see what she was pointing at, and read it, and felt the floor of her argument shift under her.

"Half the tellers thought it was a cage," her grandmother said, "and half thought it was a promise." She slid the paper back across the table and picked up her crossword pen again, as if the matter had been handed back where it belonged. Charlie looked at the clipping, then at the clock, which said eleven forty, and pulled the laptop toward her and began to type.

Xavier had been standing in the lobby of First Meridian for forty minutes with a laminated badge that said STUDENT OBSERVER, and so far the only thing he had learned was that the pen chained to the deposit counter was missing its cap. His economics teacher had arranged the shadow day as research for a class debate, and Xavier was supposed to argue that central banks should raise interest rates to fight inflation. He had a page of notes. He did not, he realized, actually understand them.

The branch manager, Ms. Adeyemi, called him over to her desk near the loan offices. "You'll sit in on my appointments this afternoon," she said. "Mostly routine. If a customer asks you a question, you can answer it, or you can say you're observing. Your choice."

The first appointment was a man named Mr. Okafor who wanted a loan to expand his dry cleaning business. Ms. Adeyemi walked him through the new rates, and Mr. Okafor set his cap on the desk like an encumbrance he was tired of carrying and said, "So I'm supposed to pay more to borrow because prices went up. Explain to me how that helps. You." He pointed at Xavier, who had been caught chewing his pen.

Xavier began with what his notes said, that higher rates reduce spending, but the words came out flat and Mr. Okafor's expression turned truculent, arms crossed, jaw set, waiting for the boy in the visitor badge to say something worth his lunch hour. Xavier stalled, repeated himself, and felt the whole argument slip through his fingers. Ms. Adeyemi rescued him by shifting the conversation to the loan terms, and Xavier sat back, ears burning, knowing he had just failed at the one thing he'd come to do.

That night his mother drove him to his grandfather's house for his aunt Ruth's birthday, and Xavier, still raw from the afternoon, mentioned at the table that he was preparing to praise the rate hikes of the early 1980s, the ones that had finally beaten inflation. Aunt Ruth set down her fork. She had been twenty-three that year, she said, working at a sheet metal plant in Ohio, and when the recession hit she was laid off and did not find steady work for a long time. She remembered the newspaper front page, she said, when unemployment rose above 10 percent. "Ten percent," she repeated. "You can look it up. It went above ten."

The table went quiet. Xavier's grandfather said the hikes worked, prices calmed down eventually, and Aunt Ruth said, "They worked, and it cost jobs. Both of those are true, and I don't want to hear one without the other." She wasn't angry at Xavier, exactly, but she wasn't not angry either, and on the drive home he sat with the window cracked open, turning the whole thing over. Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs. That was the sentence. He tested it against what he'd watched happen at the bank that afternoon, Mr. Okafor's loan getting more expensive, his expansion getting smaller, maybe a hiring plan getting shelved. The mechanism of his notes and the history of his aunt assembled themselves into one picture.

The next afternoon, Xavier returned to the branch for his second shadow day. Ms. Adeyemi raised an eyebrow. "Back for more humiliation?" "Back to fix it," he said. Mr. Okafor had an appointment to sign refinancing papers, and when he spotted Xavier he gave a short laugh and said, "You going to try explaining again, or just watch me suffer?" Xavier asked if he could try once more. Ms. Adeyemi leaned back in her chair, which augured well, or at least did not augur a refusal.

"When rates go up, borrowing costs more, like yours did today," Xavier said. "So people and businesses spend less and expand less, and that takes the pressure off prices. That's how it slows inflation. But it's not free. It usually costs jobs, because when businesses cut back, they cut workers. In the early eighties, when the rates went up to beat inflation, unemployment rose above 10 percent. My aunt lost her job that year. So when I argue for rate hikes, I have to say that part too, or I'm not telling the truth." He stopped, having run out of prepared material and arrived, abruptly, at honesty.

Mr. Okafor looked at him for a long moment, then picked up the pen, signed the papers, and slid them across the desk. "First useful thing anyone's said to me in this building all week," he said. "Expensive, but useful." He put on his cap and stood, and at the door he turned back. "Tell your aunt I said the ones who paid for it ought to be in the speech." Xavier wrote that down on the back of his notes, under the part he still wasn't sure about, whether the trade was worth it, and left it there, unsigned.

Kate had told everyone at dinner that calculus was going fine, which was true the way a map of a country at war is true. The borders were drawn. The interior was unknown. She sat at the kitchen table with the textbook open to the chapter on integration, a sharpened pencil, and a glass of water she kept forgetting to drink, while her brother Danny, fourteen and unbearably awake for a Sunday evening, dropped into the chair across from her.

"What's that squiggle," he said, pointing at the long slender curve before the x squared.

"That's the integral sign," Kate said. "It's an elongated letter s." Danny looked blank, so she went on, the way she did when she half knew something, which was most of the time lately. "Leibniz introduced it in 1675. He thought of an integral as an infinite sum. That's why it's a stretched s, for sum." Danny nodded slowly, the way people nod at weather.

"And the squiggle does what?"

"It finds the area under a curve." She tapped the graph in the book, the shaded sliver trapped between the parabola and the x-axis. "The area under this curve, from here to here." Danny frowned at it, then at her, then said the thing that undid the whole evening: "How can adding up infinity give you a normal number?"

She should have said she didn't know. Instead she said something about limits that she could not finish, and Danny, who was not cruel but was fourteen, said, "You don't know either," and got up to find a banana. Kate sat with the shaded region and felt the old familiar heat in her face, the one she'd carried out of every math classroom since seventh grade, when Mr. Ruiz had called her method "creative" in front of thirty people and the word had stuck to her like a burr. She had spent years maligning the subject, calling it a sorting machine, calling teachers charlatans with answer keys, and the strange thing was that the insults had never once helped her solve anything.

From the doorway, Danny watched his sister bend over her book and felt a complicated pity he would not have been able to name. He knew she'd told their mother she was "basically tutoring herself," which was maybe true in the way his own claim of having "basically" cleaned his room was true. He also knew that last week he had heard her on the phone with Priya saying she might drop to regular math, and that she'd said it lightly, the way you say a thing you have already decided. He ate his banana and thought that Kate was the smartest person he knew who was also, somehow, the most frightened, and that these two facts lived in her at the same time without either one winning.

She waved him back over, which surprised them both. "Sit. Help me think." He sat. She drew a rectangle under the curve, then another, then a stack of thin slices, each one narrow, each one easy, the area of a rectangle being nothing but base times height. "Leibniz thought of it as an infinite sum," she said again, and this time she heard it. "Like if you cut the area into slices this thin, and thinner, and you never stop cutting, the little errors just vanish." She was not sure that was exactly right. She wrote it anyway. Danny leaned in and said, "So the squiggle is a stretched s because it means sum," and she said yes, and drew the sign long and elegant down the margin of her paper, over and over, until it looked less like a squiggle and more like a letter she was learning to write.

Here is what Kate would tell you afterward: that she sat down that night already understanding integration, and that the evening was ancillary, a pleasant review, and that Danny's questions merely sharpened what was there. The paper tells a different story. The paper shows crossed-out attempts, a torn corner, and then, near midnight, a worked integral with the area under x squared from zero to three computed correctly, the answer circled twice, and beneath it in small handwriting: still not sure why the errors vanish. She left that line in. She could have erased it, and in her retelling of the evening she did erase it, but the paper kept it, honest where she was not, and in the morning Danny found the page and read the circled answer and the small confession underneath.

He carried it to the kitchen where she was eating cereal, and set it down beside her bowl. "You got it," he said.

"I got it," she said. Then, quieter, looking at the small line of doubt in her own handwriting: "Most of it. I still don't know why it works, only that it does."

"That's basically everything," Danny said, and stole the last of her milk.

Mr. Pavlik's classroom smelled like whiteboard marker and the radiator's particular burnt dust, and on the board he had written, in his handwriting that leaned like a man walking into wind, "Historiography: the history of history." Rachel copied it, then underlined it twice, which was what she did instead of understanding things.

The assignment sheet was one page. Trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800, it said, and cite at least six historians. Rachel had six names already, copied from the back of the textbook, and a thesis she'd drafted in the margin of her chemistry notes: for a long time everyone thought the Revolution was a class struggle, the bourgeoisie rising against the nobility, and then historians began to question that. It was a fine thesis except for one detail, which was that she could not name when the questioning started. The paragraph ended, at the moment, with the words "and then things changed," which even she knew was a sentence that meant nothing.

She brought the problem to Dana at lunch, because Dana had already written four pages and kept saying "per my outline" like a person who owned a filing cabinet. "You need the turning point," Dana said, spearing a tater tot. "The moment somebody first seriously went after the Marxist view. My brother says it was the sixties. Everything was the sixties, according to my brother."

"The whole decade?" Rachel said. "I can't cite a decade."

"Cite a person. Somebody in the sixties."

That night Rachel wrote the sentence anyway: In the 1960s, historians began to challenge the Marxist interpretation. It sat on her screen looking recalcitrant, refusing to become more specific, and she ate three crackers over the keyboard, which was against her own rules. She found names, dates attached to names, a confusing amount of both. One book called another book "influential." Another called the same book "overrated." She began to suspect that historians spent half their careers reviewing each other, like restaurants reviewing restaurants.

The confounder was the library's database, which sorted results by relevance in a way that seemed personal. She typed "French Revolution Marxist interpretation challenged" and got a lecture given in 1954, published in 1955 as a little pamphlet called The Myth of the French Revolution. She read the first page standing at the printer, because the chair by the computer was missing, someone had apparently needed it more than the library did. The lecture was by a man named Alfred Cobban, and it had been his inaugural lecture at University College London, which meant, she gathered, the speech you give when you've just gotten the job of professor, the one where you announce what you intend to do to your field. Cobban intended to do quite a lot. He went at the Marxist social interpretation the way her brother went at a durian, with visible delight and total commitment. Rachel thought of the verb "eviscerate," which Mr. Pavlik had used once about a student essay and which she'd had to look up, and thought that Cobban had done it to a half-century of scholarship in an hour.

So Dana's brother was wrong, ish. It wasn't the sixties. It was earlier, and it was one man, standing at a lectern in London in 1954, telling a room full of people that the story they all told was a myth.

The problem was the essay itself, which now had two options and Rachel had to choose. She could write the paper as a march: old view, Cobban, new view, done, tidy as a lab report. Or she could write what she'd actually seen in the database, which was that after Cobban, the Marxists didn't concede, they fortified, and the anti-Marxists fortified right back, and fifty years of argument produced not a winner but a field so divided that her textbook just... summarized both sides and moved on to Napoleon. She sat with this. The tidy version would get an A, probably. The other version was harder to outline and she couldn't yet see its shape.

She tried telling Dana about it the next day, in the hallway by the gym, where Dana was taping a poster for a French Club event that featured, inexplicably, a drawing of a baguette wearing a beret. "So it's not just that views changed," Rachel said. "It's that Cobban made them change by attacking, and the attack itself became the thing later historians had to respond to, so the field is like a family that had one huge fight at Thanksgiving in 1954 and everyone's still choosing sides."

"That's not an outline," Dana said.

"It's a thesis with a limp."

Dana considered the poster, smoothing a corner. "My brother's going to say it was still basically the sixties."

"He wasn't there. Nobody was there. That's the whole problem with historians."

Rachel wrote it that weekend anyway, the limping version, with Cobban's 1954 lecture as her hinge and both sides given their paragraphs, and an ending that admitted what she couldn't resolve: whether Cobban had found a flaw in the old view or only made it unfashionable, she couldn't say, and neither, as far as she could tell, could anyone else. On Monday she handed it in face-down, which changed nothing but felt safer. Mr. Pavlik took the stack, tapped it twice against the desk to align the pages, and read the first page of the top essay right there in front of them, unbothered, the way he did.

"Rachel," he said, without looking up, "do you know what happened to the chair by the library printer?"

The cones were still out from the morning session when Justine began her fourth consecutive day of sprints, though her legs had begun filing complaints somewhere around the second. She had planned the week herself, in a notebook with a cracked spine: Monday through Sunday, drills in the morning and conditioning at dusk, because the college tryouts were eleven days away and she intended to arrive at them faster than anyone on the field. On Thursday she timed herself at the forty-meter mark and found she was two tenths slower than Monday. On Friday she was slower still, and she stood at the touchline with her hands on her knees, watching her breath hang in the cold air, wondering what kind of arithmetic made you slower the harder you worked.

Her friend Priya sat on the bleachers with a granola bar and no plans to move. "You look like a phone at two percent," she said.

"I have eleven days."

"So does everyone, and everyone else is going home at six."

Justine wanted to adjudicate the matter right there, to weigh her plan against Priya's loafing and declare a winner, but the stopwatch had already voted, and it had not voted for her. She walked off the field carrying the notebook, and that night she did what she always did when something refused to make sense: she read. She read until a word surfaced in a coaching forum, a word she'd never heard spoken aloud, and she read the sentence under it three times. The body gets fitter during recovery, after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level. Not during the workout itself. She sat very still, because if that was true, then her whole week had been an argument against her own body, and she had been losing on purpose.

The next morning she found Priya stretching by the goalposts and read the word aloud from her phone. "Supercompensation," she said. "That's what they call it."

"Sounds like something a bank would do."

"Kind of is. You deposit the work, but the interest shows up later, when you're resting."

Priya chewed on that, and on the granola bar. "So your plan is what, to nap strategically?"

Justine laughed, but the question stayed with her through the warm-up laps, a gentle, nagging kind of wondering. How much rest? Enough to rebuild, not so much that everything you'd built quietly dissolved. The forum gave her shapes, not answers: a hard day, then an easy one; a hard week, then a lighter one. Nobody could tell her exactly where her own body fell on that curve, and she liked that and feared it in equal measure. She would have to test it on herself and watch what happened.

She rebuilt the week on a fresh page, leaving Sunday blank except for the word nothing, which she underlined twice. Monday became speed work after a full warm-up, the kind she used to skip as a formality, and Tuesday became passing and jogging, barely enough to sweat. Wednesday hard again. She taped the page inside her locker like a contract with a version of herself she hadn't met yet, and the odd thing was that the blank days frightened her more than the sprint days ever had. Rest felt like debt. Rest felt like the solvency of her training was in question, as if a single empty afternoon could bankrupt the whole enterprise.

On the first hard day of the new plan, she caught herself inventing reasons to add just one more session, and she made herself stop. On the rest day, she watched from the bleachers while the boys' team ran patterns, and she noticed things she never noticed while running: how the good players slowed down a half-second before receiving, how the keeper set her feet early. She was not, she realized, doing nothing. Her legs, meanwhile, did whatever quiet rebuilding they did, unobserved, unrehearsed.

Eight days in, she timed the forty again. Faster than Monday of the first week, faster than any day before. Not by much. Not by enough to guarantee anything about tryouts, which were now three days off, and she held that uncertainty carefully, turning it over like a stone. Maybe the rest had done it. Maybe the weather. Maybe she had simply measured badly before. She couldn't separate the threads, and she decided she could live with that, because the stopwatch had moved in the right direction and she had a theory with her name on it.

On the last morning before tryouts, she arrived before anyone else, laid out her cones, and began the warm-up she once would have skipped: jogging the width, then the strides, unhurried, deliberate. Priya came over the hill with her bag on one shoulder.

"You're here early."

"I'm testing something," Justine said, and set the stopwatch to zero.

The robotics room smelled like solder and cold pizza, and the scrimmage was in four days. Thomas watched Yasmin run the arm code for the third time, and for the third time the gripper closed a half second late and knocked the block off the platform. Marcus, who had been with the team since freshman year and could read a motor stutter from across the room, said nothing. He wound a zip tie around a loose wire and told her the run looked smoother.

Afterward, in the hallway, Thomas asked him why. "Because she stayed until eleven last night," Marcus said. "You don't tell someone who stayed until eleven that her code is broken. You tell her it's getting better." Thomas said the code was getting worse, actually, and Marcus shrugged and said the scrimmage didn't really matter, which was a strange thing for someone who wanted the regional slot as badly as he did.

At home, Thomas's sister had left a book on the kitchen table next to her car keys. It was called Radical Candor, by Kim Scott, published in 2017, and he read forty pages standing up while the pasta water boiled. He did not expatiate on it to anyone that night; he kept it to himself, because he was not yet sure the idea survived contact with an actual person. The idea was simple enough on the page. Scott argued that good feedback combined caring personally about someone with challenging them directly, and that most people gave up one half to keep the other.

The next morning he tested the halves in his head like fractions. Marcus had the caring and had thrown out the challenge. There was also a version where you kept the challenge and lost the caring, and Thomas knew that version too, because he had done it in September, when he had told a sophomore her wiring diagram was a disaster and she had quit the team by Friday. He still thought about the diagram, which had been a disaster, and about Friday.

He found Yasmin in the library at lunch, sitting with her laptop open and the arm code on the screen. He had a prepared sentence, and he abandoned it. "The grip timing is off by about half a second," he said. "I saw it in all three runs yesterday. You stayed late, and I should have said something then instead of letting Marcus go on about smoother runs, because it isn't smoother, and you're the only one who can fix it." He heard how clumsy it sounded, the apology stacked on the criticism, but he let it sit there.

Yasmin did not look up right away. Then she turned the laptop toward him, and he saw that she already had the timing loop open, with a comment marked TODO beside a delay constant. "I found it at midnight," she said. "I was waiting to see if anyone else would." She closed the lid. "Marcus thinks being kind means never telling me I'm wrong. Do you know how loud that silence gets? It's like he thinks I'll shatter." Thomas said the book on the kitchen table called it radical candor, caring personally and challenging directly at the same time, and she said, "Somebody wrote a whole book about that? My mother runs a bakery on that."

They worked through the timing that period, and Yasmin was mercurial about it, cheerful when a fix worked, sharp and certain the world was against her for the ten minutes it didn't, so that Thomas had to adjust his tone three times before lunch ended. The fix turned out to be one constant, changed from 500 to 200, and the arm picked up the block on the first try after school. Marcus watched from the doorway with his arms crossed.

"You went behind my back," he said, though it had happened in an open library. Thomas said he hadn't, and then said that he had, a little, and that he was sorry for that part but not for the rest. Marcus said he wasn't paid enough for this, which was a joke, because none of them were paid, though the team's insurance carried some indemnity against injury at competitions, a fact Marcus recited whenever he wanted to sound like the adult in the room.

At the scrimmage, the arm ran clean through all three rounds, and they took the regional slot by four points. Afterward Marcus stood next to the field, unscrewing a battery cover that didn't need unscrewing. "Next time something's wrong with my code," he said, not quite looking at Thomas, "you'd tell me? Straight, like that." Thomas said he would, and honestly did not know if he would get the mixture right, whether caring and challenging could be held in the same hand every time, or only some of the time, and only by luck. "Okay," Marcus said, and handed him the screwdriver. "Hold this while I check the leads."

Kyle signed the peer health form because Ms. Adeyemi had said the program needed boys, and because refusing would have meant explaining why he'd rather not, which he could not do. She called the position something like a trust, a fiduciary role, meaning that younger students would believe what he told them and he owed them accuracy instead of comfort. He wrote his name in the last box and then sat with the pen capped, staring at the curriculum sheet: consent, contraception, testing for infections. Three workshops, all of them his to run.

The first practice session went badly. He had the words, roughly, but they came out in the order of the handout, and when Dev from his chemistry class asked what "enthusiastic consent" actually meant at a party where everyone was drinking, Kyle said something about clear yeses that sounded like a poster. Dev said that was fine but didn't answer anything. Another boy started a tangential story about his cousin, and Kyle let it run because the silence after stopping it felt worse. Afterward he told Ms. Adeyemi he needed to see how any of this worked outside a classroom. She gave him a slip for the student clinic on Thursday.

He went partly for himself. He had decided this on the walk over, though the decision felt older than the walk. At the front desk a girl from his year, Priya, was already waiting with her hood up, and when she saw him she said, loudly enough for the receptionist to hear, that she was there for a friend. Kyle said nothing, because he understood the grammar of it, and sat two chairs away.

The nurse, whose badge said Rosa, called Priya first, then Kyle, and at some point the doors between the waiting room and the back stayed propped and the two of them ended up in the same consultation room, which Kyle suspected Rosa had arranged. Priya had come for a test and, having started talking, kept going: she'd been with a boy who hadn't used anything and hadn't asked, and she hadn't said to, and she kept circling the word "let," as if naming what she'd permitted would extenuate what he hadn't offered. Kyle said, carefully, that the asking was supposed to be his job too, not just her refusal. Priya looked at him like he'd spoken a language she'd read but never heard.

Rosa ran through the testing, the swab, the urine cup, the window periods, the clinic's quiet door on Delancey Street where nobody checked school ID. Then Priya asked about the pill versus other things, because a friend was on the pill and kept forgetting it, and Rosa pulled a plastic model from a drawer. She said hormonal IUDs and the implant fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once a clinician places them they don't depend on taking something daily. Kyle wrote it on his hand because his notebook was in his bag under Priya's coat, and Priya said, "Fewer than one in a hundred? For a whole year?" and Rosa nodded and moved on to cost and confidentiality.

Kyle ran his own numbers in the waiting room afterward, on the back of the curriculum sheet. The pill worked in theory, he knew, nearly always; it was the days, the ordinary days, that broke it. A method that survived forgetting was a different kind of method, not a better chemical but a different relationship to being human. He was not sure whether the workshop should say that or whether he was about to make a poster again.

The second workshop, he started differently. He asked who had ever forgotten something they meant to do every day, and thirty hands went up, including a teacher's at the back, and he wrote on the board what Rosa had said about IUDs and implants, the number, the year, the placement, the not depending on daily use, and let them copy it down. Then he asked them what the difference was between consent and not being stopped, and a quiet girl in the second row said, "One of them is a question that gets asked," and the room went still in a way that felt earned.

Dev raised his hand and asked whether asking felt strange, whether it killed things. Kyle said it could feel strange, and that he'd said it wrong once, too formally, and the other person had laughed, and they'd laughed, and then actually talked. He didn't say it always worked out. Some of what stayed uncertain he said out loud: that alcohol blurred things the way forgetting blurred the pill, and he didn't have a rule for exactly where the line was, only that being on the safe side of it cost less than the other side of it cost Priya, who was still waiting on results.

After the last session Priya found him by the water fountain. She said everything came back clear, and that she'd gone back and gotten the implant, and that she'd told the boy exactly what she hadn't said before, in sentences she'd rehearsed on the bus. Kyle asked if it had gone badly. She shrugged, and pulled the curriculum sheet out of her bag, the one he'd left in the clinic with his half-written numbers on the back, and smoothed it out and handed it to him.

"You can have this one back," she said. "I made my own."

The cultural festival had taken over the synagogue parking lot, folding tables of baklava and lentil soup and a debate booth that nobody was visiting. Nathan had signed up three weeks ago because Rabbi Sternman said the topic was ancient rules in modern life, and because Priya had dared him to, and because a boy who had nothing to say at his grandfather's shiva needed somewhere to practice having opinions. The topic card he drew from the coffee can read, in the rabbi's cramped hand: corners of the field.

His opponent was Miriam Auerbach, a senior from the day school across town, who was already spreading her notes across the table like she was setting a table for Shabbat. She wore a button that said TEAM MOUNT SINAI, which Nathan suspected she had made herself the night before, and she looked at the topic card over her glasses. "You go to public school," she said. It wasn't a question.

He had prepared, in his way. He'd spent two evenings at the kitchen table with his mother's old chumash, the one with her maiden name in gold on the cover, looking for something he could argue. He'd found it on a page he almost skipped: Leviticus 19:9-10, where farmers are commanded not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings too, for the poor and the stranger. He'd underlined it twice, then felt vaguely guilty, as if underlining were a kind of vandalism, and smoothed the page flat again. Before the debate, he'd texted his sister Dalia, away at her first year of college, because she was the only person he knew who would answer honestly.

The message was still on his phone when he sat down. "You're asking the wrong question," she'd written. "It's not whether the rule applies. It's what counts as your field. Figure out what you're a farmer of, and then tell me if you leave the corners." Then, a second bubble: "Also don't interpolate some grand philosophy from one verse. Rabbis hate that. Love, the smarter sibling." He'd read it four times on the bus, and once more now, under the table, while Miriam arranged her index cards in a fanning arc like a card trick.

"Resolved," the rabbi announced to the eleven people who had drifted over, some holding paper plates of kibbeh, "that this law obligates only farmers, and means nothing to the rest of us." Miriam took the affirmative, which meant Nathan had to argue that a rule about not reaping the corners of a field, and leaving the fallen gleanings for the poor and the stranger, could bind a seventeen-year-old who had never grown so much as a basil plant. She opened with the plain meaning of the text, the plain setting, agriculture, and a line about how not everything ancient must be stretched to fit. It was clean and it was reasonable and it landed on the folding chairs like a bromide, something true and useless at once.

Nathan lost the first exchange badly. He tried to talk about charity in the abstract and Miriam asked him, twice, to point at the verse he was using, and he couldn't, because he was using the idea of the verse rather than the verse itself. Eleven people watched him shuffle his notes. Somewhere behind them a band started tuning. He thought about Dalia's text under the fluorescent light of the debate booth. Then he stopped arguing about meaning and started arguing about the shape of the thing.

"The text doesn't say give money," he said, slower now, finding it as he said it. "It says don't reap all of it. The farmer doesn't travel anywhere, doesn't find the poor, doesn't decide who deserves it. The corners stay where they grew. The gleanings stay where they fell." He looked up from the page. "I don't farm. But I have a field. My grades, my time, whatever I'm good at. The rule isn't telling me to be generous. It's telling me not to take everything when I harvest it. Leave the corners for the poor and the stranger, and don't turn it into a ceremony. Just don't reap to the edge."

The judges conferred, and Miriam leaned across the table before they finished. "That's not proof," she said quietly. "That's you deciding the verse means whatever's convenient. Rashi would eat you alive." "Probably," Nathan said. "But you didn't say I was wrong about the corners." She held his eyes a moment, then looked down at her cards, and he understood that she had conceded something small and would never say so out loud.

They gave the round to Miriam on technical grounds, which felt right to him, the way a coin toss feels right. Afterward he found a quiet spot near the falafel stand and typed out a message to Dalia, deleting the part about losing and keeping the part about the corners. Behind him, the band started to play, and someone was dancing badly, and Priya appeared with two paper cups of lemonade and said, "So? Did you leave anything for the poor and the stranger, or did you reap the whole debate?" Nathan took his cup and said, "Ask Miriam. She got the win. I got the corners."

The book club met in the back room of the Lavender Street library, where the radiators clanked all winter and the folding chairs had been arranged in a circle so lopsided that whoever sat at the gap had to crane sideways to see anyone. Ashton took the gap chair because he always arrived last, pedaling from soccer practice with his backpack still smelling of grass and mud. Eleven of them were there, all sixteen or seventeen, no adult in the room. That was the club's one rule, laid down by Priya, who had founded it the previous spring and who guarded the discussion agenda like a fiduciary guarding someone else's money, exactly and a little obsessively.

They had read Jane Eyre. Priya opened her copy with a decisive snap and said they were going to try something new tonight, a critical lens, which meant reading the book through a particular question rather than just talking about whether they liked it. She had written two questions on an index card. "The feminist one asks how gender shapes what the characters can do," she said. "The Marxist one asks how money and class shape it. We'll do both, and then, if we're brave, we'll see whether they can be done at the same time." Ashton noticed she said "if we're brave" and looked directly at him, which he chose not to interpret.

The passage was the one where Jane, a governess, stands in a drawing room full of people above her station. Lena, who wanted to be a poet and said so at every meeting, read it aloud, her finger moving under the words, and the radiator hissed through the pause afterward. Ashton said the first thing that came to him, that Jane was invisible, that nobody saw her because she was a woman and poor and the two things together made her furniture. Priya wrote "woman + poor = furniture" on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

Then Marcus, who mostly came for the cookies and stayed for the arguments, said the poverty was the real engine, that a rich woman in that room would have been seen perfectly well, so gender was doing less work than they thought. Ashton countered that a poor man could still become a clerk, could sign contracts, could leave. "But Jane does leave," Marcus said. "She leaves and comes back with money, and then everything opens up for her." Nobody had an answer to that, and the circle went quiet in the way that meant thinking rather than boredom. Someone's chair squeaked. Lena tore the corner off a napkin and folded it into a small triangle.

Ashton sat with the silence and found, assembling it piece by piece, that the two lenses were not fighting so much as leaning on each other. Money without the room, the freedom without the means, either one alone was half a door. He was reaching for a way to say this when Marcus, flipping idly through his copy, found something penciled in the margin of an old library sale stamp inside the back cover, a note in faded graphite. He read it out: "Room, own money, 1929, Woolf." He looked up. "What's that supposed to mean?"

"It's A Room of One's Own," Lena said, in the tone of someone who had read it twice. "Virginia Woolf. Published 1929. It argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction." Ashton felt the note click into place like the last piece of something he hadn't known he was building. Here it was, both lenses in one sentence, the money and the room, the Marxist fact and the feminist fact, bound together on a page sixty years before any of them was born. "So the woman who writes the book we're reading," he said slowly, "Brontë, her sisters, all of them, they'd need both first. Before a single word."

Priya turned to the shelf behind her, where the club's year of reading stood in a ragged row, and counted under her breath. Twelve books, one by a woman, Jane Eyre itself. She counted again, as if the count were capricious and might change, and it did not. "We chose these," she said. "We chose them and we didn't notice." Marcus said the list had mostly come from a college syllabus he'd found online, so in a sense the omission had been inherited rather than committed, and Priya said that inheriting a thing does not abrogate your responsibility for it once you see it. They looked at each other across the crooked circle.

What stayed uncertain, Ashton thought but did not say aloud, was whether the old books were worth the rereading or should simply be set down, and whether a lens that explained everything might also flatten it; he liked Jane Eyre, he realized, precisely for what his questions couldn't quite hold. Priya wrote "next term: Woolf" on the whiteboard and boxed it. Lena read the passage again, the invisible woman in the drawing room, and this time Ashton heard it differently, as if someone had moved a lamp and the shadows had shifted.

The radiators clanked. Priya closed her copy and said, "Same chair next month, Ashton," and pointed at the gap.

Tyson folded the towel into quarters and set it on the bleacher like a paper he was about to hand in, because what he'd brought to the court this morning was, in a way, homework. He had a spiral notebook with seven boxes drawn across the top of the page, one for each day, and inside each box he had written something: ball handling, sprints, legs, rest, shooting, rest, scrimmage. He was eighteen, a senior, and next fall he would be a walk-on at a college three states away, and the assistant coach there had emailed him a single line before summer break. Come in with a plan, not just a body.

The plan was the problem. Tyson had never planned anything athletic before; he had only played, the way water only flows downhill. When he felt good, he played more. When he felt wrecked, he stopped. Now he sat on the bleachers at the far end of Emerson Park waiting for Rique, who was late in the way Rique was always late, and he studied his seven boxes and wondered whether rest days were for people who lacked hunger or for people who understood it.

Rique arrived with his history textbook under one arm, because summer session existed and Rique's mother did not believe in an idle July. "I got a test Monday," he said, dropping the book on the concrete. "On Iran. Whole thing's basically who turned a monarchy into a theocracy and who got left out." He bent to tie his shoe. "You still doing that coach's thing?"

"Trying." Tyson turned the notebook toward him. "First week I did everything hard, every day. Figured I'd rest when I was dead."

"And?"

Tyson laughed, short and rueful. "Monday I felt incredible. Tuesday I felt incredible. Wednesday morning I couldn't get down the stairs sideways." He mimed gripping a banister with both hands. "Thursday was worse. Then Friday it kind of let go of me."

Rique squinted at the notebook as if it were in a foreign alphabet. "So you got hurt?"

"No, that's the thing. Nothing was hurt. It was just soreness, the delayed kind, but it didn't show up right after the workout like I expected. It peaked days later." He tapped the page. "Somewhere between twenty-four and seventy-two hours after the first hard day. So I kept adding more on top of it because I felt fine, and then it all landed on me at once."

"Huh," Rique said, in the tone of a person filing something away for no reason he could name.

They played one-on-one to eleven, and Tyson lost 11-7, which was closer than usual, and his legs felt heavy in a way he recognized now as Tuesday's work arriving on Friday. Between games he sat on the ball and looked at his boxes again. The problem wasn't that he had trained too hard, exactly. It was that he had made one way of thinking fight another. The old Tyson said pain proved effort, and rest was a moral failure. The new Tyson was trying to believe that a rest day was a tool, like a screen or a crossover. He didn't fully believe it yet. He believed it maybe sixty percent, the way you believe a bridge you haven't driven across.

The two perspectives kept circling each other all week, and he let them argue in his head while his hands did the work. Monday: warm-up first, ten minutes, easy movement until his shoulders stopped feeling like borrowed equipment, then skills, moderate. He wrote the warm-up into the box and then, after some thought, into every box, because a warm-up wasn't an event, it was a door. Tuesday: nothing but stretching and the stationary bike, and he hated the stillness until he noticed that his shot was sharper on Wednesday than it had been in a month. Thursday: legs, hard, but he stopped one set earlier than the old Tyson would have, and he made himself write why in the margin. Feels fine now. That means nothing. Peaks later.

Saturday he drove to the court at seven because the heat came early and the court's blacktop by afternoon could desensitize the soles of your feet until you couldn't feel a pebble under your pivot foot, and he liked to know what was under him. Rique was already there, sitting on the bleachers with his textbook open to a chapter called "1979."

"You know what's funny," Rique said, not looking up. "The way they talk about a revolution, it's all one event, one date. But it was years. The real change came months after anybody was looking." He shut the book. "That's on the test, probably."

Tyson stood at the free-throw line and bounced the ball three times, his small ritual, and thought that his legs had arrived somewhere new without his noticing, the way things that matter apparently do. The notebook sat open on the bleacher with Sunday's box still empty except for the word he'd written and rewritten: rest, rest, rest. He wasn't sure the plan would survive contact with a real college weight room, or that sixty percent belief would hold. But he shot the ball, and it went in clean, and from somewhere behind him Rique called, "Again," so he did it again.

The debate topic was printed on the whiteboard in Señora Ives's handwriting: should schools monitor students' social media for signs of distress? Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no notes after the first thirty seconds. Chloe had volunteered because Marcus had dared her to, which was a bad reason, and because she actually had an opinion, which was a worse one, since opinions in a second language had a way of dissolving mid-sentence.

She practiced in the empty drama room at lunch, arguing with the folding chairs. Her position was the complicated one: monitoring might catch some kids, but it also taught everyone else to hide better, and a system that only worked when people were careless seemed to her tautological, proving only what it assumed. She did not know the Spanish for tautological, so she said it in English and kept going, and the chairs offered no objection.

Her opponent was Dani, who had lived in Madrid until fifth grade and spoke the way water runs, without visible effort. Dani's side was the simple one: kids were struggling, adults should pay attention. Chloe suspected it was also partly a truism dressed as an argument, the kind of sentence nobody could disagree with and nobody could use, but she needed Spanish words to say so, and she had exactly four days to find them.

On Wednesday she found "patologizar" in the dictionary app, hovering near the English word she wanted, pathologize. She wrote it on her palm in pen. Monitoring students' posts, she would argue, tended to pathologize ordinary teenage misery, the sad song posted at midnight that meant nothing, the joke that meant even less. Whether that was worth the risk of missing the kid who meant everything, she still had not decided. That was the part that kept her awake.

The debate happened Friday, fourth period, with the whole class pulled into a circle of desks and Señora Ives scoring on a clipboard. Dani went first and was flawless for two minutes, and then Chloe stood, and her mouth went dry in the specific way it does when you have memorized the wrong thing perfectly. She got through her opening. She gestured at the word on her palm without looking at it, and it came out, patologizar, and Dani nodded slowly, conceding the ground.

Then Chloe reached for the sentence she had rehearsed most, the one about how the program would humiliate students, and she said embarazada instead of avergonzada, because the two words had shadowed each other in her head all week. A ripple of laughter went around the circle. Sam actually fell off the arm of his chair. "Embarazada means pregnant," Dani said, grinning, "not embarrassed. False friends. They look alike, they aren't."

Chloe's ears burned. She looked at the clock: two minutes and forty seconds left, an ocean. She could quit, or she could stand there bleeding out in front of thirty people. Instead she took the word and kept it. "De acuerdo," she said slowly, "estoy embarazada de errores," and she did not fully know if that worked grammatically, but the laughter turned with her, warm now instead of at her. She argued the rest in plain, short sentences, simpler than she had planned, and slower. When she could not find a word she circled it, the way you point at a shape you cannot name. Señora Ives wrote something long on the clipboard.

Afterward, in the hallway, Dani caught up with her. "You know you lost, right? On points. Your grammar fell apart after the laughing." Chloe said she knew. "But it was the better argument," Dani went on, as if this were a technical complaint. "The part about how monitoring teaches hiding. I hadn't thought of that. My dad's a counselor and I still hadn't." She stopped at the water fountain. "Also, nobody ever survives saying embarazada wrong. Usually they stop talking. You sped up."

Chloe told her about the dictionary app, the palm, the four days of lunch in the drama room. Dani drank, wiped her mouth, and pulled out her phone. "I made a list once. False friends, like forty of them. My cousin sent it. Wanna see?" She scrolled, and Chloe leaned in, and there in the glow between them was the whole minefield, laid out in two neat columns.

The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and road dust, because Aaron had been sitting at the counter for twenty minutes reading the driver's manual while his mother scraped the black off the bread with the edge of a knife. He had his test in four days. He could do three-point turns in his sleep, could reverse around corners, but parallel parking still undid him, and merging onto the highway undid him more. His father had taken him out that morning for practice, and it had gone badly in a way Aaron was still turning over.

"You're quiet," his mother said, setting a plate in front of him.

"The truck didn't move."

"What truck?"

"On the ramp. I got on the acceleration lane and there was a truck in the right lane and I kept waiting for it to move over, and Dad grabbed the wheel and we ended up on the shoulder." He pushed the toast around the plate. "Dad said the truck should have gone over. He was honking at it after, out the window, on the shoulder, like that helped."

His mother sat down across from him with her own coffee. "And what did you think?"

Aaron had thought the truck driver was rude. He had also thought, in a smaller voice he didn't like, that he had been the one going sixty down a ramp expecting a gap to open. "I don't know.
