He was a lawyer, the kind who could hold forth on the jurisprudence of trespass at length, and he'd offered that lecture on the drive out this morning while she held the map rolled on her knees like a baton. She'd said yes, sure, she'd be careful, and mostly she'd been thinking about Seager.

The fact was she'd loved the old story. A warm river crossing an ocean to hold a continent's winters open, that was a story with a hero in it. Seager's version had no hero, just prevailing winds doing their quiet work and the ocean taking in heat all summer and letting it go slowly, like a stone that stays warm after sunset. She'd spent an hour the night before trying to find some way both could be true at once, some generous arithmetic, and had gotten nowhere except a page of crossed-out paragraphs.

Her phone buzzed against the limestone. A message from Priya, and Morgan could hear the grin in it before she'd finished reading. "Dear Morgan, breaker of hearts, inventor of buffets. My grandmother wants to know if you're coming to dinner Sunday. Also I found the actual paper, not just the summary, and it's worse for you than you think, it's very persuasive. Also also, your hero the Gulf Stream is still real and still warm, nobody's taking your ribbon away, they're just making it share. Bring the map Sunday. Bring sunscreen. Bring an argument, not a shrug. Yours in turmoil, Priya." Morgan laughed once, out loud, alone, the sound bouncing off the quarry wall and coming back smaller.

She stripped off her sneakers and waded in to her shins, map behind her on the rock, and stood looking at the far wall while the cold climbed her calves. The water here stored the sun the same way the paper said the ocean did, she supposed, and then caught herself doing it, converting everything into evidence. Still, she let the thought stand. Her father had once explained that a good argument doesn't hide the cases it loses, it absorbs them, and that the law was mostly this, not a set of verdicts but a record of what survived. She'd rolled her eyes at fifteen. She could admit now, at eighteen, standing in a quarry, that the idea might underwrite what she said on Thursday.

So she would say it like this: the Gulf Stream carries real warmth north, and that part of the old story holds. But the study argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters, and she could not make that sentence go away, so she would hand it to the seminar whole. What she couldn't yet say was how much of the mildness belonged to each part, whether anyone could say that at all, and she would end her eight minutes on that open question and stand there while her classmates looked at her.

She waded back out, dripping, and knelt over the map. With the red pen she wrote in the margin, in letters big enough to read from a podium, "most of it, not all of it, and the rest is a question." Then she folded the printout into her back pocket, gathered her four slates, and climbed the trail toward the chain and the road, phone already buzzing again in her hand.

Levi had signed up for the language exchange because the form was due at five and everything else was full. Now he sat at a carrel near the library's back window with a photocopied German newspaper article in front of him and a sophomore named Maren across the table, waiting.

The article was short, six paragraphs, about a town voting on whether to close its tram line. His assignment was to read it aloud and then summarise it in his own words, in German, without notes. He had spent forty minutes on the first paragraph the night before and still could not find the verbs.

"Start anywhere," Maren said. She had a coffee she wasn't supposed to have, and she turned the paper sideways to look at it. "You're stalling."

"I'm surveying." He ran his finger along the second line. Half the words began with capital letters, and it wasn't the start of sentences, and it wasn't names. He counted on his fingers: four capitalized words in one short line, then a comma, then three more. "Why is this one big," he said, pointing at a word in the middle. "Fahrzeug. That's not a name."

"German capitalizes every noun," Maren said. "Not just names."

Levi looked at the sentence again. He had assumed the capitals were decoration, or an alphabet with different rules he would never learn, and instead they were doing work. He put his pencil under each capitalized word and the skeleton of the sentence came up out of the page: the nouns, one after another, marked. The little words between them, the lowercase ones, were the connective tissue. He could not translate the sentence yet, but he could see its shape.

He tried the third paragraph, the one with the vote. Two capitalized words sat next to each other, and he recognised the second one from a class handout: Plebiszit. "Plebiscite," he said. "There's a vote. The town is voting on something." Maren made him say it again with the proper stress and wrote the article's actual word on the margin, which turned out to be a different word for the same thing, and she said both were used, the borrowed one in headlines because it was shorter.

The reading aloud went badly for a while. He pronounced one word three ways in three sentences and Maren corrected him each time until he could hear the difference himself. In the fourth paragraph a councillor was quoted calling the tram company's chairman bellicose, and Levi had to stop, because the word looked like a name to him and he had capitalised it in his head as a person. "It's an adjective," Maren said. "It means aggressive, warlike." He underlined it and moved on.

The summary was the real test. He had to put the article down and say what happened in it, out loud, in German. He assembled his sentences in his head and then said them too fast, and one of them came out with the wrong noun capitalized, a verb dressed up as a thing, and Maren laughed and told him to slow down. He tried again. The town had voted on the tram line. The vote was close. A company director had absconded with the maintenance funds two years earlier, which was why the line was losing money, which was why the vote was happening at all, and Levi managed the whole chain of events in five crooked sentences and then sat back.

"Better," Maren said. "Your summary said the director absconded with the funds and then everyone voted. The article says the vote came first." She tapped the paper. "Order matters in news."

He looked at the paragraphs again, following the capitals, and saw that she was right; the vote was announced in the first paragraph, and the absconding didn't appear until near the end, as background, as the thing the town was still angry about. He had flattened the story into a cause-and-effect chain because that was how he would have written it. The German article had arranged the same events in an order he hadn't expected, and he wasn't sure yet whether that was the newspaper's style or something about how the language held information, whether the nouns came first in German the way they had come first for him on the page.

He asked Maren. She thought about it with the coffee halfway to her mouth.

"I don't know," she said. "Read me another one."

The usher gave the score in Thomas's hands a suspicious look, as if he might be planning to read along in secret code, but she let him through with his three sticky notes fluttering from the pages: blue, yellow, green. He had a seat at the end of row F, close enough to see the pianist's hands, and forty minutes before the lights dimmed he spread the score across his knees and tried to codify what Mr. Alvarez kept telling him he heard but could not yet hear.

The exam was on Tuesday. Analyse the first movement, mark the form, justify your marks. Thomas had listened to the recording eleven times in his bedroom, headphones on, pencil hovering, and every time the movement dissolved into a bright river of sound that carried him along without ever showing him its floor. His father, querulous from the doorway about the volume, had asked what the point was of studying something you already liked, and Thomas had not had an answer. That was part of what bothered him. He liked it too much to take it apart, and he needed to take it apart to pass.

The blue note went on the first page, because that much was certain. He knew the names now, had copied them from the whiteboard until they stopped feeling like a foreign language: the exposition, which presented the themes. Two of them, in this one, a firm little march and then a softer, singing answer. He had written them out in his own hand and could hum each on command. That was the beginning. Blue for beginning.

The green note was the problem. The recapitulation, the coming back. Somewhere in the last third of the movement, he believed, the march would return and everything would settle, and he had to be able to say where. The yellow note, the development, was the part between, where the themes were worked through other keys, taken apart and reassembled, traveling somewhere else and then, somehow, arriving home. On paper this seemed simple. In sound it was like trying to mark the exact moment a river becomes a lake.

A girl dropped into the seat beside his, saw the score, and leaned over. "K. 331?" she said, reading the number off the cover. "That's tonight's opener."

"Is that cheating, bringing this?" Thomas asked.

"Nobody's checking." She had a scarf pushed back off her hair and a programme folded into a fan she wasn't using. "You a student?"

"Exam Tuesday. I have to mark the whole thing and I can't find where the exposition stops."

"Where the second theme settles in the new key," she said, as if it were obvious, and then looked as if she wished she'd said less. Her mother shushed her from the next seat. The lights went down.

The pianist walked out, sat, and did not pause. The march began, and Thomas followed with his finger, and for the first time the page matched the sound: there was his first theme, there the singing answer, and there, unmistakable, a small cadence, a closing of a door. His hand moved in the dark and pressed the blue note down, its edge just catching the light. The girl beside him nodded once.

Then the development, and he understood immediately why he had failed in his bedroom. It wasn't chaos; it was the same two themes, but restless, each one tugged into a new key like a word repeated until it sounded foreign. He tried to track the march and lost it, found the singing theme wearing a minor key like a borrowed coat, lost that too. The music was doing precisely what his teacher had promised and he could not hold any of it. He felt a familiar despair, the kind that made him want to decide analysis was a fraud, that the music was an animal and the score was immunology, the study of something alive done through things already dead.

He stopped trying to track everything. Instead he waited for the one thing he could wait for: the march, in the original key, at full voice. A return. When it came, it came so cleanly that he laughed out loud, one syllable, quickly smothered, earning a glare from the row behind. He pressed the green note onto the page while the music was still declaring itself, then worked backward and placed the yellow one where the traveling had begun. Three colours. He could see the whole shape of it now, a leaving and a straying and a homecoming, and the fact that the homecoming felt inevitable only after it arrived was, he decided, not a failure of his analysis but the thing itself.

At intermission the girl stood to stretch. "Where'd you put the green?" she asked. He showed her. She studied it, and her mouth twitched. "You're one bar early. Listen to the bass." She hummed the low line, and there it was, the harmony still leaning, arriving home one measure later than the melody pretended to. He moved the note, and his ears agreed with the paper.

On Tuesday, he thought, he would draw the three sections in three colours and write underneath: the return is where the harmony says it is, not where you want it to be. He put the pencil behind his ear and followed the second half of the concert with no score at all.

William had failed the projectile quiz on Tuesday, and by Saturday he was at the playground with his textbook, a calculator, and a basketball he had brought mostly out of spite. The quiz had asked where a ball would land, and he had guessed, because the numbers in his notes swam together into a single anxious blur. His friend Ada had texted him a single line that morning: swing sets, 3 o'clock, bring your sorry grade.

She was already there, sitting cross-legged on the mulch under the monkey bars with her own book open. She did not look up when he dropped his bag beside her. "You look blase about failing," she said, meaning his shrug, his slow amble, the way he let the basketball roll out of his hand and bump against the slide.

"I'm not blase. I'm conserving energy."

"Uh-huh." She flipped to a page, and he saw his own handwriting in the margin, a small desperate question mark. "Okay. Tell me what you remember."

"Gravity pulls down. The ball goes forward. Something about angles."

"That's it? That's what you wrote for a whole quiz?" She lobbed a pinecone at him, and he caught it without thinking, and then he looked at his hand as though it had acted without permission. "Throw it back," she said. "Overhand, kind of flat."

He threw it. It sailed over the mulch in a shallow arc and landed near the tire swing. Ada watched it the whole way. "Your arm knows more physics than your brain does," she said. "Same speed forward the entire flight. Gravity only messes with up and down. Those are two separate things happening at once."

William sat down on the mulch. He was quiet long enough that a jogger passed the fence, long enough for a toddler at the sand pit to fill and empty a red bucket twice. "Separate," he repeated. He drew it, an arrow going sideways and an arrow going straight down, then a curve connecting where the pinecone had started to where it had landed. "So if I figure out how long it's in the air..."

"Then you know how far it goes," Ada said. "Horizontal distance is just the constant horizontal velocity multiplied by the time in the air."

He copied the sentence exactly, underlined it, and then, because underlining felt like something his September self would do to feel productive, he tested it. He took the basketball to the end of the mulched area, walked off ten paces, and threw the ball flat and hard, counting under his breath. One, two, one-halves. It bounced once on the packed dirt near the fence.

"That's one second," Ada called. "Roughly."

"Roughly one second, roughly ten paces." He went back, threw again with the same arm, the same flick of the wrist, and got roughly the same bounce. The ball did not care that he had failed a quiz. It went the same distance every time because it was doing what it did, not what he felt about it.

They sat with the numbers after that. Ada wrote a time on her palm in pen, and William found the horizontal speed in his notes, and he multiplied, and the answer came out to a distance, and he checked it against the answer key in the back of the book, and it matched. He laughed once, short, surprised. "That's all it is? You find the time first, and then one multiplication gives you the landing point?"

"That's all it is. Ignoring air resistance, which we always do, which is a lie, but a useful lie."

He thought about that. He threw the pinecone again, flatter, with more pace, and this time it landed short of where he expected, and he could not tell whether his throw had changed or the wind had or whether his counting had drifted. The book gave him a world with no air, and the playground gave him one with air, and both of them were true enough to be worth knowing. He wrote a second line under the first: the numbers work if you hold the world still.

"It's like bio," Ada said, gathering her pens. "We spent all week on parasitism, one thing living off another, and I kept thinking the chapter was lying too, because tapeworms don't sit politely in their hosts the way the diagram shows."

"You're saying physics and tapeworms have the same problem."

"I'm saying diagrams are always cleaner than playgrounds."

The afternoon was thinning. The toddler had gone, and the swing set chains hung still, and William stood at his ten paces with the ball one more time. He counted the throw, watched the bounce, marked the landing spot with the heel of his shoe in the dirt.

"One and a half seconds," he said. "So it went one and a half times farther than the first one." He dragged his heel sideways, measuring it out. "Now I beseech you, tell me the quiz on Monday is exactly this."

Ethan spread the ocean current map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with his sister's smoothest skipping stones, four of them borrowed from the coffee can by the back door. The map had come folded in the packet from the summer program at the marine science institute, along with a letter that said, in the friendliest possible font, that all incoming students should arrive able to explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. He had eleven days. He had also, according to his sister Dee, promised to help her build the thing she was currently dragging across the lawn.

The thing was a rabbit hutch, or the idea of one, a lean-to of pallet wood and zip ties that Dee, who was thirteen and had been saving for a rabbit since March, intended to finish before their mother changed her mind about the rabbit entirely. She dropped her end of a board in the grass and came to stand over the map, casting a shadow across the North Atlantic.

"What is that, the ocean?"

"Currents," Ethan said. "The red parts move warm water north, the blue parts move cold water south." He traced the wide red ribbon that peeled off the American coast and aimed itself toward Europe like a thrown rope. What he could not yet do, and what the letter implied he should be able to do, was say why that ribbon made London rainy and green instead of frozen like Labrador, which sat at the same latitude and was, on the map, ice.

"I want the hutch done before Saturday," Dee said. "That's my want, and I'm stating it out loud so you can't say you didn't know."

"Tonight," he said. "After I figure this out."

She went back to her boards, and he bent over the map with his phone, because the packet's reading was dense and he hoped for something a person could actually picture. What he found instead was a story, and the story was better than the reading. Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769. Franklin, who had crossed the Atlantic multiple times and never once thought to wonder why some voyages dragged, got the crucial knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain. The captains had known for years. They rode the current going east and dodged it coming home, saving days, while the British packet ships plowed straight through it and lost those days, their masters complaining about fogs and delays and never once connecting the complaints to the warm water under their keels. There were no satellites. There was a whaler who watched the water, told his cousin, and the cousin had it printed.

Ethan sat back on the bench. What snagged him was not the physics of the current, which he could more or less parrot, but the shape of the discovery: the people who knew the thing best were the ones nobody thought to ask. He thought about his own essay for the program, which he had titled, with a seventeen-year-old's confidence, "The Utility of Ocean Circulation," a title chosen mostly because he had recently learned the word utilitarianism in ethics class and liked the sound of applying it to water. Utilitarianism said you judged an action by its consequences, by the days saved, and the captains had been quietly consequentialist for a century before anyone charted what they knew. He also suspected, sitting there, that his essay was worse than Dee's hutch, which at least existed.

"That is the most boring thing you've ever looked at," Dee said, hammering something. "Your face is doing the concentrating face."

"There were whalers," Ethan said, "who knew the ocean better than the scientists, and nobody asked them for a hundred years."

"So ask somebody," she said, with the brutality of thirteen.

He looked at the map again, then at the fence, then at the gray sky that had begun, in a way that did not portend anything good for the hutch, to thicken over the neighbor's poplar. He thought about his grandfather, who had driven trucks for forty years and who claimed he could tell you the best route to Tulsa in any weather, and about how nobody in the family had ever once written it down. Then he did what he should have done an hour ago, which was to read the map the way Folger would have, as a driver reads a road: not as an explanation but as a set of lanes. Warm lane going east, cold lane coming back. The warm lane delivered its heat to the boreal edge of Europe, to places that by all rights should have been tundra and were instead mild and damp, and that was the sentence he would say in September, plain, no essay title required. He could say it now. He tried it out loud to the yard: "Warm water moves north across the Atlantic and releases its heat near Europe, so northern Europe stays warmer than other places at the same latitude." It sounded almost too simple, and he trusted it more for that, though he still could not have said exactly why the water moved, and he was honest enough with himself to note the gap rather than paper over it.

The first drops hit the map and he lunged for the stones, and Dee was already shouting about the hutch, and they carried the boards two at a time under the porch roof while the rain came down through the poplar in long silver ropes. They worked until dark, Ethan holding, Dee hammering, the map drying in a safe curl on the porch swing.

"Say the ocean thing again," Dee said, driving a nail. "The whaler part."

"My cousin is a whaler," Ethan said, in his best old-timey voice, "and he says you're sailing against a river in the sea."

Dee laughed so hard she bent the nail.

Brody had claimed the living room for the weekend because the school stage was booked for the jazz band, and the one-act he was directing opened in eleven days. His mother had moved the coffee table against the wall without being asked, which he took as a kind of blessing. On the carpet he had laid out the stage with painter's tape, a rectangle roughly to scale, and inside it he arranged two kitchen chairs, a footstool, and the long sofa from the den to stand in for the set.

The play was a two-hander about brothers dividing their dead father's tools, twelve pages that had enraptured Brody the first time he read it, though he could not have said exactly why. Something about how little the brothers said while handing each other wrenches. He had assumed directing would mean deciding what the lines meant and telling the actors. He was learning, slowly, that it mostly meant deciding where people stood.

Priya and Marcus arrived at ten with bags of chips and a printed script Priya had already annotated in three colors. They ran the first scene in the taped rectangle, and almost immediately the sofa began to travel. Marcus dragged it forward to sit on it, then Priya angled it while crossing to the window, and by the fourth run-through it had migrated nearly two feet from where it started, drifting toward the edge of the taped stage like a slow barge. "You're losing your light," Brody kept saying, although there was no light in the living room, only the lamp his mother kept switching on in the hallway.

He tried the polite version of authority, asking whether they might reset between runs. Marcus, who was garrulous even for someone playing a taciturn brother, narrated each reset like a golf announcer, and Priya reset with theatrical sighs. The sofa crept anyway. It crept because actors, Brody realized, watch each other rather than the floor, and each of them nudged the furniture a little to clear a path, and none of the nudges agreed. He sat on the arm of the couch with his chin in his hand and wondered whether professional directors had this problem or whether it was only him, only this room, only a footstool standing in for a workbench.

He remembered then the floor of the real stage at school, how it had looked after the fall musical struck. There had been little Xs of colored tape everywhere, orange and green and yellow, leftovers from some earlier production, and he had assumed they were garbage. On Monday he went in early, found the tape still there, and peeled up a green X to examine it. It was stiff, matte, thinner than duct tape, and when he pressed it back down his thumbnail left no residue on the pad of his thumb. In the drama room's supply cabinet, on a shelf between gaff rolls, he found a roll labeled the same way, and a label is not an explanation, but it was a start.

"That's spike tape," said Jules, the senior who ran the light board and was, as far as Brody could tell, always in the building. She was coiling cable and did not look up. "It marks where furniture and actors go on the stage floor." Brody asked if it came in colors, and she said all of them, and that was the whole conversation, which he appreciated.

He took the roll home. That evening, before Priya and Marcus arrived, he tore short strips and laid them at each corner of the sofa, a small bright X at every leg, and one on the carpet where Marcus sat, and one where Priya had to end her cross to the window. When the actors came in, Priya looked at the tape and said it looked like a crime scene, but she stood on her mark.

The strange thing was how little he had to say after that. The sofa stopped wandering. Every time it drifted a few inches, somebody glanced down, saw the tape, and pulled it back, and the correction became part of the action, so that Marcus's character now hauled the couch into place as though it were a stubborn thing his father had owned, which in the play it was. Priya found a moment where she toed her mark before speaking, a little hesitation, like someone checking that the floor would hold her. Brody had not asked for any of it. He wrote in his notebook, where he was keeping a running list of things he did not understand about directing, that the tape had given him back about ten minutes of every rehearsal, and that those minutes had somehow become the best part.

He did not fully believe his own note. It was possible the tape was a fix and the moments were accidents, and it was possible the moments were the point and the tape only a trick, and he could not yet tell those apart. In math class they had been proving things all year, and his teacher kept insisting that every theorem rests on a smaller statement, a lemma, something you prove first so the big thing follows. Brody thought the sofa's position might be the lemma of his whole production, the small settled thing that made everything after it possible to argue. Or the metaphor might be wrong. He put a question mark next to it.

The night before they moved to the real stage, Priya and Marcus ran the entire twelve pages without stopping, and the sofa did not travel an inch. At the last line, Marcus picked up the footstool and set it down on one of the green Xs with a small deliberate bang, and Priya laughed the way people laugh when something is true. Brody stayed in his chair after they gathered their bags, looking at the little field of tape on the carpet, the Xs glowing faintly under the lamp. On Sunday, before his mother reclaimed the room, he knelt and peeled up each strip, one by one, and pressed them onto the inside back cover of his notebook, where they stuck and held.

Grayson laid the cones out in the grass before anyone arrived, ten meters apart, the same distance his brother's team kept losing the ball. He had spent two evenings thinking about it and one evening writing on graph paper, and what he had decided was this: no scrimmage today. The boys would stand between the cones and pass, and every time a pass went astray, they would do it again, immediately, with the same foot, until the ball went where it was meant to go.

The first three to arrive noticed the cones and groaned. Danny Feeney, who was eleven and had the loudest opinions, dropped his bag on the picnic table and said, "We're not scrimmaging? Coach, we always scrimmage."

"That's the problem," Grayson said. "You scrimmage every practice and you still can't complete three passes in a row. I watched the whole game Saturday. You lost the ball forty-two times."

"That's a facetious number," Danny said, though he clearly didn't know what the word meant, and neither did Grayson until he looked it up that night. Right now he only said, "It's an exact number. I counted."

They started the drill anyway. Grayson stood at the line between the cones and watched each pass, and after each one he called out what he saw: inside of the foot, hips open, look first. When Marcus bent the pass wide of the cone, Grayson made him take it again before anyone moved on. Again, and again. Marcus got frustrated, kicked the grass, then completed five in a row, and Grayson made a small check on his clipboard and did not say anything triumphant about it, because he remembered being fourteen and how praise from a coach could feel like being managed.

The harder part was the feedback. He had read about a study once, in a book his mother left on the counter, about violinists in Berlin. He'd taken a photo of the page because something about it had enthralled him, though he couldn't have said why at the time. Now, standing in his own backyard with eleven boys and a bag of nearly deflated balls, he found the photo on his phone and read the line under his breath. Ericsson, 1993. What separated the best violinists wasn't hours logged; it was effortful work on specific weaknesses, with immediate feedback. Somebody had given it a name.

"It's called deliberate practice," he told Danny, holding the phone out. "Not just doing the thing a lot. Doing the weak part, and knowing right away what went wrong."

"That's why you're making us do the boring cone thing," Danny said.

"That's why."

Danny took the phone and read the paragraph twice, his lips moving. He was the kind of kid who read everything twice, who kept a Spanish vocabulary list folded in his sock because his mother quizzed him in the car, who had once explained to the whole bench the phonetics of rolling a double r, demonstrating until the kid beside him could do it too. He handed the phone back slowly.

"Okay," he said. "But it can't only be cones. That's not a game. In a game somebody's running at you."

Grayson stopped. He looked at the cones, at the clipboard, at the graph paper in his pocket, and he understood that the kid had found the edge of what he'd planned. The study was about violinists alone in a room, and a field with opponents was a different instrument. He didn't know yet how to keep the feedback and add the pressure. "Then we do both," he said. "Cones first, then I put a defender in the passing lane, and we run the same pass until it works with someone in the way. And if that's still not like a game, we'll figure out the next thing on Thursday."

They ran it. The defender was Danny, who took the role seriously, waving his arms, calling out the passer's name the way opponents at a real match would, and the passes started arriving at the cones on the first try. Marcus, who had sulked through the first half hour, began calling for the ball in space he hadn't noticed before. When Ben tripped over a sprinkler head and sat down hard in the clover, Danny jogged over and pulled him up by both wrists before Grayson could get there, and Ben stayed in the drill.

Danny had decided, somewhere during the second round of defender drills, that this was the best practice of the season, and he wanted to know what Thursday would hold. He asked while collecting cones. He asked while pumping the flat balls back up with the hand pump Grayson's father kept in the garage. He asked a third time on the picnic table, eating the orange slices Grayson's mother had left out without being asked, and Grayson finally said, "I don't know yet. I'll figure out what's still broken and build the next thing around that."

"Okay," Danny said. He folded his Spanish list back into his sock and slung his bag over one shoulder. At the gate he turned around. "Forty-two, though. You really counted?"

The driving school on Route 9 smelled of burnt coffee and vinyl, and Charlie spent every waiting-room minute with two apartment leases spread across her knees. Her instructor, a patient man named Del, had learned not to comment. Between her turns behind the wheel he drank his coffee and read the paper while she worked, because her mother had been clear: Charlie could have the apartment near campus only if she proved she could figure out what it would actually cost, and the driving lesson was already paid for, so the math would happen in the gaps.

"Parallel park, then we switch," Del said from the passenger seat, and Charlie eased the car toward the curb while Lease A slid off the dashboard into the footwell. Lease A said utilities included, which she had repeated to her mother like a slogan until her mother said, slow and suspicious, "Read what 'included' includes."

She read it now, in the parking lot, while Del filled out a form on his clipboard. Water included. Trash included. Heat included. Then, in a clause so quiescent it might have hoped never to be read, a line saying that electricity was the tenant's responsibility, billed separately by the provider. Electricity. The thing that ran the lamp, the fridge, the laptop, the fan in August. She had told her mother the total was rent plus nothing, and the total was rent plus something, and the something was the something she had not checked.

"Rough day?" Del asked, glancing over. He was not the kind of instructor students lionized, the sort with stories about high-speed chases; he was quiet and thorough, and Charlie had come to prefer that.

"I found a trap in a lease," she said. "The first one says utilities included, but that only means the utilities it lists. Electricity isn't on the list." She held the page out, and he looked at it without taking it from her, tapping the clause with one finger.

"Fine print," he said. "That's where they hide things."

The second lease, Lease B, from the building her cousin Rosa was already raving about, said nothing sweeping at all. Instead it assigned each utility its own line: tenant pays electric, tenant pays internet, landlord covers water and heat. Lower rent, too. Charlie copied the numbers into her notebook, column by column, and discovered that if electricity in the city averaged what the provider's website said it averaged, Lease A and Lease B landed within twenty dollars of each other, close enough that the cheaper-looking one was not cheaper, only honest in a different way.

That was the afternoon she thought about her father, three years ago, signing the papers for the shop he'd wanted for a decade. He had lionized the landlord at the closing, called him the last fair man in the county, and six months later stood in the empty storefront reading a clause about "standard maintenance" that turned out to mean only the pipes, not the wiring, not the roof. Charlie had been thirteen, sitting on a folding chair with a juice box, watching his face change. He hadn't blamed anyone out loud. He'd just said, "Words mean what they say, not what I want them to mean," and she had carried that sentence around since, not fully understanding it until now, in a driving school parking lot, with two leases and a Tuesday evening going dim around her.

A boy about her age, waiting for his lesson, leaned over from the next chair. He had been circling listings on his phone for half an hour. "That first one's got utilities included, right? That's the one I'd take."

"Check the list," Charlie said. She turned the page so he could see. "Included only covers what's actually named. Electricity's missing." He read the clause, went pale in the fluorescent light, and started scrolling back through his own listing with his thumb moving fast. She slid her notebook over so he could see her two columns, the rent plus the electric line, the totals almost twins.

"That's it, then," he said. "The other one's better."

"I don't know yet," Charlie said. "They're about even, and I haven't called about internet. So I'm not done deciding." She said it plainly, and it felt like the first honest sentence she'd built all day.

Del rapped the roof of the car. "Your turn behind the wheel, Charlie. Bring the paperwork."

She gathered the leases, folded them along the same creases, and slid them into the folder under the notebook, then pulled the door shut and checked her mirror.

The bus smelled of diesel and orange peel, and Alyssa had The Catcher in the Rye open on her knees with a highlighter uncapped and going nowhere. Across the aisle, Dev was failing the same book for the second time, which he announced by dropping his copy on the seat between them like an accusation. "The guy says he's a liar," Dev said. "Page whatever. So why am I supposed to care about anything after that?"

Alyssa found the line and read it aloud, quiet enough that the freshmen up front wouldn't turn around. "I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life." She'd read it four times already that week, and each time it had shifted under her, the way a word repeated too often goes strange in the mouth. "He tells us he lies," she said. "Right at the start. In 1951, when the book came out, that must have knocked people flat."

"So it's all fake?"

"That's the question, isn't it." She tapped the cover. The problem had been circumscribing itself in her notes all week: if he lies, does the lying make everything false, or does admitting it make him honest, or does the honesty itself become a performance she was falling for? Her English teacher had refused to answer, which Alyssa had found obnoxious until she started to suspect the refusal was the whole assignment.

Dev leaned over and flipped to the back, as if the answer were printed there. "Holden," he said. "Where do they get these names. Holden."

"That's actually the interesting part." She had looked it up at midnight instead of sleeping. "The etymology people trace it to 'hold,' like hollow land, or a keeper of something. I don't know if Salinger knew or cared. I might be making that matter more than it does." Dev made a face that said he had stopped listening at the word etymology, so she moved on.

The bus hit the pothole by the credit union, and her highlighter rolled, and Dev caught it without looking, an old habit from years of shared bus seats. "Okay," he said. "Say I believe half of it. How do I know which half?"

"Exactly." This was the part she'd been chewing on. "You don't audit him line by line. You watch what the voice does. When he tells you he's a liar, that's a confession, but it's also a contract. He's saying, you're inside this with me now, you know my rules. It's like..." She searched the bus for it. The seat fabric was old and friable, wearing through to yellow foam at the corners where decades of students had picked at it. "It's like this seat. It's coming apart, and you can see the stuffing, and somehow seeing the stuffing makes you trust it more than a new seat, because at least you know what you're sitting on."

Dev considered the foam. "That's the dumbest analogy I've ever heard," he said, but he wrote it down. He wrote it in the margin of her book, actually, in pen, which she would have killed him for a year ago.

Then the twist, which came from behind them: Priya, who never spoke on the bus, who had earbuds in for the entire four years Alyssa had known her, pulled one out and said, "He's lying about lying. That's the trick. The stuff he calls lies are the true parts, because they're the ones he's ashamed of." The bus went quiet in that way it did when someone unexpected talked. Priya put the earbud back in, apparently finished with public speaking until graduation.

Alyssa sat with that for three more stops. It was a better reading than hers, and it undid her seat analogy entirely, and she found she didn't mind, or minded and wanted it anyway. Maybe Holden's confessed lies were the honest material and his confident parts were the performance. Maybe both were true at once, and the narrator's unreliability wasn't a flaw to correct but the actual weather of the book. She couldn't prove any of it, and the paper was due Friday, and Priya would not elaborate.

"Did you get her number?" Dev whispered, grinning.

"She's been behind us since freshman year, Dev."

"So did you?"

The bus turned onto Marsh Road, and Alyssa marked the liar line in yellow, then, after a second, boxed it. Priya got off two stops early, as always, and walked the rest, and Alyssa watched her go and thought: unreliable narrator, and turned the phrase over until the bus hissed to a stop at her corner. She left Dev her highlighter. He'd need it, and she could get another, and somehow that felt like the first honest thing she'd said all week.

The choir room at St. Brigid's smelled of dust and old hymnals, and on Thursday afternoons it belonged to Natalie and Mrs. Okafor, who had played the organ there for thirty-one years and had agreed, after some coaxing from Natalie's mother, to teach her composition instead of piano. "You already play," Mrs. Okafor had said at the start. "What you don't know is how a song gets built. So we will build one. Sixteen bars, chord changes, written properly. Not memorized. Written."

Natalie sat at the scarred upright piano with a staff notebook open on the music rack, and her problem sat there with her: the melody in her head would not come out. It arrived whenever she was walking home from school or lying awake, a line that rose and then settled, and by the time she got to the choir room it had thinned to nothing. She had four bars written, in the key of G, and she could hear exactly how the fifth bar should end on a long held note under a D chord, a note that would hang in the air the way the last note of the offertory anthem hung in the sanctuary on Sundays. But she could not figure out how long to make it.

Mrs. Okafor was at the organ bench across the room, running a quiet scale with the swell shades half closed, and she had a rule about questions. "Ask the piano first," she would say. "Then ask me what the piano told you." So Natalie played the four bars through, then stopped at the edge of the fifth, and held the G she wanted, counting under her breath. One, two, three, four. A whole bar. In the time signature at the top of her page, the four told her the bar held four beats.

She looked at what she had written and saw the trouble. The bar before ended with a quick note on the fourth beat, a pickup into the held G, so the G began on beat one and she wanted it to last through the whole bar and then some, to spill into the next measure the way a held note in the anthem seemed to. She wrote a half note, two beats, and played it, and the silence afterward felt like a hole. She wrote a whole note instead, four beats, and that swallowed the pickup she wanted in the next bar. Neither was the note in her head.

Her phone buzzed against the bench. It was her brother Marcus, three hundred miles away at his first semester of college, who had taught himself guitar from videos and had opinions about everything.

"Are you still doing the church thing?" he'd texted. "Don't let the organ lady turn you into a hymn machine. Church music is all rules. Rules circumscribe you. You should be writing whatever comes out, like me. I don't even read notation."

Natalie typed back, "you circumscribe yourself by not reading notation. you can only play what you can copy." Then she put the phone face down, because she was not sure that was true. Mrs. Okafor's rules had felt like walls when Natalie started, but lately they had started to feel like the walls of an instrument itself, something you touched to make sound. Marcus made whatever noise he pleased and it all sounded like other people's noise. She didn't want to say that to him, though. He was the one who had shown her a video of a jazz pianist last spring, the performance that had been, for her, seismic, the moment she understood that a person could make music that hadn't existed five minutes earlier. Without Marcus there would be no Thursday afternoons at St. Brigid's at all.

She turned back to the page. The held G. She looked at the dotted rhythms elsewhere in her melody, where a dot after a shorter note stretched it a little, and she thought, for the first time, about what the dot was actually doing. A dot after a note adds half the note's value. She said it to herself the way she rehearsed French vocab, then tested it against her fingers. A half note was worth two beats. Half of two was one. Two and one made three. She penciled in a dot beside the half note, making a dotted half note, and played the bar, counting: the G held for one, two, three, and then a short note filled the fourth beat and lifted her into the next measure exactly the way the anthem did, the way the line in her head had done all along. Three beats out of the four. She sat very still, then wrote the next two bars without stopping.

"You found something," Mrs. Okafor said from the organ bench. She had stopped playing.

"My bar kept coming out one beat short," Natalie said. "Every time I counted it. I put a dot on the half note and now it's three beats and it works."

Mrs. Okafor came over and looked at the page for a long moment. "Sing it for me," she said, and Natalie did, and Mrs. Okafor nodded once, which was the most she ever gave.

That evening Natalie sat on her bed with the notebook, eight bars done, and found another text from Marcus: "fair point about notation lol. maybe I'll learn to read this summer. send me what you wrote?"

She photographed the page, the pencil marks, the small dot she'd had to press twice to make dark enough, and then she held her thumb over the send button. The melody was half invented and she didn't know if the second eight bars would match the first; the rules had given her one honest bar and then handed the rest back to her. She thought about Mrs. Okafor saying ask the piano first, and she set the phone down unfinished, picked the notebook back up, and played the eighth bar into the tenth, slowly, counting.
